Supporters say federal education money should go to students and teachers, not to providing shelter for people who entered the country illegally.
Supporters say schools can still help during official disasters like floods and fires, so emergency response is protected.
critics: Critics say this stops public schools and colleges from helping vulnerable non-citizens who need shelter in their communities.
Critics say removing the ability of federally-funded schools to provide housing takes away an important community safety net.
Critics say the disaster exception only covers official declarations and won't help during other emergencies when schools could provide shelter.

118-hr-3981.one_liner: Add reporting rules for schools that take veteran education money
provisions: Schools that take veteran education benefits must report within 30 days when state or federal agencies take action against them
Schools applying for approval of non-accredited courses must also follow these reporting rules
State agencies and the VA must revoke approval for schools that do not report these actions
Veterans who cannot finish courses because the VA removes school approval will not lose their education benefits
The VA must create a database within 180 days to track surveys of schools that take veteran education money

supporters: Supporters say the 30-day reporting rule will help veterans avoid schools that state and federal agencies have taken action against.
Supporters say veterans will keep their education benefits if they cannot finish courses when the VA removes school approval.
Supporters say the new database will help track which schools have problems with their veteran education programs.
critics: Critics say the 30-day reporting deadline is too short for schools to properly notify state agencies and the VA.
Critics say automatic revocation of approval is too harsh and could limit education choices for veterans.
Critics say creating the database within 180 days will cost money and may be rushed.

118-hr-3935.one_liner: Fund the FAA and airports through 2028
provisions: Funds the FAA and National Transportation Safety Board through 2028
Requires the FAA to hire more air traffic controllers
Requires airlines to install voice and video recorders in cockpits
Stops aircraft dispatchers from working from home except during emergencies
Requires airlines to refund passengers with disabilities if their wheelchair cannot fit in the cargo area
Makes airlines seat young children next to adults for free if seats are available next to each other
Creates new rules for flying drones beyond where pilots can see them

supporters: Supporters say hiring more air traffic controllers will make flying safer by reducing delays and preventing accidents.
Supporters say requiring cockpit voice and video recorders will help investigators figure out what went wrong after plane crashes.
Supporters say making airlines refund passengers with disabilities when their wheelchairs cannot fit will protect people who need mobility equipment.
critics: Critics say requiring airlines to install new voice and video recording equipment will cost millions of dollars that could raise ticket prices.
Critics say stopping aircraft dispatchers from working from home will hurt workers who need flexible schedules and increase company costs.
Critics say video recording pilots in cockpits invades their privacy and could distract them from flying safely.

118-hr-400.one_liner: Raise the limit for banks investing in small business funding companies from 5% to 15%
provisions: Raises the limit for banks to invest in small business funding companies from 5% to 15% of their money
Small business funding companies provide loans and investment money to small businesses
Applies to certain types of banking entities

supporters: Supporters say raising the limit from 5% to 15% would let banks put three times more money into small business funding companies.
Supporters say small businesses would get more loans and investment money because banks could invest more in the companies that fund them.
critics: Critics say allowing banks to invest 15% instead of 5% of their money in small business companies increases risk to the banking system.
Critics say banks might lose more money if small business investments fail because they can now put three times more capital at risk.

118-hr-406.one_liner: Give Southeast Asian organization legal protections from lawsuits and taxes
provisions: ASEAN gets protection from certain types of lawsuits in U.S. courts
ASEAN does not pay property taxes on buildings it owns in the U.S.
ASEAN is a group of 10 countries in Southeast Asia including Indonesia, Singapore, and Vietnam

supporters: Supporters say this gives ASEAN the same lawsuit protection that other international organizations already have in the U.S.
Supporters say this helps the U.S. build better ties with the 10 Southeast Asian countries in ASEAN, including Indonesia and Singapore.
critics: Critics say ASEAN will not pay property taxes on buildings it owns in the U.S. while American groups must pay these taxes.
Critics say giving lawsuit protection to ASEAN makes it harder for Americans to take legal action if the organization causes them harm.

118-hr-4366.one_liner: Fund military construction and veterans programs for 2024
provisions: Pays for building new military bases and facilities in 2024
Pays for VA offices that handle veterans disability and school benefits
Pays for VA hospitals and medical care for veterans
Pays for upkeep of veterans cemeteries
Pays for building and fixing homes for military families

supporters: Supporters say this bill ensures veterans get medical care through VA hospitals and disability benefits they earned through service.
Supporters say military families need safe housing and the bill funds construction and repairs for Army, Navy, and Air Force family homes.
Supporters say the military construction funding for all branches keeps bases ready to defend the country.
critics: Critics say the military construction funding for new Army, Navy, and Air Force facilities often exceeds original budgets, costing taxpayers more than planned.
Critics say the bill spreads funding across too many different agencies like the American Battle Monuments Commission instead of focusing on core veteran and military needs.

provisions: Gives money to border security to guard the U.S. borders
Gives money to immigration enforcement to find and deport people who entered the country illegally
Gives money to airport security workers who check passengers and bags
Gives money to the Coast Guard to patrol U.S. waters
Gives money to the Secret Service to protect the President and other government officials
Gives money to FEMA to respond to hurricanes, floods, and other disasters
Gives money to the agency that protects government computer systems
Sets rules on how the agencies can spend the money

supporters: Supporters say this funding helps U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents stop illegal border crossings and drug smuggling at ports of entry.
Supporters say Transportation Security Administration funding keeps airports safe by screening passengers and bags for weapons and explosives.
Supporters say FEMA funding helps communities rebuild after hurricanes, floods, and wildfires destroy homes and businesses.
critics: Critics say too much money goes to Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportations instead of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services processing legal immigration cases.
Critics say border security agencies get more funding than the Federal Emergency Management Agency that helps disaster victims.
Critics say this money could instead fund the Department of Education or Department of Health and Human Services programs that help families.

provisions: Gives money to pay military salaries for 2024
Provides funds to buy weapons and military equipment
Pays for military research and testing programs
Funds military health care programs
Gives money to intelligence agencies
Pays for destroying old chemical weapons

supporters: Supporters say this bill ensures military service members receive their salaries and health care benefits in 2024.
Supporters say funding for weapons and equipment keeps the military ready to defend the country.
Supporters say money for intelligence agencies helps protect national security.
critics: Critics say the billions spent on weapons and military equipment could go to schools and health care instead.
Critics say funding military research and testing programs wastes taxpayer money.
Critics say giving more money to intelligence agencies increases government surveillance.

118-hr-443.one_liner: Require Labor Department workers to get training on finding human trafficking
provisions: Requires the Department of Labor to train its workers on human trafficking
Training covers how to spot signs of trafficking
Training covers how to help law enforcement with trafficking cases

supporters: Supporters say training Department of Labor workers to spot trafficking signs would help rescue victims during workplace inspections.
Supporters say teaching Department of Labor staff how to assist law enforcement would give police more trained eyes to identify trafficking cases.
critics: Critics say requiring Department of Labor to train all its workers on trafficking detection creates new costs without specifying funding.
Critics say this expands Department of Labor duties beyond workplace safety into law enforcement work.

118-hr-4368.one_liner: Fund food assistance programs, farm support, and food safety for 2024
provisions: Funds food assistance programs like SNAP that help families buy groceries
Pays for food safety inspections at meat plants and other food facilities
Funds rural housing loans and business development programs
Provides crop insurance payments to farmers
Pays for international food aid to other countries
Funds agricultural research and farm statistics

supporters: Supporters say SNAP food assistance programs help families buy groceries when they cannot afford food.
Supporters say food safety inspections at meat plants protect people from getting sick from unsafe food.
Supporters say crop insurance payments help farmers stay in business when bad weather destroys their crops.
critics: Critics say SNAP food assistance programs are expensive and cost taxpayers billions of dollars each year.
Critics say this bill spends taxpayer money on international food aid to other countries instead of helping Americans.
Critics say crop insurance payments give taxpayer money to farmers who should buy their own insurance.

118-hr-497.one_liner: Cancel a rule requiring healthcare workers to get COVID-19 vaccines
provisions: Cancels a 2021 rule that said healthcare workers must get COVID-19 vaccines
The rule applied to hospitals and clinics that take Medicare and Medicaid payments
Stops the government from making similar vaccine rules in the future
Healthcare facilities can now take Medicare and Medicaid payments without making staff get vaccinated

supporters: Supporters say this protects healthcare workers' freedom to choose about COVID-19 vaccines without losing jobs at hospitals and clinics that take Medicare and Medicaid payments.
Supporters say healthcare facilities can keep their Medicare and Medicaid funding even if staff are not vaccinated against COVID-19.
Supporters say this stops the government from making similar vaccine rules for healthcare workers in the future.
critics: Critics say unvaccinated healthcare workers could spread COVID-19 to patients in hospitals and clinics that take Medicare and Medicaid payments.
Critics say elderly and sick patients who use Medicare and Medicaid could face higher risk of getting COVID-19 from unvaccinated staff.
Critics say this removes a safety rule that protected vulnerable patients from COVID-19 in healthcare settings.

118-hr-4470.one_liner: Continue a chemical plant security program through September 2025
provisions: Keeps a Department of Homeland Security program running through September 2025
The program sets security rules for chemical plants
Without this bill, the program would stop operating

supporters: Supporters say this bill keeps the Department of Homeland Security's security program for chemical plants running through September 2025.
Supporters say the program protects communities near chemical facilities from terrorist attacks.
Supporters say without this bill, chemical plants would lose federal security rules.
critics: Critics say the program forces chemical companies to follow federal security rules that cost them money.
Critics say extending the program through September 2025 continues federal control over private chemical facilities.

118-hr-485.one_liner: Stop federal health programs from using disability-based pricing
provisions: Blocks federal health programs from using a pricing method that treats disabled lives as worth less
Applies to Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee health plans, and other federally funded programs
Affects decisions about treatment coverage and payment amounts

supporters: Supporters say this bill would stop Medicare, Medicaid, and federal employee health plans from using quality-adjusted life years that discount the value of disabled people's lives.
Supporters say this would protect disabled patients from having their treatment coverage and payment amounts decided by measures that treat their lives as worth less.
critics: Critics say removing quality-adjusted life years from Medicare, Medicaid, and federal employee health programs could increase costs without a tool to measure treatment effectiveness.
Critics say federal health programs need this pricing method to make fair coverage and reimbursement decisions with limited budgets.

118-hr-467.one_liner: Make all fentanyl-related substances illegal under federal drug laws
provisions: Classifies all fentanyl-related substances as illegal drugs with the same penalties as heroin
Creates a new registration process for researchers studying these substances with government funding
Allows researchers to use one registration for multiple related study sites
Lets researchers make small amounts of these substances for studies without separate manufacturing permits

supporters: Supporters say placing all fentanyl-related substances in Schedule I gives law enforcement the same penalties to use against fentanyl dealers as heroin dealers.
Supporters say the new registration process for government-funded research will help scientists study these substances faster.
Supporters say allowing one registration for multiple research sites will reduce paperwork for scientists.
critics: Critics say classifying all fentanyl-related substances as Schedule I could block medical research into potential treatments.
Critics say the broad classification may criminalize substances that have not been proven dangerous.
Critics say researchers will still face barriers studying these substances even with the new registration process.

118-hr-4665.one_liner: Fund State Department foreign programs and international aid for 2024
provisions: Provides money for State Department operations in other countries
Funds foreign aid programs through USAID
Pays for international security assistance to other nations
Supports Peace Corps volunteers and U.S. embassies abroad
Funds programs that promote democracy and human rights overseas

supporters: Supporters say this funds State Department operations needed to protect Americans abroad and run U.S. embassies in other countries.
Supporters say this provides foreign aid through USAID that helps respond to humanitarian crises and promotes stability in key regions.
Supporters say this supports Peace Corps volunteers and democracy programs that build relationships with other nations and advance American values overseas.
critics: Critics say this spends taxpayer money on foreign programs when domestic infrastructure and social services need more funding.
Critics say this sends international security assistance to countries that may not always support American interests or use the aid effectively.
Critics say this funds democracy and human rights programs that other nations may view as unwanted interference in their internal affairs.

118-hr-500.one_liner: Let investment companies delay withdrawals when they suspect elder financial abuse
provisions: Lets investment companies delay withdrawals for up to 15 days if they think someone 65 or older is being financially exploited
Lets them delay another 10 days if they confirm exploitation is happening
Also applies to adults 18 or older who cannot protect themselves
Companies must keep the money in a bank account during delays
Requires the SEC to make recommendations about stopping financial exploitation of older adults

supporters: Supporters say this bill would protect adults 65 and older from scammers who try to steal their retirement savings by giving investment companies 15 days to investigate suspicious withdrawals.
Supporters say the additional 10-day delay gives companies time to work with authorities to stop financial theft before victims lose their money.
Supporters say this bill helps adults 18 and older who cannot protect themselves from being tricked into giving away their investments.
critics: Critics say the 15-day delay keeps people from accessing their own money when they need it for emergencies or bills.
Critics say investment companies could misuse these rules to block legitimate withdrawals from customers for up to 25 days total.
Critics say adults 65 and older should have the right to withdraw their own money without companies deciding if they are being exploited.

118-hr-5110.one_liner: Let schools use federal education funds to buy weapons for archery and shooting sports training
provisions: Lets schools use federal education money to buy weapons for teaching archery, hunting, and shooting sports
Changes a rule that currently stops schools from using these funds to buy weapons or train students to use them
Creates an exception only for archery, hunting, and shooting sports classes

supporters: Supporters say this lets schools use federal education money to teach students archery, hunting, and shooting sports skills.
Supporters say this gives schools the ability to offer outdoor education programs that were blocked by current federal funding rules.
critics: Critics say this allows schools to spend federal education money on weapons that are currently banned from school purchases.
Critics say this changes federal safety rules that prevent schools from using education funds to buy weapons or train students to use them.

118-hr-5.one_liner: Give parents rights to review school curriculums and meet with teachers
provisions: Parents can review what their children learn in school
Parents can meet with their child's teachers at least twice each school year
Parents can see school budgets and how money is spent
Parents can review lists of books in school libraries
Schools must post what they teach online for parents to see
Schools cannot sell student information to make money
Schools must tell parents about violence at their child's school

supporters: Supporters say this gives parents the right to see what their children learn by requiring schools to post all curriculum online and allow parents to review teaching materials.
Supporters say this ensures parents stay connected to their child's education by requiring teachers to meet with parents at least twice each school year.
Supporters say this protects student privacy by stopping schools from selling student information to companies for money.
critics: Critics say requiring schools to post all curriculum online and provide extensive documentation to parents will create extra work and costs for already busy school staff.
Critics say allowing parents to review library book lists could lead to book removal when parents object to certain materials.
Critics say requiring teachers to meet with parents twice per year for every student could take time away from classroom instruction and planning.

118-hr-538.one_liner: Require companies to tell customers when smart devices have cameras or microphones
provisions: Companies must tell customers when smart devices have cameras or microphones
Does not cover phones, laptops, and other devices where people normally expect cameras
Applies to smart home devices like connected appliances and other products

supporters: Supporters say this helps consumers know when smart home appliances have cameras or microphones that could record them.
Supporters say the disclosure requirement protects privacy by telling people about recording features in devices like smart TVs and connected appliances.
critics: Critics say the disclosure requirements add new rules and costs for companies making internet-connected devices.
Critics say consumers can already find information about cameras and microphones in product manuals and descriptions.

provisions: Extends wildlife conservation programs through the year 2028
Continues the Partners for Fish and Wildlife Program
Continues money for protecting African elephants, Asian elephants, rhinoceroses, tigers, great apes, and marine turtles
Changes how several wildlife conservation programs work

supporters: Supporters say this bill protects African elephants, Asian elephants, rhinoceroses, tigers, great apes, and marine turtles through 2028.
Supporters say this continues the Partners for Fish and Wildlife Program that helps private landowners protect animal habitats.
Supporters say these conservation programs prevent endangered species from going extinct.
critics: Critics say extending these wildlife programs through 2028 costs taxpayers money that should go to other priorities.
Critics say the changes to how conservation programs work could make them work worse or cost more.
Critics say this spends money on protecting animals in other countries like African elephants instead of helping Americans.

118-hr-5585.one_liner: Make it a federal crime to flee from Border Patrol officers near the border
provisions: Makes it a federal crime to drive away from Border Patrol officers within 100 miles of the US border
Sets prison sentences for people who commit this crime
Requires longer prison sentences if someone gets badly hurt or dies during the chase
Permanently bans non-citizens from getting legal status if they commit this crime while in the US illegally

supporters: Supporters say this would protect Border Patrol officers from dangerous car chases in the 100-mile border zone where they work.
Supporters say the required longer prison sentences for cases with death or serious injury would stop people from putting officers and others at risk.
Supporters say the permanent ban on getting legal status would deter people in the US illegally from running from Border Patrol.
critics: Critics say the 100-mile border zone covers nearly 200 million Americans who live far from the actual border.
Critics say the required minimum prison sentences take away judges' power to look at each case differently.
Critics say the permanent ban on ever getting legal status is too harsh and ruins people's chances for life.

118-hr-5528.one_liner: Require a study of government buying rules for security risks
provisions: Tells the Office of Management and Budget to study how government agencies buy things
The study checks if rules about buying the cheapest option create security problems
The office must report what they find to Congress

supporters: Supporters say the Office of Management and Budget study will identify when lowest price procurement rules create national security risks.
Supporters say the report to Congress will help lawmakers understand if cheap foreign equipment threatens government security.
critics: Critics say requiring the Office of Management and Budget to evaluate all agency procurement activities adds unnecessary bureaucracy.
Critics say the study could be used to justify abandoning lowest price rules and waste taxpayer money on expensive contracts.

118-hr-5856.one_liner: Continue funding programs that fight human trafficking around the world
provisions: Continues funding for programs that fight human trafficking in other countries
Requires all U.S. aid projects to include anti-trafficking work
Adds organ trafficking to the government's yearly trafficking report

supporters: Supporters say reauthorizing international anti-trafficking programs will continue funding that helps rescue victims in other countries.
Supporters say requiring all U.S. foreign aid projects to include anti-trafficking strategies will catch more traffickers.
Supporters say adding organ trafficking information to the annual Trafficking in Persons Report will help governments track this crime.
critics: Critics say mandating anti-trafficking work in all foreign aid projects will increase costs and slow down other assistance programs.
Critics say requiring organ trafficking data in the yearly report will create more work for government agencies.

118-hr-5862.one_liner: Give customs agents more authority to reorganize customs revenue jobs and staffing
provisions: Lets Customs and Border Protection add duties to existing customs workers
Lets CBP create new job types and pay grades for customs revenue workers
Lets CBP reduce staffing in some customs areas if it will not go below optimal levels
Adds national account managers and international trade analysts to jobs that cannot be cut easily

supporters: Supporters say letting CBP add duties to existing import specialists, entry specialists, and customs auditors makes the agency more flexible without hiring more staff.
Supporters say adding national account managers and international trade analysts to the list of jobs that cannot be easily cut gives more workers stronger job protections.
Supporters say allowing staffing reductions only down to the level set by CBP's own resource allocation model keeps a data-based floor in place, preventing cuts that go too far.
critics: Critics say relaxing the rule that currently blocks any reduction in import specialists, entry specialists, and customs auditors could lead to fewer workers processing the billions of dollars in goods that enter the U.S. each year.

Critics say letting CBP define its own 'optimal' staffing level through an internal model — rather than a fixed number set by Congress — gives the agency too much power to justify cuts to revenue enforcement jobs.
Critics say adding new duties to existing customs positions, without new pay, could stretch workers thin and slow down trade processing at ports of entry.

118-hr-5860.one_liner: Fund the federal government through November 17, 2023
provisions: Funds federal agencies at the same spending levels as 2023 through November 17, 2023
Prevents a government shutdown that would otherwise start October 1, 2023
Provides emergency funding for disaster relief through FEMA
Extends the National Flood Insurance Program through November 17, 2023
Extends airport improvement grants and FAA programs through December 31, 2023
Extends funding for community health centers and diabetes programs through November 17, 2023

supporters: Supporters say the bill stops a government shutdown by keeping all federal agencies funded at 2023 spending levels from October 1 through November 17, 2023, giving Congress time to pass a full-year budget.

Supporters say it gives FEMA emergency money to respond to natural disasters and extends the National Flood Insurance Program through November 17, 2023, so homeowners in flood-prone areas do not lose coverage.

Supporters say it extends funding for community health centers, the National Health Service Corps, and diabetes programs through November 17, 2023, so low-income patients and tribal communities can keep getting care without a gap.
critics: Critics say the bill funds the government for only 47 days at the same 2023 spending levels, meaning no spending cuts are made and Congress will face the same budget deadline again on November 17, 2023.

Critics say Section 2401 exempts the bill's costs from the PAYGO Act, which normally requires new spending to be paid for with cuts or new revenue, so the emergency and extension spending adds to the deficit without any offsets.

Critics say Section 104 bars federal agencies from starting any new programs or projects that did not receive funding in 2023, which delays approved services and investments for the full length of the stopgap period.

118-hr-663.one_liner: Fund programs preventing child abuse in Native American communities through 2028
provisions: Continues funding programs that prevent child abuse in Native American families through 2028
Lets tribes use grant money to pay for child protective services and other family help
Expands a national center that trains people working with Native American children
Creates model agreements between tribes and states to handle child abuse cases

supporters: Supporters say this bill protects Native American children by continuing funding for abuse prevention programs through 2028
Supporters say tribes can now use grant money to pay for child protective services instead of just treatment programs
Supporters say the expanded national center will train more people who work with Native American children in urban areas
critics: Critics say this bill costs taxpayers money to fund these programs for five more years through 2028
Critics say expanding the national center adds more government workers and bureaucracy
Critics say the model agreements between tribes and states could create confusion about which government handles child abuse cases

118-hr-589.one_liner: Require sanctions on Iran's Supreme Leader and President for human rights abuses
provisions: Freezes money and property of Iran's Supreme Leader and President in the United States
Stops Iran's top leaders from getting permission to enter the United States
Requires the President to check every few months if sanctions should apply to Iranian officials
Targets Iranian groups that help with human rights abuses or terrorism

supporters: Supporters say freezing the Supreme Leader and President's money in the United States will stop Iran's top officials from using American banks to fund oppression.
Supporters say blocking visas for Iran's leaders will prevent them from traveling to the US while they abuse their own people.
Supporters say targeting Iranian groups that help with human rights abuses will cut off support for violence against protesters.
critics: Critics say blocking Iran's President from entering the United States could hurt talks to solve nuclear and other problems.
Critics say freezing Iranian leaders' property won't change how Iran treats protesters since most of their money is kept in other countries.
Critics say requiring the President to check sanctions every few months creates too much work without clear benefits.

118-hr-6126.one_liner: Fund military aid and defense systems for Israel
provisions: Replaces military equipment that was given to Israel
Pays back the Defense Department for training and services given to Israel
Buys Iron Dome and David's Sling defense systems for Israel
Develops Iron Beam defense system for Israel
Funds State Department security programs
Gives the President more power to transfer military equipment to Israel
Takes back unspent money from the IRS

supporters: Supporters say funding Iron Dome and David's Sling gives Israel the ability to shoot down rockets and missiles aimed at civilians, and that replacing equipment the U.S. already sent keeps American stockpiles ready.
Supporters say labeling the spending as emergency funding lets the U.S. respond quickly to the October 7 attacks without waiting for the normal budget process.
Supporters say rescinding unspent IRS funds offsets part of the cost, so not all of the money adds to the deficit.
critics: Critics say expanding the President's power to transfer defense articles to Israel without the usual congressional approval reduces oversight of how and when U.S. weapons are used.
Critics say the bill funds offensive military procurement, like the Iron Beam system still in development, on top of defensive systems, which goes beyond replacing what was already given.
Critics say pulling back unobligated IRS funds weakens tax enforcement capacity that was set aside to collect revenue the government is owed.

118-hr-662.one_liner: Give states block grants to help farmers with 2022 disaster losses
provisions: Lets the Department of Agriculture give block grants to states and territories
Uses existing funding to help farmers who lost crops or livestock in 2022
Covers losses from droughts, wildfires, hurricanes, floods, and other natural disasters
Only applies to disasters that happened in calendar year 2022

supporters: Supporters say this would help farmers and ranchers who lost crops and livestock during the droughts, wildfires, hurricanes, and other natural disasters that hit in 2022.
Supporters say block grants let states decide how to distribute the aid to farmers who need it most in their area.
Supporters say this uses existing Department of Agriculture funding instead of requiring new taxpayer money.
critics: Critics say limiting aid to only 2022 disasters leaves out farmers who suffered losses from natural disasters in 2021, 2023, and other years.
Critics say block grants could lead to unequal distribution of aid, with some states getting more help per affected farmer than others.
Critics say this sets a precedent of using federal money to bail out farmers for weather-related losses that are part of normal farming risks.

118-hr-6363.one_liner: Fund the federal government through early 2024 to prevent shutdown
provisions: Funds most federal agencies through February 2, 2024 at 2023 spending levels
Funds farm, energy, veterans, and transportation agencies through January 19, 2024
Extends farm programs that were set to expire
Extends public health programs and the U.S. Parole Commission
Prevents government shutdown that would start November 17, 2023

supporters: Supporters say this prevents a government shutdown that would start November 17, 2023 by funding federal agencies through February 2024.
Supporters say this extends farm programs and public health programs that were set to expire, keeping essential services running.
Supporters say this maintains funding for veterans affairs, transportation, and agriculture agencies through January 19, 2024 at 2023 levels.
critics: Critics say this only provides temporary funding through February 2024 instead of full-year budget certainty for federal agencies.
Critics say maintaining 2023 spending levels fails to account for inflation affecting government operations.
Critics say extending programs temporarily instead of long-term reauthorization creates ongoing uncertainty.

118-hr-6914.one_liner: Require colleges to provide pregnancy information to students
provisions: Requires colleges that receive federal student aid to give students information about pregnancy rights and resources
Colleges must list places that help pregnant students carry their baby to term and care for the baby after birth
Colleges must explain what support they offer pregnant students and new parents
Colleges must tell students how to report pregnancy discrimination

supporters: Supporters say colleges that get federal student aid must give pregnant students a list of resources to help them carry their baby to term and care for the baby after birth, which they often do not receive today.
Supporters say the bill fills a gap by requiring schools to explain what accommodations are available to pregnant students and new parents, helping them stay enrolled.
Supporters say requiring colleges to tell students how to file a pregnancy discrimination complaint gives students a clear path to protect their rights under existing law.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires colleges to share information about carrying a pregnancy to term and parenting, and does not require schools to inform students about all legal options, leaving out part of what students may need.

Critics say the bill does not set a standard for what resources colleges must actually offer, only what they must list, so students in areas with few services may get information that does not lead to real help.
Critics say the bill places new reporting and disclosure requirements on colleges without providing federal funding to cover the cost of creating and distributing the required materials.

118-hr-6678.one_liner: Make Social Security fraud grounds for deportation and blocking entry for non-citizens
provisions: Makes creating fake IDs without permission grounds for deporting non-citizens
Makes lying on Social Security disability applications grounds for deporting non-citizens
Blocks non-citizens from entering the U.S. if convicted of these Social Security fraud crimes
Applies to people convicted of the crimes or who admit to doing them

supporters: Supporters say that making fake ID creation grounds for deportation will stop non-citizens from using false documents to collect Social Security disability benefits they are not entitled to.

Supporters say that linking lying on a Social Security disability application to deportation protects a program that pays benefits to about 8 million disabled Americans, reducing fraud that drains those funds.
Supporters say the bill covers people who admit to these acts, not just those convicted in court, which closes a loophole that lets admitted fraudsters stay in the country.
critics: Critics say the bill could lead to deportation for a single false statement on a disability application, which may be too harsh a punishment for a paperwork error versus intentional fraud.
Critics say the bill does not set a dollar threshold or define how serious the false statement must be, meaning minor mistakes and large-scale fraud are treated the same way.
Critics say applying this rule to people who only admit to the acts — without a court conviction — removes standard legal protections that non-citizens normally have before facing deportation.

118-hr-6679.one_liner: Block Hamas members and October 7 attackers from US immigration benefits
provisions: Blocks Hamas members from entering the United States
Blocks Palestinian Islamic Jihad members from entering the United States
Blocks people who took part in the October 7, 2023 attacks on Israel from entering the United States
Blocks all Palestinian Liberation Organization members from entering the United States
Stops October 7 attackers from seeking asylum
Stops October 7 attackers from getting protection from deportation

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects the U.S. by blocking Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad members from entering the country, keeping out people tied to groups the U.S. already labels as terrorist organizations.
Supporters say that people who took part in or helped plan the October 7, 2023 attacks on Israel should not be able to use U.S. asylum laws or deportation protections as a way to stay in the country.
Supporters say expanding the PLO admissions bar to cover all PLO members, not just officers and spokespersons, closes a gap that let some members enter the U.S. while others were blocked.
critics: Critics say the bill bars all PLO members from the U.S., which could block Palestinian leaders, diplomats, and civilians with past PLO ties who were not involved in any violence.

Critics say removing deportation protections from anyone linked to the October 7 attacks — even before a court has ruled on their case — takes away a legal process that exists to prevent people from being sent to places where their life is at risk.

Critics say the bill does not define what it means to have 'facilitated' the October 7 attacks, which could allow immigration officials to bar people based on loose or unclear connections to the events.

118-hr-676.one_liner: Require NOAA to work with local communities on ocean acidification problems
provisions: NOAA must work with state, local, and tribal groups on ocean acidification problems
NOAA must help these groups improve their programs for dealing with acidification
NOAA must help groups share their successful work as examples for other communities
A federal advisory board on ocean acidification must include two tribal representatives

supporters: Supporters say this would help coastal communities fight ocean acidification by requiring NOAA to work directly with state, local, and tribal groups on their programs.
Supporters say adding two tribal representatives to the federal advisory board ensures Native American voices are heard on ocean acidification decisions.
Supporters say this would help communities learn from each other by requiring NOAA to share successful acidification programs as examples.
critics: Critics say this creates new federal mandates requiring NOAA to collaborate with state, local and tribal groups without providing additional funding.
Critics say requiring NOAA to assist groups in improving their programs and share information could create administrative burden and duplicate existing work.

118-hr-6918.one_liner: Block a rule change for pregnancy centers that get welfare program money
provisions: Stops the government from applying a new funding rule to pregnancy centers
Lets pregnancy centers keep getting money from a program that helps poor families
Covers centers that offer pregnancy counseling, testing, diapers, baby clothes, and family support
The blocked rule would make states prove the money is used reasonably for program goals

supporters: Supporters say this bill protects pregnancy centers that give out diapers, baby clothes, and prenatal education to low-income families from losing TANF funding under a new federal rule.

Supporters say the blocked rule would let the federal government cut off state spending for centers that counsel pregnant women, even when those centers provide direct material help to mothers and families.
Supporters say states should be able to use TANF funds for pregnancy centers without having to prove to federal officials that the spending fits a narrow definition of program goals.
critics: Critics say TANF was designed to help poor families reach financial independence, and the bill stops the government from checking whether money spent on pregnancy centers actually serves that goal.

Critics say the federal rule being blocked would simply require states to show that TANF spending meets one of the program's four legal purposes, and exempting pregnancy centers removes that basic accountability check.

Critics say the Administration for Children and Families found that counseling women only after they become pregnant has little connection to TANF's goal of reducing out-of-wedlock pregnancies, and this bill prevents that finding from being enforced.

118-hr-6976.one_liner: Make drunk driving a reason to deport or block non-citizens from entering
provisions: Stops non-citizens from entering the US if convicted of drunk driving
Stops non-citizens from entering the US if they admit to drunk driving
Lets the government deport non-citizens convicted of drunk driving

supporters: Supporters say the bill would bar non-citizens from entering the US if they have been convicted of drunk driving, which they argue protects American communities from repeat offenders who have already shown dangerous behavior on the road.

Supporters say the bill also covers non-citizens who admit to the acts of drunk driving — not just those with a formal conviction — closing a loophole that could let some offenders enter the country anyway.
Supporters say allowing deportation of non-citizens convicted of DUI gives the government a tool to remove people who have broken laws that put other drivers and pedestrians at risk.
critics: Critics say the bill would allow deportation based on a DUI conviction, which in many states can include first-time offenders or people with very low blood alcohol levels, potentially separating long-term residents from their families over a single offense.
Critics say the provision that bars entry for people who only 'admit' to drunk driving — without a conviction — removes standard legal protections, since a formal court process is bypassed.

Critics say the bill does not distinguish between a one-time misdemeanor DUI and more serious repeat offenses, meaning non-citizens could face permanent deportation under the same rules regardless of the details of their case.

118-hr-734.one_liner: Ban people born male from competing in women's and girls' sports at federally funded schools
provisions: Stops people born male from competing in women's and girls' sports at schools that get federal money
Says this rule applies under Title IX, the law that stops sex discrimination in schools
Defines sex by a person's biology at birth
Lets people born male practice with women's teams if it does not take away spots from women

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects female athletes by stopping people born male from competing in women's and girls' sports at schools that receive federal funding, which they argue gives those athletes a physical advantage.
Supporters say defining sex by a person's biology at birth under Title IX creates a clear, consistent rule for all federally funded schools to follow.
Supporters say the bill still allows people born male to practice with women's teams, as long as doing so does not take away spots or opportunities from female athletes.
critics: Critics say the bill requires schools to check students' reproductive biology and genetics at birth, which they argue invades student privacy and could force schools to demand medical records.
Critics say applying this rule under Title IX redefines what counts as sex discrimination, which could be used to exclude transgender girls who have lived as female throughout their school years.

Critics say the bill does not include any process for individual schools to review specific cases, leaving no flexibility for students whose situations do not fit neatly into the birth-biology definition.

118-hr-7217.one_liner: Fund military aid to Israel and US operations after attacks in Israel
provisions: Provides emergency military funding for the year starting October 2023
Pays to replace weapons and equipment the US gave to Israel
Covers costs of current US military operations in the Middle East region
Funds Israel's Iron Dome and other missile defense systems
Increases security funding for US embassies affected by the Israel attacks
Pays for emergency evacuations of US government workers and citizens
Lets the President transfer more military equipment to Israel

supporters: Supporters say the bill replaces weapons and equipment the US already gave to Israel, making sure US stockpiles are not left empty after the transfer.
Supporters say funding Israel's Iron Dome and David's Sling missile defense systems helps protect Israeli civilians from short-range rocket attacks.
Supporters say the bill pays for emergency evacuations of US government workers and citizens in the region, which protects Americans caught in the conflict.
critics: Critics say the bill expands the President's power to transfer military equipment to Israel without the normal approval process, reducing congressional oversight.
Critics say the funding is labeled as emergency spending, which means it is exempt from budget limits and adds to the national debt without offsets.
Critics say covering the costs of current US military operations in the Middle East region could pull the US deeper into the conflict.

118-hr-7024.one_liner: Expand tax credits for families and increase business tax breaks
provisions: Increases tax credits for families with children
Lets businesses write off equipment costs faster to reduce their taxes
Sets different tax rules for Taiwan residents who earn US income
Increases tax breaks for people who lost money in disasters and wildfires
Increases tax credits for building affordable housing

supporters: Supporters say the child tax credit changes would allow parents who earn too little to claim the full $2,000-per-child credit to get more money back, reaching about 16 million children in low-income families who currently get little or nothing.

Supporters say restoring 100% first-year write-offs for business equipment — which had been phasing down to 60% in 2024 — would push companies to buy new tools and machines, which can lead to more hiring.
Supporters say raising the low-income housing tax credit would help developers build more rental units for people who cannot afford market-rate housing.
critics: Critics say the bill costs roughly $78 billion over 10 years, and that the business tax breaks — like the faster equipment write-offs — deliver more in savings to corporations than to working families.
Critics say the special tax rules for Taiwan residents who earn U.S. income create a carve-out that workers from other countries do not get, treating one nationality differently from all others.
Critics say the child tax credit increases are set to expire after a few years, meaning families cannot count on the extra money staying in place.

118-hr-7463.one_liner: Keep the government running through March 2024 and change student aid rules
provisions: Funds federal agencies through March 8, 2024 for some and March 22, 2024 for others to prevent government shutdown
Sets a floor of negative $1,500 for student income when calculating financial aid in 2024-2025
Sets a floor of $0 for student income when calculating financial aid starting in 2025-2026
Provides additional funding for Federal Pell Grants starting in 2025

supporters: Supporters say the bill prevents a government shutdown by keeping federal agencies funded through March 8 or March 22, 2024, which protects workers who depend on federal services and pay.
Supporters say setting a student income floor of -$1,500 for 2024-2025 means more students will qualify for federal aid, because their income calculation cannot drop below that number.
Supporters say adding more money to Federal Pell Grants starting in 2025 will help low-income students pay for college without taking on more debt.
critics: Critics say the bill only extends funding for a few weeks — some agencies through March 8 and others through March 22, 2024 — which means Congress will face the same shutdown risk again very soon.
Critics say changing the student income floor to $0 starting in 2025-2026 is stricter than the 2024-2025 rule of -$1,500, which could reduce aid for students who report zero or negative income.
Critics say the bill does not pass full-year spending bills, so federal agencies are stuck operating at 2023 funding levels with no new investments or program updates.

118-hr-753.one_liner: Require VA hospitals to install on-site medical waste treatment systems
provisions: Requires VA hospitals to install systems that treat medical waste on-site instead of shipping it elsewhere
VA must create a cost analysis to figure out which hospitals would save money with these systems
Only hospitals that would save money get the new waste treatment systems

supporters: Supporters say installing on-site medical waste treatment systems at VA hospitals would save money by ending the need to ship waste to outside facilities.
Supporters say the required cost analysis model ensures taxpayer money is only spent at hospitals that would actually save money.
critics: Critics say the upfront costs to install and operate medical waste treatment systems at VA facilities could be expensive for taxpayers.
Critics say operating medical waste treatment systems on-site at VA hospitals could create safety risks for staff and patients.

118-hr-815.one_liner: Remove the 24-month care requirement for new veterans' emergency treatment reimbursement
provisions: Removes the rule that veterans must have received VA care within 24 months before getting emergency treatment to qualify for reimbursement
Lets veterans get VA reimbursement for emergency treatment at non-VA hospitals if the treatment happens within 60 days of enrolling in VA healthcare
Covers emergency treatment costs for newly enrolled veterans who have not yet used VA services

supporters: Supporters say this helps veterans who just signed up for VA care get emergency treatment paid for at non-VA hospitals within 60 days.
Supporters say removing the 24-month rule means new VA patients can get emergency care covered without waiting two years.
critics: Critics say covering emergency treatment for newly enrolled veterans will cost the VA more money by paying for additional non-VA hospital bills.
Critics say this may cause more veterans to go to non-VA emergency rooms instead of VA hospitals.

118-hr-788.one_liner: Stop the federal government from sending settlement money to outside groups
provisions: Stops the government from making legal settlements that send money to outside groups
Allows payments to repair damage caused by the defendant or pay for services
Lets officials be fired or lose money if they break this rule
Requires agencies to report their settlements for 7 years
Requires government watchdogs to report on rule violations

supporters: Supporters say this stops settlement money from going to outside groups that were not harmed, ensuring taxpayer funds return to the Treasury instead.
Supporters say the 7-year reporting rule will show the public how agencies spend settlement dollars and which groups receive payments.
Supporters say officials who break these rules can be fired or lose money, creating real consequences for violations.
critics: Critics say the narrow exceptions for 'actual harm' and 'services' could block settlement funds from going to community programs that help areas affected by corporate wrongdoing.
Critics say the 7-year reporting requirement will create extra paperwork and costs for agencies that must track and report all settlement details.
Critics say this rule could make companies less willing to settle cases if they cannot direct money to environmental cleanup or community restoration projects.

118-hr-813.one_liner: Require a government study of how well America attracts foreign business investment
provisions: Requires the Department of Commerce and Government Accountability Office to study foreign investment in America
The study examines how well America attracts businesses from trusted countries to invest here
Agencies must review current government policies that affect foreign investment
The study includes recommendations for bringing more foreign businesses to America

supporters: Supporters say the Department of Commerce and GAO review will find specific policy gaps that stop trusted foreign companies from choosing the U.S. over other countries.
Supporters say the required recommendations give Congress a clear action list for bringing more foreign business investment and the jobs that come with it to American communities.
Supporters say reviewing federal policies that affect foreign direct investment will show which rules are working and which ones may be pushing companies away.
critics: Critics say the bill only orders a study and report, with no requirement that the government act on any of the recommendations it receives.
Critics say the terms 'trusted countries' and 'responsible private-sector entities' are not defined in the bill, which could make the review results hard to use or compare.
Critics say the GAO and Commerce Department already track foreign investment data, so a new interagency review may repeat work that has already been done.

118-hr-7888.one_liner: Extend FBI surveillance powers for 5 years with new rules
provisions: Lets the FBI keep using a surveillance program for 5 more years to spy on people outside America
Requires FBI supervisors to approve searches about Americans caught in this surveillance
Makes the FBI Deputy Director approve any searches about elected officials or government workers
Bans political appointees from approving searches about politicians
Creates punishments for FBI agents who break surveillance rules including firing for intentional misconduct
Increases criminal penalties for people who violate surveillance laws
Requires sworn statements for surveillance requests and limits using information from political groups or news sources

supporters: Supporters say this bill adds important oversight by requiring FBI supervisors to approve searches about Americans caught in surveillance.
Supporters say the ban on political appointees approving searches about elected officials prevents partisan misuse of surveillance powers.
Supporters say the penalties including firing for intentional misconduct will stop FBI agents from breaking surveillance rules.
critics: Critics say this extends mass surveillance of people outside America for 5 more years without ending warrantless searches of Americans' data.
Critics say FBI supervisors can still approve searches about Americans without a warrant, which violates privacy rights.
Critics say the exception allowing searches to prevent threats to life or serious harm is too broad and could be misused.

118-hres-104.one_liner: Condemn China for flying a spy balloon over the United States
provisions: Condemns China for violating US territory with a spy balloon
Says China lied about what the balloon was for
States US policy should stop foreign spy aircraft from entering US territory

supporters: Supporters say this resolution makes it official US policy to stop foreign spy aircraft from violating US territory.
Supporters say this condemns China for sending the spy balloon over US airspace without permission.
Supporters say this calls out China for lying about the balloon's true purpose as a surveillance tool.
critics: Critics say this resolution only makes statements but creates no new laws to actually stop spy balloons.
Critics say condemning China could make diplomatic relations worse without fixing the surveillance problem.
Critics say existing US policy already prevents foreign aircraft from entering US territory without permission.

118-hres-11.one_liner: Create a House committee to study competition with China
provisions: Creates a committee in the House of Representatives
Committee has up to 16 members chosen by House leaders
Committee studies how China competes with the US in business, technology, and security
Committee writes recommendations for Congress about competing with China

supporters: Supporters say the 16-member committee will investigate China's economic, technological, and security progress to help the US compete.
Supporters say the committee will write policy recommendations for Congress about competing with China.
critics: Critics say the 16-member committee costs money for staff and operations that could be used elsewhere.
Critics say creating a committee focused on China competition could harm diplomatic relations with China.

118-hres-12.one_liner: Create a House subcommittee to investigate federal agencies' information gathering on citizens
provisions: Creates a House subcommittee with up to 13 members to investigate federal agencies
The subcommittee investigates how executive branch agencies collect information on U.S. citizens
Looks for activities that are illegal, unconstitutional, or unethical
Must report findings by January 2, 2025
The subcommittee ends 30 days after filing its report

supporters: Supporters say the 13-member subcommittee will protect citizens from illegal government spying by investigating how executive agencies collect information on Americans.
Supporters say requiring a final report by January 2, 2025 ensures Congress gets answers about unconstitutional surveillance activities within a clear deadline.
critics: Critics say creating another subcommittee wastes taxpayer money on partisan investigations instead of focusing on real legislative priorities.
Critics say the subcommittee interferes with legitimate law enforcement work by second-guessing how agencies investigate threats to national security.

118-hres-114.one_liner: Remove Representative George Santos from the House of Representatives
provisions: Removes George Santos from his seat in Congress
Stops him from voting in the House
Ends his pay and benefits from Congress
Leaves an empty House seat that needs to be filled

supporters: Supporters say this would remove Santos from his seat in Congress and stop him from voting on laws
Supporters say this would end Santos's pay and benefits from Congress paid by taxpayers
Supporters say this would open the House seat so voters can elect a new representative
critics: Critics say this would remove an elected representative before his term ends
Critics say this would leave the House seat empty until a special election is held
Critics say this removes Santos without letting voters decide in the next regular election

118-hres-166.one_liner: Allow votes on requiring inflation estimates and canceling retirement investment rules
provisions: Allows a House vote on requiring inflation estimates for Executive orders that cost money
Allows a House vote on canceling rules about how retirement plans invest money
Sets time limits for debate on both issues

supporters: Supporters say H.R. 347 would require the Executive Office of the President to publish an inflation estimate before any Executive order with a large budget effect takes place, giving Congress and the public a clearer picture of what each order costs.

Supporters say H.J. Res. 30 would cancel a Department of Labor rule that let retirement plan managers pick investments based on factors beyond financial return, arguing that plan managers should focus only on getting the best financial outcome for workers in those plans.
Supporters say setting time limits for debate on both bills prevents either measure from being blocked through extended delay on the House floor.
critics: Critics say canceling the Department of Labor rule through H.J. Res. 30 would stop retirement plan managers from using all available information when picking investments, which could affect the long-term value of 401(k) and pension accounts held by millions of American workers.

Critics say the rule for consideration limits how much time members of Congress can debate H.R. 347 and H.J. Res. 30, which reduces the chance to fully examine how each bill would affect federal agencies and retirement savers.

Critics say requiring a new inflation estimate for every Executive order that touches the federal budget could slow down time-sensitive government actions without adding useful information beyond what budget offices already produce.

118-hres-132.one_liner: Express condolences for earthquake victims in Turkey and Syria
provisions: Expresses sadness for people who died in earthquakes in Turkey and Syria on February 6, 2023
Thanks aid workers and rescue teams helping earthquake victims
Criticizes Syria's government for using the disaster to avoid international pressure

supporters: Supporters say the resolution formally mourns the deaths of tens of thousands of people killed by the February 6, 2023 earthquakes in Turkey and Syria, giving Congress a way to express solidarity with victims.
Supporters say the provision thanking aid and rescue workers on the ground recognizes the people who risked their lives to help earthquake survivors in both countries.

Supporters say condemning the Assad regime for blocking UN aid through border crossings between Turkey and Syria puts international attention on a specific action that kept help from reaching victims.
critics: Critics say the resolution includes no funding or concrete commitments to send aid, so it does not directly help the people affected by the February 6, 2023 earthquakes.

Critics say mixing a mourning resolution with political condemnation of the Assad regime turns a humanitarian statement into a foreign policy tool, which could make it harder to negotiate open border crossings for UN aid.

Critics say a non-binding resolution has no enforcement power, meaning the Assad regime faces no real consequence for blocking UN assistance through the Turkish-Syrian border crossings named in the bill.

118-hres-240.one_liner: Condemn Russia for forcing down a US military drone
provisions: Officially condemns Russia for forcing down a US military drone
States the drone was operating in international airspace when forced down
Declares Russia's attempts to recover the drone threaten US national security

supporters: Supporters say this resolution sends a clear message that Russia violated international law by forcing down a US drone in international airspace.
Supporters say condemning Russia's attempts to recover the drone protects US national security interests.
Supporters say this official condemnation shows America will not tolerate attacks on US military equipment operating legally in international waters.
critics: Critics say this resolution could make tensions with Russia worse without solving the drone problem.
Critics say formal condemnations like this might lead Russia to take more aggressive actions against US military operations.
Critics say this resolution is just words that do not actually stop Russia from threatening US national security.

118-hres-241.one_liner: Set rules for the House to consider a bill about parental rights in schools
provisions: Sets the rules for how the House will debate H.R. 5 about parental rights in public schools
Allows the House to vote on H.R. 5 under specific time limits and procedures

supporters: Supporters say parents have the right to know what curriculum their children are taught in public schools and should be notified about lesson plans.
Supporters say this bill would give parents access to school library books and materials so they can stay involved in their child's education.
Supporters say parents should be told when schools discuss topics about gender identity or sexuality with their children.
critics: Critics say these rules could let parents remove books from school libraries and limit what teachers can teach in classrooms.
Critics say the bill could harm LGBTQ+ students by forcing schools to tell parents private information about their children's conversations with counselors.
Critics say this could create conflicts between parents and teachers over science lessons and social studies topics.

118-hres-298.one_liner: Set House debate rules for Title IX sports and DC police bills
provisions: Allows the House to consider a bill about Title IX sports requirements
Allows the House to consider disapproving DC's police reform law
Sets the debate time and voting procedures for both bills

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows Congress to require schools to use biological sex at birth for Title IX sports teams.
Supporters say the rule lets Congress block DC's police reform law that changes how officers work.
Supporters say the debate rules give both sides time to discuss these issues.
critics: Critics say using biological sex at birth would ban transgender students from sports teams matching their identity.
Critics say blocking DC's police reform ignores what local voters wanted in 2022.
Critics say the debate time limits prevent full discussion of these complex issues.

118-hres-199.one_liner: Set up House votes on federal employee speech restrictions, water regulations, and COVID information release
provisions: Allows the House to vote on a bill that stops federal employees from pushing for censorship while working
Allows the House to vote on canceling EPA water regulations that expand which areas count as federal waters
Allows the House to vote on requiring intelligence agencies to release secret information about how COVID started

supporters: Supporters say H.R. 140 would protect free speech by stopping federal employees from pushing tech companies to remove legal content while on the job.
Supporters say H.J. Res. 27 would stop the EPA from claiming control over more private land through expanded water rules that hurt farmers and property owners.
Supporters say S. 619 would give the public the right to know how COVID started by forcing intelligence agencies to release hidden information about the virus origins.
critics: Critics say H.R. 140 would make it harder for federal agencies to work with social media companies to stop dangerous misinformation about health and elections.
Critics say H.J. Res. 27 would weaken clean water protections by allowing more pollution in streams and wetlands that flow into drinking water sources.
Critics say S. 619 could put national security at risk by forcing the release of secret information that reveals how intelligence agencies gather information and protect sources.

118-hres-260.one_liner: Allow a vote on increasing American oil and gas production
provisions: Sets rules to allow a vote on an energy bill
The energy bill would increase American oil and gas production
The energy bill would speed up permits for oil wells and pipelines
The energy bill would increase exports of American oil and gas
The energy bill would make it easier to mine minerals needed for batteries

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows a vote on a bill that would increase American oil and gas production, reducing energy costs for families.
Supporters say the rule enables consideration of legislation that speeds up permits for oil wells and pipelines, creating thousands of jobs.
Supporters say this allows a vote on a bill that makes it easier to mine minerals needed for batteries, helping America compete with China.
critics: Critics say this rule enables a bill that increases oil and gas production, worsening air pollution in communities near drilling sites.
Critics say the rule allows consideration of legislation that speeds up permits without proper environmental review of oil wells and pipelines.
Critics say this enables a bill that prioritizes oil and gas exports over keeping energy affordable for American families.

118-hres-363.one_liner: Express support for National Police Week and honor officers killed while working
provisions: Expresses support for recognizing National Police Week
Honors law enforcement officers across the United States
States that officers need equipment, training, and resources to stay safe while working
Honors law enforcement officers for acts of sacrifice and heroism
Expresses sympathy to families of officers killed while working

supporters: Supporters say this resolution honors law enforcement officers across the United States who died protecting people.
Supporters say recognizing National Police Week helps families of fallen officers know their sacrifice is remembered.
Supporters say stating that officers need equipment, training, and resources shows Congress knows police work is dangerous.
critics: Critics say this resolution talks about officers needing equipment and training but gives them no actual money for these things.
Critics say this resolution honors law enforcement officers but takes no action to actually improve police safety.

118-hres-311.one_liner: Encourage more countries to sign peace agreements with Israel
provisions: Encourages the US and Israel to work together more closely on economic and security matters
Urges other countries to normalize relations with Israel like the UAE, Bahrain, Morocco, and Sudan have done
Calls for peace agreements to deliver real economic and security benefits to people in those countries

supporters: Supporters say expanding the Abraham Accords beyond UAE, Bahrain, Morocco, and Sudan would bring economic and security benefits to more people in the region.
Supporters say stronger US-Israel cooperation on economic and security matters would help create stable relationships between Israel and Arab nations.
Supporters say the focus on delivering real benefits to citizens would ensure peace agreements help ordinary people.
critics: Critics say the resolution adds more countries without checking if the current four Abraham Accords members are getting promised benefits.
Critics say encouraging more nations to normalize relations with Israel while ignoring Palestinian concerns could hurt peace efforts.
Critics say the emphasis on US-Israel cooperation benefits those two countries more than Arab nations being asked to normalize relations.

118-hres-377.one_liner: Call for Russia to release detained American citizens and residents
provisions: Calls on Russia to release Evan Gershkovich, an American news reporter detained since March 2023
Tells all US government officials to bring up Gershkovich's case when talking with Russia
Calls for Russia to release Paul Whelan
Shows support for all American citizens and residents detained in Russia and other countries
Shows sympathy for the families of detained Americans

supporters: Supporters say this puts pressure on Russia by requiring all US government officials to bring up Gershkovich's case in every meeting with Russian officials.
Supporters say this shows Congress backs four specific Americans detained in Russia: Gershkovich, Whelan, Fogel, and Kara-Murza.
Supporters say this gives comfort to families of detained Americans by showing the US government will not forget them.
critics: Critics say this resolution has no legal power to force Russia to release any of the four detained Americans.
Critics say requiring all US officials to raise these cases in every meeting with Russia could hurt other important diplomatic talks.
Critics say making these detention cases more public could lead Russia to treat Gershkovich, Whelan, and other detained Americans worse.

118-hres-382.one_liner: Recognize Jewish American Heritage Month and call for leaders to fight antisemitism
provisions: Recognizes Jewish American Heritage Month as time to celebrate Jewish Americans
Calls on elected officials to condemn antisemitism
Calls on faith leaders to fight antisemitism
Calls on community leaders to fight antisemitism

supporters: Supporters say recognizing Jewish American Heritage Month celebrates the specific contributions of Jewish Americans to American society and culture.
Supporters say calling on elected officials, faith leaders, and community leaders to condemn antisemitism helps fight rising antisemitic incidents.
critics: Critics say the call on faith leaders to fight antisemitism interferes with religious freedom and separation of church and state.
Critics say the call for elected officials to condemn antisemitism creates government interference in speech issues.

118-hres-327.one_liner: Set debate rules for a debt ceiling bill and a trade duties resolution
provisions: Sets the rules for how the House will debate a bill about raising the debt ceiling
Sets the rules for how the House will debate a resolution to cancel a Commerce Department rule about trade duties

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the House to vote on the debt ceiling increase bill and the resolution about Commerce Department trade duties.
Supporters say this follows standard House procedures for bringing these measures to the floor for debate and voting.
critics: Critics say this rule limits debate time for the debt ceiling increase and prevents members from offering amendments.
Critics say this rule rushes consideration of the Commerce Department trade duties resolution without full discussion.

118-hres-398.one_liner: Allow House votes on three bills related to law enforcement
provisions: Lets the House vote on a bill that makes attacking a police officer a reason to deport non-citizens
Lets the House vote on a bill that allows federal law enforcement officers to buy their retired service weapons
Lets the House vote on a resolution supporting local police and opposing efforts to defund police departments

supporters: Supporters say making assault of law enforcement officers a deportable offense would protect police and remove non-citizens who attack officers from the country.
Supporters say allowing federal law enforcement officers to buy their retired service weapons helps officers keep familiar firearms for personal protection after they leave service.
Supporters say the resolution backing local police and opposing defunding efforts sends a strong message of support to law enforcement agencies across the country.
critics: Critics say the deportation provision for assaulting officers could separate immigrant families and lacks protections for due process rights.
Critics say allowing federal officers to purchase retired weapons could put more firearms into circulation without proper tracking.
Critics say the resolution opposing police defunding efforts blocks needed reforms and ignores community calls for police accountability.

118-hres-383.one_liner: Set rules for House votes on border security and unemployment fraud recovery bills
provisions: Allows the House to debate and vote on a border security bill
Allows the House to debate and vote on a bill about recovering stolen unemployment money
Sets the time limits and rules for discussing both bills

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the House to consider border security legislation in an orderly manner
Supporters say this rule provides floor time for legislation to recover fraudulently obtained unemployment payments
critics: Critics say this rule limits the time available to debate border security measures
Critics say this rule restricts opportunities to offer amendments to the unemployment fraud legislation

118-hres-461.one_liner: Condemn using school buildings to house non-citizens who are not admitted to the US
provisions: Condemns using elementary school buildings to house non-citizens
Condemns using high school buildings to house non-citizens
Applies to schools that currently serve students
Targets non-citizens who are not admitted to the United States
Creates a formal congressional statement of disapproval

supporters: Supporters say elementary and secondary school facilities should be used for students' education, not to house non-citizens who are not admitted to the United States.
Supporters say using school buildings that serve children for shelter takes away resources and space from students.
critics: Critics say this resolution only creates a formal statement of disapproval without solving housing problems for non-citizens.
Critics say condemning the use of elementary and secondary school facilities could prevent communities from providing emergency shelter during humanitarian crises.

118-hres-456.one_liner: Set up rules for Congress to vote on raising the debt ceiling
provisions: Sets up the rules for the House to vote on H.R. 3746 about raising the debt ceiling
Decides how long members can debate the debt ceiling bill
Sets rules for what changes members can make to the bill
Moves the debt ceiling bill toward a final House vote

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the House to have an organized debate on raising the debt ceiling to avoid a government default.
Supporters say the rule gives members time to discuss the debt ceiling increase while moving toward a needed vote.
Supporters say structured rules help the House consider important bills like H.R. 3746 in an orderly way.
critics: Critics say the rule limits how long members can debate such an important issue as raising the debt ceiling.
Critics say the rule restricts what changes members can make to the debt ceiling bill.
Critics say the rule rushes consideration of H.R. 3746 without allowing enough time for full review.

118-hres-429.one_liner: Set House voting rules for bills on fentanyl, truck pollution, and student loans
provisions: Sets voting rules for a bill that would change how fentanyl-like drugs are regulated
Schedules a vote to cancel EPA pollution standards for heavy trucks
