Supporters say the rule lets the House go on record on immigration enforcement and U.S. policy toward Israel and Gaza through H. Res. 1112 and H. Res. 1117.
critics: Critics say the rule packages four unrelated items — a surveillance law change, a maritime border expansion, an immigration statement, and a foreign policy statement — into a single floor procedure, limiting members' ability to vote on each one separately.
Critics say the rule sets tight time limits on debating H.R. 7888, which would change how intelligence agencies spy on people in the U.S., leaving little room for members to offer amendments.
Critics say H. Res. 1112 and H. Res. 1117 are non-binding statements that do not create law, and using floor time for them delays action on legislation that would have direct legal effects.

118-hres-1102.one_liner: Pass a $1.2 trillion bill to fund the federal government through September 2024
provisions: Approves about $1.2 trillion in total spending to keep the federal government running through September 30, 2024
Funds the military, including money for weapons, operations, and troop pay
Funds health programs, including the National Institutes of Health and community health centers
Funds education grants, housing assistance, and other domestic programs
Completes the House's agreement with the Senate version of the bill, sending it to the President to sign

supporters: Supporters say the bill approves about $1.2 trillion to keep the government open through September 30, 2024, which prevents a shutdown that would stop pay for federal workers and pause services for millions of people.
Supporters say the bill funds the National Institutes of Health and community health centers, which provide care to low-income patients who cannot afford private doctors.
Supporters say the bill covers military pay, weapons, and operations, keeping U.S. armed forces funded and ready.
critics: Critics say the bill adds about $1.2 trillion to federal spending in one package, which increases the national deficit without requiring cuts to offset the cost.

Critics say bundling military funding, health programs, education grants, and housing assistance into one bill forces lawmakers to vote yes or no on everything at once, with no way to reject specific programs.
Critics say the process of sending a last-minute amended bill from the House to the Senate left little time for members to read and debate the full spending plan before the vote.

118-hres-1149.one_liner: Set the House debate rules for votes on Iran sanctions and a privacy bill
provisions: Sets the rules for how the full House will debate and vote on six separate bills
Lets the House vote on changing the rules for waiving Iran financial sanctions
Lets the House vote on requiring Congress to approve any decision to lift Iran sanctions
Lets the House vote on canceling certain permissions that loosened Iran sanctions
Lets the House vote on labeling Yemen's Houthi group as a terrorist organization and adding new penalties against them
Lets the House vote on condemning Iran's drone and missile attack on Israel
Lets the House vote on stopping police and government agencies from buying your phone or internet account records from companies

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the House to vote on H.R. 4691, which would require Congress to approve any White House decision to lift Iran sanctions — a check that does not currently exist in law.

Supporters say H.R. 6046, brought to the floor by this rule, would label Ansarallah as a foreign terrorist organization, which supporters say reflects the group's ties to Iran and its ongoing attacks on ships in the Red Sea.
Supporters say H.R. 4639, also included in this rule, would stop police and federal agencies from paying companies for users' phone or internet account records instead of getting a court order.
critics: Critics say bundling six unrelated bills — ranging from Iran sanctions to online privacy rules — into one debate rule limits members' ability to slow down or amend individual bills they oppose.
Critics say fast-tracking bills like H.R. 6323 and H.R. 5947 to cancel Iran sanctions waivers and licenses removes flexibility the executive branch uses to manage diplomacy with Iran.
Critics say the rule brings H.R. 6046's Houthi designation to a vote without debate on how the new sanctions against Ansarallah would be enforced or what agencies would carry them out.

118-hres-1085.one_liner: Schedule House floor votes on six energy-related bills
provisions: This sets the rules for how the House will debate and vote on six energy-related bills.
One bill cancels a $27 billion federal fund that pays for projects to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
One bill stops the federal government from banning fracking, a method used to drill for oil and gas.
One bill blocks a proposed federal rule that would change how companies lease land from the government to drill for oil and gas.
One is a non-binding statement that Congress believes a new tax on carbon emissions would hurt the U.S. economy.
One states that Congress believes the current administration's energy decisions have hurt the country.
One locks current federal permit rules for digging in or filling waterways into law.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the $27 billion greenhouse gas reduction fund stops what they call wasteful federal spending and returns that money to taxpayers.
Supporters say blocking a federal fracking ban protects oil and gas jobs and keeps U.S. energy production from dropping.
Supporters say locking current waterway permit rules into law gives construction and energy companies a stable set of rules to follow instead of changing regulations.
critics: Critics say repealing the $27 billion greenhouse gas reduction fund cuts off money that was already set aside to pay for clean energy projects and reduce pollution.
Critics say stopping any future fracking ban removes the government's ability to limit a drilling method that environmental groups link to water and air pollution.
Critics say blocking the new Bureau of Land Management leasing rule keeps in place rules that critics argue give oil and gas companies too easy access to public lands.

118-hres-288.one_liner: Ask the European Union to label Iran's Revolutionary Guard a terrorist group
provisions: This is a non-binding resolution — it does not change any U.S. laws or spending.
It asks the European Union to officially label Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization.
The EU has existing terrorism rules it could use to make that label official.
It asks the Biden Administration to push for this EU label as a top goal in diplomatic meetings with EU leaders.

supporters: Supporters say the EU already has rules under EU Common Position 931 that allow it to label groups as terrorist organizations, and this resolution calls on the EU to use those existing rules to officially label the IRGC.
Supporters say making the EU designation a diplomatic priority would pressure Iran by cutting the IRGC off from financial and political ties across Europe.
Supporters say because this is a non-binding resolution, it carries no cost and no change to U.S. law, making it a low-risk way to push allies toward a shared goal.
critics: Critics say this resolution is non-binding, meaning the U.S. government and EU are not required to do anything, so it may produce no real result.
Critics say pressing the EU to designate the IRGC as a top diplomatic priority could strain relations with EU leaders who prefer to set their own foreign policy agenda.
Critics say an IRGC designation by the EU could complicate ongoing diplomatic talks with Iran, since the IRGC plays a central role in Iran's government and military.

118-hres-149.one_liner: Condemn Russia for taking children from Ukraine by force
provisions: Says the Russian government is responsible for taking children out of Ukraine without legal right
Says that forcing Ukrainian children into Russian adoptions goes against a 1948 international agreement that bans genocide
Says Russia is trying to erase a generation of Ukrainian children
Says Russia's invasion has put Ukrainian children at greater risk of trafficking, forced labor, violence, hunger, and death

supporters: Supporters say the resolution holds the Russian government responsible for taking Ukrainian children out of their country without legal right, and that naming this responsibility is a step toward getting those children returned.

Supporters say that forcing Ukrainian children into Russian adoptions breaks the 1948 Genocide Convention, and that Congress should go on record saying this practice fits the legal definition of genocide.

Supporters say Russia's invasion has put Ukrainian children at direct risk of trafficking, forced labor, and violence, and that the U.S. must speak clearly against these harms to press for international action.
critics: Critics say the resolution is non-binding, meaning it does not require any government action, set aside funding, or create a legal path to return the children who have already been taken.

Critics say the resolution uses the word genocide under the 1948 convention without a court ruling to back that claim, and that applying that label without a legal finding could weaken the term's meaning in future cases.
Critics say the resolution lists serious harms — trafficking, forced labor, hunger, death — but does not include any plan, deadline, or agency responsible for addressing those harms.

118-hres-883.one_liner: Declare the slogan 'from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free' antisemitic
provisions: The House of Representatives states that the slogan 'from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free' is antisemitic.
The resolution calls for the slogan to be condemned.
This is not a law — it is a formal statement of opinion by the House and does not create any rules or penalties.

supporters: Supporters say the House formally labels the slogan 'from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free' as antisemitic. They say the phrase targets Jewish people by covering the land where Israel currently exists.
Supporters say the resolution calls for the slogan to be condemned. They argue this gives Congress a recorded stance against language they say threatens Jewish communities in the U.S. and abroad.

Supporters say the resolution names Israelis and Palestinians who seek peace as groups harmed by the slogan. They argue that condemning the phrase protects those specific groups from rhetoric they say blocks peace.
critics: Critics say the resolution does not create any rules or penalties. They argue that because it is only a statement of opinion, it has no legal effect on who can use the slogan.

Critics say calling the slogan antisemitic could be used to silence Palestinian advocacy groups. These groups say they use the phrase to call for equal rights for Palestinians living between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea.

Critics say the resolution condemns the slogan without defining what it means. They argue that different speakers use the phrase in different ways, so a blanket label does not account for those differences.

118-hres-987.one_liner: Expresses Congress's opposition to Biden-era energy and land policies
provisions: States that Congress disagrees with how the Biden administration handled energy policy
States that Congress disagrees with how the Biden administration managed federal land
Calls for more domestic energy production inside the United States

supporters: Supporters say the resolution formally states that Congress disagrees with Biden administration decisions that restricted domestic energy production on federal lands.
Supporters say the call for more domestic energy production inside the United States supports industries like oil, gas, and coal that operate on federal land.
Supporters say the resolution signals that Congress wants a different direction on energy policy, including how federal land is managed for resource development.
critics: Critics say the resolution does not change any laws or spending, so it has no binding effect on energy prices or production levels.
Critics say the call for more domestic production on federal lands could increase long-term fossil fuel extraction, which some energy analysts say conflicts with existing U.S. climate commitments.
Critics say the resolution targets Biden administration policies without proposing specific replacement rules, leaving no clear standard for how federal land should be managed going forward.

118-s-2051.one_liner: Keep funding programs that find missing children and fight exploitation through 2028
provisions: Keeps federal money for programs that help find missing children running through September 2028

Gives the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) official legal backing to ask websites to remove child sexual abuse images — NCMEC was already doing this work without it written into law
Lets NCMEC offer counseling advice and community support to children, parents, and families after a child goes missing or is sexually exploited
Requires NCMEC to add new numbers to its yearly public report: how many children went missing from foster care or group homes, how many were found, and how many were likely sex trafficking victims
Requires NCMEC to publicly report each year on how it picks forensic experts and labs to recommend to police
Changes the legal term 'child pornography' to 'child sexual abuse material' throughout the law

supporters: Supporters say giving NCMEC official legal authority to ask websites to remove child sexual abuse images strengthens a program that was already running but had no written backing in the law.

Supporters say requiring NCMEC to report each year on how many children went missing from foster care and group homes — and how many were likely sex trafficking victims — will make it easier for the public and lawmakers to track gaps in the system.

Supporters say letting NCMEC offer counseling advice and community support to families after a child goes missing or is sexually exploited fills a gap in services that currently has no formal legal standing.
critics: Critics say the bill gives NCMEC new authority to ask websites to take down content but does not set clear rules or oversight for how those removal requests are made, which could raise due process concerns.
Critics say the new reporting requirements about children missing from foster care do not come with added funding or staffing to actually improve outcomes for those children.
Critics say reauthorizing funding through September 2028 without specifying new dollar amounts means programs may continue at current levels even if demand for services has grown.

119-hr-1958.one_liner: Block or deport non-citizens who commit or admit to fraud or making fake IDs
provisions: Non-citizens who are convicted of or admit to certain fraud crimes can be blocked from entering the US or removed from it.
The crimes covered include lying to get food stamps (SNAP), Social Security benefits, or any other program funded by federal money.
Making fake ID documents is also covered.
These rules apply whether a person has been found guilty in court or simply admits to doing the act.
People covered by this bill cannot get protection from deportation, even if they say they would face torture in their home country.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects federal programs like SNAP and Social Security by allowing the government to deport or block non-citizens who have been convicted of fraud against those programs.
Supporters say the fake ID provision closes a loophole that lets people use false documents to access federal benefits, and that removing such individuals reduces losses to taxpayer-funded programs.
Supporters say that requiring deportation even when someone only admits to fraud — not just when convicted in court — makes the rule harder to avoid through legal technicalities.
critics: Critics say the bill removes all deportation protections, including protections against torture, for people who may have committed minor fraud like incorrectly reporting income on a SNAP application.
Critics say the rule applies to people who only admit to an act — without a court conviction — which means someone could be deported without being found guilty by a judge or jury.
Critics say the bill could affect legal immigrants, asylum seekers, and green card holders who made errors in federal benefit applications, not just people who intentionally cheated the system.

119-hr-556.one_liner: Stop three federal agencies from banning lead ammo and lead fishing gear on public land
provisions: Three federal agencies cannot ban or limit lead ammo or lead fishing gear on public land or water.
Those agencies are the Fish and Wildlife Service, the Bureau of Land Management, and the Forest Service.
An agency can still limit lead if field data from that specific area shows lead is mainly causing wildlife numbers to drop.
The state where that land is located must also agree before any new lead limit can take effect.
Lead rules already in place before this bill stay in effect.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects hunters and anglers from federal bans on lead ammunition and lead fishing tackle on public lands managed by the Fish and Wildlife Service, the Bureau of Land Management, and the Forest Service.

Supporters say agencies can still limit lead if field data from that specific area shows lead is the main cause of wildlife population decline, and the state agrees — so the bill keeps local control in place.
Supporters say existing lead rules stay in effect, meaning the bill does not remove any current protections that are already working.
critics: Critics say blocking the Fish and Wildlife Service, the Bureau of Land Management, and the Forest Service from setting lead limits means wildlife like eagles and condors — which die from eating animals shot with lead bullets — lose federal protection across most public lands.

Critics say the requirement that a state must approve any new lead limit before it can take effect could stop federal agencies from acting quickly when field data shows lead is harming wildlife at a specific site.
Critics say the bill removes a tool federal land managers use to respond to lead poisoning risks, since three major agencies can no longer limit lead ammunition or tackle except in narrow cases.

119-hr-4294.one_liner: Create a program to buy invasive catfish from Chesapeake Bay area fishermen
provisions: NOAA sets up a program to buy blue catfish caught in the Chesapeake Bay and the rivers that flow into it
The program connects fishermen with companies that make pet food, animal feed, or fish farm feed — those companies buy the catfish
NOAA sets a minimum price per pound for the catfish, looking at market prices and input from fishermen
Fishermen can get different prices depending on whether they sell whole fillets or leftover parts
Before the program starts, NOAA works with outside partners to count how many blue catfish are in the watershed and makes that number public

supporters: Supporters say the program would give watermen a guaranteed minimum price per pound for blue catfish, with separate price points for fillets versus byproducts, creating a more predictable income from catching an invasive species.

Supporters say connecting watermen and seafood processors to pet food, animal feed, and aquaculture feed manufacturers creates a new market that gives fishermen a financial reason to catch more blue catfish, which are invasive in the Chesapeake Bay Watershed.
Supporters say requiring NOAA to publish a count of blue catfish in the watershed before the program starts gives the public a baseline number to measure whether catfish removal is actually working.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a specific dollar amount or cap for the pilot program, making it unclear how many watermen or seafood processors would be able to participate or receive payments.
Critics say the requirement for NOAA to first complete an abundance estimate with nonfederal partners adds a step before the program can begin, which could delay any income support reaching watermen.

Critics say limiting buyers to pet food, animal feed, and aquaculture feed manufacturers — rather than also including restaurants or grocery retailers — may not generate enough demand to make a measurable reduction in blue catfish numbers across the full Chesapeake Bay Watershed.

118-s-382.one_liner: Transfer about 17 acres in Washington state into trust for the Puyallup Tribe
provisions: About 17 acres of land in Pierce County, Washington will become part of the Puyallup Tribe's reservation.
The federal government holds this land in trust — the tribe controls and benefits from it.
The federal government is not responsible for any pollution or contamination that happened on the land before the transfer.
No casino or gambling is allowed on this land.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would add about 17 acres in Pierce County to the Puyallup Tribe's reservation, giving the tribe legal control over land within the boundaries of the tribe's original reservation.
Supporters say the no-gaming clause means the 17 acres cannot be used for a casino or gambling, so the land can be used for tribal housing, cultural centers, or other community purposes.
Supporters say federal trust status means the tribe does not pay state or local property taxes on the 17 acres, freeing up tribal funds for services like health care and education.
critics: Critics say moving the 17 acres into federal trust removes the land from Pierce County's property tax rolls, reducing local government revenue.
Critics say the bill's provision that the federal government is not liable for pollution that happened before the transfer could leave the tribe or nearby residents responsible for cleanup costs.
Critics say placing land into federal trust limits Pierce County's authority to apply local zoning and land-use rules to the 17 acres.

119-hres-1115.one_liner: Set floor debate rules for three bills on lead ammunition and immigration
provisions: Stops the federal government from banning lead bullets or lead fishing weights on federal lands and waters
Makes non-citizens who were convicted of cheating the US government or illegally taking public benefits unable to enter or stay in the US
Makes non-citizens who were convicted of hurting police dogs or horses unable to enter or stay in the US
Sets the rules for how these three bills will be debated and voted on in the House

supporters: Supporters say that stopping the federal government from banning lead bullets and fishing weights on federal lands protects the rights of hunters and anglers who rely on these tools on public land.

Supporters say that making non-citizens who cheated the U.S. government or illegally received public benefits deportable closes a gap in current immigration law that lets people who broke federal law stay in the country.
Supporters say that making non-citizens convicted of harming police dogs or horses deportable protects law enforcement animals that are used to keep officers and the public safe.
critics: Critics say that lead from bullets and fishing weights can poison wildlife and contaminate water on federal lands, and blocking any future ban on lead tackle or ammunition removes a tool the government could use to protect ecosystems.

Critics say that the provision making non-citizens deportable for harming law enforcement animals could be applied broadly, since the bill does not define what level of harm or what type of conviction triggers deportation.
Critics say that bundling three separate immigration and public lands bills into one procedural resolution limits debate time on each issue and reduces the ability of members to offer amendments.

119-s-3971.one_liner: Extend and update two federal programs that give research money to small businesses
provisions: Keeps the Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) and Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) programs running through 2031.
Federal agencies must check whether small businesses that apply for these awards pose security risks.
If an agency turns down a small business for security reasons, it must tell the business why.
Each agency must set a cap on how many applications one small business can submit each year.
Staff at agencies who handle these awards must get more training on how to bring new technology to market.

Creates a new pool of extra awards for small businesses working on technology in areas the government considers important — but only if the business already has working technology and can get matching money from another source.

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps the Small Business Innovation Research and Technology Transfer programs running through 2031, giving small businesses six more years of access to federal research funding they rely on.
Supporters say a new rule requires agencies to explain in writing why a small business was turned down for security reasons, so businesses know what happened and can respond.

Supporters say a separate pot of extra second-round awards — only for businesses that already have working technology and can bring in matching money from outside — directs more funding toward ideas closest to reaching the market.
critics: Critics say the new yearly cap on how many proposals one small business can submit may hurt firms that depend on applying to several programs at once to keep their research funded.
Critics say adding a security check to every application could make the review process take longer, slowing down the time it takes small businesses to get an answer.

Critics say the rule requiring businesses to find matching money from outside sources before they can receive extra awards will favor small businesses with outside investors or partners over newer firms that have not built those connections yet.

117-hconres-11.one_liner: Set the U.S. government's total spending plan for 2021 through 2030
provisions: Sets how much the federal government can spend and take in for the year starting October 2020.
Sets spending limits for each major area of government — like defense, healthcare, and housing — through 2030.
Tells 12 House committees to write laws that would add to the national deficit, each with a set dollar cap.
Those 12 committees must send their proposed laws to the House Budget Committee by February 16, 2021.
Bills written under these budget rules can skip the normal Senate filibuster vote.
Lets the House Budget Committee adjust spending limits for laws that don't add to the deficit.

supporters: Supporters say using the budget reconciliation process lets Congress pass spending changes with a simple majority, avoiding a Senate filibuster that could block laws approved by 12 House committees.
Supporters say setting spending limits for healthcare, housing, and defense through 2030 gives the government a long-term plan instead of making budget decisions year by year.
Supporters say allowing the House Budget Committee to adjust spending limits for laws that do not add to the deficit makes it easier to pass bills that pay for themselves.
critics: Critics say telling 12 House committees to write laws that increase the deficit — each with its own dollar cap — adds to the national debt without requiring those costs to be offset.
Critics say skipping the normal Senate filibuster vote removes a check that forces both parties to agree before major spending changes become law.
Critics say setting spending levels for areas like defense and healthcare all the way through 2030 locks in budget decisions that future Congresses may not be able to easily change.

117-hr-1002.one_liner: Let the DEA block companies from getting licenses to handle controlled substances
provisions: The DEA can block a company or person from getting a license to make, sell, or give out controlled substances.
The DEA can use this block on any company whose license has already been suspended or taken away.
The DEA can also block any company it finds unfit to handle controlled substances.
The block can be temporary or permanent, depending on the situation.

supporters: Supporters say the DEA needs this power because right now it can only suspend or revoke a license after a company already has one, and this bill lets the DEA block bad actors before they get registered in the first place.

Supporters say companies that have already had their licenses suspended or revoked for mishandling controlled substances could be permanently barred from re-entering the market under this bill, closing a loophole they currently use to reapply.

Supporters say giving the DEA authority to block any entity it finds unfit to handle controlled substances adds a layer of protection against opioid diversion that existing revocation rules do not cover.
critics: Critics say the bill gives the DEA broad power to permanently bar a company or person from the controlled substances market without clearly defining what 'unfit' means, which could lead to inconsistent or unfair decisions.
Critics say small distributors or pharmacies that had a past license issue could face a permanent block under this bill with no clear process described for appeal or review.
Critics say the temporary or permanent bar can be applied to any entity that merely 'meets conditions' for suspension, which critics argue is a lower standard than an actual finding of wrongdoing.

117-hr-1029.one_liner: Drop the fee to hold veterans events at war memorials near Washington DC
provisions: Groups that hold veterans events at war memorials in and around Washington DC no longer have to pay a fee to apply for a permit.
The fee waiver only applies when the event is entirely a veterans event — not just any event that veterans happen to attend.
The memorials covered are on land run by the National Park Service.

supporters: Supporters say veterans groups should not have to pay a fee just to hold events at war memorials on National Park Service land in Washington DC, since these memorials were built to honor their service.
Supporters say the waiver only applies to events that are entirely veterans events, which keeps the benefit focused on the groups it is meant to help.
critics: Critics say waiving permit fees for veterans events on National Park Service land could reduce money the agency collects to manage and maintain those memorial sites.
Critics say the bill does not define what counts as a 'veterans special event,' which could make it hard for park staff to decide which groups qualify for the fee waiver.

117-hr-1065.one_liner: Require employers to make job changes for pregnant workers
provisions: Employers must give pregnant workers changes to their job or schedule if asked.
Employers cannot force a pregnant worker to take time off if another solution is available.
Employers cannot deny a job to someone because they need pregnancy-related changes at work.
Employers cannot punish workers for asking for or using pregnancy-related changes.
A federal agency called the EEOC must publish examples of changes employers should offer.
States can be sued in court for breaking this law.

supporters: Supporters say the law protects pregnant workers from being forced onto unpaid leave when other options — like a schedule change or lighter duties — are available, helping them keep their income during pregnancy.
Supporters say the rule that employers cannot deny a job to someone because they might need pregnancy-related changes will open doors for women who were passed over for work before this law existed.
Supporters say requiring the EEOC to publish a list of example accommodations gives both workers and employers clear guidance, making it easier to follow the law without going to court.
critics: Critics say the 'undue hardship' standard is vague, and small businesses with few employees may struggle to know when they are legally required to provide accommodations versus when they can refuse.
Critics say allowing workers to sue state governments by removing Eleventh Amendment protections could expose state agencies to costly lawsuits, shifting public money away from other services.

Critics say the interactive process requirement — where employers and workers must negotiate accommodations — adds a new legal obligation that could increase compliance costs for businesses that do not currently have HR staff to manage these processes.

117-hr-1085.one_liner: Award gold medals honoring law enforcement that protected the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021
provisions: Gives three gold medals to groups that protected the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021
One medal goes to the U.S. Capitol Police
One medal goes to the Washington D.C. Metropolitan Police Department
One medal goes to the Smithsonian Institution to put on display, along with a plaque listing every law enforcement group that helped that day

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives one medal each to the U.S. Capitol Police and the Metropolitan Police Department of D.C., formally naming both agencies for their role in protecting the Capitol on January 6, 2021.

Supporters say the third medal will be displayed at the Smithsonian Institution alongside a plaque listing every law enforcement agency that responded that day, creating a lasting public record of which groups were present.
critics: Critics say the bill awards medals to the U.S. Capitol Police and the Metropolitan Police Department as organizations, not to any named individual officers, so no specific person receives the honor.

Critics say the Congressional Gold Medal has historically recognized sustained careers or lifetime achievement, and this bill applies it to a single day of duty without explaining how that meets the usual standard.

117-hr-1.one_liner: Change how Americans vote, how campaigns raise money, and what federal officials must disclose
provisions: States must register voters automatically when people apply for a driver's license or state ID, and must let people register on the same day they vote.
Any voter can ask to vote by mail, and states must offer at least 15 days of early voting before Election Day.
States cannot remove voters from the rolls only because they skipped a recent election.
States must use a panel of regular citizens — not state lawmakers — to draw the maps for U.S. House districts.
Any group that spends money on political ads must publicly name who gave them the money to pay for those ads.
Supreme Court Justices must follow a written code of conduct, and members of Congress cannot sit on the board of a for-profit company.
The President, Vice President, and people running for those offices must release their last 10 years of tax returns to the public.

supporters: Supporters say automatic voter registration for people who apply for a driver's license or state ID, plus same-day registration, would make it easier for eligible citizens to vote without extra paperwork.
Supporters say requiring at least 15 days of early voting and allowing any voter to request a mail ballot gives people more ways to cast a vote that fits their schedule.
Supporters say making political groups publicly name who funded their ads would let voters know who is paying to influence elections before they go to the polls.
critics: Critics say requiring states to set up independent citizen redistricting commissions takes map-drawing power away from state lawmakers who were elected to make those decisions.
Critics say the rule barring members of Congress from serving on company boards would force people currently serving as board members to give up those roles, limiting who can run for office.
Critics say requiring the President, Vice President, and candidates for those offices to release 10 years of tax returns sets a disclosure standard not required of other federal officeholders.

117-hr-1195.one_liner: Require employers in health care and social services to protect workers from violence
provisions: The Department of Labor must create a safety rule for employers in health care, social services, and similar fields.
The rule requires those employers to have plans to keep workers safe from violence.
The government must first release a temporary rule, then finalize a permanent one by a set deadline.

supporters: Supporters say health care and social service workers face higher rates of on-the-job violence than most other workers, and this bill would require their employers to create written plans to protect them from that violence.

Supporters say requiring the Department of Labor to release a temporary rule first means workers in hospitals, clinics, and social service agencies would get legal protections faster, without waiting years for a final rule.
Supporters say the bill covers not just hospitals but also social service workers and workers in similar fields, closing a gap where many high-risk jobs had no required safety plans.
critics: Critics say the bill gives the Department of Labor broad power to set rules for employers in health care, social services, and any field with "similar" activities, which could pull in many businesses without clear limits on who must comply.

Critics say requiring employers to develop, implement, and maintain workplace violence prevention plans creates new paperwork and compliance costs that could be especially hard for small clinics or nonprofits to afford.

Critics say the two-step process — a temporary rule followed by a permanent one — means employers may have to change their safety plans twice, creating ongoing uncertainty about what the final requirements will look like.

117-hr-1154.one_liner: Study whether the Great Dismal Swamp area should become a national heritage area
provisions: The Department of the Interior would study cities and counties in Virginia and North Carolina to see if they qualify as a National Heritage Area.
The study would look at whether the area has natural, historic, and cultural features that stand out in American history and culture.
The study would also decide if the area is worth protecting, recognizing, and making available for public use.
This bill only starts the study process — it does not create the heritage area or set aside any money yet.

supporters: Supporters say the study would examine whether cities and counties in Virginia and North Carolina hold natural, historic, and cultural features connected to the Great Dismal Swamp — including its role as a refuge for enslaved people — that deserve national recognition.
Supporters say because this bill only starts a study and does not create a heritage area or spend any money, it lets Congress gather facts before making a bigger decision.

Supporters say the study would look at whether the area is worth protecting and making available for public use, which could bring visitors and attention to local communities in Virginia and North Carolina.
critics: Critics say that even a study requires staff time and resources from the Department of the Interior, and the bill does not cap how much federal time or money can go toward it.

Critics say starting a study often leads to a full National Heritage Area designation later, which some local landowners and county governments worry could bring new federal rules about how they use their land.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for the study to be finished, so cities and counties in the study area could face uncertainty about their status for years.

117-hr-1187.one_liner: Require public companies to report environmental, social, and governance data to shareholders
provisions: Companies that sell stock to the public must report data every year about their environmental impact and how they treat workers and communities.
Those reports must also explain how the company is run at the top and how those choices connect to its long-term plans.
A new group called the Sustainable Finance Advisory Committee is created.
That committee must give the SEC — the federal agency that oversees stock markets — ideas for how to direct more investment money toward environmentally friendly businesses.

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires companies that sell stock to the public to report data every year on their environmental impact, how they treat workers, and how top leaders make decisions — giving investors facts they currently cannot access in a standard format.

Supporters say the new Sustainable Finance Advisory Committee must give the SEC (the agency that oversees stock markets) concrete policy ideas for directing investment money toward environmentally friendly businesses, creating a formal process that did not exist before.

Supporters say requiring companies to explain how their environmental and governance choices connect to their long-term plans helps investors see risks that are not always visible in standard financial reports.
critics: Critics say the bill forces every public company — regardless of size or industry — to produce annual environmental, social, and governance reports, adding compliance costs that fall hardest on smaller companies with fewer resources.

Critics say creating the Sustainable Finance Advisory Committee and tasking the SEC (the agency that oversees stock markets) with steering capital toward certain types of investments goes beyond the SEC's core mission of protecting investors and keeping markets fair.

Critics say the bill does not define clear standards for what counts as an 'environmentally sustainable investment,' which could lead to inconsistent reporting across companies and make the data hard to compare.

117-hr-1155.one_liner: Block imports from a Chinese region and sanction those using forced labor there
provisions: Stops products made in China's Xinjiang region from entering the U.S. unless the government confirms they were not made with forced labor
Requires the President to publish a list of foreign companies and people who use forced labor in Xinjiang
Freezes the U.S. bank accounts and assets of anyone on that list, and blocks listed individuals from entering the U.S.
Requires companies that trade on U.S. stock markets to report if they worked with groups building prisons or surveillance systems in Xinjiang
Requires the State Department to report to Congress on whether the treatment of Muslim groups in Xinjiang counts as genocide under U.S. law

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects an estimated 1.8 million Uyghurs, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, and other Muslim minorities in Xinjiang by blocking goods made with their forced labor from entering U.S. markets.

Supporters say requiring companies listed on U.S. stock markets to disclose ties to prison-building or surveillance projects in Xinjiang holds American investors accountable for funding human rights abuses.
Supporters say freezing the U.S. bank accounts and banning the entry of foreign individuals and companies on the forced labor list gives the U.S. government a direct way to punish those responsible.
critics: Critics say the import ban on all Xinjiang goods — a region that produces about 85% of China's cotton — could disrupt supply chains for U.S. clothing and manufacturing companies that rely on those materials.

Critics say placing the burden of proof on importers to show goods were not made with forced labor, rather than on the government to prove they were, makes it harder for businesses to legally import goods even when no forced labor was used.

Critics say requiring the State Department to formally determine whether treatment of Muslim groups in Xinjiang meets the legal definition of genocide could damage U.S.-China diplomatic relations and limit cooperation on other issues.

117-hr-1192.one_liner: Require professionals in Puerto Rico debt cases to disclose all their connections
provisions: Lawyers, financial advisors, and other paid professionals working on Puerto Rico's debt cases must list all their connections — professional, personal, and financial — with any party in the case.
These disclosures must be filed as sworn written statements before the professional can be paid for their work.
The rule covers any professional seeking payment for services in cases about reducing Puerto Rico's debt.

supporters: Supporters say requiring lawyers and financial advisors to file sworn statements listing all their connections before getting paid will help catch conflicts of interest in Puerto Rico's debt cases.
Supporters say the rule covers any professional seeking payment in Puerto Rico debt cases, making sure no one profits while hiding ties to creditors or debtors.
Supporters say sworn written disclosures create a paper trail that lets courts and the public see who has financial or personal links to parties in the case.
critics: Critics say the requirement to list all professional, personal, and financial connections may be hard to define clearly, leading to disputes over what must be disclosed.
Critics say adding sworn statement requirements before professionals can be paid may slow down debt adjustment cases in Puerto Rico, delaying relief for residents.
Critics say the rule applies broadly to all professionals seeking payment, which could create extra paperwork burdens for smaller firms working on Puerto Rico's debt cases.

117-hr-1204.one_liner: Let Washington DC set the pay for its own Chief Financial Officer
provisions: Right now, the DC Chief Financial Officer's pay is set by federal rules.
This bill lets DC set that salary on its own, as long as it pays at least what the officer currently earns.
Once a salary is set under this bill, it cannot be cut while that officer is still in the job.

supporters: Supporters say this bill gives DC the power to set its own CFO salary instead of relying on federal pay rules, which is a step toward the city controlling its own finances.
Supporters say the salary floor provision means the current CFO will not take a pay cut, which helps DC keep experienced financial leadership in place.
Supporters say letting DC set this salary locally means the city can compete with other major governments for qualified candidates without waiting for Congress to act.
critics: Critics say the rule that a salary cannot be cut once set could make it harder for DC to reduce costs if the city faces a budget shortfall.
Critics say giving DC full control over this salary removes a federal check on how the city pays its top financial officer, which could lead to pay that is hard to justify to residents.
Critics say the bill does not set a cap on how high the salary can go, so there is no limit on what DC could pay the CFO using public funds.

117-hr-1215.one_liner: Create a government group and FTC office to protect older adults from scams
provisions: Creates a group called the Senior Scams Prevention Advisory Group to build training materials for employees at stores, banks, and wire-transfer companies so they can spot and stop scams targeting older adults.
The FTC sets up a new office inside its consumer protection division to watch for scams aimed at older adults, take complaints, and teach people how to avoid them.
Training materials from the advisory group cover mail, phone, and internet scams.

supporters: Supporters say the Senior Scams Prevention Advisory Group would give employees at stores, banks, and wire-transfer companies real training materials to spot and stop scams before older adults lose money.
Supporters say the new FTC office inside the Bureau of Consumer Protection would give older adults one place to report scams by mail, phone, or internet and get help fast.
Supporters say training employees who handle cash and wire transfers is one of the last chances to stop a scam, since many older adults do not know they are being tricked until money is already sent.
critics: Critics say the bill does not require stores, banks, or wire-transfer companies to use the advisory group's training materials, so employees may never see them.
Critics say the new FTC office does not give the agency any new power to punish scammers, so watching for fraud and taking complaints may not lead to fewer scams.
Critics say the bill sets no deadline for the advisory group to finish its training materials, which could delay help for older adults for years.

117-hr-1228.one_liner: Place sanctions on people blocking peace in Libya and send aid to Libyans
provisions: Blocks the money and travel of foreign people who help Russia operate militarily in Libya
Blocks the money and travel of foreign people who steal Libyan government money or natural resources
Blocks the money and travel of foreign people responsible for serious human rights abuses in Libya
These blocks on money and travel end on December 31, 2026
Calls on the U.S. foreign aid agency to send food, shelter, health care, and COVID help to people in Libya
Requires the State Department to help Libya build working government institutions and hold free elections
Requires the U.S. Treasury to push international banks to support Libya's economic recovery

supporters: Supporters say blocking the money and travel of foreign people who help Russia operate militarily in Libya will pressure outside forces to stop fueling the conflict there.
Supporters say requiring the State Department to help Libya build working government institutions and hold free elections gives Libyans a path to a stable, self-governed country.
Supporters say calling on the U.S. foreign aid agency to send food, shelter, and health care to people in Libya addresses urgent needs for civilians caught in the conflict.
critics: Critics say the sanctions on people who threaten Libya's peace or stability are broad and do not clearly define what counts as a 'significant action,' which could lead to uneven enforcement.
Critics say the sanctions expire on December 31, 2026, giving foreign actors who steal Libyan state assets or natural resources a fixed end date after which consequences are removed.

Critics say requiring the U.S. Treasury to push international banks to support Libya's economic recovery does not come with specific funding commitments or benchmarks, making the outcome hard to measure.

117-hr-1280.one_liner: Create a national police misconduct database and restrict when officers can use force
provisions: Makes it easier to charge a police officer with a crime for misconduct — prosecutors no longer have to prove the officer meant to break the law, only that they knew or should have known their actions were wrong
Reduces the legal protection that currently blocks people from suing police officers personally when officers violate their rights
Bans police from using chokeholds or entering a home without knocking and announcing themselves in most situations
Creates a national database that stores misconduct complaints and discipline records for individual police officers across the country
Requires police departments to report data on use of force, stops, and searches to the federal government
Requires all police officers to complete training on racial profiling, personal bias, and when to step in if another officer uses too much force

supporters: Supporters say lowering the legal standard from 'willful' to 'knowing or reckless' makes it possible to charge officers who violate people's rights even when prosecutors cannot prove the officer intended harm.

Supporters say limiting qualified immunity gives victims a real path to sue police officers personally in civil court when their constitutional rights are violated, which is currently blocked in most cases.

Supporters say the National Police Misconduct Registry would let departments see an officer's full complaint and discipline history before hiring them, closing a gap that allows problem officers to move from department to department.
critics: Critics say reducing qualified immunity protections could expose individual officers to personal lawsuits for split-second decisions made in dangerous situations, making it harder to recruit and keep police officers.
Critics say banning chokeholds and no-knock warrants in most situations removes tools officers sometimes need to protect themselves and others during unpredictable encounters.
Critics say the lower criminal intent standard means an officer could face federal charges for a mistake made in the field, even without any intent to break the law.

117-hr-1333.one_liner: Limit the President's power to ban groups of people from entering the U.S.
provisions: The President can only block people from entering the U.S. if the Department of State finds a specific, real threat — not just a general concern.
That threat must be to U.S. interests, like national security or public safety.
Any block on entry must be as narrow as possible and only go as far as needed to address the threat.
Before blocking entry, the government must consult with Congress and send a report within 48 hours — if no report is sent, the block ends immediately.
The government cannot deny a visa based on a person's religion unless a separate law specifically allows it.
People in the U.S. who are hurt by an unlawful entry block can take the government to federal court.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) can block travelers on airlines that fail to check for fake travel documents.

supporters: Supporters say the bill stops the President from blocking people from entering the U.S. based on a general concern — it requires the Department of State to find a specific, real threat to national security or public safety first.

Supporters say the bill closes a gap that let the government deny visas based on a person's religion, since it now bans religious discrimination in visa decisions unless a separate law specifically allows it.
Supporters say the 48-hour congressional reporting rule creates real oversight — if the government does not send a report to Congress within 48 hours of blocking entry, that block ends automatically.
critics: Critics say requiring the government to prove a 'specific and credible' threat before acting could slow the response to a fast-moving security risk, giving the President less flexibility to act quickly.
Critics say the 'least restrictive means' rule could force the government to use weaker measures even when a broader entry block is needed to fully address a security threat.

Critics say letting people inside the U.S. sue in federal court over entry restrictions could pull national security decisions into long legal battles that delay or block the government from protecting the country.

117-hr-1374.one_liner: Give states federal money and help to build energy emergency plans
provisions: The federal government can give money to states to create or update plans for keeping their energy systems running during a crisis.
Each state plan must look at the risks to its energy systems, including physical attacks and hacking.
State plans must include steps to lower those risks and keep power and fuel running if something goes wrong.
States can ask the Department of Energy for advice and technical help when building or updating their plan.

supporters: Supporters say the bill helps states build plans that cover both physical attacks and hacking threats to power and fuel systems, which the federal government currently does not require.

Supporters say states can ask the Department of Energy for technical help when writing or updating their energy security plans, giving smaller states access to expert guidance they may not have on their own.
Supporters say requiring each state plan to include steps to keep power and fuel running during a crisis could reduce damage from future outages like the 2021 Texas winter storm.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a funding amount, so states have no guarantee they will receive enough money to actually build or update their energy security plans.
Critics say the bill lets states ask for help but does not require the Department of Energy to provide it, meaning federal assistance is optional and may not reach the states that need it most.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for states to complete their plans, so there is no guarantee any state will act on the new requirements.

117-hr-1443.one_liner: Require banks to report credit data for LGBTQ-owned businesses to federal regulators
provisions: Banks must collect and send data about credit applications from businesses owned by LGBTQ people to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
This data is used to check whether LGBTQ-owned businesses are being treated fairly when they apply for loans.
Right now, banks already report this same data for businesses owned by women, minorities, and small business owners.
This bill adds LGBTQ-owned businesses to that list.

supporters: Supporters say that adding LGBTQ-owned businesses to the credit reporting list — alongside women-owned, minority-owned, and small businesses — would let the CFPB check whether banks are denying loans to LGBTQ business owners at higher rates.
Supporters say that because banks already collect this type of data for other groups, the cost and process of adding LGBTQ-owned businesses to the reporting requirement would be small.
Supporters say the CFPB could use this data to enforce fair lending laws if the numbers show LGBTQ-owned businesses are being turned down or charged more for credit.
critics: Critics say requiring banks to collect and report whether a business owner is LGBTQ raises privacy concerns, since owners would need to self-identify to their lender in order to be counted.
Critics say the bill does not define how a business qualifies as 'LGBTQ-owned,' which could make it hard for banks to collect consistent data and lead to compliance problems.
Critics say adding a new reporting category to the CFPB's small business lending data system could increase costs and paperwork for financial institutions, especially smaller community banks.

117-hr-1446.one_liner: Extend the wait time before gun dealers can sell without a finished background check
provisions: Gun dealers must now wait 10 business days — up from 3 — before selling a gun if the background check is not done yet.
If the background check is still not done after 10 days, the buyer can file a request asking for a final decision.
If another 10 days pass with no final decision, the gun dealer can go ahead and complete the sale.

supporters: Supporters say extending the background check wait time from 3 to 10 business days gives the FBI more time to complete checks, which could stop gun sales to people who are legally blocked from buying firearms.

Supporters say the current 3-day limit has allowed guns to be sold before checks are finished — including the 2015 Charleston church shooting, where the gunman got a gun through a default proceed sale.
critics: Critics say the new 10-business-day wait — plus a possible additional 10 days after filing a petition — could leave law-abiding gun buyers waiting up to 20 business days before receiving a firearm they have a legal right to own.

Critics say the bill does not fix the reason background checks are slow in the first place, and that delays in the federal system should not be used to block or postpone transfers for buyers who have done nothing wrong.

117-hr-1339.one_liner: Create a federal group to plan for flying taxis and cargo drones
provisions: The Department of Transportation must set up a group of federal agencies to work together on new kinds of aircraft, including flying taxis and cargo drones.
The group will look at safety rules, ground infrastructure, cybersecurity, and how much money the government should put into this type of air travel.
The goal is to bring these new aircraft into the same airspace already used by regular planes.
The working group will cover flights in cities, suburbs, rural areas, and between regions.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would require the Department of Transportation to bring multiple federal agencies into one working group, so safety rules, cybersecurity standards, and infrastructure plans for flying taxis and cargo drones are built together instead of separately by each agency.

Supporters say the working group would cover flights in cities, rural areas, and between regions, which means the federal government would plan for the full range of places these new aircraft could operate before they enter shared airspace.

Supporters say having one group look at both ground infrastructure and federal investment needs would give aircraft companies clearer signals about what the government expects before they spend money building new systems.
critics: Critics say the bill sets up a coordination group but does not require any specific funding amounts, safety rules, or deadlines, so there is no guarantee the working group will produce binding results.

Critics say adding a new interagency body on top of existing agencies like the FAA could create overlapping responsibilities and slow down the process of writing the actual rules that flying taxi and cargo drone companies need to operate.

Critics say the bill does not define how many agencies must join the group, what voting or decision-making rules it follows, or what happens when agencies disagree, leaving the structure of the group unclear.

117-hr-1392.one_liner: Block U.S. weapons sales to Saudi Arabia and require reports on Jamal Khashoggi's death
provisions: For 120 days after this bill becomes law, the U.S. cannot sell or ship weapons to Saudi Arabia.
After 120 days, the weapons ban stays unless the President tells Congress Saudi Arabia met three conditions.

Those three conditions are: Saudi Arabia has not silenced or killed people in other countries, has not unjustly jailed U.S. citizens or legal U.S. residents inside Saudi Arabia, and has not tortured people in its custody.
The President must tell Congress that Saudi officials in the U.S. are not using their diplomatic status to track or harass Saudi citizens here.
If the President cannot make that statement, the U.S. must close at least one Saudi embassy or consular office in the country.
Congress gets a report on whether any Saudi officials harassed people inside the United States.
Congress gets a report on whether U.S. intelligence agencies warned journalist Jamal Khashoggi about threats to his life before he was killed in 2018.

supporters: Supporters say the 120-day weapons ban gives Saudi Arabia a clear deadline to change its behavior, and the ongoing certification requirement means the U.S. can stop arms sales any time Saudi Arabia kills or silences people in other countries.

Supporters say requiring the President to close a Saudi embassy if officials are found tracking Saudi citizens in the U.S. gives the government a real tool to protect people living here from foreign harassment.
Supporters say the required report on whether U.S. intelligence warned Jamal Khashoggi about threats to his life before his 2018 killing will hold American agencies accountable for what they knew.
critics: Critics say a 120-day blanket ban on all defense sales to Saudi Arabia could hurt U.S. defense contractors and their workers who depend on those contracts, without a guarantee it changes Saudi behavior.

Critics say the certification conditions — covering actions inside Saudi Arabia, in other countries, and inside the U.S. — set a standard that may be difficult to verify, making the ongoing arms restriction hard to lift even if Saudi Arabia cooperates.
Critics say closing a Saudi diplomatic facility as punishment could damage U.S.-Saudi relations on issues beyond human rights, including regional security cooperation and oil supply agreements.

117-hr-1460.one_liner: Fund carbon monoxide alarm installation in homes of low-income families and older adults
provisions: The government gives money to states and Native American tribal groups to buy and install carbon monoxide alarms.
The alarms go in homes where low-income families or people 65 and older live.
The alarms also go in buildings that regularly serve children or older adults, like day care centers or senior centers.
All alarms installed through this program must meet safety standards set by the government.

supporters: Supporters say the grants will put carbon monoxide alarms in homes of low-income families and adults 65 and older, who may not be able to afford detectors on their own.
Supporters say placing alarms in day care centers and senior centers will protect children and older adults who spend time in these buildings each day.
Supporters say requiring all installed alarms to meet government safety standards means the devices will actually work when carbon monoxide is present.
critics: Critics say the bill creates a new federal grant program that adds to government spending without setting a clear dollar limit on how much states can receive.
Critics say the program focuses only on low-income households and select facilities, leaving out middle-income families who also cannot always afford carbon monoxide detectors.
Critics say the bill gives the Consumer Product Safety Commission new responsibilities without specifying how much staff or funding the agency needs to run the grant program.

117-hr-147.one_liner: Give veterans more information and money options for apprenticeship programs
provisions: When service members leave the military, the Department of Labor must tell them about apprenticeship job training programs.
Veterans using the Post-9/11 GI Bill get a monthly housing payment — this bill lets them use that money for other costs too.
The Department of Veterans Affairs must build a website where veterans can search for apprenticeship programs approved for GI Bill benefits.

supporters: Supporters say that requiring the Department of Labor to share apprenticeship information during the Transition Assistance Program means every service member separating from active duty receives this information at the exact moment they are planning their next steps.

Supporters say that letting veterans use their Post-9/11 GI Bill monthly housing payment for costs beyond housing gives them more flexibility to cover expenses that come up during job training programs.

Supporters say the new VA-run website would let veterans search in one place for apprenticeship programs already approved under GI Bill education benefits, instead of searching across multiple government sources.
critics: Critics say that expanding the Post-9/11 GI Bill housing stipend to cover 'other purposes' removes limits that were designed to make sure those funds go toward housing costs while veterans are in training.

Critics say the bill requires the VA and the Department of Labor to build and maintain a new public-facing website but does not identify a funding source or set a deadline for when it must be completed.

Critics say the Transition Assistance Program already covers a wide range of topics for separating service members, and adding new apprenticeship information requirements without adjusting the program's existing content could reduce the quality of other guidance veterans receive.

117-hr-1482.one_liner: Add oversight rules for companies that help small businesses get SBA loans
provisions: Gives a federal office the job of watching over companies that help small businesses get loans through the SBA's 504 program.
The office must review the files for each loan that closes under the program.
The office can take action — formal or informal — against a company that breaks the rules.
The office can charge each of these companies a fee.
The SBA must write new rules explaining how these companies need to follow environmental requirements.

supporters: Supporters say giving the Office of Credit Risk Management direct oversight of certified development companies (CDCs) in the 504 Loan Program will help catch problems before small businesses are harmed by bad loan practices.
Supporters say requiring the office to review files for every loan closing under the 504 program creates a clear record of what each CDC is doing, making it easier to spot rule-breaking early.

Supporters say allowing the office to take formal or informal enforcement action against CDCs that break the rules gives the federal government real tools to hold these companies accountable, instead of just watching.
critics: Critics say the new fee the office can charge each CDC could raise costs for these companies, and those costs may get passed on to small businesses trying to use the 504 Loan Program.
Critics say requiring file reviews for every single loan closing in the 504 program adds paperwork and review time for CDCs, which could slow down how fast small businesses get approved for loans.

Critics say adding a requirement for the SBA to write new rules on environmental compliance gives CDCs another set of rules to follow, which could make it harder for smaller CDCs to keep up with the program's requirements.

117-hr-1487.one_liner: Require the SBA to report data on its small business microloan program
provisions: The Small Business Administration must report each year on its microloan program, which gives small loans under $50,000 to small businesses.
The report must show how many microloans went unpaid, the total dollar amount of those loans, and what percentage of all microloans went unpaid that year.
The report must show how many microloans went to small businesses in rural areas.
The report must include the average loan size, the interest rate charged, and the fees borrowers paid.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the SBA to report how many microloans went unpaid — and the total dollar amount of those defaults — will help Congress spot problems in the program before they grow.
Supporters say tracking how many microloans go to rural small businesses will show whether those communities are getting a fair share of loans under $50,000.
Supporters say publishing the average loan size, interest rate, and fees will let small business owners compare SBA microloan terms before they borrow.
critics: Critics say the SBA already collects loan data internally, so adding a formal annual report creates paperwork for agency staff without changing how loans are made.
Critics say the bill does not set any rules about what default rates or fee levels are too high, so the reports may be published without anyone acting on them.

117-hr-1490.one_liner: Raise the loan limit for small manufacturers and update SBA 504 loan rules
provisions: The top loan amount for small manufacturers goes from $5.5 million to $6.5 million.
Small manufacturers can now put less of their own money toward a project to get one of these loans.
Small manufacturers must show they kept more jobs to qualify.
Companies that connect businesses to these loans can fix paperwork errors and shift up to 10% of project costs to close a deal.
These loans can now go to businesses in areas hit by disasters, or to businesses that want to cut energy use or make renewable energy.
Every SBA office must team up with a local partner to offer training for small manufacturers.

supporters: Supporters say raising the loan limit for small manufacturers from $5.5 million to $6.5 million gives these businesses access to more money for equipment and facilities they could not afford before.
Supporters say allowing small manufacturers to put less of their own money into a project makes it easier for smaller or newer companies to qualify for a loan without draining their savings.
Supporters say expanding 504 loans to cover disaster areas and energy-efficiency projects helps businesses in struggling communities rebuild and lower their operating costs.
critics: Critics say requiring small manufacturers to show they kept more jobs adds a stricter condition that could disqualify businesses going through hard times or workforce changes.
Critics say allowing loan intermediaries to shift up to 10% of project costs without full review could lead to changes that borrowers did not originally agree to.
Critics say the new training requirement at every SBA district office adds an unfunded obligation that local offices may not have the staff or budget to carry out.

117-hr-1619.one_liner: Add 17 acres of land in North Carolina to the Catawba Indian Nation's reservation
provisions: Makes about 17 acres of land in Cleveland County, North Carolina, part of the Catawba Indian Nation's reservation.
The federal government will hold this land in trust for the tribe.
The tribe can run gambling and gaming on this land.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives the Catawba Indian Nation formal, long-term federal ownership of about 17 acres in Cleveland County, North Carolina, making it part of the tribe's official reservation.
Supporters say allowing the tribe to run gaming on this land would bring jobs and money to the Catawba Indian Nation and the surrounding area in Cleveland County.
critics: Critics say the bill lets the tribe open a casino on this land without following a federal law that normally requires a state to sign a gaming agreement with a tribe before gambling can begin.

Critics say adding 17 acres in Cleveland County to the Catawba Reservation sets a pattern where Congress bypasses the usual process for approving tribal land and gaming, which could affect how other tribes make similar requests.

117-hr-1620.one_liner: Renew and expand funding for domestic violence and sexual assault programs through 2026
provisions: Keeps funding active through 2026 for programs that help victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, dating violence, and stalking.
Creates new programs to help victims keep their housing and stay financially stable.
Changes federal gun rules so people convicted of abusing a dating partner or stalking someone can no longer legally buy or own a gun.
Before this change, only people who abused a spouse or household member faced that restriction.

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a gap in federal gun law by extending the ban on gun ownership to people convicted of abusing dating partners or stalking victims, not just spouses or household members.
Supporters say reauthorizing funding through 2026 keeps shelters, hotlines, and legal services running for victims who rely on those programs each year.
Supporters say the new housing and financial stability programs give victims a way to leave dangerous situations without losing their home or income.
critics: Critics say expanding the gun restriction to dating partners and stalking convictions is too broad and could strip gun rights from people based on minor or disputed convictions.
Critics say extending the law through 2026 without a full review of how current funds are being spent adds more federal spending without proof the existing programs are working.
Critics say some of the new housing protections could create legal conflicts with landlords' rights under state property laws.

117-hr-1502.one_liner: Update rules for the Small Business Administration's small-loan program
provisions: Lenders in this program can now offer a line of credit — money a small business can borrow from as needed — instead of only one-time loans.
Lenders who give out bigger average loans to small businesses now qualify for a lower interest rate on the money they borrow from the SBA.
Sets a maximum time limit for borrowers to pay back their loan, and stops the SBA from cutting that time limit shorter.
The SBA must set aside 15% of new loan money for states that have not received many of these loans, and make the other 85% available to any state.
Lenders must share borrower payment records with the major credit bureaus, which affects a borrower's credit score.
Each year, the SBA must report on how loan money is being spread across different groups and states.

supporters: Supporters say allowing lenders to offer lines of credit — instead of only one-time loans — gives small businesses more flexible access to money when they need it most.
Supporters say reserving 15% of new loan funds for underutilized states will send more money to places that have been left out of the program.
Supporters say requiring lenders to report borrower payments to credit bureaus will help small business owners build credit history they can use to get better loans later.
critics: Critics say requiring lenders to report borrower payment records to credit bureaus could hurt small business owners if they miss a payment, lowering their credit scores and making it harder to borrow in the future.
Critics say giving lenders a lower interest rate when they make bigger average loans could push them to favor larger borrowers over the smallest businesses the program is meant to help.
Critics say setting a fixed maximum repayment term and blocking the SBA from adjusting it removes flexibility that may be needed to protect borrowers who run into financial trouble.

117-hr-1573.one_liner: Give people stopped at the U.S. border the right to speak with a lawyer
provisions: People with green cards, visas, or refugee status who are pulled aside for extra questioning at a U.S. border must be allowed to speak with a lawyer within 1 hour of the questioning starting.
During the extra questioning, a lawyer or a relative can speak up for the person and give information to the officer.
Green card holders cannot sign away their green card status during a border stop unless they first had a real chance to talk to a lawyer.
If a green card holder decides to skip their right to a lawyer, they must say so in writing and it must be their own free choice.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would protect green card holders, visa holders, and refugees from losing their immigration status during a border stop without first talking to a lawyer, since officers cannot accept a signed waiver unless the person had a real chance to get legal advice.

Supporters say allowing a lawyer or relative to give information to the officer during secondary questioning could help clear up mistakes faster, since the officer would have more facts about the person being questioned.

Supporters say the 1-hour rule gives people with legal status — like green card holders and refugees — enough time to reach someone who can help them before they say anything that could hurt their case.
critics: Critics say requiring border officers to wait up to 1 hour before continuing secondary inspections could slow down processing at busy ports of entry and delay questioning of all travelers in line.

Critics say letting lawyers speak during secondary inspections could interfere with the officer's ability to ask questions freely, since the bill allows counsel to provide evidence and information directly to the examining officer.
Critics say the bill does not say who must provide or pay for a lawyer, so people who cannot afford one may not actually get meaningful legal help within the 1-hour window the bill requires.

117-hr-1603.one_liner: Give legal work status to undocumented farm workers and change farm visa rules
provisions: Undocumented farm workers who worked at least 1,035 hours on farms in the two years before March 2021 and have stayed in the U.S. since then can apply for a work permit that lasts 5.5 years.
While their application is being decided, the government cannot deport them and they can work legally.
Their spouse and children can also receive protected status.
After getting the permit and continuing to work in agriculture for a set number of years, they can apply for a green card.
Changes how the minimum wage for H-2A farm visa workers is calculated, and opens the program to year-round farm jobs, not just seasonal ones.
Lets H-2A workers who leave a job have 60 days to find a new farm employer before having to leave the country.
Makes a housing program permanent that provides loans and grants to build or fix housing for farm workers in rural areas.
