Supporters say having the Government Accountability Office check whether agencies and workers are actually joining the program adds accountability and helps Congress see if the program is doing its job.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a minimum number of agencies or workers that must take part, so the program could end up with very low participation and little real impact.
Critics say letting each agency write its own rules for which jobs qualify may lead to uneven standards across the government, making it hard for workers to move between agencies smoothly.

Critics say the bill gives the Office of Personnel Management the job of writing the operation plan but does not set a deadline for when that plan must be finished, which could delay the program from starting.

117-hr-3635.one_liner: Change how the government stores, maintains, and shares its emergency medical supply stockpile
provisions: The government can share emergency supplies from the national stockpile with other federal agencies through September 2024.
The government must keep all stockpile supplies in working order and can hire companies to maintain them.
The government must build U.S.-made reserves of certain supplies and can partner with manufacturers to produce them through September 2024.
States can get grants to build their own stockpiles of emergency supplies for public health crises.
The government must publish clear rules for how it decides who gets supplies from the stockpile.
It must also explain when requests are denied or only partly filled.
During the COVID-19 emergency, the government must release monthly reports showing what states, tribes, and local governments asked for and received.

supporters: Supporters say requiring monthly reports during the COVID-19 emergency — showing what states, tribes, and local governments asked for and received — will stop the confusion that happened when states did not know why their requests were denied or only partly filled.

Supporters say building U.S.-made reserves of key supplies and allowing the government to partner with domestic manufacturers through September 2024 will reduce dependence on foreign sources that were cut off during COVID-19.

Supporters say grants to states to build their own emergency stockpiles will let local governments respond faster during public health crises without waiting for the federal government to ship supplies.
critics: Critics say the authority to build domestic manufacturing partnerships and share stockpile supplies with other federal agencies both expire on September 30, 2024, meaning these fixes are temporary and leave the same gaps open after that date.

Critics say the Government Accountability Office study on user fees could lead to states being charged to access emergency supplies from the national stockpile, which could make it harder for states with smaller budgets to get help during a crisis.
Critics say the bill does not set specific funding levels for state grants, leaving it unclear how many states will actually receive money to build their own stockpiles of emergency equipment.

117-hr-3616.one_liner: Study whether Bear River areas in Utah and Idaho should become a National Heritage Area
provisions: The Department of the Interior must study land along the Bear River in Utah and Idaho
The study checks whether this area should be named a National Heritage Area
No final decision is made by this bill — it only calls for the study

supporters: Supporters say the study would look at whether the Bear River drainage area in Utah and Idaho meets the requirements for a National Heritage Area, which could bring federal tourism and preservation funding to those communities.

Supporters say because this bill only orders a study — not a final designation — no land is restricted or controlled yet, giving local governments and landowners time to weigh in before any decision is made.
critics: Critics say a Department of the Interior study of the Bear River area is often the first step toward federal designation, which can lead to new rules that affect farmers, ranchers, and other landowners in Utah and Idaho.

Critics say the study uses federal staff time and resources, and once completed, the findings could be used to push for a National Heritage Area designation even if local communities in Utah and Idaho oppose it.

117-hr-3709.one_liner: Review and improve how FEMA checks damage after disasters
provisions: FEMA must send Congress a report explaining how it checks damage after disasters, covering the last five years.
FEMA must form a panel of advisors to help improve how those damage checks are done.

supporters: Supporters say the five-year report will show Congress exactly how FEMA has been checking damage after disasters, making it easier to spot problems and fix them.
Supporters say the new advisory panel will bring in outside experts to help FEMA improve how it decides which areas get disaster relief.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires a report and a panel, but does not change any FEMA rules or speed up how quickly disaster victims get help.
Critics say forming an advisory panel adds process without setting a deadline or requiring FEMA to actually adopt any of the panel's recommendations.

117-hr-3593.one_liner: Fund new science research programs at the Department of Energy
provisions: Sets up new research programs at the Department of Energy covering topics like energy, climate, coastal zones, and the basic building blocks of matter.
Creates a program called QUEST that gives more scientists access to quantum computing tools.
Keeps U.S. scientists involved in the Large Hadron Collider, a major physics experiment based in Europe.
Creates a research program on fusion energy, which uses the same process as the sun to produce power.
Starts a high-powered laser research program.
Requires the Department of Energy to hire more science, technology, engineering, and math workers and bring in people from more backgrounds.

supporters: Supporters say the QUEST program will give more U.S. scientists access to quantum computing tools, which could help American researchers keep pace with other countries investing in the same technology.
Supporters say the fusion energy research program studies the same process the sun uses to make power, and success could produce electricity without carbon emissions.
Supporters say requiring the Department of Energy to hire STEM workers from a wider range of backgrounds will grow the number of trained scientists working across these new programs.
critics: Critics say the bill creates many new research programs — covering energy, climate, coastal zones, high-energy physics, lasers, and dark matter — without specifying funding amounts or timelines for each one.

Critics say continuing U.S. involvement in the Large Hadron Collider, a physics experiment based in Europe, sends federal research dollars to a foreign facility instead of fully funding domestic labs.
Critics say the new diversity, equity, and inclusion hiring rules added to DOE staffing could slow down the agency's ability to fill research positions quickly.

117-hr-3730.one_liner: Create a VA advisory committee for veterans in U.S. territories and Pacific island nations
provisions: Creates a new group inside the Department of Veterans Affairs made up of advisors who focus on veterans living in U.S. territories and nearby Pacific nations.
The committee covers eight places: American Samoa, Guam, Puerto Rico, the Northern Mariana Islands, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, and Palau.
The committee will review VA programs and services and suggest ways to better reach veterans in those areas.

supporters: Supporters say the new advisory committee would give veterans in all eight listed areas — American Samoa, Guam, Puerto Rico, the Northern Mariana Islands, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, and Palau — a formal way to bring VA service gaps to the department's attention.
Supporters say the committee's job of reviewing VA programs and suggesting improvements is a direct path to fixing unequal access to benefits for veterans who live far from mainland VA offices.

Supporters say the bill creates a defined advisory role inside the VA, giving territory and Pacific-nation veterans a structured channel to push for program changes through the committee's official review and recommendation process.
critics: Critics say the committee is advisory only, with no power to require the VA to act on its recommendations, meaning veterans in the eight listed areas may see little change in actual services.

Critics say adding a new committee layer inside the VA could slow decision-making without guaranteeing better outcomes for veterans in places like the Marshall Islands or Palau, which are not U.S. territories and face different legal barriers to VA benefits.

Critics say the bill does not include funding amounts or timelines, making it unclear how the committee would reach and represent veterans spread across eight remote locations in the Pacific and Caribbean.

117-hr-3985.one_liner: Add 8,000 more visas for Afghans who helped U.S. or NATO forces
provisions: Adds 8,000 more special visas for Afghan people who worked for the U.S. government or a NATO mission in Afghanistan
These visas are available until all 8,000 have been given out — there is no deadline to use them
Spouses and children of the main applicant do not count against the 8,000 limit
Removes the rule that required applicants to submit a sworn statement describing the danger they face because of their work
Removes the rule that required certain applicants to prove their job duties were sensitive or trusted

supporters: Supporters say the 8,000 new visas give Afghan nationals who worked for the U.S. government or NATO a path to safety, since the existing visa supply ran out while thousands of applicants were still waiting.

Supporters say removing the sworn statement requirement will speed up processing for Afghans who are already at risk because of their work — making them write out the threat they face slowed down approvals without making anyone safer.
Supporters say counting only the main applicant against the 8,000 limit means families can leave together without using up extra visas, so more workers can be helped with the same number of slots.
critics: Critics say removing the sworn statement means the government loses a key way to verify that each applicant actually faces danger tied to their U.S. or NATO work, which could let through people who do not need protection.

Critics say dropping the rule that required certain applicants to prove their duties were sensitive or trusted makes it harder to confirm that an applicant had real access to U.S. operations — widening who qualifies beyond the original intent of the program.

Critics say the bill sets no deadline for using the 8,000 visas, which makes it harder for Congress to track how long the program runs or how many total family members will enter alongside the 8,000 principal applicants.

117-hr-391.one_liner: Create a U.S. council to coordinate responses to global disease outbreaks
provisions: Creates a new government council to coordinate how U.S. agencies work together on global disease threats.
The council gives policy recommendations, helps agencies do their jobs, and checks whether the U.S. is meeting its commitments.
The bill covers help given to other countries to prepare for disease outbreaks.
The President picks a single person to lead and report on the U.S. response when a global health emergency happens.

supporters: Supporters say creating a single U.S. Coordinator for Global Health Security would give the country one clear leader to manage responses when a global disease emergency happens, instead of having agencies act without coordination.
Supporters say the new council would check whether the U.S. is keeping its promises to help other countries prepare for disease outbreaks, making the government more accountable.
Supporters say directing agencies to prioritize the Global Health Security Agenda would help stop infectious diseases from spreading to the U.S. before they become emergencies.
critics: Critics say the bill creates a new government council and a new coordinator position without specifying a budget, making it hard to know how much this will cost taxpayers.
Critics say giving a President-appointed coordinator power to lead interagency responses could reduce Congress's ability to oversee how global health funds are spent.
Critics say the bill requires helping other countries meet disease preparedness targets but does not set limits on how much U.S. money can be sent abroad for that purpose.

117-hr-3919.one_liner: Stop the FCC from approving equipment that poses a national security risk
provisions: The FCC must stop reviewing or approving new applications for equipment it has flagged as a national security risk
Equipment already on the FCC's risk list cannot get new government approval to be used in the U.S.
The FCC must write new rules putting this ban into effect

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a gap where companies could still get FCC approval for equipment already on the national security risk list, like gear made by Huawei and ZTE.
Supporters say blocking new FCC approvals for flagged equipment stops risky technology from entering U.S. networks through a side door that current rules leave open.
Supporters say requiring the FCC to write rules enforcing this ban gives the agency a clear legal duty to act, rather than leaving it as a choice.
critics: Critics say the bill does not define a process for companies to challenge being placed on the FCC's covered equipment list, which could harm smaller telecom firms with limited legal resources.

Critics say banning all new applications for listed equipment could disrupt rural carriers that already use some flagged gear and are still working to replace it under the FCC's rip-and-replace program.
Critics say the bill gives the FCC no timeline or funding to write the new rules, which could slow down enforcement.

117-hr-390.one_liner: Rename a federal building in Memphis after Odell Horton
provisions: Changes the official name of the federal building at 167 North Main Street in Memphis, Tennessee
The building was previously named the Clifford Davis and Odell Horton Federal Building
After this bill, the building is officially called the Odell Horton Federal Building

117-hr-4026.one_liner: Require a federal report on how HHS tracks health factors like income and education
provisions: The GAO, a federal watchdog office, must write a report on what HHS has done about social factors that affect health.
The report covers how HHS collects data on factors like income, education, and where people live.
The report checks whether that data collection follows privacy laws.

supporters: Supporters say the GAO report will show whether HHS is actually using data on income, education, and where people live to improve health outcomes — holding the agency accountable for results.
Supporters say requiring a review of privacy law compliance protects patients whose personal information on income and housing is collected by HHS.
Supporters say the report gives Congress concrete facts about what HHS has and hasn't done, so lawmakers can decide if new laws are needed.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires a GAO report — it does not require HHS to change how it collects data or fix any problems the report finds.
Critics say Congress already has tools to request GAO reports, so a separate law to mandate this one report adds little new oversight.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for HHS to act on the report's findings, which could let problems with data collection continue without a fix.

117-hr-3992.one_liner: Stop employers from treating job applicants differently based on their age
provisions: Employers cannot stop someone from applying for a job because of their age.
Employers cannot put job applicants into separate groups based on their age.
Employers cannot label or rank job applicants differently because of their age.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would stop employers from putting older job applicants into separate groups or lower-ranked lists, giving workers over 40 a fair shot at the same jobs as younger applicants.

Supporters say that banning age-based labeling and ranking of applicants would close a gap in how the Age Discrimination in Employment Act is applied, since courts have sometimes limited its reach to current employees rather than job seekers.

Supporters say older workers — a group that already faces longer unemployment spells than younger workers — would have a clearer legal path to challenge hiring practices that screen them out before an interview.
critics: Critics say the bill does not define what counts as age-based 'classification' in hiring software or algorithms, making it hard for employers to know which screening tools would violate the law.

Critics say small businesses that use third-party applicant tracking systems could face legal risk for automated sorting they did not design or control, since the bill holds employers responsible for how applicants are grouped.
Critics say the bill lacks an explicit enforcement mechanism or penalty structure, leaving it unclear how violations would be investigated or what consequences employers would face.

117-hr-4032.one_liner: Have a federal agency teach small phone companies about open network technology
provisions: The National Telecommunications and Information Administration must reach out to small phone and internet companies to tell them about Open RAN networks.
Open RAN networks are wireless systems that use shared, open technology standards instead of equipment that only works with one company's products.
The agency must offer technical help to small companies that want to learn more about or use this type of network.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would help small phone and internet companies learn about Open RAN networks, which use shared technology standards that let providers mix equipment from different companies instead of being locked into one vendor.

Supporters say the National Telecommunications and Information Administration offering free technical help could lower the cost and complexity for small carriers to upgrade their networks using open technology.

Supporters say wider use of Open RAN standards could increase competition among equipment makers, which may reduce costs for small network providers who often have fewer purchasing options than large carriers.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires outreach and technical assistance, but does not provide funding to small companies to actually build or switch to Open RAN networks, which may limit real-world impact.

Critics say Open RAN technology is still developing, and pushing small providers toward these networks through a government outreach program could lead companies to adopt systems that are not yet proven at scale.
Critics say the bill does not define what counts as a small communications provider or set measurable goals for the outreach program, making it hard to know if the effort is working.

117-hr-4028.one_liner: Require a government report on U.S. technology supply chain risks and trusted vendors
provisions: Tells the National Telecommunications and Information Administration to write a report on where U.S. tech companies get their equipment and software
The report must list which technologies are most important for the U.S. economy
The report must measure how much U.S. internet and phone companies depend on technology from companies that are not considered trusted
The report must identify what the federal government needs to do and spend to support trusted tech companies
After the report, the agency must create a plan to help trusted tech vendors compete and reduce reliance on untrusted ones

supporters: Supporters say the bill would require the National Telecommunications and Information Administration to identify which technologies are most critical to the U.S. economy, giving Congress a clear picture of where the country is most at risk.

Supporters say the required report would measure how much U.S. phone and internet companies depend on equipment from untrusted vendors, which could help reduce reliance on foreign technology that poses security risks.

Supporters say the strategy developed after the report would give trusted U.S. tech vendors a roadmap for competing globally, backed by specific federal actions and resources identified in the report.
critics: Critics say the bill does not require any action beyond writing a report and a plan, meaning it could produce findings that are never acted on or funded.
Critics say the bill does not define what makes a vendor 'trusted' or 'untrusted,' which could lead to an unclear report that does not give useful guidance to policymakers or companies.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline or budget for the required report, leaving it unclear when results would be delivered or how much the effort would cost taxpayers.

117-hr-4.one_liner: Require states with voting violations to get federal approval before changing voting rules
provisions: States with 15 or more voting rights violations in the past 25 years must get approval from the Justice Department before changing any voting rule — and that requirement lasts 10 years.
States with 10 or more violations in the past 25 years, where at least one was committed by the state itself, must also get federal approval before changing voting rules.
States that run their own elections and had 3 or more violations in the past 25 years must get federal approval before changing voting rules.
Cities and counties with 3 or more voting rights violations in the past 25 years must get federal approval before changing their local voting rules, for 10 years.
States and local areas must tell the public when they change how voting works.
The Justice Department can require states to hand over documents or answer questions about their voting rules.
When courts hear cases about voting rules, judges must consider whether a state has a history of treating voters differently based on race.

supporters: Supporters say the preclearance requirement for states with 15 or more voting rights violations in the past 25 years would stop discriminatory voting rules before they take effect, protecting Black, Latino, and other minority voters from being harmed by changes that courts would later strike down anyway.

Supporters say requiring cities and counties with 3 or more violations to get federal approval before changing local voting rules closes a gap that opened after the Supreme Court's 2013 Shelby County decision, which removed preclearance protections for most states.
Supporters say the public notification rule means voters will actually know when their polling place, ID requirements, or registration rules have changed before an election happens.
critics: Critics say giving the Justice Department power to block state voting laws before any court reviews them takes away states' constitutional authority to run their own elections, which the Constitution gives to state governments.

Critics say the 10-year preclearance requirement based on violations from the past 25 years punishes states for decisions made decades ago, even when those states have since passed new laws or changed their practices.

Critics say the DOJ's authority to demand documents and answers from states about their voting rules gives the federal government too much power to investigate and slow down election administration decisions that belong to state and local officials.

117-hr-4067.one_liner: Give legal backing to an FCC advisory council on communications network safety
provisions: Creates a law that officially sets up a council to advise the FCC on how to keep phone and internet networks safe and working
The council gives recommendations on how to improve the security and reliability of communications networks across the country
Before this bill, the council existed without a law behind it — this bill makes it official

supporters: Supporters say this bill gives the council that advises the FCC on network security a permanent legal foundation, so it cannot be dissolved without Congress acting.
Supporters say making the council official in law means its recommendations on phone and internet network reliability will carry more weight with the FCC.
Supporters say the bill keeps a structure in place that helps coordinate security and reliability improvements across communications networks nationwide.
critics: Critics say the bill gives the council no enforcement power, meaning the FCC can ignore its recommendations on network security without any legal consequence.
Critics say the bill sets no funding rules or budget for the council, leaving it unclear how it will operate or who pays for its work.
Critics say formalizing an advisory body that already exists does little to actually fix gaps in the security or reliability of communications networks.

117-hr-4055.one_liner: Require the federal government to run a public cybersecurity education campaign
provisions: A federal office called the NTIA must create a campaign to teach Americans about staying safer online.
The campaign covers best practices — steps people can take every day to lower the chance of getting hacked or having their data stolen.
The NTIA must both build the campaign and run it so that it reaches real people.
The campaign teaches cybersecurity literacy — knowing how online threats work and what to do about them, not just knowing they exist.

supporters: Supporters say the NTIA campaign would teach Americans specific steps — like using strong passwords and spotting phishing emails — that lower the chance of getting hacked or having personal data stolen.
Supporters say that requiring the NTIA to both build and run the campaign means it will actually reach real people, not just exist as a website that no one visits.
Supporters say that teaching cybersecurity literacy — how online threats work, not just that they exist — gives people tools to protect themselves as more of daily life moves online.
critics: Critics say the bill gives the NTIA broad authority to run a national campaign but sets no budget limit, no deadline, and no way to measure whether Americans actually learn anything from it.
Critics say a federal awareness campaign run by the NTIA may duplicate work already done by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which runs its own public education programs.

Critics say the bill does not require the campaign to reach specific groups — like seniors or small business owners — who face higher cybersecurity risks, so the effort may not go where it is needed most.

117-hr-4045.one_liner: Create a federal task force to study and report on 6G wireless technology
provisions: Sets up a new group called the 6G Task Force inside the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), which is the government agency that oversees phone and internet networks.
The task force will look at where 6G wireless technology stands today and what standards are being developed for it.
It will also look at possible uses for 6G technology once it is built.
The task force will include people from phone and internet companies, universities and public interest groups, and federal, state, local, and tribal governments.
The task force will produce a report with its findings.

supporters: Supporters say the 6G Task Force will bring together phone companies, universities, and local and tribal governments to agree on shared standards before 6G networks are built, which could help avoid the delays that slowed 5G rollout.

Supporters say having the FCC lead this task force gives the federal government an early seat at the table on 6G rules, which could help U.S. companies compete with other countries already working on 6G standards.
Supporters say the task force's report will map out possible uses for 6G technology, giving Congress and the FCC concrete information to guide future decisions.
critics: Critics say the bill creates a new FCC task force without setting a budget, a deadline for the report, or any requirement that the FCC act on the task force's findings.
Critics say the task force is limited to producing a report, which means it has no power to set actual 6G standards or require any company or agency to change what they are doing.
Critics say the bill does not define what makes a company or organization 'trusted,' which leaves it unclear who will actually have a seat on the task force.

117-hr-4089.one_liner: Require car rental companies to report suspicious behavior to police
provisions: The Department of Homeland Security must create a list of warning signs for car rental employees to watch for when customers rent or buy vehicles.
Car rental companies and dealers would use these guidelines to decide when to call law enforcement about a customer.
The guidelines would be shared with rental companies and dealers across the country.

supporters: Supporters say requiring DHS to create a list of warning signs for rental employees could help law enforcement stop attacks like the 2017 New York City bike path attack, which killed Darren Drake and seven others when a renter used a truck as a weapon.
Supporters say sharing these guidelines with rental companies and dealers across the country gives frontline workers a clear, consistent standard for when to call police, which they do not have now.
Supporters say this bill does not require companies to deny rentals — it only gives employees a tool to report suspicious behavior before a vehicle is handed over.
critics: Critics say the bill does not define what counts as 'suspicious behavior,' which could lead rental employees to report customers based on race, religion, or national origin rather than actual warning signs.
Critics say the guidelines are voluntary best practices with no enforcement mechanism, so rental companies may simply choose not to follow them, leaving the program with no guaranteed impact.

Critics say targeting rental companies puts the burden of security screening on private employees who are not trained in law enforcement, which could create legal risk for companies and employees who make the wrong call.

117-hr-4111.one_liner: Push for better rules to help poorer countries review their debt contracts
provisions: Tells the U.S. Treasury to have its representative at the International Monetary Fund push for global standards on how countries write debt contracts with private lenders.
Calls for the IMF to offer help to lower-middle-income countries so they can better understand the legal and money terms in their debt deals.
The goal is to give those countries the tools to review and compare loan contracts before signing them.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would give lower-middle-income countries IMF technical help to review the legal and financial terms of debt contracts before signing, so they are not locked into bad deals with private lenders.

Supporters say pushing for global standards on sovereign debt contracts through the U.S. Treasury's IMF seat costs little but could protect dozens of countries from hidden contract terms that favor lenders.
Supporters say that when countries understand their loan terms better, they are less likely to default, which lowers the risk of debt crises that can spread to other economies.
critics: Critics say the bill directs the IMF to promote standards and offer assistance but sets no timeline, budget, or way to measure whether lower-middle-income countries are actually getting help.
Critics say the bill does not require private sector creditors to follow any new standards, so lenders can keep writing contracts the same way even after the IMF promotes better practices.
Critics say technical assistance from the IMF already exists through other programs, and adding another directive without new funding may duplicate work already being done.

117-hr-4300.one_liner: Give free national park passes to veterans, active military, and Gold Star Families
provisions: Active military members, veterans, and Gold Star Families get a free America the Beautiful pass, which normally costs $80 per year.
The free pass covers entry fees and standard fees at all federal parks and recreation areas across the country.
Gold Star Families are families of U.S. service members who died while serving.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would give active military members, veterans, and Gold Star Families a free America the Beautiful pass that normally costs $80 per year, removing a cost barrier to visiting federal parks.

Supporters say Gold Star Families — who lost a service member in active duty — would gain free entry and standard amenity access at all federal recreational lands, giving them the same park benefits as other military groups.
critics: Critics say giving free $80 passes to all veterans regardless of disability rating or income level could reduce fee revenue that federal parks rely on to fund maintenance and visitor services.

Critics say active duty service members already receive a free America the Beautiful pass under the National Defense Authorization Act, so that portion of the bill repeats a benefit that is already in place.

117-hr-4250.one_liner: Expand State Department rewards for tips about war crimes suspects
provisions: The State Department pays rewards for tips that lead to the arrest, trial, or transfer of a foreign national.
That person must be accused of war crimes, crimes against humanity, or genocide.
Before this bill, the crime had to match the definition used by the specific international court handling the case.
This bill also counts crimes defined under U.S. law or the laws of the country where the crime happened.

supporters: Supporters say the bill allows tips to be rewarded when a crime matches U.S. law or the law of the country where it happened, not just the rules of one specific international court, which means more accused war criminals could be brought to justice.

Supporters say the current law leaves gaps when no international tribunal has opened a case, and this bill lets the State Department still offer rewards using other legal definitions to reach suspects who might otherwise go free.

Supporters say expanding the definition to include crimes under applicable national laws means local governments and U.S. prosecutors can work together more closely to act on tips about genocide or crimes against humanity.
critics: Critics say allowing crimes to be defined by individual countries' laws — rather than a single international tribunal standard — could let politically motivated governments label opponents as war criminals to trigger U.S. reward money.

Critics say the bill removes a key safeguard: the requirement that an international court, not just the U.S. or a foreign country, has formally accused someone of a war crime before rewards are paid out.

Critics say layering three different legal definitions — international tribunal law, U.S. law, and local country law — into one program could create confusion about who qualifies and make the program harder to oversee.

117-hr-4233.one_liner: Give veterans using education benefits access to VA counseling
provisions: Veterans who use VA or military education benefits can get counseling through the VA.
This includes counseling at Vet Centers, which are VA community offices that offer mental health support.
Active-duty service members using these education benefits are also covered.
The VA is required to offer this counseling — not just allowed to.

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires the VA to provide counseling — not just allow it — meaning student veterans using VA or military education benefits cannot be turned away from services.
Supporters say active-duty service members using education benefits would be covered for the first time, giving them access to Vet Center mental health support while they attend school.
Supporters say Vet Centers are community-based offices, so student veterans would not have to travel to a VA hospital to get counseling while taking classes.
critics: Critics say the bill expands the VA's mandatory counseling load to include all veterans and active-duty members using education benefits, but does not include new funding to hire more Vet Center staff.
Critics say requiring the VA to serve this larger group could create longer wait times at Vet Centers for veterans who already qualify for those services.
Critics say the bill does not define how many people would become newly eligible, making it hard for the VA to plan for the added demand on counseling resources.

117-hr-4256.one_liner: Raise the cap on bank investments in small business funds from 5% to 15%
provisions: This bill raises the amount banks can put into small business investment funds from 5% of their capital to 15%.
A federal banking regulator must approve the investment before a bank can move forward.
Banks can also invest in a company whose only purpose is to put money into these small business funds.

supporters: Supporters say raising the investment limit from 5% to 15% of a bank's capital means banks can put three times as much money into small business investment funds, giving small businesses more access to financing.

Supporters say that requiring a federal banking regulator to approve each investment adds a safety check that protects banks and their depositors while still allowing more lending to small businesses.
Supporters say allowing banks to invest in companies set up solely to fund these small business investment pools makes it easier for banks to pool resources and reach more small businesses at once.
critics: Critics say raising the cap from 5% to 15% of capital means banks could put significantly more depositor money into small business investment funds, which carry higher risk than traditional bank investments.
Critics say the federal approval requirement does not set clear standards for when a bank's investment will be approved or denied, which could lead to uneven rules across different banks.

Critics say the bill allows banks to invest in intermediate companies whose only job is to funnel money into these funds, which adds a layer between the bank and the actual small business investment and makes oversight harder.

117-hr-4352.one_liner: Let the federal government take land into trust for all federally recognized tribes
provisions: The federal government can place land into federal trust for all 574 federally recognized tribes.
Land held in federal trust is protected from state taxes and some state laws.
Before this bill, a 2009 Supreme Court ruling blocked this for tribes recognized after 1934.
This bill overrules that court decision and extends the rule to all tribes.
The changes apply as if they were always part of the original 1934 law.

supporters: Supporters say this bill allows the Department of the Interior to take land into trust for all 574 federally recognized tribes, giving every tribe access to the same federal land protections regardless of when they were recognized.

Supporters say land held in federal trust is removed from state tax rolls and shielded from some state laws, which tribal nations say lets them govern and develop their land without state interference.

Supporters say tribes recognized after 1934 have been denied trust land since the 2009 Carcieri v. Salazar ruling, and this bill extends the updated rule to those tribes by treating it as part of the original 1934 law.
critics: Critics say removing land from state tax rolls reduces local tax revenue in counties near tribal land, since property in federal trust is no longer subject to state or local property taxes.

Critics say applying the changes retroactively — as if they were always part of the 1934 law — could reopen past land decisions and create legal uncertainty about land that states and counties have already taxed or regulated for decades.

Critics say the bill overrides the Supreme Court's 2009 decision in Carcieri v. Salazar through an act of Congress rather than through the courts, which shifts how disputes over tribal land authority get resolved.

117-hr-4489.one_liner: Put Forest Service lawsuit and settlement money in interest accounts to fund repairs
provisions: When the federal government collects money from lawsuits or settlements tied to Forest Service activities, that money goes into an account that earns interest.
The interest earned in those accounts pays for cleanup or repair work on national forests.
The money is only invested when it is not needed for immediate use.

supporters: Supporters say investing Forest Service settlement and lawsuit money in interest-bearing accounts means the interest earned pays for forest cleanup, so taxpayers do not have to cover those repair costs directly.
Supporters say the bill ensures that settlement funds do not sit idle — when the money is not needed right away, it earns interest that can be used for restoration work tied to the original damage.
Supporters say this links the source of funding to the cause of the damage, since money collected from those responsible for harm to national forests goes toward fixing that harm.
critics: Critics say the amount of interest earned depends on how much settlement money is collected each year and on interest rates, with no guaranteed minimum set aside for cleanup work.
Critics say the bill only makes interest 'available' to cover repair costs but does not require that any specific repairs be completed or set a timeline for when forests must be restored.
Critics say that because the money is only invested when not needed for immediate use, some funds may sit uninvested for long periods and earn no interest for restoration work.

117-hr-446.one_liner: Require the FTC to track and share information about scams targeting older adults
provisions: The Federal Trade Commission must publish a report on scams that target older adults.
The report must include recommendations for how to stop those scams.
The FTC must update its website with current information about scams targeting older adults.
The website must list contact information for law enforcement and adult protective services.
The FTC must work with news outlets and law enforcement to spread that information.

supporters: Supporters say the FTC report on scam types and numbers will give Congress real data to write stronger laws protecting older adults.
Supporters say updating the FTC website with contact information for law enforcement and adult protective services will make it easier for seniors and their families to report scams quickly.
Supporters say coordinating with news outlets and law enforcement to spread this information will reach older adults who may not use the internet.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires reports and website updates, but does not create new penalties or enforcement tools to stop scammers from targeting older adults.
Critics say the FTC already collects data on fraud and runs consumer education programs, so this bill may duplicate work the agency is doing without adding new resources.
Critics say without dedicated funding attached to the bill, the FTC may not have enough staff or budget to carry out the reporting, website updates, and media coordination the bill requires.

117-hr-4369.one_liner: Create federally funded university centers to research faster drug manufacturing
provisions: The FDA picks colleges or universities to become official Centers of Excellence in continuous drug manufacturing.
Each center gets federal grant money to run its research program.
Each center studies new ways to make drugs using continuous manufacturing.
Each center shares what it learns with the FDA.
Continuous manufacturing makes drugs faster than the batch method most factories use today.

supporters: Supporters say the FDA picking colleges as Centers of Excellence would bring together university researchers and drug makers to develop continuous manufacturing, which makes drugs faster than the batch method used in most factories today.
Supporters say each center would share what it learns with the FDA, which could help the agency update its rules and speed up drug approvals for medicines made using continuous manufacturing.
Supporters say federal grant money going to these centers would fund research that could reduce drug shortages by making production faster and more flexible.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a specific dollar amount for the grants, making it hard to know if the funding will be enough for centers to do meaningful research.

Critics say requiring each center to share its research findings with the FDA could discourage drug companies from partnering with universities if they worry about losing control of private research data.
Critics say the bill focuses only on colleges and universities, leaving out private research labs and manufacturers that already have experience with continuous manufacturing technology.

117-hr-447.one_liner: Fund and expand job training apprenticeships across the country
provisions: Creates an official office inside the Department of Labor to oversee and run apprenticeship programs nationwide.
Sets quality rules for apprenticeships, including what training must be provided and what agreements employers and workers must sign.
Gives money to groups that want to start or grow apprenticeship programs, including programs for teens and young adults.
Gives money to help more businesses offer apprenticeships to workers.
Sets up state offices to manage local apprenticeship programs and help workers and employers get started.
Links apprenticeship programs with high schools, colleges, and adult education to help workers connect their training with formal schooling.
Works to bring more people from underrepresented groups into apprenticeship programs.

supporters: Supporters say creating a permanent Office of Apprenticeship inside the Department of Labor would give apprenticeship programs stable, long-term oversight instead of relying on rules that can change without Congress.
Supporters say the grants to help businesses start apprenticeship programs would bring more employers into the system, giving workers a path to a paying job while they train.

Supporters say linking apprenticeship programs to high schools, colleges, and adult education would let workers earn school credits at the same time they learn on the job, helping them finish degrees faster.
critics: Critics say giving the federal Office of Apprenticeship power to set quality standards and approve new occupations could make it harder for states to run programs that fit their local job markets.
Critics say the bill adds a new layer of federal grant programs and state offices without a clear limit on spending, and that cost falls on taxpayers.
Critics say employers — especially small businesses — may avoid apprenticeships if new federal agreements and compliance rules make the process too complicated.

117-hr-4481.one_liner: Require agents who help small businesses get SBA loans to register and pay a fee
provisions: Creates a registration system run by the Small Business Administration for agents who help small businesses apply for government-backed loans.
Agents who connect small businesses with SBA 7(a) loans must sign up in this system each year.
Agents must pay a yearly registration fee to stay in the system.
The SBA can collect data on these agents through the registration system.
The 7(a) loan program gives loans to small businesses that cannot get regular bank loans on normal terms.

supporters: Supporters say the new SBA registration system would let the government track which agents are helping small businesses apply for 7(a) loans, making it easier to spot fraud or bad actors in the program.
Supporters say requiring agents to sign up each year and pay a registration fee gives the SBA data it currently lacks about who is getting paid to guide small businesses through the loan process.
Supporters say small businesses that rely on 7(a) loans — because they cannot get regular bank loans — deserve to know that the agents helping them are registered and accountable to a federal system.
critics: Critics say the annual registration fee adds a new cost for agents, which could push smaller or independent loan agents out of the market and leave fewer options for small businesses seeking 7(a) loans.
Critics say the bill does not set limits on how much the SBA can charge for the yearly fee or what the agency can do with the data it collects on agents.
Critics say adding a registration requirement on top of existing rules could slow down the process for small businesses trying to get 7(a) loans quickly.

117-hr-4555.one_liner: Run a public education campaign to improve oral health knowledge
provisions: The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), a federal health agency, must run a public education campaign about oral health.
The campaign must focus on children, pregnant women, and parents.
The campaign must also reach older adults, people with disabilities, and racial and ethnic minorities.

supporters: Supporters say requiring HRSA to run a public education campaign could help groups with lower rates of dental care — including racial and ethnic minorities, people with disabilities, and older adults — learn about preventive oral health steps.
Supporters say focusing the campaign on children and pregnant women could reduce cavities and gum disease early in life, before bigger health problems develop.
Supporters say using an existing federal agency like HRSA to run the campaign avoids creating new programs from scratch.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a specific funding amount, making it unclear how HRSA would pay for the campaign without cutting other health programs.
Critics say a public education campaign alone does not fix the cost of dental care or expand access to dentists, which are the main barriers for the groups the bill targets.
Critics say the bill sets no measurable goals or deadlines, so there is no clear way to know if the campaign is working.

117-hr-4515.one_liner: Help small business owners build cybersecurity plans through trained local advisors
provisions: The Small Business Administration must create a program to certify workers at small business development centers in cybersecurity planning.
Depending on the size of the center, at least 5% or 10% of each center's workers must complete this certification.
Once certified, these workers help small business owners make plans to protect their businesses from cyber threats.
Small business development centers are local offices — there are about 1,000 across the country — that already provide free or low-cost business advice.

supporters: Supporters say that requiring 5% to 10% of workers at each of the roughly 1,000 small business development centers to get certified in cybersecurity will give small business owners access to free, local help making plans to protect their businesses from cyber attacks.
Supporters say that using centers that already offer free or low-cost business advice means small businesses can get cybersecurity help without paying for a private consultant.
Supporters say that setting a clear certification requirement gives the Small Business Administration a measurable goal and makes sure the training actually happens.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include funding to pay for the certification program, which could put the cost burden on individual small business development centers that may already have limited budgets.
Critics say that requiring only 5% or 10% of staff to be certified may not be enough to meet demand at busy centers, leaving many small business owners without access to a certified adviser.
Critics say the bill does not define what the certification must cover, which could lead to uneven training quality across the roughly 1,000 centers.

117-hr-4611.one_liner: Make software vendors report security weaknesses to the Department of Homeland Security
provisions: Companies selling technology products or services to the Department of Homeland Security must provide a full list of all software components.
Each vendor must certify that their components have no known security weaknesses.
If a vendor finds a security weakness, they must notify DHS about it.
Vendors must also submit a plan to fix any weaknesses they find.
DHS must issue rules covering both new contracts and contracts already in place.

supporters: Supporters say requiring vendors to submit a full list of all software components gives DHS a clear view of what is inside the technology it buys, making it easier to spot hidden security risks.
Supporters say the rule that vendors must notify DHS when they find a security weakness means problems get reported quickly instead of staying hidden until attackers exploit them.
Supporters say covering both new and existing contracts closes gaps where older DHS systems could still carry unreviewed software from unknown sources.
critics: Critics say requiring every vendor to certify that all their software components have no known weaknesses may be impossible for large products built from hundreds of open-source parts, which could push smaller companies out of bidding for DHS contracts.

Critics say the bill does not set a deadline or budget for DHS to issue the new rules, which means guidance could be delayed for years while current contracts stay in place without the new requirements.
Critics say vendors who find and report a weakness under this bill have no legal protection spelled out in the text, which may discourage honest disclosure if companies fear losing their contracts.

117-hr-4531.one_liner: Require the SBA to report annually on loan agents who help small businesses borrow money
provisions: Requires the Small Business Administration to publish a yearly report on agents who help small businesses apply for government-backed loans.
The report must include how many agents are working with loan applicants and what types of services they provide.
The report must count how many fraudulent loans were made where the borrower used one of these agents.
The report must show how much money in referral fees these agents were paid in total.

supporters: Supporters say the yearly report will show how many fraudulent 7(a) loans involved a paid agent, which gives Congress and the SBA data to identify whether agents are connected to fraud in the loan program.

Supporters say requiring the SBA to track the total dollar value of referral fees paid to agents will make it clear how much money flows through this part of the 7(a) program, which currently has no public accounting.
Supporters say counting the number and types of agents helping applicants will show whether certain agent categories have higher rates of fraud, letting regulators target oversight more precisely.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires the SBA to count and report fraud cases linked to agents — it gives the agency no new authority to remove, fine, or block those agents from working on future 7(a) loans.

Critics say small businesses that rely on agents to navigate the 7(a) application process may face fewer agent options if agents exit the market to avoid being tracked and included in a fraud-linked federal report.

Critics say the SBA already faces resource limits, and adding a new annual reporting requirement pulls staff time away from processing loans for small business borrowers who cannot get credit elsewhere.

117-hr-4502.one_liner: Fund the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education for 2022
provisions: Pays for the Department of Labor for the year starting October 2021, covering job training, workplace safety, and worker pay enforcement.
Pays for the Department of Health and Human Services, including the CDC, the National Institutes of Health, and Medicare and Medicaid programs.
Pays for the Department of Education, covering student financial aid, special education, school improvement, and college programs.
Funds the Social Security Administration, which sends monthly payments to about 70 million retired, disabled, and low-income Americans.
Sets rules for how all of this money can and cannot be spent.

supporters: Supporters say this bill keeps monthly Social Security payments going to about 70 million retired, disabled, and low-income Americans who depend on those checks to pay for food, housing, and medical care.

Supporters say funding the CDC and National Institutes of Health through this bill lets those agencies continue tracking disease outbreaks and running medical research programs that serve the whole country.
Supporters say the Department of Education money covers student financial aid and special education services that federal law already requires schools to provide to students with disabilities.
critics: Critics say packaging funding for the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education into one bill makes it harder for lawmakers to cut or change specific programs they believe are wasteful or ineffective.

Critics say some spending rules in the bill would remove limits on how federal health dollars can be used, including restrictions tied to abortion-related services that have been in place for decades.
Critics say paying for Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security Administration operations without any reforms allows the cost of those programs to keep growing and adds to the federal deficit.

117-hr-485.one_liner: Renew and expand federal child abuse prevention programs through 2027
provisions: Keeps federal child abuse prevention and treatment programs funded through September 2027
Creates national rules for how states track and report child deaths and serious injuries caused by abuse
Builds an online system so states can share child abuse records with each other across state lines
Adds steps for child protective services to follow when a family is dealing with drug or alcohol problems
Calls for a review of racial bias in how child protective services handles cases
Orders a study on unregulated custody transfers — when a parent hands a child to a stranger outside the legal system — and how to stop them

supporters: Supporters say the online system for sharing child abuse records across state lines will help stop cases where a parent moves to another state to avoid a prior abuse report.
Supporters say requiring national rules for tracking child deaths from abuse will give Congress and states better data to find out where prevention is failing and fix it.
Supporters say the review of racial bias in child protective services will show whether Black and Native families are being treated differently than white families in the same situations.
critics: Critics say adding new federal rules for how states run their child protective services — including steps for drug and alcohol cases — reduces the ability of states to decide what works best for their own families.
Critics say the bill extends federal funding only through September 2027, which is a short window that could leave states scrambling to replace money for programs they have already built.
Critics say an online system letting states share abuse registry records raises privacy concerns for families, since a report on a registry does not always mean abuse was proven in court.

117-hr-4616.one_liner: Set replacement interest rates for contracts still tied to the retired LIBOR benchmark
provisions: LIBOR was an interest rate that banks used to set prices on loans and other money contracts. It stopped being used in 2023.
Many contracts — including some home loans and business deals — were tied to LIBOR and had no backup rate written in.
For those contracts, the Federal Reserve picks a replacement rate to use instead of LIBOR.
The switch to the new rate happens automatically — no one has to go to court or sign new paperwork.
People and companies that switch to the new rate cannot be taken to court just for making that switch.
The switch does not count as selling or trading property, so no extra taxes are owed because of it.

supporters: Supporters say the automatic switch means home loan borrowers and businesses with LIBOR-tied contracts that had no backup rate will not need to go to court or sign new paperwork when LIBOR ended in 2023.

Supporters say the legal protection in the bill means lenders and borrowers cannot be taken to court just for switching to the Federal Reserve's replacement rate, removing a major legal risk tied to the 2023 LIBOR retirement.
Supporters say the tax rule stops the switch from being treated as a property sale, so no extra taxes are owed by anyone whose contract moves to the new rate.
critics: Critics say the bill gives the Federal Reserve the power to set a replacement rate for private contracts, which some argue should be left to the two parties who signed the original deal.

Critics say the Federal Reserve's replacement rate may not work the same way as LIBOR for all contracts, since LIBOR tracked unsecured bank-to-bank lending costs while the Fed's likely pick is based on a different kind of borrowing.

Critics say the broad legal protection in the bill may make it harder for borrowers to challenge a replacement rate even if it leads to higher payments than they expected under the original LIBOR terms.

117-hr-4660.one_liner: Rename a federal building and courthouse in Wheeling, West Virginia
provisions: Changes the official name of the federal building and courthouse at 1125 Chapline Street in Wheeling, West Virginia.
The building will be called the Frederick P. Stamp, Jr. Federal Building and United States Courthouse.
The building serves as both a federal office building and a U.S. courthouse.

117-hr-4679.one_liner: Name a federal building in Washington DC after Norman Yoshio Mineta
provisions: The federal building at 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE in Washington, DC will be officially called the Norman Yoshio Mineta Federal Building.
Norman Mineta served as U.S. Secretary of Transportation from 2001 to 2006 — the cabinet department whose main office is at that address.
He also served more than 20 years as a U.S. Representative from California, representing the San José area.
Mineta served in the U.S. Army as a first lieutenant after being held in a Japanese American internment camp during World War II.
The name change is official but does not change how the building is used or how it is funded.

supporters: Supporters say naming the building after Norman Mineta honors his five years as Secretary of Transportation from 2001 to 2006, during which he led the department whose main offices are at 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE.
Supporters say the name change recognizes Mineta's more than 20 years representing the San José area in Congress, making him one of the longest-serving Japanese American members of the House.
Supporters say the designation acknowledges that Mineta was held in a Japanese American internment camp as a child but went on to serve as a U.S. Army officer and later in two presidential cabinets.

117-hr-4686.one_liner: Freeze the assets and block the US entry of Cambodian officials who hurt democracy
provisions: Freezes the US bank accounts and property of senior Cambodian government, military, or security officials who took actions to undermine elections or violated human rights
Blocks those same officials from entering the United States
Covers companies owned or controlled by those officials
Does not apply to goods imported from Cambodia — trade continues as normal
The President can cancel sanctions for a specific person if doing so is in the US national interest
The President can pause all sanctions if Cambodia takes real steps to stop actions against democracy or human rights

supporters: Supporters say freezing the US bank accounts and blocking US entry of senior Cambodian officials who rigged elections or committed human rights abuses gives the US a direct way to hold those specific people responsible.
Supporters say keeping trade with Cambodia open while targeting only named officials means everyday Cambodian workers and US businesses are not hurt by the sanctions.

Supporters say the bill gives the President the power to lift sanctions if Cambodia takes real steps toward fair elections and human rights, so it pushes for change without locking the two countries into a permanent standoff.
critics: Critics say the national interest waiver lets the President cancel sanctions for any official at any time, which could allow the same people the bill targets to avoid punishment if other US policy goals take priority.
Critics say the bill does not set clear, measurable steps Cambodia must take to get sanctions lifted, making it hard to know what counts as real progress toward democracy or human rights.

Critics say targeting officials while leaving trade untouched may limit pressure on the Cambodian government, since trade revenue can still flow to the state even when individual officials are blocked.

117-hr-4981.one_liner: Give a government opioid commission more time to finish its report
provisions: A government commission studying how synthetic opioids enter the U.S. now has 390 days to finish its report, instead of the original 270 days.
That adds about 4 extra months to the deadline.
The commission's job is to study the problem and suggest ways to stop synthetic opioids like fentanyl from coming into the country.

supporters: Supporters say the extra 4 months gives the commission time to gather more complete data on how fentanyl and other synthetic opioids enter the U.S., leading to stronger recommendations.
Supporters say rushing the final report in 270 days could produce incomplete findings, and extending to 390 days allows for a more thorough review before policy changes are made.
critics: Critics say delaying the final report by 4 months means Congress and federal agencies must wait longer to act on recommendations to stop synthetic opioids from entering the country.
Critics say the original 270-day deadline was already set with enough time built in, and pushing it to 390 days slows down the process of addressing fentanyl trafficking without a clear reason.

117-hr-4881.one_liner: Put land already owned by the Pascua Yaqui Tribe into federal trust and allow gaming
provisions: The federal government will hold land in Pima County, Arizona in trust for the Pascua Yaqui Tribe of Arizona.
The land is already owned by the Tribe — this bill changes its legal status to federal trust, which gives it added protections.
Once in trust, the land becomes part of the Pascua Yaqui Reservation.
The Tribe can run casino gaming on this land.

supporters: Supporters say that placing the Tribe's land in Pima County, Arizona into federal trust gives it legal protections it does not have now, making it harder for the land to be sold or taken away from the Pascua Yaqui Tribe.
Supporters say that adding this land to the Pascua Yaqui Reservation expands the Tribe's land base, which tribal leaders argue is needed to support housing and community services for tribal members.
Supporters say allowing casino gaming on this land could bring jobs and tax revenue to the Tribe and the surrounding Tucson area.
critics: Critics say that allowing gaming on newly acquired trust land skips the usual federal review process that decides whether a tribe can open a casino on land it did not hold before a certain date.
Critics say that adding gaming rights to this land transfer goes beyond simply fixing the land's legal status and sets a precedent for future tribes seeking casinos on newly acquired land.
Critics say that nearby non-tribal governments and businesses in Pima County were not given a formal role in deciding whether a casino should be allowed on this land.

117-hr-5.one_liner: Ban discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in housing, jobs, and public places
provisions: Federal law would ban discrimination based on sex, sexual orientation, and gender identity in hiring, housing, schools, lending, and most businesses.
Stores, restaurants, gyms, and other businesses could not turn away customers based on sexual orientation or gender identity.
People could not be denied access to restrooms, locker rooms, or dressing rooms that match their gender identity.
The Department of Justice could step into federal court cases to support people who face discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity.
The law would apply to more types of businesses than current civil rights law, including places that offer entertainment, transportation, or recreational activities.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would make it illegal under federal law to fire, refuse housing to, or deny loans to people because of their sexual orientation or gender identity, protections that currently do not exist in many states.

Supporters say businesses like gyms, restaurants, and stores that offer entertainment or transportation services would be added to the list of places covered by civil rights law, meaning they could not turn away LGBT customers.

Supporters say the Department of Justice would be able to join federal court cases where someone claims discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, giving individuals more legal support.
critics: Critics say the bill requires schools, gyms, and other facilities to give people access to restrooms and locker rooms based on gender identity, which they argue removes privacy protections for women and girls in shared spaces.

Critics say expanding the definition of public accommodations to include nearly all businesses would force religious-owned stores, venues, and service providers to serve customers in ways that conflict with their beliefs, with no religious exemption in the bill.

Critics say the bill does not include language from the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, which means religious individuals and organizations could not use that law as a defense in discrimination cases brought under the Equality Act.

117-hr-4996.one_liner: Add new rules for shipping companies operating in U.S. waters
provisions: Stops shipping companies from punishing customers who use a different carrier or file a complaint against them
Requires the Federal Maritime Commission to post a public list of shipping companies that lied on paperwork or were fined
Forces shipping companies to meet basic service standards set by the government
Stops shipping companies from charging unfair fees when cargo sits waiting at ports
Requires shipping companies to report to the government each quarter on how much cargo they moved in and out of U.S. ports
Gives the Federal Maritime Commission the power to investigate and fine shipping companies for unfair charges

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects U.S. exporters by stopping shipping companies from punishing customers who file complaints or use a different carrier, which would give smaller businesses more freedom to choose who ships their goods.
Supporters say requiring the Federal Maritime Commission to post a public list of companies that lied on paperwork or were fined would make it easier to identify bad actors in the shipping industry.
Supporters say ending unfair fees for cargo sitting at ports would lower costs for American importers and exporters, who have faced large demurrage and detention charges during port delays.
critics: Critics say giving the Federal Maritime Commission new power to investigate and fine shipping companies could raise operating costs for carriers, which may pass those costs on to importers and exporters through higher rates.
Critics say the new quarterly reporting rules on cargo tonnage and container counts would create extra paperwork for shipping companies, adding administrative costs without a clear benefit to trade.
Critics say requiring the government to set minimum service standards for private shipping companies could interfere with how carriers manage their own fleets and schedules.

117-hr-51.one_liner: Make Washington D.C. the 51st state of the United States
provisions: Washington D.C. would become the 51st state, called Washington, Douglass Commonwealth.
DC residents would gain two U.S. Senators and one member of the House of Representatives.
The White House, the Capitol, and the Supreme Court stay under federal control.
Those buildings and nearby federal land are not part of the new state.
A new commission would help manage the switch from DC government to state government.
Current DC laws stay in effect until the new state is ready to take over.

supporters: Supporters say the roughly 700,000 people living in DC would gain two U.S. Senators and one House member, giving them the same voting power in Congress that residents of every other state already have.
Supporters say the bill keeps the White House, Capitol, and Supreme Court under federal control, so the federal government would not lose authority over its key buildings and nearby land.
Supporters say a new Statehood Transition Commission would manage the switch step by step, and current DC laws would stay in place until the new state is ready to take over.
critics: Critics say making DC a state would give one small area — with fewer people than most states — two Senate seats, shifting the balance of power in the Senate.

Critics say the Twenty-third Amendment, which gives DC residents electoral votes for president, would need to be repealed as part of this process, requiring a separate constitutional change that is not guaranteed to happen.
Critics say the bill does not resolve whether Congress has the power to create a new state from DC territory without a constitutional amendment, which some legal experts believe would be required.

117-hr-5323.one_liner: Send $1 billion to Israel to restock its Iron Dome missile defense system
provisions: Sends $1 billion to Israel's government to buy more Iron Dome interceptor missiles and equipment
The Iron Dome is a system that shoots down short-range rockets fired at Israel
The money comes from the U.S. Department of Defense budget

supporters: Supporters say the $1 billion would let Israel buy more Iron Dome interceptor missiles to protect civilians from short-range rocket attacks.
Supporters say the Department of Defense has funded Iron Dome before, and this continues a defense partnership that has worked for years.
Supporters say the Iron Dome is a defensive system only — it shoots down incoming rockets and does not launch attacks.
critics: Critics say the bill sends $1 billion from the Department of Defense budget with no conditions or limits on how Israel uses the funds.
Critics say the bill includes no language requiring oversight or reporting on how the $1 billion is spent after it reaches Israel's government.
Critics say $1 billion in Defense Department funds could instead go to U.S. military needs at home.

117-hr-5293.one_liner: Extend several VA programs that were set to expire
provisions: Makes the VA dental insurance plan for veterans and some of their family members permanent — it no longer needs to be renewed
Extends through September 2022 a program that pays for travel costs when veterans go to a Vet Center for care
Lets the VA accept donations of land or buildings from state or local governments through December 16, 2026

supporters: Supporters say making the VA dental insurance plan permanent means veterans and their family members enrolled in VA health care will no longer risk losing this coverage if Congress does not renew it each year.

Supporters say extending travel payment coverage through September 2022 helps veterans who use Vet Centers get reimbursed for the cost of getting to their appointments, removing a barrier to mental health and readjustment care.

Supporters say allowing the VA to accept donated land or buildings from state and local governments through December 2026 gives the VA more options to expand facilities without spending federal construction dollars.
critics: Critics say making the dental insurance plan permanent removes Congress's ability to review whether the program is working before deciding to continue funding it.
Critics say the travel reimbursement extension only runs through September 2022, meaning Vet Center patients face uncertainty about whether this benefit will continue after that date.

Critics say the donation authority for real property runs only through December 2026, which may not give the VA enough time to complete agreements with state and local governments for larger or more complex properties.

117-hr-5119.one_liner: Give tribal governments more time to spend COVID relief money
provisions: The Coronavirus Relief Fund gave tribal governments money to cover costs from the COVID-19 pandemic.
The old deadline to spend that money was December 31, 2021; this bill moves the deadline to December 30, 2022.
Tribal governments can use the money for costs like public health services, emergency response, and other needs tied to the pandemic.
This bill applies only to tribal governments — not to states or cities.

supporters: Supporters say moving the spending deadline from December 31, 2021 to December 30, 2022 gives tribal governments more time to use Coronavirus Relief Fund money for public health services and emergency response that are still needed.

Supporters say tribal governments faced unique challenges during COVID-19 and this bill lets them spend the money on costs directly tied to the pandemic without losing access to funds they were already given.
Supporters say since this bill only applies to tribal governments — not states or cities — it targets a specific group that may need more time to complete pandemic recovery work.
critics: Critics say extending the deadline to December 30, 2022 keeps funds open longer than other government groups are allowed, which some argue creates unequal treatment compared to states and cities that had earlier cutoff dates.

Critics say allowing more time to spend Coronavirus Relief Fund money past the original December 31, 2021 deadline makes it harder to track whether the spending is still tied to actual COVID-19 pandemic needs.

117-hr-5221.one_liner: Require more federal health agencies to meet with urban Native American groups
provisions: Right now, only the Indian Health Service must meet with groups that represent Native Americans living in cities.
This bill requires the Department of Health and Human Services to make sure IHS and other HHS offices meet with those groups.
These meetings must cover health care rules under the Indian Health Care Improvement Act and other federal health laws.

supporters: Supporters say the bill fixes a gap by requiring all offices within the Department of Health and Human Services — not just the Indian Health Service — to meet with urban Indian organizations, giving city-based Native Americans more ways to shape federal health rules.

Supporters say American Indians and Alaska Natives living in cities are covered by the Indian Health Care Improvement Act and other federal health laws, but right now most HHS offices have no duty to hear from urban Native groups before making decisions under those laws.

Supporters say adding the full HHS department to the meeting requirement means urban Indian organizations can raise concerns about a wider range of health care programs, not just those run by the Indian Health Service.
