critics: Critics say the bill does not include any funding to help the many offices within HHS carry out the new meeting requirement, which could leave agencies without the staff or budget to hold these conferences.
Critics say the bill does not set a clear schedule or process for how HHS offices must confer with urban Indian organizations, which may make the new requirement hard to enforce.

Critics say adding multiple HHS agencies to the meeting requirement — beyond the Indian Health Service, which already has experience with these groups — could create confusion about which office is responsible for following up on urban Native health concerns.

117-hr-5290.one_liner: Keep the government's livestock price reporting program running through 2022
provisions: Keeps a USDA program running that requires meat companies to report the prices they pay for cattle, hogs, and other livestock
The program was set to expire and this bill lets it continue through the year ending September 2022

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps a USDA program running that requires meat companies to report the prices they pay for cattle, hogs, and other livestock, giving farmers access to real market price data.
Supporters say extending the program through FY2022 means cattle and hog producers can continue to see what prices packers are paying, which helps them decide when and where to sell their animals.
critics: Critics say requiring meat companies to report their purchase prices to the USDA forces them to share business information that could be used by competitors.
Critics say continued reporting requirements could reduce the prices meat companies offer to cattle and hog producers, since companies may adjust bids to avoid revealing their full buying strategies.

117-hr-550.one_liner: Fund states to upgrade vaccine record systems and set new data standards
provisions: The Department of Health and Human Services must create a plan to improve the databases that track who has gotten which vaccines.
HHS must set rules for what technology and data formats these tracking systems must use.
HHS gives money to state and local health departments to upgrade their vaccine record systems.
Health departments that receive the money must use the data formats HHS requires.
HHS must send a report to Congress on what it has done.

supporters: Supporters say requiring state and local health departments to use the same data formats set by HHS would let vaccine records be shared across states, so doctors can see what shots a patient has already received.
Supporters say the grant program would give state and local health departments money to upgrade vaccine tracking systems that public health officials say often cannot communicate with each other.
Supporters say requiring HHS to send a report to Congress would create accountability and show where gaps in vaccine record systems still exist.
critics: Critics say the rule that health departments must use HHS-chosen data formats to receive grant money gives the federal government control over how states manage their own health records.
Critics say linking vaccine records across state and local health departments through a shared system could put the personal medical data of millions of people at risk if the system is breached.

Critics say the bill does not set a specific dollar amount for the grants, leaving state and local health departments without a clear promise of how much money they would receive to complete the required upgrades.

117-hr-5487.one_liner: Fund programs to collect data and spread awareness about stillbirths
provisions: Lets the Department of Health and Human Services give money to states and organizations to track and collect data on stillbirths.
Requires the Department of Health and Human Services to create guidelines for health departments on how to collect stillbirth data.
Requires the Department of Health and Human Services to create educational materials about stillbirths and make them free to the public.
Creates a training program for doctors who do after-birth examinations on stillborn babies.
Requires the Surgeon General to publish a report with guidelines about stillbirths and what raises the risk of one.

supporters: Supporters say the HHS grants for stillbirth surveillance would give states and organizations funding to track data that the U.S. does not currently collect in a standard way, which could help researchers find patterns in why stillbirths happen.

Supporters say the fellowship program to train doctors in perinatal autopsy would increase the number of specialists who can examine stillborn babies and find causes, since that field currently has too few trained doctors.

Supporters say the Surgeon General's report on stillbirth risk factors, combined with free HHS educational materials, would give pregnant people and their doctors clear information about what raises the risk of a stillbirth.
critics: Critics say the bill does not name a specific dollar amount for the HHS grants, which means Congress has not committed funding and states may not receive enough money to build new data collection systems.

Critics say requiring HHS to create guidelines for health departments, produce public educational materials, and run a fellowship program all at the same time adds new federal duties without a clear timeline or budget for each one.

Critics say the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention already collects some birth and death data from states, and new HHS guidelines for vital statistics units could create overlapping or conflicting reporting rules for local health departments.

117-hr-5551.one_liner: Keep CDC programs running that study and prevent birth defects in children
provisions: Keeps the CDC's National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities funded through the year starting October 2025.
The center runs programs for babies born with birth defects, children with developmental disabilities, and people with blood disorders.
Keeps a CDC program running that studies how folic acid helps prevent birth defects and spreads information about it.

supporters: Supporters say keeping the National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities funded through October 2026 lets the CDC continue programs that help babies born with birth defects, children with developmental disabilities, and people with blood disorders.
Supporters say the folic acid program, which studies how the vitamin prevents birth defects and shares that information with families, would keep running without interruption under this bill.
critics: Critics say the bill only keeps programs funded through October 2026, a short window that forces Congress to revisit the issue quickly and leaves families and researchers who depend on these CDC programs uncertain about the future.

Critics say the bill does not set specific funding amounts for the National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities, meaning the center's budget could be reduced even while the programs are technically kept alive.

117-hr-546.one_liner: Stop the Justice Department from reading messages between prisoners and their lawyers
provisions: The Justice Department cannot read private electronic messages between a person in prison and their lawyer.
This covers emails and other digital messages that are protected by attorney-client privilege.
Attorney-client privilege means a person has the right to speak privately with their lawyer without the government listening.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects attorney-client privilege by stopping the Justice Department from reading emails and digital messages between people in prison and their lawyers.
Supporters say that without this law, incarcerated people cannot speak freely with their lawyers, which makes it harder to get a fair defense in court.
Supporters say digital messages between lawyers and their clients should have the same protections as in-person conversations, since many people in prison can only reach their lawyers by email.
critics: Critics say blocking the Justice Department from monitoring electronic messages between inmates and lawyers could make it harder to catch cases where the privilege is being misused to pass illegal information.
Critics say the bill does not spell out how prison staff will verify which messages are truly protected by attorney-client privilege before they are blocked from review.

117-hr-5434.one_liner: Keep federal road, transit, and safety funding running through October 2021
provisions: Keeps road, bus, and safety program funding at 2021 levels through October 31, 2021
Raises the spending cap for large freight and highway projects from $600 million to $700 million
Extends research into technology that stops drunk drivers from starting their cars through 2022
Keeps loan programs running for fixing up railroads near train stations through October 31, 2021
Extends funding for the Appalachian Regional Commission, a federal agency that helps rural communities in 13 states, through 2022
Guarantees federal workers get paid as soon as possible if the government runs out of approved spending authority and they are sent home or made to work without pay
Keeps two trust funds for boating safety and cleaning up underground gas tank leaks running through November 1, 2021

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps road, bus, and safety program funding running at 2021 levels through October 31, 2021, preventing a gap that would pause federal payments to states.
Supporters say raising the freight and highway project spending cap from $600 million to $700 million lets the Department of Transportation fund more large-scale projects in the same budget cycle.
Supporters say the bill guarantees federal workers get paid as soon as possible if a funding lapse forces them home or makes them work without pay.
critics: Critics say extending funding only through October 31, 2021 means Congress will need to act again in weeks, creating repeated uncertainty for state and local transportation agencies.
Critics say holding highway and transit funding at 2021 levels does not account for changes in construction costs, leaving states with the same dollar amounts to cover their programs.

Critics say the bill raises the freight project spending cap to $700 million without adding new oversight rules, giving DOT more money to commit to large projects under the same existing approval process.

117-hr-5561.one_liner: Keep funding hearing screening and early care programs for newborns and young children
provisions: Keeps money flowing to federal programs that test newborns' hearing in hospitals
Funds services that help families get early care when a baby is found to be deaf or hard of hearing
Extends this funding through the year starting October 2025
Supports three federal agencies — HRSA, CDC, and NIDCD — in running these programs

supporters: Supporters say reauthorizing HRSA funding through FY2026 keeps newborn hearing screening programs running in hospitals, so babies born deaf or hard of hearing are identified before they go home.

Supporters say the early intervention services funded by this bill help families connect with speech and language support in the first few years of life, when language learning is easiest for young children.
Supporters say having HRSA, CDC, and NIDCD all working on this issue means more data, better tracking, and stronger outreach to families who might not know help is available.
critics: Critics say the bill funds three separate federal agencies — HRSA, CDC, and NIDCD — to run related programs, and argue that overlapping agency roles can lead to duplicated spending without clear results.

Critics say most states already run newborn hearing screening programs on their own, so extending federal reauthorization through FY2026 adds a layer of federal oversight to work that states are already doing.
Critics say the bill does not set new performance goals or require agencies to show whether current programs are actually getting more children into early intervention services.

117-hr-5574.one_liner: Require TSA to make airport signs and materials easier to understand for all travelers
provisions: The TSA must create a plan to make materials at major airports easier to read and understand.
The plan must cover people who speak languages other than English.
The plan must also cover people who are blind, have low vision, or are deaf or hard of hearing.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would help foreign language speakers at major airports by requiring the TSA to create a plan for materials in languages other than English, which could reduce confusion and missed security steps.
Supporters say travelers who are blind, have low vision, or are deaf or hard of hearing would benefit because the TSA would have to plan ways to make airport security information accessible to them.
Supporters say requiring a written plan holds the TSA accountable for actually reaching travelers who may not understand current English-only or visual-only materials.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires the TSA to develop a plan, not to carry one out, meaning no materials may actually change for foreign language speakers or people with disabilities.
Critics say the bill does not include a deadline or funding amount, so there is no guarantee the TSA will complete the plan or have money to put it into action.
Critics say the bill does not define which languages must be covered or how many airports must be included, leaving the scope of the plan unclear.

117-hr-5608.one_liner: Create a USDA program to study and manage a disease killing deer, elk, and moose
provisions: Creates a program inside the USDA to research and manage Chronic Wasting Disease, which is a deadly brain disease spreading through deer, elk, and moose herds across the country.
The USDA works with state and tribal wildlife agencies, universities, and research centers to study how the disease spreads, how animals resist it, and how to detect it.
The USDA works with state and tribal agencies to build and carry out plans to control the disease in their local animal populations.
The USDA creates materials to teach the public about the disease and how to help stop it from spreading.
The USDA asks the public for ideas on how to improve the rules for certifying that deer herds are free of the disease.

supporters: Supporters say the new USDA program would bring together state wildlife agencies, tribal agencies, and universities to study how CWD spreads through deer, elk, and moose herds — creating a shared national effort that no single state can run alone.

Supporters say requiring USDA to help states and tribes build local management plans would give smaller or less-funded wildlife agencies real tools to control the disease before it reaches more herds.

Supporters say the public education materials and the process to update herd certification standards would help hunters and ranchers identify safe animals and reduce the risk of spreading CWD across state lines.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a specific dollar amount for the USDA program, so there is no guarantee that state and tribal agencies will receive enough funding to actually carry out management plans.

Critics say the bill only requires USDA to 'offer' agreements with state and tribal agencies — it does not require those agencies to join, which may lead to uneven action in states where CWD is already spreading fast.
Critics say asking the public for ideas on herd certification standards is not the same as changing those standards, because the bill does not require USDA to act on any of the feedback it receives.

117-hr-5609.one_liner: Create a public database of contracts between cattle buyers and ranchers
provisions: The USDA must build and keep a public list of every type of contract that large meat-buying companies offer to cattle ranchers.
The list must include any bonus or penalty payment schedules tied to those contracts.
The USDA must publish updates to the list every week or every month, depending on the type of contract.
Meat-buying companies that refuse to share accurate contract information with the USDA can be fined or penalized.
The government must give grants to universities and research stations to teach ranchers how to use the contract and market information.

supporters: Supporters say the USDA's public list of packer contracts, including bonus and penalty payment schedules, would let cattle ranchers compare deals before signing, since ranchers currently have no way to see what contracts other producers are being offered.

Supporters say that requiring meat-buying companies to share accurate contract data with the USDA — under threat of fines — would reduce the information gap between large packers and individual ranchers.
Supporters say the grants to universities and research stations would give ranchers the training they need to actually use the contract and market data that gets published.
critics: Critics say the bill puts a new reporting burden on meat-buying companies by requiring them to submit detailed contract and payment schedule information to the USDA on a weekly or monthly basis, which could raise their operating costs.

Critics say that publishing contract terms publicly could reduce packers' ability to offer ranchers customized deals, since competitors would be able to see pricing structures that are currently kept private.

117-hr-567.one_liner: Give legal backing to a U.S. counterterrorism program in Africa that has run since 2005
provisions: Turns the Trans-Sahara Counterterrorism Partnership Program into an official program backed by law — it has operated since 2005 without one
The State Department runs the program, working with the Defense Department and USAID
The program works with countries in North and West Africa on fighting terrorism — including training their militaries, securing borders, and pushing back on terrorist messaging online and in media
The State Department must write a 5-year plan covering what the program will do in both the Sahel and Maghreb regions of Africa
The State Department must tell Congress before spending money on the program
The State Department must send Congress a yearly report on what the program did

supporters: Supporters say giving the program statutory authority means it can no longer be quietly shut down or changed without Congress knowing, since the State Department must notify Congress before spending money and send a yearly report on what the program did.

Supporters say the required 5-year plan forces the State Department to set clear goals for both the Sahel and Maghreb regions, so it is easier to see if training foreign militaries and securing borders is actually working.

Supporters say coordinating all U.S. counterterrorism programs in North and West Africa under one program — run by the State Department with the Defense Department and USAID — reduces overlap and makes the effort more organized.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a spending limit, so Congress has no cap on how much the State Department can obligate for military training, border security, and media programs across North and West Africa.

Critics say the rule that activities must only happen where there is 'adequate partner country commitment' is not defined in the bill, giving the State Department wide power to decide which countries qualify with no clear standard.
Critics say the program has run since 2005 without a law behind it, and the bill does not require a review of what the program achieved in those 16 years before locking it into permanent law.

117-hr-5720.one_liner: Require federal judges to report stock trades and post their financial disclosures online
provisions: Federal judges must file a report within 45 days of buying, selling, or trading stocks, bonds, or other investments worth more than $1,000.
The U.S. Courts office must build a public website where people can search, sort, and download these financial reports.
Reports must be posted online within 90 days of when they are due.
If a judge's personal safety could be at risk from sharing certain information, that information can be kept private.

supporters: Supporters say the 45-day reporting rule for stock trades over $1,000 would let the public quickly find out if a judge has a financial interest in a case they are deciding.
Supporters say the searchable public website would make it easier for journalists and citizens to look up a judge's financial records without filing paper requests.
Supporters say the safety exception, which lets judges keep certain personal details private, means the law protects judges while still requiring disclosure.
critics: Critics say the 90-day window for posting reports online is too slow, since a judge could rule on a case involving a stock they own before the public ever sees the report.
Critics say building and maintaining a new searchable federal database creates an unfunded technology cost that the Administrative Office of U.S. Courts would have to absorb.
Critics say judges who hear sensitive national security cases may feel the disclosure rules, even with the safety exception, put their families at risk of being identified and targeted.

117-hr-654.one_liner: Let some anti-drug community groups skip a funding match requirement
provisions: Groups that get federal money to reduce drug use among kids normally have to raise matching funds from their community.
This bill lets the program skip that matching requirement for groups that cannot raise those funds because of COVID-19.
The program must confirm a group truly cannot raise the money before waiving the requirement.

supporters: Supporters say community coalitions that fight youth drug use should not lose federal grants just because COVID-19 made it harder to raise local matching funds.

Supporters say the bill protects groups already doing drug prevention work by letting the Drug-Free Communities Support Program waive the matching requirement only after confirming a group truly cannot raise the money.
Supporters say keeping these coalitions funded during the pandemic helps prevent a rise in substance use among kids at a time when schools and community programs were disrupted.
critics: Critics say waiving matching fund requirements removes a check that ensures local communities are invested in the program, which could lead to less accountability for how federal grant money is spent.
Critics say the bill does not set a clear dollar limit on how much the federal government could end up covering without community matching funds, which may increase costs to taxpayers.

Critics say the program's ability to simply confirm a group 'cannot raise funds' is a vague standard that could be applied too broadly, allowing groups to skip matching requirements even when local fundraising is possible.

117-hr-8.one_liner: Require background checks for all private gun transfers between individuals
provisions: Right now, background checks are only required when buying a gun from a licensed store. This bill adds the same requirement to private transfers between individuals.
To transfer a gun privately, the person giving the gun must first bring it to a licensed gun dealer, who runs a background check on the person receiving it.
Some transfers are exempt — for example, a gun given as a gift between spouses.

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a gap in current law by requiring background checks for private gun transfers between individuals, not just purchases from licensed stores.

Supporters say people who are legally barred from owning guns — such as those with felony convictions — can currently get firearms through private transfers with no check at all, and this bill would block that.
Supporters say routing private transfers through a licensed dealer gives law enforcement a record of transactions between strangers, the same way store sales are tracked today.
critics: Critics say the bill requires gun owners to involve a licensed dealer in private transfers, adding steps and potential fees even for simple exchanges between neighbors or acquaintances.
Critics say the bill does not specify what dealers may charge to process these transfers, meaning the cost to comply is unknown and could vary widely from person to person.

Critics say the spousal gift exemption in the bill shows the law treats some private transfers differently than others, and critics argue the line between exempt and non-exempt transfers is not clearly defined.

117-hr-5763.one_liner: Keep federal road, transit, rail, and safety programs funded through December 2021
provisions: Keeps federal funding for road, transit, rail, and highway safety programs at their 2021 levels through December 3, 2021.
Lets the Highway Trust Fund, Sport Fish and Boating Trust Fund, and Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund keep spending money through December 4, 2021.

supporters: Supporters say extending FY2021 funding levels through December 3, 2021 keeps road, transit, rail, and highway safety programs running without a gap in service.

Supporters say allowing the Highway Trust Fund, Sport Fish and Boating Trust Fund, and Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund to keep spending through December 4, 2021 prevents construction projects and cleanup work from stopping mid-stream.
critics: Critics say extending funding only through December 3, 2021 gives Congress just weeks to pass a long-term transportation bill, creating pressure that may lead to another short-term patch instead of a full plan.
Critics say holding programs at FY2021 spending levels means no new money for roads, transit, or safety improvements during the extension period, leaving unmet needs unaddressed.

117-hr-6.one_liner: Give green cards to non-citizens who came to the US as children
provisions: Non-citizens who entered the US as children and have lived here since January 1, 2021 can apply for a 10-year green card.
To qualify, they must pass a background check and be in school or have completed a school program.
Children of certain visa holders — such as people on work visas — can also qualify.
People with TPS (a program that pauses deportation during foreign crises) or DED (a program that delays deportation for certain groups) can apply for a full permanent green card within 3 years.
After 10 years, people who got a green card under this bill can make it permanent by finishing school, joining the military, or holding a job.
Information from these applications cannot be used to find or deport people.
States can offer in-state college tuition to undocumented students without having to offer that same discount to all U.S. citizens.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives people who entered the U.S. as children and have lived here since January 1, 2021 a 10-year green card, letting them stay legally in a country they grew up in.
Supporters say people with TPS or DED status — who have been waiting for years while their home countries face crises — could get a full permanent green card within 3 years of the bill passing.
Supporters say the rule blocking states from offering in-state tuition to undocumented students would be removed, making college more affordable for students who have lived in a state for years.
critics: Critics say allowing children of certain work visa holders to qualify expands the bill beyond its stated focus on long-term U.S. residents, adding a group that was not part of the original DACA program.

Critics say the provision blocking the government from using application information for deportation cases limits immigration enforcement tools, even for people who may not qualify or who submit false information.

Critics say letting states offer in-state tuition to undocumented students without extending that same benefit to U.S. citizens from other states creates an unequal system that favors non-citizens over American nationals.

117-hr-983.one_liner: Make it a federal crime to steal veterans' benefits
provisions: Creates a new federal crime for running a scam to steal someone's veterans' benefits.
Anyone caught doing this can go to prison for up to five years, pay a fine, or both.
The law covers both completing the scam and trying to do it.

supporters: Supporters say the bill creates a federal crime that specifically targets scams against veterans' benefits, filling a gap they say exists in current federal law.
Supporters say covering both completed scams and attempts means prosecutors can charge someone who tried to steal benefits even if the fraud was stopped before it finished.
Supporters say the up-to-five-year prison term gives federal prosecutors a tool to seek meaningful sentences in veterans' benefits fraud cases.
critics: Critics say existing federal fraud statutes — like mail fraud and wire fraud — already make it a crime to run the same kinds of schemes this bill targets, making a new law unnecessary.
Critics say the bill sets no minimum prison sentence, which means a court could convict someone under this law and still impose little or no prison time.
Critics say the bill does not specify which veterans' benefits programs are covered, which could create confusion in court about how broadly the law applies.

117-hr-941.one_liner: Renew federal funding for bone marrow and cord blood transplant programs through 2026
provisions: Keeps a federal program running that helps patients find donors for bone marrow and umbilical cord blood transplants.
The program is funded through the end of the government's budget year in 2026.
Requires the Department of Health and Human Services to review research on treatments using adult stem cells and tissue from births.
Requires a government watchdog office to write a report on how many workers are trained in regenerative medicine.

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps the C.W. Bill Young Cell Transplantation Program running through FY2026, which connects patients with bone marrow and umbilical cord blood donors when transplants are their only treatment path.
Supporters say requiring HHS to review adult stem cell and birthing tissue research gives the federal government an updated picture of which therapies have enough evidence to scale.
Supporters say the GAO report on the regenerative medicine workforce will show whether the U.S. has enough trained workers to meet patient demand for these treatments.
critics: Critics say extending the C.W. Bill Young Cell Transplantation Program through FY2026 adds years of federal spending without a review of whether the program's donor-matching outcomes justify the cost.
Critics say the HHS science review and GAO workforce report create new government reporting requirements but do not include binding rules that would require agencies to act on what they find.

117-hr-803.one_liner: Set aside lands in Colorado as protected wilderness areas
provisions: Turns certain federal lands in Colorado into protected wilderness areas, which means no roads, buildings, or motorized vehicles are allowed there
Adds some of those lands to the existing West Elk Wilderness area
Keeps allowing competitive running races that are already permitted in the Redcloud Peak and Handies Peak areas
Lets the Colorado Army National Guard continue flying training missions over the new wilderness areas
Creates two new wilderness areas — Pisgah East and Pisgah West — once any current uses that are not allowed in wilderness stop
Secures federal water rights for some of the new wilderness areas
Requires the Defense Department to study how expanding wilderness areas across the Western U.S. affects military flight training

supporters: Supporters say the bill would protect federal lands in Colorado from roads, buildings, and motorized vehicles by adding them to the National Wilderness Preservation System, keeping those areas undeveloped for future generations.
Supporters say the bill secures federal water rights for the new wilderness areas, which prevents those water sources from being claimed or diverted for other uses.

Supporters say the bill lets the Colorado Army National Guard keep flying training missions over the new wilderness areas and requires the Defense Department to study how wilderness expansion affects military flight training across the Western U.S.
critics: Critics say banning roads and motorized vehicles in the new wilderness areas would block off-road vehicle users, ranchers, and timber workers from land they currently use.

Critics say creating the Pisgah East and Pisgah West wilderness areas depends on all current non-conforming uses stopping first, which could create long delays and legal disputes over when those uses have fully ended.

Critics say requiring a Defense Department study on how Western wilderness expansion affects military aviation training suggests the bill could limit where the military trains, which may hurt readiness before the study is even complete.

117-hr-842.one_liner: Expand union and worker protections under federal labor law
provisions: More workers — including some contractors and people previously counted as supervisors — would get the same union protections as other employees.
Workers can join strikes started by workers at a different company, and their union cannot be sued for supporting that strike.
Union contracts can require all workers covered by the contract to pay union fees, even in states that currently have laws blocking this.
Employers cannot fire or penalize workers for going on strike, or permanently replace them with other workers.
Employers cannot require workers to attend meetings designed to talk them out of joining a union.
Employers cannot make workers sign papers giving up their right to join a class-action lawsuit.
Companies that break these rules can face fines and court orders from the National Labor Relations Board.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would protect more workers by extending union rights to contractors and some supervisors who are currently excluded from labor law protections.
Supporters say banning employer-required anti-union meetings and permanent strike replacements would stop companies from pressuring workers who try to organize.
Supporters say allowing union contracts to require fee payments from all covered workers — even in states with laws against it — would give unions more stable funding to represent those workers.
critics: Critics say letting union contracts override state fee laws would eliminate worker protections in the 27 states that currently allow workers to opt out of paying union fees.

Critics say expanding secondary strikes — where workers can join strikes at a different company — could cause work stoppages to spread beyond the original employer dispute, affecting businesses that are not part of the conflict.

Critics say new fines and court orders from the National Labor Relations Board against companies that break these rules would increase legal costs and uncertainty for employers, especially small businesses.

117-hr-826.one_liner: Require reports to Congress on reuniting Korean Americans with family in North Korea
provisions: The State Department must report to Congress on talks with South Korea about reuniting Korean Americans with family in North Korea.
A special government official focused on North Korean human rights must also report to Congress.
That official's reports cover conversations held with Korean Americans who have family in North Korea.
Both sets of reports must happen more than once — not just a single time.

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires the State Department to report to Congress more than once on talks with South Korea about reuniting Korean Americans with family in North Korea, keeping the issue active over time.
Supporters say requiring a special government official on North Korean human rights to also report to Congress creates direct accountability for progress on family separation.
Supporters say the reports must include conversations with Korean Americans who have family in North Korea, giving this group a formal voice in U.S. policy discussions.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires reports and does not include any steps to reunite families separated between the U.S. and North Korea.
Critics say there is no requirement for South Korea or North Korea to respond to U.S. consultations, meaning the reporting process may produce no results for Korean American families.
Critics say the bill does not set a timeline or minimum number of required reports, which could allow years to pass between updates to Congress.

117-hres-134.one_liner: Condemn the 2021 military takeover in Burma and call for release of detained leaders
provisions: Says the U.S. opposes the military takeover that happened in Burma on February 1, 2021
Calls on Burma's military to free everyone who was arrested during the takeover
Calls on Burma's military to restore phone and internet access that was shut down
Calls on Burma's military to give power back to the elected civilian government

supporters: Supporters say the resolution puts the U.S. on record opposing the February 1, 2021 military takeover and calling for the release of all people arrested during the coup, including elected leaders like Aung San Suu Kyi.

Supporters say requiring Burma's military to restore phone and internet access is important because cutting communications kept millions of people from knowing what was happening or organizing peacefully.
Supporters say calling on the military to return power to the elected civilian government backs the results of Burma's November 2020 election, where the military's party lost badly.
critics: Critics say a resolution with no legal force or penalties gives the Burmese military no real reason to free detainees or restore civilian rule.
Critics say the U.S. calling on Burma's military to act could push them closer to China or Russia, making it harder to pressure them through international coalitions.
Critics say the resolution does not include any specific actions — like sanctions or aid cuts — that would back up its demands to restore communications and return power to elected officials.

117-hres-1.one_liner: Let the Speaker swear in all newly elected members of Congress
provisions: The Speaker of the House gives the oath of office to all newly elected members of Congress.
Every newly elected member must take the oath before they can vote or do any official work.
This happens at the start of every new Congress, usually in early January.
This is a standard step to open a new Congress, not a change in law.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution lets the Speaker give the oath of office to all Representatives-elect, which is required before any of them can vote or do official work.
Supporters say this is a standard step taken at the start of every new Congress, usually in early January, to formally open the legislative session.
Supporters say without this resolution, newly elected members would have no legal authority to act on behalf of their districts.

117-hres-147.one_liner: Set the rules for debating two bills in the House
provisions: Sets the time limit and debate rules for a bill that would protect certain lands in Colorado as wilderness
Sets the time limit and debate rules for a bill that would ban discrimination based on sex, gender identity, and sexual orientation
This is a procedural step — it does not pass either bill, it just controls how the House will discuss them

supporters: Supporters say this rule gives the House a structured way to debate H.R. 803, which would add Colorado land to the National Wilderness Preservation System, and H.R. 5, which would ban discrimination based on sex, gender identity, and sexual orientation.
Supporters say bringing both bills to the floor through this rule means members get a set amount of time to make their case for each bill before the full House votes.

Supporters say setting debate rules for H.R. 5 is needed because federal law does not currently include gender identity and sexual orientation as protected categories in areas like employment and housing.
critics: Critics say the debate rules limit how many changes members can propose to H.R. 5, which would expand federal anti-discrimination law to cover gender identity and sexual orientation across schools, workplaces, and housing.
Critics say using a rule to fast-track H.R. 5 blocks members from offering amendments that would add religious liberty protections to the bill.
Critics say the rule prioritizes floor time for H.R. 803 and H.R. 5 over other bills, which means other legislation waits while the House debates these two measures.

117-hres-130.one_liner: Formally condemn China and Hong Kong for breaking rights promised to Hong Kong people
provisions: When Britain gave Hong Kong to China in 1997, China promised Hong Kong could keep its own laws and freedoms until at least 2047.
Starting in 2020, China and Hong Kong passed national security laws that limit what people in Hong Kong can say, protest, and do.
Under these laws, people can be arrested for things that were allowed before 2020.
Congress says these laws break the promises China made to Hong Kong's people and to the world.
This resolution is a formal statement — it does not create new US laws or change any rules.

supporters: Supporters say China broke its 1997 promise to let Hong Kong keep its own laws and freedoms until 2047, and Congress should go on record saying so.

Supporters say the national security laws passed starting in 2020 allow people in Hong Kong to be arrested for speech and protest that were legal before, and the US should formally condemn that change.
Supporters say this resolution sends a clear message to Hong Kong's people that the US recognizes their rights were taken away, even though the resolution does not create new US laws.
critics: Critics say this resolution is only a formal statement and does not change any US laws, impose costs on China, or create any new protections for people in Hong Kong.
Critics say that condemning China without pairing this statement with concrete policy action — like sanctions or trade rules — gives China no reason to change its behavior in Hong Kong.
Critics say the resolution could make it harder for the US and China to work together on other issues without offering any real help to the people of Hong Kong.

117-hres-101.one_liner: Set the federal government's spending and budget plan through 2030
provisions: Sets a budget for the federal government for the year starting October 2020.
Outlines spending and revenue targets for each year from 2022 through 2030.
Includes instructions for lawmakers to pass separate bills that could add to the national deficit.

supporters: Supporters say setting spending and revenue targets for each year from 2022 through 2030 gives Congress a ten-year framework to coordinate how money is raised and spent across the full federal budget.

Supporters say the reconciliation instructions allow lawmakers to pass separate spending bills with a simple majority in the Senate instead of 60 votes, making it faster to respond to economic needs tied to the FY2021 budget year.
critics: Critics say the reconciliation instructions are written specifically to allow bills that increase the national deficit, which adds to federal debt at a time when annual deficits have already grown sharply.
Critics say budget targets set through 2030 are not legally binding on future Congresses, so the ten-year spending and revenue levels in this resolution carry no enforcement mechanism.

117-hres-188.one_liner: Set the rules for debating three bills on workers and gun checks
provisions: Sets the time and debate rules for voting on a bill that changes how unions and workers can organize
Sets the rules for voting on a bill that requires a background check for every gun sale, including private sales
Sets the rules for voting on a bill that closes a gap that lets gun sales go through before a background check is finished

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows a vote on H.R. 842, which would change rules under the National Labor Relations Act to make it easier for workers to organize and form unions.
Supporters say this rule brings H.R. 8 to a vote, which would extend background check requirements to private gun sales — a category of sales currently not covered by federal law.
Supporters say this rule enables a vote on H.R. 1446, which would close a gap that lets gun dealers transfer a firearm to a buyer before a background check result comes back.
critics: Critics say this rule packages a labor bill (H.R. 842) and two gun bills (H.R. 8 and H.R. 1446) together, which limits the debate time available for each separate topic.

Critics say the rule advances H.R. 8, which would require private gun sellers to process sales through a licensed dealer to run checks — adding steps and potential costs for individual sellers who currently face no such federal requirement.

Critics say the rule moves H.R. 1446 forward, which would extend the background check window from 3 business days to 10, delaying firearm transfers for buyers whose checks have not yet returned a result.

117-hres-179.one_liner: Set debate rules for two bills on voting access and police reform
provisions: This bill sets the rules for how the House will debate H.R. 1.
H.R. 1 covers changing voting rules, limiting campaign money, and adding ethics rules for government workers.
This bill also sets the rules for how the House will debate H.R. 1280.
H.R. 1280 covers holding police accountable in court and collecting data on officer misconduct.
Passing this bill does not make either H.R. 1 or H.R. 1280 law — it only decides how each bill gets debated.

supporters: Supporters say this rule gives both H.R. 1, which covers voting access and campaign finance, and H.R. 1280, which covers police accountability, a floor vote in the House.
Supporters say structured debate rules for H.R. 1 ensure that changes to voting and ethics laws get a fair hearing without being blocked before a vote.
Supporters say setting debate rules for H.R. 1280 allows the House to move forward on proposals to collect data on officer misconduct and hold police accountable in court.
critics: Critics say this rule limits how much time members can spend debating H.R. 1, which covers broad changes to voting rules, campaign money limits, and ethics requirements for government workers.
Critics say combining debate rules for two separate bills into one procedural vote pressures members to approve the process for both, even if they only support one.
Critics say the rule for H.R. 1 does not allow enough amendments, which restricts members from changing specific provisions before the bill goes to a final vote.

117-hres-198.one_liner: Set the rules for how Congress will vote on a budget bill
provisions: Sets the time limit and debate rules for the House to vote on a budget bill that came back from the Senate
Decides how long members of Congress can speak before the vote happens
Controls what changes or additions can be made to the bill before the final vote

supporters: Supporters say the time limit on debate allows the House to vote on the Senate amendment to H.R. 1319 without extended delay, moving the reconciliation process forward.
Supporters say the rule controls what changes can be made before the final vote, keeping the Senate amendment intact and avoiding a second round of changes between chambers.
Supporters say setting clear debate rules gives all members equal time to speak before the House votes on the amended bill.
critics: Critics say the debate time limits set by this rule reduce how long House members can speak on the Senate amendment to H.R. 1319, cutting short discussion on a budget bill.
Critics say the rule blocks most amendments from being added before the vote, removing the House's ability to change the bill after it returned from the Senate.
Critics say limiting debate and amendment options concentrates procedural control in House leadership rather than the full membership.

117-hres-21.one_liner: Call on the Vice President to declare the President unable to serve using the 25th Amendment
provisions: Calls on Vice President Mike Pence to use Section 4 of the 25th Amendment, a part of the Constitution that lets the Vice President and Cabinet declare the President unable to do his job.
Calls on Pence to gather the heads of the Cabinet departments to vote on whether the President can carry out his duties.
If that group agrees, Pence would take over and act as President.
Requires Pence to send written notice to the top leader of the Senate and the Speaker of the House that he is taking over as Acting President.

supporters: Supporters say Section 4 of the 25th Amendment was written for situations where the President is unable to carry out his duties, and that Congress has the right to call on the Vice President and Cabinet to use it.

Supporters say the bill asks Pence to gather the heads of all Cabinet departments to vote on whether the President can carry out his duties, which follows the exact steps laid out in the Constitution.

Supporters say if the Cabinet agrees, Pence would send written notice to the top-ranking senator and the Speaker of the House before taking over as Acting President, keeping Congress informed as the law requires.
critics: Critics say Section 4 of the 25th Amendment was meant for cases where the President has a physical or mental condition that stops him from doing his job, not for political disagreements about how he leads.
Critics say Congress cannot force the Vice President to call a Cabinet meeting or take over as Acting President, because the decision belongs to the executive branch alone under the Constitution.
Critics say this resolution sets a risky example by using a medical and legal tool to try to remove a President based on how members of Congress feel about his actions in office.

117-hres-166.one_liner: Set the rules for how the House debates and votes on H.R. 1319
provisions: This bill sets the rules for how the House of Representatives will debate H.R. 1319.
It controls how long lawmakers can speak and whether they can offer changes to the bill during debate.
It is a procedural step — it does not create or change any policy on its own.

supporters: Supporters say the rule sets clear time limits on how long lawmakers can speak, which helps the House move through debate on H.R. 1319 in an orderly way.
Supporters say controlling whether changes can be offered to the bill during debate keeps the process focused and prevents delays.
critics: Critics say limiting how long lawmakers can speak reduces the amount of time members have to explain their concerns about H.R. 1319 before a vote.
Critics say restricting the ability to offer changes during debate means all lawmakers have less opportunity to shape the final bill, regardless of their position on it.

117-hres-243.one_liner: Remove Representative Eric Swalwell from the House Intelligence Committee
provisions: Removes Representative Eric Swalwell from the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.
The House Intelligence Committee oversees U.S. spy agencies and gets access to classified national security information.
This is a House-only resolution — it does not go to the Senate or need the President's signature to take effect.

supporters: Supporters say the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence gives members access to classified information from U.S. spy agencies, and they argue Swalwell should not hold that access.

Supporters say this resolution takes effect with only a House vote — it does not need the Senate or the President — which they say makes it a proper use of the House's power to set its own committee membership.

Supporters say the Intelligence Committee's role overseeing classified national security programs makes it different from other committees, and they cite that difference as the specific reason Swalwell's removal is from this committee and not others.
critics: Critics say removing Swalwell from the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence reduces the number of members available to oversee U.S. spy agencies.
Critics say this resolution targets a Democratic member of Congress and does not point to a specific rule he violated or a formal investigative process that was followed.
Critics say the Intelligence Committee handles ongoing classified oversight work, and removing a sitting member mid-term disrupts that work without a stated finding of wrongdoing.

117-hres-303.one_liner: Set the rules for debating equal pay and workplace violence bills
provisions: Sets the time limits and voting rules for debating a bill that would change how workers can sue over unequal pay based on sex
Sets the time limits and voting rules for debating a bill that would require health care employers to make plans to stop workplace violence

supporters: Supporters say H.R. 7 would strengthen the Fair Labor Standards Act by giving women stronger legal tools to sue employers who pay them less than men for the same work.

Supporters say H.R. 1195 would require health care and social service employers to create written plans to prevent workplace violence, protecting nurses, social workers, and other staff who face high rates of on-the-job attacks.
Supporters say bringing both bills to the floor under set time limits gives all members a clear chance to vote on equal pay and worker safety rules without delay.
critics: Critics say the changes in H.R. 7 to how workers can file pay discrimination lawsuits could expose businesses to more legal costs and make it easier to bring cases that are hard to defend against.

Critics say the OSHA standard in H.R. 1195 would force health care employers — including small clinics and social service agencies — to spend money and staff time building and maintaining violence prevention programs, even if their workplaces have low risk.
Critics say using a procedural rule to limit debate time on both H.R. 7 and H.R. 1195 together reduces the chance for members to offer changes or amendments to either bill.

117-hres-275.one_liner: Condemn the 2021 Atlanta shootings and violence against Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders
provisions: The House says the March 16, 2021 shootings in Atlanta, Georgia were wrong and should not have happened.
Eight people were killed in those shootings.
The House says it will keep working against hate and violence toward Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders.
This resolution does not create any new laws or change any existing rules.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution formally recognizes the deaths of eight people killed in the March 16, 2021 Atlanta shootings, giving Congress an official record of condemnation.

Supporters say the House reaffirming its commitment to fight hate and violence against Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders responds to a rise in reported attacks on that community during 2020 and 2021.
Supporters say even without creating new laws, a formal statement from the House puts members on record standing against bigotry toward the AAPI community.
critics: Critics say the resolution creates no new laws and changes no existing rules, meaning it will not lead to any concrete action to prevent future violence.
Critics say the resolution calls the Atlanta shootings hate-motivated, but law enforcement at the time did not charge the shooter with a hate crime, making that label premature.
Critics say a House resolution with no policy provisions does not address the specific safety concerns of the Asian American and Pacific Islander community it claims to protect.

117-hres-233.one_liner: Set the rules for how Congress debates five separate bills
provisions: Decides how long Congress can debate a bill to renew protections for victims of domestic violence
Decides how long Congress can debate a bill on letting certain non-citizens stay in the country legally
Decides how long Congress can debate a bill on visas for farm workers
Decides how long Congress can debate a bill on stopping automatic cuts to government spending
Decides how long Congress can debate a proposal to remove the deadline for adding an equal rights amendment to the Constitution

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the House to debate H.R. 1620, the Violence Against Women Act reauthorization, which would restore federal protections and funding for domestic violence victims that have lapsed.

Supporters say the rule moves five bills to the floor at once—covering domestic violence, immigration status for certain non-citizens, farm worker visas, automatic spending cuts, and the ERA deadline—which lets Congress act on multiple priorities in one session.
Supporters say the rule sets debate time for H.R. 1868, which would stop automatic across-the-board cuts to government programs that would otherwise take effect without a vote.
critics: Critics say bundling five separate bills—on immigration, farm labor visas, domestic violence, spending, and the ERA—into one rule limits lawmakers' ability to debate or amend each issue on its own terms.

Critics say the rule controls how much time Congress gets to debate H.R. 6, which would grant legal status to certain non-citizen groups, and a restricted debate clock could block amendments that would change who qualifies.

Critics say setting a short debate window for H.J. Res. 17, which removes the ratification deadline for the Equal Rights Amendment, prevents full discussion of whether that deadline was legally binding under Article V of the Constitution.

117-hres-317.one_liner: Condemn China's treatment of Uyghurs and call on the President to act
provisions: States that China's government is responsible for ongoing abuses against Uyghurs and other minority groups
Calls these abuses genocide and crimes against humanity
Calls on the President to take steps to stop these actions

supporters: Supporters say formally naming China's actions against Uyghurs as genocide and crimes against humanity gives the U.S. government a legal and moral basis to pressure China through sanctions, trade limits, or diplomatic action.
Supporters say the resolution calls on the President to take direct steps to stop the abuses, which could lead to real policy changes that protect Uyghurs and other minority groups inside China.

Supporters say putting this on record in Congress sends a clear message to other countries that the U.S. will not stay silent about mass detention, forced labor, and cultural erasure targeting ethnic and religious minorities.
critics: Critics say the resolution does not include any specific policy tools, dollar amounts, or enforcement steps, so calling these acts genocide may not lead to any real change for Uyghurs on the ground.

Critics say labeling China's actions as genocide without a formal legal process or court ruling could weaken the word's legal meaning and set a precedent where Congress makes findings that belong to international courts.

Critics say the resolution's call for the President to act is vague — it does not name which actions, sanctions, or diplomatic steps should be taken, making it hard to hold the executive branch accountable.

117-hres-380.one_liner: Set the rules for debating two bills on debt collection and pregnancy workplace rights
provisions: Sets the time limits and debate rules for the House to vote on a bill about debt collection
Sets the time limits and debate rules for the House to vote on a bill about workplace rights for pregnant workers
This is a procedural step — it does not change any laws on its own

supporters: Supporters say this is a procedural vote that does not change any laws — it only sets the time and debate rules so the House can move forward on H.R. 2547, which deals with debt collection protections for consumers, students, servicemembers, and small businesses.

Supporters say allowing a vote on H.R. 1065 gives the House a chance to decide whether pregnant workers should get workplace accommodations — this procedural step is required before that debate can happen.
critics: Critics say that by setting the debate rules for H.R. 2547 and H.R. 1065, the majority party controls how much time is spent discussing these bills, which can limit the ability of members to offer changes or amendments.

Critics say procedural votes like this one are used to fast-track bills without enough public debate — in this case, moving two separate bills on debt collection and pregnancy accommodations through the House under one rule.

117-hres-331.one_liner: Formally censure a House member for public statements about a court trial
provisions: Censures Representative Maxine Waters, which is an official formal rebuke by the House of Representatives
The censure is tied to statements Waters made about the trial of Derek Chauvin, a former police officer
A censure does not remove a member from office but puts an official mark of disapproval on record

supporters: Supporters say Waters made public statements during the Chauvin trial urging protesters to "get more confrontational," and that these words from a sitting House member could have influenced the jury or inflamed tensions around an active criminal case.

Supporters say a formal censure — an official mark of disapproval on the House record — is the right response because it holds elected members accountable for statements made in their public role without removing her from office.
Supporters say the House has a duty to act when a member's words could be seen as interfering with a court proceeding, and a censure makes clear that such statements fall outside accepted conduct.
critics: Critics say the censure targets Representative Waters, a Black congresswoman, for encouraging protesters to "stay in the streets" and demand justice — speech they argue is protected and no different from what other members have said about high-profile cases.

Critics say a censure is a formal rebuke that would go on Waters' permanent House record, and that applying it here sets a standard that could be used to silence members who speak out on policing and racial justice issues.
Critics say the resolution does not point to any specific rule of the House that Waters broke, making the censure a political move rather than an enforcement of clear conduct standards.

117-hres-403.one_liner: Let the House vote on rare disease drug rules and condemn the Atlanta shootings
provisions: Sets the rules for how the House will debate and vote on two separate bills
One bill changes how long a drug company can be the only seller of a drug made for rare diseases
The other bill is a formal statement from the House condemning the March 16, 2021 shootings in Atlanta that killed 8 people
The condemnation statement says the House stands against hate and violence targeting Asian American and Pacific Islander people

supporters: Supporters say bringing H.R. 1629 to the floor gives Congress a chance to limit how long one drug company can be the only seller of a rare disease drug, which could lead to lower-cost options for patients who currently have no alternatives.

Supporters say scheduling H. Res. 275 for a vote lets the full House go on record against the March 16, 2021 shootings in Atlanta that killed 8 people, including 6 Asian women, sending a direct message against violence targeting the Asian American and Pacific Islander community.
critics: Critics say that shortening the period when one company is the only seller of an orphan drug — as H.R. 1629 would do — could make drug companies less willing to invest in developing treatments for rare diseases in the first place.

Critics say packaging the orphan drug bill and the Atlanta condemnation resolution into a single rule forces members to vote yes or no on both at once, which could block passage of one item because of disagreement with the other.

117-hres-330.one_liner: Set the House debate rules for three bills on D.C. statehood and immigration
provisions: Sets the terms for how the full House will debate a bill that would make Washington D.C. the 51st state
Sets the terms for how the full House will debate a bill about legal rights for people held at border checkpoints or inside immigration detention centers
Sets the terms for how the full House will debate a bill that would move the power to ban groups of non-citizens from entering the country from the president to Congress
This bill does not change any law itself — it only controls how and when the House can vote on these three other bills

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the full House to vote on H.R. 51, which would make Washington D.C. the 51st state and give its roughly 700,000 residents two senators and a voting member of Congress for the first time.
Supporters say this rule opens debate on H.R. 1573, which would set clear legal rights for people held at border checkpoints or inside CBP and ICE detention facilities.
Supporters say this rule lets the House vote on H.R. 1333, which would move the power to ban groups of non-citizens from the president alone to Congress, so elected lawmakers make that decision.
critics: Critics say this rule pushes forward H.R. 51, which they argue conflicts with the U.S. Constitution's requirement that the seat of the federal government not be part of any state.
Critics say this rule advances H.R. 1573, which they argue would add legal protections for people in detention that could slow down removals and border enforcement operations.

Critics say this rule moves H.R. 1333 to the floor, a bill that would take away the president's ability to quickly restrict entry of specific groups of non-citizens, which they say weakens the executive branch's power to respond to fast-moving national security threats.

117-hres-38.one_liner: Allow the House to vote on asking the VP to take over as acting President
provisions: This resolution sets the debate rules for H. Res. 21 in the House.
H. Res. 21 would ask Vice President Pence to use Section 4 of the 25th Amendment.
Under Section 4, the VP can temporarily act as President if the Cabinet says the President cannot serve.
The President keeps the title and can contest the declaration.
The resolution also lets the House fine any member who does not wear a mask on the floor.
The mask rule was announced on January 4, 2021 during a public health emergency.

supporters: Supporters say H. Res. 21 asks Vice President Pence to use Section 4 of the 25th Amendment, which lets the Cabinet temporarily transfer presidential power while allowing the President to keep his title and contest the declaration.
Supporters say Section 4 is designed for situations where the President cannot carry out his duties, and this resolution gives the House a formal process to urge that step.

Supporters say the mask fine rule enforces a public health policy announced on January 4, 2021, giving the Sergeant-at-Arms a way to hold members accountable during a declared public health emergency.
critics: Critics say Section 4 of the 25th Amendment was written for cases of medical incapacity, and using it here sets a new standard for when a VP can challenge a sitting President over conduct rather than health.

Critics say the mask fine provision gives the Speaker's office authority to charge members money for not following an announced policy, which critics argue limits members' independence on the House floor.
Critics say the resolution moves quickly through debate rules without enough time for members to fully review the process for invoking a constitutional transfer of executive power.

117-hres-479.one_liner: Set debate rules for a House vote on making Juneteenth a federal holiday
provisions: This resolution sets the rules for how the House of Representatives will debate S. 475.
S. 475 is a bill that would make Juneteenth National Independence Day a legal federal holiday.
The resolution controls how long members can speak on the bill and what changes can be offered during debate.

supporters: Supporters say S. 475 would add Juneteenth, June 19, to the list of legal federal holidays in title 5 of U.S. Code, giving federal workers a paid day off tied to the day in 1865 when enslaved people in Texas learned they were free.
Supporters say the rule sets debate time limits so the House can vote on S. 475, which already passed the Senate.
Supporters say making Juneteenth a federal holiday puts it on the same level as the other 10 holidays already listed in title 5.
critics: Critics say adding a new paid holiday under title 5 raises costs because all federal employees would receive paid time off on June 19 each year.
Critics say the rule restricts what changes members can offer to S. 475 during debate, which limits the ability to change or improve the bill before a vote.
Critics say the federal government already observes 10 paid holidays under title 5, and adding an 11th means federal offices are closed more days each year.

117-hres-41.one_liner: Set the debate rules for a House vote on impeaching President Trump
provisions: Gives the House a set amount of time to debate whether to impeach President Trump
Controls how much time each side gets to speak during the debate
Limits what changes can be made to the resolution before the House votes on it

supporters: Supporters say the rule gives both sides equal time to speak during the debate, making the process fair before the House votes on H. Res. 24.
Supporters say limiting changes to the resolution before the vote keeps the debate focused on the specific charges against President Trump rather than allowing unrelated additions.
Supporters say setting a fixed debate time ensures the House moves to a vote instead of allowing the process to be slowed down or blocked.
critics: Critics say limiting what changes can be made to H. Res. 24 before the vote stops members of the House from offering amendments that could narrow or adjust the charges.
Critics say the rule controls how much time each side gets to speak, which critics argue may not give enough time to fully examine the evidence behind the impeachment charges.
Critics say the structured debate format is being used to push the resolution to a vote quickly, rather than allowing a longer review of the facts.

117-hres-409.one_liner: Set the rules for debating two bills in the House
provisions: Set time limits and voting rules for debating a bill to create a commission to investigate the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol
Set time limits and voting rules for debating a bill to send emergency money to cover government costs through September 30, 2021
Decided which changes to those bills could be voted on during debate

supporters: Supporters say the rule allows the House to debate H.R. 3233, which would create an official commission to investigate the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol, giving Congress a structured way to find out what happened that day.

Supporters say the rule sets clear time limits and voting procedures for H.R. 3237, which would send emergency money to cover government costs through September 30, 2021, helping avoid funding gaps before the fiscal year ends.
Supporters say by deciding in advance which changes to H.R. 3233 and H.R. 3237 could be voted on, the rule keeps debate focused and prevents delays.
critics: Critics say the rule limits which amendments can be offered to H.R. 3233, which means members of Congress could be blocked from changing how the January 6 commission is set up, including who gets to appoint members.

Critics say bringing H.R. 3237 emergency spending to the floor under strict time limits does not give lawmakers enough time to review how the money would be spent before the September 30, 2021 deadline.
Critics say packaging both the January 6 commission bill and the emergency spending bill under one rule forces members to accept the debate terms for both at once, with no way to separate them.

117-hres-473.one_liner: Let the House vote on repealing the Iraq war law and new company rules
provisions: Lets the House vote on repealing the 2002 law that gave the president approval to send troops to Iraq.
Limits debate time on the Iraq war law vote to one hour, split equally between supporters and opponents.
Lets the House vote on requiring public companies to disclose more information and creating a new government committee on sustainable finance.
This bill only sets the rules for how those two votes happen — it does not repeal the Iraq war law or create the committee itself.

supporters: Supporters say this rule lets the House vote on repealing the 2002 Iraq war authorization, which they argue is no longer needed since the U.S. military mission in Iraq has changed.
Supporters say the one-hour debate limit, split 30 minutes per side, gives both supporters and opponents equal time to make their case before the vote.
Supporters say this rule also brings H.R. 1187 to the floor, which would require public companies to share more information and create a Sustainable Finance Advisory Committee.
critics: Critics say one hour of debate is not enough time for members of Congress to fully discuss repealing the 2002 Iraq war authorization, a law that affected U.S. military operations for nearly two decades.
Critics say this rule brings the H.R. 1187 vote to the floor quickly, limiting the time available to examine how its new disclosure rules would affect public companies.

Critics say this bill only controls the process for two votes and does not itself repeal the Iraq war authorization or create the Sustainable Finance Advisory Committee — those outcomes depend on separate votes.

117-hres-414.one_liner: Update mask rules in the House to match CDC guidance for vaccinated members
provisions: Tells the House doctor's office to update its mask rules for the House floor and committee rooms
The new rules would apply to members and staff who are vaccinated against COVID-19
The update must match CDC guidance from May 13, 2021, which said vaccinated people can go without masks in most indoor settings

supporters: Supporters say the CDC's May 13, 2021 guidance already allows vaccinated people to go without masks in most indoor settings, and this resolution would let vaccinated House members and staff follow those same rules on the House floor and in committee rooms.

Supporters say the House Attending Physician's office has not updated its mask rules to match the CDC's May 13, 2021 guidance, and this resolution would direct that office to make the change for vaccinated members and staff.
critics: Critics say the House floor and committee rooms include both vaccinated and unvaccinated members and staff, and removing mask rules for vaccinated people in those spaces could increase exposure risk for those who are not vaccinated.
Critics say the resolution does not include any way to check or confirm that members or staff are actually vaccinated before they stop wearing masks in the House chamber or committee meeting spaces.

117-hres-508.one_liner: Set the House debate rules for voting on the roads and transit funding bill
provisions: This bill sets the rules for how the House of Representatives debates and votes on H.R. 3684, the highways and transit funding bill.
It controls things like how long members can speak and what changes can be offered during the debate.
It does not itself spend money or change any laws — it only controls the process for considering H.R. 3684.

supporters: Supporters say the rule allows the House to move to a vote on H.R. 3684, the highways and transit funding bill, by setting time limits on debate and controlling what changes members can offer.
Supporters say having set debate rules helps members know exactly how the process will work before it starts.
critics: Critics say the rule limits how long members can speak and what changes they can offer to H.R. 3684, reducing the number of voices that can shape the final bill.
Critics say debate rules that limit amendments mean some members may not get a chance to propose changes to the highways and transit funding provisions in H.R. 3684.

117-hres-503.one_liner: Create a House committee to investigate the January 6th attack on the Capitol
provisions: Creates a 13-member House committee to look into the January 6th, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol.
The committee can hold hearings, collect evidence, and issue subpoenas — legal orders to get documents and testimony from people.
Other House committees must hand over any related records within 14 days.
The committee must suggest ways to prevent future attacks, domestic terrorism, and politically motivated violence.
The committee will write a report with findings and steps to improve security at the Capitol and other government buildings.

supporters: Supporters say the 13-member committee's power to issue subpoenas will force witnesses to testify and hand over documents, giving investigators tools to find out what led to the January 6th attack.
Supporters say the committee's required report will produce concrete steps to improve security at the Capitol and prevent future acts of domestic terrorism.
Supporters say the 14-day deadline for other House committees to share records will keep the investigation moving and stop delays in getting key evidence.
critics: Critics say the committee is made up of Members appointed by the Speaker, with only 5 chosen after talking to the minority leader, which they argue gives one party too much control over the investigation.
Critics say a select committee with subpoena power could be used to target political opponents rather than focus on finding security failures at the Capitol.
Critics say existing committees — such as the House Homeland Security Committee — already have the authority to investigate the January 6th attack, making a new 13-member body unnecessary.

117-hres-504.one_liner: Set rules for debating four separate bills in the House
provisions: Sets the time limit and debate rules for four different bills before the full House votes on them
One bill changes how inspectors general — government watchdogs — can be fired or removed
One bill replaces a statue of a judge who ruled against Black Americans with one of the first Black Supreme Court Justice, Thurgood Marshall
One bill provides money for highways, road safety, and public transportation
One bill creates a committee to investigate the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the full House to vote on H.R. 3684, which authorizes federal money for highways, road safety, and public transit — funding that states use to build and repair roads.
Supporters say the rule brings H. Res. 503 to the floor, which would create a committee with the power to subpoena witnesses and documents to investigate the January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol.

Supporters say the rule allows a vote on H.R. 3005, which would remove statues of people who voluntarily served the Confederacy from public areas of the Capitol and replace the bust of Roger Taney — who ruled against Black Americans in the Dred Scott case — with a bust of Thurgood Marshall, the first Black Supreme Court Justice.
critics: Critics say the rule packages four unrelated bills together, forcing members to move all four forward at once rather than debating each bill on its own merits and timeline.
Critics say the rule advances H. Res. 503, which they argue creates a one-sided committee to investigate January 6 rather than a bipartisan commission with equal representation from both parties.

Critics say the rule limits how much time members have to debate and offer changes to H.R. 3684, the highway and transit bill, which authorizes large amounts of federal spending without enough floor review.
