117-hres-535.one_liner: Set House debate rules for three bills on chemicals, the FTC, and Afghan visas
provisions: Sets the rules for how the House will debate and vote on three separate bills.
One bill would require the EPA to label certain man-made chemicals called PFAS as hazardous waste, making companies legally responsible for cleaning them up.
Another bill would confirm that the FTC can go to court to stop companies from breaking consumer protection laws.
A third bill would speed up the visa application process for Afghans who helped the U.S. military or government.
This bill itself does not change any laws — it only sets the debate rules so Congress can vote on the three bills above.

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the House to vote on H.R. 2467, which would require the EPA to label PFAS chemicals as hazardous waste, forcing companies to pay for cleanup of contaminated water and soil.

Supporters say the rule also brings H.R. 2668 to a vote, which would confirm the FTC's power to get court orders to stop companies permanently from breaking consumer protection laws — a power the Supreme Court said was unclear in 2021.
Supporters say H.R. 3985 under this rule would speed up visas for Afghan allies who worked with the U.S. military or government and are still waiting to enter the country.
critics: Critics say this rule bundles three unrelated bills — PFAS cleanup, FTC powers, and Afghan visas — into one debate process, limiting members' ability to amend or separate them.
Critics say the PFAS hazardous waste label in H.R. 2467 could make small businesses and local water utilities legally responsible for cleanup costs even if they did not make the chemicals.
Critics say the expedited visa process in H.R. 3985 may not allow enough time for full security screening of Afghan applicants before they enter the United States.

117-hres-486.one_liner: Set the House debate rules for voting on six pending bills
provisions: Allows the House to vote on a bill that changes how workers prove age discrimination against the federal government in court.
Allows the House to vote on a bill that would lower the cost of birth control for veterans who get it through VA hospitals.
Allows the House to vote on a bill that would require banks to track and report loan data for small businesses owned by LGBTQ people.
Allows the House to vote on canceling an EPA rule that set air pollution limits for oil and gas operations.
Allows the House to vote on canceling a banking rule that determined when a national bank counts as the official lender on a loan.
Sets aside money to pay for the work of a House committee focused on economic differences between groups of Americans.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution allows the House to vote on lowering birth control costs for veterans who get contraception through VA hospitals, which could reduce out-of-pocket expenses for that group.
Supporters say the resolution allows the House to vote on canceling an EPA rule that set air pollution limits on oil and gas operations, which they argue removes a burden on that industry.
Supporters say the resolution allows the House to vote on clearer rules for how federal workers must prove age discrimination in court under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967.
critics: Critics say the resolution allows a vote to cancel the EPA's emission standards rule for oil and gas sites, which would remove limits on air pollution that affects people living near those operations.

Critics say the resolution allows a vote to cancel the OCC's 'true lender' rule, which determined when a national bank is the official lender on a loan — removing it could make it easier for lenders to avoid state interest rate limits by partnering with banks.

Critics say bundling six separate bills into one procedural vote limits debate time on each individual measure, including the requirement for banks to collect loan data on LGBTQ-owned small businesses under H.R. 1443.

117-hres-555.one_liner: Set the rules for debating the Labor, Health, and Education spending bill
provisions: Set a time limit and debate rules for the House to vote on a spending bill for the Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education departments
The bill covered government spending for the year ending September 30, 2022
Decided which changes to the spending bill could be offered during the debate

supporters: Supporters say the time limit on debate allows the House to move quickly on funding the Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education departments before the September 30, 2022 deadline, preventing a funding gap.
Supporters say the rule's control over which amendments could be offered keeps debate focused and prevents unrelated additions to the FY2022 spending bill.
Supporters say setting clear debate rules gives all members advance notice of how the vote on H.R. 4502 will be structured, making the process more predictable.
critics: Critics say the rule's limits on which amendments could be offered blocks members from proposing changes to how money is divided among the Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education departments.
Critics say a time-limited debate on a spending bill covering three major departments does not give members enough time to fully review and challenge specific funding decisions for FY2022.
Critics say restricting amendments to H.R. 4502 gives the majority party too much control over the final shape of government spending through September 30, 2022.

117-hres-554.one_liner: Urge the Speaker to seat five Republicans on the January 6th committee
provisions: Condemns the Speaker of the House for refusing to seat five Republican members on the committee set up to investigate the January 6th attack on the Capitol.
The five members named are Jim Banks of Indiana, Jim Jordan of Ohio, Rodney Davis of Illinois, Kelly Armstrong of North Dakota, and Troy Nehls of Texas.
Calls on the Speaker to appoint all five of them to the committee.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution calls on Speaker Pelosi to seat all five Republicans she blocked — Jim Banks, Jim Jordan, Rodney Davis, Kelly Armstrong, and Troy Nehls — who were chosen by House Minority Leader Kevin McCarthy.
Supporters say blocking members chosen by the minority leader breaks with the long-standing practice of letting each party's leadership pick their own committee members.
Supporters say leaving out members chosen by Republican leadership makes the January 6th committee look one-sided, which could weaken public trust in its findings.
critics: Critics say Speaker Pelosi rejected two of the five members — Jim Banks and Jim Jordan — because she said their past actions related to January 6th would hurt the committee's work.
Critics say the resolution does not change the rules that give the Speaker final say over who sits on select committees, so the resolution has no legal force.
Critics say the House already approved the committee's structure and membership process by a majority vote, and this resolution asks the Speaker to go against that approved process.

117-hres-567.one_liner: Set the rules for debating three government spending bills in Congress
provisions: Decided how the House of Representatives would debate and vote on three separate spending bills
The first bill covered money for Congress itself for the year ending September 30, 2022
The second bill covered money for the State Department and programs in other countries for the same year
The third bill covered money for the Commerce Department, Justice Department, and science programs for the same year
Set time limits and rules for how long Congress could debate each bill before voting

supporters: Supporters say setting time limits on debate for H.R. 4346, H.R. 4373, and H.R. 4505 lets Congress move faster on funding Congress, the State Department, and science programs before the September 30, 2022 deadline.
Supporters say bringing all three spending bills under one set of debate rules gives members a clear schedule and prevents any single bill from being stalled by long delays.
Supporters say the structured rules give every member a fair and equal chance to speak on funding for the Commerce Department, Justice Department, and foreign operations programs.
critics: Critics say capping debate time on three large spending bills — covering Congress itself, the State Department, and the Justice Department — limits members' ability to fully examine how the money will be used.

Critics say combining debate rules for all three bills into one procedural vote means members who oppose one of the spending plans, such as funding for foreign programs under H.R. 4373, must accept or reject all three rules at once.
Critics say strict time limits on H.R. 4505, which covers the Commerce and Justice Departments and science agencies, reduce the chance to question specific funding decisions before the final vote.

117-hres-601.one_liner: Set the House floor rules for voting on three separate bills
provisions: Sets the rules for how the House will debate and vote on a bill that changes which states must get federal approval before changing their voting laws
Sets the rules for how the House will debate and vote on a $1.2 trillion infrastructure bill covering roads, bridges, and public transit
Sets the rules for how the House will debate and vote on a budget plan covering 2022 through 2031

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the House to move forward on the $1.2 trillion infrastructure bill (H.R. 3684), which would fund roads, bridges, and public transit across the country.

Supporters say this rule lets the House debate and vote on H.R. 4, which would update the Voting Rights Act of 1965 by setting new criteria for which states must get federal approval before changing their voting laws.
Supporters say this rule opens debate on a budget plan that sets spending levels for every year from 2022 through 2031, giving Congress a long-term financial framework.
critics: Critics say this rule packages three separate and large bills together — including a $1.2 trillion spending bill and a 10-year budget plan — which limits the time members can debate each one on its own.

Critics say this rule advances changes to Section 4 of the Voting Rights Act that would force states to meet new preclearance criteria, which they argue gives the federal government too much control over state election laws.

Critics say moving the 2022-2031 budget resolution under this rule rushes a multi-trillion-dollar spending framework through the House without enough time for members to review the full fiscal impact.

117-hres-667.one_liner: Set the rules for debating three bills in the House
provisions: Sets the time limits and debate rules for a vote on a bill about abortion access
Sets the time limits and debate rules for a vote on the 2022 military budget and troop levels
Sets the time limits and debate rules for a vote on a short-term government funding bill to keep the government running through September 30, 2022

supporters: Supporters say this rule sets structured debate time for three major bills, including the FY2022 National Defense Authorization Act (H.R. 4350) and a continuing resolution (H.R. 5305) needed to keep the government funded through September 30, 2022.
Supporters say setting firm time limits on debate for H.R. 5305 helps avoid a government shutdown by moving the funding bill to a vote quickly.
Supporters say the rule allows the House to take up H.R. 3755 on abortion access and H.R. 4350 on military spending in an organized way without unlimited delay.
critics: Critics say a closed or structured rule on H.R. 4350, the defense authorization bill, blocks members from offering floor amendments to change military spending levels or troop numbers.
Critics say bundling debate rules for three separate bills — abortion access, defense spending, and government funding — into one rule limits members' ability to vote on each issue independently.
Critics say restricting amendment time on H.R. 3755, which would affect abortion providers and patients nationwide, prevents lawmakers from proposing changes to specific provisions in the bill.

117-hres-688.one_liner: Allow the House to vote on a bill about physical activity guidelines for Americans
provisions: Sets the rules for how the House will debate and vote on a separate bill called S. 1301.
The bill being voted on would have the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services publish physical activity guidelines for Americans.
This bill itself does not create any guidelines — it only sets up the process for considering the guidelines bill.

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the House to move forward with debating S. 1301, which would require the Department of Health and Human Services to publish physical activity guidelines for Americans.
Supporters say setting a structured debate process ensures the House can vote on the physical activity guidelines bill in an orderly way.
critics: Critics say this type of rule can limit how many changes lawmakers can propose to S. 1301 before a final vote.
Critics say rules like this can restrict how much time the full House gets to debate the physical activity guidelines bill.

117-hres-716.one_liner: Set the rules for how Congress debates four bills on workers and families
provisions: Sets the time and rules for debate on a bill about preventing family violence
Sets the time and rules for debate on a bill about breastfeeding breaks at work
Sets the time and rules for debate on a bill about age discrimination in hiring
Sets the time and rules for debate on a bill about physical activity guidelines from the government

supporters: Supporters say H.R. 2119 would update the Family Violence Prevention and Services Act to improve how federal funds reach shelters and services for domestic violence survivors.

Supporters say H.R. 3110 would require employers to provide break time and a private space for nursing mothers, extending protections to workers not currently covered under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

Supporters say H.R. 3992 would amend the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 to ban employers from using job classifications that screen out applicants based on age before they are even hired.
critics: Critics say the rule limits debate time on H.R. 3992, which they argue is not enough to review how banning age-based job classifications would affect employer hiring systems under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967.

Critics say H.R. 3110 requires employers to give nursing mothers break time but does not clearly state whether that time must be compensated, which small businesses say creates uncertainty about labor costs.

Critics say combining S. 1301, a bill directing the Secretary of Health and Human Services to issue physical activity guidelines, with workplace and anti-discrimination bills in one rule limits separate debate on each bill.

117-hres-730.one_liner: Find Steve Bannon in contempt of Congress for refusing to comply with a committee subpoena
provisions: Finds that Steve Bannon refused to follow a subpoena — a legal order to appear and provide documents.
That subpoena came from the House committee investigating the January 6th attack on the U.S. Capitol.
Tells the Speaker of the House to send this finding to federal prosecutors in Washington, D.C.
Federal prosecutors can then decide whether to bring criminal charges against Bannon.
Tells the Speaker to take any other steps needed to enforce the subpoena.

supporters: Supporters say Bannon refused to follow a legal subpoena from the January 6th committee, and ignoring a congressional subpoena undermines Congress's power to investigate.
Supporters say sending this finding to federal prosecutors in Washington, D.C. is the correct legal step to hold Bannon accountable for not providing documents or testimony.
Supporters say the Speaker must take all steps needed to enforce the subpoena, or future witnesses could also refuse to cooperate with Congress.
critics: Critics say the January 6th committee was set up by House Democrats without equal Republican input, which they argue makes its subpoenas politically motivated rather than fair.
Critics say Bannon was advised by lawyers that executive privilege — a rule that can protect communications with the White House — may cover the documents the committee requested.
Critics say referring Bannon to federal prosecutors in D.C. turns a legal dispute about the scope of a subpoena into a criminal matter before the courts have settled what he must hand over.

117-hres-727.one_liner: Set the rules for the House to debate the January 6th contempt report
provisions: Set the rules for how long the House could debate the January 6th Committee report and the contempt vote against Steve Bannon
Let the House vote on whether Steve Bannon should be held in contempt for ignoring a congressional subpoena
A subpoena is an official order requiring someone to hand over documents or appear before Congress
This resolution only set the terms for the debate — it did not make any final decision on the contempt question itself

supporters: Supporters say setting debate rules allowed the full House to vote on whether Steve Bannon should be held in contempt for ignoring a congressional subpoena, which they argue is needed to enforce Congress's legal authority.
Supporters say the resolution gave the House a clear, structured process to act on the January 6th Committee's report without unlimited debate slowing down the contempt vote.
critics: Critics say the resolution was a procedural move to fast-track a contempt vote against Steve Bannon before the House had fully reviewed the January 6th Committee's findings.
Critics say limiting debate time on the committee report and the contempt resolution prevented members from raising concerns about whether the subpoena process followed proper legal steps.

117-hres-72.one_liner: Remove Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene from two House committees
provisions: Takes Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene off the House Committee on the Budget
Takes Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene off the House Committee on Education and Labor
Only the full House votes on this — it does not go to the Senate or the President

supporters: Supporters say removing Rep. Greene from the House Committee on the Budget and the House Committee on Education and Labor stops her from shaping federal spending and education policy.
Supporters say the full House — not one party or leader — gets to vote on whether Rep. Greene stays on these two committees.
critics: Critics say this resolution targets one member, Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, and removes her from two committees without a finding of rule violations.
Critics say taking a member off the Budget and Education and Labor committees reduces the voice of the voters who elected her to those roles.

117-hres-789.one_liner: Formally censure a House member for posting a video showing violence against colleagues
provisions: The House formally censures Representative Paul Gosar.
The censure is a response to a video Gosar posted on social media that showed images of violence toward Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and President Biden.
A censure is an official statement of disapproval by the House — it does not remove a member from office or change their pay.
The censured member is required to stand in the well of the House while the resolution is read aloud.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution holds Gosar accountable by requiring him to stand in the well of the House while the censure is read aloud — a formal, public act of disapproval from his peers.

Supporters say the video Gosar posted showed images of violence against a sitting member of Congress and the President, and the House issuing an official statement of disapproval sends a clear message about conduct standards.
Supporters say a censure is a direct response to the specific video posted on Gosar's social media accounts, targeting the act itself rather than punishing him beyond what the resolution allows.
critics: Critics say the censure does not remove Gosar from office or change his pay, meaning the punishment has no practical effect on his ability to serve.

Critics say the resolution punishes a member for content posted on his personal social media accounts, which raises questions about where the House draws the line on member speech outside the chamber.
Critics say the censure requires Gosar to stand in the House well while the resolution is read aloud, which they argue is a performative act rather than a meaningful consequence.

117-hres-760.one_liner: Express U.S. support for Cuban citizens peacefully protesting for freedom
provisions: Congress states it stands with Cuban people who are protesting peacefully.
Congress condemns Cuba's government for arresting peaceful protesters and journalists.
Congress calls on Cuba to stop detaining people who protest peacefully.
Congress calls on Cuba to free all political prisoners.
Congress calls on the U.S. government to take steps to support Cuban people's right to protest.

supporters: Supporters say Congress standing with Cuban protesters sends a clear message that peaceful demonstrations — like those seen across Cuba in July 2021 — deserve international backing, not prison sentences.
Supporters say calling on Cuba to release all political prisoners puts direct pressure on the Cuban government, which human rights groups say holds hundreds of people jailed for protesting.
Supporters say urging the U.S. government to take action gives the resolution teeth beyond words, pushing federal agencies to find ways to support Cubans' right to protest.
critics: Critics say a resolution like this has no legal force — it cannot make Cuba free prisoners or stop arrests, so it may change nothing on the ground for detained Cubans.
Critics say the resolution does not name specific U.S. actions or funding amounts, leaving it unclear what steps the U.S. government is actually expected to take.

Critics say focusing on Cuba's internal affairs through a congressional resolution may give the Cuban government reason to frame protesters as tools of foreign interference, which could put those protesters at greater risk.

117-hres-795.one_liner: Set the rules for the House to vote on formally rebuking Representative Paul Gosar
provisions: This bill sets the debate time limits and procedures the House will follow before voting on H. Res. 789.
H. Res. 789 is a censure of Representative Paul Gosar, a House member from Arizona — censure is a formal rebuke recorded in the congressional record.
A censure is an official condemnation by the full House, but it does not remove the member from office or take away their right to vote on legislation.
The bill has no effect outside of Congress — it only controls how this one internal vote will be run.

supporters: Supporters say this rule gives the full House a structured way to vote on H. Res. 789, using set debate time limits so every member has a fair chance to speak before the censure is recorded in the congressional record.

Supporters say the House has the right to formally rebuke its own members, and this procedure creates an official condemnation of Representative Gosar without removing him from office or taking away his vote.
Supporters say a censure through this process puts a permanent mark in the congressional record, which they argue holds a House member accountable in a way that is on the record for voters to see.
critics: Critics say this rule is being used for partisan reasons, not because the censure process itself changes anything — a censure does not remove Representative Gosar from office or stop him from voting on legislation.

Critics say the debate time limits set by this rule rush a serious vote, giving members little time to fully discuss whether a formal rebuke of a sitting House member from Arizona is the right action.

Critics say the bill has no effect outside of Congress and only controls one internal vote, making the whole process a political statement rather than a meaningful consequence for Representative Gosar.

117-hres-774.one_liner: Set the rules for how the House debates a budget bill
provisions: This resolution controls how the House will debate H.R. 5376, a budget bill Congress is handling through a process called reconciliation.
It sets time limits for debate and controls what changes to the bill members can offer during the floor vote.
This resolution only covers the debate rules for H.R. 5376 in the House — it does not pass the bill or affect how the Senate votes on it.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution sets clear debate rules and time limits, which keeps the House floor moving without delays during the vote on H.R. 5376.
Supporters say limiting what changes members can offer during the vote prevents unplanned changes that could slow down the budget process.
Supporters say the resolution only controls how the House debates the bill — it does not bind the Senate or change what is in H.R. 5376 itself.
critics: Critics say the time limits on debate give members little time to fully discuss a major budget bill before voting.
Critics say the rules controlling what changes members can offer block lawmakers from fixing parts of H.R. 5376 they disagree with during the floor vote.
Critics say passing a resolution to control debate through reconciliation (a special budget process) limits the normal back-and-forth that lets all members have a say.

117-hres-8.one_liner: Set the rules for how the House of Representatives will operate in 2021
provisions: Sets the rules for how the House of Representatives will run during the 117th Congress, which covers 2021 to 2023.
Makes the Office of Diversity and Inclusion a permanent part of the House.
Keeps rules in place requiring the House to protect employees from harassment and discrimination, and adds protections for people who report wrongdoing.
For COVID-19 relief bills, the Budget Committee chair can skip the normal rules for calculating how much a law will cost.
For bills related to climate change, the Budget Committee chair can skip the normal rules for calculating how much a law will cost.
Requires the House Clerk to keep a public list showing which members support bills already passed by the Senate.
Lets investigators demand documents or testimony in a probe into political interference at federal health agencies during the COVID-19 response.

supporters: Supporters say making the Office of Diversity and Inclusion a permanent part of the House ensures staff dedicated to equal opportunity for House employees will remain in place beyond any single Congress.
Supporters say allowing the Budget Committee chair to skip normal cost calculations for COVID-19 relief bills removes a procedural step that can slow down emergency spending responses.

Supporters say requiring the House Clerk to publish a public list showing which members support Senate-passed bills that have not yet received a House vote gives voters direct information about where their representatives stand.
critics: Critics say allowing the Budget Committee chair to skip normal cost-tracking rules for both COVID-19 and climate change bills means large amounts of spending can move forward without the standard budget review process.

Critics say granting subpoena power to investigators probing political interference at the Department of Health and Human Services and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention before those investigators have adopted their own operating rules removes a standard oversight step.

Critics say adding climate change bills to the same budget exemption created for COVID-19 emergency spending applies a rule designed for a short-term crisis to an open-ended and broadly defined category of legislation.

117-hres-85.one_liner: Set the rules for how Congress debates an apprenticeship bill and a budget plan
provisions: Sets the time limit and debate rules for a vote on a bill that expands apprenticeship programs across the country
Sets the time limit and debate rules for a vote on the federal budget plan covering 2021 through 2030
Does not change any laws itself — only controls how the House of Representatives runs its debate on these two items

supporters: Supporters say this rule brings H.R. 447 to a House floor vote, giving Congress the chance to expand the National Apprenticeship Act of 1937 to cover youth apprenticeships and pre-apprenticeships for the first time.
Supporters say scheduling debate on H. Con. Res. 11 lets the House set federal spending levels for fiscal years 2021 through 2030, giving the country a 10-year budget framework.
Supporters say the rule gives members of both parties set time to speak before any vote, so both the apprenticeship bill and the budget plan get a public hearing on the House floor.
critics: Critics say the debate time limits in this rule do not give members enough time to fully question the new federal labor standards that H.R. 447 would require apprenticeship programs to meet.
Critics say rushing H. Con. Res. 11 to a vote under a timed rule makes it harder to challenge spending levels that would cover 10 fiscal years, from 2021 through 2030.
Critics say combining debate rules for an apprenticeship expansion bill and a multi-year budget resolution into one procedural vote makes it harder to oppose either item separately.

117-hres-838.one_liner: Set the rules for debating three separate bills in the House
provisions: Decides how much time members of Congress get to debate three different bills
One bill would limit presidential power and add rules about elections
One bill would name a memorial in Orlando, Florida after the Pulse nightclub shooting
One bill would address mental health support for doctors and nurses

supporters: Supporters say this rule gives members of Congress time to debate H.R. 5314, which would add new limits on presidential power and set rules to block foreign interference in U.S. elections.
Supporters say the rule allows a vote on S. 1605, which would name the Orlando memorial at 1912 South Orange Avenue as the official National Pulse Memorial to honor the victims of the 2016 shooting.
Supporters say the rule also brings S. 610 to a vote, which would create mental health support programs for doctors and nurses who face high rates of burnout and suicide.
critics: Critics say this rule limits debate time on H.R. 5314, a bill that makes major changes to presidential authority, giving members too little time to review what those changes would mean in practice.
Critics say H.R. 5314's provisions on election interference would expand federal oversight of elections in ways that go beyond what Congress has the authority to do under the Constitution.

Critics say bundling three unrelated bills — one on presidential power, one naming a memorial, and one on nurse mental health — into a single rule makes it harder for members to vote on each issue separately.

117-hres-829.one_liner: Set the rules for debating a bill to keep the government funded through 2022
provisions: Set the time limit and debate rules for the House to vote on a bill that kept the government running through September 2022
Controlled which changes to the bill could be voted on during debate

supporters: Supporters say the rule set a time limit on debate, which allowed the House to vote quickly on keeping the government funded through September 30, 2022, avoiding a government shutdown.
Supporters say controlling which amendments could be considered during debate helped prevent delay tactics that could have stalled the vote on the continuing appropriations bill.
critics: Critics say the rule blocked members from offering amendments to the continuing appropriations bill, limiting their ability to change how the government's money was spent.
Critics say giving the majority party control over which changes could be voted on during debate shut out the minority party from shaping the terms of the September 2022 funding bill.

117-hres-803.one_liner: Set the rules for how the House debates the Build Back Better spending bill
provisions: Sets the terms for how the House can debate and vote on H.R. 5376, known as the Build Back Better Act.
Requires a technical fix to the bill to be treated as already approved before debate begins.
This is a procedural step — it does not create or change any policy on its own.

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the full House to begin floor debate on H.R. 5376, the Build Back Better Act, moving it one step closer to a final vote.
Supporters say requiring the technical amendment to be treated as already adopted clears up drafting errors before debate starts, preventing procedural delays on the floor.
Supporters say this is a standard step the House uses to bring major bills to a vote, and it follows the same process used for other large legislation.
critics: Critics say this rule limits the ability of members to offer their own amendments to H.R. 5376 during floor debate, reducing the number of voices that shape the final bill.
Critics say treating the technical amendment as pre-approved skips the normal process where all members cast a separate vote on changes to the bill's text.
Critics say using a rule to fast-track a bill as large as H.R. 5376 — which covers dozens of programs — gives members less time to review what they are voting on.

117-hres-837.one_liner: Call on China to release tennis player Peng Shuai and stop hiding her case
provisions: Says the House believes the International Olympic Committee did not protect Peng Shuai's right to speak freely
Calls on China to allow an outside investigation into Peng Shuai's claims that a top Chinese official sexually assaulted her
Calls on China to stop blocking news reports and online discussions about Peng Shuai's case
Calls on China to let Peng Shuai leave the country if she wants to
Calls on China not to punish Peng Shuai's family members who are still in China

supporters: Supporters say the IOC failed its own human rights rules by working with the Chinese Communist Party instead of pushing for an outside investigation into Peng Shuai's claim that a top Chinese official sexually assaulted her.
Supporters say China should stop blocking news reports and online posts about Peng Shuai's case so the public can learn what happened and hold abusers accountable.
Supporters say China should let Peng Shuai leave the country if she chooses and should not punish her family members who are still living in China.
critics: Critics say this resolution does not require China or the IOC to do anything, so calling for an independent investigation or an end to censorship has no legal force behind it.

Critics say publicly pressuring China through a House resolution could cause the Chinese government to retaliate against Peng Shuai's family members still in China, which the resolution itself says should not happen.
Critics say the IOC did conduct video calls with Peng Shuai after her posts were removed, and that labeling the IOC's response a failure to protect free speech ignores those direct contacts.

117-s-1502.one_liner: Protect what police officers tell peer counselors and set national program standards
provisions: When a law enforcement officer talks to a peer support specialist, those conversations generally cannot be shared with others.
A peer support specialist is a fellow officer trained to provide counseling — the privacy rule covers their side of the conversation too.
The Department of Justice must create best practices and professional standards for how these counseling programs should run.

supporters: Supporters say making peer support conversations private will encourage more law enforcement officers to seek help, since officers may avoid counseling if they fear their words could be used against them at work.

Supporters say requiring the Department of Justice to set professional standards will make sure peer support programs across the country follow consistent, tested practices instead of varying by department.
Supporters say protecting the peer support specialist's side of the conversation too means trained officers can speak openly without risk, making the counseling more effective.
critics: Critics say the bill does not define clear exceptions for when a peer support communication could be disclosed, which may make it harder for departments to act if an officer reveals a serious safety threat.
Critics say requiring the Department of Justice to develop best practices adds a federal role in programs that local law enforcement agencies have traditionally managed on their own.
Critics say the bill does not include funding to help smaller law enforcement agencies build or improve peer support programs, so the new standards may be hard to meet without extra resources.

117-hres-91.one_liner: Set the rules for a House vote on removing a Member from committees
provisions: The House will follow a set of rules when it votes on H. Res. 72
H. Res. 72 is a resolution to remove a specific House Member from certain committees
The rules control how the vote on that resolution will be run on the House floor

supporters: Supporters say the rule ensures the full House can vote on H. Res. 72 in an orderly way, with set time limits so the debate does not drag on without a decision.
Supporters say setting floor rules in advance stops last-minute procedural moves that could delay or block a vote on removing the Member from their committees.
critics: Critics say the specific floor rules in this measure may limit how many amendments members can offer during debate on H. Res. 72, cutting off chances to change the resolution before the final vote.
Critics say bringing a rule to the floor for a committee-removal vote speeds up a process that affects one Member's ability to do their job, without giving enough time for full debate.

117-s-108.one_liner: Let the Seminole Tribe of Florida sell, lease, or transfer land it owns outright
provisions: The Seminole Tribe of Florida can lease, sell, or transfer land it owns directly.
This only applies to land the federal government does not manage on behalf of the tribe.
The tribe can make these property deals without needing extra approval from the federal government.

supporters: Supporters say the bill lets the Seminole Tribe of Florida lease, sell, or transfer land it owns directly, without waiting for federal approval on each deal.
Supporters say removing the federal approval requirement for non-trust land transactions is consistent with the tribe's right to manage its own property.
Supporters say this change applies only to land the federal government does not already manage for the tribe, so it does not affect the tribe's protected trust lands.
critics: Critics say that removing federal oversight from these land transactions could make it harder for the government to ensure deals are fair to the tribe and its members.
Critics say the bill does not specify what types of non-trust land are covered, which could create disputes about which properties the new rules apply to.
Critics say there are no requirements in the bill for tribal members to be consulted before the tribe completes a land sale or transfer under the new authority.

117-s-1095.one_liner: Cut off GI Bill survivor benefits at colleges that charge out-of-state tuition to veterans' families
provisions: If a public college charges veterans' surviving family members more than in-state tuition rates, the VA stops approving that school for GI Bill survivor benefits.
This applies to family members using the Survivors' and Dependents' Educational Assistance program, which covers children and spouses of veterans who died or were disabled in service.
Schools that want to keep accepting these students' GI Bill benefits must charge them the same tuition rate as in-state students.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects children and spouses of veterans who died or were disabled in service by making sure they pay the same tuition as in-state students at public colleges, instead of the higher out-of-state rate.

Supporters say that tying VA approval to in-state tuition rates gives public colleges a clear reason to lower their charges for Survivors' and Dependents' Educational Assistance program users, since schools risk losing all DEA students if they do not comply.

Supporters say military families often move across state lines because of service, so survivors who end up living outside their home state should not be penalized with higher tuition when using earned benefits.
critics: Critics say that requiring public colleges to charge in-state rates for out-of-state DEA students shifts the cost difference onto the school or state, since the federal government does not reimburse colleges for the gap between in-state and out-of-state tuition.

Critics say that if a public college refuses to lower its tuition for DEA students, those students lose access to VA-approved benefits at that school entirely, which could reduce the number of schools available to surviving family members rather than expand it.

117-s-1064.one_liner: Sanction people in Nicaragua blocking elections and report on corruption and human rights abuses
provisions: Adds Nicaragua to a list of countries whose citizens can have their U.S. visas blocked if they interfere with elections or take part in serious corruption.
Requires the U.S. to push international banks and financial groups to add oversight to any loans or aid they give to Nicaragua.
Requires the State Department and Treasury to make a plan to use sanctions — such as freezing money and blocking travel — to pressure Nicaragua toward free and fair elections.
Requires the president to impose targeted sanctions on people found to be blocking free and fair elections in Nicaragua.
Requires a report on corruption by Nicaragua's President Daniel Ortega, his family members, and top government officials.
Requires a report on Russian activity in Nicaragua and on human rights abuses against rural farming communities and native groups.
Requires a plan to support independent news and media in Nicaragua and remove obstacles to people getting outside information.

supporters: Supporters say the bill's visa-blocking sanctions will target Nicaraguan officials who interfere with elections or engage in serious corruption, giving the U.S. a direct tool to punish individuals without cutting off aid to ordinary Nicaraguans.

Supporters say requiring the State Department and Treasury to create a joint sanctions plan will push Nicaragua's government toward free and fair elections by freezing money and blocking travel for those who obstruct the process.

Supporters say the required reports on President Ortega, his family, and top officials — plus a separate report on Russian activity in Nicaragua — will create a public record that can support further action by the U.S. and its partners.
critics: Critics say adding Nicaragua to the visa-blocking sanctions list could hurt Nicaraguan citizens and family members who have no role in government actions, cutting off legal pathways to the U.S.
Critics say pushing international banks to add oversight conditions on loans to Nicaragua may slow down aid that reaches rural farming communities and indigenous groups who depend on those funds.

Critics say the law's focus on reports and diplomatic pressure gives the U.S. government wide room to decide when — or whether — to act, with no set deadlines for imposing sanctions on specific individuals.

117-s-189.one_liner: Raise pay for disabled veterans whenever Social Security gets a raise
provisions: When Social Security payments go up to keep pace with rising prices, veterans' disability payments go up by the same percentage
The raise also applies to extra payments veterans get for supporting a spouse or children
The raise includes a clothing allowance paid to veterans with certain service-related disabilities
Surviving spouses and children of veterans who died from service-related causes get the same raise too

supporters: Supporters say tying veterans' disability payments to Social Security cost-of-living increases means veterans, their dependents, and surviving spouses and children would get automatic raises without Congress having to pass a new bill each year.

Supporters say the bill protects the real value of payments like the clothing allowance for disabled veterans and dependency payments for spouses and children, so inflation does not slowly cut what these families receive.
Supporters say automatic adjustments remove the risk that veterans miss a raise simply because Congress did not act in time.
critics: Critics say linking veterans' disability payments to Social Security COLA percentages could cost the Department of Veterans Affairs billions of dollars over time without a separate review of whether the VA budget can support those increases each year.

Critics say the bill does not set a floor or cap on the adjustment, meaning a large Social Security COLA — like the 8.7% increase in 2023 — would automatically trigger an equally large increase across all VA disability, dependent, clothing allowance, and survivor payments at the same time.
Critics say Congress gives up direct oversight each year over how much VA compensation goes up, which some members argue is a spending decision that should stay with elected officials.

117-s-164.one_liner: Require the FDA to teach doctors about biosimilar drugs
provisions: The FDA must create or improve training programs that teach doctors about biological drugs and their lower-cost versions called biosimilars.
Biosimilars are drugs that work the same as a brand-name biological drug but are made by a different company.
The FDA can build a website where doctors and health workers can find information about these drugs.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the FDA to create or improve training programs will help doctors learn the difference between brand-name biological drugs and biosimilars, which could lead to more prescriptions of the lower-cost biosimilar versions.

Supporters say an FDA-run website giving doctors and health workers easy access to information about biological products and biosimilars could reduce confusion about when it is safe to switch a patient to a biosimilar.
Supporters say better education for health care providers about biosimilars could increase competition in the biological drug market, which tends to lower prices for patients.
critics: Critics say the bill does not require the FDA to set a deadline for completing the new training programs, which means the agency could delay action with no consequences.
Critics say the bill allows the FDA to build an educational website but does not require it, so the agency may never create the resource that doctors are supposed to rely on.
Critics say the bill focuses only on educating providers but does nothing to address the rules that allow brand-name drug makers to block biosimilars from reaching the market in the first place.

117-s-1828.one_liner: Pay government workers who suffer brain injuries from hostile acts while on assignment
provisions: Lets CIA officers, diplomats, and other government workers receive payments if they suffer a brain injury while on assignment.
The worker's family members can also receive payments if they are harmed the same way.
The injury must be linked to war, insurgency, hostile acts, terrorism, or another situation designated by the agency.
The injury cannot be the result of the worker's own wrongdoing.
Workers who were injured before this bill passed can still receive payments.
Each agency must send a classified report to Congress listing how many payments were made and how much each one was.
This bill was created after U.S. government workers began reporting a condition called Havana Syndrome starting in 2016.

supporters: Supporters say this bill allows CIA officers, diplomats, and other government workers who have reported brain injuries from Havana Syndrome since 2016 to receive payments for the first time.
Supporters say the bill covers not just workers but also their family members if they are harmed the same way, and applies to injuries that happened before the bill was passed.
Supporters say required classified reports to Congress listing the number of payments and amounts will help track how the program is used.
critics: Critics say the bill does not define a dollar amount or cap on payments, which makes it hard to know how much the program will cost taxpayers.
Critics say linking payments to injuries designated by the agency gives agencies broad power to decide who qualifies, with limited outside review.
Critics say the cause of Havana Syndrome is still under investigation, and paying claims before a confirmed cause is established could set a difficult precedent for future injury programs.

117-s-1910.one_liner: Approve VA hospital construction and repair projects for 2021
provisions: The Department of Veterans Affairs gets the go-ahead to build or repair specific medical facilities for veterans.
Each project has a set dollar limit so costs cannot go above a fixed amount.
The projects are scheduled for the year starting in October 2020.
Congress sets the spending cap on each project one by one.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives the Department of Veterans Affairs permission to start building or repairing medical facilities for veterans in FY2021, so veterans can get care closer to home.
Supporters say each project has a fixed spending cap set by Congress, which keeps costs from going over budget and protects taxpayer money.
Supporters say approving each project one by one lets Congress check that every dollar is going to a real, planned facility before any money is spent.
critics: Critics say the bill sets per-project spending caps but does not require any rules about which regions or states get new facilities, meaning some veterans may still live far from VA medical care.
Critics say the one-by-one approval process in Congress can slow down construction timelines, which delays care for veterans who need updated or expanded medical facilities now.

117-s-1511.one_liner: Expand death and disability benefits for police, firefighters, and first responders
provisions: Adds traffic-control firefighters and police cadets in training to the program that pays money to public safety workers killed or badly hurt on the job.
Covers officers who respond to emergencies outside their normal work area.
Raises the up-front payment families get while waiting for a final decision on a death claim, and adjusts that amount each year to keep up with rising prices.
Raises the payout on any claim that has been waiting more than 365 days for a final answer.
Adds brain and memory disorders — like dementia — as injuries that qualify for disability payments.
Changes education payments for surviving spouses and children from optional to required.
Lets 9/11 first responders or their surviving family members file death or disability claims in certain situations.
Gives the Department of Justice the power to demand documents from outside groups, like government agencies, to speed up claims processing.

supporters: Supporters say the bill fills gaps in who qualifies for benefits, adding traffic-control firefighters and police cadets in training — two groups currently left out of the program when they are killed or badly hurt on the job.

Supporters say families waiting more than 365 days for a final decision on a death or disability claim will get a higher payout under the bill, which addresses a known problem with long delays in the system.

Supporters say adding brain and memory disorders, like dementia, as qualifying injuries means officers who develop these conditions from job-related causes can now receive disability payments they currently cannot get.
critics: Critics say expanding the program to cover officers working outside their normal area and to include 9/11 responders in new claim situations will increase the number of claims the Department of Justice must process, raising program costs without a clear funding source.

Critics say giving the Department of Justice the power to demand documents from outside government agencies through subpoenas could create new legal disputes that slow down — rather than speed up — the claims process.

Critics say changing education benefits for surviving spouses and children from optional to required removes the government's flexibility to manage the program's budget, locking in spending regardless of future funding levels.

117-s-325.one_liner: Give a federal commission on Native children two more years to finish its report
provisions: A federal commission studying programs for Native children now has 5 years to finish its report, instead of 3 years.
The commission looks at programs run by federal, state, local, and tribal governments that serve Native children.
The final report goes to the President and Congress and includes plans for federal policies on Native children.

supporters: Supporters say the 2-year extension gives the commission enough time to study programs run by federal, state, local, and tribal governments that serve Native children — a task too large to finish in 3 years.

Supporters say a rushed report could lead to weak federal policy recommendations, and that 5 years allows the commission to gather more complete data before sending findings to the President and Congress.
critics: Critics say the original 3-year deadline was already enough time, and that Native children need federal policy changes now — not two years later.

Critics say extending the deadline to 5 years delays action on programs serving Native children across federal, state, local, and tribal governments with no clear explanation of why more time is needed.

117-s-796.one_liner: Require the VA to run a care program for pregnant and postpartum veterans
provisions: The VA must run a program that connects pregnant and postpartum veterans with doctors and care providers outside the VA system.
Doctors and care providers outside the VA get training on the specific health needs of veterans who are pregnant or recently gave birth.
The training includes mental and behavioral health issues that can come from military service.
A government watchdog office must write a report on how many veterans die or get seriously hurt during or after pregnancy.
That report must look at whether Black, Hispanic, and other veterans of different racial and ethnic backgrounds have worse health outcomes.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would connect pregnant and postpartum veterans with outside doctors who are trained on military-related mental and behavioral health conditions, filling a gap in care the VA cannot always provide on its own.

Supporters say requiring a government report on maternal deaths and serious injuries among veterans — broken down by race and ethnicity — will show whether Black, Hispanic, and other veterans face worse outcomes so those gaps can be addressed.
Supporters say training community maternity care providers on the specific needs of veterans will improve care for a group whose health needs are often misunderstood by civilian doctors.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a set funding amount, which makes it unclear whether the VA will have enough money to actually run the maternity care coordination program.
Critics say the bill focuses on reports and training but does not require the VA to fix any problems found in the maternal health data, so outcomes for veterans may not improve.
Critics say community providers outside the VA are not required to complete the training, which means veterans could still see doctors who are not prepared for their specific needs.

117-s-475.one_liner: Make June 19 a federal public holiday called Juneteenth National Independence Day
provisions: June 19 becomes a federal public holiday, called Juneteenth National Independence Day.
Federal workers get a paid day off on June 19 each year.
Juneteenth joins the 10 other federal holidays, such as July 4th and Labor Day.
Private employers are not required by this bill to give workers the day off, but many follow federal holiday schedules.

supporters: Supporters say making June 19 a federal holiday gives federal workers a paid day off each year to mark the end of slavery in the United States.
Supporters say adding Juneteenth as the 11th federal holiday puts it alongside July 4th and Labor Day, giving it the same official recognition as other national days.
Supporters say that because many private employers follow federal holiday schedules, millions of workers beyond the federal workforce may also get the day off.
critics: Critics say adding a new paid federal holiday increases costs for the government because federal workers are paid to not work that day, adding to the federal payroll budget.
Critics say private employers are not required by this bill to give workers the day off, meaning most non-federal workers may not actually benefit from the holiday.

117-s-578.one_liner: Require sesame to be listed as an allergen on food labels
provisions: Makes sesame an official food allergen that must appear on food labels, joining peanuts, milk, eggs, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish, and tree nuts.
Food companies must add sesame to their labels starting January 1, 2023.
Requires the Department of Health and Human Services to report on food allergy research and data collection.
About 1.6 million Americans have sesame allergies — this law gives them the same label warnings already required for the other eight major allergens.

supporters: Supporters say the law gives the approximately 1.6 million Americans with sesame allergies the same label warnings already required for peanuts, milk, eggs, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish, and tree nuts.
Supporters say that before this law, sesame was not required on food labels, which forced people with sesame allergies to contact manufacturers directly to find out if a product was safe to eat.
Supporters say the requirement for the Department of Health and Human Services to report on food allergy research will help identify gaps in data collection for all food allergies, not just sesame.
critics: Critics say some food companies responded to the January 1, 2023 deadline by adding sesame as an actual ingredient in their products rather than listing it as a possible trace allergen, which reduced the number of sesame-free products available to people with the allergy.

Critics say food manufacturers — especially small companies with large product lines — face significant costs to update labels and production processes to meet the January 1, 2023 compliance deadline.

117-s-272.one_liner: Require federal agencies to post their budget requests online for the public
provisions: Each federal agency must put its budget request documents on its own website and on a single searchable government site like USAspending.gov.
The documents must be posted within two weeks of being sent to Congress.
People must be able to download individual reports, all reports at once, or just the results of a search.
The Office of Management and Budget must keep a public webpage listing which agencies submitted budget documents, when they were sent to Congress, and when they were posted online.

supporters: Supporters say requiring agencies to post budget documents on USAspending.gov and their own websites within two weeks of sending them to Congress gives the public faster access to how federal money is being requested.
Supporters say the rule that people can download all reports at once or search and download just what they need makes it easier for journalists, researchers, and voters to track government spending.
Supporters say the OMB tracking page — which lists which agencies submitted documents and when — creates a clear record that shows if any agency is late or missing from the process.
critics: Critics say the two-week posting deadline may be hard for smaller agencies with limited staff and technology budgets to meet consistently.
Critics say converting existing budget documents into open, searchable formats that allow bulk downloads could require agencies to spend money on new systems or staff training.

118-hr-1797.one_liner: Require safety rules for rechargeable batteries used in electric bikes and scooters
provisions: The Consumer Product Safety Commission must create new safety rules for rechargeable lithium-ion batteries.
The rules apply to batteries used in electric bikes, electric scooters, and similar small electric vehicles.
Single-use batteries are not covered — only rechargeable ones fall under these rules.
The rules must lower the risk of fires caused by these batteries.
The safety rules apply to products sold to regular consumers, not to commercial or industrial equipment.

supporters: Supporters say that requiring the Consumer Product Safety Commission to set fire safety rules for lithium-ion batteries in electric bikes and scooters will reduce the number of battery fires that have killed and injured people in cities like New York.

Supporters say that covering rechargeable batteries in consumer e-bikes and e-scooters — but not commercial equipment — keeps the rules focused on the products most likely to be used in homes and apartments where fires are most dangerous.
Supporters say that having one federal safety standard will replace a patchwork of local rules and push manufacturers to sell safer battery products to all consumers.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for the Consumer Product Safety Commission to finish the new rules, which means the agency could take years to act while unsafe batteries are still being sold.
Critics say that leaving out single-use batteries and commercial equipment creates gaps in the law, since some fire risks come from battery types and uses the bill does not cover.

Critics say the bill gives the Consumer Product Safety Commission broad power to write the rules without specifying what fire-risk levels are acceptable, which could lead to standards that are too costly for small e-bike and e-scooter makers to meet.

117-s-957.one_liner: Require VA hospitals to have drop boxes for unused prescription drugs
provisions: Every VA medical facility that has an on-site pharmacy must have a physical drop box where anyone can leave unused prescription drugs
Every VA location that has a dedicated law enforcement space must also have one of these drop boxes
Any person — not just veterans — can use these drop boxes to safely get rid of controlled substance medications

supporters: Supporters say placing drop boxes at every VA medical facility with an on-site pharmacy gives veterans and their families a safe, easy way to get rid of unused opioids and other controlled substances without flushing them or throwing them in the trash.

Supporters say opening the drop boxes to any person — not just veterans — means more people in the community can safely dispose of prescription drugs, which reduces the chance those medications are stolen or misused.
Supporters say putting drop boxes at VA locations that already have dedicated law enforcement space means trained staff are nearby to handle the collected drugs properly.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include any dedicated funding, which means VA facilities must find money within their existing budgets to buy, install, and maintain the drop boxes.

Critics say the bill does not set rules for how often the drop boxes must be emptied or who is responsible for transporting the collected controlled substances, which could create safety gaps at busy VA pharmacies.

Critics say limiting the program to VA facilities leaves out many communities that do not have a VA medical center nearby, meaning most people who need a safe disposal option still won't have one close to home.

117-s-848.one_liner: Change how federal teaching grants get turned into loans when teachers miss service requirements
provisions: Teachers whose federal teaching grants were turned into loans can ask the Department of Education to review that decision.
The Department of Education can review and reverse a grant being changed to a loan.
Teachers whose required teaching service was disrupted by COVID-19 can get extra flexibility to meet their teaching terms.
The bill updates the process the government uses to check whether teachers have met their required years of service.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives teachers a way to ask the Department of Education to review a decision that turned their TEACH grant into a loan, which can help teachers who lost grant status due to paperwork problems rather than failing to complete their service.

Supporters say teachers whose required teaching service was disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic will get extra time to meet their teaching obligations without being penalized by having their grant changed to a loan.
critics: Critics say the reconsideration process does not include a deadline for how long teachers have to request a review, which could delay loan repayment from teachers who did not complete their required years of service.

Critics say the COVID-19 flexibility rules do not set a clear limit on how much extra time a teacher can receive, which may reduce the accountability built into the TEACH grant program's service requirements.

118-hr-1767.one_liner: Keep veterans' education benefits when schools are closed by fraud or a VA inspection
provisions: If a VA inspection causes a school to shut down a program, veterans enrolled in that program keep their benefits.
If the Department of Education finds a school harmed student loan borrowers, veterans in that program keep their benefits.
To offer VA-funded programs, schools must agree to repay the VA if they close or cut a program due to fraud.

supporters: Supporters say veterans who lose access to a VA-approved program because of fraud or a VA risk survey should not have their GI Bill or other VA education benefits charged for that incomplete coursework.

Supporters say requiring schools to repay the VA if they close or cut a program due to Federal Trade Commission or Department of Education fraud findings protects taxpayer dollars and shifts the financial risk onto the school, not the veteran.
Supporters say the bill closes a gap where veterans could lose benefit months through no fault of their own when a school is found to have harmed student loan borrowers.
critics: Critics say the repayment requirement — schools must pay back all VA education assistance if they close a program due to fraud — could cause smaller schools to stop offering VA-approved programs rather than take on that financial liability.

Critics say the bill ties benefit protection to VA risk-based survey findings, but does not define a timeline or standard for when a survey result triggers the no-charge rule, which could create delays for veterans waiting to know if their benefits are safe.

Critics say the Department of Education actionable harm standard was written for federal student loan borrowers, not VA education programs, and applying it to VA benefits may create confusion about which veterans qualify for protection.

118-hr-192.one_liner: Stop non-citizens from voting in Washington DC local elections
provisions: Non-citizens cannot vote in any DC election, including local races for mayor, city council, or school board.
DC passed a law in 2022 letting non-citizens vote in local elections if they live in the city and meet certain rules — this bill cancels that law.
Federal law already blocks non-citizens from voting in national elections like presidential or congressional races — this bill extends that block to DC local elections too.

supporters: Supporters say voting in any election — including local races for mayor, city council, and school board — should be limited to U.S. citizens, and this bill makes DC's rules match that standard.
Supporters say DC's 2022 law let non-citizens vote in local elections, and this bill cancels that law to keep a clear line between the rights of citizens and non-citizens.
Supporters say federal law already blocks non-citizens from voting in national elections, and this bill closes a gap by applying the same rule to DC local elections.
critics: Critics say DC's 2022 law gave non-citizens who live in the city, pay local taxes, and follow local rules a voice in elections — like for mayor and school board — that directly affect their daily lives.
Critics say Congress is using this bill to cancel a law that DC's own elected council passed, which takes away DC residents' ability to decide who can vote in their local elections.

Critics say non-citizens living in DC have no say in national elections under federal law, and stripping their local voting rights too means they pay taxes and follow laws with no vote on any of the officials who make those rules.

118-hr-2964.one_liner: Require disposable wipes to carry a 'Do Not Flush' label on packaging
provisions: Companies that make or sell disposable wipes must put a 'Do Not Flush' label and symbol on the packaging.
This includes baby wipes, cleaning wipes, and personal care wipes.
The label and symbol must follow specific industry guidelines for how they look.
The Federal Trade Commission — a government agency that enforces consumer rules — will create the rules for how this works.
The FTC can take action against companies that do not follow the labeling rules.

supporters: Supporters say requiring a 'Do Not Flush' label on baby wipes, cleaning wipes, and personal care wipes will stop people from flushing them, which clogs sewer systems and costs cities millions of dollars each year to fix.
Supporters say giving the FTC power to enforce the labeling rule means companies that skip the label can be held accountable, making the rule more than just a suggestion.
Supporters say using a standard symbol from industry guidelines makes the warning easy to understand for people who do not read English well.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for the FTC to finish writing the rules, which could mean companies go years without clear guidance on what the label must look like.

Critics say small wipe manufacturers may face higher packaging costs to redesign labels to include the required 'Do Not Flush' phrase and symbol, and the bill does not include any help for smaller businesses.
Critics say the bill only covers retail packaging, so wipes sold in bulk or distributed without standard packaging — like in hospitals or schools — would not have to carry the warning.

118-hr-3019.one_liner: Create a system to inspect and oversee federal prisons
provisions: The DOJ Inspector General must inspect all federal prisons, with higher-risk prisons checked more often.
Inspections can happen with or without advance notice.
A new official called an Ombudsman is created inside DOJ to receive complaints about federal prisons.
The Ombudsman can look into problems, ask questions, and suggest fixes — or choose not to act on a complaint.
Federal prisons cannot punish anyone for filing a complaint or triggering an inspection.
The Ombudsman must work with prisons to let people inside, their families, and the public know this role exists.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the DOJ Inspector General to inspect all federal prisons, with more frequent checks at higher-risk facilities, will create consistent oversight where it has been missing.
Supporters say unannounced inspections will stop prisons from hiding problems before inspectors arrive, giving a more honest picture of conditions inside.
Supporters say the new Ombudsman gives incarcerated people and their families a direct way to report problems without fear, since the bill bans prisons from punishing anyone who files a complaint.
critics: Critics say the bill gives the Ombudsman the power to decline complaints without acting, which means serious problems inside federal prisons could still go unaddressed.
Critics say the bill does not set a fixed schedule or minimum number of inspections for lower-risk facilities, which could leave some prisons rarely checked.

Critics say creating a new Ombudsman office inside DOJ — the same department that runs the Bureau of Prisons — may limit how independently that office can act against the prisons it is meant to oversee.

118-hr-3354.one_liner: Name a Virginia post office after former Secretary of State Madeleine Albright
provisions: Renames the post office at 220 North Hatcher Avenue in Purcellville, Virginia as the 'Secretary of State Madeleine Albright Post Office Building'.
Madeleine Albright served as U.S. Secretary of State from 1997 to 2001 and was the first woman to hold that office.
Only the name of the building changes — all mail services, hours, and operations at that post office stay the same.
The new name takes effect when the bill is signed into law.

supporters: Supporters say the renaming honors Madeleine Albright's role as the first woman to serve as U.S. Secretary of State, a position she held from 1997 to 2001.
Supporters say the designation at 220 North Hatcher Avenue in Purcellville, Virginia gives the local community a permanent way to recognize a historic national figure.
Supporters say the bill changes only the name of the building and does not affect mail services, hours, or operations at the post office.
critics: Critics say the post office at 220 North Hatcher Avenue in Purcellville, Virginia has no known direct connection to Madeleine Albright, making the location choice unclear.
Critics say naming a local post office after a national figure who has no documented ties to Purcellville may not reflect the wishes of the people who use that facility.

118-hr-3195.one_liner: Reopen federal land in Minnesota's Superior National Forest to mining
provisions: A 2020 federal order blocked mining on about 225,000 acres of forest land in Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties, Minnesota — this bill cancels that order.
Mining companies can apply to operate mines in the Superior National Forest, and the government must finish all required reviews within 18 months of getting a plan.
Mineral leases and permits that were taken back under the 2020 ban are restored to the companies that held them.
Once restored, those leases and permits cannot be challenged in court.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the 2020 order reopens about 225,000 acres in Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties to mining, which they argue creates jobs and tax revenue for northern Minnesota.
Supporters say requiring the government to finish all mine plan reviews within 18 months gives companies a clear timeline instead of delays that have lasted years.
Supporters say restoring cancelled leases and permits lets mining companies recover rights they held before the 2020 ban took effect.
critics: Critics say the bill removes the ability to challenge restored leases and permits in court, which they argue takes away a legal check on mining operations near the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness.

Critics say completing full environmental reviews for all mine plans within 18 months may not leave enough time to study how sulfide-ore mining could affect water quality in the Superior National Forest.
Critics say reopening 225,000 acres to mineral leasing reverses a decision the federal government made specifically to protect the watershed that feeds into the Boundary Waters.

118-hr-2925.one_liner: Let mining companies build roads and structures on public land before finding minerals
provisions: Mining companies can build roads, buildings, and other structures on public land even before they find any minerals there.
Right now, companies must show they found minerals before they can do major construction on public land — this bill removes that requirement.
This applies to land owned by the federal government, which makes up about 28% of all land in the United States.

supporters: Supporters say removing the requirement to find minerals before building roads and structures will let mining companies explore federal land faster and at lower cost, making it easier to find minerals the U.S. currently imports from other countries.

Supporters say the current rule forces companies to prove a mineral deposit exists before they can build access roads, which makes early-stage exploration on the 28% of U.S. land owned by the federal government too expensive to attempt.
Supporters say allowing construction during exploration — not just after a discovery — brings mining activity in line with how oil and gas companies are already allowed to operate on public land.
critics: Critics say the bill lets mining companies build permanent roads and structures on federal public land with no guarantee that any minerals will ever be found there, leaving the land disturbed even if a mine never opens.
Critics say removing the mineral discovery requirement takes away one of the few checks that currently limits how much of the 28% of federally owned land can be used for mining infrastructure.
Critics say the bill does not include new rules for cleanup or reclamation if a company builds on public land and then finds no minerals worth mining.

118-hr-3950.one_liner: Require ticket sellers to show the full price before you pick a seat
provisions: Ticket sellers must show the total price — including all fees — before you choose a ticket, not at the end of checkout.
The full price must also appear in any ad or price listing, not just at the checkout page.
Sellers must list each fee separately, such as service fees, processing fees, delivery fees, and taxes.
If a seller does not actually have the ticket yet, they must tell you that before you pick it.
The Federal Trade Commission enforces these rules.

supporters: Supporters say requiring sellers to show the total price — including all service fees, processing fees, and delivery fees — before a buyer selects a ticket will stop the surprise charges that appear at checkout today.
Supporters say making the full price appear in ads and price listings means buyers can compare real costs across sellers before they even visit a checkout page.
Supporters say the rule that sellers must tell buyers when they do not actually have the ticket yet protects people from buying something that may not be delivered.
critics: Critics say the law puts a heavy compliance burden on small ticket resellers who will need to rebuild their websites and ad systems to show itemized fees and total prices at the first step of a transaction.

Critics say requiring every fee to be listed separately — service fees, processing fees, delivery fees, and taxes — may clutter listings and make it harder for buyers to quickly compare prices across platforms.

Critics say giving the Federal Trade Commission enforcement power over ticketing practices could lead to inconsistent penalties across sellers of different sizes with no set fine amounts written into the bill.

118-hr-354.one_liner: Let active and retired police officers carry concealed guns in more places across state lines
provisions: Active and retired police officers can carry a hidden gun in school zones, which was not allowed before
Active and retired police officers can carry a hidden gun in national parks
Active and retired police officers can carry a hidden gun in businesses and other places open to the public
Active and retired police officers can carry a hidden gun in certain federal buildings open to the public
States can let retired officers go through gun qualification tests less often than current rules require
