supporters: Supporters say allowing qualified active and retired officers to carry concealed firearms in school zones gives trained law enforcement a way to respond to threats in places where they are often already present.

Supporters say expanding carry rights to national parks, public businesses, and certain federal buildings means that off-duty and retired officers can act quickly in emergencies without being blocked by location-based rules.

Supporters say letting states reduce how often retired officers must re-qualify keeps experienced law enforcement engaged without placing a heavy burden on officers who are no longer working full-time.
critics: Critics say removing the school zone restriction for retired officers lowers the standard for who can carry guns near children, since retired officers may not train as regularly as active-duty police.
Critics say allowing concealed carry in federal buildings open to the public, such as post offices or courthouses, creates security risks in places that already have their own armed security staff.

Critics say letting states reduce qualification testing for retired officers means some carriers may not meet the same readiness standards, since the current federal rule requires regular re-qualification to keep the permit valid.

118-hr-3738.one_liner: Create a new VA office to run economic and education programs for veterans
provisions: Creates a new office inside the Department of Veterans Affairs to run economic programs for veterans, their families, and survivors.
The new office takes over job training, employment programs, and the program that helps service members move into civilian jobs.
The new office takes over education programs that help veterans pay for school.
The new office takes over the VA's home loan programs and the database that tracks small businesses owned by veterans.
Before programs move to the new office, the VA must confirm the move will not disrupt services to veterans.
Sets a cap on how many full-time workers the new office can hire in 2024 and 2025.
Sets a matching cap for the Veterans Benefits Administration.

supporters: Supporters say that creating a separate office just for economic programs — covering job training, education benefits, and home loans — will let veterans get faster, more focused help instead of being one priority among many inside the larger Veterans Benefits Administration.

Supporters say the requirement that the VA must confirm services will not be disrupted before any programs move protects veterans from losing access to benefits like the GI Bill or the Transition Assistance Program during the changeover.

Supporters say grouping the small business database, home loan programs, and employment services under one roof makes it easier for veterans and their families to find and use all the economic help they are entitled to.
critics: Critics say the hiring caps set for 2024 and 2025 limit how many full-time workers the new office and the Veterans Benefits Administration can employ, which could reduce the staff available to process education, home loan, and job training claims.

Critics say standing up a brand-new administration adds overhead and management layers, and that the cost of building new leadership structures could pull funding away from direct services to veterans and their dependents.

Critics say the VA's self-certification process — where the agency confirms its own readiness before transferring programs — may not be a strong enough check to prevent disruptions to services like vocational rehabilitation that veterans depend on.

118-hr-3397.one_liner: Block a Bureau of Land Management conservation rule from taking effect
provisions: Requires the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) to pull back its proposed conservation rule.
Stops BLM from finishing, putting in place, or enforcing that rule.
Blocks BLM from making final or putting in place any future rule that is substantially similar to its proposed conservation rule.

supporters: Supporters say the BLM's proposed conservation rule would have let the agency treat conservation as a land use equal to grazing and mining, which they argue goes beyond what Congress authorized BLM to do on public lands.

Supporters say blocking the rule protects ranchers, energy producers, and mining companies in western states who depend on BLM-managed land for their livelihoods and say the rule would have limited their access.

Supporters say the bill also blocks BLM from issuing any future rule that is substantially similar, which they argue prevents the agency from finding workarounds to impose the same restrictions under a different name.
critics: Critics say the bill stops BLM from completing a rule designed to improve the health of public land ecosystems, which BLM manages across more than 245 million acres in the western United States.

Critics say the provision blocking any 'substantially similar' future rule would limit BLM's ability to write new conservation policies even if Congress or courts later support them, removing a tool the agency uses to manage land over the long term.

Critics say the bill does not replace the withdrawn rule with any other conservation standard, leaving BLM without updated guidance on how to protect soil, water, and wildlife habitat on the lands it oversees.

118-hr-3602.one_liner: Add prison time for tipping off criminals about border agents or destroying border equipment
provisions: Anyone who tells criminals where border agents are, to help with an immigration, customs, or drug crime, can get up to 10 years in prison.
Destroying or damaging a device used to watch the border or a border crossing can get someone up to 10 years in prison.
Using a gun while helping someone with a felony record enter the country illegally adds extra prison time on top of the original sentence.

supporters: Supporters say the 10-year prison penalty for spotting border agents — sharing their location to help with an immigration, customs, or drug crime — will make it harder for cartels to move people and drugs across the border.

Supporters say that adding extra prison time for using a gun while helping someone with a felony record enter the country illegally will discourage armed criminal networks from operating at the border.
Supporters say making it a federal crime to destroy border monitoring devices protects equipment that agents rely on to catch smugglers and stop illegal crossings.
critics: Critics say the bill's language around 'transmitting the location of law enforcement' is broad enough to cover journalists, lawyers, or aid workers who share information about where border agents are operating, even without criminal intent.

Critics say the enhanced gun penalties apply to people helping someone with a felony record enter — but that category can include family members of long-term U.S. residents trying to reunite, not just armed cartel members.
Critics say the bill does not define what counts as a border 'device,' which could make it unclear whether damaging a fence post or a sensor triggers the 10-year maximum sentence.

118-hr-4016.one_liner: Speed up repayment to veterans whose benefits were stolen by their caretakers
provisions: When a person in charge of a veteran's money misuses those funds, the VA must pay the veteran back faster.
The VA cannot hold up repayment just because it hasn't finished deciding whether it made a mistake in choosing that caretaker.
The VA does not have to investigate its own role in every single case of stolen benefits before sending repayment.

supporters: Supporters say the bill stops the VA from holding up repayment to veterans while it is still deciding whether it made a mistake in choosing the person placed in charge of their money.
Supporters say the bill removes the rule that required the VA to complete a negligence review for every single case of misuse before sending repayment to the affected veteran.
Supporters say veterans whose money was misused by the person managing their account will receive repayment sooner, because the VA can no longer delay payment while its internal review is pending.
critics: Critics say that because the VA is no longer required to check its own role in every case, repeated problems in how it selects people to manage veterans' money may go undetected.
Critics say allowing repayment to proceed while a negligence review is still pending means the VA does not have to determine whether it made a mistake before closing a case.

Critics say the bill does not set a specific deadline for when repayment must arrive — only that the VA cannot hold it up — leaving veterans without a guaranteed timeframe for getting their money back.

118-hr-4581.one_liner: Add stillbirth prevention research to a federal health funding program
provisions: A federal program that gives money to states for mother and child health services will now also cover research on preventing stillbirths.
States can use the grant money to run programs that work to reduce the number of stillbirths.

supporters: Supporters say adding stillbirth prevention to the Maternal and Child Health Services Block Grant means states can now use this money to fund research and programs that could reduce the number of babies lost to stillbirth each year.
Supporters say giving states the ability to run stillbirth prevention programs through an existing federal grant makes it easier to reach mothers who are already using state maternal health services.
critics: Critics say the bill does not add new funding, so states may have to take money away from other maternal and child health programs already running under the block grant.

Critics say the bill does not set any specific goals, required outcomes, or reporting rules for how states must use the stillbirth prevention money, which could make it hard to know if the programs are working.

118-hr-4143.one_liner: Expand a federal team's power to investigate collapses of bridges, towers, and other structures
provisions: A federal team at NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) can only investigate when buildings collapse or almost collapse.
People must have died or been at risk of dying.
This bill lets the team also investigate other structures, like bridges or towers.
The team finds out what likely caused the structure to fail.
The team also looks at how people were evacuated and whether emergency responses worked.
The team recommends changes to engineering rules and standards based on what it finds.

supporters: Supporters say expanding the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) investigation team beyond buildings to cover bridges, towers, and other structures means more failures will be studied and more engineering standards can be improved.

Supporters say the team's review of evacuation and emergency response procedures — currently limited to building collapses — would now apply to a wider range of dangerous structure failures, helping communities respond better in the future.
Supporters say requiring NIST to find the likely cause of non-building failures and recommend rule changes could prevent future collapses before people are killed or put at risk.
critics: Critics say the bill does not define which 'other types of structures' qualify for investigation, leaving it unclear whether the team has the staff and budget to cover bridges, towers, dams, and other infrastructure.

Critics say the current trigger — that people must have died or been at serious risk — may be hard to apply to non-building structures like bridges or towers, where failure conditions work differently.
Critics say expanding the team's authority without adding funding or staff could stretch NIST's existing resources thin, slowing down investigations of both buildings and other structures.

118-hr-4310.one_liner: Ban consumer products that contain 10% or more sodium nitrite
provisions: Makes it illegal to sell any consumer product that contains 10% or more sodium nitrite.
Sodium nitrite is a chemical that can be deadly in large amounts — a small quantity can kill a person.
A 10% concentration means 1 out of every 10 parts of the product is sodium nitrite.
Products with lower concentrations of sodium nitrite, like some cured meats, are not affected by this rule.

supporters: Supporters say banning products with 10% or more sodium nitrite will protect young people, since even a small amount of the chemical can be lethal.
Supporters say the rule targets concentrated sodium nitrite sold directly to consumers, not food products like cured meats that have much lower levels.
Supporters say removing high-concentration sodium nitrite from consumer sale cuts off easy access to a substance that has been used in self-poisonings.
critics: Critics say the bill does not define which specific consumer products are covered, which could create confusion about what sellers must remove from shelves.
Critics say the 10% threshold may be set without enough scientific review, and that some legitimate industrial or food-preservation uses could be affected.
Critics say enforcement details are missing from the bill, leaving it unclear how the ban would be monitored or what penalties sellers would face.

118-hr-4510.one_liner: Reauthorize and expand the federal office that manages wireless signals and internet policy
provisions: Keeps the NTIA — the federal office that manages wireless signals and internet policy — funded through 2025.
Raises the head of NTIA to a higher rank within the Department of Commerce.
Gives the NTIA official authority over spectrum — the frequencies that carry Wi-Fi, phone calls, and TV signals.
Requires the NTIA to run a public campaign to help Americans learn how to stay safe online.
Requires the NTIA to report on whether foreign companies in the U.S. telecom supply chain pose security risks.
Requires the NTIA to create a plan to get more Americans connected to the internet.
Requires the NTIA to review whether foreign ownership of U.S. telecom companies creates national security risks.

supporters: Supporters say raising the NTIA head to Under Secretary gives the agency more power to push internet and wireless policy inside the Department of Commerce, which could speed up decisions on spectrum use and the digital divide plan.
Supporters say requiring the NTIA to report on foreign companies in the U.S. telecom supply chain will help the government find and fix security risks before they become bigger problems.

Supporters say the plan to get more Americans connected to the internet, combined with the online safety campaign, gives the NTIA clear legal duties to close the gap between people who have internet access and those who do not.
critics: Critics say the bill only funds the NTIA through 2025, which means Congress will have to reauthorize it again soon, creating uncertainty for the agency's long-term programs like the digital divide strategy.

Critics say adding new duties — like running a cybersecurity literacy campaign, reviewing foreign telecom ownership, and managing spectrum sharing — without setting a specific budget could spread NTIA resources too thin.

Critics say the bill gives NTIA authority to review foreign ownership of U.S. telecom companies, but does not set clear deadlines or enforcement tools, which could make the national security reviews slow or inconsistent.

118-hr-4824.one_liner: Expand a Department of Energy program for carbon storage research, testing, and commercialization
provisions: The Department of Energy's carbon storage program now includes storing carbon in plants and soil, and storing it underground in rock formations and water-filled rock layers.
The program covers research, testing, real-world demonstrations, and bringing carbon storage to commercial use — not just lab work.
DOE must submit a long-term, strategic, and prioritized plan once a year that identifies the biggest obstacles to using these carbon storage methods at a large scale.
The first long-term strategic plan must be submitted within two years of this bill becoming law.

supporters: Supporters say requiring DOE to submit a new strategic plan every year will keep carbon storage research moving forward and force the agency to name the biggest barriers to storing carbon in soil, plants, and underground rock layers.
Supporters say expanding the program to cover real-world testing and commercial use — not just lab work — gives companies a clearer path to actually deploying carbon storage at large scale.
Supporters say adding terrestrial storage, like carbon in plants and soil, alongside underground storage in rock formations and aquifers gives researchers more tools to find what works best.
critics: Critics say the bill sets no funding levels, so without a budget attached, the new annual planning requirement may produce reports that sit on a shelf without leading to real action.
Critics say the two-year deadline to submit the first strategic plan means carbon storage research priorities could go without a guiding framework for up to 24 months after the bill becomes law.
Critics say the bill focuses on expanding DOE research programs but does not set measurable targets for how much carbon must be stored or by when, making it hard to hold the program accountable.

118-hr-4755.one_liner: Fund federal research into tools that keep personal data private
provisions: The National Science Foundation must fund research on tools that make personal data harder to trace back to specific people.
The foundation must include this type of privacy research in its computer security grant program.
A network of 24 federal agencies must work together to speed up the creation and use of these privacy tools.
The National Institute of Standards and Technology must work with businesses and the public to create voluntary rules for using these tools when collecting and sharing data.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the National Science Foundation to fund research on de-identification tools will make it harder for companies and hackers to trace collected data back to specific people.

Supporters say coordinating 24 federal agencies under the Networking and Information Technology Research and Development Program will speed up how quickly these privacy tools get built and used across government.
Supporters say having NIST create voluntary standards gives businesses a clear guide for using privacy tools when they collect and share data, without forcing them to start from scratch.
critics: Critics say the standards NIST creates are voluntary, meaning businesses can ignore them, leaving people's data just as exposed as before.
Critics say spreading responsibility across 24 federal agencies and multiple offices like NSF, NIST, and the FTC could slow decisions and create confusion over who is actually in charge.
Critics say the bill does not set a funding amount for the National Science Foundation's privacy research, making it unclear whether enough money will be available to produce useful tools.

118-hr-4691.one_liner: Require Congress to approve or block Iran sanctions changes before they take effect
provisions: The President must send Congress a written notice before lifting, pausing, or changing any Iran sanctions.
After getting that notice, Congress has 30 days to vote on whether to allow the action.
If Congress is in summer recess between July 10 and September 7, the review window extends to 60 days.
The President cannot take the action until Congress approves it with a vote.
If Congress votes to block the action, the President cannot move forward with it.

supporters: Supporters say the 30-day review window gives Congress a real chance to check whether the President is trading away sanctions without a vote, keeping that power in elected hands.
Supporters say requiring a written notice before any licensing action that changes U.S. policy toward Iran means Congress gets the facts — what the action is and why — before it happens, not after.
Supporters say the 60-day extension during the July 10–September 7 recess period makes sure Congress is not bypassed just because members are out of session.
critics: Critics say requiring a full congressional vote before the President can lift or waive any Iran sanction slows down diplomacy, since deal terms often need fast, flexible responses that a 30-day clock does not allow.

Critics say the rule that the President cannot act until Congress passes a joint resolution of approval gives Congress a veto over routine licensing decisions that have traditionally been executive branch tools.

Critics say the bill's broad definition of actions that 'significantly alter' foreign policy is unclear, which could mean almost any Iran-related decision triggers the review process and ties the President's hands.

118-hr-4763.one_liner: Set rules for which government agency oversees different types of digital money
provisions: Creates a set of rules deciding whether digital assets like crypto tokens are watched over by the CFTC (a trading watchdog) or the SEC (the stock market regulator)
If a digital asset runs on a blockchain that no single person or company controls, the CFTC oversees it — the same agency that watches over gold and oil trading
A blockchain counts as not controlled by one party if no person or company owns 20% or more of the digital asset or its voting power
If a digital asset runs on a blockchain where one person or company is still in charge, the SEC oversees it — the same agency that watches over stocks
Some digital assets can skip SEC rules if they cap how much they sell each year and limit sales to experienced investors who meet certain financial thresholds
Stablecoins — digital tokens tied to a fixed dollar value — are not regulated by either agency, except when it comes to stopping fraud

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives crypto companies a clear rule for the first time: if no single person or company controls 20% or more of a digital asset or its voting power, the CFTC — the same agency that oversees gold and oil — takes charge instead of the SEC, removing years of legal confusion.

Supporters say smaller crypto projects can skip full SEC registration if they cap yearly sales and limit access to experienced investors who meet financial thresholds, which lets early-stage digital asset companies raise money without the same costs as a public stock offering.

Supporters say stablecoins — tokens tied to a fixed dollar value — are kept outside of both the CFTC and SEC rulebooks, except for anti-fraud rules, which supporters say removes barriers for dollar-backed digital payment tools.
critics: Critics say the 20% ownership threshold for deciding if a blockchain is decentralized is easy to work around, letting token issuers spread ownership just enough to move from SEC oversight to the lighter CFTC rules.

Critics say pulling digital assets out of SEC oversight removes investor protections that apply to stocks — like required disclosures and rules against insider trading — from assets that everyday people are buying.

Critics say leaving stablecoins outside both the CFTC and the SEC, except for fraud cases, means there is no agency requiring the companies behind them to prove they hold enough real dollars to back every token in circulation.

118-hr-4639.one_liner: Stop law enforcement from buying your private data without a court order
provisions: Right now, police and spy agencies can buy your personal data from data brokers without a warrant. This bill makes that illegal.
Data brokers are companies that collect and sell information about people — like where you go, what you buy, and who you talk to.
Under this bill, the government must get a judge's approval before getting your personal records from any outside company.
Government agencies cannot share data they bought with police or intelligence agencies to get around this rule.
Any data the government got this way cannot be used against you in court.
This bill also covers a new type of company — middlemen that move or store your data between tech services — and gives them the same rules as other tech providers.

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a loophole that lets police and spy agencies buy personal data — like location history and purchase records — from data brokers without getting a warrant, which they argue bypasses Fourth Amendment protections.

Supporters say the bill requires the government to get a judge's approval before obtaining personal records from any outside company, including middlemen that move or store data between tech services.
Supporters say that banning the use of purchased data in any trial or court hearing removes the government's incentive to buy its way around warrant requirements.
critics: Critics say requiring court orders to access commercially available data broker records could slow down time-sensitive law enforcement and national security investigations.

Critics say extending Stored Communications Act rules to intermediary service providers — companies that move or store data between tech services — creates a broad new category that may be hard to define and enforce.

Critics say blocking government agencies from sharing purchased records with law enforcement or intelligence agencies limits coordination between federal offices in ways that could leave gaps in criminal and national security cases.

118-hr-4877.one_liner: Start a five-year government research program on abandoned oil and gas wells
provisions: The Department of Energy must start a research program on abandoned oil and gas wells — wells that were drilled but no longer in use.
The program works to find where abandoned wells are located, including ones that were never officially recorded.
It studies how to plug, clean up, and repurpose those wells.
It looks for ways to reduce harm to the environment from abandoned wells.
The program runs for five years and then ends.

supporters: Supporters say the DOE program would help find and fix the estimated hundreds of thousands of abandoned wells across the U.S. that leak methane and other harmful gases into the air and water.
Supporters say requiring DOE to track down wells that were never officially recorded closes a gap in current data, helping communities near those wells know about risks they did not know existed.
Supporters say the five-year time limit keeps the program focused and avoids open-ended government spending.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include any funding amount, so there is no guarantee DOE will have the money needed to actually plug or clean up abandoned wells — only to study them.
Critics say a research-only program that ends after five years may not lead to real action, since the bill does not require DOE to plug any wells or set cleanup targets.
Critics say the bill does not say who pays for plugging wells once they are found, leaving that cost question unanswered for states and taxpayers.

118-hr-5403.one_liner: Stop the Federal Reserve from creating or issuing a digital dollar
provisions: Stops Federal Reserve banks from opening accounts for individual Americans
Stops the Federal Reserve from creating a digital version of the U.S. dollar
Stops the Federal Reserve from using a digital dollar to control interest rates or the money supply

supporters: Supporters say the bill would stop the Federal Reserve from opening accounts for individual Americans, which they argue would protect people from government tracking of every purchase they make.
Supporters say banning a digital dollar would prevent the Federal Reserve from using it to control how people spend money, such as blocking certain purchases or penalizing savings.

Supporters say the bill stops the Federal Reserve from using a central bank digital currency to set interest rates or adjust the money supply, which they say keeps that power out of one agency's hands.
critics: Critics say blocking the Federal Reserve from issuing a digital dollar could put the U.S. behind other countries that are already building their own central bank digital currencies, weakening the dollar's role in global trade.
Critics say the bill removes a tool the Federal Reserve could use to send money directly to Americans faster and at lower cost than the current banking system allows.
Critics say banning Federal Reserve accounts for individuals could limit access to basic financial services for the roughly 5.9 million U.S. households that do not have a bank account.

118-hr-529.one_liner: Extend the ocean zone where U.S. customs officers can board and check ships
provisions: The zone where U.S. customs rules apply at sea expands from 12 nautical miles to 24 nautical miles from the U.S. coast.
U.S. customs officers can board and search ships anywhere in this 24-nautical-mile zone.
Ships found carrying undeclared or illegal goods within 24 nautical miles of shore can be stopped and inspected.
The 24-nautical-mile boundary matches a limit the U.S. set under international law in 1999.
The old boundary — 4 leagues, which equals 12 nautical miles — is replaced by the new 24-nautical-mile line.

supporters: Supporters say expanding the customs zone from 12 to 24 nautical miles gives officers more space to stop ships carrying illegal or undeclared goods before they reach shore.

Supporters say the 24-nautical-mile limit already matches a boundary the U.S. set under international law in 1999 through Presidential Proclamation 7219, so this change brings customs law in line with rules already in place.
Supporters say customs officers would be able to board and search ships at 24 nautical miles instead of 12, giving them twice as much range to catch smuggling at sea.
critics: Critics say giving customs officers the power to board and search any ship within 24 nautical miles could affect foreign commercial vessels that are operating legally under international rules.
Critics say the bill does not include funding or staffing to enforce the expanded 24-nautical-mile zone, which could make the new authority hard to use in practice.
Critics say moving the inspection boundary from 12 to 24 nautical miles may lead to legal disputes with other countries over where U.S. customs authority ends and international waters begin.

118-hr-5863.one_liner: Remove federal income taxes on payments received for wildfire and certain disaster losses
provisions: Money you get for wildfire disaster losses from fires declared after 2014 is not taxed as income.
People who lost money in the East Palestine, Ohio train derailment on February 3, 2023, don't pay taxes on relief payments.
The bill extends a rule that lets disaster victims deduct personal losses from their federal taxes.

supporters: Supporters say wildfire victims who received disaster relief payments after 2014 should not have to pay income tax on that money, since they are already dealing with major losses.

Supporters say people who lost property or income due to the East Palestine, Ohio train derailment on February 3, 2023 should not be taxed on compensation payments they received to cover those losses.
Supporters say extending the rule that lets disaster victims deduct personal casualty losses from their federal taxes gives families more financial help when they are trying to rebuild.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a clear spending limit or cap on how much tax-free compensation one person can receive for wildfire or train derailment losses.
Critics say covering losses from a single train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio creates a special carve-out that other disaster victims in different states did not receive.
Critics say extending personal casualty loss deductions adds to the federal deficit without a plan to offset the lost tax revenue.

118-hr-4866.one_liner: Create new programs to improve wildfire tracking and coordination across agencies
provisions: NOAA sets up a new program to help federal, state, and local groups share information about wildfires and how they spread.
The program funds research and tools to detect wildfires earlier and better understand how weather affects fire behavior.
NOAA can hire private companies to collect data from planes and satellites to help predict and monitor wildfires.
NOAA can test drones to gather weather data in areas where wildfires occur.
A new group made up of different federal agencies is created to help state and local governments manage wildfires without doing the same work twice.
A separate advisory group is created to give guidance to the coordinating group and other agencies on wildfire management.

supporters: Supporters say the new NOAA program will help federal, state, and local groups share wildfire data faster, which could mean earlier warnings before a fire spreads.
Supporters say allowing NOAA to hire private companies to collect data from planes and satellites will give agencies better tools to predict where wildfires are heading.
Supporters say the new Interagency Coordinating Committee will stop different agencies from doing the same work twice, which wastes time and money during active wildfires.
critics: Critics say creating two new groups — the Interagency Coordinating Committee and the National Advisory Committee — adds more layers of government without a clear plan for how they will make decisions faster than existing agencies.
Critics say the bill does not set a specific funding amount for the NOAA program, so there is no guarantee the research, drone testing, and private data contracts will actually be paid for.
Critics say state and local fire agencies already deal with too many federal contacts, and adding a new coordinating committee could slow down communication instead of helping it.

118-hr-6093.one_liner: Extend NOAA weather forecasting programs and add new weather data tools
provisions: Keeps NOAA weather research programs funded through 2028
Requires NOAA to improve radar accuracy and expand weather forecasting in areas that currently get less coverage
Requires NOAA to buy weather data from private companies and test whether that data works with government systems
Requires upgrades to weather warning systems so they reach more people, including in rural areas, using newer technology like cloud-based services
Adds a program to improve flood forecasts along coastlines
Adds programs to improve weather forecasts for farmers and water managers in western and central states, plus a network to track soil moisture

supporters: Supporters say reauthorizing NOAA weather research programs through 2028 gives forecasters stable funding to run the VORTEX-USA tornado research program, which could reduce response times in tornado-prone areas.

Supporters say the bill requires NOAA to expand radar coverage and improve forecasts in areas that currently get less service, including rural communities that now miss out on timely weather warnings.
Supporters say the new soil moisture monitoring network and pilot programs for western and central states give farmers and water managers better data to make decisions during droughts or floods.
critics: Critics say requiring NOAA to buy weather data from private companies and then test whether it works with government systems creates a two-step process that may duplicate data the agency already collects.

Critics say the coastal flooding forecasting program and the soil moisture monitoring network are added as requirements without a stated dollar amount attached, leaving it unclear how NOAA will pay for them on top of existing workloads.

Critics say upgrading warning systems to cloud-based services in rural areas may take years to implement, meaning communities that need better coverage the most could wait a long time before seeing any change.

118-hr-615.one_liner: Stop federal agencies from banning lead ammunition and fishing tackle on federal land
provisions: Stops federal agencies from banning lead bullets or lead fishing tackle on federal land open to hunting or fishing.
This applies to land run by the Department of the Interior and the Department of Agriculture.
Agencies can still ban lead if field data from that specific area shows it is causing a drop in local wildlife.
The state where that land is located must also approve the ban before it can take effect.
Some lead rules that were already in place before this bill stay in effect.

supporters: Supporters say the bill stops the Department of the Interior and the Department of Agriculture from banning lead ammunition or fishing tackle on federal land open to hunting and fishing, keeping access to affordable gear that hunters and anglers have used for generations.
Supporters say agencies can still restrict lead if field data from that specific land unit shows it is causing a wildlife decline, so the bill allows regulation where there is direct local evidence.
Supporters say requiring state approval before any new lead ban takes effect gives states a role in managing wildlife on federal land within their borders.
critics: Critics say the bill removes federal agency authority to act on lead pollution across wide areas of federal land, even when research links lead from ammunition and tackle to harm in birds like bald eagles and condors.

Critics say the bill requires showing a wildlife decline at one specific land unit before any restriction can take effect, meaning agencies cannot act on broader patterns of lead exposure across connected habitats.
Critics say the state-approval requirement adds a second step before protections can be put in place, which could delay or block restrictions even when field data at a specific site supports them.

118-hr-6046.one_liner: Label Ansarallah a terrorist group and freeze the money and visas of its members
provisions: The State Department must officially label Ansarallah, also known as the Houthis, as a foreign terrorist organization.
The President must freeze any money or property that Ansarallah holds in the United States.
Members, helpers, and partners of Ansarallah are banned from getting U.S. visas and have their U.S. money frozen.
Groups or businesses that Ansarallah owns or controls face the same money freeze and visa ban.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the State Department to officially label Ansarallah as a foreign terrorist organization gives the U.S. government legal tools to cut off funding and support to a group that has attacked U.S. Navy ships and international cargo ships in the Red Sea.
Supporters say freezing any U.S.-held money or property belonging to Ansarallah, its members, and businesses it controls would make it harder for the group to buy weapons or pay fighters.
Supporters say banning Ansarallah members and affiliates from getting U.S. visas would stop people connected to the group from entering the country.
critics: Critics say the foreign terrorist organization label could make it harder for aid groups to deliver food and medicine inside Yemen, where the United Nations says more than 21 million people need humanitarian help.
Critics say freezing the assets of businesses Ansarallah owns or controls could affect ordinary Yemeni civilians who depend on those businesses for basic services like banking and fuel.

Critics say the bill removes presidential flexibility by making the designation mandatory, even if the President is in active negotiations or ceasefire talks that could reduce attacks on U.S. interests.

118-hr-6090.one_liner: Require the Education Department to use a set definition of antisemitism in discrimination reviews
provisions: The Education Department's civil rights office must consider the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism when looking into discrimination complaints.
The IHRA definition describes antisemitism as a certain perception of Jews, which may be expressed as hatred toward Jews.
This rule applies to schools and other programs that get federal money.
Right now, the civil rights office considers this definition as a guide, but this bill writes that requirement into law.

supporters: Supporters say writing the IHRA definition into law gives the Education Department's Office for Civil Rights a clear, consistent standard to use when investigating antisemitism complaints at federally funded schools, instead of treating it as optional guidance.

Supporters say the bill protects Jewish students at schools that receive federal money by making sure investigators apply the same definition of antisemitism every time a discrimination complaint is filed.
Supporters say the IHRA definition has already been used as a guide by the civil rights office, so making it a legal requirement simply locks in a practice that is already happening.
critics: Critics say the IHRA definition — which describes antisemitism as 'a certain perception of Jews' — is too vague to be a legal standard, and writing it into law could lead to inconsistent enforcement across federally funded schools.

Critics say some examples included in the IHRA definition could classify criticism of Israeli government policies as antisemitism, which could restrict protected speech at colleges and universities that receive federal funds.

Critics say the bill removes flexibility from the Education Department's civil rights office by requiring it to apply one specific definition in every discrimination review, even in cases where that definition may not fit.

118-hr-5947.one_liner: Cancel a deal that moved $6 billion in Iranian funds and block future ones
provisions: Cancels the waiver that let about $6 billion in Iranian money move from bank accounts in South Korea to bank accounts in Qatar.
Those funds had been frozen, and the move was tied to the release of five American citizens held in Iran.
Ends the Treasury Department licenses that made those fund transfers possible.
Stops the President from using waiver power to free up certain Iranian accounts in the future.

supporters: Supporters say the bill cancels the transfer of about $6 billion in Iranian funds from South Korea to Qatar, arguing that moving those funds gave Iran access to money it had not previously been able to use.
Supporters say ending the Treasury licenses that made the $6 billion transfer possible prevents future administrations from using the same mechanism to move frozen Iranian assets.
Supporters say that trading $6 billion in fund access for five detained Americans could encourage Iran to detain more Americans as a negotiating tool in future disputes.
critics: Critics say the bill reverses a deal that secured the release of five U.S. citizens held in Iran, and canceling the waiver could make it harder to negotiate for Americans detained abroad in the future.

Critics say blocking the President from using waiver authority over certain Iranian accounts removes a diplomatic tool that past administrations have used to resolve hostage situations without military action.

Critics say the $6 billion was Iranian money already held in restricted accounts, not U.S. taxpayer funds, and the bill misrepresents the nature of the transfer by treating it as a payment made by the United States.

118-hr-6323.one_liner: Change when the President can lift limits on foreign banks that helped Iran move money
provisions: Right now, the President can lift limits on foreign banks that helped Iran move money, but only when needed for national security.
This bill adds a second reason the President can lift those limits: if Iran stops supporting terrorism in other countries.
Congress gets the power to pass a vote blocking the President from using the national security reason to lift those limits.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives the President a new reason to lift banking limits on foreign banks that helped Iran — if Iran stops supporting terrorism abroad, those limits can be removed, which could encourage Iran to change its behavior.

Supporters say giving Congress the power to vote to block the President from lifting these limits on national security grounds adds a check so one branch cannot act alone on decisions about Iranian banks.
Supporters say tying the removal of banking limits to Iran stopping support for terrorism in other countries creates a clear, specific condition Iran must meet before getting any financial relief.
critics: Critics say allowing the President to lift restrictions on foreign banks that moved money for the Central Bank of Iran or Iranian nationals — even with new conditions — could reduce pressure on Iran before it has made verifiable changes.

Critics say the joint resolution process that lets Congress block the President only applies to the national security reason, leaving the new terrorism-related waiver without the same congressional check.

Critics say the bill does not define what counts as Iran having 'ceased to provide support for acts of international terrorism,' which could make the standard hard to enforce or easy to interpret loosely.

118-hr-6543.one_liner: Require hotels and short-term rentals to show all fees in the listed price
provisions: Hotels, motels, inns, and short-term rentals must include all required fees in the price they show when advertising or listing a room.
When you browse for a place to stay, the price you see must already include fees like resort fees or cleaning fees — not add them at checkout.
This rule does not apply to travel booked through a company, government, or school travel program.
The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general can take action against businesses that break this rule.

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires hotels, motels, and short-term rentals to include all mandatory fees — such as resort fees and cleaning fees — in the price shown when advertising or listing a room, so travelers see the full cost before they book.
Supporters say the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general are authorized to take enforcement action against any lodging provider that does not follow the price display requirement.
Supporters say requiring the full price to appear in the first price shown prevents businesses from advertising a low rate and then adding required fees only at checkout.
critics: Critics say the bill exempts travel booked through corporate, government, or institutional travel programs from the price display rule, leaving a large category of lodging bookings outside the requirement.

Critics say the bill's requirement that all mandatory fees be included in every price 'displayed or advertised' means lodging providers must update listings across every booking platform and advertisement they use to stay in compliance.

Critics say that because both the FTC and all state attorneys general can take action against businesses under this bill, a single lodging provider could face overlapping enforcement from multiple agencies for the same violation.

118-hr-6285.one_liner: Reopen federal land in Alaska for oil and gas drilling
provisions: Brings back oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR) in Alaska that were canceled by the Biden administration.
The Department of the Interior must accept bids on canceled leases within 30 days and reissue them.
A second round of lease sales must happen by December 22, 2024.
Cancels two federal rules and two executive orders that paused or limited drilling in the area.
Limits the ability of the President and the Department of the Interior to cancel future drilling leases in this area.
Limits the ability of courts to block lease approvals under this program.

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires the Department of the Interior to reissue canceled ANWR leases within 30 days and hold a second lease sale by December 22, 2024, which would open new areas for oil production and create jobs in Alaska.

Supporters say the bill removes two executive orders and two federal rules that blocked the Coastal Plain Oil and Gas Leasing Program, which Congress first approved in 2017 and which had already issued permits to oil companies.
Supporters say limiting the President's power to cancel future leases in the 1002 Area gives oil companies more certainty before they spend money on exploration and drilling.
critics: Critics say the bill limits courts' ability to block lease approvals in ANWR, which removes a legal tool that Alaska Native communities and other groups use to challenge drilling decisions.

Critics say requiring a second lease sale by December 22, 2024 would bring drilling into the 1002 Area, which Gwich'in Alaska Native communities say is calving ground for the Porcupine caribou herd they rely on for food.

Critics say the bill states that reissued leases automatically meet Endangered Species Act requirements, bypassing the normal agency review meant to check impacts on polar bears, migratory birds, and other wildlife in the refuge.

118-hr-6571.one_liner: Create a federal program to track and fix weak spots in U.S. supply chains
provisions: A group inside the Department of Commerce tracks where important U.S. goods come from and flags weak spots that could cause shortages.
The government picks which industries, goods, and supply chains need the most attention and monitoring.
A team of federal agencies works together to respond when a supply chain problem hits.
The program works with other countries to find ways to reduce the risk of shortages.
Businesses can choose to follow new guidelines the government creates to lower their supply chain risk.
The program must report regularly on what it finds and how well it is working.

supporters: Supporters say the bill sets up a group inside the Department of Commerce to map where important U.S. goods come from and spot weak spots before they cause shortages, giving the government early warning it does not have today.
Supporters say a team of federal agencies working together to respond to supply chain problems means the government acts faster and in a more organized way when shortages hit.
Supporters say working with other countries to find ways to lower shortage risks helps protect U.S. access to critical goods that American companies and consumers depend on.
critics: Critics say the guidelines the government creates for businesses are voluntary, so companies are not required to change how they manage their supply chains, which limits how much the program can actually reduce risk.

Critics say the bill does not include direct funding or incentives for businesses to fix supply chain gaps, meaning the program mostly produces reports and maps without giving companies tools to act on them.

Critics say giving the government power to pick which industries, goods, and supply chains get monitored could leave some critical sectors without attention if political or budget pressures shift priorities.

118-hr-6192.one_liner: Give the government more ways to cancel energy rules for home appliances
provisions: Appliance energy standards no longer need to be reviewed or updated on a 6-year schedule
The government can cancel an energy rule if it raises costs for consumers
The government can cancel an energy rule if it does not save a meaningful amount of energy or water
The government can cancel an energy rule if it makes a product — like a gas stove — unavailable to some buyers
New energy rules must be both technically possible and cost-justified before taking effect

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects consumer choice by allowing the government to cancel any energy rule that makes a product — such as a gas stove — unavailable to some buyers in the United States.
Supporters say requiring new energy rules to be both technically possible and cost-justified before taking effect will stop rules that raise appliance prices without delivering real savings.
Supporters say removing the 6-year mandatory review schedule lets the Department of Energy focus on updates that are actually needed, rather than being forced to revisit rules on a fixed clock.
critics: Critics say that allowing the government to cancel a rule simply because it raises costs for consumers could be used to block most new efficiency standards, since almost any new requirement adds some upfront cost to a product.
Critics say removing the 6-year review requirement means old energy standards could stay in place indefinitely, even as more efficient technology becomes widely available and cheaper.

Critics say the provision letting DOE cancel rules that do not result in 'significant' conservation of energy or water lacks a clear definition of 'significant,' which could be used to weaken a wide range of appliance standards.

118-hr-6960.one_liner: Keep federal funding for children's emergency medical programs through 2029
provisions: A federal program that helps states pay for emergency medical care for children will keep running.
The program gives money to state governments and medical schools to treat children who are badly hurt or very sick.
Federal funding for this program is approved through September 2029.

supporters: Supporters say keeping the Emergency Medical Services for Children program funded through 2029 means state governments and medical schools can keep getting federal grants to treat children who need emergency or critical care.

Supporters say children in trauma situations need care that is different from adult emergency care, and this program helps make sure states have the money to train staff and buy equipment built for kids.
Supporters say without this reauthorization, the program would lose its approved funding, which could force states to cut back on emergency services for seriously hurt or sick children.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include specific dollar amounts or funding caps, making it hard to know how much federal money will actually be spent on the program through 2029.
Critics say reauthorizing the program without requiring states to report clear results means there is no built-in check on whether the grants to state governments and medical schools are working.

118-hr-6983.one_liner: Name a post office in Lakeland, Georgia after Nell Patten Roquemore
provisions: Gives the official name 'Nell Patten Roquemore Post Office' to the post office at 15 South Valdosta Road in Lakeland, Georgia.
The name is set by Congress, making it an official federal designation.
The name change applies only to that one building — no other post offices are affected.

supporters: Supporters say that naming the post office at 15 South Valdosta Road in Lakeland, Georgia after Nell Patten Roquemore gives Congress a way to honor a community member through an official federal designation.
Supporters say that post office naming bills like this one cost nothing to carry out, since the building at 15 South Valdosta Road already exists and no new spending is required.
critics: Critics say that using congressional floor time to rename a single post office in Lakeland, Georgia delays action on bills that affect larger numbers of people or involve federal spending.
Critics say that post office naming bills, which apply to only one building and change no federal policy, are a low-priority use of the formal legislative process in Congress.

118-hr-7423.one_liner: Name a post office in Rayville, Louisiana after Luke Letlow
provisions: The post office at 103 Benedette Street in Rayville, Louisiana will be officially named the Luke Letlow Post Office Building.
Luke Letlow was elected to represent Louisiana's 5th district in Congress but died in December 2020 before taking office.
The name change is honorary and does not change how the post office runs or the services it offers.
Only the one building at 103 Benedette Street in Rayville is affected by this bill.

supporters: Supporters say naming the post office at 103 Benedette Street after Luke Letlow honors a man elected to represent Louisiana's 5th district who died in December 2020 before he could serve.
Supporters say the name change does not alter any services or operations at the Rayville post office, so it costs the community nothing while recognizing a local figure.
critics: Critics say Congress has limited floor time, and using it to rename a single building in Rayville rather than pass bills affecting more people is a poor use of that time.
Critics say honorary naming bills like this one set no policy, move no money, and change nothing about how the post office at 103 Benedette Street runs or who it serves.

118-hr-7109.one_liner: Add a citizenship question to the census and exclude non-citizens from House seat counts
provisions: The census form would ask every person in every household whether they are a U.S. citizen, a U.S. national, a non-citizen living here legally, or a non-citizen living here without legal status.
The government would publish the count of people in each of those four groups for every state.
Non-citizens would not be counted when the President sends Congress the population totals used to divide up House seats.
Right now, all people — citizens and non-citizens — are counted when deciding how many House seats each state gets.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would make House seat counts fairer by counting only citizens, since only citizens can vote — right now, states with large non-citizen populations get extra House seats that represent people who cannot vote.

Supporters say requiring the census to ask about citizenship status and publish the count of all four groups — citizens, nationals, legal non-citizens, and undocumented non-citizens — for each state would give Congress better data when making laws about immigration and federal funding.

Supporters say that under the current system, a state with many non-citizens gains more seats in Congress than a state with the same number of citizens, shifting political power away from states with fewer non-citizens.
critics: Critics say the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution requires that House seats be based on the count of all 'persons' in each state — not just citizens — and that this bill would conflict with that rule.

Critics say removing non-citizens from the reapportionment count would cost states like California, Texas, and New York one or more House seats, cutting their power in Congress even though those states still must provide schools, roads, and services to all residents.

Critics say adding a question about legal status to the census form could cause non-citizens — including people here legally — to skip the census out of fear, leading to an undercount that affects not just House seats but also federal funding that is tied to population totals.

118-hr-7219.one_liner: Make federal agencies post the data and methods behind their rules
provisions: The Office of Management and Budget must update its rules for how federal agencies use data when writing or updating regulations.
Federal agencies must use the best available data and science when writing any rule or guidance.
Any agency that writes a rule must post online the data sources, models, and methods it used so the public can see them.
These posting rules apply to any information that has a clear or large effect on how a rule is written or explained to the public.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would force agencies to post the data sources, models, and methods they used to write rules, so the public and outside experts can check the government's work.
Supporters say requiring agencies to use the best available science and data when writing regulations means rules will be based on stronger evidence, not outdated or cherry-picked studies.

Supporters say the Office of Management and Budget updating its guidelines for all federal agencies creates one clear standard for how influential information — data with a large effect on rules — must be handled.
critics: Critics say the requirement to post all data sources, models, and methods for every rule that has a 'clear or substantial impact' could slow down the rulemaking process, since agencies would need extra time and staff to prepare and publish that documentation.

Critics say the bill does not define what counts as 'best reasonably available' data, which could let regulated industries challenge agency rules in court by arguing the agency picked the wrong studies.
Critics say small agencies with limited budgets may struggle to meet the new publishing requirements for every rule that affects the public, without any added funding provided by the bill.

118-hr-6572.one_liner: Create a federal program to promote blockchain and digital ledger technology
provisions: The Department of Commerce must create a program to support blockchain and other digital ledger technologies.
Blockchain is a system that stores and shares verified digital records across many computers at once.
The program also covers digital tokens — transferable online records — and the process of creating them.
Commerce must form advisory groups to develop best practices for using blockchain and related technologies.
Commerce must send Congress a yearly report on the program.
The report must include recommendations for new laws to strengthen U.S. competitiveness in blockchain.

supporters: Supporters say the bill directs the Department of Commerce to create a Blockchain Deployment Program, which would help U.S. companies develop and use blockchain technology before other countries pull ahead.
Supporters say the required yearly report to Congress — including recommendations for new laws — gives lawmakers a regular way to track U.S. blockchain progress and close any gaps in federal policy.

Supporters say the advisory groups will produce best practices for using blockchain and digital tokens, giving businesses and government agencies clear, tested guidance instead of having to figure it out on their own.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a spending limit or budget for the Blockchain Deployment Program, leaving Congress without a clear cap on how much the Department of Commerce can spend.
Critics say the bill requires Commerce to promote digital tokens and tokenization but does not include any consumer or investor protections for people who use those tokens.

Critics say the bill requires Commerce to form advisory groups but includes no conflict-of-interest rules or membership disclosure requirements, meaning there is no way for the public to know who is shaping the best practices.

118-hr-7343.one_liner: Require federal detention of non-citizens who assault police or first responders
provisions: Non-citizens who are arrested for, charged with, or convicted of assaulting a police officer, firefighter, or other first responder must be taken into federal custody.
The Department of Homeland Security is required to detain these individuals — it does not have the option to skip detention.
This rule applies to non-citizens who already meet certain grounds for being denied entry into the United States.
Once detained, these individuals can be removed from the country.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects police officers, firefighters, and other first responders by requiring the Department of Homeland Security to take non-citizens into federal custody if they assault these workers.
Supporters say the bill removes DHS discretion by making detention mandatory, so non-citizens who assault first responders cannot be released back into communities while their cases are pending.
Supporters say non-citizens who already meet grounds for being denied entry into the U.S. and then assault a first responder can be removed from the country under this bill.
critics: Critics say the bill requires federal detention based on an arrest or charge alone — before any conviction — which means people who are later found not guilty could still be detained and deported.

Critics say removing DHS discretion means immigration officers cannot consider individual circumstances, such as how long a person has lived in the U.S. or whether they have U.S. citizen family members.
Critics say the bill does not define what counts as 'assault,' which could lead to detention for minor physical contact during a stop, not just serious attacks on first responders.

118-hr-7581.one_liner: Require a federal report on attacks against police officers and their mental health resources
provisions: The Department of Justice must write a report on attacks that targeted police officers on purpose.
The report must look at whether these attacks can be added to existing crime tracking systems.
The report must also list what mental health support is available to police officers.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the DOJ to report on targeted attacks against police officers will give lawmakers real data to understand how often officers are attacked on purpose, which is not currently tracked in one place.
Supporters say adding mental health resource information to the report could help agencies find gaps in support for officers, who have higher rates of suicide than line-of-duty deaths.
Supporters say studying whether targeted attacks can be added to existing crime tracking systems could improve national crime data without creating a new system from scratch.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires a report, not any action, so it may not lead to real changes in officer safety or mental health support.
Critics say existing systems like the FBI's National Use-of-Force Data Collection already track some officer-related incidents, making a new DOJ report potentially duplicative.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline or funding amount for the report, leaving it unclear when or how the DOJ would complete the work.

118-hr-7659.one_liner: Keep the Coast Guard funded and update its rules through 2026
provisions: Keeps the Coast Guard running at current staffing levels through the end of 2026.
Lets the Coast Guard respond to cyberattacks, crime by foreign groups, and threats from other countries.
Gives Coast Guard Academy teachers a faster path to getting hired.
Gives some Coast Guard Reserve members up to 12 days of parental leave when they have a new child.
Requires the Coast Guard to make evacuation plans for its bases in areas at high risk of a tsunami.
Requires a higher-level review before keeping an officer who has a sexual assault on their record.
Provides money to buy new ships and planes, update computer systems, and fix buildings.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives some Coast Guard Reserve members up to 12 inactive-duty training periods of parental leave when they have a new child, a benefit they do not currently have.
Supporters say the bill requires a higher-level review before the Coast Guard can keep an officer who has a sexual assault on their record, adding a check that is not currently required.
Supporters say the bill provides money to buy new ships and planes, update computer systems, and fix Coast Guard buildings through the end of FY2026.
critics: Critics say the bill lets certain ship repair programs skip some standard oversight steps, which could reduce checks on how federal money is spent.
Critics say the parental leave benefit of up to 12 inactive-duty training periods only covers certain Reserve members, not all Coast Guard personnel.
Critics say the bill only requires the Coast Guard to send Congress a report on the Polar Security Cutter program, rather than setting deadlines or requiring specific fixes.

118-hr-764.one_liner: Remove federal protections for gray wolves in the lower 48 states
provisions: Takes gray wolves off the federal protected species list in the lower 48 states.
A 2020 rule took wolves off the protected species list.
A federal court struck that rule down in 2022 — this bill puts it back.
One separate subspecies, the Mexican wolf found in the Southwest, stays on the protected list.
Courts cannot challenge or block this rule change.

supporters: Supporters say the bill restores the 2020 federal rule that removed gray wolves in the lower 48 states from the endangered species list, reversing the February 2022 court decision that struck that rule down.
Supporters say state wildlife agencies, not federal law, should manage wolf populations, and removing ESA protections lets states set their own hunting and livestock protection rules.
Supporters say the Mexican wolf subspecies in the Southwest stays on the protected list under the ESA, so the bill targets only the broader gray wolf population that has recovered.
critics: Critics say blocking courts from reviewing this rule change removes the legal process used to challenge federal agency decisions under the Endangered Species Act, which is how the 2020 rule was struck down in the first place.

Critics say wolf populations in states like the Northern Rockies are still rebuilding, and removing ESA protections in the lower 48 states could allow hunting and habitat loss to reduce those numbers again.
Critics say Congress is overriding a federal court's February 2022 ruling without addressing the scientific findings the court used to vacate the 2020 rule.

118-hr-7530.one_liner: Remove DC's power to lower criminal sentences and tighten youth offender rules
provisions: Takes away DC's power to change any criminal sentences that are in place when this bill becomes law.
Lowers the age for youth offender status from 24 to 18 — meaning 18-to-24-year-olds no longer qualify for lighter sentences.
Removes the ability for DC judges to give a sentence below the lowest sentence required by law for youth offenders.
Removes the option for DC judges to give probation instead of jail time to youth offenders.
Requires DC's Attorney General to post monthly crime data about youth offenders on a public website.

supporters: Supporters say removing DC's power to change criminal sentences will stop the DC Council from weakening penalties that are already in place, keeping tougher sentences on the books.

Supporters say lowering the youth offender age from 24 to 18 means adults aged 18 to 24 who commit crimes will face the same mandatory sentences as other adults, rather than getting reduced sentences.
Supporters say requiring the DC Attorney General to post monthly youth crime data on a public website gives residents regular, up-to-date information on how often young people are committing crimes.
critics: Critics say removing judges' ability to give probation instead of jail time to youth offenders takes away a tool that courts use to keep young people out of prison when their cases call for it.

Critics say cutting the youth offender age from 24 to 18 means 18-to-24-year-olds can no longer receive sentences below the mandatory minimum, even when a judge believes a shorter sentence is the right call.

Critics say blocking DC from changing any of its own criminal sentencing laws takes away the city's ability to adjust rules based on what local leaders and residents decide works best for their community.

118-hr-7525.one_liner: Help local special districts qualify to receive federal grant money
provisions: The budget office called OMB has 180 days to put out rules on how federal agencies decide if a special district can get grants.
A special district is a local government body created by state law to do one specific job, like running a water system or fire department.
It has its own budget and is separate from other local governments in the area.
All federal agencies must follow those rules within one year of when they come out.

supporters: Supporters say the bill fixes a real problem: many special districts — like water authorities and fire districts created by state law with their own budgets — have been turned away from federal grants because agencies do not agree on whether they count as a local government.
Supporters say requiring OMB to issue clear rules within 180 days gives special districts a defined timeline to expect change, instead of waiting on each federal agency to decide differently.

Supporters say the one-year deadline for all federal agencies to follow OMB's guidance means thousands of special districts across the country would have a consistent path to apply for federal financial assistance.
critics: Critics say the bill's definition of a special district — requiring its own budget and separation from other local governments — may leave out some existing districts that currently receive federal grants but do not fully meet those terms, cutting off funding they already rely on.
Critics say giving OMB 180 days to write new rules and then giving agencies another full year to carry them out means special districts could wait nearly two years before any real change happens.

Critics say the bill does not require OMB or agencies to actually approve more special districts for grants — only to clarify the rules — so the guidance could be issued without expanding access at all.

118-hr-8070.one_liner: Fund the military and set pay and rules for U.S. armed forces in 2025
provisions: Raises base pay for lower-ranked enlisted troops (E-1 through E-4) by an average of 15%, on top of a 4.5% raise already set for 2025
Sets the number of active duty and reserve troops allowed to serve
Lets the military buy aircraft, ships, and missiles
Requires the military to build a new missile defense site on the East Coast by December 31, 2030
Requires the military to set up a quantum computing center at a military research lab
Lets the Marines test AI and machine learning software to improve how supplies and equipment are tracked and delivered

supporters: Supporters say the 15% pay raise for E-1 through E-4 enlisted troops, on top of the 4.5% raise already set for 2025, will help the military compete with private sector jobs and keep more young service members from leaving.
Supporters say building a new missile defense site on the East Coast by December 31, 2030 closes a gap in the current system, which only has interceptor sites on the West Coast and in Alaska.
Supporters say letting the Marines test AI and machine learning software for tracking supplies will cut waste and get equipment to troops faster without requiring new spending.
critics: Critics say the 15% pay raise for lower-ranked troops, while leaving higher grades with smaller increases, does not address pay gaps for mid-career enlisted personnel in grades E-5 and above who also face rising costs.

Critics say the requirement to build a new East Coast missile interceptor site by 2030 sets a deadline without a confirmed budget, and past missile defense programs have run billions of dollars over their original cost estimates.
Critics say authorizing new purchases of aircraft, ships, and missiles without a detailed cost breakdown makes it hard for Congress and the public to know the full price tag of the bill.

118-hr-8036.one_liner: Send money to the Pentagon and State Department to support U.S. allies in Asia and the Pacific
provisions: Sends extra money to the Department of Defense and the State Department to support U.S. allies in Asia and the Pacific in the year starting October 2023.
Pays to replace military equipment and supplies that the U.S. sent to Taiwan and countries that helped Taiwan.
Puts money into building more submarines faster.
Funds military needs in the Pacific that were not yet covered in the regular budget.
Lets the President send more military equipment to other countries or international groups.
Adds money to a program that helps other countries buy U.S. military equipment.
Gives money to an international group that makes low-interest loans to poorer countries.

supporters: Supporters say the bill strengthens U.S. security in Asia by funding military needs of the Indo-Pacific Command that were left out of the regular budget, closing gaps before they become threats.
Supporters say paying to replace equipment sent to Taiwan keeps U.S. military readiness strong while still helping an ally resist pressure from China.
Supporters say investing in the submarine industrial base will let the U.S. build more submarines faster, which defense planners say is key to deterring conflict in the Pacific.
critics: Critics say the bill labels all its spending as 'emergency' to skip the normal budget limits, which means the cost is added directly to the national debt without offsets.
Critics say expanding the President's power to send military equipment to foreign countries or international groups with fewer restrictions reduces Congress's oversight of how weapons are shared.

Critics say some funding — like the contribution to the International Development Association for low-interest loans to poorer countries — goes beyond direct U.S. security needs and should go through the regular foreign aid budget process.

118-hr-8035.one_liner: Send about $61 billion in emergency military and economic aid to Ukraine
provisions: The bill sends about $61 billion in emergency funding — labeled as outside the normal budget limits — to support Ukraine in its war with Russia.
The Department of Defense gets money to replace weapons and equipment already sent to Ukraine and to cover the cost of military training it provided.
The State Department and the U.S. foreign aid agency get money to send to Ukraine to help keep its government and economy running.
The President must send long-range missiles called Army Tactical Missile Systems to Ukraine.
Ukraine must sign an agreement to pay the U.S. back for the economic money it receives.
Other countries must chip in matching funds for some of the aid, so the U.S. is not the only one paying.
New rules require regular updates to Congress on how the money is being used and whether it is reaching its stated goals.

supporters: Supporters say the $61 billion in emergency funding helps Ukraine keep fighting Russia without putting U.S. troops in the conflict, and that the requirement for other countries to match some funds means the U.S. is not paying alone.
Supporters say requiring Ukraine to repay the economic aid and setting up regular reports to Congress adds accountability, so the money is tracked and not wasted.
Supporters say replacing weapons already sent to Ukraine restores the U.S. military's own supply, so American defense readiness is not weakened by the aid.
critics: Critics say labeling $61 billion as emergency spending lets the government bypass normal budget limits, adding to the national debt without going through the usual approval process.
Critics say the bill requires the President to send long-range Army Tactical Missile Systems to Ukraine, which critics argue could pull the U.S. deeper into a war with a nuclear-armed country.
Critics say the repayment agreement with Ukraine is not guaranteed to work, and if Ukraine cannot pay back the economic assistance, U.S. taxpayers will be left covering the full cost.

118-hr-8034.one_liner: Send military weapons and aid money to Israel during the conflict
provisions: Sends money to the U.S. military to cover the cost of operations in the Middle East
Buys new weapons to replace ones the U.S. already sent to Israel, including Iron Dome and David's Sling missile defense systems
Pays to send additional weapons and military equipment directly to Israel through a government arms program
Sends money to help refugees and people forced from their homes by the conflict
Adds money to protect U.S. embassies and government buildings in other countries
Gives the President more power to send military equipment to other countries without going through the normal approval steps
Stops any of this money from going to the U.N. Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA)

supporters: Supporters say the bill pays to replace Iron Dome and David's Sling missile defense systems that the U.S. already sent to Israel, so the U.S. military does not have a gap in its own supply of weapons.
Supporters say the bill covers the cost of U.S. military operations already happening in the Middle East and adds money to protect U.S. embassies in the region, keeping American personnel safe.
