Supporters say the bill includes money for refugees and people displaced by the conflict, so it addresses both military and humanitarian needs at the same time.
critics: Critics say the bill gives the President new power to send military equipment to other countries without going through the normal Congressional approval steps, reducing oversight of arms transfers.
Critics say the bill blocks all funds from reaching UNRWA, the main U.N. agency delivering food and supplies to Palestinian refugees, cutting off aid to civilians who depend on it.

Critics say the bill sends advanced weapons and military equipment directly to Israel through the Foreign Military Financing Program while the conflict is still ongoing, which could make the fighting worse.

118-hr-8038.one_liner: Add sanctions and bans targeting fentanyl traffickers, Iran, and TikTok
provisions: Freezes the money and property of people outside the US who are linked to bringing fentanyl into the country.
Lets the US take Russian government money and send it to Ukraine to pay for war damage and rebuilding.
Bans TikTok and its parent company ByteDance from operating apps or websites in the US.
Stops companies that sell personal data from sharing Americans' private information with China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.
Freezes money and blocks travel for foreign people who help Iran sell oil to other countries.
Freezes money of foreign governments that give weapons or funding to Hamas or Palestinian Islamic Jihad.
Stops US banks from doing business with Chinese banks that help Iran sell oil.

supporters: Supporters say freezing the money and property of people linked to fentanyl trafficking will cut off the flow of the drug that killed over 70,000 Americans in one year.
Supporters say banning TikTok and ByteDance stops a Chinese-owned app from collecting data on 170 million American users and passing it to a foreign government.
Supporters say blocking US banks from working with Chinese banks that help Iran sell oil will squeeze Iran's ability to fund military programs and armed groups.
critics: Critics say seizing Russian government money and sending it to Ukraine sets a new rule that lets the US take foreign government assets, which could make other countries stop trusting US banks and financial systems.
Critics say the TikTok ban blocks a platform used by 170 million Americans without giving them or the company a clear path to keep the app running under new ownership.
Critics say broad sanctions on foreign governments that support Hamas could limit the US government's ability to shape peace talks, since some of those governments are also diplomatic partners.

118-hr-8580.one_liner: Funds military construction and veterans services for the year starting October 2024
provisions: Sends money to the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force, National Guard, and reserve units to build and repair military bases and facilities.
Pays for the NATO Security Investment Program, which funds shared military buildings and infrastructure with U.S. allies.
Funds health care, benefits, and burials for about 9 million veterans through the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Pays for building, fixing, and running housing for military families and service members who live on base.
Pays to close and clean up old military bases no longer in use.
Funds the Armed Forces Retirement Home, which provides housing and care for retired military veterans.
Also pays for national war memorials and a court that handles veterans legal appeals.

supporters: Supporters say the bill funds health care, benefits, and burial services for about 9 million veterans through the Department of Veterans Affairs, making sure those who served can access the care they earned.

Supporters say funding for on-base housing construction and repairs helps military families and single service members who live where they are stationed, improving conditions for active-duty personnel.
Supporters say the NATO Security Investment Program pays for shared military buildings and infrastructure with U.S. allies, which they argue spreads the cost of defense across multiple countries.
critics: Critics say spending money on the NATO Security Investment Program uses U.S. funds to build facilities that benefit allied countries, and argue those countries should pay a larger share of their own defense costs.

Critics say the bill funds base closure and cleanup of old military sites, a process that has historically gone over budget and taken decades, raising questions about whether those funds are well managed.

Critics say the VA appropriation, while serving about 9 million veterans, has faced repeated backlogs in benefits claims and health care wait times, and argue that more oversight requirements should be attached to how those funds are spent.

118-hr-8146.one_liner: Require a government report on how border policies affected police officers
provisions: Tells the Department of Justice to write a report on how border policies from 2021 to 2025 affected police officers at the federal, state, local, and tribal levels.
The report covers officers from all levels of government — not just federal border agents.

supporters: Supporters say the DOJ report would document how border policies from 2021 to 2025 affected officers at all four levels of government — federal, state, local, and tribal — putting that information in one official record for the first time.

Supporters say requiring this report gives Congress a factual basis to decide whether to change funding or policy for the law enforcement officers who dealt with border-related demands during that period.
critics: Critics say the bill only covers border policies from 2021 to 2025, which limits the report to one administration and does not compare those years to earlier periods when border policy also affected law enforcement.

Critics say the bill requires the DOJ to write a report but does not require any action based on what the report finds, so conditions for federal, state, local, and tribal officers may not change as a result.

118-hr-8369.one_liner: Require the U.S. to deliver all weapons and military aid to Israel
provisions: Stops the government from blocking or pausing weapons deliveries to Israel.
Stops federal money from being used to pay any Pentagon or State Department worker who holds back military aid to Israel.
Requires the Pentagon and State Department to deliver all weapons and military equipment that were scheduled to go to Israel in 2024 and 2025.
Freezes some Pentagon and State Department office budgets until those offices confirm all held-back weapons have been delivered to Israel.
Requires the Pentagon and State Department to file regular reports to Congress on what weapons and military support have been sent to Israel.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would stop the Pentagon and State Department from blocking or pausing weapons deliveries to Israel, which they argue keeps the U.S. committed to a formal security partner.
Supporters say requiring delivery of all military equipment scheduled for 2024 and 2025 ensures Congress-approved aid actually reaches Israel instead of being held up by executive branch decisions.
Supporters say the regular reporting requirement gives Congress direct oversight of what weapons and military support are sent to Israel.
critics: Critics say the bill would freeze budgets for Pentagon and State Department offices until they confirm all held-back weapons are delivered, which could disrupt unrelated government operations.

Critics say stopping the government from paying any Pentagon or State Department worker who slows military aid to Israel removes the ability of U.S. officials to pause deliveries while reviewing civilian harm concerns.
Critics say requiring delivery of all scheduled 2024 and 2025 weapons removes the executive branch's ability to adjust military aid based on changing conditions on the ground.

118-hr-8289.one_liner: Keep FAA programs and airport funding running through May 17, 2024
provisions: Keeps FAA drone testing programs running until May 17, 2024, including programs that track where drones are flying.
Keeps the airport grants program going — it gives money to public airports for building projects and reducing noise near airports.
Keeps taxes on airline tickets and jet fuel in place so the FAA can keep collecting money to fund aviation programs.
Keeps a program running that lets smaller airports use remote-operated towers instead of having staff on-site.
Lets the Department of Homeland Security and the Justice Department keep taking action against drones that get too close to high-risk sites inside the United States.

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps the Airport Improvement Program running so public airports can continue receiving federal grants for construction and noise reduction projects without a funding gap through May 17, 2024.
Supporters say extending FAA drone tracking programs, including the UAS Test Site Program and the remote identification pilot program, lets safety research continue without interruption.

Supporters say keeping DHS and DOJ authority in place lets those agencies continue acting against drones that fly near high-risk sites inside the United States, protecting facilities that could be targeted.
critics: Critics say the extension only lasts until May 17, 2024, giving airports, airlines, and drone program operators just weeks of certainty before facing another potential funding lapse.
Critics say extending authority for DHS and DOJ to act against drones near high-risk sites does not define which U.S. facilities qualify as high-risk, leaving the scope of that power unclear.

Critics say a short-term extension of the Airport and Airway Trust Fund's taxing authority delays any debate in Congress over how those airline ticket and jet fuel taxes are structured or how the money is spent.

118-hr-8282.one_liner: Cut US funding to the ICC and sanction people who help it investigate protected persons
provisions: Cuts all US government money going to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and blocks future payments.
Puts visa bans and property freezes on any foreign person who helps the ICC investigate, arrest, or prosecute a protected person.
Also bans the family members of sanctioned people from getting US visas.
Protected persons include US citizens, US companies, and anyone living in the US.
They also include citizens or legal residents of US-allied countries that have not joined the ICC.
The US signed but never ratified the ICC treaty, and formally withdrew its signature in 2002.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects US citizens, US companies, and people living in the US from being investigated or prosecuted by a court that the US never ratified and formally withdrew from in 2002.
Supporters say cutting all US funding to the ICC and blocking future payments stops American tax dollars from going to a court with no legal authority over Americans.

Supporters say visa bans and property freezes on foreign persons who help the ICC go after protected persons give the US real leverage to defend its citizens and those of allied countries that also never joined the ICC.
critics: Critics say the visa bans extend to immediate family members of sanctioned persons, punishing people who had no role in any ICC action.

Critics say sanctioning foreign persons from US-allied countries who work with the ICC could damage relationships with those allies, since many US partners are ICC members and cooperate with it regularly.
Critics say cutting all ICC funding removes US influence over a court that prosecutes war crimes and could leave cases involving US allies or partners without American support.

118-hres-1209.one_liner: Remove the current Speaker of the House from their position
provisions: Declares the Speaker of the House seat empty, which would require the House to vote for a new Speaker
Any member of the House can call this vote, and it passes with a simple majority of members present

supporters: Supporters say the bill would give any one of the 435 House members the power to call a vote to remove the Speaker, which they argue returns control of House leadership to the full membership instead of a small group of party leaders.
Supporters say because the vote only needs a simple majority of members present to pass, it makes it easier for the House to act quickly if they believe the Speaker is not doing the job.
critics: Critics say allowing any single member to trigger a Speaker removal vote could be used as a political threat, making it hard for the Speaker to lead without the constant risk of being removed.
Critics say if the Speaker seat is declared vacant, the House cannot move forward on pending legislation until a new Speaker is chosen, which could delay votes affecting all 435 districts.

118-hres-1173.one_liner: Set debate rules for seven bills covering mining, hunting, wildlife, and antisemitism
provisions: This resolution sets the terms for how the House will debate seven separate bills.
One bill would let hunters and anglers use lead bullets and lead fishing gear on federal lands and waters.
One bill would give mining companies more stable rights to use land near their mine sites for support operations.
One bill would bring back mining leases and permits in the Superior National Forest in Minnesota that were canceled.
One bill would remove the gray wolf from the federal list of protected endangered animals.
One bill would cancel a federal rule that required the Bureau of Land Management to protect and preserve federal land health.
One bill would lock in the permits and approvals already given to oil and gas companies to drill on Alaska's coastal plain.

One bill would require schools and colleges that get federal money to use a definition of antisemitism from a group called the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance when handling discrimination complaints.

supporters: Supporters say H.R. 615 would stop federal agencies from banning lead bullets and lead fishing tackle on federal lands and waters, protecting access to gear that millions of hunters and anglers currently use.

Supporters say H.R. 764 would direct the Secretary of the Interior to reissue regulations removing the gray wolf from the federal endangered species list, returning wolf management to state wildlife agencies in states like Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho.

Supporters say H.R. 6090 would require schools and colleges that get federal money to use the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism when handling discrimination complaints, which Jewish student groups say gives campuses a clear tool to identify antisemitic acts.
critics: Critics say H.R. 615 would allow lead bullets and lead fishing tackle across federal lands and waters. Studies have found that lead from ammunition and tackle poisons bald eagles, California condors, and other wildlife that eat animal carcasses or swallow lost tackle.

Critics say H.R. 6285 would lock in all permits and approvals for oil and gas drilling on Alaska's coastal plain, an area where polar bears den and caribou calve each year, and would prevent future administrations from reviewing those approvals.

Critics say H.R. 6090 would require schools to apply an antisemitism definition that some civil liberties organizations argue includes examples that could restrict campus speech about the policies of the Israeli government.

118-hres-1160.one_liner: Set House voting rules for five foreign aid and sanctions bills
provisions: The House set the rules for debating and voting on five bills at once.
One bill provided emergency money for Israel through September 30, 2024.
A second bill provided emergency money for Ukraine through the same date.
A third bill provided emergency money for countries in the Indo-Pacific region.
A fourth bill let the President place sanctions on Russia and Iran.
The House voted to accept changes the Senate made to a combined foreign aid bill called H.R. 815.

supporters: Supporters say the rule let the House debate and vote on emergency aid for Israel (H.R. 8034), Ukraine (H.R. 8035), and the Indo-Pacific region (H.R. 8036) in a single session, moving faster toward the September 30, 2024 spending deadline.

Supporters say bundling all five bills under one rule allowed the House to also pass sanctions on Russia and Iran (H.R. 8038) and accept the Senate's changes to H.R. 815 without holding separate floor debates for each.
Supporters say the rule was needed to get foreign aid packages to a final vote quickly, since delays could have left Israel and Ukraine without emergency funds before the fiscal year ended.
critics: Critics say the rule forced members to vote on aid for Israel and aid for Ukraine under the same procedural package, removing the ability to approve one without the other.

Critics say bundling H.R. 8034, H.R. 8035, H.R. 8036, H.R. 8038, and H.R. 815 into one rule prevented separate amendments to each bill, limiting debate on the specific dollar amounts and terms for each country.

Critics say packaging the Russia and Iran sanctions bill (H.R. 8038) together with unrelated aid bills pressured members to accept all five measures as a group rather than voting on the sanctions authority on its own.

118-hres-1112.one_liner: Formally oppose Biden administration immigration policies in Congress
provisions: This resolution is a formal statement from Congress that does not change any laws or spend any money.
It states that Congress disagrees with how the Biden administration handled immigration at the border.
It calls on the administration to use different immigration policies, including stricter border enforcement.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution puts Congress on record disagreeing with Biden administration border policies, which they say led to record numbers of illegal crossings.
Supporters say calling for stricter border enforcement sends a clear message to the administration to change course without needing to pass a new law.
Supporters say this formal statement reflects the views of voters who want tougher immigration rules at the southern border.
critics: Critics say this resolution does not change any laws or require any action, so it has no real effect on immigration policy.
Critics say the resolution calls for stricter enforcement without naming specific policies or numbers, making it too vague to guide any real change.
Critics say denouncing the administration without offering a detailed plan does not address the causes of border crossings or help the people affected.

118-hres-1194.one_liner: Set rules for House floor votes on energy, census, crypto, and mining bills
provisions: Allows a House vote on energy appliance rules. That bill would stop the Energy Department from setting new standards unless proven to work and worth the cost.
Allows a House vote on adding a citizenship question to the U.S. Census. That bill would base House seat counts on citizens only, not all residents.
Allows a House vote to cancel an SEC rule on crypto. That rule required banks to list customers' crypto holdings as debts on their books.
Allows a House vote on a mining bill. That bill would give mining companies more secure rights to use land around their mines for support work.

supporters: Supporters say the rule allows a House vote on stopping the Energy Department from setting new appliance standards unless they are proven to work and worth the cost, which they argue protects consumers from rules that raise product prices without clear benefits.
Supporters say the rule allows a vote on basing House seat counts on citizens only instead of all residents, which they argue gives citizens more direct representation in Congress.

Supporters say the rule allows a vote to cancel the SEC rule that required banks to list customers' crypto holdings as debts, which they argue removes an accounting burden that discouraged banks from offering crypto services.
critics: Critics say the rule bundles four separate and unrelated bills into one debate process, which limits the amount of time members can spend reviewing each bill on its own terms.

Critics say the rule allows a vote on the citizenship census question, which they argue would cause noncitizen residents — who are counted in the current census — to lose representation in Congress and reduce federal funding for states with large immigrant populations.

Critics say the rule allows a vote to cancel the SEC crypto accounting rule, which they argue would remove a protection that helps banks and regulators track financial risk tied to customer crypto holdings.

118-hres-1210.one_liner: Condemn Biden Administration border policies and call on leaders to support law enforcement
provisions: Congress states that border policies during the Biden Administration put extra pressure on law enforcement officers
Congress says that law enforcement officers face dangers and stress because of conditions at the border
Congress calls on leaders at all levels of government to support and encourage law enforcement officers
Congress expresses sympathy for the stress that law enforcement officers deal with on the job

supporters: Supporters say the resolution draws attention to the extra pressure that Biden Administration border policies placed on law enforcement officers, who the resolution says faced increased dangers and stress.
Supporters say calling on leaders at all levels of government to support and encourage law enforcement officers gives Congress a clear role in backing the people who work at the border.
Supporters say that Congress expressing sympathy for the stress officers face on the job is an acknowledgment that their work carries real risks.
critics: Critics say the resolution does not include any funding, policy changes, or specific steps to reduce the dangers and stress it says law enforcement officers face.
Critics say the resolution focuses only on condemning one administration's policies without naming any specific border rules that were changed or how many officers were affected.

Critics say a resolution that only expresses sympathy and calls on leaders to offer encouragement does not give law enforcement officers any concrete tools or resources to address the conditions it describes.

118-hres-1215.one_liner: Call on leaders to speak out against antisemitism and recognize Jewish American contributions
provisions: Calls on elected officials and faith leaders to speak out against antisemitism
Calls on government and civic leaders to take steps to protect Jewish American communities
Calls on the executive branch and civic leaders to tell the public about the history and contributions of Jewish Americans

supporters: Supporters say the resolution calls on elected officials and faith leaders to speak out against antisemitism, which they say creates a public message that comes from many parts of society, not just the government.
Supporters say directing the executive branch to educate the public about Jewish American history and contributions gives civic leaders a specific task they can act on.

Supporters say asking government and civic leaders to take 'all possible steps' to protect Jewish American communities signals a commitment that covers safety efforts across multiple levels of leadership.
critics: Critics say the resolution is non-binding, so elected officials and faith leaders face no legal duty to speak out against antisemitism or take steps to protect Jewish American communities.

Critics say calling on the executive branch to educate the public about one specific ethnic and religious community's contributions, without naming other groups, raises questions about equal treatment.
Critics say involving faith leaders and civil society groups — which are not government agencies — in carrying out a government resolution may blur the line between public and private roles.

118-hres-1213.one_liner: Express Congress's condemnation of calls to cut or eliminate police funding
provisions: Says Congress condemns any calls to cut or eliminate police funding
States that police officers need proper equipment, training, and resources to keep the public safe
Expresses condolences to the families of officers who died in the line of duty

supporters: Supporters say the resolution's condemnation of calls to cut or eliminate police funding sends a clear message that Congress stands behind law enforcement officers.
Supporters say recognizing that officers need proper equipment, training, and resources addresses real gaps that put both officers and the public at risk.
Supporters say expressing condolences to families of officers killed in the line of duty gives formal recognition to a sacrifice that affects thousands of families each year.
critics: Critics say the resolution does not include any funding, specific dollar amounts, or binding rules, so it does not actually require any changes to police equipment or training.

Critics say by condemning all calls to cut police funding, the resolution blocks the conversation about how police budgets are divided among cities and what other services those dollars could support.

Critics say the resolution does not address concerns raised by community groups about how police resources are currently used, which is part of why some local officials have called for budget reviews.

118-hres-1243.one_liner: Schedule House votes on digital money rules and DC voting limits
provisions: Sets up a vote on rules for who oversees digital currencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum — two agencies would share that job: the CFTC and SEC
Sets up a vote to stop the Federal Reserve from creating a government-run digital dollar that people could use directly
Sets up a vote to block non-citizens from voting in Washington DC elections

supporters: Supporters say this resolution brings H.R. 4763 to the floor, which would give the CFTC and SEC clear, shared rules for overseeing digital assets like Bitcoin and Ethereum — filling a gap where no clear federal oversight exists today.

Supporters say H.R. 5403, included in this package, would stop the Federal Reserve from issuing a digital dollar directly to individual Americans, which they argue would give the government too much visibility into personal spending.

Supporters say H.R. 192 reinforces that only U.S. citizens should vote in Washington DC elections, reversing a 2022 DC law that allowed non-citizens, including those in the country without legal status, to vote in local races.
critics: Critics say bundling three unrelated bills — crypto regulation, a Federal Reserve ban, and a DC voting rule — into one resolution limits debate time and forces members to move all three forward together or block all three.

Critics say H.R. 5403 would prevent the Federal Reserve from even researching or piloting a central bank digital currency, putting the U.S. behind countries like China and the European Union that are already developing their own digital currencies.

Critics say H.R. 192 overrides a law passed by DC's own elected council, and that Congress using its authority over DC to strip away local voting decisions sets a precedent for further federal control over the District.

118-hres-1227.one_liner: Schedule House votes on bills about law enforcement, DC crime, and Israel defense
provisions: The House can vote on a bill to send defense equipment to Israel
The House can vote on a bill to limit youth offender status in Washington, D.C. to people 18 and under
The House can vote on a bill to hold non-citizens in jail if they assault a police officer
The House can vote on bills requiring reports on how the southern border affects local, state, and federal police
The House can vote on a bill updating rules for off-duty and retired police officers carrying guns in public

supporters: Supporters say this rule opens debate on eight bills at once, including H.R. 8369 to send defense equipment to Israel and H.R. 354 to update carry rules for off-duty and retired police officers.
Supporters say H.R. 7343 would require mandatory detention of non-citizens who assault law enforcement officers, which they argue closes a gap in current immigration enforcement.
Supporters say H.R. 7530 would cap youth offender status in Washington, D.C. at age 18 and require the D.C. Attorney General to run a public website with current juvenile crime data.
critics: Critics say H.R. 7343 allows detention of non-citizens based on an assault charge with no requirement that a court first find the charge is supported by evidence.
Critics say H.R. 7530 would remove the D.C. Council's authority to change criminal sentences, limiting a locally elected government's control over its own laws.
Critics say bundling unrelated matters — defense aid to Israel, D.C. crime rules, and border enforcement reports — into one rule limits the House's ability to debate each issue on its own.

118-s-546.one_liner: Expand a federal grant program to help police departments hire more officers
provisions: Lets police departments use federal COPS grant money to cover the cost of background checks, psychological tests, and other fees that job applicants have to pay
Creates new grants for police departments that team up with schools and colleges to run job fairs and recruiting events
Tells the Department of Justice to create a guide to help police departments that are short-staffed apply for these grants
Requires the Government Accountability Office to study how recruiting problems and officers leaving the job affect police departments at the federal, state, tribal, and local levels

supporters: Supporters say the bill lets police departments use federal COPS grant money to cover the cost of background checks, psychological tests, and other hiring fees, which can be hundreds of dollars that some job applicants cannot afford to pay.
Supporters say new competitive grants for police departments that team up with schools and colleges on job fairs will help recruit people who might not have considered law enforcement as a career.

Supporters say the Department of Justice will be required to create a guide specifically to help short-staffed police departments apply for COPS grants, so the agencies that need help the most have a clearer path to funding.
critics: Critics say the school and college partnership grants are competitive, meaning the bill does not guarantee that every understaffed police department that applies will receive money.

Critics say the GAO study required by the bill will only produce a report on how recruiting problems and officer attrition affect federal, state, tribal, and local agencies — the bill does not require the Department of Justice or Congress to act on what the study finds.

Critics say the bill allows COPS funds to be used to reduce application fees like background checks and psychological evaluations, but it sets no minimum reduction amount, so agencies could lower fees by only a small amount.

118-hres-1287.one_liner: Set the House debate rules for the 2025 military spending bill
provisions: This resolution controls how the House of Representatives debates H.R. 8070, the 2025 defense spending bill.
It sets how much time members of Congress get to speak about the bill on the House floor.
It decides which changes to the bill members can propose during debate.
After debate ends, it allows the full House to hold a final vote on the defense bill.

supporters: Supporters say this rule moves H.R. 8070 forward by setting up a final House vote on the full 2025 defense bill, which covers funding for the Department of Defense, military construction, and Department of Energy national security programs.

Supporters say the debate time limits set by this rule keep the House on schedule so defense programs and military personnel funding do not go without authorization past the start of fiscal year 2025.
Supporters say the amendment rules protect the bill from changes that could stall or reopen negotiations on the defense programs already agreed to in the bill.
critics: Critics say the amendment restrictions in this rule block members of Congress from proposing changes to specific defense programs or spending levels in H.R. 8070 during floor debate.
Critics say limiting debate time prevents members from fully discussing all the programs covered in the bill, including military construction projects and Naval Petroleum Reserve policies.
Critics say the rule gives leadership too much control over which parts of the 2025 defense bill can be changed before the final House vote, cutting out rank-and-file members.

118-hres-1269.one_liner: Allow the House to vote on veterans funding and ICC sanctions bills
provisions: Allows the House to vote on a bill that sets funding for military building projects and the Department of Veterans Affairs through September 30, 2025.
Allows the House to vote on a bill that would put restrictions on the International Criminal Court if it investigates, arrests, or takes to trial any American or person from a U.S. ally country.
Sets the rules for how long the House can debate each bill and how the votes will work.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution clears the way for a vote on H.R. 8580, which funds military construction projects and the Department of Veterans Affairs for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2025, giving veterans and military families access to needed resources.

Supporters say H.R. 8282 would protect Americans and citizens of U.S. ally countries from being investigated, arrested, or put on trial by the International Criminal Court, which they argue has no authority over U.S. personnel.
Supporters say the resolution sets clear debate time limits so the House can move efficiently on both funding and national security matters.
critics: Critics say combining VA and military construction funding with International Criminal Court sanctions into one procedural package forces members to accept or reject both at once, limiting their ability to vote on each issue separately.
Critics say H.R. 8282 could block the ICC from prosecuting war crimes cases involving U.S. allies, which critics argue weakens international accountability for serious human rights violations.

Critics say the debate rules set by this resolution limit how much time members have to discuss H.R. 8580's spending levels for veterans programs, reducing oversight of how those dollars are allocated.

118-s-138.one_liner: Set a U.S. position on Tibet's legal status and counter China's claims about Tibet
provisions: The U.S. defines Tibet to include not just the Tibet Autonomous Region, but also Tibetan areas in four other Chinese provinces: Qinghai, Sichuan, Gansu, and Yunnan.
A U.S. government office focused on Tibet gets a new job: push back on false information about Tibet's history spread by China's government.
The U.S. officially states that the conflict between Tibet and China is not resolved and that Tibet's legal status is still an open question under international law.

supporters: Supporters say the bill's definition of Tibet — covering the Tibet Autonomous Region plus Tibetan areas in Qinghai, Sichuan, Gansu, and Yunnan provinces — matches how Tibetan exile groups define their homeland, giving their view official U.S. recognition.

Supporters say requiring the U.S. Special Coordinator's office to push back on China's government statements about Tibet's history gives the U.S. a formal tool to challenge what they call false claims.
Supporters say declaring Tibet's legal status unresolved under international law keeps open the possibility of a future political settlement between Tibetan leaders and China.
critics: Critics say the bill's definition of Tibet — which goes beyond China's official Tibet Autonomous Region to include parts of four other provinces — directly challenges China's position on its own borders, which could damage U.S.-China relations.

Critics say directing a U.S. government office to counter China's statements about Tibet's history puts the U.S. in the role of judging another country's internal historical claims, which China's government says violates its sovereignty.

Critics say declaring Tibet's conflict with China 'unresolved' and its legal status open under international law contradicts decades of U.S. policy that recognized Chinese sovereignty over Tibet, which could create legal and diplomatic confusion.

118-hres-1292.one_liner: Find Attorney General Merrick Garland in contempt of Congress for ignoring a subpoena
provisions: Says AG Merrick Garland broke the rules by not turning over what the House Judiciary Committee asked for in a subpoena.
The House votes to officially find him in contempt of Congress.
Tells the Speaker of the House to send the case to federal prosecutors in Washington, D.C.
Federal prosecutors would then decide whether to bring criminal charges against Garland.
Tells the Speaker to take any other steps needed to force Garland to follow the subpoena.

supporters: Supporters say Garland broke the law by ignoring the House Judiciary Committee's subpoena, which asked for audio recordings from a special counsel investigation, and that the House has a duty to hold him accountable through a formal contempt vote.

Supporters say the resolution directs the Speaker to send the case to federal prosecutors in Washington, D.C., which is the standard legal path for enforcing a contempt finding against a government official.

Supporters say the resolution also tells the Speaker to use civil enforcement or the House's own power to compel compliance, giving Congress tools beyond the criminal referral to force Garland to hand over the subpoenaed materials.
critics: Critics say President Biden issued a presidential order blocking the release of the audio recordings before Garland refused to turn them over, meaning Garland was following that order and cannot be held personally responsible for not complying with the subpoena.

Critics say sending the case to federal prosecutors in Washington, D.C. creates a problem since those prosecutors work for the same Justice Department that Garland leads, making it unlikely they would bring charges against their own boss.

Critics say the House Judiciary Committee was told in writing why the materials were being withheld before the contempt vote, and that moving forward anyway turns a legal dispute into a political action rather than a real enforcement effort.

117-hr-1218.one_liner: Add pregnancy and birth outcome data to an FCC internet health map
provisions: The FCC runs an online map that shows where people have internet access and how that connects to health outcomes. This bill adds data about what happens to mothers during and after pregnancy to that map.
The FCC must work with the CDC to decide which pregnancy and birth outcomes to include on the map.
A government watchdog agency must study whether having internet access improves health outcomes for pregnant women and new mothers.

supporters: Supporters say adding maternal health outcome data to the FCC's broadband health map will help researchers and policymakers see where gaps in internet access line up with poor pregnancy outcomes, making it easier to target resources.
Supporters say requiring the FCC to work with the CDC ensures the map includes accurate, medically meaningful data about what happens to mothers during and after pregnancy.
Supporters say the GAO study will produce evidence on whether internet access actually improves health outcomes for pregnant women and new mothers, giving Congress real data to act on.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include any funding, so the FCC and CDC may not have the staff or budget to add maternal health data to the map in a meaningful way.

Critics say collecting and displaying sensitive maternal health data at the county level could raise privacy concerns for women in rural areas where small population sizes make individuals easier to identify.
Critics say a GAO study on internet access and maternal health outcomes may take years to complete, delaying any real action on the high rates of maternal mortality in the United States.

117-hconres-70.one_liner: Condemn threats against historically Black colleges and recognize Black History Month
provisions: Congress states that threats and violence against historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs) are wrong
Congress says the federal government will work to protect HBCU students, teachers, and staff from violence
Congress recognizes Black History Month

supporters: Supporters say this resolution is needed because HBCU campuses received a wave of bomb threats in 2022, forcing evacuations at more than 50 schools and disrupting classes for thousands of Black students.
Supporters say that Congress putting its support in writing sends a clear message to law enforcement that protecting HBCU students, faculty, and staff is a federal priority.
Supporters say recognizing Black History Month alongside this resolution connects the safety of HBCUs to the broader history of Black education in America, which HBCUs have led since the 1800s.
critics: Critics say this resolution has no enforcement power — it does not create new laws, add funding, or require any federal agency to take specific action to protect HBCU campuses.
Critics say that without a budget or a plan attached, the promise to 'work to protect' HBCU students, teachers, and staff is a statement of intent, not a binding commitment.

117-hr-1916.one_liner: Require private health insurance to cover treatment of birth defects and congenital conditions
provisions: Private health insurance plans must cover diagnosis and treatment of birth defects and conditions a person is born with.
Coverage must include surgeries, procedures, and items that improve, fix, or restore body parts — if a doctor says it is needed for normal function or appearance.
Insurance plans cannot set stricter limits or higher out-of-pocket costs for these services than they do for other medical or surgical care.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would require private insurance plans to cover surgeries and procedures for children born with birth defects, such as cleft palates or missing limbs, when a doctor says treatment is needed for normal function or appearance.
Supporters say the bill stops insurance companies from charging higher copays or setting stricter limits on birth defect care than they do for other medical or surgical services.

Supporters say families with children born with congenital conditions would no longer have to pay out of pocket for reconstructive care that a treating physician has determined is medically necessary.
critics: Critics say requiring private insurers to cover all doctor-approved reconstructive services for birth defects, with no stricter cost limits than general surgical care, could raise premiums for all plan members.

Critics say the bill gives treating physicians alone the power to determine what counts as medically necessary for normal appearance, which could lead to broad and hard-to-define coverage obligations for insurance plans.
Critics say the bill does not set a dollar cap or limit on covered services, which may create unpredictable costs for employers and insurers who offer private health plans.

117-hr-2116.one_liner: Ban discrimination based on hair texture or style tied to race or national origin
provisions: Makes it illegal to treat someone differently because of their hair texture or style.
This applies when that style or texture is tied to their race or where their family is from.
The law covers jobs, housing, public places, and any program that gets federal money.
Anyone discriminated against under this law can take legal action to enforce their rights.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would protect Black Americans and others who face job or housing rejections because of hairstyles like locs, braids, or afros, which are tied to their racial identity.
Supporters say the law covers jobs, housing, public places, and federally funded programs, closing gaps in existing civil rights protections that do not mention hair.
Supporters say people who face this type of discrimination would have the right to take legal action under the same enforcement rules used for other civil rights violations.
critics: Critics say the bill's definition of hairstyles 'commonly associated with a particular race' is vague and could lead to courts deciding which styles count, creating inconsistent rulings.
Critics say adding hair texture and style to federal anti-discrimination law could increase lawsuits against employers and landlords, even when their policies apply the same rules to everyone.
Critics say workplace grooming and safety standards — such as rules about loose hair near machinery — could be challenged under this law, putting employers in a difficult position.

117-hr-2074.one_liner: Set up a federal program to help tribes own and manage buffalo on their lands
provisions: The federal government sets up a program inside the Department of the Interior.
The program helps Native American tribes own and manage buffalo on their own lands.
The government can give tribes money, contracts, and support for bringing buffalo back or managing them.
Before taking any action that affects buffalo or their habitat — including dealing with sick buffalo — the government must talk with tribes first.
The government will write a policy for how buffalo and their habitat are managed on tribal lands.
The government can move extra buffalo from federal land onto tribal land if a tribe agrees.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives Native American tribes direct ownership and management of buffalo on their own lands, which tribes say is tied to their cultural and spiritual traditions.

Supporters say the requirement for the Department of the Interior to consult with tribes before taking any action — including dealing with sick buffalo — gives tribes a say in decisions that affect their land and wildlife.
Supporters say allowing the government to move surplus buffalo from federal land onto tribal land gives tribes a way to grow their herds without having to pay to acquire animals.
critics: Critics say the bill creates a new permanent program inside the Department of the Interior without specifying a budget or cost limit, making it hard to know how much taxpayers will spend.

Critics say the rule requiring the government to consult tribes before containing or removing diseased buffalo could slow down disease response and put other herds — including those on non-tribal land — at risk.
Critics say the bill leaves key details, like what the buffalo habitat management policy will actually say, to be decided later, giving the public little certainty about how the program will work.

117-hr-1621.one_liner: Stop judges from using not-guilty charges to give longer prison sentences
provisions: Right now, a federal judge can give someone a longer prison sentence based on crimes a jury found them not guilty of.
This bill stops that practice.
Judges can still consider the crimes someone was found guilty of when deciding a sentence.
This applies to federal courts across the country.

supporters: Supporters say that under current federal law, judges can give someone more prison time for crimes a jury found them not guilty of, and this bill would end that practice.
Supporters say the 6th Amendment guarantees the right to a jury trial, and using crimes a jury cleared someone of to increase their sentence undermines that right.
Supporters say judges would still be able to consider the crimes the person was convicted of when deciding a sentence, so public safety is not affected.
critics: Critics say that in cases like drug trafficking and organized crime, prosecutors often cannot prove every charge to a jury, but judges need to consider the full picture of what happened when deciding how long someone should be in prison.

Critics say federal sentencing rules allow judges to weigh facts that did not meet the higher bar required for a conviction, and this bill would remove that tool from judges in courts across the country.
Critics say removing this practice could lead to shorter sentences for people involved in serious crimes where some charges were dropped or not proven at trial.

117-hr-1836.one_liner: Let National Guard and Reserve members count more service time toward GI Bill education benefits
provisions: National Guard and Reserve members can now count paid training days, inactive duty training, and general duty service toward their GI Bill education benefits.
Before this bill, some types of service that came with pay did not count toward qualifying for education benefits.
This change lets more Guard and Reserve members qualify for the Post-9/11 GI Bill, which covers tuition, housing, and books at colleges and trade schools.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would let National Guard and Reserve members count paid training days, inactive duty training, and general duty service toward Post-9/11 GI Bill eligibility, which covers tuition, housing, and books at colleges and trade schools.

Supporters say current rules exclude some paid service — including inactive duty training — from counting toward education benefits, meaning Guard and Reserve members who receive basic pay for that service still cannot qualify for the GI Bill.

Supporters say this change would allow more Guard and Reserve members to be eligible for Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits under one standard: if the federal government paid them for the service, it counts toward their education benefit.
critics: Critics say adding paid training days, inactive duty training, and general duty service to the list of qualifying time would make more of the roughly 800,000 National Guard and Reserve members eligible for GI Bill benefits, increasing federal spending on tuition, housing allowances, and book stipends with no funding source named in the bill.

Critics say counting part-time inactive duty training toward the same GI Bill benefits tied to extended active-duty service would give part-time reservists access to benefits built around a longer and more continuous period of service.

Critics say the bill's broad definition of 'general duty service for which basic pay is warranted' could allow a wide range of short or routine duties to count toward education benefits, expanding the program beyond its original scope.

117-hr-2842.one_liner: Rename a post office in Petaluma, California after Lynn C. Woolsey
provisions: Gives the federal post office at 120 4th Street in Petaluma, California the official name 'Lynn C. Woolsey Post Office Building'
This is a federal action covering a U.S. Postal Service building, not a state or city decision
The bill does not change how the post office runs, who works there, or what services it offers
No money is spent and no other rules are changed by this bill

supporters: Supporters say this bill honors Lynn C. Woolsey, who represented the Petaluma area in Congress for 20 years, by naming the federal post office at 120 4th Street after her.
Supporters say the bill costs no money and changes none of the post office's services or staff, making it a low-cost way to recognize local public service.
critics: Critics say Congress spends limited floor time on bills like this one that only change a building's name and have no effect on postal operations or federal policy.
Critics say naming the facility at 120 4th Street after a former officeholder is a symbolic act that does not benefit the residents who use that post office.

117-hr-2324.one_liner: Rename a post office in Tallahassee, Florida after D. Edwina Stephens
provisions: Changes the official name of the post office at 2800 South Adams Street in Tallahassee, Florida to the 'D. Edwina Stephens Post Office'

117-hr-3113.one_liner: Put public land maps online showing which roads, trails, and waters are open
provisions: Three federal agencies — the Department of the Interior, the Forest Service, and the Army Corps of Engineers — must agree on shared data standards so their maps work together.
These agencies must put digital maps online showing which roads and trails on public land are open or closed.
The maps must show what types of vehicles — like ATVs, trucks, or bikes — are allowed on each road or trail.
The maps must show the dates when roads and trails open and close each season.
The maps must show where hunting and shooting are allowed and where they are restricted.
The maps must show which parts of rivers or lakes are closed to boats or have limits on engine power.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the Department of the Interior, Forest Service, and Army Corps of Engineers to use one shared set of data standards will let hikers, hunters, and ATV riders check road and trail status in one place instead of searching three separate agency websites.

Supporters say publishing digital maps that show which vehicle types — such as ATVs, trucks, or bikes — are allowed on each trail segment will help off-road users follow the rules and avoid fines for using restricted routes.
Supporters say showing the exact boundaries where hunting or recreational shooting is restricted will help hunters and sport shooters stay within legal areas on public land.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a funding amount or a completion deadline, leaving it unclear how the three agencies will pay for new digital mapping systems or when they must finish.
Critics say digitizing and publishing federal interests — including easements and rights-of-way — in private land could expose sensitive property information about landowners without their input.
Critics say requiring three large agencies with different existing IT systems to agree on shared data standards is a complex process that could take many years to complete.

117-hr-2954.one_liner: Change rules for workplace retirement savings accounts
provisions: Requires many employers to sign workers up for retirement savings plans automatically, instead of waiting for workers to sign up themselves
Raises the age at which retirees must start taking money out of their retirement accounts from 72 to 75
Lets older workers put more money into their retirement accounts each year to catch up on savings

supporters: Supporters say that automatic enrollment will get more workers into retirement savings plans without requiring them to take any action, reaching workers who might otherwise never sign up.
Supporters say raising the required withdrawal age from 72 to 75 gives retirees three more years to let their savings grow before they are forced to take money out.
Supporters say the higher catch-up contribution limits will help older workers who started saving late build a bigger retirement fund in their final working years.
critics: Critics say automatic enrollment may take money out of paychecks for workers who cannot afford to save right now and would prefer to opt in on their own.
Critics say raising the withdrawal age to 75 mainly helps higher-income retirees who do not need the money at 72, while lower-income retirees already take their distributions as soon as they can.
Critics say the expanded catch-up contribution rules benefit workers with high salaries who can afford to save more, not lower-wage workers who are already saving as much as they can.

117-hr-2501.one_liner: Require two federal agencies to update their agreement on handling radio frequency disputes
provisions: Tells the FCC and a Commerce Department office called NTIA to update the written agreement they share on how radio frequencies get managed
The update must improve how the two agencies settle conflicts when different users share or are close to the same radio frequencies
The update must make sure radio frequencies are used as efficiently as possible

supporters: Supporters say updating the FCC and NTIA's written agreement would create a clearer process for resolving conflicts when commercial wireless companies and federal agencies share the same radio frequencies.
Supporters say requiring the two agencies to improve spectrum efficiency could free up more radio frequencies for new uses without needing to find entirely new spectrum bands.

Supporters say a stronger coordination process between the FCC and the Commerce Department's NTIA would help spectrum decisions better reflect both economic needs and national security at the same time.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for the FCC and NTIA to finish updating the MOU, which means the agencies could delay making any real changes.

Critics say giving the two agencies broad authority to redesign how they resolve frequency disputes could lead to new rules that favor large federal users over smaller commercial operators in shared spectrum bands.
Critics say updating the MOU alone does not require either agency to act on the new coordination process, so the agreement could change without improving how disputes are actually settled.

117-hr-3359.one_liner: Give murder victims' families the right to request a review of unsolved cases
provisions: Family members of murder victims can ask federal investigators to review the case file if the murder happened more than 3 years ago
To qualify, investigators must have already followed all leads and have no named suspect
Immediate family members — like parents, spouses, and children — are the ones who can make this request

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives parents, spouses, and children of murder victims a formal way to request a federal case review after 3 years with no named suspect, which families currently cannot do.
Supporters say the review is limited to cases where investigators have already followed all leads, so it does not disrupt active investigations or waste resources on cases still being worked.
Supporters say family members of unsolved federal murder cases deserve a process to get answers, and this bill creates that process without expanding the definition of who can be prosecuted.
critics: Critics say the bill does not define how federal agencies must respond to a family's request, which could mean reviews happen with no real action or timeline.
Critics say limiting the request to 'immediate family members' could leave out relatives — like grandparents or siblings — who were primary caregivers or next of kin for the victim.

Critics say requiring that 'all probative investigative leads' be exhausted before a review is allowed sets a bar that investigators themselves define, giving agencies full control over when the process can even start.

117-hr-3531.one_liner: Let a private foundation build a WWII home front women's memorial
provisions: A private group called the Women Who Worked on the Home Front Foundation gets permission to build a memorial on federal land in Washington, D.C.
The memorial honors women who worked jobs in the U.S. to support the war effort during World War II.
The private foundation must raise and pay for all costs to build the memorial — no federal money can be used.
The memorial must follow the rules set by the Commemorative Works Act, which covers how memorials are built on federal land.

supporters: Supporters say the bill honors the millions of women who took over factory, farm, and industrial jobs in the U.S. during World War II, a group that has no dedicated memorial in Washington, D.C.
Supporters say the Women Who Worked on the Home Front Foundation must pay all costs to build the memorial, so no federal tax dollars will be spent on construction or setup.
Supporters say the memorial must follow the rules of the Commemorative Works Act, which sets clear standards for how and where memorials are built on federal land.
critics: Critics say giving a private foundation the right to build on federal land in Washington, D.C. adds another permanent structure to a limited and already crowded public space.
Critics say Congress has not set a cost estimate or cap on what the foundation may spend, leaving the total size and scope of the memorial open-ended.

117-hr-3539.one_liner: Rename a post office in Hagatna, Guam after Atanasio Taitano Perez
provisions: Names the post office at 223 West Chalan Santo Papa in Hagatna, Guam the 'Atanasio Taitano Perez Post Office'.
This is a ceremonial naming — it changes only the official name and nothing else about the post office.
The bill does not include any information about who Atanasio Taitano Perez was.

117-hr-3197.one_liner: Transfer federal land in Eunice, Louisiana to the city for free
provisions: The federal government gives specific parcels of land in Eunice, Louisiana to the city at no cost.
The land being transferred is part of the original townsite of Eunice.
Once the land is transferred, it is removed from the boundaries of Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve in Jefferson Parish, Louisiana.

supporters: Supporters say the city of Eunice would receive specific parcels of the original townsite at no cost, giving the city ownership it needs to restore the Liberty Theatre without spending money on land acquisition.

Supporters say removing these parcels from Jean Lafitte National Historical Park boundaries gives the city of Eunice direct control over land inside its own townsite, instead of that land being managed by a federal agency.
critics: Critics say removing the parcels from Jean Lafitte National Historical Park means the land would no longer be subject to National Park Service land-use restrictions, which currently limit commercial development and require conservation standards.

Critics say the federal government conveys the land 'without consideration,' meaning the public receives no payment or exchange of value for transferring publicly owned property to a local government.

117-hr-3485.one_liner: Block foreign nationals who violate LGBT and intersex rights abroad from getting U.S. visas
provisions: Blocks foreign nationals from getting U.S. visas if they violated people's rights based on sexual orientation, gender identity, or sex characteristics.
This covers violations against people who are LGBT or intersex — or who others think are, even if they are not.
The President must create a list of foreign nationals responsible for these violations and update it regularly.
People on that list can also face other U.S. penalties beyond being blocked from getting visas.
The State Department must assign a senior officer to track violence and discrimination against LGBT and intersex people in other countries.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would block foreign nationals from getting U.S. visas if they took part in violating the rights of LGBT or intersex people — or people others believed to be LGBT or intersex — giving the U.S. a direct way to hold those individuals accountable.
Supporters say requiring the President to build and regularly update a named list of violators creates a public record that goes beyond visa denial and can lead to other U.S. penalties.

Supporters say placing a dedicated senior officer at the State Department to track violence and discrimination against LGBT and intersex people in other countries fills a gap in how the U.S. monitors these abuses.
critics: Critics say the bill gives the President broad power to decide who goes on the sanctions list, with few limits written into the law on how that list is built or reviewed.
Critics say the bill's language covering people who are 'perceived' to be LGBT or intersex makes it hard to define exactly which cases qualify, which could make enforcement uneven.

Critics say applying visa sanctions and other U.S. penalties to foreign nationals based on actions taken under their own country's laws could create friction with governments the U.S. relies on for other foreign policy goals.

117-hr-3743.one_liner: Raises the money the FDA and NIH must send to their research foundations each year
provisions: The FDA must send at least $1,250,000 to the Reagan-Udall Foundation each year — up from $500,000.
The NIH must send at least $1,250,000 to the Foundation for the NIH each year — also up from $500,000.
Both agencies can now send up to $5,000,000 a year to their foundations — up from $1,250,000.
Both foundations use this money to support scientific research that helps the FDA and NIH do their work.

supporters: Supporters say raising the minimum transfer from $500,000 to $1,250,000 gives the Reagan-Udall Foundation and the Foundation for the NIH more stable funding to support research that helps both agencies do their jobs.
Supporters say allowing transfers up to $5,000,000 — four times the old cap of $1,250,000 — lets the FDA and NIH scale up research partnerships when they have more funding available.
Supporters say the foundations use this money to fill gaps in scientific research that the agencies cannot fund directly, so more dollars mean faster progress on public health questions.
critics: Critics say directing up to $5,000,000 a year from each agency to outside foundations moves public funds away from the FDA and NIH core budgets, where Congress has more direct oversight.

Critics say the Reagan-Udall Foundation and the Foundation for the NIH receive money from private companies, and higher government transfers could give those companies more influence over research priorities.
Critics say the bill does not require the foundations to report how they spend the extra funds, making it harder for the public to track where the money goes.

117-hr-4445.one_liner: Let people take sexual assault and harassment cases to court instead of forced arbitration
provisions: If someone signs a contract that says they must use private arbitration for sexual assault or harassment claims, that part of the contract no longer counts.
People can still choose arbitration after an incident happens, but companies cannot force it ahead of time.
This applies to new claims filed after the law takes effect.
Courts — not private arbitrators — decide whether this law applies to a specific case.

supporters: Supporters say that pre-signed arbitration clauses block sexual assault and harassment victims from going to court, and this bill removes that barrier by making those clauses unenforceable.
Supporters say the bill lets people still choose arbitration after an incident if they want to — it only stops companies from forcing that choice ahead of time through a contract.
Supporters say putting courts in charge of deciding whether this law applies keeps private arbitrators from ruling on their own power, which has favored employers in the past.
critics: Critics say removing pre-dispute arbitration agreements will push more sexual harassment and assault cases into public courts, which can take years longer to resolve than private arbitration.

Critics say businesses — especially small ones — will face higher legal costs because court cases are more expensive to defend than arbitration, and those costs may be passed on through higher prices or fewer jobs.
Critics say the bill applies to all pre-signed agreements without exception, which removes a process that some employees have voluntarily used and found faster and more private than a public trial.

117-hr-4380.one_liner: Name a garden in El Paso, Texas an official national memorial
provisions: Makes the Healing Garden at 6900 Delta Drive in El Paso, Texas an official national memorial
The garden is renamed the El Paso Community Healing Garden National Memorial

supporters: Supporters say that giving the garden at 6900 Delta Drive an official national memorial designation tells El Paso residents that the federal government recognizes the site as a place of lasting public importance.

Supporters say the new title — El Paso Community Healing Garden National Memorial — puts this site in the same category as other federally recognized memorials, which can draw visitors and attention to the community it serves.
Supporters say the designation costs Congress nothing to pass and gives the local healing garden a permanent place in the official national record.
critics: Critics say that designating a single local garden at 6900 Delta Drive as a national memorial sets a precedent that could lead to many more such requests, adding to the list of federally recognized sites that may later seek federal funding.

Critics say the bill does not include any rules about how the El Paso Community Healing Garden National Memorial will be managed or maintained, leaving questions about who is responsible for the site after the name change.
Critics say Congress has limited floor time, and spending it on symbolic name changes for local sites takes time away from bills that affect larger numbers of people.

117-hr-3894.one_liner: Require Medicaid to update its guidance on health issues linked to poverty
provisions: Tells the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to update its rules for states on how to handle health problems tied to poverty, housing, and other life conditions
Covers both Medicaid and the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), which together serve over 90 million Americans
States must get updated guidance from the federal government on a regular basis to help them respond to these issues

supporters: Supporters say the bill would require CMS to regularly update guidance for all 50 states on how to use Medicaid and CHIP to address health problems tied to poverty, housing, and other life conditions, helping the more than 90 million Americans enrolled in those programs.
Supporters say that without regular federal guidance updates, states have had to figure out social determinant programs on their own, and this bill gives them a clearer federal framework to follow.
Supporters say updated CMS guidance would help states respond faster to emerging issues — like housing instability — that affect the health of Medicaid and CHIP enrollees.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a specific timeline for how often CMS must update its guidance, which means states could still wait long periods without new direction.

Critics say the bill adds new federal compliance requirements to state Medicaid agencies that manage large and complex programs, without providing any new funding to help cover the cost of meeting those requirements.

Critics say that guidance alone does not change what states can actually do — without changes to Medicaid and CHIP funding rules, states may receive updated instructions they still lack the resources to act on.

117-hr-3617.one_liner: Remove marijuana from federal drug laws and wipe federal marijuana conviction records
provisions: Removes marijuana from the federal list of illegal substances, so no one can face federal charges for making, selling, or having marijuana.
Creates a process for people with federal marijuana convictions to have those records cleared.
Adds a federal tax on cannabis products made or brought into the US.
Creates a fund to support people and businesses in communities that faced heavy marijuana enforcement.
Lets cannabis businesses apply for small business loans and services from the federal government.
Stops the federal government from taking away benefits like housing or food assistance based on marijuana-related offenses.
Stops immigration officials from denying someone's immigration case because of a marijuana-related event.

supporters: Supporters say removing marijuana from the federal list of illegal substances would end federal criminal charges for people who make, sell, or possess marijuana, which they argue has led to millions of arrests, especially in Black and Latino communities.

Supporters say the bill's expungement process would clear federal marijuana convictions for people who have already served time, letting them apply for jobs, housing, and benefits without a criminal record blocking them.

Supporters say cannabis businesses would gain access to Small Business Administration loans for the first time, and people with marijuana offenses would no longer lose federal benefits like housing assistance or food stamps.
critics: Critics say removing marijuana from the federal schedule conflicts with state laws in places where marijuana is still illegal, and say the federal government would lose its ability to enforce restrictions across state lines.
Critics say the new federal excise tax on cannabis products could raise prices and push buyers toward untaxed illegal markets, making it harder for legal cannabis businesses to compete.

Critics say stopping immigration officials from considering marijuana-related events in immigration cases removes a tool that enforcement agencies use to screen people entering or staying in the country.

117-hr-4738.one_liner: Create a public archive of personal stories from the COVID-19 pandemic
provisions: The Library of Congress will collect personal stories from people who lived through the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States.
The project will gather video and audio recordings of people sharing their experiences.
All collected stories and records will be made available to the public.

supporters: Supporters say the Library of Congress will collect video and audio recordings from people across the U.S. who lived through the COVID-19 pandemic, creating a lasting public record of what Americans experienced.

Supporters say the project will make all collected stories available to the public, so researchers, students, and families can access firsthand accounts from survivors, healthcare workers, and others affected by the pandemic.
Supporters say the American Folklife Center already runs similar history projects, making it a ready home for this collection without building a new government office.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a specific funding amount, leaving it unclear how many recordings can actually be collected or how the project will be staffed.
Critics say the bill sets no deadline for when the project must be completed or when stories must be made publicly available.
Critics say the bill includes no cost cap or sunset clause, meaning there is no limit on how long the project can run or how much it can spend.

117-hr-4673.one_liner: Automatically sign up veterans for VA health care when the Defense Department confirms they qualify
provisions: Veterans who qualify for VA health care get signed up automatically — they do not have to apply on their own.
The VA uses data from the Defense Department to confirm which veterans qualify, then signs them up.
Each veteran gets online access to proof of their enrollment and a way to opt out if they choose.

supporters: Supporters say automatic enrollment would connect veterans who qualify for VA health care but never applied on their own, giving them access to medical benefits without extra steps.
Supporters say using Defense Department data to confirm eligibility removes the paperwork burden from veterans and speeds up the process of getting them signed up.
Supporters say the online opt-out option gives veterans full control — those who do not want VA care can leave the system quickly without calling an office or filling out forms.
critics: Critics say enrolling veterans without their direct request could create VA records for people who already have private insurance or military retiree coverage and have no plan to use VA services.
Critics say automatically sharing personal data between the Defense Department and the VA — before a veteran asks to enroll — raises questions about how that data is stored, accessed, and protected.
Critics say the opt-out process, even with an online tool, shifts the burden onto veterans who must now take action to leave a system they never chose to join.

117-hr-4476.one_liner: Create a new council inside DHS to give advice on protecting the U.S. economy
provisions: Creates a new group inside the Department of Homeland Security called the DHS Trade and Economic Security Council.
The council gives advice and suggestions to DHS leaders about protecting the country's economy.
The council looks for situations where the U.S. depends too heavily on one country or one company for important goods.
The council helps DHS decide what economic security problems to focus on first.

supporters: Supporters say creating the DHS Trade and Economic Security Council would give DHS a dedicated group to spot situations where the U.S. depends too much on a single country or company for important goods, which they say is a gap in current government structure.
Supporters say the council would help DHS leaders decide which economic security problems to fix first, rather than reacting to crises without a clear plan.
Supporters say having one council focused on trade and economic risks inside DHS would make it easier to coordinate advice across the department.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a budget or staffing number for the new council, making it unclear how much it will cost taxpayers to run.
Critics say the council is only allowed to give advice and make recommendations, with no power to enforce rules or require action, which may limit its real-world impact.
Critics say adding a new advisory body inside DHS could create overlap with existing trade and economic security offices already operating across the federal government.

117-hr-5001.one_liner: Extend federal programs to protect endangered fish in two Colorado river systems
provisions: Gives the Department of the Interior more time — through the 2024 budget year — to build facilities that help endangered fish survive in the Upper Colorado and San Juan rivers.
Moves the deadline for a progress report on these fish recovery programs to 2022.

supporters: Supporters say extending the Department of the Interior's authority through FY2024 gives engineers more time to finish building the facilities that endangered fish in the Upper Colorado and San Juan rivers need to survive.
Supporters say moving the progress report deadline to 2022 gives recovery program managers enough time to collect meaningful data before reporting to Congress.
critics: Critics say extending the construction authority through FY2024 delays accountability for how federal money is being spent on fish recovery facilities in the Upper Colorado and San Juan river basins.
Critics say pushing the report deadline to 2022 means Congress will wait longer to find out whether these recovery programs are actually working.

117-hr-4706.one_liner: Add the Blackwell School in Marfa, Texas to the National Park System
provisions: Makes the Blackwell School in Marfa, Texas a national historic site managed by the federal government
The school was used during a time when Black and white students were forced into separate schools, from 1885 to 1965
The site cannot be created until the federal government signs a written deal with the Marfa school district to hand over or jointly manage the property
The federal government can only get land for the site through donations or land trades — not by taking it
No private land can be added to the site without the owner's written agreement
The Department of the Interior must write a plan for how the site will be managed

supporters: Supporters say making Blackwell School a National Park System site would protect its history as a school that served students during 80 years of forced school segregation in Texas, from 1885 to 1965.

Supporters say the bill blocks the federal government from taking any private land by force — it can only get land through donations or trades — which protects property owners near the school in Marfa.
Supporters say the bill requires a written deal with the Marfa school district before the site can open, giving the local community a direct say in whether the project moves forward.
