critics: Critics say the bill requires the Marfa school district to donate or hand over joint management of the Blackwell School to the federal government, which shifts control of a local building to Washington.
Critics say the Department of the Interior would write the management plan for the site without specifying how much money Congress must set aside to run it, leaving the funding level unclear.

Critics say placing the school under federal management as a National Park System unit adds a new layer of federal oversight to a building that the Marfa community and local school district currently control.

117-hr-5577.one_liner: Rename a post office in Atlanta, Georgia after John R. Lewis
provisions: Gives the post office at 3900 Crown Road Southwest in Atlanta, Georgia the official name 'John R. Lewis Post Office Building'

supporters: Supporters say renaming the post office at 3900 Crown Road Southwest honors John R. Lewis, who represented Atlanta in Congress for over 30 years and was a leader in the 1960s civil rights movement, including the 1965 Selma to Montgomery marches.
Supporters say placing Lewis's name on a federal building in the Atlanta community he served gives residents a lasting public reminder of his work to expand voting rights for Black Americans.
Supporters say naming federal facilities after notable figures is a low-cost way for Congress to recognize public servants without spending federal program dollars.
critics: Critics say Congress spends floor time on symbolic bills like renaming the facility at 3900 Crown Road Southwest instead of passing legislation that changes federal policy or spending.
Critics say post office naming bills move through Congress with little debate, which means the public record on why this specific location was chosen over other Atlanta facilities is limited.

117-hr-5343.one_liner: Require FEMA to report to Congress on how often case managers leave their jobs
provisions: FEMA must send Congress a report showing how often case managers quit or leave their jobs
The report must include the average and middle length of time case managers stay employed
FEMA must describe what steps it is taking or plans to take to reduce turnover among case managers

supporters: Supporters say the bill would give Congress data on how often FEMA case managers quit, so lawmakers can see whether staffing is stable enough to serve people after disasters.
Supporters say requiring FEMA to report both the average and median length of employment for case managers gives Congress a baseline to measure whether staffing improves over time.
Supporters say requiring FEMA to put its turnover-reduction plans in writing creates a record Congress can check to see whether FEMA follows through on those steps.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for FEMA to submit the report, so there is no guarantee Congress will receive the staffing data in a timely way.
Critics say the bill only requires a report and does not require FEMA to hit any turnover targets, so case managers' employment conditions may not change as a result.
Critics say Congress can already request this kind of staffing data through GAO investigations or the annual appropriations process, making a separate standalone report potentially duplicative.

117-hr-55.one_liner: Make lynching a federal hate crime with prison time and fines
provisions: Lynching is now listed as a hate crime under federal law.
People found guilty can be sent to prison, fined, or both.
This applies to any attack where a group of people kills or seriously harms someone because of their race, religion, or other protected identity.

supporters: Supporters say the bill adds lynching to the federal list of hate crimes for the first time, closing a gap in federal law that had existed for over 100 years.

Supporters say people convicted under this law face prison time, a fine, or both, giving federal prosecutors a clear legal tool when a group targets someone because of their race, religion, or other protected identity.
Supporters say making lynching a named federal crime means federal law enforcement can step in when state governments do not prosecute group attacks based on protected identity.
critics: Critics say federal hate crime laws passed in 2009 already cover murder and serious injury based on race, religion, and other protected identities, making a separate lynching category a duplicate.
Critics say the bill's penalties may be lower than existing federal murder charges, which could give prosecutors less power, not more, in the most serious cases.
Critics say decisions about how to charge violent group attacks should remain with state governments, not the federal government.

117-hr-5547.one_liner: Require economic development grant applicants to include child care plans
provisions: Groups applying for public works or economic development grants must add a section to their planning documents describing how they will expand access to child care, elder care, disability care, or early childhood education in their area.
This applies to grants given out under the Economic Development Administration program.
The new requirement is added to the planning document that grant applicants already have to submit — called a comprehensive economic development strategy.

supporters: Supporters say that requiring Economic Development Administration grant applicants to include a care access plan in their existing comprehensive economic development strategy will push local leaders to treat child care, elder care, and disability care as part of economic growth — not just social services.
Supporters say that adding this section to a document applicants already have to submit means communities can plan for care access without creating a separate process or new paperwork.

Supporters say that when families cannot find affordable child care or elder care, adults — especially women — often leave the workforce, and this requirement asks grant recipients to address that barrier directly in their planning.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires applicants to describe how they will increase care access, but does not require them to actually provide funding or build new child care, elder care, or disability care services — meaning plans may be written but never acted on.

Critics say the Economic Development Administration grant process already involves detailed planning requirements, and adding a care access section may slow down approvals for public works projects without a clear connection to the infrastructure being funded.
Critics say the bill does not set any standard for what a care access plan must include or how it will be measured, so applicants could write broad or vague descriptions and still qualify for grants.

117-hr-5314.one_liner: Add new rules limiting presidential power and blocking foreign money in elections
provisions: The President cannot pardon himself or herself.
If a sitting President or Vice President commits a federal crime, the clock on filing charges stops until they leave office.
Anyone running for President or Vice President must hand over their last 10 years of tax returns to the Federal Election Commission.
The Department of Justice must keep a written record of all calls and meetings between its staff and the White House.
If Congress issues a subpoena and someone ignores it, Congress gets new tools to force compliance in court.
Presidential emergency declarations get new time limits and rules that Congress can use to push back.
Political campaigns must report any contact with foreign governments, and foreign donations of money or private information about a candidate stay banned.

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a legal gap by stopping the clock on federal charges if a sitting President or Vice President commits a crime, so they cannot run out the clock on prosecution while in office.

Supporters say requiring candidates for President or Vice President to give the Federal Election Commission 10 years of tax returns lets voters see possible conflicts of interest before they cast a ballot.

Supporters say requiring campaigns to report all contacts with foreign governments and keeping the ban on foreign donations of money or private information about a candidate protects elections from outside interference.
critics: Critics say banning self-pardons and giving Congress new court tools to enforce subpoenas shifts power away from the executive branch in ways the Constitution does not support.

Critics say forcing presidential and vice-presidential candidates to hand over 10 years of tax returns adds a new requirement for running for office that goes beyond what the Constitution lists as qualifications.
Critics say putting new time limits and congressional override rules on presidential emergency declarations could slow the government's ability to respond to fast-moving national security threats.

117-hr-5657.one_liner: Create a new registration process for medical marijuana research
provisions: Creates a new sign-up process so doctors and scientists can get permission from the DEA to study medical marijuana
Lets companies register with the DEA to grow and supply marijuana specifically for medical research
The Department of Health and Human Services must keep running its existing marijuana growing program through the National Institute on Drug Abuse
Lets researchers access the same types of marijuana sold in state-licensed dispensaries, not just government-grown research strains
The government-supplied marijuana stays available until private companies can provide enough on their own

supporters: Supporters say the new DEA sign-up process for doctors and scientists removes a major barrier that has slowed medical marijuana studies for decades, making it easier for researchers to get legal access to the drug.
Supporters say allowing researchers to study the same marijuana sold in state-licensed dispensaries — instead of only government-grown strains — means studies will reflect what patients actually use.
Supporters say keeping the National Institute on Drug Abuse supply program running until private companies can fill the gap ensures researchers will not face a shortage during the transition.
critics: Critics say creating a separate DEA registration track for marijuana research still keeps the drug under federal Schedule I rules, which they argue will continue to limit what researchers can study and publish.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for the DEA to approve or deny research registrations, leaving scientists uncertain about how long the process will take.
Critics say relying on state-licensed dispensary products for research could create quality-control problems, since those products are not made to the same standards as drugs approved by the FDA.

117-hr-5616.one_liner: Require DHS to track and improve accreditation for its law enforcement training programs
provisions: DHS must report to Congress on whether each of its basic training programs is accredited.
If a DHS training program loses accreditation, that part of DHS must notify the department within 30 days.
DHS must research new tools and systems to let state, local, tribal, and territorial agencies access DHS training.
The focus is on departments in rural or hard-to-reach areas.
The goal is to help these agencies prepare for terrorism and other homeland security threats.

supporters: Supporters say requiring DHS to report to Congress on whether each basic training program is accredited will make it easier to spot programs that have fallen below standard before problems grow.
Supporters say the 30-day notification rule for lost accreditation means Congress and department leaders will find out quickly instead of learning about it months later.

Supporters say researching new ways to give rural and tribal law enforcement access to Federal Law Enforcement Training Centers will help small departments that cannot afford to send officers to distant training sites prepare for terrorism threats.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set any deadline for DHS to fix a training program that loses accreditation, meaning a 30-day notice requirement alone may not lead to real improvements.

Critics say the bill focuses research dollars on expanding access to existing training systems but does not require DHS to evaluate whether those training programs are actually effective at reducing terrorism risk.
Critics say rural and tribal agencies may still struggle to use new training tools if the bill provides no direct funding to help those departments cover the costs of participating.

117-hr-5673.one_liner: Update rules for a federal loan program that helps communities prepare for disasters
provisions: The federal government runs a loan program that helps cities and towns reduce damage from natural disasters before they happen.
Cities and towns that get money from this program must follow the two most recent published versions of building safety codes and construction standards.
The bill makes small fixes to how this loan program works.

supporters: Supporters say requiring cities and towns to follow the two most recent building code editions means disaster loan money goes toward stronger, up-to-date construction — not outdated standards that have since been replaced.
Supporters say the technical corrections make the hazard mitigation loan program easier to administer, reducing errors and delays for cities applying for pre-disaster funds.
critics: Critics say requiring the two most recent code editions could put the program out of reach for smaller towns that haven't yet adopted the latest building standards in their local laws.
Critics say the bill does not add new funding to the loan program, so the updated code requirements may create compliance burdens without giving communities more resources to meet them.

117-hr-5665.one_liner: Create a State Department office to track anti-Muslim acts in foreign countries
provisions: Creates an office inside the State Department to monitor anti-Muslim acts in other countries.
Creates a government position called the Special Envoy for Monitoring and Combating Islamophobia to lead the office.
Requires the State Department's yearly reports to Congress to cover anti-Muslim acts in foreign countries.
Those reports must include information about violence, harassment, and hate speech targeting Muslim people.
The reports must also cover what each country's government did in response to those acts.

supporters: Supporters say the new Special Envoy position would give the U.S. a dedicated person to track and respond to violence and harassment against Muslim people in foreign countries, similar to existing envoys for antisemitism and religious freedom.

Supporters say requiring the State Department's yearly human rights reports to include data on anti-Muslim acts — like hate speech in government media and physical attacks — would give Congress better information when making foreign policy decisions.
Supporters say the office would help the U.S. hold foreign governments accountable by documenting what steps each country took in response to acts targeting Muslim people.
critics: Critics say creating a new office and Special Envoy position inside the State Department singles out one religious group, while existing offices like the Ambassador-at-Large for International Religious Freedom already cover all religions including Muslims.

Critics say adding Islamophobia-specific reporting requirements to annual State Department reports to Congress could conflict with First Amendment values by having the U.S. government label foreign speech as 'hate speech' without a clear legal definition in the bill.
Critics say the bill does not include a cost estimate or staffing limit for the new office, leaving Congress without information about how much the office would cost to run each year.

117-hr-5641.one_liner: Raise the dollar limit that qualifies a disaster recovery project as small
provisions: Raises the cutoff for what counts as a small project to $1 million, letting more disaster recovery projects use a faster, simpler approval process.
Small projects get approved under a shorter set of steps, which means communities can start rebuilding sooner after a disaster.
The government must check and possibly update this $1 million cutoff every three years.

supporters: Supporters say raising the small project cutoff to $1 million means more disaster recovery projects can skip the long approval process and get started faster, helping communities rebuild sooner after storms, floods, or other disasters.

Supporters say the current threshold was set too low, so many projects that should qualify for the simpler process are stuck in longer reviews, slowing down recovery efforts for local governments and towns.
Supporters say the required review every three years keeps the $1 million limit from becoming outdated as construction costs rise over time.
critics: Critics say setting the small project limit at $1 million with less oversight could make it easier to misuse federal disaster funds, since simplified procedures involve fewer checks on how money is spent.
Critics say the bill does not set a clear method for how the three-year review must be done, which could allow the threshold to rise without enough public input or review by Congress.

Critics say moving more projects into the fast-track process reduces accountability for federal spending, since small projects under the Stafford Act require less documentation and fewer audits than larger ones.

117-hr-5681.one_liner: Give Shadow Wolves tracking unit officers a higher ICE rank
provisions: Lets ICE upgrade Shadow Wolves officers to special agent rank after required training.
Shadow Wolves is a tracking unit that patrols land belonging to the Tohono O'odham Nation.
Officers in similar tracking units at other locations can also be upgraded to special agent rank after the same training.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) must study and report on the best ways to expand the Shadow Wolves program.
The Government Accountability Office (GAO) must do a separate study on expanding the program.

supporters: Supporters say reclassifying Shadow Wolves officers as ICE special agents after training would give them more authority to stop illegal border crossings on Tohono O'odham Nation land.
Supporters say allowing officers in similar tracking units at other locations to earn special agent rank would grow the number of trained agents across more parts of the border.
Supporters say requiring both DHS and the GAO to study how to expand the Shadow Wolves program ensures decisions are backed by research before the program grows.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a limit on how many officers can be reclassified as special agents, which could lead to higher personnel costs without a clear budget.
Critics say expanding the Shadow Wolves model to locations outside Tohono O'odham Nation land may not work, since the unit was built around the tracking traditions of that specific community.
Critics say ordering two separate studies from DHS and the GAO on the same expansion question may produce conflicting results and delay any real action.

117-hr-5689.one_liner: Expand disaster prevention funding and coverage for wildfires, tsunamis, and ice storms
provisions: Lets unused disaster prevention money be moved to other projects after 7 years or when a grant closes, whichever comes first.
Raises the share of national disaster prevention grants for public buildings and roads from 6% to 15%.
Lets private nonprofit buildings — like food banks or community centers — get money and help to prepare for disasters before they happen.
Adds wildfires, tsunamis, and ice storms to the list of disasters that prevention money can be used for.
Requires FEMA to set aside 10% of yearly disaster prevention funds to help buildings meet the latest published safety codes.
Creates a test program where states and cities give money directly to homeowners to make their homes more disaster-proof.

supporters: Supporters say raising the national pre-disaster grant share from 6% to 15% for public buildings and roads means more infrastructure gets reinforced before a disaster hits, which costs less than rebuilding after.

Supporters say letting private nonprofits like food banks and community centers apply for hazard mitigation funds means more community hubs can stay open after wildfires, tsunamis, or ice storms — disasters now added to the eligible list.

Supporters say the pilot program that sends money directly to homeowners for retrofits, and the rule requiring FEMA to set aside 10% of funds for updated building codes, helps people protect their homes before the next disaster rather than waiting for recovery aid.
critics: Critics say moving unused disaster prevention funds after 84 months could pull money away from long-term projects in slow-recovering communities that still need those dollars.

Critics say adding wildfires, tsunamis, and ice storms to the eligible disaster list — while also expanding nonprofit eligibility and increasing the infrastructure grant share to 15% — spreads a fixed pool of FEMA money across more uses, leaving less for existing priorities.
Critics say requiring FEMA to set aside 10% of yearly funds specifically for building code upgrades limits how local governments can spend disaster prevention dollars based on their own needs.

117-hr-5695.one_liner: Update internal government bookkeeping references in federal law
provisions: Changes page and chapter numbers inside the U.S. law books so they point to the right place after a 2016 reorganization
No new rules, spending, or rights are created or removed — only the location codes inside the legal text change

supporters: Supporters say this bill corrects internal references in Title 25 of the U.S. Code to match the 2016 reorganization of Chapters 14 and 19, so that citations in federal law point to the right location.
Supporters say no new rules, spending, or rights are created or removed — only the location codes inside the legal text change.
Supporters say fixing these broken references helps courts, lawyers, and tribal governments find the correct law without confusion caused by outdated chapter numbers.
critics: Critics say that even a technical correction to Title 25, which governs Indian land claims and tribal affairs, should include input from the tribes affected by those provisions before it is enacted.
Critics say the bill was passed without further review of whether the 2016 reclassification itself was done correctly, meaning any errors from that reorganization would be locked in.
Critics say updating references to Chapters 14 and 19 without a full legal review could cause problems if any provisions were misplaced or mislabeled during the original 2016 transfer.

117-hr-5679.one_liner: Fix outdated cross-references in federal law across ten titles of U.S. Code
provisions: Updates internal bookkeeping in federal law so that references to old section numbers point to the correct, current section numbers
Does not change any policy, funding, or rules — only corrects where one law points to another
Affects sections across ten areas of federal law, including agriculture, education, and public lands
No dollar amounts, deadlines, or rules for people are changed

supporters: Supporters say updating the cross-references in Title 7 (Agriculture), Title 20 (Education), and Title 43 (Public Lands) prevents situations where a law points to a section number that no longer exists, which can cause confusion for courts and agencies trying to apply the law.
Supporters say this bill does not change any policy, funding levels, or rules — it only fixes where one part of federal law points to another, making the U.S. Code easier to read and use correctly.

Supporters say correcting outdated section references across ten titles of federal law helps lawyers, judges, and government workers find the right legal text without having to trace through old amendments.
critics: Critics say that even technical fixes to cross-references in federal law can introduce new errors if a wrong section number is inserted, potentially causing a law in areas like agriculture or public lands to point to the wrong provision.

Critics say bills that update references across ten different titles of federal law — including the Internal Revenue Code (Title 26) and Bankruptcy code (Title 11) — should go through careful review, since a small drafting mistake in a technical bill can have unintended effects.

117-hr-5677.one_liner: Fix outdated cross-references in federal law without changing any rules
provisions: This bill corrects technical errors in federal law where internal references point to the wrong place.
It updates how laws in Title 2 (laws about Congress), Title 50 (laws about national security), and Title 52 (laws about elections) refer to each other.
No rights, benefits, or rules change as a result of this bill.
Only the internal numbering and references used by lawyers and courts are updated.

117-hr-6434.one_liner: Create a National Park Service network about Japanese American history in World War II
provisions: Tells the National Park Service to set up a network focused on Japanese American history during World War II
The network will look at existing studies about places where Japanese Americans were held during the war so it does not repeat work already done
The network will create and share materials like maps, guides, and online information about what Japanese Americans went through during World War II

supporters: Supporters say the bill directs the National Park Service to create materials like maps, handbooks, and online guides about relocation centers and confinement sites where Japanese Americans were held during World War II, making that history easier for the public to access.
Supporters say the network must review existing studies before starting new ones, so the National Park Service does not repeat research already done on Japanese American experiences during the war.

Supporters say the bill specifically requires coverage of Japanese American confinement sites, which are currently spread across multiple NPS locations with no single program coordinating information about them.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a specific funding amount, so it is unclear how the National Park Service will pay to create and distribute the handbooks, maps, and electronic materials the network requires.
Critics say the National Park Service already manages some Japanese American confinement sites and related programs, and adding a new network may overlap with coordination work already underway.

Critics say the bill sets no timeline for when the network must be established or when educational materials must be produced, and includes no enforcement mechanism if the Department of Interior does not act.

117-hr-5705.one_liner: Update internal code references after crime law sections were moved to a new title
provisions: Congress moved crime and law enforcement laws to a new section of U.S. law called Title 34 in 2017.
Other laws that pointed to the old section numbers now have broken references.
This bill updates those old references so they point to the correct new location in Title 34.
No laws change — only the internal addresses used to find them.

supporters: Supporters say this bill fixes broken reference numbers left behind when Congress moved crime and law enforcement laws to Title 34 in 2017, so courts and agencies can find the correct law without confusion.
Supporters say updating these internal addresses prevents citation errors in enforcement documents and legal filings that still point to the old section numbers.
critics: Critics say that even a technical cleanup bill that touches crime and law enforcement references in Title 34 should be reviewed carefully to confirm no unintended changes to existing law slip through.
Critics say Congress should clearly document which specific section numbers are being updated so the public can verify that only the addresses changed and no substantive rules were altered.

117-hr-5982.one_liner: Update and reorganize existing space program laws into one place in the U.S. Code
provisions: Moves existing space program laws into a single section of federal law called Title 51
Does not change what the laws say — only reorganizes where they appear in the U.S. Code
Makes small technical fixes so the laws read clearly and consistently

supporters: Supporters say moving all space program laws into a single section of federal law — Title 51 — makes it easier for government agencies, contractors, and courts to find and follow those rules without searching across multiple parts of the U.S. Code.
Supporters say the technical fixes in this bill make the laws read more clearly and consistently, which reduces the chance of confusion about what the rules require.
Supporters say this bill does not change what any law says or does, so no programs, funding levels, or affected groups are altered — only where the laws appear in the Code.
critics: Critics say that even technical rewrites of existing laws — ones that are supposed to change nothing — can accidentally shift the meaning of words in ways that affect how courts or agencies interpret the rules later.

Critics say consolidating many space program laws into Title 51 at once, without changing the rules, makes it harder for the public to track what moved where and whether anything quietly changed in the process.

117-hr-5706.one_liner: Require transportation companies to have policies against sexual assault and harassment
provisions: Passenger airlines, buses, trains, and rideshare companies like Uber and Lyft must create written policies on sexual assault and harassment, train their staff, and set up ways for people to report incidents.
People who physically or sexually assault transportation workers face civil fines.
The Department of Transportation must collect data on how many sexual assault and harassment reports each company receives and post that information online for the public to see.
People who experience sexual assault or harassment on transportation can report it to police in a way that keeps their name and personal details private.
The Department of Transportation must write and publish an official definition of what counts as sexual harassment in transportation.

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a gap by requiring airlines, buses, trains, and rideshare companies like Uber and Lyft to have written sexual assault and harassment policies and trained staff — rules that do not currently exist at the federal level.
Supporters say requiring the Department of Transportation to post each company's incident report totals online gives riders a way to compare safety records before choosing a carrier.
Supporters say the private reporting option lets passengers report sexual assault or harassment to police without giving up their name or personal details, which may lead more people to come forward.
critics: Critics say the bill places new training and policy requirements on transportation network companies and carriers without providing federal funds to help cover the cost of building those programs.
Critics say civil penalties only cover assaults on transportation workers, leaving gaps in how the law handles passengers who assault other passengers on buses, trains, or rideshares.

Critics say that publishing each company's raw incident counts online could mislead the public, because a company with better reporting systems may show higher numbers than one that simply records fewer complaints.

117-hr-5961.one_liner: Update the federal rulebook for government advisory committees and financial disclosures
provisions: Rewrites the rules for federal advisory committees — groups of outside experts that give advice to the government — without changing what those rules actually say
Rewrites the rules for Offices of Inspector General, which are the government offices that look for waste and fraud, without changing what those rules say
Rewrites the financial disclosure rules for federal workers, including the President and Vice President, without changing what those rules say
Rewrites the rules about how much money federal workers can earn from outside jobs without changing what those rules say

supporters: Supporters say the bill cleans up the wording in federal law covering advisory committees, Inspectors General, and financial disclosure rules without changing what any of those rules actually require.

Supporters say restating the rules for federal advisory committees — the outside expert groups that advise agencies — in cleaner language makes the U.S. Code easier for agencies and the public to read and use.

Supporters say updating the legal text around financial disclosure requirements for the President, Vice President, and executive branch employees helps keep Title 5 of the U.S. Code organized and current.
critics: Critics say that when rules about Offices of Inspector General and financial disclosures are rewritten, even without intended changes, small wording differences could be used in court to argue the rules now mean something different.

Critics say that because the bill rewrites rules covering outside earned income limits for federal workers alongside financial disclosure requirements, without a side-by-side comparison, it may be difficult to confirm nothing was changed.

Critics say Congress should use the regular lawmaking process to restate rules this significant — covering the President, Vice President, and all executive branch employees — so any unintended changes can be caught through normal review.

117-hr-6865.one_liner: Fund the Coast Guard and update its safety and environmental rules through 2023
provisions: Sets the Coast Guard's budget for the years ending September 2022 and September 2023
Changes how the Coast Guard handles reports of sexual assault and sexual harassment among its members
Changes safety rules for ships and boats on the water
Changes rules for how ships and boats are built
Updates rules for navigation on U.S. waterways
Changes rules for dealing with aquatic invasive species — plants and animals that spread into waters where they don't belong and can damage local ecosystems
Changes rules for how oil spills are reported and cleaned up

supporters: Supporters say the bill sets steady Coast Guard funding for FY2022 and FY2023, which lets the agency maintain its ships, crews, and rescue stations without budget gaps.
Supporters say changing how sexual assault and sexual harassment are reported inside the Coast Guard will make it easier for members to file complaints and get support.
Supporters say updated rules for aquatic invasive species will help stop plants and animals from spreading into U.S. waters and damaging local fish and wildlife.
critics: Critics say new ship construction rules could raise costs for U.S. boat builders, since companies would need to update their building processes to meet the new standards.
Critics say combining budget authorization with changes to oil spill rules, vessel safety, and navigation in one bill makes it harder to debate each provision on its own.
Critics say updated oil spill reporting requirements could add paperwork and compliance costs for shipping companies that operate on U.S. waterways.

117-hr-897.one_liner: Transfer 2,560 acres of California land to the Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians
provisions: Puts about 2,560 acres of land in California into federal trust for the Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians, a federally recognized tribe
Land held in trust becomes part of the tribe's reservation
No gambling is allowed on the land transferred through this bill

supporters: Supporters say putting 2,560 acres into federal trust for the Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians restores land that is part of the tribe's historical territory in California.
Supporters say making the land part of the tribe's reservation gives the Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians legal control over how the land is used and managed.
Supporters say the bill includes a rule that blocks any gambling on the 2,560 acres, which addresses a common concern about trust land transfers.
critics: Critics say transferring 2,560 acres into federal trust removes that land from California's local tax base, which can reduce funding for county services in the area.
Critics say once land is taken into trust for the tribe's reservation, state and local governments lose the ability to enforce zoning or land-use rules on those 2,560 acres.

Critics say the bill bypasses the standard Bureau of Indian Affairs fee-to-trust application process, which normally includes an environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) before land status is changed.

117-hr-963.one_liner: Stop companies from forcing workers and customers into private arbitration
provisions: Right now, many companies make workers and customers sign contracts that say any dispute must go to a private arbitrator instead of a court.
This bill makes those contract clauses unenforceable for disputes about jobs, shopping, competition, and civil rights.
Workers and consumers would be able to bring these disputes to court or join class-action lawsuits instead.
The change applies to new disputes after the bill becomes law.

supporters: Supporters say workers and consumers required by contract to use private arbitrators for employment, consumer, antitrust, or civil rights disputes would be able to take those disputes to court instead.
Supporters say the bill allows people to join class-action lawsuits, which individual workers and consumers currently cannot do when arbitration clauses block court access.
Supporters say the change applies to new disputes after the bill becomes law, so it does not affect cases already in arbitration.
critics: Critics say businesses that currently use arbitration to resolve employment and consumer disputes quickly and at lower cost would face more expensive and slower court proceedings.
Critics say allowing class-action lawsuits in antitrust and civil rights cases could expose companies to much larger financial penalties than individual arbitration outcomes.
Critics say workers and consumers who signed contracts with arbitration clauses agreed to those terms, and the bill removes a dispute option some parties prefer.

117-hr-735.one_liner: Name a Cotati, California post office after Arturo L. Ibleto
provisions: The post office at 502 East Cotati Avenue in Cotati, California will officially be called the Arturo L. Ibleto Post Office Building.
Arturo Luis Ibleto was a person from the Cotati, California area whom Congress chose to honor with this public building designation.
No postal services, hours, staff, or operations at this location change — only the official name changes.
The U.S. Postal Service will update its records and building signs to use the new name.

supporters: Supporters say the bill honors Arturo Luis Ibleto by giving his name to the post office at 502 East Cotati Avenue in Cotati, California, recognizing his contributions to the local community.
Supporters say the name change does not affect any postal services, hours, or staff at the location, so there is no cost or disruption to residents who use the building.
Supporters say Congress chose this building because it is a public landmark in the community where Ibleto lived, making it a fitting way to preserve his memory.

117-hres-1017.one_liner: Set the House debate rules for cannabis and insulin cost bills
provisions: This is a procedural resolution — it sets the rules for how the House will debate two other bills, not a policy change itself.
The first bill (H.R. 3617) would remove cannabis from the federal list of illegal substances, making it no longer a federal crime to possess or use it.
H.R. 3617 would also let people with past federal cannabis convictions apply to clear their records.
H.R. 3617 would create a fund to send money to communities that faced heavy drug enforcement over the past decades.
The second bill (H.R. 6833) would cap how much people with health insurance have to pay out of pocket each month for insulin.

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows a vote on H.R. 3617, which would remove cannabis from the federal list of illegal substances and let people with past federal cannabis convictions apply to clear their records.

Supporters say H.R. 6833, brought to the floor by this rule, would cap monthly out-of-pocket insulin costs for people with health insurance, making the drug more affordable for the millions of Americans who depend on it.

Supporters say H.R. 3617 would create a fund to send money back to communities that faced heavy drug enforcement over the past decades, directing resources to people directly harmed by those policies.
critics: Critics say this rule packages cannabis descheduling under H.R. 3617 with insulin pricing under H.R. 6833, combining two unrelated policy areas in a single debate process that limits separate review of each bill.

Critics say H.R. 3617's removal of cannabis from the federal controlled substances list conflicts with current federal law and could affect how states enforce their own drug rules, raising concerns about law enforcement coordination.

Critics say the insulin cost-sharing caps in H.R. 6833 impose new requirements on private insurance plans under ERISA and the Internal Revenue Code without fully accounting for how those mandates might affect employer-sponsored coverage costs.

117-hres-849.one_liner: Set House debate rules for a bill creating a State Department anti-Islamophobia office
provisions: This is a procedural rule that sets the terms for how the House of Representatives can debate and vote on H.R. 5665.
It controls how much time members of Congress get to speak about the bill and what changes to the bill can be considered.
The underlying bill, H.R. 5665, would create a new office inside the State Department to track and respond to discrimination against Muslims around the world.
The procedural rule does not itself create the office — it only governs how the House handles the debate over whether to do so.

supporters: Supporters say this rule is needed to bring H.R. 5665 to a House vote, which would create a new office inside the State Department focused on tracking anti-Muslim discrimination in other countries.

Supporters say the State Department already monitors religious discrimination abroad through existing offices, and H.R. 5665 would add a dedicated office so anti-Muslim incidents receive the same level of tracking as other forms of religious bias.
Supporters say the rule sets structured debate terms and controls which amendments can be considered, keeping the House focused on the core question of whether to create the new office.
critics: Critics say the rule limits which amendments members can offer, so Congress cannot adjust the scope or staffing of the new State Department office before the vote.

Critics say creating a State Department office focused on one religious group, rather than expanding the existing religious freedom office to cover anti-Muslim discrimination, sets up an unequal structure inside the department.
Critics say the debate time the rule allows is not enough for members to examine how the new office would define anti-Muslim discrimination or decide which countries it would monitor.

117-hres-831.one_liner: Call on the US to push NATO to create a center focused on democracy
provisions: Calls on the President to use the US vote at NATO to update NATO's core plan so it states support for shared democratic values among member countries
Calls on the President to use the US vote at NATO to create a Center for Democratic Resilience inside NATO's main office in Brussels
This center would work to strengthen democratic systems in NATO member countries, partner countries, and countries that want to join NATO
This is a resolution, meaning it expresses the opinion of Congress but does not create a law or spend money

supporters: Supporters say updating NATO's core plan to clearly name shared democratic values would give the alliance a stronger, unified message when member countries face pressure from authoritarian governments.

Supporters say a Center for Democratic Resilience at NATO headquarters in Brussels would give member, partner, and aspirant countries a dedicated resource to strengthen their voting systems, courts, and free press.
Supporters say because this is a resolution and not a spending bill, it costs no money and simply directs the President to push for these changes using the US vote at NATO.
critics: Critics say calling on the President to use the US vote to change NATO's core plan could create disagreements with the 31 other NATO members who may not want democratic values written into the alliance's main strategy.

Critics say creating a new center inside NATO headquarters could expand the alliance's role beyond its military mission, which some member countries and US lawmakers argue goes outside what NATO was built to do.
Critics say the resolution does not set any rules, funding, or timeline for the proposed center, leaving key details about how it would work and who would run it unanswered.

117-hres-852.one_liner: Set the rules for how Congress will vote on raising the debt limit
provisions: Sets the process Congress will follow to debate and vote on a bill that raises the federal debt limit
Limits how long Congress can debate the debt limit bill before taking a vote
Does not change the debt limit itself — only controls how the vote on changing it will work

supporters: Supporters say the time limit on floor debate set by this rule gives the debt limit vote a clear path forward, stopping the process from being blocked by unlimited debate.
Supporters say this rule brings S.J. Res. 33 to an up-or-down vote, which supporters argue is the only way to avoid a federal default when the debt limit must be raised.
Supporters say setting a fixed debate window through this rule treats both parties equally by giving each side the same amount of time to speak before the vote.
critics: Critics say the time limit on floor debate set by this rule cuts short the time members of Congress have to challenge or amend S.J. Res. 33 before a final vote.
Critics say rushing S.J. Res. 33 through a capped debate process means fewer members can put their objections to raising the debt limit into the public record.
Critics say this rule, by controlling how S.J. Res. 33 is debated, shifts power to House leadership and away from rank-and-file members who want more time to review the resolution.

117-hres-848.one_liner: Allow the House to vote on charging Mark Meadows with contempt of Congress
provisions: Lets the full House vote on a report from the committee that investigated the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol.
The report says Mark Meadows, who was White House Chief of Staff under President Trump, should be charged with contempt of Congress.
Contempt of Congress means the House believes a person refused to hand over documents or answer questions that Congress asked for.
This is a procedural step — it opens debate and a vote on the contempt report, but does not itself charge anyone.

supporters: Supporters say allowing the full House to vote on the contempt report holds Mark Meadows accountable for refusing to hand over documents and answer questions about the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack.
Supporters say this step is needed because Meadows, as White House Chief of Staff, had direct knowledge of events on January 6 and Congress has a right to that information.
Supporters say opening debate and a vote on the contempt report follows the normal process Congress uses when a witness does not cooperate with an investigation.
critics: Critics say this resolution is a political move against Meadows rather than a fair use of the contempt process, since the select committee was set up by House Democrats without equal Republican input.
Critics say Meadows had legal reasons to limit what he shared, because some of his communications with President Trump may be protected under executive privilege.
Critics say moving forward with a contempt vote before courts ruled on the executive privilege question skipped an important legal step.

117-hres-851.one_liner: Find Mark Meadows in contempt of Congress for ignoring a legal order
provisions: Congress sent Mark Meadows a legal order to appear and hand over documents — called a subpoena.
Meadows was White House Chief of Staff when the January 6th attack on the Capitol happened.
He refused to follow that order.
This resolution says Congress officially finds him in contempt — meaning he broke the law by refusing.
The Speaker of the House must send his case to federal prosecutors for possible criminal charges.
The Speaker must also take steps to force Meadows to follow the subpoena.

supporters: Supporters say Meadows broke federal law by refusing to follow a legal subpoena issued by the January 6th Select Committee, and Congress must enforce its own oversight power or lose the ability to investigate future attacks on the Capitol.

Supporters say that as White House Chief of Staff on January 6th, Meadows had direct knowledge of events that day, and the committee cannot complete its investigation without the documents and testimony he was ordered to provide.
Supporters say the resolution correctly requires the Speaker to send Meadows's case to federal prosecutors, which is the standard legal step Congress must take when someone defies a subpoena.
critics: Critics say Meadows stopped cooperating after the committee sought documents and communications that he believes are protected by executive privilege — a legal rule that shields some White House conversations from outside review.
Critics say the contempt resolution moves too fast, because courts have not yet settled whether executive privilege covers the specific materials Meadows was subpoenaed to hand over.

Critics say referring Meadows to the Justice Department for criminal charges turns a legal dispute over privilege into a political fight, since the same administration whose allies sit on the committee would decide whether to prosecute him.

117-hres-860.one_liner: Schedule votes on two bills about veteran education and VA healthcare enrollment
provisions: Allows the House to vote on a bill that counts time spent in active duty training toward GI Bill education benefits
Allows the House to vote on a bill that would sign eligible veterans up for VA healthcare automatically instead of requiring them to apply
Sets the debate time and rules for how each of these two bills will be considered on the House floor

supporters: Supporters say H.R. 1836 would count time spent in active duty training toward GI Bill education benefits, helping Guard and Reserve members who currently do not get credit for that service.
Supporters say H.R. 4673 would automatically enroll eligible veterans in VA healthcare, removing the application step that causes some veterans to miss out on care they earned.
Supporters say this rule sets a fixed amount of debate time for each bill and brings both to a House floor vote.
critics: Critics say combining H.R. 1836 and H.R. 4673 into one rule limits the ability to vote on each bill separately, reducing options for members who support one but not the other.
Critics say automatic enrollment under H.R. 4673 could pull veterans into the VA system without their explicit consent, raising questions about whether enrollment should require an active choice.
Critics say expanding GI Bill eligibility under H.R. 1836 to cover active duty training periods would increase education benefit costs without a clear funding source identified in the bill.

117-hres-912.one_liner: Set the rules for how Congress would vote on postal service and spending bills
provisions: Set a time limit and voting rules for debating the postal service bill (H.R. 3076) on the House floor
Set a time limit and voting rules for debating a spending bill (H.R. 6617) that kept the government funded through September 30, 2022
Decided which changes to those bills could be proposed and voted on during debate

supporters: Supporters say the rule's structured debate time for H.R. 3076 allows the full House to vote on postal service reforms without delay, moving the bill closer to becoming law.
Supporters say the rule brings H.R. 6617 to the floor for a vote, which kept the federal government funded through September 30, 2022 and avoided a government shutdown.

Supporters say limiting which amendments can be offered during debate on both bills keeps the process focused and prevents the bills from being stalled or altered in ways that would lose enough votes to pass.
critics: Critics say the amendment restrictions on H.R. 3076 block members from proposing changes to specific postal service rules, meaning the bill moves forward without allowing fixes that some members believe are needed.

Critics say the debate time limits set by the rule give members only a short window to raise concerns about the government funding levels in H.R. 6617, which covered spending through September 30, 2022.

Critics say controlling which amendments can be voted on for both bills gives House leadership too much power over what changes are allowed, cutting out members who want to offer different funding or postal policy options.

117-hres-868.one_liner: Set the rules for how the House votes on a NASA property leasing bill
provisions: The House can debate the Senate's version of the NASA leasing bill under a set time limit with no extra changes allowed.
Once the time limit is up, the House votes up or down on the Senate version of the bill.
The House can move to a final vote on the rule itself without additional debate once it is brought up.

supporters: Supporters say the set time limit on debate keeps the House from stalling on the Senate's NASA leasing bill, moving it to a final vote faster.
Supporters say the up-or-down vote process means the House gets a clear, simple choice on the Senate version without delays.
Supporters say allowing the House to move straight to a vote on the rule itself without extra debate saves floor time for other business.
critics: Critics say the rule blocks House members from offering any changes to the Senate version, even if they disagree with specific leasing terms NASA could offer.
Critics say cutting off debate with a strict time limit prevents members from fully questioning how NASA will use its expanded authority to lease non-excess property.
Critics say forcing a clean up-or-down vote means the House must accept or reject the entire Senate bill, with no way to fix parts they find problematic.

117-hres-950.one_liner: Set the rules for debating a veterans toxic exposure health care bill
provisions: Sets the time limit and debate rules for Congress to vote on H.R. 3967, a bill about health care for veterans exposed to toxic substances
Controls which changes to the bill can be proposed during debate
Does not change any health care rules itself — only controls how the vote on the main bill will be run

supporters: Supporters say the rule sets a defined time limit for debate on H.R. 3967, which would let Congress move quickly to vote on expanding health care for veterans exposed to toxic substances.
Supporters say that by controlling which amendments can be proposed, the rule keeps the debate focused on H.R. 3967 as written, preventing last-minute changes that could delay a vote.
Supporters say the rule is the required step to bring H.R. 3967 to the full House floor, meaning without it, veterans waiting for toxic exposure benefits cannot get a final vote.
critics: Critics say the rule restricts which amendments members can offer, blocking lawmakers from proposing changes to specific parts of H.R. 3967 — such as which toxic substances or which groups of veterans are covered.
Critics say using a structured rule limits the ability of members to fix problems in H.R. 3967 before it passes, meaning errors in the benefit or eligibility rules could become law without debate.
Critics say the rule gives House leadership control over what gets debated, rather than letting all members weigh in on a bill that affects veterans' health care access.

117-hres-900.one_liner: Set the rules for debating three separate bills in the House
provisions: This is a procedural bill that sets the time limits and debate rules for three other bills before the House votes on them.
The first bill would place sanctions on foreign individuals who violate the rights of LGBTQI people.
The second bill would stop companies from forcing workers and customers to use private arbitration in sexual assault or sexual harassment cases.
The third bill would create a federal research program focused on engineering biology to keep the U.S. competitive globally.

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the House to move forward on three bills at once, including H.R. 3485 to sanction foreign individuals who violate LGBTQI rights and H.R. 4445 to end forced arbitration in sexual assault and harassment cases.

Supporters say the rule sets structured debate time so members can vote on H.R. 4445, which would give workers and customers the right to take sexual assault and harassment claims to court instead of private arbitration.
Supporters say the rule brings H.R. 4521 to a floor vote, which would create a coordinated federal research program in engineering biology to keep the U.S. competitive with other countries.
critics: Critics say the rule packages three unrelated bills together, covering LGBTQI sanctions, arbitration law, and federal research programs, which limits members from voting on each issue separately.
Critics say the rule limits floor debate time, which reduces the chance to consider how the arbitration changes in H.R. 4445 could affect existing contracts between companies and employees.
Critics say the rule brings H.R. 4521 to a vote without enough debate about the scope and cost of creating a new coordinated federal research initiative in engineering biology.

117-s-1226.one_liner: Name a federal courthouse in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania after Judge Sylvia H. Rambo
provisions: The courthouse at 1501 North 6th Street in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania gets an official new name: the Sylvia H. Rambo United States Courthouse.
Sylvia H. Rambo was appointed as a federal judge in 1979 — one of the first women to serve as a federal judge in Pennsylvania — and served on the bench for over 30 years.
The courthouse serves the Middle District of Pennsylvania, which handles federal court cases for the central part of the state.
The name is official and permanent — it applies to all signs, records, and documents tied to that building going forward.

supporters: Supporters say the bill honors Judge Sylvia H. Rambo, who was appointed in 1979 as one of the first women to serve as a federal judge in Pennsylvania and served on the bench for over 30 years.

Supporters say renaming the courthouse at 1501 North 6th Street in Harrisburg makes her contributions to the Middle District of Pennsylvania a permanent part of the building's official records, signs, and documents.
Supporters say the designation costs nothing and requires no funding — it is a formal recognition with no impact on courthouse operations or federal court cases.

117-hres-956.one_liner: Call for a cease-fire in Ukraine and continued support against Russia
provisions: Calls for an immediate stop to fighting in Ukraine
Calls for all Russian military forces to leave Ukrainian territory
Supports keeping economic penalties on Russia in place
Calls on the U.S. and its allies to send more military equipment to Ukraine for defense

supporters: Supporters say calling for a full Russian military withdrawal from Ukrainian territory would restore Ukraine's recognized borders and stop ongoing civilian casualties.
Supporters say keeping economic sanctions on Russia cuts off funding that the Putin government uses to continue military operations.
Supporters say sending more defensive military equipment to Ukraine through U.S. allies gives Ukraine the tools to protect its own land without U.S. troops entering the conflict.
critics: Critics say calling for more military aid to Ukraine commits the U.S. and its partners to open-ended spending with no dollar limit or end date stated in the resolution.
Critics say demanding a full Russian withdrawal sets conditions that make a negotiated cease-fire harder to reach, which could extend the length of the conflict.
Critics say the resolution does not address how the U.S. will pay for additional defensive security assistance or which specific weapons systems would be sent.

117-s-2126.one_liner: Name a federal building in Cheyenne, Wyoming after Louisa Swain
provisions: The federal building at 308 W. 21st Street in Cheyenne, Wyoming will be officially named the Louisa Swain Federal Office Building.
Louisa Swain was the first woman to vote in a U.S. election, casting her ballot in Laramie, Wyoming in 1870.
Wyoming gave women the right to vote in December 1869, more than 50 years before the 19th Amendment made it a right for women across the country in 1920.

supporters: Supporters say naming the building at 308 W. 21st Street after Louisa Swain honors the first woman to vote in a U.S. election, a right she exercised in Laramie, Wyoming in 1870.

Supporters say Wyoming gave women the right to vote in December 1869 — more than 50 years before the 19th Amendment reached all women in 1920 — and a named federal building in the state capital marks that lead.
Supporters say placing Louisa Swain's name on a federal office building in Cheyenne creates a lasting public record of Wyoming's role in expanding voting rights.
critics: Critics say Louisa Swain cast her ballot in Laramie in 1870, not in Cheyenne, so naming a building at 308 W. 21st Street — roughly 50 miles from where the vote actually happened — does not mark the true historic site.

Critics say the bill sets no funding for new signs or plaques at 308 W. 21st Street, meaning any costs from the name change would have to come out of the agency's existing budget without a clear dollar amount approved by Congress.

117-hres-979.one_liner: Set the rules for debating two bills in the House
provisions: Sets the time limit and rules for how the House can debate a bill about arbitration agreements
Sets the time limit and rules for how the House can debate a bill about hair texture and style discrimination
Controls which changes lawmakers can propose during debate on each bill

supporters: Supporters say the rule brings H.R. 2116 to a full House vote, giving people who face discrimination based on hair texture or style — including many Black Americans — a path to federal protection.

Supporters say the rule allows the House to debate H.R. 963, which would change title 9 of the US Code to limit when companies can force workers or consumers into private arbitration instead of court.
Supporters say setting firm time limits on debate for both bills keeps the legislative process on track and prevents either bill from being stalled indefinitely.
critics: Critics say the rule controls which changes lawmakers can propose during debate, blocking members from offering amendments that could alter key parts of the arbitration or hair discrimination bills.

Critics say bringing H.R. 963 forward under a restricted rule limits the ability to address how changes to title 9 of the US Code would affect existing contracts and arbitration agreements already in place.
Critics say the structured debate rules give members too little time to fully examine the legal effects of rewriting federal arbitration law under title 9 of the US Code.

117-hres-973.one_liner: Set the rules for the House to vote on four separate bills
provisions: Allowed the House to vote on a government spending bill to fund federal agencies through September 2022
Allowed the House to vote on a short-term spending extension to keep the government running
Allowed the House to vote on a ban on importing oil and energy from Russia
Allowed the House to vote on emergency COVID-19 relief spending for 2022
Set time limits and debate rules for each of those four votes

supporters: Supporters say this rule allowed the House to vote on a full-year government funding bill to keep federal agencies running through September 2022, preventing a government shutdown.
Supporters say the rule allowed a vote to ban Russian oil and energy imports, which supporters argued would cut off a key source of money for Russia amid the Ukraine conflict.
Supporters say the rule also allowed a vote on emergency COVID-19 relief spending for 2022, giving lawmakers a path to send more funds to people and programs still dealing with the pandemic.
critics: Critics say procedural rules like this one set strict time limits on debate, which limits how long members of Congress can speak against or offer changes to major spending bills.
Critics say bundling votes on a Russian oil ban, COVID relief, and government funding into one rule made it harder for members to vote against one bill without slowing down the others.

117-s-2629.one_liner: Set up a national system to track and count cybercrime reports
provisions: The Department of Justice must work with the National Academy of Sciences to create a system for sorting different types of cybercrime into categories.
The DOJ must add a cybercrime section to the national database that police departments use to report crimes.
The national crime survey that the government runs each year must start asking people questions about cybercrime.
A government watchdog must check whether people are actually reporting cybercrime and whether some groups report it less than others.

supporters: Supporters say adding a cybercrime section to the National Incident-Based Reporting System will give police departments across the country a standard way to record and share cybercrime data for the first time.

Supporters say requiring the National Crime Victimization Survey to ask about cybercrime will capture attacks that people never reported to police, giving a fuller picture of how many individuals and businesses are affected each year.
Supporters say having the Government Accountability Office check whether certain groups report cybercrime less than others will help identify gaps in outreach and enforcement.
critics: Critics say creating a new taxonomy through the National Academy of Sciences and adding cybercrime categories to federal databases will take years to implement, delaying any real improvement in data collection.

Critics say the bill does not require agencies to act on the data once it is collected, meaning the new reporting systems could produce information that sits unused without changing how cybercrime is investigated or prosecuted.

117-s-3294.one_liner: Place statues of Justices Sandra Day O'Connor and Ruth Bader Ginsburg in the Capitol
provisions: A government committee must get statues of Supreme Court Justices Sandra Day O'Connor and Ruth Bader Ginsburg.
The statues must be placed permanently inside the U.S. Capitol building or on its grounds.
Sandra Day O'Connor was the first woman on the Supreme Court, serving from 1981 to 2006.
Ruth Bader Ginsburg served on the Supreme Court from 1993 until her death in 2020.

supporters: Supporters say placing statues of O'Connor and Ginsburg in the U.S. Capitol honors the first two women to serve on the Supreme Court, giving them a permanent place alongside other figures recognized in the building.
Supporters say the bill marks O'Connor's 25 years on the Court (1981–2006) and Ginsburg's 27 years (1993–2020) as a lasting record of their service in the nation's most visible civic space.
critics: Critics say space in the U.S. Capitol and its grounds is limited, and adding two statues requires the Joint Committee on the Library and the Architect of the Capitol to go through a formal process that takes time and public funds.

Critics say decisions about who is honored with a permanent statue in the Capitol should follow a consistent set of criteria applied to all former justices, not be made case by case through separate bills.

117-s-321.one_liner: Award a Congressional Gold Medal to the women of the 6888th Central Postal Battalion
provisions: Gives a Congressional Gold Medal to the women who served in the 6888th Central Postal Directory Battalion during World War II
The 6888th was made up of Black women in the U.S. Army who sorted mail for American troops stationed in Europe
The medal will be kept at the Smithsonian Institution where people can see it and researchers can study it

supporters: Supporters say the medal honors the roughly 855 Black women of the 6888th who sorted millions of pieces of mail for U.S. troops in Europe during World War II — service that went without national recognition for more than 75 years.
Supporters say placing the medal at the Smithsonian Institution will let the public view it and allow researchers to study the history of the 6888th's contributions to troop morale during the war.
critics: Critics say the bill provides only a symbolic award and does not include financial compensation or veterans' benefits for any surviving members of the 6888th or their families.

Critics say the medal goes to the Smithsonian Institution rather than to the veterans or their descendants, meaning the women who served will not personally receive any item of recognition from Congress.

117-s-2959.one_liner: Let school districts use 2022 data for a key federal school funding program
provisions: School districts that get federal money through the Impact Aid Program can use their data from 2022 instead of collecting new data for 2023.
The Impact Aid Program gives money to schools that lose property tax income because federal land nearby does not get taxed.
Schools that have more students living on military bases or Native American lands also get money through this program.
Districts can use either their 2022 student count numbers or their 2022 federal property values — whichever applies to how they qualify for the program.

supporters: Supporters say that letting school districts use their 2022 student count or federal property data for 2023 applications saves time and reduces paperwork for districts near military bases and Native American lands.

Supporters say this protects funding for schools that already lost property tax income because nearby federal land is tax-exempt, making sure those districts do not have to reapply with new data during a difficult transition year.
critics: Critics say that using 2022 data for 2023 funding means some districts may receive more or less money than they should, since student populations on military bases and Native American lands can change from year to year.
Critics say the bill does not explain what happens if a district's 2022 numbers were wrong or disputed, which could lock in errors for the full 2023 program year.

117-s-400.one_liner: Name the Department of Transportation headquarters building after William T. Coleman Jr.
provisions: The Department of Transportation building at 1200 New Jersey Avenue in Washington, DC gets a new official name: the William T. Coleman, Jr., Federal Building.
William T. Coleman Jr. was the first Black person to serve as U.S. Secretary of Transportation, a role he held from 1975 to 1977 under President Gerald Ford.
This is a name-only change — no rules change, no money moves, and the building works exactly as before.

supporters: Supporters say renaming the building honors William T. Coleman Jr., who made history in 1975 as the first Black U.S. Secretary of Transportation, and that a federal building name is a lasting way to mark that milestone.
Supporters say the change costs nothing — no rules change, no money moves, and the building at 1200 New Jersey Avenue keeps working exactly as before — so there is no downside to the recognition.
Supporters say naming a Department of Transportation building after the first Black person to lead that department connects the agency's history to the people who walk through its doors every day.
critics: Critics say Congress has limited floor time, and spending it on a name-only bill for a building at 1200 New Jersey Avenue takes time away from bills that change policy, move funding, or affect large numbers of people.
Critics say ceremonial renaming bills like this one do not change any rules or programs at the Department of Transportation, so the impact on the public is close to zero.

Critics say if Congress wants to honor Secretary Coleman's service from 1975 to 1977, there are ways to do that — like updating transportation policy — that would have a real effect on the people the department serves.

117-s-566.one_liner: Rename a Rhode Island post office after Specialist Matthew R. Turcotte
provisions: Changes the official name of the post office at 42 Main Street in Slatersville, Rhode Island to the 'Specialist Matthew R. Turcotte Post Office'

117-s-658.one_liner: Let the Department of Homeland Security partner with nonprofits to teach cybersecurity skills
provisions: The Department of Homeland Security can team up with a group of nonprofit organizations to build and run cybersecurity training programs.
The training is meant to help protect the country from online attacks.
The nonprofit group can create new training, update existing training, and teach it to people who need it.

supporters: Supporters say teaming DHS with nonprofit organizations lets the government use outside experts who already run cybersecurity training, rather than building new programs from scratch.
Supporters say keeping training programs updated through the nonprofit consortium means people defending against online attacks will learn the latest methods, not outdated ones.
Supporters say this gives DHS a formal way to reach more people who need cybersecurity skills, which could reduce gaps in how well different parts of the country are protected.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a spending limit or budget for the DHS-nonprofit partnership, making it hard to know how much taxpayer money could be committed.
Critics say giving nonprofit groups the power to create and deliver homeland security training without clear oversight rules could lead to uneven quality across different training programs.
Critics say the bill does not define who qualifies to join the nonprofit consortium, which could limit competition and favor certain organizations over others.

117-s-583.one_liner: Require DHS to publish yearly reports on new government buying methods
provisions: DHS must post a yearly report on its website showing which new buying methods it used and whether they saved money, worked faster, or led to better results.
DHS must write guides and offer training to staff on new ways to buy goods and services from outside companies.
DHS must share what works across the agency and make that information available to other federal agencies.
A council of top government buyers from across federal agencies must meet to look at better ways to handle purchasing and contracts.
One of the goals DHS must track is whether more contracts are going to small businesses.

supporters: Supporters say the yearly public report on DHS's website will let taxpayers see which new buying methods saved money, cut the time it takes to award contracts, or got better results — making the agency more accountable.
Supporters say the requirement to track whether more contracts go to small businesses will help small companies compete for federal work inside DHS.
Supporters say sharing what works across DHS and with other federal agencies could stop agencies from spending time and money figuring out the same procurement problems on their own.
critics: Critics say the bill requires DHS to write guides, hold trainings, and publish yearly reports, but sets no specific cost savings targets or deadlines, so there is no way to measure whether the new rules are actually working.
Critics say forming a new Chief Acquisition Officers Council adds meetings and coordination costs across agencies without giving the council power to require any agency to change how it spends money.

Critics say the bill tracks whether small business contract goals are being met but does not change the actual rules about how many contracts must go to small businesses, so the outcome may not change.

117-s-452.one_liner: Award a gold medal to hockey player Willie O'Ree for his role in growing the sport
provisions: Gives Willie O'Ree, or a family member if he is not available, a Congressional Gold Medal
The medal honors his work in hockey and his efforts to open the sport to more people

supporters: Supporters say O'Ree broke the NHL's color barrier in 1958 as the first Black player in league history, and a Congressional Gold Medal would formally recognize that milestone for a group that was excluded from professional hockey for decades.
Supporters say the bill honors O'Ree's ongoing work as the NHL's Ambassador for Youth Development, where he has helped bring hockey to children who would not otherwise have access to the sport.
critics: Critics say the bill does not define what 'unavailable' means, leaving no clear standard for when the medal would go to a family member instead of O'Ree himself.
Critics say Congress did not include a cost estimate for producing the gold medal, which under existing law requires gold, silver, and bronze versions to be struck and distributed.

118-hr-1513.one_liner: Create a federal task force to study sixth-generation wireless technology
provisions: The FCC (the federal agency that oversees communications) must set up a group called the 6G Task Force.
The task force will include people from communications companies, public interest groups and universities, and federal, state, local, and tribal governments.
The task force will study the current state of 6G wireless technology and how standards for it are being set.
The task force will report on possible uses of 6G technology.

supporters: Supporters say the 6G Task Force would bring together communications companies, universities, and federal, state, local, and tribal governments to coordinate early planning for 6G technology before standards are locked in by other countries.
Supporters say requiring the FCC to study how 6G standards are being set gives the U.S. a chance to shape those standards rather than adopt rules set by foreign competitors.
Supporters say the task force's report on possible uses of 6G technology would help lawmakers and agencies make informed decisions before spending money on deployment.
critics: Critics say the bill only creates a study group and requires a report, but does not require the FCC or Congress to act on any findings, making it unlikely to produce real change in U.S. 6G policy.
Critics say limiting task force membership to 'trusted' companies and organizations gives the FCC broad power to exclude certain voices without defining what 'trusted' means in the law.
Critics say a task force reporting on technology that does not yet exist commercially may produce recommendations that are outdated by the time 6G standards are actually finalized.

118-hr-1398.one_liner: Restart a Justice Department program to investigate Chinese government spying
provisions: Brings back a DOJ program that was shut down in 2022, now called the CCP Initiative.
The program looks into spying, hacking, and theft of U.S. trade secrets tied to the Chinese Communist Party.
