It also watches for threats to U.S. power grids, water systems, and other key infrastructure.
DOJ must report to Congress once a year on what the program is doing and what problems it faces.
The program runs for six years and then automatically ends.

supporters: Supporters say bringing back the CCP Initiative will give DOJ a focused team to catch spying, hacking, and trade secret theft tied to the Chinese Communist Party, which the original China Initiative had been doing before it ended in 2022.

Supporters say the program protects U.S. power grids, water systems, and other key infrastructure from foreign threats, and the six-year time limit with yearly reports to Congress keeps the program accountable.
Supporters say the annual briefing requirement means Congress can track what the initiative is doing and cut it off if it stops working.
critics: Critics say the original China Initiative, which this bill brings back under a new name, led to wrongful prosecutions of Chinese-American researchers and academics who were later acquitted or had charges dropped.
Critics say the bill does not include rules to prevent racial or ethnic profiling, which civil rights groups argued was a problem with the first program before DOJ shut it down in 2022.
Critics say focusing a DOJ program specifically on one country's political party could sweep in people based on national origin rather than actual evidence of wrongdoing.

118-hr-1157.one_liner: Set up a fund to push back against Chinese government influence in the US and other countries
provisions: Creates a fund to pay for activities that push back against the Chinese government's efforts to gain power and control over other countries
Defines Chinese government influence as actions that help China gain control over other countries or hurt the security and independence of the US or its allies
Covers Chinese government efforts that threaten other countries' economies or governments

supporters: Supporters say the fund would give the U.S. government money and tools to push back when China tries to control other countries' governments or economies.

Supporters say the bill's definition of malign influence covers actions that hurt U.S. national security, economic security, or the independence of U.S. allies — giving agencies a clear target for their work.
Supporters say countering Chinese government efforts to build a rival world order protects the ability of smaller countries to make their own decisions.
critics: Critics say the bill does not name a specific dollar amount for the fund, making it hard to know how much will be spent or how Congress will oversee it.
Critics say the definition of 'malign influence' is broad enough to cover normal trade and diplomacy by China, which could pull the U.S. into conflicts that don't directly threaten American security.
Critics say the bill does not name which agencies will run the fund or what rules they must follow, leaving key decisions to the executive branch without clear limits.

118-hr-1103.one_liner: Require yearly reviews of whether Hong Kong's US offices can stay open
provisions: Hong Kong has three offices in the US that get special protections, like not being taken to court and not paying property taxes.
The President must check at least once a year whether those offices should keep those protections.
If the President decides the offices no longer deserve those protections, the offices must close within 180 days.
If the President decides the offices can stay open, Congress can still vote to overrule that decision.
US government agencies can only work with these offices if they are still approved to operate under this law.

supporters: Supporters say the yearly review gives Congress a way to check whether Hong Kong's three US offices still deserve special protections like immunity from lawsuits and no property taxes, since Hong Kong's status has changed under Chinese rule.
Supporters say the 180-day shutdown rule means the offices cannot keep operating with full legal protections if the President decides they no longer qualify, closing a gap in current law.
Supporters say the rule blocking US agencies from partnering with these offices — unless they are approved under this law — adds a clear accountability step that does not exist today.
critics: Critics say giving the President alone the power to certify each year whether these offices stay open puts too much control over a foreign policy decision in one person's hands, even though Congress can vote to overrule.
Critics say requiring the three Hong Kong offices to shut down within 180 days of a negative certification could cut off trade and business ties that US companies and Hong Kong businesses depend on.
Critics say the annual review process creates uncertainty for the offices and the people who work with them, making it harder to plan long-term agreements or partnerships with US government agencies.

118-hr-1425.one_liner: Require Senate approval before the U.S. joins any WHO pandemic treaty
provisions: Any pandemic agreement made through the World Health Organization must be approved by the U.S. Senate before it takes effect.
The Senate must vote to approve it like a treaty — it cannot take effect by presidential action alone.
This applies to any agreement made through a WHO group formed in December 2021 to work on pandemic rules.

supporters: Supporters say that requiring a Senate vote on any WHO pandemic agreement keeps the treaty power in Congress, where the Constitution puts it — not with the president alone.

Supporters say that the WHO group formed in December 2021 is writing rules that could affect how the U.S. responds to future outbreaks, and those rules should need approval from 67 senators before binding the country.
Supporters say that without this bill, a president could accept a WHO pandemic agreement without a Senate vote, bypassing the two-thirds approval that all other treaties require.
critics: Critics say that calling this WHO agreement a treaty under U.S. law could slow down the country's ability to work with other nations during a fast-moving outbreak, since Senate approval can take months or years.
Critics say the bill targets one specific WHO negotiating body — the one formed in December 2021 — but does not explain what happens to other international health agreements, creating uneven rules.
Critics say the U.S. already has tools to reject WHO agreements it does not like, so a separate law singling out pandemic deals is not needed.

118-hr-2789.one_liner: Require studies on fighting drug smuggling and expanding services in nearby countries
provisions: The State Department must send Congress a plan to work with Mexican states and cities to stop fentanyl and opioid smuggling.
The State Department must study whether space-based phone and internet technology could help Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean.
The State Department must review how to help people in Caribbean countries get better access to banks and financial services.

supporters: Supporters say the plan to work with Mexican states and cities on fentanyl and opioid smuggling could help cut off drug supply chains before they reach the U.S. border.
Supporters say the study on space-based phone and internet technology could help millions of people in Central America and the Caribbean get connected where ground-based networks do not reach.
Supporters say the review of banking access in the Caribbean could help people there send and receive money more safely, which can reduce poverty and reliance on informal financial systems.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires studies and reports, not any real action, so fentanyl trafficking and limited banking access may not actually improve.
Critics say the State Department already has programs in these areas, and adding more required reports could pull staff time away from work that is already underway.

Critics say the bill does not set deadlines, funding amounts, or clear goals, so Congress will have no way to measure whether the work on opioid trafficking or Caribbean financial access is making a difference.

118-hr-1631.one_liner: Let private groups keep copyright on technical standards written into law
provisions: Private organizations that write technical standards keep their copyright even when those standards become part of a law or government rule.
To keep copyright protection, the organization must post the standard for free on a public website so anyone can read it.
If someone argues that a standard has lost its copyright, that person must prove it — the burden is on them, not the organization.

supporters: Supporters say the bill solves a legal conflict by setting a clear rule: private organizations that write technical standards — like electrical or building codes — keep their copyright even after a government rule adopts those standards.

Supporters say the bill protects public access by requiring standards development organizations to post their full standards for free on a public website, so anyone can read the rules they are legally required to follow.

Supporters say this setup lets organizations keep funding the work of writing and updating safety standards, because they can still control commercial use of their work while giving the public free reading access.
critics: Critics say that when a government rule requires people to follow a private standard, that standard becomes part of the law — and letting a private organization hold copyright over the law means citizens cannot freely copy, print, or share the legal rules they must obey.

Critics say the bill shifts the burden of proof onto anyone who challenges a copyright claim, making it harder for small businesses, states, or the public to argue that a standard incorporated into law has entered the public domain.

Critics say free online reading access is not the same as full public use — organizations can still block people from reproducing or distributing the standards, even though compliance with those standards is legally required.

118-hr-5179.one_liner: Keep labeling rules for goods made in the West Bank and Gaza
provisions: Goods made in the West Bank or Gaza must carry labels showing where they were made
This labeling rule already exists, but this bill writes it into law so it is harder to remove
The State Department and U.S. Customs cannot spend any money to change or end this labeling rule

supporters: Supporters say the bill writes the existing West Bank and Gaza origin labeling rule into law, making it harder for the State Department or U.S. Customs to reverse or discontinue it without an act of Congress.

Supporters say the bill blocks the State Department and U.S. Customs from spending any funds to change or end the labeling rule, which they say protects consumers who want to know where imported goods come from.

Supporters say requiring clear origin labels on goods from the West Bank and Gaza gives American buyers and businesses specific information at the point of purchase that they currently rely on under existing policy.
critics: Critics say the bill targets goods from the West Bank and Gaza specifically, and that singling out these two areas — rather than applying a broader labeling standard — puts Palestinian producers at a trade disadvantage compared to other foreign exporters.

Critics say locking the labeling rule into statute and barring the State Department and U.S. Customs from using any funds to revisit it removes the executive branch's ability to adjust trade policy in response to changing conditions in the region.

Critics say the bill's title references the BDS movement but the text applies to all goods from the West Bank and Gaza, meaning it affects Palestinian producers regardless of whether they or their buyers have any connection to BDS.

118-hr-3724.one_liner: Change the rules colleges must follow to keep their accreditation
provisions: Colleges that have accreditation can receive federal student aid — this bill changes the rules accrediting groups must follow to stay recognized by the government.
Accrediting groups cannot require colleges to take sides on political or social issues in order to keep their accreditation.
Accrediting groups cannot require colleges to treat people differently based on sex, race, or ethnicity.
Accrediting groups cannot stop a college from having a religious mission, requiring a statement of faith, or setting a code of conduct for students and employees.
Accrediting groups cannot add new rules beyond what Congress has specifically approved.

supporters: Supporters say accrediting groups should not be able to force colleges to take political or social positions as a condition of keeping their accreditation, which affects access to federal student aid.
Supporters say the bill protects religious colleges by stopping accrediting groups from blocking schools from requiring a statement of faith or enforcing a code of conduct for students and employees.
Supporters say limiting accrediting groups to only the rules Congress has approved stops them from adding new requirements that were never voted on by elected officials.
critics: Critics say removing accreditor standards on how colleges treat people based on sex, race, or ethnicity could weaken civil rights protections at schools that receive federal student aid.

Critics say accrediting groups use broad standards to check education quality, and limiting them to only Congress-approved rules could make it harder to catch low-quality programs before students enroll.

Critics say the bill's rule against requiring colleges to avoid treating people differently by race or sex could conflict with existing federal civil rights laws that schools are already required to follow.

118-hr-1516.one_liner: Cut DHS funding to colleges with ties to Chinese government programs
provisions: Colleges that have contracts, deals, or received gifts from Chinese government-linked groups cannot get money from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
Confucius Institutes are cultural programs that get money from the Chinese government, directly or through other groups.
A college loses its DHS funding as long as it keeps that relationship.
A college can get its DHS funding back if it ends all ties with those groups.

supporters: Supporters say that colleges with contracts, deals, or gifts from Chinese government-linked groups should not receive DHS funding, because those ties could give the Chinese government access to U.S. security research.

Supporters say Confucius Institutes are funded by the Chinese government and operate on U.S. campuses, and cutting DHS dollars to schools that host them reduces that government's influence over American education.
Supporters say the bill gives colleges a clear path to keep their DHS funding by simply ending all ties with Chinese entities of concern or Confucius Institutes.
critics: Critics say the bill could cut DHS funding to colleges that received small in-kind gifts or donations from Chinese-linked groups, even if those gifts had nothing to do with security risks.
Critics say the bill does not define a dollar threshold or set a minimum level of relationship before a college loses all DHS funding, which could penalize schools for minor or outdated ties.
Critics say losing DHS funding could hurt U.S. students and researchers at those colleges who depend on DHS grants for programs unrelated to any Chinese government connection.

118-hr-7213.one_liner: Keep funding autism research, education, and tracking programs through 2029
provisions: Keeps funding a CDC program that tracks how many people have autism and studies its causes through 2029.
Keeps funding programs run by the Department of Health and Human Services that help with autism education, early detection, and early treatment through 2029.
Keeps a federal committee running through 2029 that coordinates autism research and policy across government agencies.

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps the CDC program running through 2029, which tracks how many people have autism and studies its causes — data that doctors and policymakers use to plan where to send resources.
Supporters say continuing HHS funding for early detection and early treatment through 2029 helps young children get services sooner, which research shows can improve long-term outcomes.
Supporters say keeping the Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee funded through 2029 stops federal agencies from duplicating each other's work on autism research and policy.
critics: Critics say the bill keeps money flowing to research on autism's causes through 2029 but does not add funding for services autistic adults need, like help with housing, employment, or daily living.
Critics say the Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee has no power to direct how money is spent across agencies, so coordination alone does not guarantee funds reach the highest-need programs.
Critics say reauthorizing the same programs through 2029 without expanding them does not keep pace with rising autism diagnosis rates, leaving gaps in education and intervention services.

118-hr-5339.one_liner: Require retirement plan managers to base investment choices only on financial risk and return
provisions: Managers of 401(k) and pension plans must choose investments based only on expected financial risk and return for workers.
Managers cannot use environmental, social, or other non-financial reasons when picking investments.
There is an exception: if two investment options look equal on financial grounds, a manager can use other factors to break the tie.
Workers who choose their own investments inside a retirement plan may still be offered options that use non-financial screens.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects retirement savings for 401(k) and pension holders by requiring plan managers to pick investments based only on expected financial risk and return, not on environmental or social goals.
Supporters say the current rules let fund managers use non-financial factors that could lower returns for workers, and this bill closes that gap by making financial performance the required standard.
Supporters say the bill still lets workers choose their own investment options, including funds that use non-financial screens, so individual choice is preserved.
critics: Critics say the bill would block pension and 401(k) managers from using environmental or climate-related financial data that affects long-term investment risk, even when that data is material to returns.
Critics say requiring managers to prove two options are financially equal before using other factors sets a nearly impossible standard, making the tie-breaker exception unusable in practice.
Critics say the bill limits how plan managers can respond to risks like stranded fossil fuel assets or governance failures, which can have real financial consequences for retirees.

118-hr-7152.one_liner: Create a registry of Korean American families separated from relatives in North Korea
provisions: The State Department builds a list of Korean American families who want to reconnect with family members living in North Korea.
The registry stores information about these families to help arrange future in-person reunions.
When the U.S. government holds talks with North Korea, it must push for progress on family reunions.
The State Department sends regular reports to Congress on the registry and on whether North Korea is moving toward allowing reunions.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would create a formal State Department registry of Korean American families who want to reconnect with relatives in North Korea, giving those families an official pathway that does not currently exist.

Supporters say requiring the State Department to raise family reunions in every round of U.S.-North Korea talks puts the issue on the agenda through a specific policy mandate, not through informal requests.
Supporters say the required reports to Congress will create a public record of how many families are registered and whether North Korea is taking steps toward allowing reunions.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include any funding or staffing for the State Department to build and maintain the registry, leaving the mandate without resources to carry it out.
Critics say adding a family reunion requirement to U.S.-North Korea talks could complicate ongoing diplomatic talks on other priorities such as nuclear negotiations.
Critics say North Korea has historically refused to engage on divided family issues with Korean Americans, so a registry and diplomatic mandate may produce no actual reunions.

118-hr-5441.one_liner: Keep EPA programs running to protect and restore Long Island Sound through 2028
provisions: Keeps EPA programs running through 2028 that work to protect and restore Long Island Sound.
Long Island Sound is a body of water off the coasts of New York and Connecticut where rivers meet the ocean.
Includes a grant program that gives money to local groups working to conserve the area.
Long Island Sound supports fishing, swimming, and recreation for communities across New York and Connecticut.

supporters: Supporters say keeping EPA programs funded through 2028 gives local groups in New York and Connecticut more time to restore Long Island Sound's water quality and fish populations.
Supporters say the stewardship grant program puts money directly into the hands of local organizations that protect the Sound, which supports fishing and recreation communities that depend on it.
critics: Critics say reauthorizing the program without setting specific cleanup targets or deadlines means EPA funding could continue without measurable progress in restoring the Sound.
Critics say the bill does not address how much money will actually be appropriated, leaving it unclear how many local groups will receive grants or how large those grants will be.

118-hr-7637.one_liner: Stop the Energy Department from setting stricter rules on refrigerator energy use
provisions: Stops the Department of Energy from making or enforcing new energy rules for refrigerators, freezer-refrigerators, and freezers unless three conditions are met.
The new rule must be possible to build with current technology.
The new rule must not cost consumers more money overall.
The new rule must save a meaningful amount of energy.

supporters: Supporters say the bill stops the DOE from setting new refrigerator rules unless those rules can be built with current technology and will not raise costs for consumers overall.
Supporters say the bill protects families from paying more for appliances by requiring that any new DOE energy standard must not add net costs to the consumer.
Supporters say the bill still allows DOE to act when a rule will save a meaningful amount of energy, so it does not block all new standards — only ones that fail the three required tests.
critics: Critics say the condition that a rule must not cost consumers more money could be used to block standards that have upfront costs but save money over years. The bill does not define how far into the future those savings must be counted.
Critics say removing DOE's ability to enforce refrigerator and freezer standards could slow progress on household appliance energy use, which makes up a large share of home electricity bills.
Critics say the bill adds three new legal hurdles that did not exist before, making it harder for DOE to update energy rules even when technology has improved.

118-hr-7700.one_liner: Restrict new dishwasher energy rules unless they are affordable, feasible, and save real energy
provisions: The Department of Energy can only set new energy rules for dishwashers if three tests are met.
The technology to meet the rule must already exist, and the rule must make economic sense.
The rule must not raise the total cost for buyers.
The rule must save a meaningful amount of energy.
The DOE also cannot enforce existing dishwasher energy rules that do not pass these three tests.

supporters: Supporters say the three-test requirement protects buyers by blocking DOE from setting rules that would raise the total cost of buying or running a dishwasher.
Supporters say requiring that the technology already exist before a rule is set prevents DOE from forcing manufacturers to meet standards that are not yet possible to build.
Supporters say blocking enforcement of existing rules that fail the three tests removes regulations that were already raising costs without proven energy savings.
critics: Critics say requiring that rules not raise net costs to buyers could let DOE block efficiency standards even when long-term energy savings would outweigh the upfront price increase.
Critics say the bill gives DOE no clear definition of what counts as a 'meaningful' amount of energy saved, which could be used to reject almost any new dishwasher standard.
Critics say removing enforcement of existing dishwasher energy rules could undo conservation gains already built into appliances now on the market.

118-hr-7887.one_liner: Remove degree and experience requirements from most federal contractor job bids
provisions: Right now, the government can ask contractors to hire workers with specific degrees or years of experience.
This bill removes that requirement from most federal contract bids.
An agency can still add those requirements to a bid.
But the person in charge of the contract must write down why the job cannot be done without them.
The Office of Management and Budget must send guidance to all federal agencies within 60 days of this bill becoming law.
That guidance will explain how to follow the new rules.

supporters: Supporters say the bill opens federal contract jobs to more workers by removing degree and experience requirements as the default in government bids, so agencies can no longer screen out candidates without a reason.
Supporters say requiring a contracting officer to write down why a job cannot be done without specific credentials stops those requirements from being added to bids without a clear justification.

Supporters say the 60-day deadline for the Office of Management and Budget to send guidance means all federal agencies will get clear instructions quickly instead of applying the new rules inconsistently.
critics: Critics say removing degree and experience requirements as the default could lead to unqualified workers being placed on technical federal contracts where mistakes have real costs.
Critics say the bill does not define what a written justification must include, so contracting officers across different agencies may set very different standards for when requirements are allowed.
Critics say the 60-day window for OMB to issue guidance may not give agencies enough time to train contracting staff before they must begin following the new rules.

118-hr-7909.one_liner: Make sex crimes and domestic violence grounds to deport or block non-citizens from entering
provisions: Non-citizens who admit to or are convicted of domestic violence, sex crimes, or planning a sex crime can be blocked from entering the US.
Current law lets the government deport non-citizens for domestic violence, stalking, and child abuse. This bill adds sex offenses — including crimes against children — to that list.
Non-citizens convicted of planning a sex offense can also be deported.
The bill expands what counts as domestic violence for deportation — it now includes physical or sexual abuse, or a pattern of controlling behavior, within close relationships like marriage or dating.

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a gap in current law by adding sex offenses — including crimes against children — to the list of crimes that make a non-citizen deportable, since current law only covers domestic violence, stalking, and child abuse.
Supporters say blocking non-citizens who have admitted to or been convicted of sex crimes or domestic violence from entering the US protects potential future victims before harm occurs.

Supporters say expanding the definition of domestic violence to include a pattern of controlling behavior — not just physical assault — means more abuse victims in marriages or dating relationships will have legal protection.
critics: Critics say the bill allows the government to bar or deport non-citizens based on an admission to a crime — not just a conviction — which removes the right to have guilt decided in a court before facing immigration consequences.

Critics say non-citizen victims of domestic violence may be less likely to report abuse to police if they fear their immigration status could be affected, since the bill does not include protections for victims who are undocumented.

Critics say the term 'pattern of coercive behavior' in the expanded domestic violence definition is not precisely defined in the bill, which could lead to uneven enforcement depending on who is reviewing a case.

118-hr-8281.one_liner: Require proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections
provisions: People must show a document proving U.S. citizenship — like a passport or birth certificate — when they sign up to vote in federal elections.
States cannot process a voter registration form for federal elections unless the person hands over that citizenship document.
States must set up a backup process for people who want to prove citizenship but do not have the standard documents.
States must check their voter rolls on an ongoing basis and remove anyone who is not a U.S. citizen.
Anyone can take an election official to court if that official signs up a voter who did not show citizenship proof.
Election officials who register someone without seeing citizenship proof can face criminal charges.
The federal agency that helps states run elections must send states instructions for following this law within 10 days.

supporters: Supporters say requiring a passport or birth certificate to register to vote ensures that only U.S. citizens can vote in federal elections, since noncitizens are not legally allowed to vote.
Supporters say the ongoing removal of noncitizens from voter rolls gives states a clear process to keep their voter registration lists accurate.
Supporters say allowing anyone to sue an election official who registers a voter without seeing citizenship proof creates accountability and a way for citizens to enforce the law.
critics: Critics say many eligible U.S. citizens do not have easy access to a passport or birth certificate, which could prevent them from registering to vote in federal elections.
Critics say the backup process for people without standard documents is not clearly defined, which may leave some legal citizens unable to register even if they can prove citizenship another way.
Critics say criminal penalties for election officials who make registration errors could discourage people from working as election officials, making it harder for states to run elections.

118-hr-7980.one_liner: Block EV tax credits for cars with parts from companies tied to China or adversary nations
provisions: Cars with parts made or processed by companies tied to China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea lose the EV tax credit.
This applies to the new clean vehicle tax credit created in 2022, not older EV incentives.
Companies linked to terrorist groups are also covered by this rule.
Buyers of affected vehicles would no longer qualify for the credit, which is worth up to $7,500.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would remove the $7,500 new clean vehicle tax credit from any car that uses parts made or processed by companies tied to China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea.
Supporters say the bill also blocks the credit for vehicles with supply chains connected to terrorist organizations, so no federal tax incentive flows to those sources.
Supporters say tying the 2022 clean vehicle tax credit to these supply chain rules gives automakers a financial reason to source EV parts from countries not on the excluded list.
critics: Critics say the bill would remove the $7,500 credit from vehicles using battery parts processed in China, which could limit the number of EV models that buyers can apply the credit toward.

Critics say the bill does not specify how closely a company must be linked to China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea to disqualify a vehicle, which could make it unclear to buyers whether their car qualifies.
Critics say shifting supply chains away from the four excluded countries could raise vehicle prices and further reduce the pool of EVs that qualify for the $7,500 credit.

118-hr-8752.one_liner: Fund the Department of Homeland Security for the year starting October 2024
provisions: Gives money to the agencies that check people and goods entering the United States at the border.
Funds the agency that screens passengers and bags at airports across the country.
Gives money to FEMA, the agency that sends help after hurricanes, floods, and other disasters.
Funds the agency that enforces immigration laws inside the United States.
Gives money to the Coast Guard, which patrols U.S. waters and responds to emergencies at sea.
Funds the Secret Service, which protects the President and other government leaders.
Gives money to the agency that protects government computer systems from outside attacks.

supporters: Supporters say the bill funds Customs and Border Protection and ICE, which check people entering the country and enforce immigration laws, helping control who crosses U.S. borders.
Supporters say giving money to FEMA means the agency can respond faster after hurricanes and floods, getting help to people in disaster zones.
Supporters say funding the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency protects government computer systems from attacks by other countries or criminal groups.
critics: Critics say the bill gives money to ICE, which enforces immigration laws inside the U.S., and some groups say ICE's actions break up families and target people who have lived here for years.
Critics say funding TSA and border agencies at current levels is not enough to fix long wait times at airports and ports of entry, where staffing shortages have been reported.

Critics say the bill does not include enough detail about how DHS must spend the money, which makes it hard for Congress to track whether agencies like the Secret Service and Coast Guard are using funds well.

118-hr-8314.one_liner: Fine nonprofits that take foreign money and then donate to political campaigns
provisions: If a nonprofit receives foreign money and then donates to a political campaign, it is fined.
The fine is 200% of the donation — meaning the group pays back double what it gave.
A nonprofit that does this more than twice loses its tax-exempt status.
Tax-exempt status means the group does not pay federal taxes — the bill removes that status after a third violation.

supporters: Supporters say the 200% fine — meaning a group pays back double what it donated — gives nonprofits a strong reason not to pass foreign money into U.S. elections.
Supporters say the rule targets a real gap in election law, where a foreign national could give money to a tax-exempt group, which then donates to a political committee.
Supporters say losing tax-exempt status after a third violation puts serious pressure on nonprofits to track where their money comes from before making political donations.
critics: Critics say the bill does not define how closely a foreign contribution must be linked to a political donation, which could punish nonprofits that received foreign funds long before making any political gift.

Critics say small nonprofits that rely on international donors — such as global religious or humanitarian groups — could lose their tax-exempt status over bookkeeping mistakes, not intentional wrongdoing.
Critics say the 200% penalty applies even if a nonprofit did not know the foreign money and the political donation were connected, leaving groups open to large fines without proof of intent.

118-hr-8772.one_liner: Fund Congress and its support offices for the year starting October 2024
provisions: Gives money to pay for running the House of Representatives and offices that help lawmakers do their jobs
Pays for the Capitol Police, who protect Congress and the people and buildings around it
Funds the Congressional Budget Office, which figures out how much bills would cost before Congress votes on them
Funds the Library of Congress, which includes a research service that answers policy questions for lawmakers and a copyright office that protects creative work
Funds the Government Accountability Office, which checks whether the government is spending money the way it was supposed to
Sets rules for what the money in this bill can and cannot be used for
Does not include money for the Senate — the Senate sets its own budget separately

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps the Congressional Budget Office funded, so lawmakers can see how much every bill costs before they vote on it.
Supporters say the bill funds the Government Accountability Office, which checks whether agencies spend money the way Congress intended and flags waste before it grows.
Supporters say paying for the Capitol Police through this bill keeps Congress, its staff, and the public buildings around it protected every day.
critics: Critics say the bill sends money to the Congressional Office for International Leadership Fund and the John C. Stennis Center, which are not core lawmaking functions — they argue those funds should go to oversight offices instead.

Critics say the bill sets rules on what the money can and cannot be used for, but does not require offices like the Library of Congress or the Stennis Center to report back on whether they followed those rules, leaving compliance unchecked.
Critics say leaving Senate funding out of this bill splits the full cost of running Congress across two separate bills, making total legislative spending harder to track in one place.

118-hr-8333.one_liner: Block federal funds from going to groups that use biotech from foreign adversary companies
provisions: Groups that get federal money cannot buy or use biotech equipment or services from companies linked to foreign adversaries like China.
The government must create a list of banned biotech companies; five specific companies are already named in the bill.
Any group that has a contract with a banned company also cannot receive federal funds.
The government can approve exceptions that last up to one year, with one possible extension of 180 days.
U.S. intelligence must write a report on the security risks of foreign companies collecting DNA and other body data through biotech tools.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects national security by stopping any group that gets federal money from buying biotech equipment or services from companies linked to foreign adversaries, including five specific companies already named in the bill.
Supporters say foreign companies collecting DNA and other body data through biotech tools pose a real risk, and the required intelligence report will show how serious that risk is.
Supporters say cutting off federal funds from any contractor that works with a banned company closes a loophole that could let foreign-linked firms get around the rules.
critics: Critics say the five companies named in the bill supply lab equipment and DNA sequencing tools used by hundreds of U.S. hospitals and research institutions, and those groups may not be able to find replacement equipment before the ban takes effect.

Critics say the waiver process — which allows exceptions for only up to one year plus a 180-day extension — is too short for large research centers to switch out complex biotech systems without disrupting ongoing medical studies.

Critics say cutting federal funds from any contractor that does business with a banned company could pull money from universities and hospitals that had no direct role in the security concern the bill is trying to address.

118-hr-8771.one_liner: Fund the State Department and U.S. foreign programs for 2025
provisions: Gives the State Department money to run U.S. embassies and diplomatic offices around the world for the year starting October 2024.
Funds USAID, the government agency that sends development money and aid to other countries on behalf of the U.S.
Pays for the Peace Corps, which sends American volunteers to work in communities in other countries.
Funds the Export-Import Bank and other agencies that help U.S. companies sell goods and services to foreign buyers.
Pays for security programs that send military and economic help to other countries.
Funds commissions that track issues like religious freedom abroad and U.S. relations with China.

supporters: Supporters say funding USAID and the Peace Corps keeps the U.S. present in other countries, which can stop problems like disease outbreaks and instability before they reach American borders.
Supporters say the Export-Import Bank and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation help U.S. companies win contracts in foreign markets, which supports American jobs.
Supporters say commissions that track religious freedom abroad and U.S.-China relations give Congress regular reports based on on-the-ground monitoring, not government agency self-reporting.
critics: Critics say the National Endowment for Democracy and the U.S. Agency for Global Media receive funding through this bill to operate in other countries, which critics call interference in foreign governments' internal affairs.

Critics say security assistance programs that send military and economic help to other countries direct billions of dollars outside U.S. borders each fiscal year, money critics say should stay in the U.S.
Critics say funding the U.S. Institute of Peace and the East-West Center adds to the overall foreign operations budget without a clear measure of what results those programs produce.

118-hr-8997.one_liner: Fund energy, water, and nuclear programs for the year starting October 2024
provisions: Gives money to the Army Corps of Engineers to build and maintain rivers, harbors, and flood control systems across the country
Funds the Bureau of Reclamation, which runs water supply and dam projects mostly in western states
Pays for Department of Energy programs covering nuclear power, renewable energy, electricity grid work, and fossil fuels
Funds cleanup of radioactive waste and old nuclear sites that are no longer in use
Pays to maintain the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, a government stockpile of oil held for national emergencies
Funds nuclear weapons and defense programs run by the National Nuclear Security Administration
Pays the budgets of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission

supporters: Supporters say the bill funds Army Corps of Engineers construction and maintenance of flood control systems along rivers like the Mississippi, which helps protect homes and farms in flood-prone areas from water damage.
Supporters say Bureau of Reclamation funding pays for water supply and dam projects in western states, where cities and farms rely on federal water systems to meet basic needs during dry years.
Supporters say keeping the Strategic Petroleum Reserve funded ensures the U.S. has a stored supply of oil it can release during emergencies or major supply shortages.
critics: Critics say the bill continues funding the Fossil Energy and Carbon Management program, which directs money toward fossil fuel research instead of shifting those dollars fully to renewable energy sources.

Critics say funding for the National Nuclear Security Administration's nuclear weapons programs increases spending on the U.S. nuclear arsenal, which some groups say should be reduced rather than maintained.

Critics say the Non-Defense Environmental Cleanup program, which pays to clean up radioactive waste at old nuclear sites, has fallen behind schedule in past years, and this bill may not provide enough funding to finish the work.

118-hr-8812.one_liner: Fund and update Army Corps of Engineers water and flood projects across the country
provisions: Approves new Army Corps of Engineers projects to improve rivers, ports, and harbors so ships can move through them more easily
Funds projects to reduce flood damage in communities near rivers and coasts
Pays for work to restore wetlands, fish habitats, and other water ecosystems
Supports building and fixing water supply systems, dams, and wastewater infrastructure
Cancels approval for some older water projects that were never built

supporters: Supporters say the bill funds Army Corps of Engineers work to improve rivers, ports, and harbors, which helps cargo ships move goods more efficiently and supports jobs tied to water transport.
Supporters say the bill pays for flood damage reduction projects in communities near rivers and coasts, which can protect homes and businesses from storm and flood losses.
Supporters say the bill funds restoration of wetlands and fish habitats, which benefits fishing industries and communities that rely on healthy water ecosystems.
critics: Critics say the bill approves a large number of new Army Corps projects — covering rivers, ports, dams, and wastewater systems — without a clear total cost, making it hard for Congress to weigh the full spending commitment.

Critics say some of the water infrastructure projects in the bill require local governments to share costs, which may put financial pressure on smaller communities that lack the budget to pay their share.
Critics say canceling older, never-built projects only after years of planning means federal dollars spent on those studies were wasted with nothing built to show for it.

118-hr-897.one_liner: Make an underwater cypress forest in the Gulf of Mexico a protected federal sanctuary
provisions: Makes an underwater cypress forest in the Gulf of Mexico off the Alabama coast a federally protected sanctuary.
Cutting, removing, or digging up any of the cypress trees in the sanctuary becomes illegal.
Using dredging equipment, drills, explosives, or laying cables on the seafloor in the sanctuary becomes illegal.
Fishing, diving, mooring, and other recreational or commercial water activities are still allowed in the sanctuary.
Building artificial reefs to improve fishing or diving in the area is still allowed.
Oil and gas projects that were approved before this bill passes can continue operating in the sanctuary.
The federal ocean agency (NOAA) must create a full management plan and set up an advisory council for the sanctuary.

supporters: Supporters say protecting the ancient cypress forest — which researchers estimate is over 60,000 years old — from cutting, dredging, and drilling will preserve a rare underwater ecosystem that cannot be rebuilt once damaged.

Supporters say fishing, diving, and mooring are still allowed under the bill, so local fishing businesses and tourism operators near the Alabama coast can keep working in the area without interruption.
Supporters say requiring NOAA to create a management plan and advisory council will give local communities a formal voice in how the sanctuary is run.
critics: Critics say allowing oil and gas projects approved before the bill passes to keep operating inside the sanctuary could still damage the cypress trees and seafloor that the bill is meant to protect.

Critics say adding a new federally managed sanctuary with a required management plan and advisory council creates new government costs and rules that fall on NOAA without a clear funding source named in the bill.

118-hr-8774.one_liner: Fund the U.S. military for the year starting October 2024
provisions: Pays the salaries and benefits for active-duty troops across all military branches
Covers day-to-day costs of running the military, like fuel, repairs, and training exercises
Buys new weapons, vehicles, aircraft, and other equipment for the military
Funds research to develop new weapons, technology, and defense systems
Pays for health care for troops and their families through the military's health program
Funds military efforts to stop illegal drugs from entering the country
Funds retirement and disability payments for CIA workers

supporters: Supporters say this bill pays the salaries and benefits of all active-duty troops across every military branch, keeping the armed forces fully staffed.
Supporters say the bill funds health care for troops and their families through the Defense Health Program, making sure service members do not lose medical coverage.
Supporters say the bill pays for new weapons, aircraft, and vehicles and funds research into new defense technology, which they say keeps the U.S. military ready to respond to threats.
critics: Critics say the bill continues to fund drug interdiction programs under the Defense Department that have run for decades without proof that they have cut the flow of illegal drugs into the country.
Critics say paying for CIA retirement and disability benefits through a separate intelligence account reduces the level of public oversight that applies to other federal retirement programs.
Critics say the bill adds new procurement spending on weapons and equipment while basic operating costs like fuel, repairs, and training already consume a large share of the defense budget.

118-hr-8998.one_liner: Fund national parks, the EPA, tribal programs, and the arts for 2025
provisions: Gives money to the National Park Service, which runs more than 400 parks and historic sites across the country, to keep them staffed and open.
Funds the Environmental Protection Agency to keep running programs that set rules for air and water quality.
Gives money to the Bureau of Indian Affairs and Bureau of Indian Education, which run services and schools for Native American tribes.
Funds the Indian Health Service, which provides healthcare to about 2.6 million Native Americans and Alaska Natives.
Gives money to arts and culture organizations including the Smithsonian Institution, the Kennedy Center, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the National Endowment for the Humanities.
Includes a rule that lets the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians buy back land that was historically theirs.
Sets rules for how all of the money in this bill can and cannot be spent.

supporters: Supporters say this bill funds the Indian Health Service, which provides medical care to about 2.6 million Native Americans and Alaska Natives — a group with higher rates of chronic illness and less access to private health insurance than most Americans.

Supporters say the bill gives money to the Bureau of Indian Affairs and Bureau of Indian Education, which run schools and services for Native American tribes that depend on federal funding because they do not have a state tax base to draw from.
Supporters say a rule in this bill lets the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians buy back land that was historically theirs, without requiring new federal spending beyond what the bill already provides.
critics: Critics say this bill keeps EPA funding for Clean Water Act programs that require farms, ranches, and small manufacturers to meet water quality rules — requirements those groups say cost individual operations tens of thousands of dollars each year in permits and equipment.

Critics say the bill sends federal money to the Kennedy Center, the Smithsonian Institution, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the National Endowment for the Humanities — groups that together receive hundreds of millions of dollars in taxpayer funds each year that critics say private donors and ticket sales should cover instead.

Critics say the bill bundles two separate laws — H.R. 548, which gives the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians the right to reacquire historic lands, and the America's Wildlife Habitat Conservation Act — into one spending bill, forcing members to vote on unrelated land and wildlife policies at the same time as annual agency budgets.

118-hres-1316.one_liner: Allow the House to vote on spending bills for Defense, State, and Homeland Security
provisions: Lets the full House vote on a spending bill for the Department of Defense for the year ending September 30, 2025
Lets the full House vote on a spending bill for the Department of State and foreign aid programs for the year ending September 30, 2025
Lets the full House vote on a spending bill for the Department of Homeland Security for the year ending September 30, 2025

supporters: Supporters say this resolution allows the full House to vote on the Department of Defense spending bill for FY2025, keeping military funding on schedule before the September 30, 2025 deadline.
Supporters say bringing all three bills — covering Defense, the State Department, and Homeland Security — to the floor moves the annual budget process forward and avoids a government funding gap.
Supporters say the resolution gives the full House a direct say in setting foreign aid and border security funding levels for the year ending September 30, 2025.
critics: Critics say packaging consideration of three major spending bills — for Defense, State, and Homeland Security — under one rule limits the time members have to debate each bill on its own.

Critics say the rule controls how the House considers the Department of Homeland Security spending bill, which may restrict members from offering changes to border and immigration enforcement funding.

Critics say moving the State Department and foreign operations spending bill under this rule speeds up a vote on foreign aid levels before members have fully reviewed what programs and countries receive funding.

118-hr-9456.one_liner: Require security reviews when people from China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea buy U.S. farmland
provisions: When a person from China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea tries to buy U.S. farmland, USDA must report that deal to a national security committee.
That committee, called CFIUS, decides if the deal is a security risk and whether to do a full review.
CFIUS can block or set conditions on a deal if it finds the purchase puts national security at risk.
The U.S. Secretary of Agriculture gets a seat on CFIUS when deals involve farmland, farm technology, or farm businesses.
This rule also covers farm storage, transportation, and food processing businesses, not just land.

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires USDA to report any farmland purchase by buyers from China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea to CFIUS, giving the government a clear process to catch deals that could threaten the U.S. food supply.

Supporters say adding the Secretary of Agriculture to CFIUS means farm experts will have a direct vote on whether deals involving farmland, farm storage, transportation, and food processing put national security at risk.

Supporters say the bill closes a gap by covering not just land purchases but also farm tech, food processing, and storage businesses, so foreign adversaries cannot gain control of U.S. agriculture through those back doors.
critics: Critics say the bill only targets buyers from four countries — China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea — and does not require CFIUS reviews for farmland deals involving buyers from other countries that may also pose risks.
Critics say adding a new USDA referral step before CFIUS can act may slow down routine farmland sales and create delays even for deals that end up having no connection to national security.
Critics say foreign buyers from the four listed countries could use shell companies based in other nations to avoid triggering the USDA reporting requirement, making the rule easy to get around.

118-hres-1341.one_liner: Schedule House votes on voter ID, school sex discrimination, and appliance energy rules
provisions: Lets the House vote on a bill that would require people to show proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote in federal elections.
Lets the House vote on a measure that would cancel a Department of Education rule on sex discrimination in schools and colleges that get federal money.
Lets the House vote on a spending bill that funds the U.S. Congress for the year ending September 2025.
Lets the House vote on a bill that would stop the Department of Energy from setting energy rules for dishwashers.
Lets the House vote on a bill that would stop the Department of Energy from setting energy rules for refrigerators and freezers.

supporters: Supporters say requiring proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections, as H.R. 8281 would do, ensures that only citizens cast votes in those races.

Supporters say canceling the Department of Education's sex discrimination rule under H.J. Res. 165 would stop schools and colleges that get federal money from having to follow rules they say go beyond what Congress passed.

Supporters say blocking the Department of Energy from setting energy standards for dishwashers, refrigerators, and freezers lets manufacturers make products without rules that the bills say may not be cost-effective or technically possible.
critics: Critics say the citizenship proof requirement in H.R. 8281 could block U.S. citizens who do not have documents like a passport or birth certificate from being able to register to vote in federal elections.

Critics say canceling the Department of Education's nondiscrimination rule through H.J. Res. 165 removes sex discrimination protections for students in schools and colleges that receive federal financial assistance.

Critics say removing the Department of Energy's power to set energy rules for dishwashers, refrigerators, and freezers could lead to appliances that use more energy and cost households more money over time.

118-hr-9076.one_liner: Keep funding for child welfare and foster care programs running through 2029
provisions: Keeps money flowing to child welfare programs through September 2029
Requires 3 out of every 100 dollars in child welfare funding to go directly to Native American tribes
Lets foster youth who are 18 or older choose to have caseworker visits done over video call instead of in person
Creates grants for states to test new ways to help foster children stay connected to a parent who is in prison
Requires the government to look at how much time state child welfare workers spend on paperwork and find ways to reduce it
Keeps funding running for a program that helps courts handle child welfare cases, including through video hearings
Requires a report on what services are available to families after a child is adopted or placed with a guardian

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps money flowing to child welfare programs like Stephanie Tubbs Jones Child Welfare Services through September 2029, so states do not face funding gaps that could cut services to children already in the system.

Supporters say requiring 3 out of every 100 dollars in child welfare funding to go directly to Native American tribes helps close a gap, since Native children are placed in foster care at higher rates than other groups.
Supporters say reducing the time caseworkers spend on paperwork — and allowing foster youth over 18 to choose video call visits — frees up staff to spend more time directly helping children.
critics: Critics say the bill only extends funding through 2029, which means Congress will need to act again in a few years, and programs could still face cuts or gaps if lawmakers miss that deadline.

Critics say allowing video calls to replace in-person visits for foster youth over 18, even when those youth choose it, may make it harder for caseworkers to spot signs of abuse or unsafe living conditions.
Critics say the 3% tribal funding set-aside is too small given that Native American children make up a much larger share of foster care cases than their share of the overall child population.

118-hr-9494.one_liner: Fund the government through March 2025 and require proof of citizenship to vote
provisions: The bill keeps the federal government funded at 2024 spending levels through March 28, 2025.
It stops a government shutdown that would have started on October 1, 2024.
It sends extra money to FEMA's disaster relief fund for people affected by natural disasters.
It sends extra money to the Navy's Virginia Class Submarine building program.
It keeps the National Flood Insurance Program running so homeowners can still buy flood insurance.
It extends farm livestock price reporting, federal timber sale rules, and the military's ability to fund certain building projects through March 2025.
Anyone registering to vote in a federal election must now show documents proving U.S. citizenship.

supporters: Supporters say the bill stops a government shutdown that would have started October 1, 2024, keeping federal agencies open and workers paid through March 28, 2025.

Supporters say the bill sends extra money to FEMA's Disaster Relief Fund to help people hurt by natural disasters, and keeps the National Flood Insurance Program running so homeowners can still buy flood coverage.
Supporters say the new rule requiring documents that prove U.S. citizenship to register for federal elections makes sure only eligible citizens can sign up to vote.
critics: Critics say the citizenship document requirement could block millions of eligible U.S. citizens who do not have easy access to a passport or birth certificate, making it harder for them to register to vote in federal elections.
Critics say the bill only funds the government through March 28, 2025, which delays real budget decisions and sets up another possible shutdown fight just a few months later.
Critics say adding extra money for the Navy's Virginia Class Submarine program inside a short-term spending bill skips the normal budget review process that Congress uses to check military spending.

118-hres-1367.one_liner: Create a House task force to investigate the July 2024 Trump assassination attempt
provisions: Sets up a group of up to 11 House members to look into the July 13, 2024 shooting in Butler, Pennsylvania
Up to 5 of the 11 members are picked with input from the minority party leader
The task force can take sworn statements and issue legal orders to get documents and testimony
All relevant House committee records must be handed over within 7 days
The task force must release a final report by December 13, 2024
The report must include steps Congress could take to stop future security failures

supporters: Supporters say the task force's power to issue subpoenas and take sworn statements will force federal agencies, state law enforcement, and private groups to hand over documents they might otherwise withhold about the July 13, 2024 shooting in Butler, Pennsylvania.

Supporters say the December 13, 2024 deadline for a final report will produce a fast, public record of what went wrong with Secret Service and local security — and require Congress to propose specific fixes.
Supporters say requiring all relevant House committee records to be transferred within 7 days prevents agencies from slow-walking the investigation.
critics: Critics say only up to 5 of the 11 task force members are chosen with input from the minority leader, which means the majority party controls at least 6 seats and can shape what the investigation focuses on.

Critics say the December 13, 2024 deadline gives the task force less than 5 months to investigate actions by federal agencies, multiple state and local governments, and private individuals — which may not be enough time to get full answers.
Critics say the resolution does not set rules for how evidence must be reviewed or how members with potential conflicts of interest must be handled, which could affect the fairness of findings.

118-hres-1370.one_liner: Set debate rules for two spending bills covering energy, water, and the environment
provisions: This rule allows the House to debate and vote on two separate spending bills.
The first bill covers money for energy and water programs for the year ending September 30, 2025.
The second bill covers money for the Department of the Interior and environment programs for the same year.
The rule sets limits on how long House members can speak during debate on each bill.
The rule controls which changes members are allowed to propose to each bill during debate.

supporters: Supporters say the rule allows the House to debate and vote on H.R. 8997 and H.R. 8998 before the September 30, 2025 deadline, which helps prevent a funding gap for energy, water, and environment programs.

Supporters say the debate time limits in the rule allow both spending bills to move through the floor quickly, so the Department of the Interior and energy agencies can receive their FY2025 funding on time.
Supporters say the amendment controls keep debate focused on the actual spending decisions in H.R. 8997 and H.R. 8998, rather than unrelated policy additions.
critics: Critics say the rule limits which amendments members can offer to H.R. 8997 and H.R. 8998, blocking some lawmakers from proposing changes to funding levels for energy programs or environmental agencies.
Critics say the debate time limits the rule sets do not give members enough time to fully discuss the spending decisions for the Department of the Interior and its related programs.

Critics say handling two separate spending bills — energy and water under H.R. 8997 and Interior and environment under H.R. 8998 — under one rule makes it harder for members to raise concerns about each bill on its own.

118-hres-1371.one_liner: Put Congress on record condemning Biden Administration border policies
provisions: Congress formally states its disapproval of how the Biden Administration handled the southern border.
The resolution names Kamala Harris as the person in the Biden Administration responsible for border security.
This is a statement only — it does not change any laws, rules, or spending.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution formally puts Congress on record opposing how the Biden Administration managed the southern border, using its power to issue official statements of disapproval.
Supporters say the provision naming Kamala Harris as the official responsible for border security holds a specific person accountable by name in the congressional record.
Supporters say even though the resolution does not change any laws or spending, it signals to the public and other officials that Congress believes border policy failed.
critics: Critics say the resolution does not change any laws, rules, or spending, meaning it cannot stop or reverse any of the border policies it objects to.
Critics say the provision that singles out Kamala Harris by name, rather than pointing to specific border numbers or policy failures, makes the statement more about a person than a policy.
Critics say a formal condemnation with no legal effect uses congressional time without producing any change in how the border is actually managed.

118-hres-1376.one_liner: Let the House debate a resolution about Biden's border record
provisions: This resolution sets the rules for bringing H. Res. 1371 to a vote on the House floor.
H. Res. 1371 condemns how the Biden administration handled the U.S. southern border.
This bill does not change any law, create any program, or spend any money.
It is a procedural step that controls how long the House can debate the resolution and whether changes to it are allowed.

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the House to hold a formal, on-the-record vote on H. Res. 1371, which condemns the Biden administration's handling of the southern border.
Supporters say the rule limits debate time, which prevents the vote from being delayed or talked out of consideration on the House floor.
Supporters say forcing a recorded vote makes members publicly accountable for where they stand on border policy.
critics: Critics say this resolution does not change any law, create any program, or spend any money. They argue it is a political statement rather than a real policy action.
Critics say the time used to debate H. Res. 1371 under this rule could instead be spent on bills that would actually change border enforcement or funding.
Critics say the resolution names specific officials, including Kamala Harris as 'Border Czar,' in a way that is meant to score political points rather than address specific border policies.

118-hres-1344.one_liner: Declare the Attorney General in contempt of Congress for ignoring a subpoena
provisions: The House of Representatives voted to find Attorney General Merrick Garland in contempt of Congress.
Contempt of Congress means Garland did not comply with a legal order from the House to hand over documents.
The legal order — called a subpoena — was connected to a House investigation.
After a contempt vote, Congress can send the case to the Justice Department to decide whether to bring criminal charges.
The vote itself does not immediately remove or penalize Garland from his position.

supporters: Supporters say Garland broke the law by ignoring a legal subpoena from the House, which ordered him to hand over documents tied to a House investigation.
Supporters say the contempt vote sends the case to the Justice Department, which can then decide whether to bring criminal charges against Garland.
Supporters say letting the Attorney General ignore a subpoena sets a bad example and weakens the House's ability to get documents during investigations.
critics: Critics say the Justice Department — which Garland leads — would have to decide whether to charge him, which creates a conflict of interest and makes real punishment unlikely.
Critics say the contempt vote does not remove Garland from office or penalize him right away, so the action has limited practical effect.
Critics say some documents Garland withheld may be protected under executive privilege, meaning there could be a legal reason he did not fully comply with the subpoena.

118-s-1146.one_liner: Require federal help to states for finding and protecting missing foster kids
provisions: The Children's Bureau must give states and tribes information and tools to find children who go missing from foster care.
The bureau must review how states and tribes track missing foster children and identify what works best.
The bureau must help states screen children who were missing and returned to foster care for signs of sex trafficking.
Children already in foster care who are at risk of sex trafficking must also be assessed under this bill.

supporters: Supporters say the Children's Bureau will review how every state and tribe tracks missing foster children and share what works best, which could help locate children faster.
Supporters say the bill requires workers to screen children who went missing from foster care and came back for signs of sex trafficking, directly targeting a group at high risk.
Supporters say foster children who are already in care and at risk of sex trafficking will also be assessed under this bill, not just children who went missing.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include any dedicated funding to pay states and tribes for the new screenings and assessments it requires them to carry out.
Critics say requiring the Children's Bureau to review state and tribal tracking systems adds federal oversight of child welfare programs that states currently manage on their own.
Critics say sharing information and best practices without direct resources may not be enough to change outcomes for foster children at risk of sex trafficking.

118-hres-901.one_liner: Express US support for democracy and human rights in Pakistan
provisions: The US government states it supports free and fair elections in Pakistan
The resolution calls on the President to work with Pakistan on democracy and human rights
It calls on Pakistan to protect democratic institutions and the rule of law

supporters: Supporters say the resolution puts the US on record backing free and fair elections in Pakistan, which signals to Pakistani officials that the US is watching how votes are run.
Supporters say calling on the President to work with Pakistan on human rights gives the executive branch a clear direction from Congress on how to handle that relationship.
Supporters say urging Pakistan to protect democratic institutions sends a message to groups inside Pakistan that the US stands behind civilian rule and the rule of law.
critics: Critics say the resolution has no legal force and no funding attached, so it does not require Pakistan or the President to take any specific action.
Critics say calling on a foreign government to uphold democratic institutions through a non-binding resolution puts no real pressure on Pakistani officials to change how they govern.
Critics say the resolution does not name specific human rights violations or affected groups in Pakistan, so it is unclear what concrete change it is asking for.

118-s-227.one_liner: Add two cities to the list of places where federal courts must hold sessions
provisions: Courts in the Pecos Division of the Western District of Texas must now hold sessions in Alpine, Texas.
Courts in the Western District of Washington must now hold sessions in Mount Vernon, Washington.
People in those areas can now go to a federal court closer to home instead of traveling to a more distant city.

supporters: Supporters say adding Alpine to the Pecos Division of the Western District of Texas means residents in far west Texas no longer have to travel to a distant federal courthouse, which can be several hours away.

Supporters say adding Mount Vernon to the Western District of Washington gives people in Skagit County access to a closer federal court, reducing travel costs for jurors, witnesses, and plaintiffs in that area.
Supporters say both changes expand access to the federal court system without changing any rules about how cases are decided.
critics: Critics say opening court sessions in Alpine and Mount Vernon will require the federal judiciary to allocate staff, space, and resources to additional locations, adding to operating costs.

Critics say spreading court sessions across more cities in the Western District of Texas and Western District of Washington could slow case processing if judges and clerks are divided between more locations.

118-s-2861.one_liner: Award Billie Jean King a Congressional Gold Medal
provisions: Gives Billie Jean King a Congressional Gold Medal for her work in advancing equal rights for women in sports and education.
The medal is one of the highest awards Congress can give to a civilian.

supporters: Supporters say Congress should give Billie Jean King one of its highest civilian honors — the Congressional Gold Medal — because she helped pass and enforce Title IX, the 1972 law that banned sex discrimination in school sports programs.

Supporters say King's 1973 'Battle of the Sexes' match, watched by 90 million people, directly led to equal prize money in professional tennis and showed that women's sports could draw large audiences.

Supporters say the bill recognizes King's work building the Women's Tennis Association, which created a professional league where women could earn a living playing sports, a right that did not exist before her advocacy.
critics: Critics say the bill's stated purpose — honoring 'courageous and groundbreaking leadership' — is a subjective standard that Congress has not applied consistently, since many athletes with equal social impact have not received this medal.

Critics say Congress has awarded the Congressional Gold Medal over 180 times since 1776, and some lawmakers argue the honor loses meaning when given for advocacy work rather than acts of direct national service like military leadership.

Critics say the bill does not include any funding mechanism, and the U.S. Mint charges recipients or sponsoring groups for the physical medal, shifting costs onto private parties without disclosing that in the bill text.

118-s-3706.one_liner: Let family members and guardians collect money owed to crime victims in court
provisions: When a crime victim is under 18, disabled, or has died, a parent, guardian, or family member can collect court-ordered payments from the convicted person on the victim's behalf.
The person stepping in for the victim can be repaid for money they lost from work, travel costs, and child care while helping with the investigation or going to court hearings.
They can also be repaid for costs of transporting the victim to get medical care, physical therapy, or other treatment.

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a gap in the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act of 1996 by letting parents, guardians, or family members collect court-ordered payments when the victim is a minor, disabled, incapacitated, or deceased — groups who previously could not receive those payments directly.

Supporters say a parent or guardian who lost wages or paid travel and child care costs to attend court hearings or assist with an investigation can now be repaid by the convicted defendant for those specific out-of-pocket expenses.

Supporters say family members who paid to transport a victim to medical care, physical therapy, or rehabilitation can recover those transportation and related costs from the defendant, rather than bearing them alone.
critics: Critics say defendants who are convicted of serious crimes often fail to pay even the restitution already owed to direct victims, and adding new categories of claimants — including 'any other person appointed as suitable by the court' — may further reduce what each person actually collects.

Critics say the bill does not set a dollar cap or specific documentation standard for claims like 'lost income' and 'other expenses,' which could make it harder for courts to verify and limit what third parties request from a defendant.

Critics say expanding restitution obligations increases the total amount a defendant owes, which courts and the Department of Justice must then track and enforce — adding administrative costs without a guaranteed increase in funds actually recovered.

118-s-3249.one_liner: Name a VA clinic in Kansas City, Kansas after Captain Elwin Shopteese
provisions: The VA outpatient clinic at 9201 Parallel Parkway in Kansas City, Kansas gets a new official name: the Captain Elwin Shopteese VA Clinic.
Captain Elwin Shopteese was a U.S. Army veteran from Kansas honored by Congress for his military service.
This name change applies only to this one clinic in Wyandotte County — no other VA buildings or locations are renamed.

supporters: Supporters say naming the clinic at 9201 Parallel Parkway after Captain Elwin Shopteese honors a Kansas Army veteran that Congress recognized for his military service, giving local veterans a visible reminder of their community's history.
Supporters say the name change applies to a VA facility that serves veterans in Wyandotte County, making the recognition meaningful to the specific community where Captain Shopteese is from.
Supporters say official naming designations like this cost Congress no federal funding and require no changes to VA services or staffing at the clinic.
critics: Critics say renaming the clinic does not change any medical services, staffing levels, or care access for veterans who use the facility at 9201 Parallel Parkway.

Critics say the administrative work of updating official signage, federal records, and government documents for one clinic creates costs and staff time without a direct benefit to veteran health outcomes.
Critics say Congress could use the same legislative time to pass bills that expand care or funding for VA clinics in Wyandotte County instead of a name-only designation.

118-hres-1430.one_liner: Set the rules for how Congress debates six separate bills
provisions: This resolution sets the time limits and debate rules for six different bills being considered in the House
