One of the six bills would create a program to track and respond to actions by China's government
One bill would require the Senate to vote to approve any global pandemic agreement before it becomes binding on the U.S.
One bill would cut federal money to colleges that have ties to Confucius Institutes, which are programs funded by the Chinese government
One bill would remove the $7,500 electric vehicle tax credit for cars with batteries that use materials from certain foreign countries, including China
One bill would add new rules on foreign governments buying farmland in the U.S.
One bill would keep the federal government funded through the end of 2025

supporters: Supporters say grouping these six bills under one rule is the most efficient way to bring national security measures to a vote, including a bill to cut federal money to colleges tied to Confucius Institutes and a bill to add new rules on foreign governments buying U.S. farmland.
Supporters say this rule ensures the government funding bill — which would keep the federal government running through the end of fiscal year 2025 — gets a vote before a possible shutdown deadline.
Supporters say setting a fixed debate time for each bill prevents delay on measures like the bill removing the $7,500 electric vehicle tax credit for cars that use battery materials from China.
critics: Critics say the rule bundles the government funding bill with five other bills into one vote, forcing members to accept or reject all six at once, even if they support keeping the government open but oppose removing the $7,500 electric vehicle tax credit.

Critics say the rule limits how long members can debate each bill, giving them too little time to examine the bill that would require the Senate to approve any global pandemic agreement before it becomes binding on the U.S.

Critics say the rule blocks members from proposing individual changes to any of the six bills, meaning the Confucius Institute funding cuts or the new rules on foreign farmland purchases cannot be adjusted even if members see problems with specific parts.

118-hres-1455.one_liner: Set debate rules for seven bills on education, finance, trade, immigration, and environment
provisions: Sets the rules for how the House of Representatives will debate and vote on seven separate bills
One bill stops college accreditors from requiring schools to pass political tests to keep their accreditation
One bill changes what information public companies must share with investors and creates a new advisory committee
One bill keeps 'Made in West Bank or Gaza' labels on imported goods from those areas
One bill limits what retirement fund managers can consider when making investment choices
One bill cuts federal money to cities or states that give benefits to people who are in the country without legal status
People who have been convicted of or committed sex offenses or domestic violence can be denied entry to or removed from the U.S.
One resolution cancels an EPA rule that set pollution limits for cars and trucks made in 2027 and later

supporters: Supporters say the resolution brings H.R. 7909 to a vote, which would let the U.S. deny entry to or deport people who have been convicted of sex offenses or domestic violence.

Supporters say the resolution allows a vote on H.R. 5717, which would cut federal funding to cities or states that provide benefits such as housing or health services to people who are in the country without legal immigration status.
Supporters say the resolution allows the House to vote on H.J. Res. 136, which would cancel the EPA's April 2024 rule setting pollution limits for cars and trucks made in model year 2027 and later.
critics: Critics say the resolution bundles H.J. Res. 136, which would remove the EPA's emission standards for light-duty and medium-duty vehicles starting in model year 2027, canceling rules the agency published in April 2024.

Critics say the resolution brings H.R. 5339 to the floor, which would restrict what pension and retirement fund managers are allowed to factor into investment decisions, limiting their options beyond direct financial returns.

Critics say the resolution allows a vote on H.R. 5717, which could take away federal dollars that cities and states currently use to serve residents who do not have legal immigration status, affecting local services.

117-hr-2020.one_liner: Create a public website showing how federal disaster aid money is spent
provisions: The federal government must put disaster aid spending data in one place online where anyone can look it up.
The Small Business Administration, the Department of Housing and Urban Development, and any other agency that gives out disaster aid must update this information every three months.
Each agency must show the total amount of money it gave out, how much of that money was actually spent, and what it was spent on.

supporters: Supporters say putting all disaster aid data from the SBA, HUD, and other agencies in one place online makes it easier for the public, journalists, and lawmakers to see how money is being spent.
Supporters say requiring quarterly updates means people can track whether disaster aid money was actually spent, not just promised, which helps catch waste or delays.
Supporters say showing what each project or activity the money went to gives disaster survivors a way to verify that aid reached their communities.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set any penalties if agencies miss the quarterly reporting deadlines, which may mean the data stays incomplete or outdated.
Critics say requiring the SBA, HUD, and every other disaster aid agency to build and maintain a centralized reporting system adds administrative work without new funding to pay for it.
Critics say the bill does not define what counts as a 'project or activity,' which could let agencies report spending in vague ways that still hide how money was used.

117-hr-2377.one_liner: Let federal courts order people to give up their guns if a judge finds they pose a risk
provisions: A family member or police officer can ask a federal court to take away someone's guns if they think that person is dangerous to themselves or others.
A judge can issue an order that stops a person from buying, having, or receiving guns or bullets.
People who are under one of these court orders get added to the list of people who are not allowed to own guns under federal law.

supporters: Supporters say the bill lets family members or police officers ask a federal judge to stop a dangerous person from buying or having guns or bullets before that person hurts themselves or others.
Supporters say the order goes through a judge, so the person named in the petition gets the right to a fair hearing before losing access to firearms.
Supporters say people placed under one of these orders get added to the federal list of people who cannot legally own guns, which closes a gap in current law.
critics: Critics say the bill allows a court to take away someone's guns based on a family member's claim, before that person has been charged with or convicted of any crime.
Critics say the order is not part of a criminal case, but it still removes a person's gun rights, which some legal experts argue goes beyond what civil courts should be allowed to do.

Critics say the bill does not define a clear, specific standard for what makes someone 'dangerous enough' to lose their firearms, leaving that decision up to individual judges without firm guidelines.

117-hr-224.one_liner: Rename a Houston post office after Vanessa Guillén
provisions: Changes the official name of the post office at 5302 Galveston Road in Houston, Texas to the Vanessa Guillén Post Office Building
Vanessa Guillén was a U.S. Army soldier from Houston who was murdered at Fort Hood, Texas in 2020
Her death led to a federal law called the I Am Vanessa Guillén Act, which changed how the military handles reports of sexual harassment and assault

supporters: Supporters say renaming the post office at 5302 Galveston Road honors Vanessa Guillén, a Houston-native soldier who was murdered at Fort Hood in 2020, giving her hometown a permanent place to remember her.
Supporters say the renaming connects to the I Am Vanessa Guillén Act, a federal law that changed how the military handles sexual harassment reports, and keeps public attention on those reforms.
Supporters say naming a local federal building after Guillén gives Houston residents, especially her family and community, a public space tied to her memory.
critics: Critics say Congress spends time on bills like this one — which only changes a sign at 5302 Galveston Road — while other military reform work tied to the I Am Vanessa Guillén Act still needs oversight and funding.

Critics say commemorative naming bills have grown very common, and some lawmakers argue the process should be reserved for figures with a direct connection to the specific building or neighborhood being renamed.

Critics say a post office renaming does not carry the same weight as the legislative changes in the I Am Vanessa Guillén Act, and may give the appearance of action without adding new protections for soldiers.

117-hr-209.one_liner: Rename a post office in Pontotoc, Mississippi after Lance Corporal Marc Lucas Tucker
provisions: Changes the official name of the post office at 305 Highway 15 North in Pontotoc, Mississippi to the 'Lance Corporal Marc Lucas Tucker Post Office Building'

117-hr-207.one_liner: Rename a post office in Amory, Mississippi after Command Sergeant Major Lawrence Kennedy
provisions: Renames the post office at 215 1st Avenue in Amory, Mississippi after Command Sergeant Major Lawrence E. 'Rabbit' Kennedy.
Command Sergeant Major is the highest rank an enlisted soldier can reach in the U.S. Army.
The building keeps the same address and all post office services stay the same.

supporters: Supporters say the bill honors Command Sergeant Major Lawrence E. 'Rabbit' Kennedy, who reached the highest rank an enlisted soldier can earn in the U.S. Army, by naming the post office at 215 1st Avenue in Amory, Mississippi after him.

Supporters say renaming the building gives the Amory, Mississippi community a permanent, public way to recognize CSM Kennedy's military service without changing the address or any post office services.

117-hr-2773.one_liner: Fund state programs that protect wildlife and plants at risk of dying out
provisions: Gives money to states, territories, and Washington D.C. to protect animals and plants that are at risk of dying out
The Department of the Interior runs a grant program using part of this money
Grants go to new efforts to help endangered or threatened species, or to protect the places where those species live
States can also use the money for wildlife education and outdoor recreation projects

supporters: Supporters say the bill would give states, territories, and Washington D.C. dedicated funding to protect animals and plants listed as endangered or threatened before they go extinct.
Supporters say the Department of the Interior grant program would pay for new recovery efforts that focus on the specific habitats where at-risk species live.
Supporters say states could also use the money for wildlife education and outdoor recreation, which brings more people into conservation work.
critics: Critics say the bill adds a new federal spending program without a clear cap on total dollars sent to states and territories, making the long-term cost hard to predict.
Critics say giving the Department of the Interior control over which grant projects count as 'innovative' gives one agency too much power to decide how the money is spent.
Critics say funding outdoor recreation projects through this bill stretches the definition of wildlife conservation and could divert money away from direct species recovery work.

117-hr-2543.one_liner: Require the Federal Reserve to track and reduce racial gaps in jobs and wealth
provisions: Tells the Federal Reserve to do its work in a way that reduces gaps in jobs, income, wealth, and access to loans between racial and ethnic groups
Requires the Federal Reserve to release reports showing where gaps exist in employment between different racial and ethnic groups
Requires the Federal Reserve to share its plans for how it will work to close those gaps over time

supporters: Supporters say the bill would require the Federal Reserve to track and report gaps in employment and income between racial and ethnic groups, giving the public regular data on where those gaps stand.
Supporters say the bill would require the Federal Reserve to share specific plans for how it will reduce gaps in access to loans for Black, Latino, and other minority borrowers.
Supporters say making the Federal Reserve responsible for closing racial wealth gaps adds a clear goal to its work beyond its two main jobs of keeping prices stable and keeping unemployment low.
critics: Critics say the bill would expand the Federal Reserve's role beyond its two main jobs — keeping prices stable and keeping unemployment low — without giving it new tools or funding to address racial gaps.
Critics say requiring the Federal Reserve to report on plans to close racial and ethnic employment gaps could conflict with how it currently sets interest rates and manages the money supply.
Critics say the bill does not define what counts as success in closing racial gaps, which makes it hard to measure whether the Federal Reserve's required reports and plans are working.

117-hr-2724.one_liner: Assign peer support specialists to veterans filing military sexual trauma claims
provisions: The VA must assign a peer support specialist to each veteran who files a military sexual trauma claim.
Veterans can say no if they do not want a specialist assigned to them.
Each specialist must be trained as a victim advocate.
The specialist cannot have any role in deciding whether the veteran's claim is approved or denied.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would give every veteran who files a military sexual trauma claim their own peer support specialist, someone trained as a victim advocate, to help them through the process.
Supporters say the rule that the specialist cannot have any role in deciding whether a claim is approved or denied means veterans can speak openly without worrying it will hurt their case.
Supporters say the opt-out option lets veterans who want support get it automatically, while still giving those who prefer to go it alone the choice to do so.
critics: Critics say the VA has not shown it has enough trained victim advocates on staff to assign one to every military sexual trauma claimant, and the bill does not include funding to hire more.
Critics say requiring the VA to build and run a new specialist assignment system for every military sexual trauma claim could slow down an agency that already has a backlog of pending cases.
Critics say the bill does not set a timeline for when a specialist must be assigned after a claim is filed, which could leave veterans waiting without support during the early stages of their case.

117-hr-2499.one_liner: Give federal firefighters workers' compensation for job-related illnesses
provisions: Federal firefighters, paramedics, EMTs, and hazmat workers who get heart disease, lung disease, or certain cancers are automatically covered by workers' compensation — without having to prove the job caused the illness.
To qualify, the worker must have worked in fire protection for at least 5 years and be diagnosed within 10 years of starting the job.
Workers who catch a disease during a declared pandemic or a chronic infectious disease tied to job hazards are covered regardless of how long they have worked.
Workers' compensation covers both disability and death caused by these illnesses.
Covered workers include anyone whose main job is fire suppression — including firefighters, paramedics, EMTs, rescue workers, ambulance staff, and hazmat workers.

supporters: Supporters say the bill removes the requirement that federal firefighters, paramedics, EMTs, and hazmat workers prove their job caused their heart disease, lung disease, or cancer — making it easier to receive workers' compensation.
Supporters say the 5-year work requirement and 10-year diagnosis window set the coverage window for these illnesses, while pandemic and infectious disease coverage applies from day one of employment.
Supporters say the bill covers both disability and death from these illnesses, so families of federal fire protection workers who die from job-related disease can also receive compensation.
critics: Critics say the automatic presumption for heart disease, lung disease, and certain cancers — without requiring workers to show a direct link to their job — could lead to compensation claims for illnesses that developed from causes unrelated to fire protection work.

Critics say expanding coverage to all communicable diseases during a declared pandemic, with no minimum years of service required, broadens the program beyond illnesses that can be clearly tied to fire suppression duties.

Critics say adding paramedics, EMTs, ambulance staff, and hazmat workers to the covered group — beyond traditional firefighters — increases the number of federal employees eligible for automatic workers' compensation presumptions, raising program costs.

117-hr-2992.one_liner: Create training tools to help police respond to people with brain injuries or PTSD
provisions: The Bureau of Justice Assistance must create training tools to help police and other first responders work with people who have brain injuries or PTSD.
At least one police department named as a Law Enforcement Mental Health Learning Site must use these tools.
The tools must be added to an existing resource called the Police-Mental Health Collaboration Toolkit.
The CDC must study how often first responders get concussions and report back on what they find.

supporters: Supporters say the BJA training tools would help police and other first responders recognize when someone has a brain injury or PTSD during a crisis, which could reduce harmful misunderstandings in those situations.

Supporters say adding the tools to the Police-Mental Health Collaboration Toolkit would make them available to departments across the country, going beyond the one required Law Enforcement Mental Health Learning Site.
Supporters say the CDC study on concussions among first responders would give agencies data they currently do not have about how often their own officers are getting brain injuries on the job.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires one police department — the designated Law Enforcement Mental Health Learning Site — to actually use the new training tools, meaning most departments face no requirement to adopt them.

Critics say the bill does not include a specific funding amount for creating the BJA training tools or conducting the CDC concussion study, leaving it unclear how these agencies will pay for the work.
Critics say the CDC report only measures how often first responders get concussions but does not require any follow-up action based on what the study finds.

117-hr-3508.one_liner: Name a Honeoye Falls post office after Army Chief Warrant Officer Christian Koch
provisions: The post office at 39 West Main Street in Honeoye Falls, New York gets a new official name.
That name is the CW4 Christian J. Koch Memorial Post Office.
CW4 stands for Chief Warrant Officer 4, a senior Army rank.

supporters: Supporters say the bill honors CW4 Christian J. Koch, a senior Army officer who reached the rank of Chief Warrant Officer 4, by giving his name to the post office at 39 West Main Street in Honeoye Falls, New York.
Supporters say the designation requires no new federal spending, since it only changes the official name of an existing postal facility.
Supporters say naming a local post office after a fallen service member gives the Honeoye Falls community a permanent public way to recognize his military service.
critics: Critics say updating federal records, signage, and postal databases at 39 West Main Street will require administrative work and costs that are paid by taxpayers, even if no new spending is formally authorized.
Critics say Congress uses limited floor time to pass individual post office naming bills, and that time could be used for legislation that affects larger numbers of people.
Critics say there is no formal process requiring local community input before a federal designation like this one is proposed, so residents of Honeoye Falls may not have had a clear way to weigh in.

117-hr-4693.one_liner: Direct USAID to run programs that prevent and treat malnutrition in other countries
provisions: USAID must work through a government-wide plan called the Global Nutrition Coordination Plan to guide how U.S. money for nutrition is spent.
USAID must pick which countries get help based on malnutrition data, and must update that list within five years.
USAID can create a group inside the agency called the Nutrition Leadership Council to keep all its nutrition work coordinated.
USAID can direct food and health help to the people most at risk of severe malnutrition.
USAID can work with UN agencies, private companies, and local groups to help partner countries build their own nutrition programs.
USAID must send Congress a plan and yearly reports on how these programs are running.
All these programs end seven years after the law is signed.

supporters: Supporters say requiring USAID to pick countries based on malnutrition data — and update that list within five years — makes sure U.S. nutrition money goes where the need is greatest.

Supporters say creating the Nutrition Leadership Council inside USAID and using the Global Nutrition Coordination Plan will stop different U.S. agencies from doing overlapping work with the same funds.
Supporters say the yearly reports to Congress and the seven-year end date give lawmakers a clear way to track results and decide whether to keep funding these programs.
critics: Critics say the seven-year sunset means partner countries may not have enough time to build nutrition programs that can run on their own after U.S. support ends.

Critics say the bill gives USAID broad permission to work with UN agencies, private companies, and local groups, but does not set a budget or spending limit, making it hard to know what the programs will actually cost.
Critics say sending Congress a plan and yearly reports adds reporting work to USAID without requiring the agency to hit specific targets for reducing malnutrition rates.

117-hr-4133.one_liner: Fund security and disaster programs in Caribbean countries
provisions: Sends money to Caribbean countries to help with public safety and fighting crime
Requires the State Department to make a plan for helping Caribbean countries prepare for and respond to disasters
The plan must include steps that can be measured to show progress
The State Department must submit a timeline and list of goals for carrying out the plan
Requires reports to track whether the money is being used and goals are being met

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires the State Department to create a plan with specific, measurable steps for disaster preparedness in Caribbean countries, which means progress can be tracked instead of just promised.

Supporters say the funds are directed at fighting crime, corruption, and the influence of authoritarian regimes in the Caribbean, which backers argue protects U.S. national security interests in the region.
Supporters say the required timeline and reporting on how money is used gives Congress a way to check whether Caribbean countries are actually meeting the stated goals.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a specific dollar amount for the funding, making it unclear how much money will actually flow to Caribbean public safety and disaster programs.

Critics say adding new strategy documents, implementation plans, and reporting requirements to the State Department creates more bureaucratic steps that could delay aid reaching the Caribbean countries the bill is meant to help.

Critics say the provision to counter 'influence from authoritarian regimes' is not clearly defined, which could allow funds to be used for purposes beyond crime-fighting and disaster response without clear limits.

117-hr-3807.one_liner: Add $60 billion to a fund that gives money to restaurants hurt by COVID-19
provisions: Adds $60 billion to the Restaurant Revitalization Fund, a program that gives money directly to restaurants and other food and drink businesses
This fund was created to help these businesses recover from losses during the COVID-19 pandemic
Businesses can apply for grants — money they do not have to pay back — to cover costs like rent, payroll, and supplies

supporters: Supporters say the $60 billion in grants would help restaurants and food businesses cover real costs like rent, payroll, and supplies without taking on debt they cannot afford.

Supporters say the Restaurant Revitalization Fund targets businesses that lost money during COVID-19, and adding $60 billion gives more of those businesses a chance to get help they were promised but did not receive.
Supporters say these grants do not have to be paid back, which gives small food and drink businesses a better shot at staying open and keeping workers employed.
critics: Critics say adding $60 billion to a single fund is a large cost to taxpayers, especially when other industries also suffered pandemic losses and did not get the same level of direct grant funding.
Critics say the original Restaurant Revitalization Fund had problems with fraud and mismanagement, and sending another $60 billion through the same program could repeat those issues.
Critics say the bill focuses only on restaurants and food businesses, leaving out other hard-hit small businesses like retail shops and service providers that faced similar COVID-19 losses.

117-hr-3344.one_liner: Help Central and Eastern European countries secure their phone and internet networks
provisions: The State Department will help Central and Eastern European countries make their phone and internet networks more secure.
Projects that get U.S. support must use only safe equipment — Chinese equipment is not allowed.
If a country's network already uses Chinese equipment, it must replace that equipment to qualify.
The State Department will give diplomatic support and push international banks to invest in these projects.
U.S. agencies — including a government bank called the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation — will help fund studies and cover project costs.
Projects must meet international standards and be financially sustainable.
Projects must also help connect telecom networks across the Central and Eastern European region and block interference from foreign actors.

supporters: Supporters say the bill strengthens U.S. national security by requiring that all supported projects remove Chinese equipment from Central and Eastern European telecom networks, cutting off a potential route for foreign surveillance.

Supporters say the bill uses existing U.S. agencies — like the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation — to fund feasibility studies and project costs, which helps allied countries build secure networks without bearing the full financial burden alone.

Supporters say requiring projects to meet international standards and connect networks across the Central and Eastern European region will make it harder for foreign actors to interfere with communications in countries near Russia.
critics: Critics say the rule that countries must replace all existing Chinese equipment before qualifying for help could be too costly for smaller Central and Eastern European countries, slowing down or blocking their ability to get U.S. support.

Critics say the bill does not name a specific dollar amount for funding, making it unclear how much the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and other agencies will actually spend or whether the money will be enough to complete large telecom projects.

Critics say pushing international banks to invest in these projects through diplomatic pressure — rather than binding commitments — may not produce reliable funding, leaving some projects without the money needed to finish.

117-hr-5738.one_liner: Require VA medical centers to provide clean breastfeeding rooms for mothers
provisions: Every VA medical center must have a clean room where mothers can breastfeed or pump milk
The room cannot be a bathroom
The room must be easy to find

supporters: Supporters say the bill would give veteran mothers a clean, private place to breastfeed or pump at every VA medical center, since the law requires the room to be hygienic and not a bathroom.
Supporters say requiring each lactation space to be easy to find means veteran mothers won't have to search through large medical buildings while caring for a newborn.
Supporters say the rule covers every VA medical center, so veteran mothers across the country would have access to the same basic standard of care.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a funding amount, leaving it unclear how VA facilities will pay to build or set aside dedicated rooms that meet the new specifications.
Critics say converting existing space at each VA medical center into a separate lactation room could reduce space available for medical services at already crowded facilities.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for compliance, which could mean some VA medical centers take years to provide the required rooms.

117-hr-5324.one_liner: Upgrade and expand NOAA's emergency weather radio network
provisions: Keeps NOAA Weather Radio working in areas with no or weak cell service
Makes sure broadcast towers and antennas get regular repairs and upkeep
Adds the ability to broadcast non-weather emergency alerts through the radio network
Puts real-time weather warnings online so more people can access them
Requires NOAA to study how many people can and cannot reach the weather radio network

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps NOAA Weather Radio working in rural and low-income areas where cell service is weak or missing, so residents still get emergency alerts during disasters.
Supporters say requiring regular repairs to broadcast towers means the radio network stays reliable instead of failing during storms when people need it most.
Supporters say putting real-time weather warnings online gives people without a dedicated weather radio another way to get alerts, reaching more of the public.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a funding amount, leaving it unclear how NOAA will pay for tower repairs, coverage expansion, and new online systems without a budget attached.

Critics say the added ability to broadcast non-weather emergency messages through the radio network could create confusion if listeners cannot tell which agency is sending the alert or how serious it is.
Critics say prioritizing online access to warnings may not help elderly residents or low-income households who lack reliable internet, meaning the people hardest to reach stay underserved.

117-hr-496.one_liner: Count Russia's actions in occupied Ukraine when rating its record on religious freedom
provisions: When the U.S. government decides whether to label Russia a country that violates religious freedom, it must now look at what is happening in the parts of Ukraine that Russia controls.
Russia can be put on a U.S. watchlist if it is found to be violating religious freedom — that label can lead to the U.S. pulling certain aid or taking other actions against Russia.

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a gap in current law by requiring the President to look at religious freedom violations in parts of Ukraine that Russia controls when deciding whether to label Russia a 'country of particular concern.'

Supporters say the 'country of particular concern' label can lead to the U.S. pulling development assistance from Russia, so expanding what the President must review could make that outcome more likely.
Supporters say the bill covers not just Russian forces but also Russia-affiliated non-state groups operating in occupied Ukrainian territory, making the review more complete.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires the President to 'consider' incidents in occupied Ukrainian territory — it does not require the President to actually label Russia a 'country of particular concern,' so no action is guaranteed.
Critics say the bill does not create any new penalties or enforcement tools — it only expands what the President must look at, leaving all decisions about consequences the same as before.

Critics say the bill focuses only on Ukrainian territory under Russian control and does not require the President to look at religious freedom conditions inside Russia itself when making this decision.

117-hr-5658.one_liner: Require DHS to report on who handles cyber attacks and how
provisions: The Department of Homeland Security must write a report explaining which parts of the agency are in charge of responding to cyber attacks.
DHS must work with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency when putting together the report.

supporters: Supporters say requiring DHS to write a report on which parts of the agency handle cyber attacks will help Congress see if there are gaps or overlaps in who does what.

Supporters say having DHS work with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency on the report means the findings will reflect input from the main federal group already focused on cyber threats.
critics: Critics say a report alone does not fix any problems — it only describes roles without requiring DHS or its parts to actually change how they respond to cyber attacks.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for when the report must be finished, which could mean delays before any action is taken.

117-hr-5129.one_liner: Extend and update a federal program that funds local antipoverty services
provisions: Keeps the Community Services Block Grant program running through 2031.
Opens up services to families earning up to twice the federal poverty level.
That is roughly $62,400 for a family of four in 2024, up from about $31,200.
Changes how the program is run and how results are measured.
Updates how money is divided among states, tribes, and territories.

supporters: Supporters say expanding eligibility to 200% of the federal poverty level means families earning up to $62,400 a year — not just $31,200 — can now get help with food, housing, and job training.
Supporters say keeping the program funded through 2031 gives states, tribes, and territories a stable source of money to plan long-term antipoverty work.
Supporters say the new performance measurement rules will make it easier to track whether the program is actually reducing poverty and hold local agencies accountable.
critics: Critics say raising the income limit to $62,400 for a family of four will spread limited block grant dollars across more people, leaving fewer resources for the poorest families already in the program.
Critics say the changes to how money is divided among states, tribes, and territories could shift funding away from areas with the highest poverty rates.
Critics say the updated rules on administration and measurement add new reporting requirements that smaller community agencies may struggle to meet.

117-hr-5754.one_liner: Create an online system for veterans to file and track complaints with VA patient advocates
provisions: The Veterans Health Administration must build an online system where veterans can file complaints with a patient advocate without going in person.
Veterans or someone acting on their behalf — like a family member or representative — can file and check the status of complaints through the system.
Right now, there is no standard electronic way to file or track these complaints; this bill requires one to be created.

supporters: Supporters say the new online system would let veterans file complaints with a patient advocate without going in person, which helps veterans who live far from a VA facility or have trouble traveling.

Supporters say that right now there is no standard electronic way to file or track complaints, so this bill would give veterans and their family members a clear way to see what is happening with a complaint they filed.
Supporters say allowing a veteran's family member or legal representative to file and check complaints through the system makes it easier for veterans who need help managing their own care.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a cost limit or deadline for when the Veterans Health Administration must finish building the new IT system, which could lead to delays or cost overruns.
Critics say the bill only requires the VHA to let veterans track complaints — it does not require the VHA to respond faster or fix problems within a set number of days.
Critics say the bill does not explain what privacy rules will protect veteran information when family members or outside representatives access the complaint system on a veteran's behalf.

117-hr-5900.one_liner: Rename a Los Angeles post office after Marine Corps Reserve Private Jacob Cruz
provisions: Renames the post office at 2016 East 1st Street in Los Angeles, California, to the Marine Corps Reserve PVT Jacob Cruz Post Office.
The name change is ceremonial and does not affect post office operations or services.
Jacob Cruz served in the United States Marine Corps Reserve and is being honored by this designation.

arguments.note: This bill is purely ceremonial. It renames one post office at 2016 East 1st Street in Los Angeles to honor Marine Corps Reserve PVT Jacob Cruz. It does not change policy, spending, or services. There are no policy sides to present.

117-hr-5914.one_liner: Move a senior fraud protection grant program to a new agency and extend it to 2028
provisions: Keeps a grant program running that gives money to states to protect older Americans from financial fraud, through 2028.
Moves the program from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Creates a task force to watch over how the program runs.
Removes some of the rules that states had to meet before they could get grant money.

supporters: Supporters say moving the program from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to the Securities and Exchange Commission puts it under an agency with stronger experience overseeing investment fraud, which is a common way older Americans are targeted.
Supporters say removing eligibility requirements makes it easier for more states to get grant money, so more older Americans can be protected from financial bad actors before 2028.
Supporters say the new task force will make sure grant money is being used well by keeping watch over how the program runs across all participating states.
critics: Critics say moving the program away from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau removes it from an agency focused on protecting everyday consumers, which could weaken protections for seniors who are victims of non-investment fraud.
Critics say eliminating grant eligibility requirements means states may receive funds without meeting standards that were meant to ensure the money is spent effectively on senior protection.

Critics say the bill does not include new funding amounts, so it is unclear whether the program will have enough money through 2028 to make a real difference for older Americans at risk of financial fraud.

117-hr-5911.one_liner: Let people with old criminal records work at banks and credit unions without special permission
provisions: Right now, banks and credit unions must get special permission from the government before hiring someone convicted of certain crimes involving dishonesty or fraud.
This bill removes that requirement if 7 or more years have passed since the crime happened.
It also removes the requirement if 5 or more years have passed since the person was released from jail or prison.
If the crime was committed before the person turned 21 and it has been at least 30 months since sentencing, no special permission is needed.
If a person's criminal record was erased, sealed, or pardoned, they can be hired without special permission.

supporters: Supporters say the bill helps people with old records get jobs in banking, since crimes that happened 7 or more years ago would no longer block hiring without a waiver.
Supporters say the rule for offenses before age 21 — where only 30 months must pass after sentencing — gives young people a second chance before their records follow them into adulthood.
Supporters say people whose records were erased, sealed, or pardoned should not face extra government hurdles, since the legal system already cleared them.
critics: Critics say removing the waiver requirement for crimes involving dishonesty or fraud — even after 7 years — puts banks and credit unions at higher risk, since those institutions handle other people's money and savings.

Critics say the 30-month window for offenses committed before age 21 may be too short, because it allows someone to work in a financial institution less than 3 years after sentencing for fraud-related crimes.
Critics say the bill takes away oversight from the FDIC and the National Credit Union Administration, which currently review each case before approving a hire at an insured institution.

117-hr-5879.one_liner: Change the rules for when small businesses in low-income areas get a price advantage on government contracts
provisions: The HUBZone program lets small businesses in certain low-income areas compete for government contracts.
Right now, these businesses can get a price preference, meaning the government can pay up to 10% more to choose them over a larger competitor.
This bill changes the rules for when that price preference applies during the bidding process.

supporters: Supporters say the bill fixes confusion about when the 10% price preference applies, so HUBZone small businesses in low-income areas can compete more fairly for federal contracts.
Supporters say clearer rules will help more small businesses in HUBZone areas win government contracts, which brings jobs and money into communities that need it.
critics: Critics say changing the price preference rules could make it easier for agencies to avoid giving the 10% advantage to HUBZone businesses, reducing the program's benefit to small firms in low-income areas.
Critics say the bill does not define exactly when the preference must apply, which could lead to agencies interpreting the new rules in ways that hurt small HUBZone businesses during bidding.

117-hr-6064.one_liner: Order a review of VA disability claim exams for veterans who experienced military sexual trauma
provisions: The VA must ask a national science group to review the medical exams used when veterans who were sexually assaulted file for disability pay.
The review covers exams for both mental and physical conditions tied to sexual assault during military service.
The science group must write a report on what it finds.
The VA must then write its own report on what steps it plans to take based on those findings.

supporters: Supporters say the review would check whether the medical exams given to veterans who filed disability claims tied to sexual assault during service are being done correctly, since those veterans must prove their conditions are connected to that trauma.

Supporters say the review covers both mental and physical conditions, which means veterans with PTSD and those with physical injuries from military sexual trauma would both be included in the findings.
Supporters say requiring the VA to write a report on steps it plans to take based on the science group's findings creates accountability for how military sexual trauma disability claims are handled.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires the VA to 'seek to enter into' an agreement with the science group — it does not guarantee the review will happen if no agreement is reached.
Critics say the VA's required report only covers what steps it 'plans to take,' not what it must actually do, meaning the science group's findings could be set aside without any required action.
Critics say the bill sets no deadline for when the science group must finish its report or when the VA must respond, which could delay any changes to how these disability exams are conducted.

117-hr-6052.one_liner: Require VA employees to take training on working with the Inspector General
provisions: All VA employees must complete training on how to report wrongdoing to the Inspector General.
The training also covers how to respond to requests from the Inspector General's office.
Employees learn what it means to cooperate with Inspector General investigations.
The Inspector General's office creates and manages this training.

supporters: Supporters say requiring all VA employees to complete training on reporting wrongdoing to the Inspector General will make it easier for workers to come forward when they see problems.

Supporters say having the Inspector General's office create and manage the training ensures employees learn the exact steps needed to cooperate with investigations, which could help the VA catch fraud or misconduct faster.
Supporters say teaching employees how to respond to Inspector General requests will reduce delays in investigations that affect veterans' care and benefits.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a timeline or budget for rolling out the training to all VA employees, leaving key details unclear.
Critics say mandatory training programs for large agencies like the VA can pull employees away from serving veterans without a clear measure of whether the training changes actual reporting behavior.
Critics say the bill gives the Inspector General's office full control over the training content, with no outside review to check that the material is accurate or fair to employees.

117-hr-6087.one_liner: Let nurse practitioners and physician assistants treat injured federal workers
provisions: Right now, only doctors can treat injured federal government workers under the workers' compensation program. This bill lets nurse practitioners and physician assistants do that job too.
Nurse practitioners and physician assistants would be able to recommend treatment and prescribe medicine to injured federal workers.
They could also fill out paperwork certifying what the injury is and how long the worker might be unable to do their job.
They could take part in required medical exams alongside a doctor from the Department of Labor.

supporters: Supporters say this bill would let nurse practitioners and physician assistants treat injured federal workers, giving workers more providers to choose from and reducing wait times to see someone who can help.

Supporters say that under current law, only doctors can certify an injury and how long a worker may be unable to work — this bill lets nurse practitioners and physician assistants do that paperwork too, which many already do for non-federal patients in their states.

Supporters say allowing nurse practitioners and physician assistants to prescribe medicine and recommend treatment for injured federal workers brings federal workers' comp rules in line with how most state workers' comp programs already work.
critics: Critics say that letting nurse practitioners and physician assistants certify the nature of an injury and the probable extent of disability — without requiring a doctor's sign-off — could lead to less consistent medical decisions about how long a federal worker is considered disabled.

Critics say that while nurse practitioners and physician assistants can join required Department of Labor medical exams, they would do so alongside a physician rather than replacing one, raising questions about whether the bill goes far enough or creates confusion about who has final say.

Critics say expanding who can certify federal workers' injuries and disability periods may increase the number of approved claims, which could raise costs for the federal workers' compensation program over time.

117-hr-6089.one_liner: Add armed drones to the weapons covered by U.S. Iran sanctions
provisions: U.S. law already puts penalties on people or companies that supply certain weapons to Iran — this bill adds armed drones to that list.
These penalties — called sanctions — can include travel bans, frozen bank accounts, and being blocked from doing business with American companies.
The law targets both individuals and organizations that give or sell armed drones to Iran.

supporters: Supporters say adding armed drones to the existing sanctions list means anyone who sells or gives unmanned combat vehicles to Iran can now face travel bans, frozen bank accounts, and a block on doing business with U.S. companies.
Supporters say the current law had a gap — it covered many weapons but not armed drones, which Iran has obtained and used in regional conflicts — and this bill closes that gap.
Supporters say targeting both individuals and organizations gives the U.S. more tools to stop drone transfers before they reach Iran.
critics: Critics say sanctions blocking access to U.S. businesses only work against countries and companies that trade with the U.S. — suppliers like Russia, which has transferred drone technology with Iran, may not be deterred because they already face broad U.S. sanctions.
Critics say the bill adds armed drones to a list but does not create any new enforcement powers or funding, which means detection and punishment still depend on the same systems already in place.
Critics say expanding the sanctions list without a named enforcement agency or budget may make the law hard to apply consistently against both individuals and large organizations.

117-hr-6270.one_liner: Create a grant program to plan and build landing pads for new small aircraft
provisions: The Department of Transportation can give planning money to local governments, airports, and transit agencies.
These groups would plan where to build vertiports — landing pads for small aircraft that take off straight up.
Plans must identify locations for vertiports and list available sources of money to pay for them.
If the FAA approves at least two new aircraft models, DOT can give money for construction.
Construction money can cover design costs, environmental studies, and other building expenses.
No grants can be given out after September 30, 2023.

supporters: Supporters say the program gives local governments, airports, and transit agencies planning money to figure out where to build vertiports, letting communities shape this new technology from the start.
Supporters say tying construction grants to FAA approval of at least two aircraft models means no building money goes out until the planes are proven safe.
Supporters say requiring plans to list available funding sources helps communities find money beyond federal grants to pay for vertiport construction.
critics: Critics say the September 30, 2023 deadline means no grants can be awarded after that date, leaving the program with a very short window to actually build anything.
Critics say the bill only funds planning and construction for vertiports but does not set any rules for how these aircraft will operate in neighborhoods or near homes.
Critics say the program sends money to state, local, and tribal governments and transit agencies without requiring them to show that communities actually want vertiports in their area.

117-hr-6386.one_liner: Rename a post office in Schaumburg, Illinois, to the Veterans of Iraq and Afghanistan Memorial Post Office Building
provisions: Changes the official name of the post office at 450 West Schaumburg Road in Schaumburg, Illinois, to the 'Veterans of Iraq and Afghanistan Memorial Post Office Building'
The post office keeps its address at 450 West Schaumburg Road and continues to operate the same way
No money is spent and no new programs are created by this name change
No further government action is needed once the bill passes

supporters: Supporters say renaming the post office at 450 West Schaumburg Road honors veterans who served in Iraq and Afghanistan, giving the Schaumburg community a lasting public landmark in their name.
Supporters say the bill costs no money and requires no new programs, making it a low-cost way for Congress to formally recognize military service.
critics: Critics say Congress is spending legislative time on a symbolic name change that creates no new benefits, funding, or services for Iraq and Afghanistan veterans.
Critics say the renaming at 450 West Schaumburg Road does not address veterans' concrete needs, such as healthcare or job support, that could be tackled with the same legislative effort.

117-hr-6824.one_liner: Create an annual cybersecurity contest for U.S. government workers with cash prizes
provisions: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) runs a yearly competition open to U.S. government employees and teams.
Winners can receive cash prizes.
CISA can work with outside experts and organizations to help design and run the contest.
CISA can partner with nonprofits, private companies, or state and local agencies to manage the competition.
Money for the contest can come from Congress, other federal agencies, states, tribal governments, nonprofits, and private companies.

supporters: Supporters say the yearly competition gives U.S. government cybersecurity workers a chance to sharpen their skills and earn cash prizes, which could help the federal government attract and keep people with strong cybersecurity abilities.
Supporters say allowing private companies, nonprofits, and state governments to help fund and run the competition means Congress does not have to cover the full cost.
Supporters say letting CISA work with outside experts to design the contest helps make sure the competition tests real-world cybersecurity skills that matter for protecting federal systems.
critics: Critics say allowing for-profit companies to help fund and design a federal cybersecurity competition could give those companies influence over a government program that handles sensitive security information.
Critics say the bill does not set a cap on how much can be spent on cash prizes or administration, so it is unclear how much taxpayer money could go toward the competition each year.

Critics say government cybersecurity employees already receive federal salaries and benefits, so adding cash prizes on top may not be the most cost-effective way to improve federal cybersecurity skills.

117-hr-6376.one_liner: Let more student veterans qualify for VA work-study pay
provisions: Right now, veterans must be enrolled at least three-quarter time to get paid through the VA work-study program.
This bill lowers that requirement to half-time, so more veterans can qualify.
Veterans can use the work-study program while they go to school, or are in a training or rehabilitation program.
The work-study program lets veterans earn money by doing jobs for the VA or on campus while they study.

supporters: Supporters say lowering the enrollment requirement from three-quarter time to half-time would let veterans in rehabilitation or training programs earn money through the VA work-study program who could not qualify before.
Supporters say the change helps veterans who can only attend school part-time — due to work, family, or health reasons — still access work-study jobs on campus or at VA offices.

Supporters say veterans in rehabilitation programs are already working toward recovery and skills, so they should be able to earn work-study pay at half-time just like students in regular education programs.
critics: Critics say expanding eligibility to half-time students could increase the number of veterans drawing work-study allowances, raising costs for the VA without a clear funding source identified in the bill.
Critics say veterans enrolled only half-time may have less availability to fill VA work-study positions, which could make it harder to staff those roles consistently.

117-hr-6531.one_liner: Track which communities get federal money and push more toward the poorest areas
provisions: The Census Bureau must publish a list of areas where poverty has stayed high for many years, and update it every year.
A federal office must create a plan to send more federal money to these high-poverty areas.
The same federal office must report to Congress every year on how much money went to these areas.
A government watchdog group must review the plan and report on whether more money is actually reaching the poorest communities.

supporters: Supporters say the Census Bureau's yearly updated list of high-poverty areas will make it harder for federal agencies to ignore communities that have been poor for decades.
Supporters say requiring a federal plan to direct more money to these areas gives Congress a tool to track whether poor communities are actually getting a bigger share of federal funds.
Supporters say the government watchdog review adds a check to make sure the plan works — not just on paper, but in real dollars reaching the poorest zip codes.
critics: Critics say the bill creates new reporting rules for the Census Bureau, OMB, and GAO but does not require any specific dollar amount to actually be spent in high-poverty areas.
Critics say the bill adds layers of planning and reporting without changing the formulas or laws that control how federal grants are already distributed to communities.
Critics say annual reports to Congress do not force any agency to shift spending, so the bill may produce data without producing change.

117-hr-6604.one_liner: Help veterans get their GI Bill benefits back if their school closed
provisions: If a veteran's school closes or loses approval, the VA must let them sign a written statement saying they transferred fewer than 12 credits from that school
Once a veteran signs that statement, the VA must accept it as proof and restore their full GI Bill time — meaning they don't lose the months they spent at the closed school
The VA must send veterans a certificate showing they still have their full education benefit available to use
If a veteran actually transferred 12 or more credits, they do not get the benefit restored and the VA takes back the certificate
The VA must contact veterans who qualify for this process and tell them how to apply

supporters: Supporters say the bill helps veterans whose schools closed or lost VA approval by letting them sign a written statement confirming they transferred fewer than 12 credits, which restores their full GI Bill time so they do not lose months of benefits they already used.
Supporters say the VA must send qualifying veterans a certificate showing their full education benefit is still available, which makes it easier for veterans to enroll in a new school without delays.
Supporters say the VA must contact veterans who qualify and explain the process, so veterans are not left to find this option on their own after their school closes.
critics: Critics say the bill uses self-certification — veterans sign a written statement without the VA checking their credit transfers first — which could allow some veterans to receive a certificate of eligibility they do not qualify for.

Critics say that when veterans do transfer 12 or more credits, the VA must take back the certificate of eligibility after already issuing it, creating extra steps and possible confusion for veterans who believed their benefits were restored.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for when the VA must notify veterans or issue certificates, which could leave veterans waiting without knowing if their GI Bill time has been restored.

117-hr-6873.one_liner: Create a DHS office to prevent bombing attacks in the US
provisions: Creates a new office inside the Department of Homeland Security focused on stopping bomb attacks
The office gives advice on explosive threats and helps different parts of DHS work together on the issue
Provides help to businesses and the public on how to protect important places and large events from bomb threats
Makes sure different agencies share information about research on stopping explosive attacks

supporters: Supporters say the new DHS Office for Bombing Prevention will bring all DHS bomb threat work under one roof, replacing scattered efforts spread across different parts of the department.
Supporters say the bill requires DHS to give technical help to businesses and event organizers at critical infrastructure sites and large public events, filling a gap in current federal support.
Supporters say the information-sharing requirement will make sure that research on stopping explosive attacks reaches local and federal agencies faster than current processes allow.
critics: Critics say CISA already runs a Bombing Prevention program and the TRIPwire network, which do much of what this new office would do, making a separate office redundant.
Critics say the bill does not set a budget, staff size, or timeline for the new office, which makes it hard to measure whether the office is actually working.
Critics say the 'promoting security awareness' part of the bill has no enforcement rules or measurable goals, so there is no way to verify if those efforts reduce bomb threats.

117-hr-6825.one_liner: Update and extend the federal grant program that helps nonprofits pay for security
provisions: Keeps the program running and funded through 2028.
Requires FEMA to create a new office, run by a senior FEMA official, to manage the program.
The new office will reach out to nonprofits, answer questions, and help groups apply for grants.
FEMA must publish grant rules, and can stop states from closing their application windows before those rules come out.

supporters: Supporters say extending the program through FY2028 gives nonprofits like religious organizations and community centers more time to apply for security funding they could not otherwise afford.
Supporters say the new FEMA office, led by a senior official, will help smaller nonprofits that lack staff to navigate the grant application process on their own.
Supporters say requiring FEMA to publish grant rules before states can close their application windows prevents nonprofits from missing deadlines because the rules came out too late.
critics: Critics say creating a new FEMA office adds administrative costs that take money away from the security grants themselves, without specifying how much funding nonprofits will actually receive.
Critics say giving FEMA the power to stop states from closing their own application processes reduces state control over how federal grant programs are run in their communities.

117-hr-6871.one_liner: Change how the Department of Homeland Security buys goods and services
provisions: Gives the DHS Under Secretary for Management the job of overseeing all purchases and contracts for the department
Sets new rules for what the DHS money officer and technology officer must do when the department buys things
Creates a new office inside DHS called the Program Accountability and Risk Management Office to track spending and flag problems

supporters: Supporters say making the Under Secretary for Management the Chief Acquisition Officer puts one person in charge of all DHS contracts, which could reduce confusion about who is responsible for spending decisions.
Supporters say the new Program Accountability and Risk Management Office would track DHS spending and flag problems early, which could prevent cost overruns on large contracts.
Supporters say giving the DHS money officer and technology officer clear roles in purchasing decisions could help the department avoid buying systems that go over budget or do not work together.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set spending limits or timelines for the new Program Accountability and Risk Management Office, which makes it hard to know if the office will actually reduce waste.
Critics say adding a new office and shifting duties to the Under Secretary for Management could create more layers of bureaucracy without fixing the root causes of DHS procurement problems.
Critics say the bill does not require the department to report results to Congress, so there is no clear way to measure whether these changes improve how DHS spends money on contracts.

117-hr-6891.one_liner: Block Russian government officials from major international finance meetings
provisions: Tells the Treasury Department and the Federal Reserve to keep Russian government officials out of major international finance meetings, as much as legally possible.
This covers meetings like the World Bank, International Monetary Fund, Group of 20, and Bank for International Settlements.
This rule lasts up to five years.
It ends earlier once the President tells Congress Russia has stopped its actions against Ukraine and 30 days have passed.

supporters: Supporters say that keeping Russian government officials out of World Bank, IMF, G20, and Bank for International Settlements meetings would cut off their access to top global finance leaders while Russia continues actions against Ukraine.
Supporters say the rule includes a clear off-ramp — it ends 30 days after the President tells Congress that Russia has stopped trying to undermine Ukraine's sovereignty, so it is not permanent.
Supporters say directing both the Treasury Department and the Federal Reserve to act together gives the U.S. more power to enforce this exclusion across all four major international finance forums.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires exclusion 'to the maximum extent practicable,' which means Russian officials may still attend some meetings if the U.S. cannot block them under existing rules of these organizations.

Critics say removing Russia from G20 meetings for up to five years could make it harder for member countries to coordinate responses to global economic problems that affect all members, including the U.S.

Critics say the bill gives the President sole power to decide when Russia has met the conditions to end the exclusion, with no set standards in the bill for what 'ceased activities' against Ukraine actually means.

117-hr-6868.one_liner: Create a grant program to teach cybersecurity in K-12 schools
provisions: Lets a federal agency called CISA give money to schools, cities, colleges, and nonprofits to teach students about cybersecurity and how to stay safe online
Schools from kindergarten through 12th grade can apply for this money
States, local governments, colleges, and nonprofit groups can also apply for funding

supporters: Supporters say this bill lets CISA give money to K-12 schools, colleges, and nonprofits to teach students how to stay safe online, starting as early as kindergarten.
Supporters say opening the grants to states, local governments, and nonprofit groups means more communities can apply for funding, not just large school districts with more resources.
Supporters say teaching cybersecurity skills in K-12 schools helps build a pipeline of trained workers to fill jobs in a field that has a shortage of qualified people.
critics: Critics say the bill does not name a specific dollar amount for the grants, so schools and local governments cannot plan around how much funding they might actually receive.
Critics say letting a federal agency like CISA direct education programs at local K-12 schools shifts control away from states and school districts that already manage their own curricula.
Critics say the bill sets no clear rules for how grant recipients must report results, making it hard to measure whether the money improved student learning or school security.

117-hr-6899.one_liner: Block Russia and Belarus from exchanging their international reserve funds through the IMF
provisions: The U.S. Treasury cannot exchange or trade IMF reserve funds — called Special Drawing Rights — held by Russia or Belarus.
The U.S. must push other IMF member countries to also stop trading these reserve funds with Russia and Belarus.
U.S. representatives at the IMF must vote against giving Russia or Belarus any new reserve fund allocations.
These rules last for five years, or until Russia and Belarus stop acting against Ukraine's independence — whichever comes first.

supporters: Supporters say blocking the U.S. Treasury from trading Special Drawing Rights with Russia or Belarus cuts off a financial tool that could help Russia fund its actions against Ukraine.
Supporters say requiring U.S. representatives at the IMF to vote against any new SDR allocations to Russia or Belarus adds pressure by limiting their access to international reserve assets.
Supporters say the five-year limit with an early exit — if Russia and Belarus stop acting against Ukraine's independence — gives both countries a clear reason to change their behavior.
critics: Critics say the bill targets SDR exchanges but does not specify how much in SDR value Russia or Belarus currently hold, making it hard to measure the real financial impact.
Critics say pushing all IMF member countries to stop SDR transactions with Russia and Belarus may be difficult, since the U.S. cannot force other nations to follow its lead at the IMF.

Critics say the condition for ending the rules — the President reporting that Russia and Belarus have stopped destabilizing Ukraine — gives the executive branch broad power to decide when the restrictions end.

117-hr-6943.one_liner: Expand disability and death benefits for public safety officers to cover PTSD
provisions: Public safety officers — like police, firefighters, and paramedics — can now get disability payments for PTSD or acute stress disorder.
The condition must come from a traumatic event on the job.
Family members of officers who developed PTSD on duty and later died can receive death benefits.
This expands the Public Safety Officers' Benefits Program, which already covers death, disability, and education benefits for officers hurt or killed on duty.

supporters: Supporters say the bill lets police, firefighters, and paramedics qualify for PSOB disability payments when they develop PTSD or acute stress disorder from a traumatic event on the job — groups not previously covered under the program.
Supporters say family members of officers who developed PTSD on duty and later died can now receive PSOB death benefits, closing a gap that previously left those families without support.

Supporters say the bill adds PTSD and acute stress disorder to PSOB's list of covered disability conditions, putting them on the same eligibility footing as physical injuries already covered under the program.
critics: Critics say the bill does not define what counts as a 'stressful situation' that triggers eligibility, which could make it hard to decide which officers qualify for PSOB disability payments.
Critics say no cost estimate is included, so Congress does not know how much expanding PSOB to cover PTSD and acute stress disorder will cost the federal program.

Critics say proving that a mental health condition came specifically from a single on-duty event may be difficult, and the bill does not set a clear evidentiary standard for making that causation determination.

117-hr-700.one_liner: Rename a post office in Elwood, Illinois after Lawrence M. 'Larry' Walsh Sr.
provisions: Changes the official name of the post office at 303 East Mississippi Avenue in Elwood, Illinois to the "Lawrence M. 'Larry' Walsh Sr. Post Office".
The post office is located in Elwood, Illinois, a village in Will County.
The name honors Lawrence M. 'Larry' Walsh Sr., a local Illinois figure.
No changes are made to how the post office runs, its hours, or its services — this is a name-only change.
The U.S. Postal Service will update the official designation for this location.

117-hr-6961.one_liner: Change how the VA handles claims from veterans who experienced military sexual trauma
provisions: Requires every VA appeals board member to complete yearly training on military sexual trauma before they can decide those cases
Requires the VA to quickly identify when an appeal involves a military sexual trauma claim and whether the veteran asked for a hearing
Requires the VA to review the letters it sends to veterans when denying military sexual trauma claims and rewrite any language that could cause more harm
Requires outside medical providers who do exams for these claims to follow specific guidelines for working with trauma survivors

supporters: Supporters say requiring all BVA members to complete yearly MST training before they can be assigned these cases means veterans will have their appeals decided by someone who understands trauma, not just legal procedures.
Supporters say the rule to audit and rewrite denial letters will stop the VA from sending language that could hurt veterans a second time — a problem that currently has no formal process to fix.

Supporters say requiring outside medical providers to follow trauma-informed guidelines during MST exams gives veterans the same standard of care from contract doctors that they would expect from VA staff.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include any funding for the mandatory annual BVA training, which means the VA would need to pull money from its existing budget to train every board member each year.

Critics say the requirement that BVA members finish annual training before being assigned MST cases could reduce the number of members available to hear those appeals, making wait times longer for veterans.

Critics say the bill sets no deadline for the VA to complete its review and rewrite of denial letters, so there is no guarantee veterans will see any change to those letters within a specific amount of time.

117-hr-6930.one_liner: Let the President seize assets from wealthy people who supported Putin
provisions: For two years after this bill passes, the President can take assets worth more than $5 million from people whose wealth is tied to supporting or corrupt dealings with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The President can only use this power if Russia is still fighting a war in Ukraine and has already placed sanctions on the person for corruption, human rights violations, or actions related to the conflict.
Money from selling seized assets can only go to rebuilding Ukraine after the war, helping Ukrainian refugees, buying weapons for Ukraine's military, or helping the Russian people with aid.

supporters: Supporters say the bill only lets the President take assets worth over $5 million from people who already have U.S. sanctions for corruption, human rights violations, or actions tied to the conflict in Ukraine.

Supporters say money from sold assets can only be spent on rebuilding Ukraine after the war, helping Ukrainian refugees, buying weapons for Ukraine's uniformed military, or sending aid to the Russian people — not on unrelated programs.
Supporters say the two-year time limit and the requirement that Russia still be fighting in Ukraine put clear legal boundaries on when and how the President can use this power.
critics: Critics say the phrase 'derived in part' through support for Putin is broad enough that a President could target people with only a loose or indirect connection to Russia.
Critics say using seized assets to buy weapons for Ukraine's military means the U.S. government is directly funding an active armed conflict using property taken from private individuals.
Critics say seizing private assets — even from already-sanctioned people — could face legal challenges under U.S. due process protections and international property rights rules.

117-hr-7077.one_liner: Let the U.S. Fire Administration investigate major fires and release public reports
provisions: Lets the U.S. Fire Administration send investigators to major fires to find the cause and look at broader safety patterns.
Investigators can include safety specialists, fire engineers, codes experts, researchers, and fire training specialists.
All investigations must be done alongside the right local, state, and federal officials.
After each investigation, the agency must release a public report or contribute findings to another federal agency's report.
The agency can also send investigators to fires with unusual circumstances, even if the damage is less severe than a major fire.

supporters: Supporters say giving the U.S. Fire Administration power to send safety specialists, fire engineers, and codes experts to major fires will help find patterns that cause fires to spread or kill more people.
Supporters say requiring a public report after each investigation means local and state officials get findings they can use to update fire codes and training programs.
Supporters say allowing investigators to go to fires with unusual circumstances — even smaller ones — means dangerous new fire behaviors can be caught and studied before they cause a major disaster.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a budget or limit on how many investigations the agency can open, which could lead to federal investigators duplicating work already done by local fire marshals.
Critics say requiring coordination with local, state, and federal authorities on every investigation could slow down the process of getting findings to the public in time to prevent the next fire.
Critics say the bill gives the agency broad power to define what counts as a fire with 'unusual or remarkable context,' with no clear rules about when that standard is met.

117-hr-7153.one_liner: Require the VA to send Congress a plan for updating its benefits computer systems
provisions: The VA must send Congress a plan for updating the computer systems used to process veterans' benefits claims.
The plan must cover five years, starting in October 2025.
The Veterans Benefits Administration is the part of the VA that handles benefits claims — including disability pay and education support.
Congress receives this plan as a report only — the bill does not include any money to carry out the updates.

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires the VA to send Congress a written plan for updating the computer systems that process veterans' disability pay and education support claims, covering five fiscal years starting in October 2025.

Supporters say putting a five-year modernization plan in writing gives Congress a record to use when checking whether the Veterans Benefits Administration follows through on updates to its claims systems.
Supporters say the reporting requirement creates a starting point for future legislation that could add funding or deadlines for the Veterans Benefits Administration's IT updates.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include any money to carry out updates to the Veterans Benefits Administration's systems, so the VA has no funding to act on the plan it submits to Congress.
Critics say Congress receives the plan as a report only, meaning the Veterans Benefits Administration faces no legal requirement to implement any of the changes described.

Critics say a bill that spans five fiscal years but provides no budget or enforcement leaves veterans who depend on disability pay and education support with no assurance that the systems handling their claims will actually be updated.

117-hr-7066.one_liner: Make US financial companies apply Russia and Belarus sanctions to all businesses they own
provisions: US financial companies must follow all financial sanctions on Russia and Belarus.
Any business they own or control must follow those same sanctions.
Companies must take all steps available to make sure their subsidiaries comply.
