supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a loophole by requiring U.S. financial companies to make sure their foreign-owned subsidiaries follow the same Russia and Belarus sanctions — not just the U.S. parent company.
Supporters say that without this rule, U.S. banks could indirectly help Russia or Belarus move money through businesses they own or control overseas.
Supporters say the bill gives financial institutions clear legal responsibility to take all available steps to enforce compliance across their entire network.
critics: Critics say the bill puts the burden on U.S. financial companies to control the actions of foreign subsidiaries, which may operate under different national laws that conflict with U.S. sanctions rules.
Critics say the phrase 'all necessary and available actions' is vague and could expose banks to legal risk if a subsidiary fails to comply even after good-faith efforts.
Critics say smaller U.S. financial institutions with international holdings may not have the legal or operational resources to monitor and enforce compliance across every entity they own or control.

117-hr-7081.one_liner: Direct the U.S. to push for Ukraine to stop making debt payments
provisions: Tells the U.S. Treasury to contact major international lending groups and ask them to pause all loan payments Ukraine owes them
Tells the U.S. Treasury to work with other countries to get Ukraine's private and government lenders to also pause payments
Pushes for Ukraine to get lower-interest loans from international financial institutions during this period

supporters: Supporters say pausing Ukraine's loan payments to international lenders like the IMF and World Bank would stop debt obligations from draining funds that Ukraine needs to pay soldiers, keep hospitals open, and maintain power grids during the war.
Supporters say directing the U.S. Treasury to push private and government lenders to pause payments would give Ukraine breathing room without requiring the U.S. to spend new money directly.
Supporters say requiring lower-interest loans from international financial institutions would reduce the total amount Ukraine owes over time, making it easier to rebuild after the conflict ends.
critics: Critics say pausing payments to international lenders like the IMF could set a precedent that makes those institutions less willing to lend to other countries in the future.

Critics say the bill gives the Treasury broad authority to negotiate debt relief through country-to-country deals and agreements with groups of countries, but sets no clear limits on what the U.S. can promise on behalf of American taxpayers.

Critics say commercial lenders — private banks and bondholders — are not bound by U.S. law, so Treasury's push for voluntary payment pauses may produce little result while creating uncertainty in debt markets.

117-hr-7211.one_liner: Change how FEMA handles disaster aid requests for small states and rural areas
provisions: Gives FEMA's Small State and Rural Advocate new duties to help states gather and present information when asking for disaster aid
Requires the Government Accountability Office to review how FEMA decides whether to approve a governor's request for major disaster aid
The review focuses on requests for individual assistance, which is aid that goes directly to people affected by a disaster

supporters: Supporters say the expanded role of FEMA's Small State and Rural Advocate will help small states and rural communities better organize and present the data they need to qualify for major disaster declarations, which they often struggle to do without extra staff.

Supporters say requiring the Government Accountability Office to review how FEMA evaluates disaster declaration requests will make the process more transparent, especially for individual assistance that goes directly to affected residents.

Supporters say rural areas are often denied disaster aid because they cannot show localized damage as clearly as large urban areas, and this bill directly addresses that gap by giving states a dedicated helper at FEMA.
critics: Critics say the bill adds new duties to FEMA's Small State and Rural Advocate without providing new funding or staff, which could slow down disaster response rather than improve it.

Critics say a Government Accountability Office review of FEMA's disaster declaration process could take years to complete, meaning any fixes to how individual assistance requests are evaluated would come too late for communities currently waiting on aid.

Critics say the bill focuses on the application process but does not change the actual standards FEMA uses to approve or deny requests, so small states and rural communities may still face the same barriers even with better-prepared paperwork.

117-hr-7334.one_liner: Give the government 10 years to pursue COVID loan fraud cases
provisions: The government has 10 years from the date of the fraud to bring criminal charges against someone who cheated on a COVID disaster loan
The government also has 10 years to sue in civil court to recover money lost to COVID disaster loan fraud
Before this bill, the default time limit to bring most federal fraud cases was 5 years
This applies to loans made through the COVID-19 Economic Injury Disaster Loan program, which gave out over $390 billion to businesses during the pandemic

supporters: Supporters say the 10-year window gives investigators enough time to find and prosecute fraud in the $390 billion COVID disaster loan program, since many fraud cases take years to uncover.
Supporters say doubling the time limit from 5 to 10 years lets the government recover more stolen money through civil court, instead of letting fraudsters keep funds after the old deadline runs out.
Supporters say COVID-19 EIDL fraud was large-scale and complex, so the standard 5-year limit was not enough time to build cases against everyone who cheated the program.
critics: Critics say a 10-year statute of limitations means businesses and individuals could face criminal charges or lawsuits a decade after receiving a COVID loan, creating long-term legal uncertainty for borrowers.

Critics say extending the deadline to 10 years could lead to prosecutions based on old records that are hard to find or verify, making it harder for defendants to prove they followed the rules at the time.
Critics say the longer window may be used against small business owners who made honest mistakes on loan applications, not just those who committed clear fraud.

117-hr-7311.one_liner: Require the State Department to report to Congress a plan on countering Russia in Africa
provisions: The State Department must write a plan explaining what the U.S. is doing to limit Russia's influence in Africa and send it to Congress.
After the first report, the department must send Congress an update every year.
The law covers Russia's government, military, intelligence agencies, private military companies, and other groups working on Russia's behalf in Africa.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the State Department to write a strategy and send it to Congress creates clear accountability for U.S. efforts against Russia's military, intelligence agencies, and private military companies operating in Africa.
Supporters say the yearly updates to Congress will let lawmakers check whether U.S. actions are actually reducing Russian influence in Africa over time.
Supporters say covering all groups working on Russia's behalf — including private military companies — closes gaps that would let Russia use unofficial forces to avoid U.S. oversight.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires the State Department to write reports but does not require any specific actions or add any funding to actually stop Russian military or intelligence activity in Africa.
Critics say sharing a strategy and yearly updates with Congress could expose U.S. counter-tactics to Russia, making those tactics easier to work around.

Critics say the bill does not set a firm deadline for the first report, which means the State Department could delay putting a plan in place to address Russian private military companies and other groups.

117-hr-7276.one_liner: Require the President to report to Congress on war crimes in Ukraine
provisions: Requires the President to send Congress a report on atrocities that have happened during Russia's invasion of Ukraine since February 24, 2022.
The report must describe what the U.S. government has done to collect and save evidence of war crimes.
The report must describe efforts to make Russian citizens, soldiers, and leaders aware that people are being identified for prosecution.
The report must explain how courts — in the U.S., other countries, or international — can get evidence from the U.S. government.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the President to report on evidence collected since February 24, 2022 gives Congress a way to check whether the U.S. is actually documenting war crimes committed during Russia's invasion.

Supporters say the part of the bill that explains how foreign and international courts can get evidence from the U.S. government would make it easier to bring cases against Russian soldiers and leaders responsible for atrocities.

Supporters say running information campaigns aimed at Russian soldiers and political leaders — as required by the bill — could reduce future crimes by making clear that people are being identified for prosecution.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires a report and does not create any new funding, courts, or legal tools to actually prosecute those responsible for war crimes.
Critics say the provision requiring the U.S. to explain how foreign or international courts can obtain its evidence could expose intelligence sources and methods used to collect that evidence.
Critics say public diplomacy efforts targeting Russian citizens and military, as described in the bill, could make future diplomatic talks between the U.S. and Russia harder to conduct.

117-hr-7314.one_liner: Require regular reports on whether China is helping Russia fight in Ukraine
provisions: The State Department must regularly report to Congress on whether China's government, Communist Party, or companies are helping Russia in Ukraine.
The reports must say whether China is helping Russia avoid financial penalties or restrictions on buying certain goods and technology.
The reports must cover whether China is giving Russia technology to use in its military or spy programs.
The reports must also say whether China is helping Russia spread false stories or propaganda.

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires the State Department to report to Congress on whether China's government, Communist Party, or companies are helping Russia avoid financial penalties and buying restrictions, giving lawmakers specific facts to decide next steps.
Supporters say the reports must cover whether China is sending Russia technology for its military or spy programs, letting Congress track weapons-related transfers tied to the war in Ukraine.
Supporters say requiring reports on China's role in spreading false stories gives Congress a record of propaganda activity it can use to respond.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires reports and sets no mandatory action if China's government, Communist Party, or companies are found helping Russia evade sanctions or get military technology.
Critics say the reports may be incomplete because China is not required to share information and may hide transfers of money, goods, or technology to Russia.
Critics say regularly publishing reports accusing China's government and companies of helping Russia could push China to take more open steps in support of Russia's military.

117-hr-7309.one_liner: Renew and expand job training, youth employment, and adult education programs
provisions: Keeps job training programs funded through 2028
Raises the share of business leaders required on state and local workforce boards from 20% to 30%
Creates paid job programs for young people that include job-skills training and mentoring
Expands Job Corps, a free job training program, to serve more people in U.S. territories and removes some age limits
Gives grants to groups of employers in the same industry to build more job training programs
Lets people with criminal records get job training help through new grants focused on reducing repeat offenses
Expands English literacy and job-skills classes to U.S. territories like the Northern Mariana Islands and American Samoa

supporters: Supporters say raising the share of business leaders on workforce boards from 20% to 30% means employers will have more say in shaping job training programs, making workers better matched to real jobs.
Supporters say the new paid youth job programs include job-skills training and mentoring, giving young people work experience and income at the same time.
Supporters say expanding Job Corps to U.S. territories like the Northern Mariana Islands and American Samoa gives people in those areas access to free job training they did not have before.
critics: Critics say requiring states to cover one-stop center costs out of their WIOA funding allocations could reduce the money available for direct job training services to workers.
Critics say eliminating the Selective Service compliance check for WIOA participants removes an existing legal requirement that applied to all federally funded training programs.

Critics say the grants for people with criminal records create a separate track for justice-involved youth, and it is not clear how outcomes will be measured or how funding will be divided between this group and other job seekers.

117-hr-7335.one_liner: Require the VA to coordinate support resources for veterans filing military sexual trauma claims
provisions: Veterans filing a military sexual trauma claim can choose to receive support materials during the process.
Those materials include the Veterans Crisis Line number, mental health appointment info, and other MST help resources.
For veterans who sign up for the notification system, the VA alerts health staff before any exam, hearing, or related event.
The VA also alerts health staff before the veteran gets a final decision on their claim.
The VA must include these support materials with the final decision it sends to the veteran.

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires VA health staff to be notified before a veteran attends a medical exam or hearing related to their MST claim, so mental health support can be ready at those high-stress moments.

Supporters say veterans will receive the Veterans Crisis Line number and mental health appointment information with their final claim decision, giving them direct access to help when they learn the outcome of their case.
Supporters say veterans who sign up for the notification system get an extra layer of protection because VHA staff are alerted ahead of every key step in the claims process, not just at the end.
critics: Critics say the automatic notification system only covers veterans who are enrolled in VA health care and who choose to opt in, meaning MST claimants who use outside health care or do not consent get no advance coordination.

Critics say the bill requires the VA to send materials and notifications but does not add mental health staff or funding, so veterans referred to VA mental health care may still face long wait times for appointments.

Critics say the bill does not set a timeline for how far in advance VBA must notify VHA before an exam or hearing, which could limit how useful the warning is for health staff trying to prepare support.

117-hr-7500.one_liner: Let the VA build and upgrade specific medical facilities for veterans in 2022
provisions: The VA gets approval to build or make major upgrades to specific medical facilities for veterans during 2022.
Each facility is named individually in the bill — only those specific locations are included, not VA buildings across the country.
The bill sets a dollar cap on each project so the VA cannot spend more than the listed amount on any one job.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives the VA formal approval to move forward on specific medical facility projects, which are required by law before construction money can be spent.
Supporters say setting a dollar cap on each named project protects taxpayers by preventing the VA from going over budget on any single job.
Supporters say listing each facility by name ensures that only high-priority locations get funded, rather than spreading money thin across all VA buildings.
critics: Critics say the bill covers only a small number of named locations, leaving veterans at VA facilities not on the list without upgraded care during 2022.
Critics say the spending caps on each project may be set too low to cover rising construction costs, which could delay or shrink the planned upgrades.
Critics say the bill does not include oversight rules to make sure the VA actually finishes each project on time or reports back to Congress on progress.

117-hr-7375.one_liner: Let the VA send education payments electronically to colleges outside the US
provisions: The Department of Veterans Affairs must update its payment system to send GI Bill and other education money directly to foreign colleges by electronic transfer
Right now, some foreign schools cannot receive VA payments because they lack a US tax ID or a US bank account — this bill fixes that
Veterans attending approved programs at foreign schools would get their education money sent faster and more reliably

supporters: Supporters say veterans enrolled in VA-approved programs at foreign schools currently face payment delays because those schools have no US tax ID or US bank account, and this bill would fix that gap by letting the VA send money by electronic transfer.
Supporters say the update would make GI Bill payments reach foreign schools faster and more reliably, so veterans do not have to cover tuition costs out of pocket while waiting for checks.
Supporters say the bill only applies to foreign schools already approved to offer VA-covered courses, so no new schools gain access — it just changes how approved ones get paid.
critics: Critics say sending VA education funds to foreign banks makes it harder for the VA to track whether money is used correctly, since those institutions are outside US financial oversight.
Critics say the bill does not set rules for how the VA should verify a foreign school's identity before sending electronic payments, which could create risk of funds going to the wrong place.
Critics say veterans attending foreign schools make up a small share of GI Bill users, so the cost of updating the VA payment system may not be worth the number of people who would benefit.

117-hr-7372.one_liner: Create a working group to study the war in Ukraine's impact on semiconductor supply chains
provisions: A group of federal agencies will work together to study how Russia's attack on Ukraine has affected semiconductor materials.
The group will report to Congress on shortages of materials like palladium, neon gas, and helium.
The group will study how the war has affected global supply chains and the world economy.
The group will give Congress steps it can take to protect the supply of these materials.
Each year, the group will report to Congress on world events that could disrupt semiconductor supply chains.

supporters: Supporters say the interagency working group will give Congress specific data on shortages of palladium, neon gas, and helium — materials that chip makers need — so lawmakers can act on real information instead of guessing.
Supporters say the required annual reports on world events will alert Congress early when new conflicts or crises could cut off semiconductor supply chains before shortages get severe.
Supporters say the group will recommend exact steps Congress can take to protect material supplies, giving lawmakers a clear action list rather than a broad problem with no solutions.
critics: Critics say the bill only creates a study group and requires reports — it does not change any laws, spend any money, or directly protect the supply of palladium, neon gas, or helium.
Critics say the bill focuses its study on Russia's attack on Ukraine, but semiconductor materials come from many countries, so the scope may miss other supply chain risks.
Critics say Congress already has access to agency reports on supply chain issues, and adding another working group may duplicate work already being done by existing federal bodies.

117-hr-7352.one_liner: Give prosecutors 10 years to charge fraud on COVID small business loans
provisions: Gives the government up to 10 years to charge someone with fraud on a Paycheck Protection Program loan
The PPP gave out over $800 billion in loans to businesses during COVID-19 to help keep workers paid
Before this bill, the window to bring fraud charges was shorter, which meant some cases could expire before investigators finished their work
Covers both criminal charges and civil cases where the government tries to get money back

supporters: Supporters say giving investigators up to 10 years to file charges means more PPP fraud cases can be fully investigated before the deadline runs out, since the program handed out over $800 billion in loans.
Supporters say the bill covers both criminal charges and civil cases, which gives the government more tools to pursue fraudsters and recover money.
Supporters say a longer enforcement period increases the chance the government can recover fraudulently obtained funds from borrowers who misused PPP loans.
critics: Critics say a 10-year window means the millions of businesses that took PPP loans could face legal risk for a decade, making it harder for them to know when they are in the clear.

Critics say applying the same 10-year deadline to both criminal and civil cases treats all PPP borrowers the same, even though many businesses made small paperwork errors rather than committing intentional fraud.
Critics say that over 10 years, business records and witnesses can become hard to find, making it difficult for borrowers to defend themselves against civil or criminal fraud claims.

117-hr-7667.one_liner: Renew FDA fees and add rules for drug trials and supply chains
provisions: Keeps the FDA's fee programs running through 2027 — these fees are paid by drug and device companies and fund FDA reviews
Requires drug makers to create plans to include more types of people in their medical trials
Requires the FDA to tell generic drug makers, if asked, whether their drug has the same ingredients in the same amounts as the brand-name version
Renews programs that support the development of drugs and devices for children
Sets new rules for checking drug factories and for studies companies must do after a drug is approved
Adds rules for using real-world patient data to help get drugs and devices approved

supporters: Supporters say renewing the FDA's fee programs through 2027 keeps drug and device reviews funded without using taxpayer money, since companies — not the public — pay those fees.

Supporters say requiring drug makers to create plans for including more types of people in clinical trials means that drugs get tested on patients who look more like the real population that will use them.

Supporters say the rule requiring the FDA to tell generic drug makers if their product has the same ingredients in the same amounts as the brand-name version helps more low-cost generics reach patients faster.
critics: Critics say the fee programs through 2027 give large drug and device companies too much influence over the FDA reviews that are supposed to regulate them, since the agency depends on their payments to operate.

Critics say the clinical trial diversity plans only require companies to create and report plans — not to actually meet any enrollment targets — so the rule may not change who gets included in trials.
Critics say the new rules for post-approval studies and real-world data could let companies use less rigorous evidence to get drugs approved, which may raise safety risks for patients.

117-hr-7666.one_liner: Renew and expand federal funding for mental health and addiction programs through 2027
provisions: Keeps funding going through 2027 for mental health programs that serve children, communities, and people with addiction.
Removes the rule that required people to be addicted to opioids for at least one year before they could enter a treatment program.
Adds support for helping people find stable housing while they recover from addiction.
Funds programs to find and treat eating disorders and maternal depression.
Expands mental health services for Native American tribal communities.
Checks that employer-run insurance plans follow federal rules requiring equal coverage for mental and physical health.
Funds programs that add mental health care to regular doctor visits.

supporters: Supporters say removing the one-year wait rule for opioid treatment programs will let people get help sooner, before their addiction gets worse.

Supporters say funding through 2027 for the Community Mental Health Services Block Grant and Substance Abuse Prevention and Treatment Block Grant will keep services running for children with serious emotional disturbances and adults in recovery.
Supporters say requiring employer-run insurance plans to cover mental health the same as physical health will close gaps that left many workers without access to therapy or addiction care.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set specific funding amounts for tribal mental health programs, which could leave Native American communities with less support than promised.
Critics say adding mental health screening inside regular doctor visits may strain primary care offices that are already short on staff, without enough new providers to meet the added demand.

Critics say the bill reauthorizes programs through 2027 without requiring agencies to report clear outcome data, making it hard to know if the spending is actually reducing addiction or improving mental health.

117-hr-7622.one_liner: Require small business development centers to offer apprenticeship and job training help
provisions: More than 900 Small Business Development Centers around the country give free or low-cost help to people starting or growing a small business.
This bill adds apprenticeships and work-based learning programs to the list of services every center must offer.
Work-based learning means programs where people learn job skills by doing real work — like apprenticeships, internships, or on-the-job training tied to a small business.

supporters: Supporters say that requiring all 900+ Small Business Development Centers to offer apprenticeship and work-based learning help will make it easier for small business owners to find trained workers without paying for expensive outside recruiters.

Supporters say that adding work-based learning services to the required list means small businesses in every state will have access to free or low-cost help setting up on-the-job training programs, which they currently have to figure out on their own.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include any new funding, so the 900+ Small Business Development Centers will have to offer these new apprenticeship services using the same budgets they already have, which may reduce time spent on other services.
Critics say the bill does not define clear standards for what counts as a qualifying work-based learning program, which could lead to uneven quality of help across different centers.

117-hr-7664.one_liner: Tell small business centers to help hire and support career and technical education graduates
provisions: Tells Small Business Development Centers and Women's Business Centers to help small businesses hire graduates from career and technical education programs.
Also tells both types of centers to help those graduates start their own small businesses.

supporters: Supporters say Small Business Development Centers and Women's Business Centers already help small businesses hire workers, so adding career and technical education graduates to their mission costs little and connects trained workers to jobs that need them.
Supporters say helping career and technical education graduates start their own small businesses gives a clear path for people who learned a trade but do not want to work for someone else.
Supporters say small businesses often struggle to find workers with hands-on skills, and this bill directs existing centers to actively match those businesses with graduates who have those skills.
critics: Critics say the bill adds new responsibilities to Small Business Development Centers and Women's Business Centers without providing extra funding, which could stretch their staff and reduce the quality of help they already give.

Critics say career and technical education programs vary widely by state and school, so without a standard definition in the bill, centers may not know which graduates qualify for this new assistance.
Critics say the bill does not set any goals or ways to measure whether the new matching efforts between small businesses and career and technical education graduates are actually working.

117-hr-7606.one_liner: Create a federal office to investigate unfair practices in the meat and poultry industry
provisions: Creates a new office inside the Department of Agriculture to look into whether meat companies and poultry dealers are breaking competition rules.
Gives the office the power to use subpoenas — legal orders that force companies to hand over documents or answer questions.
The office can take companies to court or start formal government actions against them for breaking the rules.
The office works with the Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission when competition problems come up in food and farming.
The office also talks with the Department of Homeland Security about safety risks in the food supply chain.
The office must hire lawyers and other experts to do this work.

supporters: Supporters say the new Office of the Special Investigator can use subpoenas to force large meat and poultry companies to hand over documents, giving the government a stronger tool to catch price-fixing that drives up food costs for families.

Supporters say the office will work directly with the Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission, so competition violations in the meat and poultry industry are investigated by multiple agencies at once instead of falling through the cracks.

Supporters say requiring the office to hire lawyers and competition experts means the government will have trained staff dedicated full-time to holding packers and live poultry dealers accountable under the Packers and Stockyards Act of 1921.
critics: Critics say creating a new office inside the Department of Agriculture adds government staff and overhead costs when existing agencies like the Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission already have the power to investigate meat and poultry companies.

Critics say giving one new office the authority to bring civil and administrative actions against packers — separate from the DOJ — could lead to duplicate investigations that create legal confusion for companies and slow down the process.
Critics say the bill does not set a budget limit or staff cap for the new office, which means Congress has no clear control over how much the office will spend on lawyers, experts, and legal actions.

117-hr-7670.one_liner: Require the Small Business Administration to report on contracts given to women-owned small businesses
provisions: The Small Business Administration must report how many contracts were given to women-owned small businesses.
The report must also include the total dollar amount of those contracts.
The Women-Owned Small Business Federal Contracting program sets aside some government contracts for businesses that are at least 51% owned and run by women.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the SBA to report the number and total dollar amount of contracts given to women-owned small businesses will let Congress check if the program is actually reaching its goals.
Supporters say this reporting will show whether businesses that are at least 51% owned and run by women are getting a fair share of federal contracts set aside for them.
Supporters say public data on contract totals will help women business owners and advocacy groups spot gaps in how the program is working.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires reporting and does not fix any problems found in how contracts are awarded to women-owned small businesses.
Critics say adding a new reporting requirement puts more paperwork on the SBA without giving the agency more staff or funding to handle it.
Critics say the bill does not set a minimum dollar amount or number of contracts the program must reach, so the reports may show problems but trigger no action.

117-hr-7790.one_liner: Give the FDA $28 million to fix the baby formula shortage
provisions: Gives the FDA $28 million in emergency money to respond to the shortage of baby formula.
The money can also be used to prevent future shortages of baby formula and medical foods.
Some of the money goes toward stopping fake or fraudulent baby formula from entering the U.S. market.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives the FDA $28 million in emergency funds to respond to the shortage of infant formula in the U.S., which affected families across the country.
Supporters say the funding can be used to prevent future shortages of baby formula and certain medical foods, not just the current crisis.
Supporters say part of the $28 million is set aside to stop fake or unsafe baby formula from entering the U.S. market, protecting infants from products that could harm them.
critics: Critics say the $28 million goes to the FDA, but the agency already has authority to inspect infant formula manufacturers and did not use that authority to prevent the shortage before it began.

Critics say the bill does not require steps to diversify who makes infant formula in the U.S., meaning a single plant closure — like the Abbott Nutrition facility in Sturgis, Michigan, which was shut down in February 2022 — could cause another shortage.
Critics say giving the FDA more money does not address the slow pace of FDA reviews that delayed foreign formula from entering the U.S. market during the shortage, which the bill does not change.

117-hr-7688.one_liner: Ban fuel price gouging during declared energy emergencies
provisions: During a declared energy emergency, sellers cannot charge prices that are unreasonably high for gas or other fuels.
The price must also show the seller is taking advantage of the emergency to count as price gouging.
The President can declare an energy emergency and set which fuels and areas are covered, and for how long.
The Federal Trade Commission can take sellers to court and fine them for breaking this rule.
State attorneys general can also enforce this rule in their states.
Fines collected from violators go to a program that helps low-income households pay their heating and cooling bills.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects consumers by letting the FTC fine sellers who charge prices that are far higher than normal for gas or other fuels during a declared energy emergency.
Supporters say the President can quickly define which fuels and areas are covered, so the rule targets the right sellers in the right places.
Supporters say fines collected from violators go directly to the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, which helps low-income households pay heating and cooling bills.
critics: Critics say the rule against prices that are far higher than normal is vague, and sellers may not know when they have crossed the line until the FTC takes them to court.
Critics say giving the President power to declare an energy emergency and set which fuels and areas are covered creates room for the rule to be applied unevenly across states.
Critics say that capping fuel prices during a shortage can discourage suppliers from moving more fuel into the affected area, which could make the shortage last longer.

117-hr-7777.one_liner: Create free cybersecurity training for workers who protect industrial systems
provisions: Sets up a free training program inside the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) for workers who protect industrial systems from hackers
The training covers systems that run factories, power plants, water treatment, and other industrial operations
Workers in the cybersecurity field can take the training at no cost

supporters: Supporters say the free training through CISA will help close the shortage of workers who know how to protect industrial control systems like power plants and water treatment facilities from cyberattacks.

Supporters say that because the training costs workers nothing, smaller companies and local governments that run industrial systems but cannot afford private training will be able to improve their cybersecurity skills.

Supporters say that factories, power grids, and water systems are high-value targets for hackers, and giving the cybersecurity workforce hands-on training specific to these systems reduces the risk of a major attack.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a specific funding amount, which makes it unclear whether CISA will have enough resources to run the program without cutting other cybersecurity efforts.

Critics say the bill does not set any standards for who qualifies as part of the 'cybersecurity workforce,' which could limit access for workers in industries like manufacturing who also need this training but may not be counted.

Critics say the program is run entirely within CISA without requiring input or coordination from the private companies that actually operate these industrial systems, which may mean the training does not match real-world needs.

117-hr-7694.one_liner: Require federal agencies to favor contractors who use small businesses as subcontractors
provisions: When the government picks a company to do a job, it must look at how much of that work the company plans to give to small businesses.
Companies bidding on government contracts must submit a plan showing how much work small businesses will get.
Federal agencies must use that small business plan as one factor when deciding who wins the contract.

supporters: Supporters say that requiring federal agencies to weigh a company's small business subcontracting plan when picking a contract winner gives small businesses a real shot at more federal work, not just a promise on paper.
Supporters say the bill closes a gap where companies could submit small business plans but agencies were not required to treat those plans as a factor in who wins, meaning the plans had no teeth.
Supporters say small businesses that cannot win a prime contract directly can still get steady work as subcontractors if agencies are required to reward bidders who commit more work to them.
critics: Critics say making small business subcontracting plans a required evaluation factor could push agencies to pick a contractor who scores well on that plan but is not the best value or lowest cost for the government.

Critics say the bill does not set a minimum percentage of work that must go to small businesses, so agencies and contractors may still interpret the requirement in widely different ways with little accountability.
Critics say larger contractors may write ambitious subcontracting plans to win the contract but face no clear penalty if they do not follow through on those commitments after the award.

117-hr-903.one_liner: Give TSA airport security workers the same job rights as other federal employees
provisions: TSA workers currently operate under a separate set of rules that gives them fewer job protections than most other federal workers. This bill moves them onto the same system used by the rest of the federal government within 180 days.
Workers keep their current pay rates, vacation time, and other rights during the switch.
The TSA must work with the workers' union during the transition.
Bans TSA workers from putting TikTok on government phones.
Requires TSA to hire more veterans, including those with disabilities.
Requires TSA to give workers clear guidance on how to protect themselves from COVID-19.
TSA must talk with groups connected to the Federal Air Marshal Service about issues facing air marshals, including mental health and suicide rates.

supporters: Supporters say moving TSA workers onto the same rules used by all other federal employees within 180 days would give them access to a federal appeals board and stronger job protections they currently do not have.
Supporters say the bill protects workers during the switch by keeping their current pay rates, vacation time, and other rights in place.

Supporters say requiring TSA to consult with the workers' union and prioritize hiring veterans, including those with disabilities, gives workers and military families a stronger voice in how the agency is run.
critics: Critics say shifting roughly 60,000 TSA workers to standard federal employee rules within 180 days may move too fast for the agency to update contracts, pay systems, and job classifications without errors.

Critics say the bill bundles unrelated items — like a TikTok ban on government phones and COVID-19 guidance requirements — into a single workforce bill, making it harder to pass or reject each issue on its own merits.

Critics say the bill does not set a funding level for the pay and benefits changes, leaving open the question of whether Congress will provide enough money to cover the cost of bringing TSA workers up to the same standard as other federal employees.

117-hr-7910.one_liner: Add new gun rules covering sales to people under 21, ghost guns, and large magazines
provisions: Stops the sale of certain semi-automatic rifles and shotguns to anyone under 21 years old
Creates new federal crimes for selling or moving guns illegally across state lines
Requires guns built at home without serial numbers to be registered and tracked like store-bought guns
Sets rules for how gun owners must store firearms in their homes
Puts bump stocks — devices that make a gun fire faster — under the same rules as other regulated weapons
Bans the import, sale, making, and ownership of magazines that hold large amounts of ammunition

supporters: Supporters say raising the purchase age for certain semi-automatic rifles and shotguns to 21 would keep these guns away from teenagers, who they say are responsible for many school shootings.
Supporters say requiring home-built guns to be registered and tracked like store-bought guns closes a gap that lets people skip background checks entirely.
Supporters say placing bump stocks under federal firearms rules targets a device used in the 2017 Las Vegas shooting, where a gunman killed 60 people by firing at a much faster rate.
critics: Critics say the bill's ban on importing, selling, and owning large-capacity magazines would make millions of gun owners into criminals for possessing equipment they bought legally.
Critics say the federal home storage rules would require gun owners to lock up their firearms, which they say slows access in a home self-defense situation.
Critics say raising the purchase age for semi-automatic rifles to 21 removes a right that 18-to-20-year-olds currently hold under federal law, including active military members.

117-hr-847.one_liner: Direct the National Science Foundation to support research on technology that protects digital privacy
provisions: The National Science Foundation is directed to support research on technology that protects digital privacy, chosen through a merit review and competition.
Existing grants for computer security research can now also cover privacy technology and keeping data confidential.
A federal program must send Congress a report on how far privacy technology research has come and what voluntary guides or resources exist.

supporters: Supporters say directing the National Science Foundation to fund merit-reviewed research on privacy enhancing technologies will push forward new tools that protect personal data online.
Supporters say expanding existing computer security grants to also cover privacy technology and data confidentiality means more research can happen without needing new standalone funding.
Supporters say requiring a federal report to Congress on the progress of privacy technology research will help lawmakers track what tools exist and where gaps remain.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a specific funding amount for privacy research, so there is no guarantee the National Science Foundation will receive enough money to make a real impact.
Critics say the bill only calls for voluntary guides and resources, which means companies are not required to use or follow any privacy standards that come out of the research.
Critics say a progress report to Congress does not create any enforcement power, so the findings may not lead to actual policy changes or protections for users.

117-hr-91.one_liner: Name a post office in Easley, South Carolina after Private First Class Barrett Lyle Austin
provisions: This bill gives an official name to the post office at 810 South Pendleton Street in Easley, South Carolina.
The building will be called the "Private First Class Barrett Lyle Austin Post Office Building."
Private First Class is the third enlisted rank in the U.S. Army — one step above the basic rank of Private.

117-hr-7791.one_liner: Give the USDA power to fix baby formula shortages for low-income families
provisions: Lets the USDA step in during emergencies to help families in WIC, a federal food program for low-income mothers and babies.
Requires companies with WIC formula contracts to have a plan for keeping families supplied if their product is recalled.
Requires the USDA to set up a written agreement with the Department of Health and Human Services within 30 days.
The agreement covers how the two agencies share information during formula shortages or recalls.
Lets the USDA temporarily waive WIC rules during emergencies — for example, lifting the monthly limit on how much formula a family can get.
Requires the USDA and state agencies to notify each other when formula supply problems happen.

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires formula companies that hold WIC contracts to have a recall plan in place, so the roughly 7 million low-income mothers and babies in the WIC program are not left without formula if a product is pulled from shelves.
Supporters say the USDA can temporarily lift the monthly limit on how much formula a WIC family can receive during a shortage, giving families access to more formula when store supplies run low.

Supporters say the 30-day deadline for a written agreement between USDA and the Department of Health and Human Services means the two agencies must have a clear plan for sharing information before the next shortage hits.
critics: Critics say the bill only protects families who are enrolled in WIC, leaving out the roughly half of U.S. infants whose families do not qualify for the program and who also faced empty shelves during the 2022 shortage.

Critics say the authority to waive 'any WIC qualified administrative requirement' is broad, and without clear time limits on those waivers, temporary rule changes could stay in place longer than intended.

Critics say requiring formula manufacturers to add recall response plans to their WIC contracts could raise the cost of winning those contracts, which may reduce competition among suppliers and drive up prices over time.

117-hres-1023.one_liner: Set rules for how the House handles the January 6th Committee report
provisions: Sets the steps the House follows to debate and vote on the January 6th Committee's report
Controls how much time members can speak and what changes can be made during the debate
Applies only to this one report from the committee that investigated the January 6th attack

supporters: Supporters say this resolution gives every House member a set amount of time to speak about the January 6th Committee's report, so no one side can block or delay the debate.
Supporters say the rules apply only to this one report from the committee that investigated the January 6th attack, keeping the process focused and limited in scope.
Supporters say by setting the debate rules in advance, the House can move to a final vote without procedural delays that would otherwise require a separate vote to waive.
critics: Critics say limiting how long members can speak and what changes they can propose cuts off the ability of some lawmakers to offer amendments or raise concerns about the January 6th Committee's report.

Critics say applying a special rule to the January 6th Committee's report — instead of using the House's standard floor process — gives leadership too much control over what can and cannot be debated.
Critics say the rule restricts the full House from shaping the report's consideration, since only the Select Committee directed what would be included in the resolution.

117-hr-92.one_liner: Name a post office in Pickens, South Carolina after Specialist Four Charles Johnson
provisions: A post office at 110 Johnson Street in Pickens, South Carolina will be officially named the 'Specialist Four Charles Johnson Post Office'.
The name honors Charles Johnson, who held the military rank of Specialist Four.
This is a naming-only action — no money is spent and no rules change.

supporters: Supporters say the bill honors Charles Johnson's military service by giving the post office at 110 Johnson Street in Pickens, South Carolina his name and rank of Specialist Four.
Supporters say this is a naming-only action — no federal money is spent and no postal rules change — making it a low-cost way for Congress to recognize a local servicemember.
critics: Critics say Congress spends floor time on naming bills like this one instead of passing laws that change policy or spending, which some members argue is a poor use of limited legislative hours.

Critics say commemorative naming bills follow no standard criteria for who qualifies, so there is no public process to explain why the post office at 110 Johnson Street was chosen to honor Specialist Four Charles Johnson over others.

117-hr-923.one_liner: Impose sanctions on people who commit human rights abuses in Russian-occupied parts of Georgia
provisions: The President must block the U.S. entry and freeze the U.S. assets of people found responsible for human rights abuses in two regions of Georgia that Russia occupies: Abkhazia and South Ossetia.
Every 180 days, the President must send Congress a list of those people.
The State Department must report to Congress on what military help the U.S. gives Georgia and how well Georgia can defend itself.
The State Department must report on cybersecurity work the U.S. and Georgia do together.
The State Department must report on a plan to help Georgia fight false information spread by Russia.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would protect people living in Abkhazia and South Ossetia by blocking the U.S. entry and freezing the U.S. assets of anyone found responsible for human rights abuses in those Russian-occupied regions.
Supporters say requiring a report to Congress every 180 days on sanctioned individuals would hold the President accountable and keep lawmakers informed about who is being targeted.

Supporters say the State Department reports on U.S. military aid, cybersecurity cooperation, and a plan to counter Russian disinformation would give Congress a clearer picture of Georgia's ability to defend itself.
critics: Critics say that imposing entry bans and asset freezes on foreign persons tied to Russia could increase tensions with Moscow and risk drawing the U.S. deeper into the conflict in Georgia.
Critics say the bill does not include funding or a timeline for the disinformation strategy, making it unclear whether the plan to help Georgia fight Russian propaganda would ever be carried out.
Critics say the 180-day reporting requirement on sanctioned individuals may be too infrequent to respond quickly if conditions in Abkhazia or South Ossetia get worse.

117-hres-1033.one_liner: Set the rules for debating a bill to add money to the restaurant relief fund
provisions: This rule sets the terms for how the House will debate and vote on H.R. 3807.
H.R. 3807 would add money to the Restaurant Revitalization Fund, which was created in 2021 to help restaurants that lost money during COVID-19.
The fund was originally given $28.6 billion, but more restaurants applied than there was money available, leaving many without aid.

supporters: Supporters say the original Restaurant Revitalization Fund was given $28.6 billion, but so many restaurants applied that the money ran out before all qualifying businesses could receive aid, leaving owners who followed the rules with nothing.

Supporters say this rule allows the House to debate and vote on H.R. 3807, which would give restaurants that lost income during COVID-19 a second chance to receive funds they were eligible for but never got.

Supporters say small restaurant owners — a group that includes many minority and independent operators — applied on time and were denied only because the fund ran dry, and this bill would fix that gap.
critics: Critics say adding more money to the Restaurant Revitalization Fund means new federal spending on a program from 2021, at a time when Congress is debating how to reduce the deficit.

Critics say the rule limits how long the House can debate H.R. 3807, which reduces the time members have to review how any new funds would be distributed and whether the same restaurants that missed out in 2021 would actually be prioritized.
Critics say the original $28.6 billion program had reports of fraud and mismanagement, and they argue Congress should audit how that money was spent before adding more to the same fund.

117-hr-935.one_liner: Let certain business sale brokers skip federal registration rules
provisions: Brokers who help sell privately owned businesses do not have to register with federal securities regulators if the company they are selling earns below a set dollar amount
This applies only to brokers helping transfer ownership of private companies — not public ones
Brokers who lend money as part of the sale do not get this pass
Brokers involved with shell companies — businesses that exist on paper but have no real operations — do not qualify
Brokers who have had their license suspended or taken away also do not qualify

supporters: Supporters say M&A brokers currently must file paperwork with the SEC and follow ongoing compliance rules built for large financial firms — this bill removes those steps for brokers who help small, privately held companies change hands, lowering the cost of getting professional help with a sale.
Supporters say the bill blocks bad actors by barring brokers who lend money during a sale, work with shell companies, or have had their license suspended or revoked from claiming the exemption.
Supporters say the exemption covers only transfers of privately held companies, so public company investors and publicly traded stocks are not affected by the looser rules.
critics: Critics say the bill does not require exempt brokers to give buyers or sellers written disclosures about fees, conflicts of interest, or past complaints — protections that SEC-registered brokers must currently provide.

Critics say the bill refers to a 'specified threshold' for company earnings but does not write a dollar amount into the law itself, leaving the cutoff to be set later and potentially changed without a new vote.

Critics say brokers who have faced fines or customer complaints — but not a full license suspension or revocation — still qualify for the exemption, leaving a gap in oversight for brokers with a record of misconduct.

117-hres-1037.one_liner: Find two former White House officials in contempt of Congress for ignoring subpoenas
provisions: Peter Navarro and Daniel Scavino refused to respond to subpoenas from the committee investigating January 6th
The House votes to hold both men in contempt of Congress
The Speaker of the House sends the contempt findings to federal prosecutors in Washington D.C.
Federal prosecutors can then decide whether to bring criminal charges against Navarro and Scavino

supporters: Supporters say Navarro and Scavino ignored legal orders from the committee investigating the January 6th attack, and this resolution forces the Speaker to send that refusal to federal prosecutors in Washington D.C. so they can decide on criminal charges.

Supporters say Congress has the power to demand information through subpoenas, and if officials can simply ignore those demands without consequence, Congress loses its ability to conduct investigations.

Supporters say the contempt referral to the U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C. is the required legal step to enforce the subpoenas — without it, the committee has no way to compel Navarro and Scavino to comply.
critics: Critics say Navarro and Scavino were following a legal claim called executive privilege — a rule that lets White House officials refuse to share certain information with Congress — and that holding them in contempt punishes them for following that legal guidance.

Critics say this resolution sends the contempt findings to a Justice Department run by the opposing political party, which they argue creates a conflict of interest in deciding whether to bring criminal charges against Navarro and Scavino.

Critics say the select committee was made up of members chosen by Democratic leadership, and they argue that allowing that committee to refer criminal charges gives one party too much control over the outcome.

117-hres-1097.one_liner: Set the rules for debating four separate bills in Congress
provisions: This bill sets the time limits and debate rules for bringing four other bills to a vote in the House.
One of those bills would give TSA airport security workers the same job protections as other federal workers.
Another would make it easier for federal firefighters to get benefits if they get sick with certain diseases.
A third would renew a program that gives money to local groups helping people in poverty.
The fourth would send emergency money to Ukraine during the 2022 conflict.

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows a vote on H.R. 903, which would give TSA airport screeners the same job protections as other federal workers, covering tens of thousands of employees who currently lack those rights.
Supporters say the rule brings H.R. 7691 to the floor, which would send emergency money to Ukraine during the 2022 conflict, and that acting quickly required a rule to speed up House debate.
Supporters say the rule also advances H.R. 2499, which would make it easier for federal firefighters to get disability benefits if they develop certain diseases linked to their job.
critics: Critics say packaging four unrelated bills — TSA worker rights, firefighter benefits, a poverty program, and Ukraine aid — into one rule limits members' ability to vote on each issue separately.
Critics say H.R. 7691 sends emergency funds to Ukraine without a set dollar cap listed in the rule itself, and that emergency spending bills added this way bypass the normal budget review process.

Critics say H.R. 903 would raise costs for the federal government by moving TSA screeners into the title 5 pay system, which provides higher wages and stronger job protections than the current TSA-specific system.

117-hres-1124.one_liner: Set the rules for debating three separate bills in the House
provisions: This bill sets the time limits and voting rules for how the House of Representatives would debate three other bills.
The first bill would create offices inside the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Justice, and the FBI to track and respond to domestic terrorism.
The second bill would set rules against charging too much for gas and other fuels sold to everyday consumers.
The third bill would send emergency money to fix a shortage of baby formula in the United States before September 30, 2022.

supporters: Supporters say this rule brings three separate issues to a vote at once: new domestic terrorism offices inside DHS, DOJ, and the FBI; consumer fuel price protections; and emergency baby formula funding — letting Congress act on all three without delay.

Supporters say the rule allows a floor vote on emergency money to fix the baby formula shortage, which left parents across the country unable to find food for infants before the September 30, 2022 deadline.

Supporters say moving forward the fuel price-gouging bill under this rule would protect everyday consumers at the gas pump by setting legal limits on how much sellers can charge during times of high demand.
critics: Critics say bundling domestic terrorism offices, fuel pricing rules, and baby formula funds into one rule limits the time lawmakers have to review each bill on its own terms before voting.

Critics say creating new offices inside DHS, DOJ, and the FBI to track domestic terrorism activity could be used to monitor Americans based on their political beliefs, without enough oversight built into the bill.

Critics say the fuel price rules included in this package could discourage fuel suppliers from bringing gas to market during shortages, which may cause supply problems rather than lower prices for consumers.

117-hres-1119.one_liner: Set the rules for debating three separate bills in Congress
provisions: Decides how long Congress can debate a bill that would send more money to low-income areas
Decides how long Congress can debate a bill that would renew job training programs around the country
Decides how long Congress can debate a bill that would rename a federal courthouse in Tallahassee, Florida after Judge Joseph Woodrow Hatchett

supporters: Supporters say the rule opens floor debate on H.R. 6531, which would increase the share of certain federal grant funding directed to areas where the poverty rate has stayed above 20% for at least 30 years.
Supporters say the rule allows a vote on H.R. 7309, which would renew the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act and keep federal funding for job training programs available to workers nationwide.
Supporters say the rule moves S. 2938 forward, which would officially name the federal courthouse at 111 North Adams Street in Tallahassee, Florida after Judge Joseph Woodrow Hatchett.
critics: Critics say the rule limits total debate time on H.R. 6531, which restricts members' ability to propose changes to how 'persistent poverty' is defined or which areas qualify for the increased funding.

Critics say the rule does not give members enough floor time to examine how H.R. 7309 would change the formulas used to distribute Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act money to states and local workforce boards.

Critics say the rule does not set aside separate debate time for S. 2938, meaning the Tallahassee courthouse renaming moves forward without a standalone discussion of whether the standard criteria for naming federal buildings after individuals have been met.

117-hres-1065.one_liner: Set House debate rules for a bill to lend weapons to Ukraine
provisions: This bill sets the rules for how the House will debate and vote on a separate bill called S. 3522.
S. 3522 would let the President sign agreements to lend or lease military equipment to Ukraine.
The military equipment would be used to protect Ukrainian civilians during the Russian invasion.
Ukraine would be expected to pay back or return the equipment after the conflict ends.
This rule does not create any programs, funding, or new laws — it only controls how Congress debates the Ukraine bill.

supporters: Supporters say this rule brings S. 3522 to a House floor vote, which would give the President authority to sign lend-or-lease agreements to send military equipment to Ukraine to protect civilians from the Russian invasion.

Supporters say S. 3522 includes a repayment requirement, meaning Ukraine must pay back or return the defense articles after the conflict ends, so the U.S. is lending equipment rather than giving it away at no cost.

Supporters say the lend-or-lease model in S. 3522 lets the U.S. move military equipment to Ukraine faster than standard foreign aid rules allow, which supporters argue is important while active fighting is happening.
critics: Critics say this rule limits how long the House can debate S. 3522, which they argue cuts short discussion of whether the President should have expanded authority to enter lend-or-lease deals without a separate vote for each agreement.
Critics say S. 3522 does not set a dollar cap or limit on how much military equipment the President can commit to Ukraine under these agreements, leaving the total cost open-ended.
Critics say the repayment terms in S. 3522 are not clearly defined, and there is no guarantee Ukraine will be able to return or pay for the defense articles once the conflict ends.

117-hres-1125.one_liner: Call on leaders to speak out against antisemitism in the US and worldwide
provisions: Calls on elected officials, faith leaders, and community leaders to publicly condemn antisemitism
Calls for more action to fight antisemitism in the United States, in other countries, and on the internet

supporters: Supporters say the resolution calls on elected officials, faith leaders, and community leaders to publicly state that antisemitism is condemned by government and community leaders, putting leaders on record against it.
Supporters say that calling for more action against antisemitism online addresses one of the two specific areas the resolution names, where hate speech can spread widely.
critics: Critics say the resolution only calls on leaders to speak out and does not create any new laws, funding, or penalties to back up those calls.
Critics say the resolution does not define what counts as antisemitism, which could make it unclear for elected officials and community leaders trying to follow through on its call to act.

117-hres-1153.one_liner: Set the rules for Congress to debate two gun safety bills
provisions: Allows Congress to vote on a bill that would let courts take guns from people a judge finds dangerous.
Allows Congress to vote on a bill that would raise the gun-buying age from 18 to 21 for some firearms.
Allows Congress to vote on a bill that would make it a crime to buy a gun for someone else.
Allows Congress to vote on a bill that would require safe storage of guns at home.
Allows Congress to vote on a bill that would make guns without serial numbers illegal.

supporters: Supporters say allowing a vote on the extreme risk protection order bill would let judges remove guns from people found to be a danger to themselves or others before a shooting happens.
Supporters say raising the gun-buying age from 18 to 21 for certain firearms and banning guns without serial numbers would make it harder for younger buyers and criminals to get untraceable weapons.
Supporters say making it a crime to buy a gun for someone else and requiring safe storage at home would reduce gun trafficking and prevent children from accessing loaded firearms.
critics: Critics say the extreme risk protection order bill could let courts take guns from people before they are convicted of any crime, which may violate Second Amendment rights.
Critics say raising the purchase age to 21 would block law-abiding adults between 18 and 20 from buying certain firearms they are legally allowed to own under current federal law.
Critics say the safe storage requirement could make it harder for gun owners to quickly access their firearms for self-defense in their own homes.

117-hres-833.one_liner: State U.S. support for Moldova's independence and call on Russia to pull out its troops
provisions: States that the U.S. backs Moldova's right to run its own government and make its own alliances
Supports the U.S.-Moldova talks as a way to build a stronger relationship between the two countries
Calls on Russia to remove its military forces and weapons from Moldova
Tells Russia to stop backing groups inside Moldova that want to break away from the country
Supports finding a peaceful solution to the conflict in the Transnistria region, a strip of land that broke away from Moldova in the 1990s and still has Russian troops in it

supporters: Supporters say this resolution sends a clear message that the U.S. backs Moldova's right to choose its own alliances, including joining the European Union, which Moldova began formal membership talks with in 2024.

Supporters say calling on Russia to remove its military forces from the Transnistria region — where Russian troops have been stationed since the 1990s — reinforces the international rule that one country cannot station troops inside another country without permission.

Supporters say the U.S.-Moldova Strategic Dialogue named in the resolution gives both countries a formal way to work together on government reforms and security at a time when Moldova shares a border with the war in Ukraine.
critics: Critics say the resolution is non-binding, meaning Russia faces no legal penalty or consequence for keeping troops in Moldova or continuing to back separatist groups in Transnistria.
Critics say asking Russia to follow through on its 1999 Istanbul summit promises — which it has ignored for over 25 years — without any enforcement tool gives the resolution little practical effect.
Critics say the U.S. has no formal defense treaty with Moldova, so making a public commitment to Moldova's territorial integrity creates expectations the U.S. may not be able to back up.

117-hres-1191.one_liner: Allow the House to debate three health-related bills
provisions: Opens floor debate on a bill that would let Americans voluntarily share their sexual orientation and gender identity in some federal surveys
Opens floor debate on a bill that would create a new federal health research agency called ARPA-H
Opens floor debate on a bill that would keep funding going for mental health and drug treatment programs
This bill sets the rules for how long each debate lasts and what changes can be proposed — it does not pass the bills itself

supporters: Supporters say allowing floor debate on H.R. 4176 gives Congress a chance to vote on letting Americans voluntarily share their sexual orientation and gender identity in federal surveys, which researchers say would help track health gaps affecting LGBTQ+ groups.

Supporters say bringing H.R. 5585 to the floor lets Congress consider creating ARPA-H, a new federal health research agency modeled after DARPA, which backers say could speed up medical breakthroughs the way DARPA sped up defense technology.

Supporters say debating H.R. 7666 keeps alive the funding for mental health and drug treatment programs under the Public Health Service Act, which currently serve millions of Americans dealing with substance use disorders.
critics: Critics say H.R. 4176 would direct federal agencies to collect sexual orientation and gender identity data in government surveys, which some groups argue goes beyond what the federal government should be tracking about private life.

Critics say setting up ARPA-H under H.R. 5585 creates a brand-new federal bureaucracy with its own budget and staff, and they argue existing agencies like NIH could do the same work without adding a new layer of government.

Critics say the rule limits what changes lawmakers can propose to H.R. 7666, which means members who want to redirect mental health and substance use funding toward different priorities may not get a vote on their amendments.

117-hres-1170.one_liner: Set debate rules for three bills about the Federal Reserve, wildlife, and farming
provisions: This bill sets the rules for how the House of Representatives will debate three separate bills.
One bill would require the Federal Reserve to collect and report data broken down by race, gender, and other groups.
That same bill would also change the official goals that guide how the Federal Reserve runs.
A second bill would send more money to states to manage animals and plants that are at risk in their area.
A third bill would create a new office inside the Department of Agriculture to look into whether large companies in farming and food are following competition rules.

supporters: Supporters say the bill that changes the Federal Reserve Act would require data broken down by race and gender, helping policymakers see whether Fed decisions affect different groups equally.

Supporters say the Pittman-Robertson change would send more money to states to protect animals and plants identified as most at risk, giving state fish and wildlife agencies direct control over which species get help.

Supporters say the new Department of Agriculture office would have a dedicated team to check whether large farming and food companies are breaking competition rules, which smaller farmers say is a gap today.
critics: Critics say changing the official goals that guide the Federal Reserve could shift focus away from controlling inflation and employment, two goals the Fed has followed for decades.
Critics say the Pittman-Robertson expansion does not set a cap on how much extra money states can receive, leaving the total cost open-ended and unpredictable for the federal budget.

Critics say creating a new Office of the Special Investigator inside the Department of Agriculture adds another layer of oversight that duplicates work already done by the Department of Justice antitrust division.

117-s-2514.one_liner: Rename a Utah veterans center after Col. Gail S. Halvorsen
provisions: Changes the official name of the VA veterans center in Orem, Utah to the Col. Gail S. Halvorsen 'Candy Bomber' Veterans Center

Col. Halvorsen was a U.S. Air Force pilot who dropped candy by parachute for children in Berlin during the 1948–1949 Berlin Airlift, when the Soviet Union blocked food and supplies from reaching the city
The renaming is a formal act by Congress and applies to the VA-operated facility in Orem, Utah

supporters: Supporters say Col. Halvorsen flew candy drops by parachute for children in Berlin during the 1948–1949 Soviet blockade, and naming the VA center in Orem after him connects the facility's mission of serving veterans to a specific act of military service and goodwill.

Supporters say the renaming formally recognizes Col. Halvorsen's U.S. Air Force career through an official act of Congress, giving veterans who use the Orem facility a name tied to a real person from their own state's history.

Supporters say the Berlin Airlift was a military operation in which U.S. forces kept a city of over 2 million people supplied for nearly a year, and honoring a pilot from that mission at a veterans' center is a fitting tribute.
critics: Critics say Congress spends limited floor time on renaming bills like this one instead of passing legislation that directly changes veterans' health care, benefits, or wait times at VA facilities.
Critics say the bill does not require any input from veterans who currently use the Provo Veterans Center in Orem, meaning the people the facility serves had no formal say in the name change.
Critics say there is no funding or process in the bill to update signage, records, and official documents at the Orem facility, leaving those costs unaddressed.

117-s-2520.one_liner: Expand federal help to state and local governments on cybersecurity
provisions: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) will give more help to state, local, tribal, and territorial governments to protect against cyberattacks.
DHS will provide grants and training to help governments understand cyber threats and how to respond when an attack happens.
A DHS center will team up with a group called the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center to run practice drills and teach cybersecurity skills.
DHS will promote cybersecurity education for government workers and the public.
DHS will start a test program that puts sensors on government networks to find and block harmful internet traffic.

supporters: Supporters say the bill helps state, local, tribal, and territorial governments get DHS grants and training they need to respond when a cyberattack hits their networks.
Supporters say teaming up the DHS center with the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center to run practice drills will help smaller governments that lack their own cybersecurity staff.
Supporters say the pilot program to place sensors on government networks will give officials an early warning when harmful internet traffic is detected, before damage is done.
critics: Critics say the bill gives DHS broad authority to deploy sensors on state and local government networks, which raises questions about federal oversight of systems that states normally control.
Critics say the bill does not set a specific funding amount for the grants and training programs, making it unclear how much help state and local governments will actually receive.
Critics say promoting cybersecurity education to the general public is a vague goal that lacks clear targets or measures for whether the program is working.

117-s-1872.one_liner: Award a Congressional Gold Medal to World War II Army Rangers
provisions: Gives a single Congressional Gold Medal to the U.S. Army Rangers who served in World War II.
The medal is a formal thank-you from Congress for their service during the war.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives the U.S. Army Rangers who served in World War II a Congressional Gold Medal, which is the highest honor Congress can give a civilian or military group.
Supporters say the Army Rangers completed missions behind enemy lines in Europe and the Pacific during World War II, and this medal is a formal record from Congress that their service mattered.
Supporters say awarding a single shared medal keeps the cost low while still giving official recognition to the whole group of WWII Army Ranger veterans.
critics: Critics say most World War II Army Rangers have passed away, so the medal would go to a display or institution rather than to the veterans themselves, making the award largely symbolic.
Critics say Congress has given out hundreds of Congressional Gold Medals in recent years, and some question whether adding another one reduces the meaning of the honor.
Critics say the bill does not include funding for outreach or education about the Rangers' WWII service, so the medal alone may not help the public learn more about what these veterans did.

117-s-1760.one_liner: Name a new VA clinic in Oahu, Hawaii after Daniel Kahikina Akaka
provisions: Gives an official name to a new VA clinic being built in Oahu, Hawaii
The clinic will be called the Daniel Kahikina Akaka VA Clinic

supporters: Supporters say naming the new Oahu clinic after Senator Daniel Kahikina Akaka honors his decades of work in Congress to expand health care access for Hawaii veterans.
Supporters say giving the planned Oahu facility an official name helps veterans in Hawaii identify and connect with their local VA clinic.
critics: Critics say Congress used floor time on a naming bill instead of addressing funding or staffing gaps at VA facilities serving veterans in Hawaii.
Critics say the bill only assigns a name to the planned Oahu clinic and does not add any new services, providers, or money for veterans who will use it.

117-s-2102.one_liner: Expand VA mammogram coverage to veterans who served in listed combat zones abroad
