provisions: Female veterans who served in Iraq between August 2, 1990 and February 28, 1991, or again from March 19, 2003 onward, can get VA mammograms.
Veterans who served in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Qatar, or other parts of the Southwest Asia region from August 2, 1990 onward can get VA mammograms.
Veterans who served in Afghanistan, Djibouti, Syria, Jordan, Egypt, Lebanon, or Yemen from September 11, 2001 onward can get VA mammograms.
Coverage for all listed locations continues until burn pits — open-air trash fires used by the military — are no longer in use there.
The VA can add more locations and time periods based on its Airborne Hazards and Open Burn Pit Registry.

supporters: Supporters say female veterans who served near burn pits in more than 13 countries — including Iraq, Afghanistan, Kuwait, and Syria — would gain access to VA mammograms they currently cannot get, because the VA's existing rules do not cover them.

Supporters say burn pit smoke has been linked to cancer, and this bill connects mammogram eligibility directly to documented burn pit use at each location, so screenings go to veterans with a known exposure risk.
Supporters say the bill lets the VA add new locations through the Airborne Hazards and Open Burn Pit Registry, which means coverage can grow as the military identifies more toxic exposure sites.
critics: Critics say the bill sets no end date for most locations — coverage runs until burn pits 'are no longer used' in each country, which creates an open-ended VA cost commitment with no fixed budget ceiling.

Critics say eligibility is based on where a veteran served, not on proof that they were exposed to burn pit smoke, which could add large numbers of veterans to VA mammogram rolls beyond those with a direct toxic exposure.
Critics say the bill covers only mammograms, leaving out other cancer screenings that may also be relevant to veterans exposed to burn pits in the same locations and time periods.

117-s-2687.one_liner: Give the VA Inspector General power to require witnesses to testify
provisions: The VA's watchdog office can now legally require people to show up and answer questions during investigations.
This subpoena power cannot be used to force witnesses to testify in criminal cases.
Before sending a subpoena, the VA watchdog must notify the Department of Justice and the person being called.
If the Department of Justice says the subpoena would get in the way of an ongoing investigation, the VA watchdog must cancel it.

supporters: Supporters say giving the VA watchdog office the power to require witnesses to show up and answer questions will help investigators get facts they could not access before, leading to stronger oversight of VA programs that serve millions of veterans.
Supporters say the rule that stops the VA watchdog from using subpoenas in criminal cases protects people's legal rights, since those cases have separate rules under the courts.
Supporters say the required notice to the Department of Justice before any subpoena is sent will prevent the VA watchdog from accidentally blocking ongoing federal investigations.
critics: Critics say requiring the VA watchdog to cancel a subpoena whenever the Department of Justice objects gives DOJ the power to slow or stop VA investigations, even when no real conflict with a criminal case exists.
Critics say the bill does not set a time limit on how long the Department of Justice can block a subpoena, which could let an investigation stall for months without any check on that delay.

117-s-2533.one_liner: Expand breast cancer screening and treatment options for veterans through the VA
provisions: The VA must create a plan to improve breast imaging services for veterans.
The VA must run a three-year program to offer mammograms by video for veterans who live far from a VA facility.
The VA must upgrade all mammogram machines at VA facilities to use 3D imaging technology.

The VA must partner with at least one National Cancer Institute cancer center in each regional network, and ensure veterans in rural areas can get cancer care through telehealth if no partner center is nearby.
The VA must update its guidelines to offer more genetic testing and counseling to veterans diagnosed with breast cancer.
The VA must check that a mammogram site can physically accommodate veterans with spinal cord injuries before sending them to a non-VA provider.
The VA must work with the Department of Defense on shared breast cancer research and care programs and report on those collaborations.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would help veterans who live far from a VA facility by starting a three-year telemammography program, letting them get mammograms by video instead of traveling long distances.
Supporters say upgrading all VA mammogram machines to 3D imaging technology and expanding genetic testing and counseling would give veterans diagnosed with breast cancer more complete care options.

Supporters say partnering with at least one NCI-designated cancer center in each regional network — and requiring telehealth access for rural veterans — would connect women veterans to specialized cancer care closer to home.
critics: Critics say upgrading all VA mammogram machines to 3D imaging technology requires capital spending the bill does not fund, leaving it unclear how the VA would cover those costs.

Critics say the bill adds several new mandates — including NCI partnerships, a telemammography pilot, and a DoD collaboration report — without specifying a budget, which could strain existing VA resources.

Critics say the requirement to verify physical accessibility of mammogram sites for veterans with spinal cord injuries before referrals applies only to non-VA providers, leaving a gap for accessibility issues at VA facilities themselves.

117-s-3527.one_liner: Let the VA move an official facility name to another nearby property
provisions: The VA can move the official name of a building or facility to a different VA property in the same city or local area.
This only applies when Congress originally gave that name to the first property through a law.
The new property must be at a different address or location from the original named property.
The VA cannot use this to rename a facility to something new — only to move an existing congressional name to a new location.

supporters: Supporters say the bill lets the VA transfer a congressionally given name to a new facility in the same city or local area without waiting for Congress to pass a new naming law each time.

Supporters say the bill keeps the transfer limited to the same 'town, city, or other local government area' named in the original designation, so veterans in that jurisdiction can still find care at a place they recognize by name.
Supporters say the VA cannot use this authority to create a new name — it can only move an existing congressional name to a different address, which limits how much the agency can act on its own.
critics: Critics say the bill does not require the VA to notify the public or veterans before moving a name, so people may show up to the original address expecting a facility that has already been relocated.

Critics say the phrase 'town, city, or other local government area' is not defined in the bill, which could allow the VA to move a name across a wide geographic area depending on how local boundaries are drawn.

Critics say Congress gave these names to specific buildings at specific addresses, and allowing the VA to reassign those names — even within the same city — removes the oversight role that Congress has over VA facility designations.

117-s-3522.one_liner: Let the U.S. lend weapons and military equipment to Ukraine faster
provisions: Lets the U.S. government lend or lease military equipment to Ukraine without the usual rules that slow the process down
Removes the normal five-year limit on how long the U.S. can lend military equipment to Ukraine
Removes the rule requiring Ukraine to pay the U.S. back for the cost of leasing the equipment
Takes away Congress's ability to block these equipment transfers while the law is active
Stays in effect until the Russia-Ukraine conflict — which started with Russia taking Crimea in 2014 — ends and Russian troops pull back to where they were before March 1, 2021
Requires the President to set up a fast-track system to get the equipment to Ukraine quickly

supporters: Supporters say removing the five-year loan limit and the repayment requirement lets the U.S. send military equipment to Ukraine faster and without waiting for payment agreements to be worked out.
Supporters say the fast-track delivery system required by the bill means weapons and gear reach Ukrainian civilians and forces more quickly than under normal Pentagon rules.
Supporters say the law stays active until Russian troops pull back to pre-March 2021 levels, giving Ukraine a steady supply of defense equipment for as long as the conflict lasts.
critics: Critics say removing Congress's ability to block equipment transfers while the law is active takes away a key check on presidential power over military aid decisions.
Critics say waiving the repayment requirement means U.S. taxpayers could be left covering the full cost of military equipment sent to Ukraine, with no guarantee of getting it back.
Critics say the open-ended timeline — tied to Russia reducing forces to pre-March 2021 levels — could keep the U.S. locked into military lending with no clear exit point.

117-s-3580.one_liner: Stop ocean carriers from refusing cargo and using unfair shipping methods
provisions: Changes the rules that govern ocean shipping to support the growth of U.S. exports.
Stops ocean carriers, marine terminal operators, and ocean transportation intermediaries from turning away cargo when space is available on their ships.
Stops those same carriers and operators from using unfair methods in ocean shipping.

supporters: Supporters say the rule stopping ocean carriers from turning away cargo when ship space is available will help U.S. exporters — especially farmers and small businesses — who lost sales during recent shipping crises when carriers skipped U.S. export ports to chase higher-paying routes.

Supporters say banning unfair methods by ocean carriers and marine terminal operators will give U.S. shippers a more level playing field against large foreign-owned shipping lines that control most of global ocean trade.
Supporters say stronger Federal Maritime Commission oversight of carrier practices will make it easier for American exporters to get their goods on ships and grow U.S. export volumes.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set specific penalties or dollar amounts for carriers that refuse cargo, which may make the new rules hard to enforce in practice.

Critics say requiring ocean carriers and terminal operators to accept all available cargo could create logistical problems at busy ports, since ships and terminals have complex scheduling needs that go beyond just whether space exists.
Critics say the bill focuses on carrier behavior but does not address port congestion or labor shortages, which are also major reasons U.S. exporters have struggled to get cargo shipped.

117-s-4089.one_liner: Protect veterans' retraining benefits if their school closes or loses approval
provisions: If a veteran's school closed or lost approval, the VA cannot count that time against their training benefits.
This applies when the veteran could not finish because of the closure or disapproval.
The protected time equals the full amount of training time the veteran was enrolled.
Schools that close or lose approval cannot receive any more payments from this program.
Any payments a closed or disapproved school already received become money owed back to the government.

supporters: Supporters say veterans who lost training time because their school closed or lost VA approval should not have that time counted against their benefits, since the veteran did nothing wrong.
Supporters say the bill protects the full amount of training time a veteran was enrolled in — meaning no benefit days are lost due to a school's failure.
Supporters say requiring closed or disapproved schools to pay back money already received holds institutions accountable and protects taxpayer funds.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a time limit or cap on how far back these benefit protections can apply, which could create large, hard-to-track liabilities for the VA.
Critics say schools that close may no longer exist as legal entities, making it difficult for the government to actually collect overpayments they now owe back.
Critics say the bill does not explain how veterans prove their inability to finish was caused by the closure, which could lead to disputes over who qualifies for the protected time.

117-s-4160.one_liner: Lets Supreme Court Police protect the families of justices and court officers
provisions: Before this bill, Supreme Court Police could only protect the justices and court officers themselves — not their families.
This bill lets the Marshal of the Supreme Court decide when to protect the immediate family members of any Supreme Court justice or court officer.
The Marshal and the Supreme Court Police can now act to protect those family members if the Marshal decides protection is needed.

supporters: Supporters say that before this bill, Supreme Court Police had no legal authority to protect the families of justices or court officers, leaving them without official security even when facing threats.
Supporters say the bill gives the Marshal of the Supreme Court the power to decide when family members need protection, so security resources are used only when there is a real need.
Supporters say that justices and court officers may be targeted through their families, and this bill closes that gap by letting police extend protection to immediate family members.
critics: Critics say the bill gives the Marshal broad, unchecked power to decide when to protect family members, with no clear rules or oversight written into the law.
Critics say the bill does not define what counts as a threat or set any standard the Marshal must meet before ordering protection for family members, which could lead to unequal treatment.

Critics say expanding Supreme Court Police duties to cover family members could stretch the agency's staffing and budget, but the bill includes no funding amounts or limits on how far that protection can go.

117-s-516.one_liner: Create a federal working group to plan for new small aircraft that carry people and cargo
provisions: The Department of Transportation must create a group of agencies to work together on a new type of air travel called Advanced Air Mobility (AAM).
AAM includes small aircraft, like air taxis, that can take off and land in cities, rural areas, and everywhere in between.
The working group will plan for safety rules, buildings and landing pads, protection from hackers, and how much federal money to spend on this.
The group will coordinate how these new aircraft fit into the airspace already used by planes and helicopters.

supporters: Supporters say the working group will bring safety agencies together to plan rules and landing pads for air taxis, so the federal government does not have multiple agencies working in separate directions.
Supporters say the bill covers rural areas along with cities, which means small aircraft could carry people and cargo to places that do not have nearby airports.
Supporters say adding cybersecurity planning now, before air taxis are in wide use, can help stop hackers from targeting aircraft flying over populated areas.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a dollar amount or spending limit for federal investment in AAM infrastructure like landing pads, so Congress has no cap on how much taxpayer money could eventually be spent.
Critics say the bill only creates a planning group and does not require that group to produce finished safety rules or build any infrastructure by a specific deadline.

Critics say the bill does not explain how new small aircraft will safely share airspace already used by planes and helicopters, leaving a key safety question unanswered before the group even begins work.

117-s-497.one_liner: Create a committee to help run grants for fishing communities
provisions: Creates a new committee under the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to help manage a grant program for fishing communities.
Divides the committee into six regional groups so different parts of the country are represented.
Committee members come from different parts of the fishing industry, chosen by region.
The committee finds out what fishing communities need, writes up grant proposals, reviews applications, and sends them to NOAA for final approval.

supporters: Supporters say the six regional groups will make sure fishing communities from different parts of the country — not just a few states — have a voice in how grant money is handed out.

Supporters say having committee members come from different parts of the fishing industry means the people reviewing grant applications will understand what fishing communities actually need, rather than leaving those decisions to government staff alone.

Supporters say giving the committee the job of finding needs, writing grant proposals, and reviewing applications will make the existing NOAA grant program work better for working waterfronts and sustainable fisheries.
critics: Critics say adding a new committee layer between fishing communities and NOAA could slow down the grant approval process, since applications must pass through the committee before NOAA gives final approval.
Critics say the bill does not set limits on how many members the committee can have or how much it will cost to run, which makes it hard to know whether the new structure is worth the added expense.
Critics say the bill gives the committee power to write the grant request-for-proposals itself, which could let certain industry groups shape the rules in ways that favor their sector over others.

117-s-3823.one_liner: Raise the debt limits for people and small businesses filing for bankruptcy
provisions: Keeps the higher debt limit for small businesses filing for bankruptcy — the limit was temporarily raised to $7.5 million and this bill makes that permanent
Adjusts that $7.5 million limit over time so it keeps up with inflation
Lets a small business that is connected to a publicly traded company still use this type of bankruptcy
If a small business owner stops running their company during bankruptcy, a court-appointed trustee can take over running it
Raises the debt limit for individuals filing under Chapter 13 bankruptcy, which is a repayment plan for wage earners
Combines the two separate debt limits for individuals — one for secured debt (like a mortgage) and one for unsecured debt (like credit cards) — into one single limit

supporters: Supporters say making the $7.5 million debt limit permanent gives small business owners a clear, stable rule to plan around when deciding whether to reorganize under bankruptcy instead of shutting down entirely.

Supporters say combining the two separate Chapter 13 debt limits into one single limit lets more wage earners qualify for a repayment plan, which keeps them out of Chapter 7 liquidation where they could lose more assets.
Supporters say tying the $7.5 million small business limit to inflation means Congress won't need to keep passing new laws just to keep the limit current as prices rise.
critics: Critics say allowing businesses that are connected to publicly traded companies to use the small business bankruptcy process — which was built for true small businesses — could let larger corporate networks use a faster, cheaper process that was not designed for them.

Critics say raising the Chapter 13 debt ceiling and merging secured and unsecured debt into one limit means individuals with more total debt, including large mortgages, can now use a repayment plan that creditors say gives them less recovery than a full liquidation would.
Critics say letting a court-appointed trustee take over and operate a debtor's business adds costs to the bankruptcy estate, which can reduce how much money is left for creditors who are owed money.

118-hr-1449.one_liner: Require more frequent lease sales and faster permits for geothermal energy on federal land
provisions: The federal government must now hold lease sales for geothermal energy land at least once a year.
Before this bill, sales were required only once every two years.
If a sale is canceled or delayed, a replacement sale must happen within the same year.
When someone applies for a permit to drill for geothermal energy, the government has 30 days to say whether the application is complete.
After telling the applicant the application is complete, the government has 30 days to make a final decision on the permit.

supporters: Supporters say requiring at least one geothermal lease sale per year — up from once every two years — gives energy companies more chances to access federal land for geothermal development.
Supporters say the 30-day deadlines for permit decisions will cut down on government delays that have held up geothermal projects.
Supporters say the requirement to hold a replacement sale within the same year means a canceled or delayed sale will not push developers back by a full year.
critics: Critics say doubling the required frequency of lease sales, from once every two years to once a year, could strain Interior Department staff and budgets without guaranteed funding to meet the new pace.
Critics say the 30-day deadline to issue a final permit decision may not give Interior enough time to fully review environmental and safety concerns for each drilling application.
Critics say the mandate to hold a replacement sale within the same calendar year as any cancellation could force Interior to rush sales when staffing or resources are limited.

118-hr-3012.one_liner: Keep funding programs that support human rights and free information in North Korea
provisions: Funds grants to groups working on human rights and free press inside North Korea through 2028
Pays for radio and other broadcasts that send uncensored news into North Korea
Gives money to groups helping North Koreans who have left the country without government permission

supporters: Supporters say the bill extends grants to nonprofit groups working on human rights, democracy, and free markets inside North Korea through 2028, keeping programs running that would otherwise lose funding.

Supporters say paying for radio and other broadcasts gives North Korean citizens access to uncensored news that their own government blocks, reaching people who have no other outside source of information.
Supporters say the bill provides money to organizations helping North Koreans who left the country without government permission, giving those people shelter, legal help, and other basic support.
critics: Critics say North Korea's government jams foreign radio signals and punishes citizens caught listening, which means the broadcast funding is unlikely to reach most people inside the country.

Critics say giving money to groups that help North Koreans who fled without permission could make the North Korean government less willing to engage with the United States on other issues, including nuclear talks.
Critics say grants to nonprofits working in a country as closed as North Korea are hard to track, making it difficult to confirm the money is being spent as intended.

117-s-66.one_liner: Order a federal assessment and plan to address algae blooms in South Florida waters
provisions: A group of federal agencies must study algae blooms and low-oxygen water conditions in South Florida.
The group must submit a plan for reducing and controlling those conditions in the region.
The bill covers algae events that make water toxic or starve fish of oxygen, setting the scope for the federal review.

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires a group of federal agencies to study algae blooms and low-oxygen water conditions in South Florida, which would give scientists and local communities a clearer picture of what is causing the problem.
Supporters say the required plan for reducing and controlling harmful algae events could help protect South Florida's fishing industry, tourism, and the health of people who live near affected water.
Supporters say setting a clear scope — covering water that turns toxic or starves fish of oxygen — means the federal review cannot ignore the most damaging types of algae events.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires a study and a plan, but does not require any agency to actually reduce algae blooms or spend money to fix the problem.
Critics say federal inter-agency task forces can take years to produce reports, meaning South Florida communities dealing with toxic water now may not see any action for a long time.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for when the plan must be completed or put in place, which could allow the process to stall without results.

117-s-812.one_liner: Require annual reports on U.S. efforts to get Taiwan into World Health Organization meetings
provisions: The State Department must include more detail in its yearly reports about Taiwan's efforts to join World Health Organization meetings as an observer.
China has blocked Taiwan from joining these meetings, which is why the U.S. tracks its own efforts to help.
After any meeting where Taiwan was not allowed in, the report must describe what changed or improved in the U.S. plan to get Taiwan a seat.
The report covers the World Health Assembly, which is the main decision-making meeting of the World Health Organization.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would hold the State Department accountable by requiring it to explain, in yearly reports, what steps it took after any World Health Assembly meeting where Taiwan was not allowed in as an observer.

Supporters say Taiwan's exclusion from the World Health Assembly — the main decision-making body of the World Health Organization — means Taiwan cannot take part in global health decisions, and this bill tracks U.S. efforts to change that.
Supporters say requiring more detail in State Department reports on the U.S. plan to support Taiwan's observer status creates a clear record of whether those efforts are improving or stalling.
critics: Critics say the bill only adds a reporting requirement and does not give Taiwan an actual seat at the World Health Assembly meetings it has been blocked from by China.

Critics say requiring the State Department to report on efforts to support Taiwan at the World Health Organization could affect U.S. relations with China, which opposes Taiwan's participation and could respond by limiting cooperation in other areas.
Critics say the bill sets no consequences if the State Department's yearly plan to help Taiwan shows no improvement, making the reporting requirement hard to enforce.

118-hr-3208.one_liner: Create a cybersecurity job training program for DHS employees
provisions: Sets up a training program inside the DHS cybersecurity agency known as CISA.
DHS workers who are not already in cybersecurity jobs can join the program to learn cybersecurity skills.
The program follows a national standard called the National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education Framework.
Each year, CISA must send Congress a report on the program.
The report shows how many people joined, what jobs they moved into, and other key details.

supporters: Supporters say the program lets DHS workers who currently hold non-cybersecurity jobs move into cybersecurity roles at CISA, which could help fill open positions without recruiting from outside the department.

Supporters say the training follows the National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education Framework, a national standard, so the skills workers learn match what federal agencies define as needed for cybersecurity work.
Supporters say the required annual report to Congress — showing how many workers joined and which jobs they moved into — gives lawmakers a way to check whether the program is working each year.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a funding amount for the program, leaving it unclear how many DHS workers could actually take part or whether CISA has the resources to run it.

Critics say the program only trains current DHS employees who are not already in cybersecurity jobs, which limits the number of people who can join and does not bring in workers with prior cybersecurity experience from outside the government.

Critics say the required annual report only tracks how many people joined and where they were placed, but does not require CISA to report on whether participants stayed in cybersecurity roles long-term or how their skills compared to existing cybersecurity staff.

118-hr-390.one_liner: Expand the Hudson River Valley Heritage Area to cover two more counties in New York
provisions: Adds the rest of Saratoga County and all of Washington County in New York to the Hudson River Valley Heritage Area
This area covers land along the Hudson River that has historic and cultural significance
A local organization manages this area with support and some funding from the federal government
The expansion gives these two counties access to the same recognition and resources the rest of the heritage area already has

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives Saratoga County and Washington County access to the same federal recognition and resources that other Hudson River Valley counties already receive.
Supporters say Saratoga County includes the Saratoga Battlefield, the site of a 1777 Revolutionary War battle, which fits the heritage area's focus on historic sites along the Hudson River corridor.
Supporters say connecting these two counties to the existing heritage area lets the managing organization coordinate historic preservation across a larger, linked region.
critics: Critics say the bill expands the heritage area to cover two full counties but does not say how much additional federal funding, if any, the managing organization would get to serve the new area.

Critics say Washington County and parts of Saratoga County were left out of the original heritage area, and the bill does not include a review of whether the managing organization has the staff or budget to take on more land.
Critics say adding counties through legislation without a formal review process could lead to more boundary expansions later, without first checking whether resources can keep up.

118-hr-5342.one_liner: Change how Social Security calculates benefits for people who also get a government pension
provisions: Some government workers — like certain teachers, firefighters, and police — pay into a pension instead of Social Security. A current rule called the WEP cuts their Social Security check when they retire.
This bill changes the math used to calculate those cuts, basing the reduction on what share of a person's career earnings went into Social Security.
People who retire between 2025 and 2067 get whichever calculation gives them the higher monthly payment.
People retiring after 2067 will only use the new formula.
Some people already affected by the current rule get an extra one-time or ongoing payment.
The Social Security Administration must add non-covered earnings to the yearly statements it sends workers.

supporters: Supporters say the new formula is fairer to teachers, firefighters, and police because it bases Social Security cuts on how much of a person's career actually went into Social Security payroll taxes, rather than using a flat penalty that treats all workers the same.

Supporters say that workers retiring between 2025 and 2067 will receive whichever monthly payment is higher — the current WEP calculation or the new formula — so no one's benefits go down during the changeover.
Supporters say people already receiving reduced Social Security checks because of the WEP will get an additional payment, giving current retirees some relief without waiting for the 2067 full switch.
critics: Critics say the new formula does not take full effect until 2067, meaning most teachers, firefighters, and police working today will retire before the new calculation applies to them and will still face cuts under the old WEP rules.

Critics say the bill adds new federal spending — through extra payments to current WEP-affected retirees — without a clear plan to fund those payments, which could add pressure to the Social Security trust fund.

Critics say that changing the WEP math still leaves a penalty in place for public workers with non-covered pensions, and that a full repeal of the WEP would do more to close the gap between what these workers paid in and what they receive.

118-hr-3334.one_liner: Ban Chinese Communist Party leaders and their families from entering the U.S.
provisions: The top ruling body of the Chinese Communist Party, called the Central Committee, has about 376 members — this bill bans all of them from getting visas to enter the United States.
Adult family members of those Central Committee members are also banned from getting U.S. visas.
Any money or property those people have in the United States gets frozen — they cannot spend it or move it.
The President can pause these sanctions for up to 30 days at a time by notifying Congress that China has changed course on four actions.

To pause the sanctions, the President must confirm that China has stopped carrying out genocide against Uyghur Muslims, threatening Taiwan, weakening Hong Kong's self-rule, and stealing American business ideas and inventions.
Any presidential pause must be posted publicly on a U.S. government website.

supporters: Supporters say banning all 376 Central Committee members and their adult family members from U.S. visas puts direct pressure on the people who make decisions about Uyghur detention camps, Taiwan military drills, and Hong Kong's government.
Supporters say freezing any U.S. money or property held by Central Committee members gives the United States a financial tool to push back on intellectual property theft from American businesses.

Supporters say the waiver process holds China to four clear tests — stopping Uyghur genocide, ending Taiwan threats, restoring Hong Kong's autonomy, and halting IP theft — and requires the President to post any pause publicly so Congress and the public can see it.
critics: Critics say extending visa bans to adult family members of all 376 Central Committee members punishes people who may have no role in Chinese government policy.

Critics say the 30-day waiver limit gives the President very little room to manage diplomatic talks with China, since any pause expires quickly and requires a public certification that could complicate negotiations.

Critics say requiring China to meet all four conditions at once — on Uyghurs, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and IP theft — before any sanctions are lifted makes it nearly impossible to reward partial progress on any single issue.

118-hr-4790.one_liner: Limit what information public companies must share with investors
provisions: Companies only have to share information with investors if the company itself decides that information affects buying or voting decisions about its stock.
The SEC must post on its website a list of every disclosure companies are currently required to make that does not affect investment decisions, along with a reason for each one.
The SEC must send that list to Congress every five years.
A company cannot be sued for not sharing information that does not affect investment decisions.
Creates a new group inside the SEC, made up of public company officials and advisors, to give the SEC advice on its rules and company policies.
The SEC must study and report on how European Union sustainability rules affect U.S. companies, consumers, and investors.

supporters: Supporters say letting companies decide what information affects buying or voting decisions will cut down on paperwork and reporting costs for public companies, freeing up resources instead of filing disclosures that do not change investor choices.

Supporters say removing the threat of lawsuits for not sharing non-material information protects companies from legal risk over disclosures that the SEC itself admits do not affect investment decisions.

Supporters say the new advisory committee, made up of public company officials and advisors, gives the SEC direct input from the people most affected by its rules before new requirements are put in place.
critics: Critics say letting companies decide for themselves what counts as material information could allow them to hide details that investors or the public would want to know, since the company has a financial interest in limiting what it shares.

Critics say the advisory committee is only made up of public company officials, senior managers from industry groups, and company advisors, with no seats for investors, consumers, or the general public who are also affected by SEC rules.

Critics say blocking lawsuits against companies that skip non-material disclosures removes a legal tool that investors currently use to hold companies accountable, even for information the SEC has required under existing federal securities laws.

118-hr-5658.one_liner: Require tracking barcodes on all mail-in ballots
provisions: Mail-in ballots must have a U.S. Postal Service barcode so voters and officials can track each ballot.
Ballot envelopes must meet postal design rules so machines can process them.
Each ballot must show the official election mail logo.

supporters: Supporters say the USPS barcode requirement would let voters track their individual ballot through the mail, giving them confirmation it was received before Election Day.
Supporters say requiring ballot envelopes to meet postal design rules for machine processing would reduce delays caused by ballots that get stuck or rejected by sorting machines.
Supporters say adding the official election mail logo helps postal workers identify and prioritize ballots during busy mail periods.
critics: Critics say printing USPS barcodes and redesigning ballot envelopes to meet postal design rules for machine processing would add printing and design costs that fall on local election offices.

Critics say requiring all ballots to follow postal design rules for machine processing may force counties to reprint or redesign existing envelope stock, creating a burden for smaller jurisdictions with limited budgets.
Critics say the bill does not include any funding to help election offices cover the cost of updating ballot materials to meet the new barcode and envelope requirements.

118-hr-5349.one_liner: Fund a high school curriculum about communism and totalitarianism
provisions: The Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation would create a curriculum for high school students about communism and totalitarianism.
The Foundation would also create oral history resources for students to learn from people who lived under these governments.
The curriculum would explain how these systems differ from U.S. democracy.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would have the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation create a high school curriculum that directly compares communist and totalitarian governments to U.S. democracy, giving students concrete knowledge about how these systems work.

Supporters say the oral history resources would let students hear firsthand accounts from real people who lived under communist or totalitarian rule, making the lessons more concrete than a textbook alone.
Supporters say teaching high school students about totalitarianism helps them understand specific rights — like free speech and free elections — that do not exist under communist governments.
critics: Critics say the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation was set up to memorialize victims of communism, which means it may not be a neutral source for building a school curriculum that all students are expected to learn from.

Critics say the bill directs curriculum only about communism and totalitarianism but does not require teaching about other systems that have also restricted rights, giving high school students a partial view of world governments.
Critics say the bill does not name a funding amount or explain how schools would be required to adopt the curriculum, leaving it unclear how many students would actually be reached.

118-hr-7073.one_liner: Fund research and testing of new materials and technology for pipelines
provisions: The Department of Energy must run a 5-year program that gives money to test new pipeline technology at different stages of development.
The Department of Energy, the Department of Transportation, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology must work together on research into new materials for pipelines.
The Department of Energy must create a National Pipeline Modernization Center to work with companies on testing and selling new pipeline products.
The National Institute of Standards and Technology must run a research program focused on keeping pipelines safe, secure, and working well.

supporters: Supporters say the DOE's 5-year program would fund real-world tests of new pipeline technology at early stages of development, helping move safer and more efficient designs toward actual use.
Supporters say creating a National Pipeline Modernization Center would bring companies and federal agencies together to turn research into products that can be sold and used across the country.

Supporters say requiring DOE, DOT, and NIST to work together under a formal agreement would reduce gaps in pipeline safety research and help set national standards for keeping pipelines secure and working well.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a specific dollar amount for the 5-year DOE program or the National Pipeline Modernization Center, making it hard to know how much taxpayer money will be spent.

Critics say directing federal research money toward liquefied natural gas facilities and liquid fuel storage could lock in fossil fuel infrastructure instead of spending those funds on cleaner energy systems.
Critics say adding a new National Pipeline Modernization Center may repeat work that DOT and NIST already do, creating overlap between agencies without clear lines on who is responsible for what.

118-hr-6513.one_liner: Let Congress send official observers to watch how federal elections are run
provisions: House committee chairs can name their employees to watch federal elections as official observers.
States must let these observers into any area where ballots are cast, counted, scanned, or certified.
Observers can watch but cannot touch ballots or election equipment.
Observers cannot campaign for any candidate or take any action that could reveal how a voter voted.
Observers cannot stop a voter from casting a ballot or an election worker from doing their job.
If an observer breaks the rules, election officials can remove them and must notify the House committee in writing.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives House committee chairs a formal, legal way to send their own employees to watch federal elections, which Congress has the power to do under Article I of the Constitution.
Supporters say observers are banned from touching ballots, talking to voters about candidates, or slowing down election workers — so states keep full control of running their elections.
Supporters say if a contested election ends up before the House, members will have firsthand information from observers who were present during counting and certification.
critics: Critics say requiring states to give House-designated observers access to every area where ballots are cast, scanned, or counted adds a new layer of federal oversight that states did not agree to and that could slow down local election administration.

Critics say the bill gives the chair or ranking member of one House committee the power to send observers anywhere in the country, and the rules for removing a misbehaving observer still require written notice back to that same committee — giving Congress influence over a process run by state and local officials.
Critics say the bill does not set a limit on how many observers a committee can send to a single location, which could create crowding or confusion at polling places and counting centers.

118-hr-5717.one_liner: Cut federal money to cities refusing to share immigration data or honor federal detention holds
provisions: Cities and states lose federal money if they have rules stopping officials from sharing immigration status.
The money at risk is only the part they planned to spend on people living in the country without legal permission.
They also lose money if they ignore a federal request to hold an immigrant in jail.
They also lose money if they don't tell federal immigration officials before letting an immigrant out of jail.
Crime victims and witnesses are not covered — cities can keep rules that protect them from immigration checks.
This rule starts in the first full budget year after the law is passed.

supporters: Supporters say that when local officials share immigration status information with DHS and comply with federal detainer requests, it helps federal agents locate and remove people who have entered the country without legal permission, which they argue reduces public safety risks.

Supporters say the bill only cuts the portion of federal money a city or state planned to spend on people living in the country without legal permission — not all federal funding the jurisdiction receives.

Supporters say the bill includes a specific carve-out so that cities can keep rules protecting crime victims and witnesses from immigration checks, meaning community members who report crimes are not affected by this law.
critics: Critics say requiring local jails to notify DHS before releasing someone — and to hold people based on federal detainer requests — turns local police departments into immigration enforcement agents, a role local law enforcement agencies say was never part of their mission.

Critics say the bill's scope goes beyond serious criminals: any jurisdiction that does not share immigration status information for any individual, regardless of their criminal history, risks losing federal funds it planned to use for that population.

Critics say the bill takes effect in the first full budget year after it passes, meaning cities and states will have to change existing laws and policies while also adjusting budgets that were already approved under different rules.

118-hr-8057.one_liner: Rename a Westminster, California post office after Little Saigon Vietnam War Veterans
provisions: Renames the post office at 9317 Bolsa Avenue in Westminster, California as the 'Little Saigon Vietnam War Veterans Memorial Post Office'
This is a ceremonial name change — no money is spent and no new programs are created
The name honors Vietnamese-American veterans who served in the Vietnam War
Once Congress passes this, only Congress can change the official name of this post office

supporters: Supporters say renaming the post office at 9317 Bolsa Avenue honors Vietnamese-American veterans who served in the Vietnam War, giving the Little Saigon community in Westminster a lasting public recognition.

Supporters say this name change costs no money and creates no new programs, making it a low-cost way to acknowledge a specific group of veterans in one of the largest Vietnamese-American communities in the United States.

Supporters say the name 'Little Saigon Vietnam War Veterans Memorial Post Office' connects the location directly to the community it serves, since Westminster's Little Saigon district is home to many Vietnamese-American veterans and their families.
critics: Critics say that once Congress passes this designation, only Congress can change the official name, which locks in the name permanently with no expiration date or built-in review process.

Critics say naming post offices after specific groups sets a precedent that can lead to many similar requests, adding to congressional workload without creating any programs or services for the veterans being honored.

Critics say a ceremonial name change does nothing to address the actual needs of Vietnamese-American veterans, such as access to VA services or benefits, since the bill creates no funding or programs.

118-hr-7409.one_liner: Remove federal permit requirements for geothermal drilling on state and private land, not tribal lands
provisions: Geothermal companies drilling on state or private land no longer need a federal drilling permit.
This applies when the U.S. government owns less than 50% of the underground geothermal rights and the company holds a state permit.
These rules do not apply on tribal lands.
These projects no longer need to go through the federal environmental review process.
These projects no longer need a federal check on how they may affect endangered species.
These projects do not need federal historic preservation review unless the state has no state law covering historic properties.

supporters: Supporters say removing the federal drilling permit requirement for projects on state or private land — where the U.S. owns less than 50% of the underground geothermal rights — will speed up clean energy projects that currently face long federal approval delays.
Supporters say skipping the federal environmental review process under NEPA will let states, which already issue their own permits, avoid doing the same review twice for the same project.
Supporters say the bill still requires federal historic preservation review in any state that does not have its own historic property law, so protections remain where no state law exists.
critics: Critics say removing the federal endangered species check means no one at the federal level will review whether geothermal drilling on state or private land could harm protected animals or plants before work begins.

Critics say cutting out NEPA review removes a process that lets nearby communities and tribes — even those not on tribal land — give public input on projects that could affect local water, land, and air.

Critics say that when the U.S. owns even a small share of underground geothermal rights, the federal government still has a financial stake in the land but would lose its ability to set drilling or environmental conditions.

118-hr-8205.one_liner: Apply federal insurance rules to cash bail and bail bond companies
provisions: Cash bail and bail bond companies would have to follow the same federal rules that insurance companies follow.
Right now, bail bond companies are not covered by those federal insurance laws — this bill would change that.
This applies to both criminal bail bonds and immigration bail bonds.

supporters: Supporters say that bringing bail bond companies under federal insurance laws would add government oversight to an industry that currently has none of those rules.
Supporters say that covering both criminal and immigration bail bonds under these laws would give defendants and detainees the same protections that insurance customers already receive.
Supporters say that requiring bail bond companies to meet federal insurance standards could reduce fraud and bad business practices in the bail industry.
critics: Critics say that applying federal insurance regulations to bail bond companies could force smaller companies out of business, leaving fewer options for people who need a bail bond to get out of jail before trial.
Critics say that extending these rules to immigration bail bonds could shrink the number of companies offering those bonds, making it harder for immigration detainees to secure release.
Critics say that the cost of meeting federal insurance requirements could be passed on to defendants and their families through higher bail bond fees.

118-hr-7673.one_liner: Limit the Department of Energy's power to set rules on washing machines
provisions: The Department of Energy can only set energy rules for washing machines if the rules are technically possible to meet.
The rules cannot end up costing consumers more money overall.
The rules must save a meaningful amount of energy — not just a small amount.

supporters: Supporters say the bill stops the DOE from setting washing machine rules that are not technically possible for manufacturers to meet, which they argue has happened with past energy standards.
Supporters say the bill protects consumers by blocking rules that would raise the total cost of owning a washing machine, even if the machine itself uses less energy.
Supporters say the bill requires any new rules to save a meaningful amount of energy, cutting out regulations that cause disruption but deliver little real savings.
critics: Critics say the bill's requirement that rules not result in 'additional net costs to consumers' could be used to block standards that save energy long-term, since calculating total consumer costs is complex and open to challenge.
Critics say removing DOE's ability to enforce standards freely could slow progress on reducing the energy used by the roughly 80 million washing machines in U.S. homes.
Critics say the phrase 'significant conservation of energy' is not defined in the bill, which could let manufacturers argue that almost any standard falls short of that bar.

118-hr-7198.one_liner: Require federal agencies to study how proposed rules affect small businesses before finalizing them
provisions: When a federal agency proposes a new rule, it must include indirect costs the rule could place on small businesses, not just direct costs.
If an agency says a rule will not significantly affect small businesses, it must tell the Office of Advocacy within 10 days.
Small businesses can file a petition asking the Office of Advocacy to review that decision.
If the Office of Advocacy reviews the petition and finds the rule does affect many small businesses, the agency must do a full cost study.
This cost study must be completed before the rule takes effect.
If the agency does not take part in that review, the rule will not apply to small businesses.
For rules that could significantly affect many small businesses, agencies must publish their policy guides and allow public comments.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects small businesses by requiring agencies to include indirect costs — not just direct costs — in their rule reviews, so small businesses get a fuller picture of what a rule will actually cost them.

Supporters say the 10-day notification rule and the petition process give small businesses a real way to challenge agency decisions, including the right to ask the Office of Advocacy to step in if an agency wrongly skips a full cost study.
Supporters say that if an agency refuses to take part in the review process, the rule simply will not apply to small businesses — giving small businesses a direct check on agency behavior.
critics: Critics say the new petition and review steps add layers to the rulemaking process, which could delay rules that protect workers, consumers, or the environment from taking effect.

Critics say the rule requiring agencies to publish policy guides and accept public comments for any rule that might affect small businesses could slow down guidance that agencies need to issue quickly.

Critics say the provision blocking a rule from applying to small businesses if an agency does not join the review could let small businesses avoid rules that were meant to apply to them, creating an uneven playing field.

118-hr-8446.one_liner: Require the government's mineral list to match the energy department's materials list
provisions: The U.S. Geological Survey keeps a list of minerals important to the country's security and economy.
The Department of Energy keeps a separate list of materials important for energy.
Right now, these two lists do not have to match.
This bill requires the USGS to add any material from the Energy Department's list to its own list.
When the Energy Department adds a new material to its list, the USGS has 45 days to add it to the USGS list.

supporters: Supporters say that requiring the USGS to add any material from the Energy Department's list within 45 days will close a gap where important energy materials had no supply chain protections under the USGS program.

Supporters say that aligning the two lists means companies and agencies working on energy projects will get the same federal support — like supply chain reviews and sourcing help — that other critical minerals already receive.
Supporters say the 45-day update rule prevents delays that could leave new energy materials unprotected during supply chain disruptions.
critics: Critics say that automatically adding Energy Department materials to the USGS list removes USGS's independent review process, which was designed to evaluate economic and national security risks separately from energy policy.
Critics say the bill does not set a limit on how many materials the Energy Department can add, which could expand the USGS list without additional resources or staff to manage the new entries.

118-hr-8219.one_liner: Study whether Lahaina, Hawaii should become a National Heritage Area
provisions: Tells the National Park Service to look into whether Lahaina, Maui should be named a National Heritage Area
The study would check if Lahaina meets the standards for that status under a federal law called the National Heritage Areas Act
No money is spent or land changed until the study is done and Congress acts on its findings

supporters: Supporters say the study would help decide if Lahaina's history as a former capital of the Hawaiian Kingdom makes it a good fit for National Heritage Area status under the National Heritage Areas Act.
Supporters say no federal money is spent and no land changes hands until the study is done and Congress takes a separate vote, so the bill carries no immediate financial cost.
Supporters say the study could help the town of Lahaina, Maui rebuild its identity after the 2023 wildfire by formally recognizing its cultural and historical significance.
critics: Critics say a federal National Heritage Area designation could bring new rules and outside oversight to Lahaina that local landowners and the Maui County government did not ask for.

Critics say starting a National Park Service study sets Lahaina on a path toward a federal designation that may not match what Native Hawaiian communities and local residents want for the area's future.

Critics say Congress has already authorized dozens of National Heritage Areas, and adding another study before finishing plans for existing ones may not be the best use of National Park Service time and staff.

118-hr-8368.one_liner: Create a coordinator to help Afghan allies, U.S. citizens, and green card holders leave Afghanistan
provisions: The State Department must hire an official called the Coordinator for Afghan Relocation Efforts to run these programs.
The coordinator moves and resettles Afghan allies who meet the requirements to come to the U.S.
The coordinator helps U.S. citizens and green card holders who ask for help leaving Afghanistan.
The coordinator makes sure all parts of the federal government work together on these efforts.
The coordinator can hire temporary workers and sign service contracts, and can extend and keep active contracts that were already in place.
This program lasts for three years after the law passes.

supporters: Supporters say creating a dedicated Coordinator for Afghan Relocation Efforts gives one official clear responsibility for moving Afghan allies through the resettlement process, instead of spreading that work across many agencies with no one in charge.

Supporters say the coordinator's power to hire temporary workers and sign service contracts quickly will help the State Department respond faster to Afghan allies and U.S. citizens still trying to leave Afghanistan.
Supporters say the three-year time limit keeps the program focused and forces the government to show results within a set window.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a budget or cap on spending for the coordinator's office, leaving taxpayers without a clear picture of what this program will cost over its three-year life.

Critics say giving one coordinator authority to extend and maintain pre-existing personal services contracts, without new oversight rules, could allow spending commitments made under earlier programs to continue with little congressional review.
Critics say the bill does not define who counts as an 'eligible Afghan ally,' which means the coordinator has wide discretion to decide who gets help and who does not.

118-hr-8790.one_liner: Set new rules for managing federal forests to reduce wildfire risk
provisions: Groups high-risk federal forest areas into zones called 'firesheds' and tracks them on a public website with maps and data
Creates a new joint center between the U.S. Forest Service and U.S. Geological Survey to track and predict wildfires
Cuts the environmental review steps required before starting certain forest management projects
Skips environmental review entirely for some forest activities
Creates small teams inside agencies to speed up approvals for forest projects
Limits how much courts can do when people sue over forest management decisions in these fire-risk zones
Funds projects to restore forests, reduce fire risk near neighborhoods, and test new technologies to fight wildfires

supporters: Supporters say the bill would reduce wildfire danger by grouping high-risk federal forest areas into trackable zones called firesheds and putting real-time maps and data on a public website, giving firefighters and local communities better information.

Supporters say cutting the number of environmental review steps before forest management projects start would let the Forest Service clear dead trees and brush faster, lowering fire risk near neighborhoods before the next fire season.

Supporters say creating a joint center between the U.S. Forest Service and U.S. Geological Survey to predict wildfires would help agencies respond earlier and protect more communities from fire damage.
critics: Critics say the bill skips environmental review entirely for some forest activities, removing the main legal process that checks whether a project could harm wildlife, water, or land before work begins.

Critics say limiting what courts can do when people sue over fireshed management decisions takes away a key tool that local communities and tribes use to stop harmful projects on federal land near them.

Critics say reducing required consultations under the Endangered Species Act for forest projects in high-risk zones could put threatened and endangered species at greater risk without public notice or legal recourse.

118-hr-8371.one_liner: Expand healthcare, housing, and benefits for veterans and their families
provisions: Lets veterans see doctors outside the VA system and protects the agreements those doctors make with veterans
Raises the spending limit on home care options so more veterans can get care at home instead of a nursing home
Gives more support to family members who are the main caregivers for veterans with serious injuries or illness
Removes the deadline on college scholarship money for surviving spouses of service members killed in the line of duty
Lets Native American veterans refinance their home loans through a VA program they previously could not use for that purpose
Pays burial and funeral costs for veterans who die in hospice care at home, if they came to hospice directly from a VA hospital or nursing home
Temporarily raises the daily payment rate the VA gives to shelters and housing programs that serve homeless veterans
Starts a program to update the VA's electronic health record system

supporters: Supporters say the bill lets veterans see doctors outside the VA system and protects the care agreements those doctors make, giving veterans more options when a VA facility is not nearby or easy to reach.

Supporters say removing the deadline on the Fry Scholarship means surviving spouses of service members killed in the line of duty will never lose their college funding just because too much time has passed.
Supporters say raising the spending cap on home care alternatives means more veterans can get care at home instead of being placed in a nursing home, which many veterans and their families prefer.
critics: Critics say the burial and funeral allowance only covers veterans who die in hospice if that hospice stay came directly after a VA hospital or nursing home stay, which leaves out veterans who entered hospice from home or from a non-VA setting.

Critics say the bill launches a new program to update the VA's electronic health record system, but the VA's last major health record overhaul cost billions of dollars and ran into serious problems, raising questions about whether a new program will do better.
Critics say the increase in daily payments to homeless veteran shelters is only temporary, which makes it hard for those programs to plan long-term budgets or keep staff.

118-hr-9598.one_liner: Keep the federal drug control office and its programs running through 2031
provisions: Keeps the Office of National Drug Control Policy running with its current powers through 2031.
Continues funding for the High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas program, which gives money and resources to local law enforcement in areas with high drug activity.
Continues the Drug-Free Communities program, which gives grants to local groups working to reduce drug use among young people.
Continues the Drug Court Training program, which helps courts that send people with drug offenses to treatment instead of jail.
Continues the National Community Anti-Drug Coalition Institute, which trains and supports local groups fighting drug use.

supporters: Supporters say keeping the High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas program funded through 2031 gives local law enforcement the resources they need to fight drug activity in the hardest-hit communities.
Supporters say the Drug-Free Communities program puts grant money directly into local groups working to keep young people away from drugs, and cutting it would leave those groups without funding.
Supporters say the Drug Court Training program helps courts send people with drug offenses to treatment instead of jail, which costs less and leads to better outcomes for people with addiction.
critics: Critics say reauthorizing the Office of National Drug Control Policy through 2031 locks in current programs without requiring Congress to review whether they are actually reducing drug use.

Critics say the High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas program sends federal money to local law enforcement, but there is limited public data showing these funds have reduced drug trafficking in targeted areas.

Critics say the Drug-Free Communities grants go to local anti-drug groups, but some research questions whether community coalition programs change teen drug use rates enough to justify continued federal spending.

118-hr-9106.one_liner: Require equal Secret Service protection staffing for presidents, vice presidents, and major candidates
provisions: The Secret Service must use the same rules to decide how many agents protect the President, Vice President, and major candidates for those offices.
Right now, the number of agents assigned can differ between those groups — this bill removes that difference.
The Department of Homeland Security decides who counts as a major candidate after talking with a committee of congressional leaders.

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a gap where major presidential and vice presidential candidates get fewer Secret Service agents than the President and Vice President, even when facing similar threats.

Supporters say requiring the Secret Service to use the same staffing rules for all four protected groups means candidates cannot be left with weaker protection due to a technicality in current policy.
Supporters say the bill keeps Congress involved by having the Department of Homeland Security consult with a committee of congressional leaders before deciding who counts as a major candidate.
critics: Critics say giving major candidates the same agent count as the President and Vice President could stretch Secret Service resources thin, since the agency would need to staff multiple protectees at the same high level at once.
Critics say the bill does not define what staffing standard the Secret Service must meet — it only says the rules must match, leaving the actual protection level up to agency discretion.
Critics say the process for deciding who is a major candidate still relies on the Department of Homeland Security, which could create delays or disputes about who qualifies before an election.

118-hr-9495.one_liner: Delay tax deadlines for hostage Americans and remove tax breaks for terrorism-supporting groups
provisions: Americans held hostage or wrongfully detained in another country get more time to file their taxes.
Their spouses also get the same extra time to file.
If a detained American already paid tax fines during the time they were held, the government refunds that money.
Groups that give money or other support to terrorist organizations lose their tax-free status.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives Americans who are wrongfully detained abroad more time to file their taxes, so they are not penalized for missing deadlines while held against their will.
Supporters say spouses of detained Americans also get extra time to file, since they may be managing family finances alone during the detention.
Supporters say groups that give money or other support to designated terrorist organizations would lose their tax-exempt status under this bill.
critics: Critics say the bill does not define how long the tax deadline extension lasts, which could create confusion for the IRS about when normal filing rules apply again.

Critics say revoking tax-exempt status from organizations requires the IRS to determine which groups qualify as terrorist-supporting, and the bill does not set clear rules for how that decision is made.
Critics say the refund process for penalties already paid by detained Americans is not explained in detail. It is unclear how a detained person or their family would apply for that money back.

118-hr-8932.one_liner: Require the student financial aid application to open by October 1 each year
provisions: The FAFSA — the form students fill out to apply for federal college money — must open every year by October 1.
Right now, the law says the FAFSA must open by January 1, with October 1 as a goal but not a hard deadline.
This bill makes October 1 a firm deadline that the Department of Education must meet every year.
Opening the FAFSA earlier gives students and families more time to compare college costs before application deadlines.

supporters: Supporters say making October 1 a firm deadline — instead of just a goal — gives students and families at least three extra months to see their financial aid numbers before college application deadlines in December and January.

Supporters say the current law lets the Department of Education delay the FAFSA until January 1, and that flexibility caused problems in 2024 when millions of students received aid information too late to make enrollment decisions on time.
Supporters say a hard October 1 deadline holds the Department of Education legally accountable in a way the current 'to the maximum extent practicable' language does not.
critics: Critics say the bill removes the January 1 backup deadline without giving the Department of Education extra funding or staff to guarantee the FAFSA is ready by October 1 every year.

Critics say that when major changes are made to the FAFSA form — as happened with the FAFSA Simplification Act — a rigid October 1 statutory deadline could force the department to release a form that has not been fully tested.
Critics say the bill does not address what happens if the Department of Education misses the October 1 deadline, leaving students with no clear remedy if the form opens late.

118-hr-8958.one_liner: Keep NASA funded and running through 2025 while adding new space and science rules
provisions: NASA keeps its funding for all of its programs through September 2025.
NASA continues working toward landing people on the Moon and eventually sending people to Mars, with help from private space companies.
Private companies can fly their own missions to the International Space Station.
When the International Space Station is eventually retired, NASA must partner with a private company to safely bring it out of orbit and dispose of it.
NASA must test how well satellites can detect greenhouse gases from space.
NASA must share Earth science data — like weather and land information — with farmers and the agriculture industry.
NASA must keep researching drones and high-speed experimental aircraft.

supporters: Supporters say keeping NASA's funding in place through September 2025 protects ongoing Moon and Mars programs from gaps that could delay crewed landings.

Supporters say allowing private companies to fly their own missions to the International Space Station opens the door to commercial spaceflight growth and reduces how much the government has to pay alone.
Supporters say requiring NASA to share Earth science data with farmers gives the agriculture industry better weather and land information to make decisions about crops and resources.
critics: Critics say requiring NASA to partner with a private company to deorbit the International Space Station hands over control of a major government asset without clear rules on cost or accountability.
Critics say the bill adds new tasks — like testing greenhouse gas satellites, researching drones, and writing multiple reports — without specifying new funding to cover those costs through FY2025.
Critics say requiring NASA to evaluate greenhouse gas detection from space could shift agency focus and resources away from its core mission of human spaceflight and exploration.

118-hr-9600.one_liner: Name a post office in Plains, Georgia after Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter
provisions: The post office at 119 Main Street in Plains, Georgia will be officially called the "Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter Post Office."
This bill only changes the name of the building — it does not change postal services, hours, or anything else at that location.
Jimmy Carter was the 39th President of the United States, serving from 1977 to 1981. He was born and raised in Plains, Georgia.
Rosalynn Carter served as First Lady from 1977 to 1981. She died in November 2023, and Jimmy Carter died in December 2024.
Plains, Georgia is a small town of about 700 people where both Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter were born and spent most of their lives.

supporters: Supporters say renaming the post office at 119 Main Street honors Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter, who were both born in Plains, Georgia and spent most of their lives there.
Supporters say the name change recognizes Jimmy Carter's service as the 39th President from 1977 to 1981 and Rosalynn Carter's role as First Lady during the same years.
Supporters say the designation gives the roughly 700 residents of Plains a lasting way to mark the Carters' ties to their hometown, since both died in 2023 and 2024.

118-hr-9668.one_liner: Create a DHS team to study and counter security threats from China's government
provisions: Sets up a team inside the Department of Homeland Security to look at security threats from China's government
The team studies terrorist threats, cybersecurity threats, border and port security threats, and transportation security threats
The team must find gaps in how the U.S. is responding to these threats and report its findings to Congress every year
The Department of Homeland Security must also research and build new tools to detect and respond to these threats
A government watchdog office reviews how well the program is working and reports back to Congress
The team and its work end seven years after it is set up

supporters: Supporters say the working group will find gaps in how DHS is currently responding to Chinese government threats across four specific areas: terrorism, cybersecurity, border and port security, and transportation security.
Supporters say requiring DHS to report to Congress every year creates accountability and keeps lawmakers informed about how the U.S. is responding to threats from China's government.
Supporters say the seven-year sunset date and the Government Accountability Office review mean Congress can check whether the program is actually working before deciding to continue it.
critics: Critics say the bill creates a new working group inside DHS without specifying a budget or staffing levels, making it unclear whether the team will have enough resources to do the job.
Critics say the bill focuses only on threats from China's government but does not explain how the working group will avoid duplicating security work that DHS and other agencies are already doing.
Critics say the bill directs DHS to research and build new detection tools without setting a timeline or cost limit, which could lead to spending without clear results.

118-hres-1449.one_liner: Condemn the rise of antisemitism and call on countries to fight it
provisions: States that antisemitism has grown around the world
Calls on countries and international groups to take steps to fight antisemitism
Supports a set of global guidelines launched in July 2024 that countries can use to track and address antisemitism

supporters: Supporters say the resolution's call for countries to adopt the July 2024 Global Guidelines gives governments a concrete tool to track and report antisemitic incidents, rather than relying on inconsistent national definitions.

Supporters say that formally condemning the global rise of antisemitism sends a clear signal to Jewish communities worldwide that their governments recognize the threat and are committed to coordinated action.
Supporters say encouraging international bodies to embrace the Global Guidelines creates a shared standard, making it easier for countries to share data and coordinate responses across borders.
critics: Critics say the resolution does not include any enforcement mechanism or funding, meaning countries can endorse the Global Guidelines without being required to take any specific action.

Critics say the July 2024 Global Guidelines have been opposed by some civil liberties groups who argue that certain definitions of antisemitism within the framework could be used to limit protected political speech, including criticism of foreign governments.

Critics say the resolution focuses on international cooperation but sets no measurable targets — such as a required number of participating countries or a reporting timeline — making it difficult to assess whether the guidelines are actually being used.

118-hres-1469.one_liner: Condemn Biden, Harris, and 13 others for their roles in the Afghanistan withdrawal
provisions: The House formally condemns President Biden and Vice President Harris for decisions made during the 2021 withdrawal from Afghanistan
The resolution also condemns 13 other named officials for their roles in planning and carrying out the withdrawal
No new laws or rules are created — this is a formal statement of disapproval by the House
