supporters: Supporters say the resolution holds 15 named officials — including President Biden and Vice President Harris — directly responsible for decisions made during the 2021 Afghanistan withdrawal, including the Abbey Gate bombing that killed 13 U.S. service members.

Supporters say the resolution's act of naming 13 specific officials beyond the President and Vice President creates a formal record of who made key planning and execution decisions during the withdrawal.
Supporters say a formal House condemnation gives Congress a way to respond to the withdrawal without needing new legislation, using its existing authority to issue statements of disapproval.
critics: Critics say the resolution creates no new rules, investigations, or penalties — meaning none of the 15 named officials face any legal consequences as a result of the condemnation.

Critics say the withdrawal followed the Doha Agreement signed in 2020, which set the terms for U.S. departure, and the resolution does not address that agreement or how it shaped the decisions made by named officials.
Critics say a resolution that names 15 individuals but includes no enforcement mechanism does not produce any findings of fact or require any official review of what went wrong during the evacuation.

118-hr-9716.one_liner: Require the government's budget office to publish more frequent spending forecasts
provisions: The Congressional Budget Office must publish at least two budget forecasts each year, instead of just one
At least one of those forecasts must include the economic data used to build it
The President must send detailed budget numbers to Congress by February 1 each year, instead of bundling that data into the full budget request later in the year

supporters: Supporters say requiring the CBO to publish at least two budget forecasts a year, instead of one, gives Congress more current information when voting on spending bills throughout the year.
Supporters say requiring the CBO to include the economic data behind at least one forecast lets lawmakers and the public check the math and see what assumptions are driving the numbers.
Supporters say moving the President's detailed budget data deadline to February 1 gives Congress weeks of extra time to study the numbers before the full budget request arrives.
critics: Critics say adding a second required CBO forecast each year could stretch the agency's staff and resources, potentially reducing the quality or depth of each report.

Critics say moving the President's technical budget data to February 1 as a separate submission could create confusion if those early numbers differ from the figures in the full budget request that follows later.

118-hres-1568.one_liner: Set House debate rules for bills on FAFSA, geothermal drilling, and critical minerals
provisions: This bill sets the terms for the House to debate and vote on three separate bills.
One bill would move the FAFSA college financial aid application window to an earlier date each year, so students get aid decisions sooner.
One bill would remove the requirement for a federal drilling permit for some geothermal energy projects on federal land.
That same bill would remove the requirement for an environmental review for those geothermal projects.
One bill would add a category called 'critical materials' to the government's official list of essential minerals.

supporters: Supporters say the FAFSA bill would move the college aid application window to an earlier date each year, giving students more time to compare financial aid offers before choosing a school.

Supporters say removing the federal drilling permit requirement for some geothermal projects on federal land would speed up clean energy development by cutting steps that can delay projects by months or years.
Supporters say adding 'critical materials' to the government's official minerals list would help secure supplies of materials needed for technology and energy production.
critics: Critics say removing the environmental review requirement for geothermal projects on federal land means drilling can begin on public land without a formal check on impacts to water, soil, or wildlife.
Critics say waiving the federal drilling permit for certain geothermal projects takes away a layer of federal oversight over activities on land owned by all Americans.
Critics say packaging three unrelated bills — covering college aid, geothermal drilling, and mineral definitions — into one debate limits the time members can give to each issue separately.

118-hres-1486.one_liner: Set floor debate rules for five measures on China, crime, forests, Afghanistan, and witness rules
provisions: This resolution sets the rules for how the House debates and votes on five separate measures.
One measure puts financial penalties on members of China's ruling Communist Party.
One bill lets local governments use federal crime grant money to build public safety reporting systems.
One bill speeds up government review of forest projects on national forests, federal land, and tribal land.
One measure calls for an investigation into Biden-Harris administration officials over decisions made during the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan.
One change updates House rules to let witnesses appear by video during official proceedings.

supporters: Supporters say the rule advances H.R. 3334, which would impose financial sanctions on members of China's ruling Communist Party, giving the U.S. a tool to pressure the Chinese government over its actions.

Supporters say H.R. 8790 would speed up the government review process under NEPA for forest projects on national forests, federal land, and tribal land, which they argue could reduce dangerous buildup of fire-prone trees.

Supporters say the Afghanistan accountability measure would require an investigation into specific Biden-Harris officials over decisions made during the 2021 U.S. military withdrawal, which resulted in the deaths of 13 U.S. service members.
critics: Critics say bundling five unrelated measures — covering China sanctions, crime grants, forest rules, Afghanistan, and House witness rules — into a single rule limits lawmakers' ability to debate and amend each one on its own merits.

Critics say H.R. 8790 would reduce required environmental reviews on national forest and tribal lands, which could let forest management projects move forward without full analysis of impacts to those communities.

Critics say the Afghanistan resolution focuses on one administration's decisions while the withdrawal itself was set in motion by agreements signed in 2020, meaning key earlier decision-makers would not face the same review.

118-hres-1576.one_liner: Set House debate rules for two bills on geothermal leasing and taxes
provisions: Sets the debate rules for the House to consider these two bills together under one process.
The first bill makes the government hold geothermal energy lease sales more often.
The first bill requires a new lease sale to be scheduled if one is canceled.
The second bill lets Americans who are held hostage or wrongfully detained abroad skip tax deadlines without penalty.
The second bill pays back any late tax fees those detained Americans already paid.
The second bill lets the government remove the tax-free status of groups found to support terrorism.

supporters: Supporters say requiring geothermal lease sales more often, and replacing any canceled sales, will increase domestic clean energy production by opening more federal land to development.

Supporters say Americans who are held hostage or wrongfully detained abroad should not face tax penalties for missing deadlines while imprisoned, and this bill lets them skip those deadlines and get back any late fees already paid.
Supporters say giving the government power to remove tax-free status from groups found to support terrorism closes a loophole that lets those groups avoid paying taxes.
critics: Critics say combining geothermal leasing rules and tax law changes into one debate process gives less floor time to each bill and limits the ability of members to fully debate either topic.

Critics say the provision to strip tax-exempt status from groups labeled as supporting terrorism does not set a clear legal standard for who decides what counts as support, which could lead to misuse against groups not involved in terrorism.
Critics say requiring a replacement lease sale every time one is canceled could pressure agencies to skip thorough environmental reviews in order to meet the new scheduling rules.

118-hres-1608.one_liner: Release the House Ethics Committee's report on Matt Gaetz to the public
provisions: The House Ethics Committee looked into allegations against Matt Gaetz, who was a member of Congress from Florida until late 2024.
The committee finished its report but never released it to the public.
This bill tells the Ethics Committee to make that report available for anyone to read.
The report covers the committee's findings from its investigation into Gaetz.

supporters: Supporters say the Ethics Committee finished its report on Matt Gaetz but never gave the public access to it, leaving the investigation's findings hidden from voters.
Supporters say Gaetz left Congress in late 2024, and releasing the report now would let people see what the committee found about a former member's conduct while in office.
Supporters say the committee's own rules do not require secrecy for reports about members who are no longer in office.
critics: Critics say releasing the report could expose witnesses or third parties named in the investigation to public attention without their consent.

Critics say the Ethics Committee has long-standing rules about keeping investigation materials private, and making an exception here could discourage people from cooperating with future investigations.
Critics say the committee, not the full House, should decide when and whether to release its own investigative findings.

118-hres-1602.one_liner: Schedule House floor votes on two bills about civic education and small business rules
provisions: Sets up a House floor vote on a bill that would create a civic education program about certain political ideologies
Sets up a House floor vote on a bill that would require the federal government to share more information when new rules affect small businesses
This is a procedural step — it does not pass either bill, it just allows the House to debate and vote on them

supporters: Supporters say this resolution allows the House to vote on H.R. 5349, which would create a civic education program teaching students about political ideologies that have caused historical harm, like fascism and communism.
Supporters say bringing H.R. 7198 to the floor gives small business owners a chance to get more information from the federal government before new rules take effect, giving them time to prepare.
Supporters say scheduling floor debate on both bills gives all House members a chance to weigh in on civic education and small business rules that affect millions of Americans.
critics: Critics say H.R. 5349 uses vague language — 'certain political ideologies' — without clearly defining which ideologies the curriculum must cover, leaving too much to be decided later.

Critics say H.R. 7198 could slow down the federal rulemaking process by adding new disclosure steps every time a regulation touches small businesses, which could delay rules meant to protect workers or consumers.
Critics say combining two unrelated bills — one on education, one on business regulation — into a single procedural vote makes it harder for members to oppose one bill without blocking the other.

118-s-3613.one_liner: Require federal building security committees to respond to security recommendations
provisions: When the Federal Protective Service sends a security recommendation to a building's security committee, that committee has 90 days to say yes or no.
If the committee says no, it must explain to the Department of Homeland Security why it is willing to accept the risk.
DHS must create a system to track all recommendations and responses.
DHS must also take steps to make sure committees follow through on responding.
DHS must report to Congress 270 days after this bill passes, and every year after that, on how committees are responding to recommendations.

supporters: Supporters say the 90-day deadline gives Facility Security Committees a clear timeline to act on Federal Protective Service recommendations, closing a gap where security issues could be ignored without a response.

Supporters say requiring committees to explain in writing why they are rejecting a recommendation — and to justify accepting the risk — creates a paper trail that holds agencies accountable for security decisions.
Supporters say the annual reports to Congress will let lawmakers track which federal buildings are ignoring security upgrades and push for action.
critics: Critics say the bill adds new reporting requirements on Facility Security Committees without providing extra staff or funding to meet the 90-day response deadline, which could strain agencies with limited security personnel.
Critics say requiring a written justification to DHS every time a committee rejects a recommendation may create paperwork burdens that slow down day-to-day security operations in federal buildings.
Critics say the bill gives DHS authority to take 'reasonable action' to enforce committee responses but does not define what that means, leaving enforcement rules unclear.

118-hres-915.one_liner: Ask Ukraine to resume letting Americans adopt Ukrainian children
provisions: Ukraine stopped allowing non-Ukrainians to adopt children on March 13, 2022.
This resolution asks Ukraine to first look at cases where American families already finished the adoption process and got approved before that date.
It also asks Ukraine to let American families who had a Ukrainian child stay with them through a hosting program start the full adoption process.
It asks Ukraine to let those same families apply to take in Ukrainian children who are in legal limbo about whether they can be adopted.

supporters: Supporters say American families who finished Ukraine's full adoption process and got approved before March 13, 2022 should not be forced to start over, since they already met all legal requirements.

Supporters say children who lived with U.S. families through hosting programs have already formed bonds with those families, and blocking the adoption process leaves those children without a permanent home.

Supporters say Ukrainian children currently in legal limbo — with no clear status on whether they can be adopted — need a defined path, and allowing pre-adoptive placements by U.S. families already in hosting programs would resolve that uncertainty.
critics: Critics say Ukraine suspended non-Ukrainian adoptions on March 13, 2022, partly to protect children during an active war, and restarting the process before the conflict ends could make it harder to verify the safety and legitimacy of each case.

Critics say the resolution asks Ukraine to prioritize U.S. families in hosting programs and pre-adoptive placements, but Ukraine may not have the government capacity to review those cases while managing wartime demands.

Critics say decisions about Ukrainian children's legal status and adoption eligibility belong to Ukraine's own courts and agencies, and a U.S. resolution urging policy changes may not reflect what Ukraine's child welfare system can safely handle right now.

118-hres-1609.one_liner: Release House Ethics Committee records on Matt Gaetz's alleged misconduct
provisions: The House Ethics Committee must keep all records from its review of Matt Gaetz, who served as a U.S. Representative from Florida.
The Committee must make those records available to the public.
The records cover the time Gaetz served as a Member of the House of Representatives.

supporters: Supporters say releasing the Ethics Committee's records on Matt Gaetz would let the public see what investigators found about his conduct while he served as a U.S. Representative from Florida.
Supporters say keeping these records sealed hides information that belongs to the public, since the review was done by a government body using public resources.
Supporters say making the records available sets a clear rule that Ethics Committee findings on sitting Members of Congress should not stay hidden when a member leaves office.
critics: Critics say releasing records from an Ethics Committee review that was never completed or voted on could be unfair to Gaetz, since no formal findings or charges were ever issued.
Critics say opening these specific records could make future subjects of Ethics reviews less willing to cooperate, knowing their files might later be made public.
Critics say the bill targets one named person — Matthew Louis Gaetz II — rather than setting a general rule, which raises questions about equal treatment under House procedures.

118-hres-1612.one_liner: Set the debate rules for three bills on energy standards, judges, and wildlife
provisions: Lets the House debate and vote on a bill that stops the Energy Department from setting efficiency rules for clothes washers unless those rules are cost-effective and technically possible
Lets the House debate and vote on a bill that adds more judges to federal district courts and makes some temporary judge positions permanent
Lets the House debate and vote on a bill that renews government programs that protect wildlife habitats and fund conservation work
Does not change any law on its own — it only controls how and when the House can debate these three bills

supporters: Supporters say H.R. 7673 would stop the Energy Department from setting clothes washer efficiency rules that manufacturers cannot meet or that cost consumers more than the energy savings are worth.
Supporters say H.R. 5009 renews federal programs that fund wildlife habitat protection, keeping grants available to landowners and conservation groups that rely on that funding.
Supporters say S. 4199 addresses court backlogs by adding district court judges and making some temporary judgeships permanent, giving courts more capacity to hear cases.
critics: Critics say this rule bundles three separate bills — clothes washer standards, federal judgeships, and wildlife conservation — into one debate package, limiting members' ability to vote on each bill on its own.

Critics say the rule allows H.R. 7673 to reach a floor vote under one debate package without separate floor debate, making it harder to examine how changes to Energy Department authority could affect long-term appliance efficiency.
Critics say S. 4199 would convert temporary judgeships to permanent ones, making those positions permanent without future review, which adds to federal judiciary costs on an ongoing basis.

118-s-2228.one_liner: Speed up environmental reviews for microchip factory projects that get federal funding
provisions: Some microchip factory projects that get federal money no longer need an environmental review before they can be built.
The Department of Commerce takes the lead on environmental reviews for chip projects that still require one.
Each chip factory project gets one combined review document instead of separate ones from multiple agencies.
States can choose to run the environmental review for chip factory projects themselves instead of the federal government doing it.
People who want to challenge a chip project in court over environmental review have a set deadline to file their lawsuit.

supporters: Supporters say that exempting some chip factory projects from the federal environmental review law will let construction start faster, helping the U.S. build more microchips at home instead of relying on foreign suppliers.

Supporters say that having the Department of Commerce lead a single combined review document for chip projects that still need one will cut down on delays caused by multiple agencies doing separate reviews.
Supporters say that letting states run their own environmental reviews for chip factory projects gives local governments more control and can speed up the process.
critics: Critics say that exempting certain chip factory projects from the federal environmental review law means some communities near those factories will not get a full review of potential air, water, or land impacts before construction begins.
Critics say that the set deadline to file a lawsuit over a chip project's environmental review could prevent nearby residents from having their concerns heard in court.

Critics say that allowing the Department of Commerce to adopt older studies instead of doing a new review for each chip factory project may mean outdated information is used to make decisions about environmental harm.

119-hr-6422.one_liner: Renew funding for five federal water programs protecting lakes, coastlines, and waterways through 2031
provisions: Keeps five federal water protection programs running through 2031, including programs for the Great Lakes, Long Island Sound, Columbia River, and coastal beaches.
Adds the Mississippi Sound to a list of nationally important water areas that can receive federal support.
Lets states and local governments use federal beach grants to track down where water pollution is coming from.
Makes federal agencies able to apply for grants under the San Francisco Estuary Partnership program.
Stops Clean Water Act grant money from going to groups based in or connected to countries the U.S. considers a security risk.
Has a government watchdog office review how well the EPA's regional water programs are working.

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps five federal water programs running through 2031, protecting water in areas like the Great Lakes and Long Island Sound that millions of people rely on for drinking water and recreation.
Supporters say adding the Mississippi Sound to the list of nationally important water areas means communities along that coastline can now get federal money to clean up and protect local waters.
Supporters say letting states use beach grants to find the exact source of water pollution will help close beaches less often and keep swimmers safer.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include new funding levels, so reauthorizing programs through 2031 may not give the EPA enough money to actually improve water quality in the Great Lakes, Columbia River, and other named areas.

Critics say the rule blocking Clean Water Act grants from groups connected to foreign countries of concern could cut off research partnerships with universities or nonprofits that do important water testing work.

Critics say making federal agencies eligible for San Francisco Estuary Partnership grants could shift limited grant dollars away from local governments and community groups that have fewer other funding options.

118-s-3764.one_liner: Keep a federal commission running that tracks threats to religious freedom around the world
provisions: The U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom gets funding and legal backing to keep running through the year starting October 2025.
The commission tracks countries and situations where people cannot practice their religion freely.
It reviews how the U.S. government responds to these situations and recommends changes to policy.

supporters: Supporters say reauthorizing the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom through FY2026 keeps a federal body running that tracks countries where people cannot freely practice their religion.
Supporters say the commission reviews how the U.S. government responds to religious freedom violations and gives policymakers specific recommendations for changing those responses.
Supporters say continued funding lets the commission monitor situations in real time and report findings to Congress and the public each year.
critics: Critics say the reauthorization only extends the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom through FY2026, giving the commission less than two years of funding before Congress must act again.
Critics say the bill does not require the U.S. government to act on the commission's recommendations, so countries identified as violators face no guaranteed policy response.
Critics say the bill adds no new tools or requirements to measure whether the commission's past recommendations have led to real changes in U.S. foreign policy.

119-hr-5103.one_liner: Set up a federal commission and cleaning program for Washington D.C.
provisions: Creates a federal commission made up of officials from U.S. Attorneys' Offices in Washington D.C., Maryland, and Virginia, plus other federal agencies.
The commission gives recommendations on enforcing federal immigration laws inside Washington D.C.
The commission works to bring in federal resources to lower crime in D.C. and helps recruit and keep more officers in the D.C. Metropolitan Police Department.
The Department of the Interior runs a program to clean and take care of monuments, parks, and roads in D.C. that many people visit.
The program also repairs or puts back federal monuments and similar properties that have been damaged or removed.
All parts of this bill end on January 2, 2029.

supporters: Supporters say the federal commission, made up of officials from U.S. Attorneys' Offices in D.C., Maryland, and Virginia, would bring more coordinated law enforcement resources to reduce crime in the District.
Supporters say the Department of the Interior program would keep monuments, parks, and roads clean and restore federal properties that have been damaged or removed.
Supporters say helping recruit and keep more D.C. Metropolitan Police Department officers would strengthen local law enforcement capacity.
critics: Critics say the commission's role in enforcing federal immigration law inside D.C. oversteps local authority, since D.C. has its own policies limiting cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
Critics say placing federal control over D.C. public safety and cleanliness through a commission that reports to the executive branch reduces the city's ability to govern itself.
Critics say the bill's sunset date of January 2, 2029 is too short to measure whether the commission's recommendations or the Interior Department's cleaning program produce lasting results.

118-s-709.one_liner: Require federal agencies to check and report their progress on goals each year
provisions: Each federal agency must review its progress on every goal it has set at least once a year.
Agencies must find and list problems that could stop them from reaching their goals.
For goals most at risk of being missed, agencies must come up with a plan to get back on track.
Each agency must appoint a Deputy Performance Improvement Officer to help run these reviews.
The government's top priority goals must be updated during the first year of each new presidential term.
Each top priority goal must include a plan to complete it within one four-year presidential term.
Each top priority goal must point to the specific parts of the federal budget that pay for it.

supporters: Supporters say requiring each agency to review progress on every goal at least once a year will catch problems early, before money and time are wasted on programs that are off track.

Supporters say linking each top priority goal to specific budget lines will make it easier for Congress and the public to see exactly where federal money is going and whether it is being used effectively.

Supporters say requiring goals to be updated in the first year of each presidential term ensures new administrations set clear plans with a realistic four-year timeline, rather than carrying over outdated priorities.
critics: Critics say creating a new Deputy Performance Improvement Officer position at each agency adds government staff and costs without proof that more oversight roles lead to better results.

Critics say requiring all priority goals to fit within a single four-year presidential term may push agencies to ignore long-term problems — like infrastructure or climate risks — that take longer than four years to solve.
Critics say annual reviews and new reporting requirements will pull agency staff away from delivering services, adding paperwork burdens that fall hardest on smaller agencies with fewer resources.

118-s-3791.one_liner: Extend and update wildlife and conservation programs through 2030
provisions: Keeps several wildlife and conservation programs running through the year starting October 2029, including programs for wetlands, fish habitat, and the Chesapeake Bay
Extends a program that tracks and manages Chronic Wasting Disease, a sickness that spreads among deer and elk
Lets one government group per state get a permit to protect farm animals from black vulture attacks
Funds the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to finish a national survey of fish habitats and build a database to track the results
Keeps a rule in place through 2030 that stops the EPA from adding rules about lead in sport fishing gear

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps the North American Wetlands Conservation Act and fish habitat programs funded through FY2030, which they say protects wetlands and fish populations that millions of hunters and anglers depend on.

Supporters say the black vulture livestock permit program gives farmers in each state a legal way to protect their cattle and sheep from black vulture attacks without needing to get individual permits from the federal government.
Supporters say extending the Chronic Wasting Disease Task Force through FY2030 helps states track and slow the spread of a disease that has infected deer and elk herds across dozens of states.
critics: Critics say the bill extends through 2030 a block on the EPA from regulating lead in sport fishing gear, which prevents the agency from acting on research linking lead sinkers and jigs to lead poisoning in fish-eating birds like loons and eagles.
Critics say limiting black vulture depredation permits to one government entity per state may leave farmers in large or rural states without timely access to protection for their livestock.

Critics say the bill funds a new national fish habitat database without setting a required deadline or budget cap for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to complete it, leaving the scope and cost open-ended.

119-hres-1128.one_liner: Express House support for keeping the Department of Homeland Security funded
provisions: The House says it supports giving the Department of Homeland Security enough money to keep running
The House says Americans face more risk every day that DHS runs out of money and has to pause its work
The House thanks DHS employees for their work protecting the country

supporters: Supporters say the resolution calls for fully funding DHS so the agency can keep running without interruption.
Supporters say the resolution warns that Americans face greater risk every day that DHS runs out of money and has to pause its work.
Supporters say the resolution formally thanks DHS employees for their work protecting the country, which they say recognizes the people who carry out that mission.
critics: Critics say the resolution does not include a specific dollar amount, so it does not commit Congress to any actual level of funding for DHS.
Critics say the resolution does not name which DHS programs should be funded first if a lapse happens, leaving no guidance on protecting the most important work.
Critics say thanking DHS employees without defining what protections they receive during a funding lapse means the resolution offers no real help to those workers.

119-hres-1131.one_liner: Set the rules for debating four bills in the House
provisions: Sets the time and rules for how the House will debate a bill to fund the Department of Homeland Security for the year ending September 30, 2026
Sets the rules for debating a statement of support for the Department of Homeland Security
Sets the rules for debating a bill to create a program to clean up and improve Washington D.C.
Sets the rules for debating a bill about which ships can use U.S. waterways and ports

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the House to move forward on H.R. 8029, which funds the Department of Homeland Security through September 30, 2026, keeping border security and immigration enforcement agencies fully funded for the year.

Supporters say the rule enables debate on H.R. 7084, which would change the rules on which ships can enter U.S. ports and waterways, giving Congress a chance to vote on tighter controls over foreign vessels.
Supporters say combining debate rules for all four bills into one resolution helps the House work through its schedule faster and keeps multiple priorities moving at the same time.
critics: Critics say bundling four separate bills — including DHS funding, D.C. cleanup, and shipping rules — into a single rule means members must accept or reject the entire package instead of voting on each issue separately.
Critics say if the rule limits debate time on H.R. 8029, members will not have enough time to examine how DHS spending is divided across its many agencies and programs before casting a vote.
Critics say restricting amendments to H.R. 7084 through the rule prevents members from proposing changes to which specific vessel types would be affected by the new port and waterway restrictions.

119-hres-1142.one_liner: Set the rules for how Congress handles Senate changes to a government spending bill
provisions: This is a procedural step that decides what happens to changes the Senate made to a spending bill called H.R. 7147.
H.R. 7147 funds many parts of the federal government through September 30, 2026.
This resolution tells the House how to respond — whether to accept, reject, or negotiate the Senate's changes.
No new spending or policy changes are made by this resolution itself.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution keeps H.R. 7147 moving forward so that federal government funding through September 30, 2026 does not lapse.
Supporters say it uses the House's constitutional role to formally respond to Senate changes on spending bills, which is a required step before any funds can be sent.
Supporters say the resolution gives the House a structured way to accept, reject, or negotiate the Senate's changes to H.R. 7147 rather than letting the bill stall.
critics: Critics say this procedural step allows House leadership to decide how to respond to Senate amendments without a full floor debate on each specific change.
Critics say skipping a conference committee — where both chambers negotiate line by line — reduces accountability over what ends up in the final version of H.R. 7147.
Critics say the resolution gives members no direct vote on the Senate's changes to a bill that funds large parts of the federal government through September 30, 2026.

119-hr-8029.one_liner: Fund the Department of Homeland Security and end its partial shutdown
provisions: The Department of Homeland Security ran out of money on February 14, 2026, and this bill gives it funding to keep running for the rest of the year.
Agencies that get funded include Border Patrol, ICE, TSA, the Coast Guard, and the Secret Service.
FEMA and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency also get money to keep operating.
Federal workers who missed paychecks during the shutdown get their back pay.
Costs the government took on during the shutdown to protect people and property are approved as valid.

supporters: Supporters say the bill ends the DHS shutdown that started on February 14, 2026, so agencies like Border Patrol, ICE, TSA, the Coast Guard, and the Secret Service can keep running.
Supporters say federal workers who missed paychecks during the shutdown will receive their back pay under the bill.
Supporters say the bill keeps FEMA and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency funded so they can respond to disasters and protect digital systems.
critics: Critics say the bill funds the full DHS budget through the rest of FY2026 without requiring any cuts or changes to how agencies like ICE or TSA spend their money.
Critics say the bill approves costs agencies spent during the shutdown without requiring a review of whether those expenses were necessary.

Critics say relying on short-term funding bills that expire — like the continuing resolution that ran out on February 14, 2026 — disrupts agency planning, and this bill does not require a longer-term fix.

119-hr-7084.one_liner: Block ships from US ports if they called at a port taken from American owners
provisions: The President can block ships from US ports if those ships stopped at an American-owned port that was seized by another government.
The rule only applies to ports seized by countries in the Western Hemisphere that have a trade deal with the US.
The block can be lifted when the country returns the property, pays the US owner, or both sides reach an agreement.
Ships in an emergency can still enter US ports even if they are otherwise blocked.
A ship can also enter if the American who owned the seized port gave it permission to use the facility.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects American property owners by giving the President power to block ships that used ports seized from U.S. companies or individuals, creating a financial cost for countries that take American-owned facilities.
Supporters say the rule targets a specific problem: Western Hemisphere countries that have trade deals with the U.S. but still seize American-owned ports without paying fair compensation.
Supporters say the bill includes safeguards, like allowing blocked ships to enter U.S. ports during emergencies and lifting the ban once a country returns the property or pays the U.S. owner.
critics: Critics say the bill gives the President broad, unilateral power to block foreign ships with no requirement for Congress to approve or review each decision.
Critics say targeting only Western Hemisphere countries with U.S. trade deals creates unequal treatment, since countries without trade deals face no penalty for the same actions.

Critics say blocking ships could disrupt trade and raise costs for U.S. businesses and consumers who depend on goods carried by those vessels, even when the dispute is between the government and a single property owner.

117-hconres-45.one_liner: Call on Serbia to prosecute those responsible for killing three American brothers
provisions: Three American brothers — Ylli, Agron, and Mehmet Bytyqi — were killed in Serbia in July 1999.
Congress states that the people responsible for those killings should be prosecuted.
Congress states that the U.S. should put enough money and staff toward watching and supporting Serbia's investigation.
This resolution does not create a law or require any action — it states Congress's position.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution puts Congress on record calling for prosecution of the people responsible for the 1999 killings of three American citizens — Ylli, Agron, and Mehmet Bytyqi — in Serbia.
Supporters say directing U.S. money and staff toward watching Serbia's investigation gives the Bytyqi family a better chance at seeing the killers held accountable after more than 25 years.
Supporters say that even though the resolution does not create a law, it sends a clear message to Serbia that the U.S. government is paying attention to how the case is handled.
critics: Critics say the resolution does not require any government action or spending, so it may not lead to real results for the Bytyqi family.
Critics say Congress has passed similar non-binding resolutions before without changing outcomes in foreign criminal cases, and this one gives Serbia no legal obligation to act.
Critics say the resolution leaves the amount of U.S. resources devoted to monitoring Serbia's investigation undefined, making it hard to hold anyone accountable for following through.

117-hconres-59.one_liner: Condemn the 2021 military takeover in Sudan and call for return to civilian rule
provisions: States that Congress does not support the October 25, 2021 military takeover of Sudan's government.
Calls on Sudan's military leaders to free all government officials and civilians they arrested during the takeover.
Calls on Sudan's military to restore the civilian-led government and constitution that was in place before the coup.
Calls on Sudan's military to end the state of emergency and turn communications back on.
Calls on other countries to join the U.S. in placing targeted sanctions on Sudan's military leaders.
Calls on international groups to suspend Sudan from regional organizations until civilian rule is restored.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution calls on Sudan's military to release all government officials and civilians arrested during the October 25, 2021 takeover and to restore the transitional constitution and civilian-led government.

Supporters say the resolution asks other countries to join the U.S. in placing targeted sanctions on Sudan's military leaders and to suspend Sudan from regional organizations until civilian rule is restored.
Supporters say calling out the coup by its specific date sends a clear message that Congress does not accept military takeovers of elected governments.
critics: Critics say a concurrent resolution has no legal force and does not require the President to take any action, so Sudan's military leaders have no reason to comply.
Critics say calling for targeted sanctions on Sudan's military leaders could push those leaders to cut off cooperation with the U.S. on counterterrorism and regional security.
Critics say suspending Sudan from regional organizations could hurt ordinary Sudanese people who depend on those organizations for aid and services, not just the military leaders who led the coup.

117-hr-1456.one_liner: Extend Peace Corps funding and expand benefits and protections for volunteers
provisions: Keeps the Peace Corps funded through September 2025
Raises the payment volunteers get when their service ends
Lets returned volunteers apply for federal jobs without going through the standard hiring process
Gives returned volunteers three months of health coverage at no cost after service ends, with an option to pay for three more months at their own cost
Requires the Peace Corps to provide mental health care to volunteers during and after service, and to supply period products
Lets volunteers who had to leave early through no fault of their own re-enroll faster
Expands protections for volunteers who report problems or wrongdoing, and raises the pay rate used to calculate workers compensation claims

supporters: Supporters say the bill helps returned volunteers by giving them three months of free health coverage after their service ends, which protects people who may not have a job lined up right away.
Supporters say allowing returned volunteers to apply for federal jobs without going through the standard hiring process rewards people who gave years of public service abroad.
Supporters say requiring the Peace Corps to provide mental health care during and after service addresses a known gap that has left volunteers without support when they return home.
critics: Critics say giving returned volunteers the ability to skip the standard federal hiring process creates an unequal system where other qualified job applicants must compete under rules that Peace Corps returnees do not have to follow.

Critics say adding three months of free health coverage, raising the readjustment payment, and increasing the pay rate used to calculate workers compensation claims all raise program costs, but the bill does not include specific dollar figures or spending caps to limit those increases.

Critics say reauthorizing Peace Corps funding through September 2025 without requiring measurable performance goals means Congress is committing federal dollars without clear proof the program is meeting its stated mission.

117-hr-1066.one_liner: Set the federal government's share of wildfire aid at 75% or more
provisions: The federal government must pay at least 75% of the cost of wildfire emergency grants, called Fire Management Assistance Grants.
FEMA must create new rules that set clear levels of fire damage that would allow the federal share to go above 75%.
The rules must use a measurement specific to fire damage — not general disaster damage — to decide when to increase federal funding.

supporters: Supporters say the 75% federal cost floor for Fire Management Assistance Grants gives states and local governments a guaranteed baseline of help, so they are not left paying most of the bill after a major wildfire.
Supporters say requiring FEMA to use a fire-specific damage measurement — instead of a general disaster formula — means funding decisions will better match the actual scale of fire destruction.
Supporters say the new rulemaking will create clear rules for when the federal share can go above 75%, which removes guesswork for states applying for aid after a fire.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a cap on how high the federal share can go above 75%, which could mean the federal government ends up covering a much larger portion of costs with no defined limit.
Critics say the bill does not specify a timeline for FEMA to finish the new rulemaking, which could delay the fire-specific damage thresholds from taking effect for years.
Critics say states that have fewer or smaller wildfires may object to a rule that raises the federal cost share for fire grants, since it shifts more of the national budget toward fire-prone states.

117-hr-1808.one_liner: Make it a federal crime to buy, sell, make, or own certain semi-automatic guns and large magazines
provisions: Makes it a crime to buy, sell, make, or own certain semi-automatic guns and magazines that hold large numbers of bullets.
Bolt-action, pump-action, lever-action, and slide-action guns are not covered by this rule, nor are antiques or guns that no longer work.
Active police, certain government workers, and retired police officers can still own these guns and magazines.
People who already own these guns can keep them but must store them safely, and a background check is required before selling or giving one to someone else.
People who already own large magazines can keep them but cannot sell or give them to anyone else.
New large magazines must have a serial number, and new guns and magazines covered by this rule must display the year they were made.
Cities and states can use federal grant money from the Byrne Justice Assistance program to pay people who turn in these guns or magazines voluntarily.

supporters: Supporters say the bill will reduce the future supply of these guns because it bans new manufacturing and new sales of semi-automatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, even though people who already own them can keep them.

Supporters say that when someone wants to sell a grandfathered assault weapon to a private buyer, a licensed gun dealer must run a background check first, which helps keep these guns away from people who are not allowed to have them.

Supporters say cities and states can use federal Byrne Justice Assistance grant money to pay people who choose to turn in these guns or magazines voluntarily, giving owners a way to get rid of them safely.
critics: Critics say the bill makes it a crime to buy or make semi-automatic guns that millions of Americans currently own legally for self-defense and sport, treating law-abiding gun owners as criminals.

Critics say that buy-back programs using Byrne grant money are optional — states and cities are not required to offer them — so many owners who want to surrender a weapon may receive no payment at all.
Critics say the bill creates two sets of rules by letting active and retired law enforcement officers keep these guns and magazines while banning the same guns for regular citizens.

117-hr-2250.one_liner: Set new rules for how the VA manages its technology projects and spending
provisions: The VA cannot spend money on any new major tech project unless it first submits a report covering the project's cost, timeline, and goals.
That report becomes the baseline — the VA must track and report any changes against it throughout the life of the project.
Each project must be run by a team that includes a certified project manager, a technical lead, a functional lead, and a contracting officer.
The VA's top tech official must take direct control over the technology staff and contractors at the VA's Financial Services Center.
The VA must review all of its tech investments to decide which ones could move to cloud computing.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the VA to submit a cost, timeline, and goals report before spending money on any new major tech project will stop the agency from repeating past overruns, like the VA's electronic health record system, which has gone hundreds of millions of dollars over budget.

Supporters say requiring a certified project manager, technical lead, functional lead, and contracting officer on every project will bring the kind of team structure that private companies use to keep tech projects on track.

Supporters say giving the VA's Chief Information Officer direct control over tech staff and contractors at the Financial Services Center will close a gap where that office had oversight responsibility but not real management authority.
critics: Critics say the requirement to submit a baseline report and track all changes throughout a project's life cycle adds a new layer of paperwork that could slow down tech upgrades veterans are already waiting for.
Critics say the bill does not set any spending limit or timeline for completing the cloud computing review, which means the VA could conduct the review without ever acting on its findings.
Critics say placing the Financial Services Center's tech staff under a new chain of command could disrupt ongoing contracts and day-to-day operations during the transition.

117-hr-263.one_liner: Limit who can own or touch big cats like lions and tigers
provisions: Makes it illegal for most private owners to get new big cats, including lions, tigers, leopards, cheetahs, jaguars, and cougars.
People who already own big cats can keep them but cannot breed them or get more.
Stops members of the public from touching or petting big cats at zoos, circuses, or other exhibits.
Only licensed facilities like accredited zoos can keep big cats under the new rules.

supporters: Supporters say the ban on new private ownership of lions, tigers, leopards, cheetahs, jaguars, and cougars will reduce the number of dangerous animals living in backyards and roadside zoos, where they pose risks to neighbors and emergency responders.
Supporters say ending public contact with big cats at zoos and circuses will stop cubs from being taken from their mothers repeatedly to be used for paid petting sessions.
Supporters say limiting big cat keeping to licensed, accredited facilities means these animals will be held to care and safety standards that private owners are not required to meet.
critics: Critics say the rule allowing current owners to keep their animals but not breed or acquire more will create a shrinking population of legally owned big cats, leaving some owners with aging animals and no way to continue their programs.

Critics say small, family-run animal exhibits that are not accredited by major zoo associations may lose the ability to display big cats even if they have good safety records, putting those businesses at risk.
Critics say the no-contact rule removes a source of funding for some facilities, since paid public interactions with big cats help cover the high cost of caring for these animals.

117-hr-2521.one_liner: Start a VA pilot program to provide doula support to pregnant veterans
provisions: The VA will run a 5-year test program to offer doula services to pregnant veterans already enrolled in VA health care.
Doulas are trained support people who help women before, during, and after childbirth.
The program will track how doula support affects birth outcomes and mental health for pregnant veterans.
Services will be provided through outside organizations that work with the VA.

supporters: Supporters say the 5-year pilot program would give pregnant veterans access to trained doula support before, during, and after childbirth — a service not currently offered through the VA health care system.
Supporters say tracking birth and mental health outcomes over five years would give the VA real data to decide if doula services should become a permanent benefit for enrolled veterans.
Supporters say using outside organizations to deliver services would let the VA expand access without needing to hire and train new VA staff.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a funding amount, making it unclear how much the 5-year program would cost taxpayers or how many pregnant veterans it could actually serve.
Critics say routing services through outside organizations instead of VA staff could create gaps in care coordination for veterans already in the VA health care system.
Critics say the bill limits the program to veterans already enrolled in VA health care, leaving out pregnant veterans who are eligible but not yet enrolled.

117-hr-203.one_liner: Name a Houston post office building after Benny C. Martinez
provisions: The post office at 4020 Broadway Street in Houston, Texas will officially be called the 'Benny C. Martinez Post Office Building'.
The name applies to the building only — mail delivery, services, and daily operations at that location stay the same.
The bill honors Benny C. Martinez by giving his name to this Houston post office as a form of public recognition.
No federal money is spent and no laws or rules change as a result of this bill.

supporters: Supporters say the bill honors Benny C. Martinez by giving his name to the post office at 4020 Broadway Street in Houston, Texas, recognizing his contributions to the local community.
Supporters say the naming costs no federal money and changes no laws or services, making it a low-cost way to preserve a person's legacy in a public building.
critics: Critics say Congress is using floor time to rename a single building with no policy effect, no spending changes, and no impact on mail delivery or federal operations.
Critics say the bill changes only the official name of the building and does nothing to affect services, funding, or rules at the 4020 Broadway Street location.

117-hr-1934.one_liner: Create a government team to boost U.S. influence in global 5G technology rule-making
provisions: Creates a group of federal agencies working together to shape international rules for 5G wireless technology
The group works to get U.S. allies and private companies more involved in setting those rules
Reports to Congress on plans for working with other countries to share safety information about 5G
Reports to Congress on what China is doing in international 5G rule-setting groups

supporters: Supporters say the interagency working group would give the U.S. a stronger voice in groups like the International Telecommunication Union, where 5G rules are being written right now.
Supporters say bringing in U.S. allies and private companies to help set 5G standards would reduce the chance that rules get written around equipment from companies like Huawei.
Supporters say requiring reports to Congress on China's role in 5G standard-setting groups gives lawmakers real information to act on, instead of guesses.
critics: Critics say the bill only creates a working group and requires reports, but does not give the group any power or funding to actually change what happens in international standard-setting bodies.
Critics say the bill does not define how many agencies must join the group or set a deadline for when the strategy must be ready, which could slow down results.
Critics say that private companies already participate in 5G standard-setting on their own, so a government-led group may duplicate work already being done without adding new resources.

117-hr-3588.one_liner: Fund grants to colleges and nonprofits for math modeling research in K-12 schools
provisions: The National Science Foundation must create a program to give grants to colleges and nonprofits for research on math and statistics teaching in public K-12 schools.
The grants will support teaching areas like data science and how to use math to solve real-world problems.
The National Science Foundation must try to set up a study with the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine on how math and statistics modeling is taught in schools.
The study will produce a report on what is working and what is not in math modeling education.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the NSF to fund grants for colleges and nonprofits will help K-12 schools get better at teaching data science and real-world math problem solving, skills that many students currently do not get.

Supporters say the required study with the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine will produce a report showing what math and statistics teaching methods are working and which are not, giving schools clearer guidance.
Supporters say putting the NSF in charge of this program means the grants will go through a competitive process, so only high-quality research on math modeling education gets funded.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a specific dollar amount for the grants, making it unclear how many schools or programs will actually receive funding.

Critics say directing the NSF to study and report on math modeling education adds a new requirement without guaranteeing that public K-12 schools will change how they teach based on the report's findings.
Critics say the grants go to colleges and nonprofits for research, not directly to K-12 teachers or schools, so classrooms may not see any real change in how math and statistics are taught.

117-hr-3372.one_liner: Fund community centers and hotlines to help people leaving prison
provisions: Lets the Department of Justice give money to community nonprofits to open reentry centers for people coming out of prison
Lets the Department of Justice give money to states, tribes, and local governments to run phone hotlines that connect people leaving prison to services in their community

supporters: Supporters say the DOJ grants for community nonprofits would give people leaving prison a single place to get housing, job, and health services, which research shows lowers the chance they return to prison.

Supporters say the reentry hotlines funded for states, tribes, and local governments would let people call for help the moment they leave prison, when they are most likely to struggle without support.
Supporters say connecting returning citizens to community-based organizations instead of government offices makes it easier to reach people who distrust the system and need services fast.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a specific dollar cap on DOJ grants, making it hard to know the total cost to taxpayers before Congress votes.
Critics say grants to nonprofits to run reentry centers may duplicate programs already funded by states and local governments, spending federal money on services that exist in some communities.
Critics say phone hotlines alone do not guarantee housing or jobs, and without tracking outcomes tied to the grant money, there is no proof the program reduces reoffending rates.

117-hr-3482.one_liner: Create a national center to support aviation education and job training
provisions: Creates a new group called the National Center for the Advancement of Aviation to connect schools, businesses, and government agencies in the aviation field.
The center will help develop school lessons and training programs for aviation and aerospace jobs.
It will help military veterans move into civilian aviation or aerospace careers through outreach and apprenticeships.
It will collect and store public data on aviation safety, jobs, and research in one place.
It will host events and conferences where people from different parts of the aviation world can share ideas.
It can give grants — money with no payback required — to schools and training programs that teach aviation, including high schools and trade schools.

supporters: Supporters say the center will help military veterans move into civilian aviation and aerospace jobs through apprenticeships and outreach programs, addressing the shortage of trained pilots and technicians in the U.S.

Supporters say the ability to issue grants to high schools, trade schools, and colleges for aviation curricula will expand career training to students who currently have no access to aviation education programs.
Supporters say storing aviation safety data, economic data, and research in one public place will make it easier for schools, businesses, and policymakers to find and use accurate information.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a funding cap or budget for the new center, leaving the total cost to taxpayers undefined before the program is approved.

Critics say the center's duties — collecting data, developing curricula, and hosting conferences — overlap with work already done by the FAA and the Department of Transportation, creating a redundant agency.
Critics say limiting grants to organizations that already have experience building aviation curricula could shut out newer schools and programs that are just starting to offer aviation training.

117-hr-2988.one_liner: Strengthen protections for federal workers who report government problems to Congress
provisions: Federal workers are protected from job punishment if they report problems to Congress.
The President, members of Congress, military members, and other federal workers cannot block an employee's right to report to Congress.
Workers cannot reveal a whistleblower's name to people outside the government.
Workers who face job punishment can ask a government board to fix it.
If the board does not decide within 180 days, workers can take the case to court.
Workers can now report problems to a supervisor in their chain of command as a protected action.
Job suspensions of 1 to 13 days not caused by budget gaps, and suspensions of 14 to 29 days, can now be appealed.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects federal workers from being fired, suspended, or punished for reporting problems to Congress, closing gaps that left some employees unprotected.
Supporters say the rule barring anyone — including the President and members of Congress — from blocking a worker's right to report to Congress makes the protection harder to ignore or work around.
Supporters say allowing workers to appeal short suspensions of 1 to 13 days, which were not previously covered, means more workers can challenge unfair punishment.
critics: Critics say expanding protected disclosures to include a supervisor in the employee's chain of command could allow agencies to handle complaints internally and keep problems from reaching outside watchdogs.
Critics say the 180-day window before a worker can take a case to court may still leave workers waiting too long for relief while facing job pressure.

Critics say prohibiting disclosure of a whistleblower's identity only to people outside the government may not fully protect workers, since people inside the government could still share that information.

117-hr-302.one_liner: Stop agencies from moving federal workers into a less-protected job category
provisions: This bill stops federal agencies from moving jobs out of the standard federal hiring system into separate, less-protected categories.
It makes it illegal to create any new job categories beyond the ones already in federal hiring rules as of September 30, 2020.
A 2020 executive order had created a new category called Schedule F, covering federal workers whose jobs involve setting or advising on government policy.
Workers placed in Schedule F lose the job protections that most federal employees have.
Reports at the time estimated around 50,000 federal workers could have been moved into Schedule F under the 2020 order.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects roughly 50,000 federal workers whose jobs involve setting or advising on government policy from losing their civil service job protections under Schedule F.

Supporters say by banning any new job categories beyond those in place as of September 30, 2020, the bill stops future presidents from using executive orders to strip career federal employees of hiring and firing protections.
Supporters say workers in the competitive service have appeal rights and due process rules that Schedule F removed, and this bill restores those protections for policy-related jobs.
critics: Critics say the bill prevents presidents from being able to remove federal workers in policy-advising roles, making it harder for a new administration to carry out the agenda voters elected them on.

Critics say positions that are policy-determining or policy-advocating in character — the jobs covered by Schedule F — should be more directly accountable to elected leadership, not shielded by civil service rules.

Critics say blocking Schedule F means federal agencies cannot easily replace workers in key policy roles who resist or slow down a president's directives, limiting executive control over the bureaucracy.

117-hr-3630.one_liner: Add Medicare coverage for compression garments that treat lymphedema
provisions: Medicare would start covering compression sleeves, stockings, and wraps prescribed to treat lymphedema.
Lymphedema is a condition where fluid builds up and causes swelling, usually in the arms or legs.
Items must be prescribed by a health care provider, such as a doctor, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant.
Coverage includes both standard sizes and custom-fitted garments made to fit a specific patient.
Other devices that help prevent or treat lymphedema could also be covered if found to work.

supporters: Supporters say Medicare would for the first time cover compression sleeves, stockings, and wraps — both standard sizes and custom-fitted garments — when prescribed by a doctor, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant to treat lymphedema.

Supporters say Medicare currently has no benefit category for compression garments, meaning people with lymphedema pay the full cost themselves — this bill would create that coverage for the first time.
Supporters say requiring a prescription from a licensed health care provider before coverage applies limits the benefit to patients with a confirmed lymphedema diagnosis.
critics: Critics say the bill's provision covering 'other devices determined to be effective' creates an open-ended coverage category tied to no defined cost ceiling, making total new Medicare spending difficult to estimate.

Critics say custom-fitted garments, which the bill explicitly covers, cost more than standard sizes and require individual measurements, adding to Medicare expenses without a cap written into the law.
Critics say the bill does not specify what evidence standard 'other devices' must meet to qualify for coverage, leaving those decisions to agency discretion rather than criteria defined in the law.

117-hr-3771.one_liner: Direct CDC to give states grants for heart disease awareness in high-risk communities
provisions: Requires the CDC to give money to states to run heart disease awareness programs.
States can use the money to create educational materials and research collections about heart disease.
The program focuses on South Asian people in the U.S., who face heart disease more often than many other groups.
Other groups that face heart disease more often than average are also covered by the program.
Research and awareness efforts include how type 2 diabetes connects to heart disease in these communities.

supporters: Supporters say the bill directs CDC grants to states to fund heart disease awareness programs aimed at South Asian Americans, a group that faces heart disease at higher rates than many other communities in the U.S.

Supporters say the bill requires states to produce educational materials that explain how type 2 diabetes connects to heart disease, giving South Asian communities and other at-risk groups access to health information tied to conditions they face more often.

Supporters say the program covers other populations that also face higher-than-average rates of heart disease, not just South Asian people, meaning CDC grant money can reach a broader set of at-risk groups.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a specific dollar amount for the CDC grants, which makes it unclear how much funding will actually reach state programs or whether states will receive enough to run meaningful awareness efforts.

Critics say the CDC's Office of Minority Health already runs community health programs for populations at higher risk of heart disease, and the bill does not explain how the new state grant program differs from or coordinates with those existing efforts.

Critics say the bill sets no outcome measures or reporting requirements for states that receive grants, so there is no way to track whether the awareness programs reduce heart disease rates in South Asian or other at-risk communities.

117-hr-4040.one_liner: Make COVID-era telehealth rules permanent for Medicare patients
provisions: Medicare patients can get telehealth visits from anywhere, not just rural areas or approved locations.
Community health centers and rural clinics can be the location where a doctor connects with a patient over video or phone.
Any type of Medicare-approved medical provider can offer telehealth visits, not just certain specialists.
Patients can have audio-only phone appointments for general care and mental health services, without needing a camera or video connection.

supporters: Supporters say making telehealth permanent for Medicare patients means seniors and people with disabilities can see a doctor by phone or video from home, without traveling to a clinic.
Supporters say allowing audio-only phone appointments for mental health services helps patients who do not own a smartphone or cannot use video, removing a barrier to care.
Supporters say letting community health centers and rural clinics serve as telehealth sites gives more providers a way to reach patients in areas with few doctors.
critics: Critics say allowing any Medicare-approved provider to offer telehealth visits without stricter oversight could make it harder to catch billing fraud or low-quality care.
Critics say removing location rules means Medicare pays for telehealth visits from anywhere, which could increase total Medicare spending without a clear cap on new costs.
Critics say audio-only visits for general and mental health care may lead to missed diagnoses that an in-person or video exam would have caught, raising safety concerns for patients.

117-hr-4118.one_liner: Create federal grants and new offices to reduce violence in communities with high homicide rates
provisions: Gives money to local programs that work to stop violence in areas where homicides happen most
Creates a new office inside the Department of Health and Human Services to run these programs
Sets up a group of advisors to help guide how violence reduction programs are run
Creates a national center to train local groups, share research, and track data on violence
Gives job training money to connect young people ages 16 to 24 to jobs in areas hit hard by gun violence

supporters: Supporters say the grants for communities hit hardest by homicides would fund proven programs where trained community members, called violence interrupters, work directly to stop conflicts before they turn deadly.
Supporters say the Department of Labor job training grants would connect young people ages 16 to 24 in high-violence areas to in-demand jobs, giving them a path away from violence.
Supporters say the new National Community Violence Response Center would track data and share research across cities, so local programs can learn what actually works instead of guessing.
critics: Critics say creating a new Office of Community Violence Intervention inside HHS adds federal bureaucracy and overhead costs that take money away from the local programs the bill is meant to fund.
Critics say the bill does not include specific funding amounts or caps, making it hard to know how much this will cost taxpayers or whether Congress will keep funding it in future years.
Critics say job training grants for ages 16 to 24 leave out adults over 24 who also live in communities disproportionately affected by gun violence and may need the same help.

117-hr-3843.one_liner: Change the fees companies pay to the government before completing a merger
provisions: Companies that want to merge must pay a fee to the government before the deal is approved — this bill changes how much that fee is
The fees are based on the size of the deal, with bigger mergers paying more
Each year, the fees go up automatically to keep pace with rising prices

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires companies seeking to merge to pay fees that cover the cost of the government review of whether their merger is legal, instead of drawing from other government funds.
Supporters say the automatic yearly increase tied to the Consumer Price Index keeps fees current with rising costs, so Congress does not need to pass a new law each year to update them.
Supporters say the graduated fee schedule means the largest mergers pay the highest fees, matching the cost of government review to the size and complexity of each deal.
critics: Critics say higher fees under the new schedule raise the cost for any company seeking government approval of a merger, which could discourage deals that allow smaller companies to grow by combining with larger ones.
Critics say the automatic yearly increase tied to the Consumer Price Index means companies cannot know their exact fee when planning a merger years in advance, making deal finances harder to predict.

Critics say setting fees through automatic yearly adjustments removes Congress from the process of deciding how much companies must pay, a decision they argue should require a vote each time fees go up.

117-hr-4404.one_liner: Add a section of the Kissimmee River in Florida to the national protected rivers list
provisions: A restored section of the Kissimmee River in Florida gets added to the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System, a federal program that protects certain rivers from development.
Rivers in this system cannot have federally funded dams, diversions, or other projects built on them without special approval.
The U.S. government manages the land along the river to keep it in its natural state.

supporters: Supporters say adding the restored Kissimmee River to the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System would permanently block federally funded dams or diversions on this section of the river, protecting the restoration work already done.
Supporters say federal protection would keep the riverbanks in their natural state, which helps wildlife and the water quality that Florida communities depend on.
Supporters say the designation locks in long-term oversight by the U.S. government, making it harder for future development projects to undo the river's restoration.
critics: Critics say putting the river under federal management could limit how Florida state and local governments make decisions about land and water use along the river.
Critics say the requirement for special approval before any federally funded water projects can be built near the river could slow down flood control or infrastructure work that the region may need.
Critics say handing oversight to the federal government removes control from the people who live near the river and understand its local needs.

117-hr-4176.one_liner: Require federal surveys to collect data on sexual orientation and gender identity
provisions: Federal agencies that run surveys must check their existing surveys to see which ones do not ask about sexual orientation or gender identity.
Agencies must review how they ask questions about sexual orientation and gender identity and figure out what changes are needed.
Any federal agency that publishes reports using survey data must include sexual orientation and gender identity information in those reports.

supporters: Supporters say requiring agencies like HHS and the Census Bureau to review their existing surveys will show exactly which datasets are missing sexual orientation and gender identity data, so gaps can be filled.

Supporters say agencies that publish reports using survey data will have to include sexual orientation and gender identity information, giving researchers and policymakers real numbers on the health and economic status of LGBTQI+ people.
Supporters say the bill's requirement to assess changes in how questions are asked will help agencies collect this data in a consistent and accurate way across the federal government.
critics: Critics say requiring every federal agency to audit its surveys and update question methods will create new costs and staff burdens without a set budget to cover them.

Critics say adding sexual orientation and gender identity fields to published federal reports could allow people to identify LGBTQI+ individuals through public records requests, raising privacy concerns.
Critics say the bill does not set clear standards for how agencies should define or measure sexual orientation and gender identity, which could lead to inconsistent data across different agencies.

117-hr-4785.one_liner: Create a U.S. government position focused on human rights in China's Xinjiang region
provisions: Creates a Special Coordinator for Uyghur Issues job at the State Department to focus on human rights in China's Xinjiang region.
Lets the State Department give money to people who speak at public events about the rights of Uyghurs and other minority groups in Xinjiang.
Requires the State Department to make Uyghur language classes available to U.S. diplomats.
Requires the State Department to place at least one Uyghur-speaking diplomat at U.S. offices in China.

supporters: Supporters say the new Special Coordinator for Uyghur Issues at the State Department would give the U.S. a dedicated person focused only on human rights in Xinjiang, instead of splitting that work across many offices.
Supporters say requiring at least one Uyghur-speaking diplomat at U.S. offices in China would help the U.S. better gather information about what is happening to minority groups in Xinjiang.
Supporters say funding human rights advocates to speak at public diplomacy forums would give Uyghurs and other minority groups in Xinjiang a voice in international conversations about their rights.
critics: Critics say placing a Uyghur-speaking diplomat at U.S. missions in China and creating a coordinator role aimed at Xinjiang could strain U.S.-China relations and make cooperation on other issues harder.
Critics say the bill allows but does not require the State Department to fund human rights advocates at public forums, meaning the money may never actually be spent on Uyghur communities.

Critics say the bill does not include specific funding amounts or enforcement tools, so the new coordinator position and language training requirements may not lead to real changes in how China treats Uyghurs.

117-hr-5118.one_liner: Finish buying land to complete the Continental Divide National Scenic Trail by 2028
provisions: The Forest Service must finish buying all land needed for the Continental Divide Trail by November 10, 2028.
