The Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management must form a joint team to work on completing the trail.
Within 3 years of passing, the Forest Service must send Congress a plan showing which parts of the trail are still missing.
The plan must include the cost to finish building and protecting each part of the trail.
The government can only buy land from sellers who agree to sell — it cannot force anyone to give up their land.
Both the Forest Service and the Continental Divide Trail Coalition must send Congress yearly updates until the trail is done.

supporters: Supporters say the November 10, 2028 deadline requires the Forest Service to close gaps in the Continental Divide Trail that have remained incomplete, giving the agency a firm end date to work toward.
Supporters say forming a joint Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management team will bring two agencies together to speed up land acquisition and reduce delays caused by working separately.
Supporters say requiring a cost plan within 3 years gives Congress specific dollar amounts and site details, making it easier to fund and oversee the trail's completion.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a funding amount, meaning Congress could pass the 2028 deadline without providing the money the Forest Service needs to buy the required land.
Critics say the ban on using eminent domain, while protecting landowners, could leave permanent gaps in the trail if key private landowners choose not to sell.

Critics say requiring both the Forest Service and the Continental Divide Trail Coalition to send separate yearly reports to Congress creates overlapping paperwork without guaranteeing faster progress on the trail.

117-hr-521.one_liner: Let injured federal first responders keep their retirement benefits if they move to a different government job
provisions: Federal law enforcement officers, border patrol officers, and firefighters pay more into retirement than other government workers and must retire by age 57.
When one of these workers gets hurt on the job and moves to a different government position to recover, this bill lets them stay in their original retirement plan.
Under current rules, moving to a different government job after an injury can knock them out of the retirement plan they paid into.
If one of these workers leaves government service before they can collect retirement, this bill lets them get back the extra retirement money they paid in.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects federal law enforcement officers, border patrol officers, and firefighters who get hurt on the job — letting them stay in the retirement plan they paid extra into, even if they move to a different government job to recover.

Supporters say current law can take away the higher retirement benefits these workers earned, even though they kept paying the larger share required of first responders — and this bill stops that from happening.

Supporters say if a first responder leaves government service before they can collect retirement, this bill lets them get back the extra contributions they made, so they do not lose money they paid in.
critics: Critics say the bill creates a two-tier system where workers in non-first-responder roles could receive first responder retirement benefits, even though they are no longer doing the high-risk work those benefits were designed for.

Critics say allowing injured workers to keep accelerated retirement benefits while working lower-risk civil service jobs could increase long-term costs to the federal retirement system, since those workers would collect higher annuities without continuing the dangerous duties that justified them.

117-hr-5274.one_liner: Give Customs and Border Protection workers tools and training to avoid fentanyl exposure
provisions: Containment devices are sealed containers or bags used to handle seized drugs safely, without direct skin contact.
Customs and Border Protection must give these sealed devices to all of its officers, agents, and other workers.
CBP must hold training at least once a year on how to use these devices correctly.
The training covers how to avoid accidental contact with fentanyl and other deadly drugs — contact that can happen even without touching the drugs directly.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects CBP officers, agents, and other workers by requiring sealed containment devices that prevent direct skin contact with fentanyl — a drug that can cause serious harm or death even through brief, indirect exposure.

Supporters say making annual training mandatory ensures that all CBP personnel — not just some — learn the correct way to use containment devices every year, reducing the chance of accidental drug exposure during seizures.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a funding amount or cost cap for buying containment devices for all CBP officers, agents, and other personnel, making it unclear how much the program will cost taxpayers.

Critics say one required training session per year may not be enough for workers who handle fentanyl seizures frequently, since skills learned once a year can fade before the next training takes place.

117-hr-5407.one_liner: Ask colleges to make plans for student mental health and suicide prevention
provisions: Tells the Department of Education to push colleges to create mental health plans for their students
Colleges that follow through would have a written plan for preventing suicide on campus

supporters: Supporters say requiring the Department of Education to push colleges to create written mental health plans would give students a clear path to get help before a crisis happens.
Supporters say colleges with formal suicide prevention plans are better prepared to identify at-risk students early, which could reduce student deaths by suicide.
Supporters say creating a written plan forces colleges to assign staff and set steps for responding to mental health emergencies, rather than leaving those decisions to chance.
critics: Critics say the bill does not require colleges to actually follow through — it only tells the Department of Education to 'encourage' schools, which may produce no real change.
Critics say colleges may write plans on paper without funding the counselors or programs needed to carry them out, since the bill does not attach any money to the requirement.
Critics say smaller colleges with limited staff may struggle to build a full mental health and suicide prevention plan without clear guidance or resources from the federal government.

117-hr-5271.one_liner: Name a Nashville post office after Tennessee state senator Thelma Harper
provisions: The post office at 2245 Rosa L Parks Boulevard in Nashville, Tennessee will be officially named the 'Thelma Harper Post Office Building.'
Thelma Harper served in the Tennessee State Senate from 1990 to 2014, representing parts of Nashville, and was the first Black woman elected to that office.
This is a ceremonial action only — it does not change how the post office runs or spend any government money.

supporters: Supporters say naming the post office after Thelma Harper honors her 24 years in the Tennessee State Senate, from 1990 to 2014, where she represented parts of Nashville.
Supporters say the designation recognizes Harper as the first Black woman elected to the Tennessee State Senate, marking a historic milestone for Nashville's community.
Supporters say this action costs no government money and does not change how the post office operates, making it a low-cost way to recognize public service.

117-hr-5441.one_liner: Tighten rules against painful training methods used on show horses
provisions: Makes it harder to use painful methods on horses' legs to change how they walk or run in shows
Creates a new system for checking horses for signs of pain or injury at shows, sales, and auctions
Raises the fines and punishments for people caught using these painful training methods

supporters: Supporters say the bill's new inspection system would catch more cases of soring — the use of painful substances or devices on horses' legs to produce an exaggerated high-stepping gait at shows and competitions.
Supporters say raising fines and penalties under the bill would make trainers and show organizers less likely to use illegal methods on horses' legs, since the risk of punishment would be higher.
Supporters say the bill removes a conflict of interest by replacing industry-run inspectors at horse shows, sales, and auctions with a system not controlled by the same groups being regulated.
critics: Critics say the bill's new federal inspection system would add costs and rules that fall heavily on small Tennessee Walking Horse shows, sales, and auctions that may not have resources to comply.
Critics say the bill increases fines and criminal penalties for violations before proving that the new inspection methods are accurate enough to correctly identify soring in all cases.

Critics say the bill could reduce or end a training and showing tradition tied to the Tennessee Walking Horse breed, affecting breeders, trainers, and show organizers who say current rules already address soring.

117-hr-5315.one_liner: Give grants to governments and colleges to use drones for inspecting roads, power lines, and water systems
provisions: The Department of Transportation gives money to state, local, and tribal governments to buy drones for inspecting roads, power lines, and water systems.
Governments that get the money must use drones made in the United States by companies not owned or controlled by China.
The Department of Transportation also gives money to colleges to train students for jobs that use drones.
The grants cover inspections, repairs, and construction of roads and other public infrastructure.

supporters: Supporters say the grants would let state, local, and tribal governments use drones to inspect roads, power lines, and water systems, keeping workers out of dangerous conditions during those jobs.
Supporters say the bill requires all grant money to be spent on drones made in the United States by companies not owned or controlled by China, which they say protects American manufacturing jobs.
Supporters say the college training grants build a pipeline of students ready for drone-related jobs in infrastructure work, filling a gap in the skilled workforce.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a specific dollar cap on the grants, so there is no fixed limit on how much the Department of Transportation can spend on the program.
Critics say the rule limiting purchases to domestically made drones cuts out competition, which could raise the price that state, local, and tribal governments pay to buy equipment.

Critics say the bill gives grants for drone inspections of roads and water systems but sets no minimum standards for how those inspections must be done, leaving no requirement that drone-based inspections meet the same safety thresholds as current inspection methods.

117-hr-5455.one_liner: Let more people sentenced for crack cocaine ask for shorter prison terms
provisions: Before 2010, courts gave much longer prison sentences for crack cocaine than for powder cocaine.
A 2010 law changed those sentencing rules to treat crack and powder cocaine more equally.
A 2018 law let some people sentenced under the old rules ask a court for a shorter sentence.
In 2021, the Supreme Court ruled that low-level offenders could not use the 2018 law to get a shorter sentence.
This bill lets low-level crack cocaine offenders use the 2018 law to ask for shorter sentences too.

supporters: Supporters say the bill fixes a gap left by the 2021 Supreme Court ruling in Terry v. United States, which blocked low-level crack cocaine offenders from asking a court for a shorter sentence, even though they were sentenced under the same pre-2010 rules that Congress already said were unfair.

Supporters say that before 2010, courts gave sentences for crack cocaine that were up to 18 times longer than sentences for the same amount of powder cocaine, and low-level offenders sentenced under those rules should be able to ask a judge to reduce their sentence just like higher-level offenders can.
Supporters say this bill does not automatically release anyone — it only lets low-level crack offenders go before a judge and ask for a shorter sentence, with the judge making the final decision.
critics: Critics say expanding who can ask for sentence reductions beyond what the 2018 First Step Act originally covered could lead to the early release of people convicted of drug offenses, which raises public safety concerns in their communities.

Critics say courts could face a large number of new sentence reduction requests from crack cocaine offenders who were ruled ineligible by the Supreme Court in 2021, adding to backlogs in the federal court system.

117-hr-5768.one_liner: Fund police and prosecutors to use new technology to solve violent crimes
provisions: The Department of Justice sets up a program to give money to police and prosecutors.
The money goes toward using new technology to help close open violent crime cases.
State, tribal, and local law enforcement agencies can apply for the money, including groups of them working together.
Prosecutors can also apply, alone or with police departments.

supporters: Supporters say the grant program would give state, tribal, and local law enforcement agencies access to new technology to help close open violent crime cases.
Supporters say prosecutors can apply for the grants on their own or alongside police departments, making it easier for the full criminal justice system to work together on unsolved violent crimes.
Supporters say allowing groups of agencies to apply together means smaller departments can pool resources and share technology they could not afford alone.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a specific dollar amount for the grants, so there is no guarantee agencies will receive enough funding to make a real difference in clearance rates.
Critics say the bill sets no required reporting standards or performance metrics, meaning agencies that receive grant money do not have to show measurable improvement in closing violent crime cases.
Critics say the bill does not define what counts as an acceptable 'technological investigative method,' leaving agencies without clear guidelines on how the money must be spent.

117-hr-5585.one_liner: Create a new federal agency to fund high-risk health and medical research
provisions: Creates a new agency inside the Department of Health and Human Services to fund health and medicine research that other agencies won't take on
The agency gets its own separate budget, not shared with the rest of HHS
A director chosen by the President runs the agency and can speak directly to Congress without getting approval from other government officials first
The agency can give out money through grants, contracts, and prize competitions to support research projects
Staff called program managers pick which projects get funded, set goals, and decide whether to keep or stop each project
The agency must work with the FDA and Medicare and Medicaid to speed up the path from new cures to patient coverage
Every year, the agency reports on what it's doing, and the National Academies of Sciences checks whether it's working

supporters: Supporters say creating a separate agency with its own budget inside HHS would let program managers take on high-risk health research that agencies like NIH typically pass on, funding projects that could lead to new cures.
Supporters say requiring the agency to work directly with the FDA and Medicare and Medicaid would help move new treatments faster from the lab to patients who need coverage.
Supporters say having the director report to Congress without approval from other officials would give lawmakers a direct, unfiltered view of what the agency is doing and how money is being spent.
critics: Critics say giving program managers broad power to pick, fund, and stop research projects without a clear oversight structure could lead to spending on projects that lack scientific consensus.
Critics say a separate agency budget, outside the normal HHS budget process, makes it harder for Congress to weigh health research spending against other priorities.
Critics say the bill does not set a dollar cap on what the agency can spend, leaving the total cost to taxpayers open-ended.

117-hr-5774.one_liner: Give FEMA power to build housing for disaster survivors in U.S. territories
provisions: After a major disaster is declared, the President can tell FEMA to pay for things people still need that no other program covers.
FEMA can give money directly to people or families to help them get a place to live.
FEMA can build permanent or semi-permanent homes in U.S. territories like Puerto Rico or the U.S. Virgin Islands.
The President can approve home construction in other locations if it costs less than other housing options.

supporters: Supporters say this bill closes a gap by letting FEMA pay for things disaster survivors still need that no other program covers — so families do not have to go without help just because existing aid runs out.
Supporters say FEMA can give money directly to households to help them get housing, which gets aid to people faster than waiting for contractors or government-run projects.

Supporters say people in U.S. territories like Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands can get permanent or semi-permanent homes built by FEMA, which helps communities that have struggled to rebuild after past disasters.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a dollar cap or define what qualifies as an 'unmet need,' so the President's power to direct FEMA spending on unmet needs is not limited by specific rules or budget constraints.

Critics say the bill allows FEMA to build permanent homes in locations the President decides are cost effective, but it does not define what cost effective means or require any outside review of that decision.

Critics say the bill gives the President authority to approve home construction in locations beyond U.S. territories with no requirement for input from local governments or the communities that would receive those homes.

117-hr-5659.one_liner: Name a post office in Oxnard, California after John R. Hatcher III
provisions: Renames the U.S. Post Office at 1961 North C Street in Oxnard, California to the 'John R. Hatcher III Post Office Building'
No money is spent and no mail service, hours, or staffing rules change as a result of this bill
The post office keeps running exactly as it does today — only the building's official name changes
Congress passes bills like this to give federal buildings official names, often to honor people from a local community
The new name takes effect when the President signs the bill into law

arguments.procedural_note: This bill only gives an official name to the post office at 1961 North C Street in Oxnard, California. No money is spent, no services change, and no policy is created. Bills like this have no debate because nothing changes except the building's name.

117-hr-6538.one_liner: Create a national alert system to warn the public during active shooter events
provisions: Assigns one person at the Department of Justice to run a national active shooter alert network
That person works with states and tribal governments to build plans for sending out active shooter alerts
Federal, state, local, and tribal agencies are encouraged to set up steps for how to respond when an active shooter is reported
The Government Accountability Office must study how states and local governments respond to active shooters and issue a report on their findings

supporters: Supporters say that naming one Department of Justice officer to run a national active shooter alert network will make sure alerts are sent faster and more consistently across states and tribal governments, which currently have no shared system.

Supporters say that asking the Government Accountability Office to study how states and local governments respond to active shooters will produce real data that Congress can use to improve future laws.
Supporters say that encouraging federal, state, local, and tribal agencies to set up response steps will help first responders act quickly when an active shooter is reported.
critics: Critics say the bill only encourages agencies to set up response plans but does not require them to do so, meaning states and tribal governments could ignore the coordinator's guidance with no penalty.
Critics say the bill creates a new coordinator role and a Government Accountability Office study without providing any funding, leaving it unclear how either will be paid for.
Critics say that because the bill does not set a deadline for states to build active shooter alert plans, the national network could take years to become useful.

117-hr-6552.one_liner: Keep funding programs that fight human trafficking in the US and abroad
provisions: Keeps money flowing through 2026 for State Department and Justice Department programs that fight human trafficking in other countries.
Keeps running the Angel Watch Center, a program that warns other countries when a convicted sex offender is about to travel there.
Lets the Department of Health and Human Services run a program to help trafficking survivors get back on their feet and support themselves.

States that get federal money for foster care must stay in contact with police and the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children when a child in their care goes missing and may be a trafficking victim.
Requires the Angel Watch Center to get lists from other countries of people who are required to register as sex offenders.
Requires federal workers to book overnight stays at hotels that have policies in place to fight human trafficking.

supporters: Supporters say reauthorizing State Department and Justice Department anti-trafficking programs through 2026 keeps funding in place for international efforts that have already built partnerships and systems to identify victims abroad.

Supporters say the requirement that states stay in regular contact with police and the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children when a foster child goes missing gives those children a better chance of being found before traffickers can exploit them further.
Supporters say the HHS reintegration program gives trafficking survivors access to support that helps them become financially independent, reducing the chance they will be exploited again.
critics: Critics say the bill does not specify how much money will be available for the HHS program to help survivors reintegrate, making it unclear whether the program will have enough resources to serve the people it is meant to reach.

Critics say the rule requiring federal workers to book hotels with anti-trafficking policies lacks a clear definition of what those policies must include, which could make the rule difficult to enforce consistently across agencies.

Critics say requiring the Angel Watch Center to collect sex offender registry lists from visa waiver countries could create friction with allied governments who may see it as a one-sided demand, potentially complicating cooperation on the broader anti-trafficking mission.

117-hr-6878.one_liner: Set health and safety rules for pregnant women held in federal prisons
provisions: Federal prisons must provide health care and services to pregnant women and women who recently gave birth
Prisons cannot put pregnant women or new mothers in solitary confinement or use physical restraints on them
A pregnant woman whose baby is due within the last year of her sentence can be released early to home or a halfway house
The government will track how many pregnant women are in federal, state, and local jails and prisons, and what health care they receive
A government watchdog office will study what health services and protections pregnant women get in state and local jails and prisons
States, local governments, tribes, and nonprofits can apply for grants to pay for pregnancy care and women's health services inside jails and prisons

supporters: Supporters say the bill would protect pregnant women in federal prisons by banning the use of physical restraints and solitary confinement during pregnancy and the recovery period after birth.

Supporters say allowing pregnant women whose due date falls within their final year of sentence to be released early to home confinement or a halfway house gives babies a healthier start outside of prison.
Supporters say collecting data on how many pregnant women are in federal, state, and local jails — and what care they receive — will show where gaps in health services exist so they can be fixed.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set minimum standards for the grants given to states, tribes, and local governments, which means the quality of pregnancy care inside jails and prisons could vary widely from place to place.

Critics say the early release provision only applies to women in the final year of their sentence, leaving out pregnant women earlier in their terms who may face the same health risks during pregnancy.

Critics say ordering a study by the government watchdog office on state and local jails stops short of requiring those facilities to change their practices, so the research may not lead to real protections for women outside the federal prison system.

117-hr-6448.one_liner: Give grants to local and tribal police departments with under 200 officers
provisions: Police departments and tribal governments with fewer than 200 officers can apply for a federal grant.
Grant money can be used to buy body cameras for officers.
Departments can use the money to train officers on how to calm down tense situations before they escalate.
Funds can also go toward recruiting new officers and keeping the ones they have.

supporters: Supporters say small police departments with fewer than 200 officers often lack money for body cameras, and this grant would help them buy that equipment.
Supporters say the grant lets departments pay for de-escalation training, which teaches officers how to calm tense situations before they turn dangerous.
Supporters say tribal governments and small local police can use the funds to recruit new officers and keep the ones they have, which helps departments that struggle to stay staffed.
critics: Critics say the bill limits grants to departments with fewer than 200 officers, leaving out mid-size departments that may also lack funds for body cameras and training.
Critics say the bill does not set a minimum amount of grant money each department must receive, so smaller or less connected governments may end up with little to no funding.
Critics say there are no clear rules in the bill requiring departments to show results, so there is no way to know if the money for training or cameras actually changes how officers behave.

117-hr-6493.one_liner: Extend and expand college drug and alcohol prevention programs through 2028
provisions: Keeps federal funding for drug and alcohol prevention programs at colleges running through the year starting October 2027.
Expands the program to cover a wider range of substance misuse, not just illegal drugs and alcohol.
Colleges that receive this funding run programs to help students avoid or recover from substance problems.

supporters: Supporters say keeping federal funding for campus drug and alcohol programs running through FY2028 gives colleges time to build programs that help students avoid or recover from substance problems.
Supporters say expanding the program beyond illegal drugs and alcohol to cover a wider range of substance misuse means more students struggling with things like prescription drug abuse can get help.
Supporters say colleges that already run these federally funded programs have systems in place to reach students early, before substance problems get worse.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include new funding amounts, so colleges may not get enough money to actually expand their programs to cover the wider range of substances the bill now requires.
Critics say reauthorizing a program through FY2028 without requiring colleges to report results means there is no clear way to know if the money is working to reduce student substance misuse.
Critics say expanding what counts as substance misuse without defining it clearly could make it harder for colleges to decide which students or situations the program is supposed to cover.

117-hr-7174.one_liner: Keep funding a Secret Service school that trains police on cybercrime
provisions: Keeps the National Computer Forensics Institute running through 2032
The institute trains police officers and others to investigate cyber crimes and electronic crimes
Adds training on how to prevent cyber crimes, not just investigate them after they happen
Requires the institute to find new ways to investigate cyber crimes
Requires the institute to send a yearly report on what it has done

supporters: Supporters say extending the National Computer Forensics Institute through 2032 ensures that local and state police officers continue to receive hands-on training in how to investigate electronic crimes and cybersecurity incidents.
Supporters say adding prevention training to the institute's mission means officers will learn to stop cyber attacks before they happen, not just respond after damage is done.
Supporters say the new requirement for a yearly report will show the public and Congress what the institute has actually done, making it easier to hold the program accountable.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a budget or spending cap for running the institute through 2032, so the total cost to taxpayers is unknown.

Critics say expanding the Secret Service's mission to include 'preventing' cybersecurity threats — without defining what that means — could allow the agency to monitor networks or individuals without clear legal limits.

Critics say the requirement to develop 'innovative approaches' to investigating cyber crimes sets no specific goals or deadlines, making it hard to measure whether the institute is actually improving.

117-hr-6929.one_liner: Restore full pension payments for Delphi Corporation workers whose benefits were cut in 2009
provisions: Workers who had pensions through Delphi Corporation, which went bankrupt in 2009, had their monthly payments cut. This bill restores those payments to the full amount.
The federal pension agency (PBGC) must recalculate each worker's monthly pension payment.
The PBGC must also go back and recalculate all past payments already made.
Workers get a one-time lump-sum check to make up for any money they were underpaid in past months.
The government sets up a fund and puts money into it to cover these payments.
The bill sets rules for how the lump-sum payments are taxed.

supporters: Supporters say this bill would restore the full monthly pension payments that Delphi Corporation workers earned before the company went bankrupt in 2009, payments that were cut when General Motors collapsed.

Supporters say the PBGC would be required to recalculate past payments already made and send workers a one-time lump-sum check to cover any months they were underpaid, giving them money they were owed but never received.
Supporters say the bill sets clear rules for how the lump-sum payments are taxed, so workers know exactly what they will owe to the IRS when they receive the back pay.
critics: Critics say the bill requires the government to set up and fund a new payment fund using taxpayer money to cover the restored benefits and back-pay lump sums for former Delphi workers.
Critics say making the PBGC go back and recalculate every past monthly payment already sent to Delphi plan participants adds a large administrative cost on top of the benefit payments themselves.

Critics say using a special government fund to cover losses from a private company's bankruptcy could set a precedent for other groups whose pension plans were reduced after corporate bankruptcies to seek the same treatment.

117-hr-6965.one_liner: Create a 10-year federal plan to bring more international tourists to the United States
provisions: The Department of Commerce must write a 10-year plan for U.S. travel and tourism, with yearly goals for how many international visitors come to the U.S. and how much money those visitors spend here.
The bill creates a new government position — Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Travel and Tourism — to lead that plan.
That official must set yearly visitor goals, work to speed up visa approvals for people who want to visit the U.S., and promote U.S. travel and tourism to people in other countries.
The new official must also write and carry out a plan to help the U.S. travel and tourism industry recover from the COVID-19 pandemic.
A group called the United States Travel and Tourism Advisory Board gets a formal legal role helping the new official carry out the COVID-19 recovery plan.

supporters: Supporters say the new 10-year plan with yearly visitor goals would give the travel and tourism industry a clear target to work toward, helping businesses like hotels and airlines plan ahead.

Supporters say creating the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Travel and Tourism would put one person in charge of speeding up visa approvals, which could bring more international visitors and increase money spent in the U.S.
Supporters say giving the U.S. Travel and Tourism Advisory Board a formal legal role means the industry has a direct voice in shaping the COVID-19 recovery plan.
critics: Critics say the bill creates a new government position — Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Travel and Tourism — without specifying how much it will cost or where the funding will come from.
Critics say writing a COVID-19 recovery plan now may be too late, since the pandemic's effects on travel happened years ago and the industry has already been recovering without this plan.
Critics say the bill sets yearly goals for international visitors but does not include any penalties or clear steps if those goals are not met, making the targets hard to enforce.

117-hr-7180.one_liner: Fund research on how COVID-19 affects the brain and thinking
provisions: The National Science Foundation will give out grants to researchers studying how COVID-19 affects thinking and memory, both short-term and long-term.
The research includes how COVID-19 affects children and teenagers.
Within 45 days of passing, the National Science Foundation must work with the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine to produce a report on how COVID-19 disrupts brain function.

supporters: Supporters say NSF grants for studying how COVID-19 affects thinking and memory will help doctors better treat the millions of people who report lasting brain fog after infection.
Supporters say including children and teenagers in the research is important because schools have reported widespread learning and attention problems since the pandemic.
Supporters say requiring a report within 45 days from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine creates a fast timeline to get findings to policymakers.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a specific dollar amount for the grants, making it hard to know if the funding will be enough to produce useful results.
Critics say the NSF already funds health and brain research, so a new law directing them to study COVID-19 cognitive effects may duplicate work already underway.
Critics say a 45-day deadline for the National Academies to begin a study on a complex topic like brain disruption may not leave enough time for a thorough review.

117-hr-7025.one_liner: Stop U.S. wildlife money from going to foreign military units that abuse human rights
provisions: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service must check that the foreign groups it sends money to are not paying or supporting military or police units accused of serious human rights abuses.
Before giving out grants, the agency must run background checks on the groups that will receive the money.
Groups getting money must share financial records and follow a safety plan to make sure funds don't reach abusive units.
The agency must post a public list of military and police units that are banned from getting this money.
The agency must work with the State Department to screen groups before sending funds.
The ban can be lifted if the foreign government is taking real steps to punish the people responsible and stop future abuses.
Grants must go through regular audits to confirm the money is being used correctly.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects human rights by requiring the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to run background checks on foreign groups before sending them grant money, so funds do not reach military or police units accused of serious abuses.

Supporters say requiring grant recipients to share financial records, follow a safety plan, and go through regular audits gives the public and Congress a way to confirm conservation money is not funding abusive units.
Supporters say the public list of banned military and police units, built in coordination with the State Department, makes the screening process transparent and harder to bypass.
critics: Critics say the new vetting requirements — including background checks, safeguard plans, financial audits, and State Department coordination — add layers of paperwork that could slow down or block conservation grants to effective but under-resourced foreign groups.

Critics say the bill gives the agency wide power to cut off funding based on a 'reasonable belief' of abuse, a standard that could be applied unevenly and end partnerships with conservation groups that have no direct link to the accused units.

Critics say the exception that allows funding to resume only if a foreign government is 'taking effective steps' to punish abusers sets a high and vague bar that may permanently block aid to regions where conservation work is most needed.

117-hr-7321.one_liner: Set new safety inspection and worker rules for foreign aircraft repair shops
provisions: Requires every foreign aircraft repair shop to get at least one surprise inspection per year from the FAA
Requires airlines to send the FAA a report every month about any work done on their planes
Sets minimum job requirements that mechanics and other workers must meet before working on U.S. planes at foreign repair shops
Stops the FAA from approving any new foreign repair shops if certain safety rules are not put in place within one year

supporters: Supporters say requiring at least one surprise inspection per year at every foreign repair shop will catch safety problems that scheduled inspections might miss, since workers won't have time to hide issues before inspectors arrive.

Supporters say the monthly reports airlines must send the FAA will let regulators track all maintenance work on U.S. planes in real time, making it easier to spot patterns that could lead to accidents.

Supporters say setting minimum job requirements for mechanics at foreign repair shops will make sure workers handling U.S. planes meet the same basic standards as mechanics working at domestic repair stations.
critics: Critics say the cost of conducting unannounced inspections at every foreign repair station each year will require the FAA to hire and deploy more inspectors overseas, straining an already limited budget.

Critics say the one-year deadline to put certain safety rules in place — with a moratorium on new foreign repair shop approvals as the penalty — may not give the FAA enough time to write and finalize the required regulations.

Critics say monthly reporting requirements placed on air carriers will increase paperwork and administrative costs for airlines, which may pass those costs on to passengers through higher ticket prices.

117-hr-7693.one_liner: Keep the National Park Foundation running through 2030
provisions: Lets the National Park Foundation keep operating and receiving money through the year ending September 2030
The National Park Foundation raises private money to support national parks across the United States

supporters: Supporters say reauthorizing the National Park Foundation through FY2030 gives the organization a set timeline to keep raising private money for national parks without interruption.
Supporters say the Foundation's role is to collect donations from private groups and individuals, which adds funding to national parks beyond what Congress appropriates each year.
critics: Critics say the bill reauthorizes the Foundation through FY2030 without adding new rules about how private donations are reported or how donors are chosen.
Critics say extending the Foundation's authority for eight years with no added oversight provisions means Congress will not review its performance again until after FY2030.

117-hr-7283.one_liner: Let states use mine cleanup funds to treat acidic water from old coal mines
provisions: States can use up to 30% of their federal mine cleanup money to treat acidic water flowing out of abandoned coal mines.
The money comes from grants already set up under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.
Acid mine drainage is water that turns toxic after mixing with rocks and minerals exposed in old coal mines.

supporters: Supporters say allowing states to use up to 30% of their Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act mine cleanup grants for acid mine drainage treatment gives states a way to address toxic water that current rules do not clearly allow.

Supporters say acid mine drainage from abandoned coal mines pollutes streams and rivers, and directing existing federal grant money toward treatment can reduce that harm without requiring new spending.
Supporters say states with many abandoned coal mines can now choose how to split their grant money between physical cleanup and water treatment, making the grants more useful for local conditions.
critics: Critics say allowing up to 30% of annual mine reclamation grants to go toward water treatment means less money available for physically cleaning up and sealing abandoned coal mine sites.
Critics say the bill only applies to coal mines, leaving out other types of abandoned mines that also cause acid drainage, which limits how many affected communities can benefit.

Critics say treating acid mine drainage is an ongoing cost, and using one-time Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act grant money for a problem that requires long-term funding may not provide a lasting fix.

117-hr-7337.one_liner: Require the National Archives to submit a plan for clearing veteran record request backlogs
provisions: The National Personnel Records Center holds service records for veterans, but requests have piled up in a backlog.
The head of the National Archives must send Congress a plan to clear that backlog.
The plan must include deadlines for when the backlog will be reduced.
The plan must describe steps to upgrade computer systems to stop backlogs from building up again.
The plan must also include steps to improve service for people waiting on their requests.

supporters: Supporters say this bill would help veterans who are stuck waiting for service records they need to apply for benefits, by forcing the National Archives to give Congress a clear plan with deadlines for clearing the backlog.

Supporters say requiring the National Archives to upgrade its computer systems would stop future backlogs from piling up at the National Personnel Records Center, which holds service records for millions of veterans.
Supporters say the bill's customer service requirements would give veterans better updates and communication while they wait on their records requests.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires a plan to be submitted to Congress, but does not set any specific deadlines or funding to actually clear the backlog, so it may not lead to real change.

Critics say without money or staffing requirements attached, the National Archives may submit a plan that looks good on paper but lacks the resources needed to reduce wait times for veterans seeking their records.

117-hr-7289.one_liner: Order studies on PFAS chemicals in the environment and human body
provisions: Tells the EPA to work with a national science group to study how people are exposed to PFAS chemicals and how dangerous they are.
Tells the EPA to work with that same science group to study how PFAS spreads in the environment and how to clean it up.
Tells the White House science office to write a plan for how the federal government will research PFAS based on what the studies find.
PFAS are man-made chemicals found in nonstick pans, waterproof clothing, and other products that may cause health problems.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the EPA to work with the National Academies of Sciences on a two-phase study will give the government solid data on how PFAS chemicals harm human health, which is needed before setting safety rules.

Supporters say the study on PFAS contamination in the environment will help identify how to clean up affected water and land, which matters for communities near military bases and factories where PFAS has been found.
Supporters say requiring the White House science office to write a federal research plan based on the study findings will help agencies coordinate instead of doing separate, repeated work.
critics: Critics say the bill only calls for more studies and a written plan, but does not set any limits on PFAS in water or require cleanup of contaminated sites, meaning no direct action is taken to protect people.
Critics say the two-phase study structure and the requirement to wait for a federal implementation plan could delay meaningful regulation of PFAS chemicals by several years.
Critics say the bill does not include any funding amounts or deadlines for the National Academies studies, making it unclear when results will be available or how the work will be paid for.

117-hr-7900.one_liner: Fund the U.S. military and set troop and equipment levels for 2023
provisions: Pays the salaries and training costs for U.S. military troops for the year starting October 2022.
Sets aside money for research and testing of new military technology and weapons systems.
Pays for aircraft — such as planes and helicopters — for the U.S. military.
Pays for missiles and ammunition to stock U.S. military supplies.
Sets the maximum number of troops allowed to serve in each branch of the military during 2023.

supporters: Supporters say the bill covers salaries and training costs for all active U.S. military troops, making sure service members are paid for their work in 2023.
Supporters say funding for research and testing of new weapons systems helps the U.S. military stay ahead of other countries in defense technology.
Supporters say buying aircraft, missiles, and ammunition keeps U.S. military supplies stocked at the levels needed to respond to threats.
critics: Critics say the bill authorizes new spending on aircraft, missiles, and ammunition procurement without cutting any existing defense programs to help pay for those costs.
Critics say research and testing funds go to new weapons systems that have not yet proven they work, putting taxpayer money at risk on unproven technology.
Critics say the troop caps set in the bill lock in personnel levels for each branch that may not match what military commanders say they actually need during 2023.

117-hr-7780.one_liner: Add mental health workers in schools and change employer health plan rules
provisions: Creates grants to put more mental health counselors and therapists in public schools
Colleges must follow new rules for supporting students with disabilities
Stops employers from requiring workers to use private arbitration instead of courts when disputing health benefit decisions
Stops employers from including clauses in health plans that let the employer make the final call on all benefit disputes

supporters: Supporters say the school-based mental health grants would put more counselors and therapists directly in public schools, giving students access to help without needing to leave campus.
Supporters say removing arbitration clauses from employer health plans means workers can take benefit disputes to court instead of a private process where employers often have the advantage.
Supporters say the new rules for colleges would make it clearer how schools must support students with disabilities, which affects millions of enrolled students.
critics: Critics say the grant programs for school mental health services create new federal spending without a clear limit on cost, and local schools may struggle to keep those positions funded after grants run out.
Critics say the ban on discretionary clauses in employer health plans could lead employers to face more lawsuits over benefit decisions, which may raise the cost of offering health coverage.
Critics say the new college requirements for students with disabilities add compliance costs to institutions of higher education without providing federal money to help cover those costs.

117-hr-7734.one_liner: Require Treasury to share bank financial crime reports with Congress within 30 days
provisions: The Treasury Department must give Congress any Bank Secrecy Act report within 30 days of being asked for it.
Banks must hand over these reports to a congressional committee if Congress issues a subpoena.
Bank Secrecy Act reports track suspicious money activity, like possible money laundering, that banks are required to flag.

supporters: Supporters say the 30-day deadline would stop Treasury from delaying delivery of Bank Secrecy Act reports to Congress, giving lawmakers faster access to data on possible money laundering.
Supporters say adding subpoena power means congressional committees can legally require banks to hand over these reports, strengthening oversight of financial crimes.
critics: Critics say forcing Treasury to share sensitive Bank Secrecy Act reports within 30 days could rush the review process and risk leaking details of ongoing law enforcement investigations.
Critics say requiring banks to turn over these reports under subpoena may conflict with BSA confidentiality provisions, which restrict who can see suspicious activity data and under what conditions.

117-hr-8296.one_liner: Stop governments from restricting access to abortion services or who provides them
provisions: Stops state and federal governments from passing laws that limit access to abortion services.
Lets providers prescribe drugs used for abortion — such as medication abortion pills — and offer abortion services through telemedicine, without added government restrictions.
Stops governments from requiring providers to delay care when the provider decides a delay puts the patient's health at risk.

Stops governments from requiring providers to do medical procedures patients do not need, share medical information that is not accurate, or meet certification or licensing requirements that do not apply to other providers who perform similar procedures.
Patients do not have to make extra in-person visits or explain their reasons before getting an abortion.
Abortion cannot be banned before a fetus can survive outside the womb; after that point, it must still be allowed if the provider decides the pregnancy risks the patient's life or health.
The Department of Justice, individual patients, and healthcare providers can all sue to enforce this law, and states can be taken to court for violations.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would stop states from banning abortion before a fetus can survive outside the womb, which they say would protect the rights of patients across all 50 states.

Supporters say the bill allows providers to prescribe medication abortion pills and offer abortion services through telemedicine without added government restrictions, expanding access for patients who cannot reach a clinic.
Supporters say the bill removes requirements that force patients to make extra in-person visits or explain their reasons for seeking an abortion, which they say removes barriers that delay care.
critics: Critics say the bill would block state laws that require in-person visits or specific licensing for abortion providers, which they say are patient safety measures that apply to other medical procedures.

Critics say the bill allows abortions after fetal viability as long as a provider decides the pregnancy risks the patient's health, and critics argue the bill does not define 'health' narrowly enough to limit this exception.

Critics say the bill lets the Department of Justice and private individuals sue states that pass abortion restrictions, which they say overrides the authority of state governments to set their own health and safety rules.

117-hr-8294.one_liner: Fund federal transportation and housing agencies for the year starting October 2022
provisions: Gives money to the Department of Transportation to run programs covering roads, highways, airlines, railroads, and public transit for the year starting October 2022.
Gives money to the Department of Housing and Urban Development for public housing, home loan programs, and efforts to reduce homelessness.
Funds the office that enforces fair housing rules, which bar landlords and sellers from turning away people based on race, religion, or other protected traits.
Funds a program that finds and removes lead paint hazards in homes, which can harm young children.
Funds safety offices at the Federal Aviation Administration and Federal Railroad Administration, which inspect planes and trains.
Funds Amtrak's inspector general, who checks whether Amtrak spends its money correctly.
Sets rules on how all the money in this bill can and cannot be spent.

supporters: Supporters say the bill funds the Office of Lead Hazard Control and Healthy Homes, which removes lead paint from houses where young children live — lead exposure can cause permanent brain damage in kids under six.

Supporters say HUD funding in this bill supports public housing and programs to reduce homelessness, giving low-income families access to stable housing and home loan programs they could not afford otherwise.

Supporters say money for safety offices at the Federal Aviation Administration and the Federal Railroad Administration pays for inspectors who check planes and trains before problems turn into accidents.
critics: Critics say the bill's spending rules for HUD's homelessness programs set no outcome benchmarks — the bill does not require the agency to show how many people were housed, so there is no way to know if the money worked.

Critics say the Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity office gets funding but the bill's spending restrictions place no time limit on resolving discrimination complaints, leaving renters and home buyers who filed cases waiting for years with no required deadline.

Critics say funding Amtrak's inspector general on a separate line from the Department of Transportation's own inspector general creates an oversight gap — spending that crosses both agencies can fall between the two offices with neither one fully accountable.

117-hr-8373.one_liner: Protect the legal right to access and provide contraception
provisions: Makes it illegal for any law or government action to block or single out people from getting contraception
Protects doctors and other health care workers who provide contraception from being penalized
Covers birth control devices, medications, sterilization procedures, and fertility-awareness methods
Lets the Department of Justice, patients, or health care providers sue in court if this law is broken
States cannot claim they are immune from being sued under this law

supporters: Supporters say the bill would make it illegal for any law or government action to single out and block access to birth control pills, IUDs, sterilization procedures, and fertility-awareness methods.
Supporters say doctors and nurses who provide contraception would be protected from being penalized by state laws that target contraception providers.

Supporters say the bill gives the Department of Justice, patients, and health care providers the power to file lawsuits to enforce these protections, and states cannot claim immunity from those suits.
critics: Critics say the bill's definition of contraception includes sterilization procedures, which some religious groups and medical providers believe should not be treated the same as other forms of birth control under federal law.
Critics say removing state immunity means states could face federal lawsuits over laws passed by their own voters, which critics argue limits states' ability to set their own health care rules.

Critics say the 'less restrictive means' legal standard in the bill makes it very hard for states to defend any law that touches contraception access, even laws that supporters of those laws say are meant to protect patients.

117-hr-8351.one_liner: Remove import taxes on baby formula through the end of 2022
provisions: Removes all import taxes and fees on baby formula from the date this passes through December 31, 2022.
During that time, baby formula coming into the country will not face any extra charges, quotas, or limits at the border.
Companies bringing in baby formula must list the correct tariff code on their customs paperwork.

supporters: Supporters say removing all import taxes and fees on baby formula through December 31, 2022 would let more foreign formula enter the U.S. quickly, which could help families who could not find formula on store shelves during the 2022 shortage.
Supporters say lifting border quotas and extra charges on formula imports means companies could bring in larger amounts without added costs, which may lower prices for parents buying formula.
Supporters say requiring importers to list the correct tariff code on customs paperwork keeps track of how much formula is coming in, so the government can watch supply levels.
critics: Critics say the duty-free period only lasts through December 31, 2022, which is a short window that may not be enough time for foreign companies to set up the supply chains needed to make a real difference in U.S. formula supply.

Critics say removing all import fees and quotas could make it harder for U.S. formula makers to compete on price once the shortage ends, possibly hurting domestic manufacturers who employ American workers.
Critics say the bill does not set any safety or quality standards for the formula coming in, and parents may not know whether foreign formula meets the same rules that U.S.-made formula must follow.

117-hr-8297.one_liner: Block states from punishing people who get or help with abortions in other states
provisions: States cannot use their laws to stop someone from going to another state to get an abortion.
States cannot punish doctors or clinics in other states for providing abortion care to patients who traveled there.
States cannot punish people who help doctors or clinics provide abortion care to patients from other states.
States cannot punish people or groups who help someone travel to another state for abortion care.
States cannot block abortion pills from being shipped across state lines.
The U.S. Justice Department can go to court to stop anyone using state law to block this.
People who are blocked from getting this care can also take whoever blocked them to court.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects people who travel to another state for an abortion by making it illegal for their home state to punish them or anyone who helped them get there.
Supporters say the bill stops states from blocking abortion pills from being shipped across state lines, which would keep access open for people in states where abortion is banned.
Supporters say both the Justice Department and private citizens can take violators to court, giving people a direct way to fight back if a state tries to block their care.
critics: Critics say the bill overrides state abortion laws by stopping states from enforcing their own rules when a resident crosses state lines, which they argue takes power away from state governments.
Critics say protecting doctors and clinics in other states from any legal action removes the ability of a person's home state to hold out-of-state providers accountable under local law.

Critics say allowing private lawsuits against anyone who 'helps' with out-of-state abortion travel is too broad and could expose ordinary people, like family members or coworkers, to federal court cases.

117-hr-8446.one_liner: Keep funding a U.S. program that fights hunger in other countries through 2028
provisions: Continues U.S. government funding for a global food and nutrition program through 2028.
Adds a new rule requiring the program to look for ways to make farming more efficient and sustainable.
Continues funding for a separate program that helps people in other countries buy food in local markets through 2028.

supporters: Supporters say reauthorizing the Global Food Security Strategy through 2028 gives U.S. agencies time to build lasting programs that reduce hunger in countries that depend on American food aid.
Supporters say the new rule requiring the program to improve farming efficiency and sustainability will help partner countries grow more food with fewer resources over time.
Supporters say the Emergency Food Security Program lets people in other countries buy food from local sellers, which keeps money in local economies instead of shipping food from the U.S.
critics: Critics say the bill extends funding through 2028 without setting clear goals for how many people should be lifted out of food insecurity, making it hard to know if the money is working.
Critics say the new sustainability requirement does not include measurable standards, so there is no way to hold the program accountable if farming practices do not actually improve.

Critics say the Emergency Food Security Program's model of helping people buy food in local markets may cost more per person served than direct food delivery programs, and the bill does not require a cost comparison.

117-hr-8326.one_liner: Set new rules for what questions the Census Bureau can add to the census
provisions: The head of the Census Bureau can only be fired if there is a specific proven reason — not just because the President wants to.
The Census Bureau cannot add a new question or topic to the census unless it first notifies Congress.
Every two years, the Census Bureau must send Congress a progress report on how it is planning for the next national population count.
Before adding a question that did not appear on the last two censuses, the Census Bureau must show that it researched and tested that question.
A federal watchdog office checks whether new census questions were properly researched and tested, then sends a report to Congress with its findings.

supporters: Supporters say that requiring the Census Bureau Director to be fired only for a specific proven reason protects the bureau from political pressure, which could affect how population counts are done and how congressional seats are assigned.

Supporters say that making the bureau notify Congress before adding new questions, and requiring research and testing for any question not on the last two censuses, helps prevent rushed or untested questions from being added to the count.
Supporters say that having a federal watchdog office check whether new questions were properly researched and then report to Congress adds an independent check on the bureau's work.
critics: Critics say that requiring Congress to be notified before any new question or topic is added could slow down the bureau's ability to respond quickly to new data needs identified by researchers or agencies.
Critics say that limiting when the Census Bureau Director can be removed makes it harder for a new administration to bring in leadership that matches its policy goals for how the census is run.
Critics say that adding biannual progress reports to Congress and GAO review of new questions creates more paperwork and review steps for the bureau without guaranteeing a more accurate count.

117-hr-8466.one_liner: Require federal agencies to post workplace safety plans during public health emergencies
provisions: Each federal agency must post a safety plan on its website.
The plan applies during a nationwide public health emergency for an infectious disease.
The plan must describe what protective equipment workers get and how testing works for people who come into the office.
It must also cover cleaning schedules and how many people can be in the building.
Workers who have to travel off-site for their job must also be covered by the plan.
New employees and contractors must receive the plan within 30 days of being hired or starting a contract.
Each agency's internal watchdog office must report on whether the agency published and followed its plan.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects federal workers by requiring each agency to post a safety plan that covers protective equipment, testing, and cleaning schedules during a public health emergency.
Supporters say the 30-day requirement ensures new employees and contractors know the safety rules quickly after being hired or starting a contract.
Supporters say the inspector general reporting requirement gives the public a way to check whether agencies actually followed their own safety plans.
critics: Critics say the bill adds paperwork burdens to every federal agency without setting a funding amount to cover the cost of writing, posting, and updating safety plans.
Critics say the bill does not set any penalty if an agency fails to post its plan or if the inspector general finds the plan was not followed, making enforcement weak.

117-hr-8542.one_liner: Create grants to send mental health workers to emergencies instead of police
provisions: Creates a program that trains and sends mental health workers to respond to emergencies instead of police.
States, tribes, and local governments can apply for grants to start these programs.
A federal health agency called SAMHSA runs the program.
SAMHSA can take back grant money if a program leads to more people being jailed or sent to institutions.
The federal government checks whether the program is working.

supporters: Supporters say sending trained mental health workers instead of police to behavioral health emergencies could reduce arrests and use of force against people in mental health crisis.

Supporters say the grant program lets states, tribes, and local governments build programs that fit their communities, and SAMHSA can pull funding if a program leads to more jailing or institutionalization.
Supporters say having both SAMHSA and DOJ evaluate the program means there is a check on whether it actually works before more money is spent.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a specific funding amount, making it unclear how many communities could actually receive grants or train enough mental health workers to cover emergency calls.
Critics say some emergencies involving people with behavioral health needs also involve safety risks that mental health workers alone may not be equipped to handle without law enforcement present.
Critics say SAMHSA managing the program instead of local agencies could add layers of federal oversight that slow down how fast communities can get help to people in crisis.

117-hr-884.one_liner: Require a federal plan for disease outbreaks in air travel
provisions: Tells the Department of Transportation to write a plan for how airports and airlines should handle disease outbreaks
The plan must require that airline workers who deal with the public have the right protective gear during a disease outbreak
Airlines and airline workers must be consulted when the plan is written
A government watchdog group called the Government Accountability Office must review the plan and report on whether it is working

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects airline workers who deal with the public every day by requiring that airlines provide them with the right protective gear during a disease outbreak.
Supporters say requiring the Department of Transportation to consult airlines and airline workers when writing the plan means the people most affected will have a voice in how the rules are made.

Supporters say the Government Accountability Office review will check whether the plan meets U.S. obligations under international treaties and whether the aviation system is truly ready for an outbreak.
critics: Critics say the bill tells the Department of Transportation to write a plan but does not set a deadline for when that plan must be finished, which could delay real protections for workers.

Critics say the bill does not define what counts as 'appropriate' protective gear, which means airlines could decide for themselves what is good enough and workers may not get the protection they need.
Critics say the Government Accountability Office can only study and report on the plan — it has no power to force changes if the plan is found to be weak or incomplete.

117-hr-8463.one_liner: Expand which countries can apply for U.S. development aid
provisions: Right now, only countries ranked among the 75 poorest in the world can apply for aid from the Millennium Challenge Corporation.
This bill raises that limit so countries ranked up to 125th poorest can apply.
The World Bank's yearly income rankings decide which countries qualify.

supporters: Supporters say expanding eligibility from the 75 poorest countries to the 125th poorest would let more developing nations compete for MCC aid, reaching countries that are poor but currently locked out by the cutoff.
Supporters say using the World Bank's yearly income rankings to set the limit means the rules update automatically as countries' economies change, keeping the program current.

Supporters say countries ranked between 76th and 125th poorest may still have weak institutions and low incomes that MCC programs are designed to address, so excluding them cuts off aid where it could work.
critics: Critics say raising the income cutoff from 75 to 125 countries could spread MCC funding across more applicants, meaning the poorest 75 countries — the original targets — compete against wealthier nations for the same pool of money.
Critics say the bill does not add new funding, so expanding the number of eligible countries without increasing the budget may reduce the size of individual grants to the neediest nations.
Critics say countries ranked 76th to 125th poorest are richer than the original targets, and MCC resources could have more impact if kept focused on the lowest-income countries.

117-hr-8454.one_liner: Set up a new DEA sign-up process for medical marijuana and CBD research
provisions: Creates a separate sign-up process through the Drug Enforcement Administration so doctors and researchers can get permission to study marijuana
Lets registered colleges, doctors, and drug makers handle marijuana and CBD for medical research
Lets companies get DEA permission to produce drugs that contain marijuana or CBD once those drugs are approved for sale
Requires the DEA to check whether there is enough marijuana available so research is never stopped by a shortage
Brings back open access for marijuana research by blocking the Department of Health and Human Services from restoring an old review process that slowed approvals
Lets doctors talk openly with patients about what marijuana and CBD might do to them
Requires a government report on whether marijuana could treat conditions like epilepsy, what it does to teenage brains, and how it affects driving

supporters: Supporters say the new DEA sign-up process removes a bottleneck that slowed marijuana research for years by blocking the Department of Health and Human Services from bringing back an old review process that delayed approvals.

Supporters say letting registered colleges, doctors, and drug makers legally handle marijuana and CBD for medical studies could speed up answers on whether marijuana treats conditions like epilepsy, which currently has limited treatment options.
Supporters say requiring the DEA to confirm there is always enough marijuana available means researchers will not have to stop studies due to supply shortages.
critics: Critics say the bill expands access to marijuana for research and commercial drug production before the required government report on how marijuana affects teenage brains and driving ability has even been completed.

Critics say blocking the Department of Health and Human Services from restoring its review process removes an oversight step that existed to check whether marijuana research proposals were safe and scientifically sound.

Critics say allowing doctors to openly discuss marijuana and CBD with patients, including possible benefits, could encourage use of a substance whose effects on adolescents and drivers the government has not yet fully studied.

117-hr-8888.one_liner: Create a new VA office to help veterans get food assistance
provisions: Creates a new office inside the Department of Veterans Affairs focused on food assistance for veterans
The office gives veterans information about which food assistance programs they can apply for
The office creates rules to find veterans who do not have enough food and connect them with help

supporters: Supporters say the new Office of Food Security inside the VA would give veterans a single place to learn which federal nutrition programs, like SNAP, they qualify for, instead of navigating multiple agencies on their own.
Supporters say the office would create rules to identify veterans who are food insecure and connect them with help, targeting a group that current VA programs do not systematically screen for.
critics: Critics say the bill creates a new VA office but does not include a budget appropriation, leaving it unclear how staffing or outreach will be funded.

Critics say the office can only provide information about existing federal nutrition programs and cannot change eligibility rules, so veterans who do not qualify for SNAP or USDA programs today would still not qualify after the bill passes.
Critics say adding a new office inside the VA to handle food assistance duplicates outreach work already done by USDA and nonprofit veterans service organizations.

117-hr-8876.one_liner: Extend and increase funding for home visits for new and expecting parents through 2027
provisions: Keeps the Maternal, Infant, and Early Childhood Home Visiting Program running through 2027
Increases the total amount of money the program receives each year
Sets rules for how that money gets divided among states and groups
Gives tribal communities a larger share of program funds than before
Creates a public website where anyone can see how the program is performing
Requires the program to find ways to reduce paperwork and reporting for staff
Lets home visitors meet with families online instead of in person, under certain conditions

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps funding for home visits running through 2027, which helps expectant and new parents in communities at risk for poor health outcomes.
Supporters say the bill gives tribal communities a larger share of program funds, directing more resources to families in those communities.
Supporters say the new public dashboard will let anyone see how the program is performing, making it easier to track whether home visits are helping children and mothers.
critics: Critics say increasing the total amount of money the program receives each year adds to federal spending without a set limit on how much costs can grow.
Critics say allowing virtual home visits, even under certain conditions, may reduce the quality of support that in-person visits provide to new parents.
Critics say the new rules for dividing funds among states and groups could shift money away from states that currently serve large numbers of at-risk families.

117-hres-1130.one_liner: Express support for Finland and Sweden joining NATO
provisions: The U.S. Congress says it supports Finland and Sweden applying to join NATO.
Congress says it opposes any move by Russia to stop Finland and Sweden from joining.
Congress calls on all NATO member countries to approve Finland and Sweden's membership quickly.

supporters: Supporters say Finland and Sweden joining NATO would add two experienced military forces to the alliance, strengthening the 32-member group's ability to defend Europe.
Supporters say Congress opposing Russia's attempts to block Finland and Sweden's membership sends a clear message that NATO decisions are made by member countries, not outside powers.

Supporters say calling on all NATO members to approve Finland and Sweden's accession quickly reduces the window of time when those two countries could be vulnerable to threats while waiting for full membership.
critics: Critics say this resolution pressures NATO member countries to rush their approval votes without enough time to review what adding Finland and Sweden means for their own defense commitments.
Critics say the resolution escalates tensions with Russia by directly naming and opposing Russian government actions, which could make diplomatic solutions harder to reach.

117-hr-8987.one_liner: Send one-time payments to 9/11 victims and their families from an existing fund
provisions: 9/11 victims, their spouses, and their children get one-time catch-up payments from the U.S. Victims of State Sponsored Terrorism Fund
The money to pay for this comes from leftover Small Business Administration funds that were set aside for the Paycheck Protection Program but never used

supporters: Supporters say 9/11 victims, their spouses, and their children have not received equal payments from the U.S. Victims of State Sponsored Terrorism Fund compared to other claimants, and these lump-sum catch-up payments would close that gap.

Supporters say the bill does not add new spending because it uses unobligated Small Business Administration funds left over from the Paycheck Protection Program that were never distributed to businesses.
Supporters say families of 9/11 victims have waited decades for full compensation, and redirecting unused federal funds is a direct way to deliver that money without increasing the deficit.
critics: Critics say rescinding unobligated Paycheck Protection Program funds removes a reserve the Small Business Administration could use for future small business relief programs or emergencies.
Critics say the bill does not specify the total dollar amount of the catch-up payments, making it unclear how much each 9/11 victim, spouse, or dependent would actually receive.
Critics say pulling funds from an SBA program to pay a separate victim compensation fund sets a precedent for redirecting unused program money in ways Congress did not originally intend.

117-hr-8873.one_liner: Change the rules for how electoral votes are cast and counted in presidential elections
provisions: Each state must use laws passed before Election Day to pick its electors, the people who officially cast electoral votes for that state.
A state can only extend its voting time because of a major disaster, terrorist attack, or widespread power outage.
The event must stop a large number of people from voting or destroy many ballots already cast.
Each state's governor must officially sign off on which electors the state is sending.
When Congress meets to count electoral votes, the Vice President's only job is to keep the process moving, not to decide which votes count.
