To object to a state's electoral votes in Congress, at least one-third of both the House and Senate must agree.
Before this bill, just one member from each chamber could raise an objection.

supporters: Supporters say raising the objection threshold to one-third of both chambers means a small group of lawmakers can no longer stop a state's electoral votes from being counted, since before this bill just one member from each chamber could trigger an objection.
Supporters say requiring each state's governor to sign off on which electors are sent means there is one official document showing which people are authorized to cast that state's electoral votes.

Supporters say limiting the Vice President's role to keeping the joint session moving removes any chance that the presiding officer could decide on their own which electoral votes to accept or reject.
critics: Critics say allowing voting time extensions only for disasters, terrorist attacks, or power outages leaves out other problems — like long lines or equipment failures — that can stop large numbers of people from casting a ballot.

Critics say requiring one-third of both the House and Senate to object to a state's electoral votes makes it much harder for Congress to flag problems, since before this bill just one member from each chamber could raise a concern.

Critics say the fast-track court review process for candidates who dispute their state's official election paperwork may not give courts enough time to fully examine complex legal questions before the electoral votes are finalized.

117-hres-1168.one_liner: Urge the President to strengthen trade between the US and Caribbean nations
provisions: The US Congress states that trade with Caribbean countries is important to the US economy.
Congress calls on the President to make Caribbean trade programs a priority.
The resolution supports trade deals with Caribbean nations that build long-term economic stability in the region.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution formally states that trade with Caribbean countries is important to the U.S. economy, giving Congress a foundation to push for new trade programs with the nations it calls the 'Third Border.'

Supporters say calling on the President to prioritize Caribbean trade programs could open formal pathways for U.S. businesses to sell goods and invest in a nearby region that shares close geographic and economic ties with the U.S.

Supporters say backing trade deals built around long-term economic stability — as the resolution directly states — could grow Caribbean economies in ways that reduce their reliance on U.S. foreign aid over time.
critics: Critics say the resolution names no specific trade programs, sets no dollar targets, and gives no timeline, so the call for the President to 'prioritize' Caribbean trade has no measurable standard to hold anyone accountable.

Critics say the resolution does not include current trade volume data or identify which U.S. industries would benefit, making it unclear why Caribbean nations should be prioritized over other trade partners the U.S. already has deals with.

Critics say that without an enforcement mechanism, the resolution's stated goal of 'sustainable and resilient economic development' in the Caribbean is advisory only and places no legal obligation on the President to act.

117-hres-1254.one_liner: Set House debate rules for three bills on health, trails, and pensions
provisions: Lets the House vote on a bill to study cardiovascular health in South Asian Americans.
Lets the House vote on a bill to finish the Continental Divide National Scenic Trail.
Lets the House vote on a bill to raise guaranteed pension payouts for certain retirees.
This rule does not change any law on its own.
It only sets up how the three bills will be debated on the House floor.

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the House to vote on H.R. 3771, which would fund research into why South Asian Americans face higher rates of heart disease than other groups.
Supporters say the rule brings H.R. 6929 to the floor, a bill that would raise the pension payments guaranteed to retirees whose pension plans have run out of money.

Supporters say moving H.R. 5118 forward would require the Secretary of Agriculture to make finishing the Continental Divide National Scenic Trail a top priority, completing a trail that still has unfinished sections across several states.
critics: Critics say bundling H.R. 3771, H.R. 5118, and H.R. 6929 into one rule limits how much floor time members get to debate each bill on its own.
Critics say the rule restricts amendments that members can offer on H.R. 6929, which changes how much money the federal government must guarantee to retirees in failed pension plans.

Critics say moving all three bills under one procedural rule reduces the chance for members to raise questions about the costs tied to H.R. 5118's trail completion mandate and H.R. 6929's expanded pension guarantees.

117-hres-1224.one_liner: Set the rules for debating five separate bills in the House
provisions: This bill set the rules for how the House would debate and vote on five other bills.
One of those bills funded the military and set troop levels for 2023.
One would have improved college grants for children of soldiers killed in Iraq or Afghanistan.
Two bills dealt with abortion access. One would protect people's ability to get an abortion. The other would stop states from blocking people from traveling out of state to get one.
One bill would have created a national alert system to warn the public about active shooter situations.

supporters: Supporters say this rule allowed the House to move forward on five bills at once, including the 2023 defense funding bill (H.R. 7900) that sets troop levels and military budgets.

Supporters say the rule brought up the Active Shooter Alert Communications Network bill (H.R. 6538) and college grant improvements for children of soldiers killed in Iraq or Afghanistan (S. 3373), giving those bills a path to a vote.

Supporters say the rule gave the House a way to vote on two abortion access bills — H.R. 8296 and H.R. 8297 — that supporters argue protect people's ability to travel across state lines for medical care.
critics: Critics say the rule packaged abortion bills H.R. 8296 and H.R. 8297 together with unrelated legislation like military funding and a shooting alert system, putting members in a position of voting on items they oppose to advance items they support.

Critics say the rule set fixed debate terms for all five bills, which blocked members from offering amendments to specific provisions — such as troop strength numbers in H.R. 7900 or the grant eligibility rules in S. 3373.
Critics say combining abortion legislation with defense funding in a single rule used military priorities as leverage to advance bills on a separate policy issue.

117-hres-1232.one_liner: Set the rules for how Congress debates three separate bills
provisions: Lets Congress vote on a bill to fund transportation and housing programs through September 2023
Lets Congress vote on a bill about the legal right to use contraception
Lets Congress vote on a bill about federal marriage rules
Sets time limits and debate rules for how each of those three bills gets discussed on the House floor

supporters: Supporters say the rule lets Congress hold a vote on H.R. 8373, which would set a legal right to use contraceptives and protect health care providers who give contraception — rights some members say need to be written into federal law.
Supporters say the rule moves forward a vote on H.R. 8404, which would replace the Defense of Marriage Act and require the federal government to recognize marriages that are legal under state law.

Supporters say the rule sets clear time limits and debate structure so all three bills — including the transportation and housing spending bill for fiscal year 2023 — can move through the House without delay.
critics: Critics say the rule packages three unrelated bills — a spending bill, a contraception bill, and a marriage bill — into one vote, which forces members to accept or reject all three debate structures together.
Critics say the debate rules for H.R. 8404 limit amendments, which prevents members from changing how the bill defines marriage or which marriages the federal government must recognize.

Critics say bringing H.R. 8373 and H.R. 8404 to the floor through this rule moves quickly on issues — contraception rights and federal marriage law — that they argue should go through committee hearings first.

117-hres-1204.one_liner: Set rules for how Congress votes on three separate bills
provisions: Lets Congress vote on renaming a federal courthouse in Tallahassee, Florida after Joseph Woodrow Hatchett
Lets Congress vote on extending a program that gives schools flexibility in how they serve meals to children
Lets Congress vote on funding for the Legislative Branch for the year ending September 30, 2022

supporters: Supporters say this rule would let Congress vote on renaming a federal courthouse in Tallahassee, Florida after Joseph Woodrow Hatchett, who was the first Black justice on the Florida Supreme Court and the first Black federal judge to serve in the South.

Supporters say extending the child nutrition waiver from the Families First Coronavirus Response Act would let schools keep serving meals to children in flexible ways, helping students who depend on school meals for daily food.
Supporters say bringing the Legislative Branch funding bill to a vote would keep Congress funded and running through the end of the fiscal year on September 30, 2022.
critics: Critics say bundling three separate bills — the courthouse renaming, the child nutrition waiver, and the Legislative Branch funding — into one procedural rule limits debate on each individual issue.

Critics say the child nutrition waivers in S. 2089 were written as a temporary COVID-19 response and extending them further moves away from the original rules schools must follow to qualify for federal meal funding.

Critics say using a special rule to fast-track the Legislative Branch appropriations bill in H.R. 4346 bypasses the normal committee review process that is supposed to check how Congress spends its own operating funds.

117-hres-1300.one_liner: Change House rules to speed up how certain resolutions get scheduled for a vote
provisions: Lets the House vote on certain rules committee resolutions the same day they are introduced, instead of waiting a day
Applies this change through July 29, 2022
Changes how bills on the Consensus Calendar — a list of bills with broad support — get scheduled for a vote

supporters: Supporters say waiving clause 6(a) of Rule XIII lets the House vote on Rules Committee resolutions the same day they are introduced, which helps avoid delays when time-sensitive legislation needs to move quickly.
Supporters say the change only applies through July 29, 2022, so it is a short, limited adjustment to House procedure rather than a permanent shift in power.
Supporters say updating how bills on the Consensus Calendar get scheduled gives broadly supported legislation a clearer path to a floor vote.
critics: Critics say removing the one-day waiting period under clause 6(a) of Rule XIII takes away time members need to read and understand resolutions before they vote on them.
Critics say allowing same-day consideration of Rules Committee resolutions could be used to bring major rule changes to the floor before members have a chance to raise concerns.
Critics say altering the Consensus Calendar scheduling process could change which broadly supported bills actually reach a vote, giving House leadership more control over the floor schedule.

117-hres-1289.one_liner: Set the rules for how Congress votes on a spending bill for its own operations
provisions: Sets the steps the House must follow to vote on a spending deal that the Senate changed
Covers government spending for Congress itself for the year ending September 30, 2022
Sets rules for how Congress runs its business between August 1 and September 12, 2022

supporters: Supporters say the rule sets clear steps for the House to vote on the spending deal the Senate changed, which keeps the process moving before the September 30, 2022 deadline for Congressional funding.
Supporters say setting recess rules for August 1 through September 12, 2022 lets members return to their districts while keeping Congress able to come back if urgent business comes up.
Supporters say passing this rule helps avoid a gap in funding for the Legislative Branch by making sure the House can act on the Senate amendment quickly.
critics: Critics say the rule limits debate time on a spending bill that covers Congress's own budget, which means members may not get a full chance to question how the money is being used.
Critics say rushing the amendment process between August 1 and September 12, 2022 reduces the number of days available for public review of changes to the Legislative Branch spending deal.
Critics say using a special rule to set the terms of the vote, instead of following regular order, gives House leadership more control over which changes members can propose to the bill.

117-hres-1316.one_liner: Set the House rules for debating a Senate budget bill
provisions: The House set specific rules for how it would debate and vote on the Senate's version of H.R. 5376, a budget bill.
H.R. 5376 was originally passed using a budget process called reconciliation, which lets Congress change spending and tax rules with a simple majority vote.
The rule controlled how much time members of Congress could spend debating the Senate's changes before voting.

supporters: Supporters say the rule gives the House a clear, structured process to debate and vote on the Senate's changes to H.R. 5376 without delay.
Supporters say using the reconciliation process allows Congress to pass budget changes with a simple majority vote, which they say reflects the will of the elected majority.
Supporters say setting firm debate time limits prevents stalling and moves the budget bill toward a final vote faster.
critics: Critics say limiting debate time on the Senate's changes to H.R. 5376 gives members of Congress too little time to review major spending and tax rule changes before voting.
Critics say the reconciliation process was used to bypass the normal 60-vote threshold in the Senate, which critics argue cuts out the minority party from having a real say.
Critics say the rule was written to control the outcome of the vote on H.R. 5376 rather than to allow open debate on the Senate's specific changes to spending levels.

117-hres-1256.one_liner: Set the rules for debating two bills in the House
provisions: This bill sets the time limits and debate rules for two other bills before the House votes on them
One of the two bills would change rules about keeping certain wild animals in captivity
The other bill would extend the ability of Medicare patients to see doctors by video or phone call

supporters: Supporters say this rule advances H.R. 4040 to a floor vote, which would extend Medicare patients' ability to see doctors by video or phone call under title XVIII of the Social Security Act.
Supporters say the rule also moves H.R. 263 forward, which would update the Lacey Act Amendments of 1981 to clarify rules about keeping certain wild animals in captivity.
Supporters say setting structured debate limits on both bills allows the full House to vote on them without delay.
critics: Critics say the rule restricts how much time members can spend debating H.R. 4040, which affects Medicare patients who rely on telehealth services under title XVIII of the Social Security Act.
Critics say using a structured rule to advance H.R. 263 limits members' ability to offer changes to the captive wildlife provisions under the Lacey Act Amendments of 1981.
Critics say combining debate rules for two unrelated bills — one on wildlife, one on Medicare — under a single rule reduces the time each bill gets on its own merits.

117-hres-1302.one_liner: Set the debate and voting rules for a bill that would limit assault weapons
provisions: This is a procedural rule — it sets the terms for how the House of Representatives debates and votes on a bill.
The bill being debated, H.R. 1808, is a separate piece of legislation that would put limits on who can own certain guns and what types of guns can be sold.
The rule gives both sides a set amount of time to speak before a vote is taken.
This rule does not change any gun laws on its own — only the final vote on H.R. 1808 would do that.

supporters: Supporters say this rule brings H.R. 1808 to the House floor for a formal debate and vote, giving lawmakers a chance to act on a bill that would set new limits on who can own certain guns and what types can be sold.
Supporters say the rule guarantees both sides a set amount of time to speak before any vote is taken, so members of Congress can hear arguments on H.R. 1808 before a decision is made.
Supporters say without this procedural rule, H.R. 1808 could never reach a full House vote — this rule is the only step that moves the gun limits bill forward.
critics: Critics say this rule should not be used because it forces a House floor vote on H.R. 1808, a bill that would restrict what types of guns can be sold and who can own them — changes they argue go too far.
Critics say the rule limits how long members can speak before the vote, cutting short debate on H.R. 1808 and the specific gun ownership rules it would change.
Critics say passing this rule is the first step toward enacting H.R. 1808, and opposing the rule is their main tool to stop the underlying gun limits bill from becoming law.

117-hres-1339.one_liner: Set the rules for debating three bills about federal jobs and the Census
provisions: Decides how long Congress can debate a bill that limits which government jobs can be removed from standard hiring rules
Decides how long Congress can debate a bill that adds protections for federal workers who report wrongdoing
Decides how long Congress can debate a bill that changes how the Census Bureau runs

supporters: Supporters say this rule brings H.R. 302 to the floor for a vote, which would limit how many federal jobs the president can move out of standard civil service hiring rules where workers have removal protections.
Supporters say allowing debate on H.R. 2988 is important because it would add new legal protections under Title 5 for federal workers who report wrongdoing to Congress or inspectors general.

Supporters say the rule also clears the way for a vote on H.R. 8326, which would change how the Census Bureau under Title 13 runs its operations — affecting how congressional seats and federal funding are divided.
critics: Critics say this rule controls and limits how long Congress can debate H.R. 302, which would reduce the executive branch's ability to restructure which federal jobs fall outside standard civil service rules.
Critics say setting a fixed debate window for H.R. 2988 leaves too little time to review how whistleblower claims would be verified before federal workers receive protections under Title 5.

Critics say the rule moves H.R. 8326 forward without enough debate time to examine specific changes to Census Bureau operations that affect population counts used to assign House seats and distribute federal dollars.

117-hres-1372.one_liner: Set the House floor debate rules for a bill on counting electoral votes
provisions: Allows H.R. 8873, a bill about how Congress counts electoral votes, to be brought up for a vote in the House.
Sets how much time members of Congress can spend debating the bill before a vote is held.
Controls which changes to the bill members can propose during the debate.

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the House to vote on H.R. 8873, which would update the Electoral Count Act — a law that has not been changed in over 130 years.
Supporters say the rule sets a fixed debate time, which gives all members a set window to speak before the vote on H.R. 8873 is held.

Supporters say the amendment controls in this rule keep floor debate focused on the specific provisions of H.R. 8873, preventing unrelated proposals from being added to the electoral vote counting reform.
critics: Critics say the limited debate time set by this rule does not give members enough opportunity to fully examine how H.R. 8873 would change the rules Congress uses to count electoral votes.
Critics say this rule restricts which changes members can propose, meaning parts of H.R. 8873 that some members want to alter cannot be brought up for a separate floor vote.
Critics say the amendment controls prevent floor votes on alternative versions of the electoral vote reform, limiting the House to an up-or-down vote on H.R. 8873 as written.

117-hres-1377.one_liner: Set House debate rules for four bills on violence, policing, and mental health
provisions: This bill sets the House debate rules for four other bills — it does not create programs itself.
One bill would give money to community groups that work to reduce violence.
A second bill would fund a program to help solve violent crimes using new technology.
A third bill would give money to police departments with fewer than 200 officers.
A fourth bill would fund states and tribes to hire mental health workers.
Those workers would respond to emergencies involving people with mental illness instead of police.

supporters: Supporters say this rule moves four bills to the House floor that together address violence through community grants under H.R. 4118, crime-solving technology under H.R. 5768, funding for police departments with fewer than 200 officers under H.R. 6448, and mental health emergency response under H.R. 8542.

Supporters say H.R. 8542 would fund states and tribes to hire mental health workers who respond to emergencies involving people with mental illness in lieu of police, giving those communities a trained specialist for mental health calls.
Supporters say H.R. 6448 targets police departments with fewer than 200 officers — smaller agencies that often cannot access the same federal resources as large city departments.
critics: Critics say H.R. 8542 directs mental health workers to respond in lieu of law enforcement officers in emergencies involving people with mental illness, which removes police from calls where responder safety may be at risk.
Critics say H.R. 4118 would send federal money to community groups for violence reduction but does not require those groups to meet specific outcome measures before receiving continued funding.

Critics say packaging all four bills under one rule sets a single combined floor debate, giving members less time to examine each bill's grant eligibility rules and funding conditions than if the bills were brought to the floor separately.

117-hres-1361.one_liner: Set debate rules in Congress for a bill to let borrowers split joint student loans
provisions: This sets the rules for how Congress will debate and vote on S. 1098.
S. 1098 would let borrowers who have a joint consolidation loan split it into two separate loans.
Right now, borrowers who took out joint consolidation loans cannot split them into separate loans.
Joint consolidation loans are federal student loans that two borrowers combined into one single loan.

supporters: Supporters say S. 1098 would help borrowers who took out joint consolidation loans but later divorced or lost contact with their co-borrower, since right now there is no way to split the loan.
Supporters say allowing borrowers to separate joint consolidation loans would let each person be responsible only for their own share of the debt, instead of being tied to someone else's payments.
Supporters say this rule sets up a fair debate process so Congress can vote on whether to give these borrowers a way out of a loan structure they cannot currently escape.
critics: Critics say this procedural rule limits how much time members of Congress can debate S. 1098, which may prevent a full review of how splitting loans would affect federal loan servicers.
Critics say separating joint consolidation loans could create extra costs for the federal student loan program, since servicers would need to process and track twice as many loan accounts.

117-hres-1396.one_liner: Set the rules for debating three bills in the House
provisions: This bill sets the time limits and rules for how the House debates three other bills.
The first bill changes the fees companies pay before merging and adds money for antitrust enforcement.
The second bill funds mental health and drug treatment support for students and school staff.
The third bill lets voting access grants go to a U.S. territory and American Indian tribal groups.

supporters: Supporters say the rule allows the House to debate H.R. 3843, which changes merger filing fees to fund more antitrust enforcement, helping stop large companies from reducing competition.

Supporters say the rule opens floor debate on H.R. 7780, which puts money toward mental health and drug treatment staff in schools, giving students and school workers more access to behavioral health support.
Supporters say the rule enables a vote on S. 3969, which would let voting access grants reach the Northern Mariana Islands and American Indian tribal groups that were left out before.
critics: Critics say the rule limits debate time on three separate bills at once, making it harder for members to fully question the merger fee changes in H.R. 3843 or the scope of school mental health funding in H.R. 7780.
Critics say bundling debate rules for bills on antitrust fees, school behavioral health, and tribal voting grants into one rule reduces each bill's chance for full review and amendment.

Critics say the structured rule blocks members from offering changes to S. 3969's grant formula, which could affect how funds are split between the Northern Mariana Islands and American Indian consortium groups.

117-hres-720.one_liner: Condemn ISIS attacks in northern Mozambique and call for action to protect civilians
provisions: The U.S. Congress condemns terrorist attacks carried out by an ISIS group in the Cabo Delgado region of Mozambique.
The resolution calls on the Mozambique government to take steps to stop the violence and keep its people safe.
No U.S. laws change and no U.S. money is spent — this is a statement of position only.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution puts the U.S. Congress on record against ISIS-Mozambique attacks in Cabo Delgado Province without spending any U.S. money or changing any U.S. laws.
Supporters say calling on Mozambique's government to take steps to protect its citizens puts public pressure on that government to act against the violence.
Supporters say naming ISIS-Mozambique as the group responsible for the attacks helps build a shared international understanding of who is behind the violence in Cabo Delgado.
critics: Critics say this resolution is only a statement of position — it provides no U.S. funding or resources to the people harmed by ISIS-Mozambique attacks in Cabo Delgado Province.
Critics say urging Mozambique's government to stop the violence does not give that government the money or military support it may need to carry out those steps.

117-hres-892.one_liner: Call on Rwanda to release Paul Rusesabagina and let him return to the US
provisions: Calls on the government of Rwanda to release Paul Rusesabagina, who is being held in prison there
Calls on Rwanda to give Rusesabagina access to doctors and the medical care he needs
Calls on the US government to push Rwanda to release him in every meeting between the two countries
Expresses support for Rusesabagina's family as they work to bring him home

supporters: Supporters say Rwanda should release Rusesabagina, a U.S. permanent resident and Belgian citizen, on humanitarian grounds because he is aging and in poor health while held in prison.
Supporters say the resolution calls on Rwanda to give Rusesabagina access to qualified doctors and all medical care needed to protect his physical and mental health.
Supporters say the U.S. government should raise his case in every meeting with Rwanda and press for his immediate release to bring him home to his family.
critics: Critics say Rwanda's courts convicted Rusesabagina in 2021 on terrorism charges, including links to armed groups responsible for attacks that killed civilians, and calling for his release ignores that legal process.
Critics say pressing Rwanda on this case in every diplomatic meeting could strain U.S. relations with a key partner in East Africa at a time when regional stability depends on that cooperation.
Critics say the resolution does not address the Rwandan government's evidence against Rusesabagina, which means U.S. pressure could be seen as interference in another country's court system.

117-hres-1499.one_liner: Set the rules for debating four bills in the House
provisions: This bill sets the time limits and debate rules the House follows when voting on four other bills
One of those bills would give money to nonprofits that help people leaving prison find housing, jobs, and services
Another bill would set rules for medical care for pregnant women who are in prison
A third bill would keep funding a program that sends nurses or social workers to visit new and expecting parents at home
The fourth measure would end a labor dispute between railroad companies and some of their workers

supporters: Supporters say the rule sets fixed time limits for floor debate on all four bills, allowing the House to schedule and complete votes on prison reentry grants, prenatal care for inmates, the home visiting program, and the railroad labor dispute without open-ended delays.

Supporters say grouping all four measures under a single structured rule gives each bill a guaranteed path to a House floor vote, rather than leaving them waiting in the schedule with no set timeline.
Supporters say the rule's debate structure prevents any one member from using unlimited debate to stall action on the railroad worker dispute or the funding programs included in the package.
critics: Critics say the rule bundles four bills covering unrelated topics — nonprofit reentry grants, medical care for pregnant inmates, home visiting program funding, and a railroad labor settlement — under one vote, reducing the floor time members get to debate each bill on its own.

Critics say the rule limits the ability of members to offer amendments to the railroad dispute resolution, forcing a take-it-or-leave-it vote on the settlement terms for railroad workers and companies.

Critics say compressing debate time on the maternal health and home visiting bills under a combined rule means members have less time to question specific provisions, such as which medical services incarcerated pregnant women must receive.

117-hres-1464.one_liner: Set the debate rules for a bill about silencing agreements in sexual assault cases
provisions: This is a procedural rule that sets the terms for how the House of Representatives will debate another bill.
The underlying bill would stop courts from enforcing contracts that require people to stay silent about sexual assault or harassment before any dispute happens.
Those silencing agreements are sometimes signed before people are hired or as part of other deals.
This rule decides how much time lawmakers get to debate, what changes they can propose, and when they vote.

supporters: Supporters say this rule would open a House floor vote on S. 4524, which would stop courts from enforcing contracts that require workers to stay silent about sexual assault or harassment before any dispute even starts.

Supporters say the rule moves forward a bill that protects people who signed nondisclosure or nondisparagement agreements before being hired, giving them the right to speak about what happened to them.
Supporters say allowing a debate and vote on S. 4524 gives lawmakers a chance to end the use of silencing clauses that are sometimes buried in job offer paperwork.
critics: Critics say the rule controls how much time lawmakers get to debate S. 4524 and limits what changes they can propose, which may prevent fixes to how the bill defines covered agreements.

Critics say moving the bill forward under a structured rule could block amendments that would address how the change affects employers who use nondisclosure agreements for reasons beyond sexual misconduct.
Critics say limiting debate on a bill that changes contract law for workers and businesses across the country reduces the chance for full review of how courts would apply the new rules.

117-hres-1404.one_liner: Set the rules for the House to vote on two bills
provisions: This bill sets the terms for how the House of Representatives will debate and vote on two separate pieces of legislation.
One of those bills would cap how much people pay out of pocket for insulin.
The other would set aside money to pay victims of terrorism sponsored by foreign governments who have not yet received their full payment.

supporters: Supporters say H.R. 6833 would limit what patients pay out of pocket for insulin by changing cost-sharing rules under the Public Health Service Act, the Internal Revenue Code, and ERISA — laws that cover most private health plans in the U.S.

Supporters say H.R. 8987 would release catch-up payments from the U.S. Victims of State Sponsored Terrorism Fund to people who won court cases against foreign governments but have not yet received full payment.

Supporters say the rule schedules dedicated floor time for both H.R. 6833 and H.R. 8987 in a single session, allowing the House to act on both bills without waiting to put each one on the calendar separately.
critics: Critics say H.R. 6833 only caps the cost-sharing amount patients pay at the pharmacy — a requirement added to the Public Health Service Act, IRC, and ERISA — but does not set any limits on the list prices insulin manufacturers charge, leaving the root cost of the drug unchanged.
Critics say linking H.R. 6833 and H.R. 8987 under one rule ties two unrelated issues together, making it harder for members to vote against one bill without also blocking the other.

Critics say the rule controls how long members can debate H.R. 6833 and H.R. 8987 on the floor, giving lawmakers less time to review the cost-sharing requirements and funding amounts before a final vote is held.

117-s-144.one_liner: Let a health agency buy land and build a road to a California youth center
provisions: Lets the Indian Health Service buy private land in Hemet, California at a fair price
Requires the agency to build a paved road on that land
The road gives people a way to reach the Desert Sage Youth Wellness Center, which serves Native American youth
Requires the agency to either maintain the road itself or make an agreement with Riverside County to maintain it

supporters: Supporters say the bill would give the Indian Health Service the authority to buy private land in Hemet, California at fair market value, removing a barrier that currently blocks reliable access to the Desert Sage Youth Wellness Center.
Supporters say building a paved road directly to the center would make it easier for Native American youth to reach mental health and wellness services they are already entitled to under federal law.
Supporters say the road maintenance requirement — either by IHS or through an agreement with Riverside County — ensures the access route stays usable long-term, not just at opening.
critics: Critics say the bill does not specify a cost cap for the land purchase or road construction, leaving the total federal expense undefined before Congress approves the project.

Critics say requiring IHS to either maintain a new road or negotiate a maintenance deal with Riverside County adds ongoing administrative and financial obligations to an agency that already has a large service backlog.

117-s-1098.one_liner: Let student loan borrowers split a joint loan into two separate loans
provisions: Right now, some people took out a single joint federal student loan with another borrower and cannot separate it.
This bill lets both borrowers apply together to the Department of Education to split their shared loan into two separate loans.
If one borrower is facing abuse — including financial control — by the other, or cannot reach them, they can apply alone.
They do not need the other person's agreement to split the loan in those cases.

supporters: Supporters say the bill fixes a problem in federal student loan rules: two borrowers who took out a joint consolidation loan currently cannot separate it, even if their financial situations have changed.
Supporters say the bill lets one borrower apply alone to the Department of Education to split the loan if the other borrower is using financial control as a form of abuse or cannot be reached.
Supporters say the bill gives borrowers a path to separate their debt without needing the other borrower's agreement in cases of abuse or when contact is not possible.
critics: Critics say the Department of Education may have difficulty verifying abuse or lack of contact claims when only one borrower submits an application, which could lead to disputes over how the debt is divided.

Critics say that splitting a joint loan without the other borrower's consent could leave that borrower responsible for a larger share of the debt than they agreed to when the loan was first taken out.
Critics say the bill does not specify how the Department of Education will decide what portion of the loan each borrower owes after a separation, which could create inconsistent outcomes.

117-s-2293.one_liner: Give FEMA disaster reservists job protections when they leave for a deployment
provisions: FEMA keeps a group of reservists, workers who can be called up when disasters hit.
This bill gives those workers job protection when they leave for a deployment.
Employers must give these workers their old jobs back when they return from a deployment.
These job protections apply even if the worker could not tell their employer before leaving.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives FEMA reservists the same job protections that military reservists already have under USERRA, closing a gap that left disaster workers without guaranteed reemployment rights.
Supporters say the no-notice rule is needed because disasters strike without warning, and FEMA reservists often cannot contact employers before they must deploy.
Supporters say requiring employers to give reservists their old jobs back when they return will make it easier for FEMA to recruit and keep trained disaster workers.
critics: Critics say the no-notice rule removes the employer's ability to plan for a worker's absence, which could be especially hard for small businesses that rely on a single employee.
Critics say the bill does not set a limit on how long a deployment can last before the job-return guarantee kicks in, leaving employers uncertain about how long they must hold a position open.

117-s-231.one_liner: Require FEMA to create safety guides for firefighters on avoiding harmful chemicals in foam
provisions: Tells FEMA to write guides for firefighters on how to avoid contact with PFAS chemicals.
PFAS chemicals are man-made substances found in some firefighting foams and have been linked to health problems.
Tells FEMA to create guides on foam, gear, and tools that do not contain PFAS chemicals.
Tells FEMA to build a public website where firefighters can find best practices for reducing exposure to these chemicals.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would protect firefighters from PFAS chemicals found in firefighting foam, which have been linked to serious health problems in people who work with them regularly.
Supporters say requiring FEMA to publish guides on PFAS-free foam, gear, and tools gives fire departments a clear path to safer equipment without having to find that information on their own.
Supporters say the public website FEMA must build will make it easier for fire departments across the country to find and share best practices for reducing PFAS exposure.
critics: Critics say the bill does not require fire departments to actually change their equipment or foam — it only asks FEMA to write guides, which departments can choose to ignore.
Critics say the bill sets no deadline for when FEMA must finish the guidance or launch the public website, which could delay any real protection for firefighters.
Critics say the bill does not include funding to help fire departments, especially smaller ones, pay for PFAS-free gear or foam if they choose to switch.

117-s-2089.one_liner: Let states bury National Guard and Reserve members at state veterans cemeteries
provisions: States that get VA grant money for veterans cemeteries can now choose to bury National Guard and Reserve members who left service with an honorable discharge.
ROTC members who died while in the program under honorable conditions can also be buried at these state cemeteries.
Spouses and children of these members can be buried at the same state cemeteries.
The VA cannot turn down a state's grant application just because the state plans to bury these members.
The VA cannot enforce old grant rules, set before this bill passed, that blocked states from burying these members.
Families of eligible members can receive money to help pay for a burial plot at these cemeteries.

supporters: Supporters say the bill lets National Guard and Reserve members who left service with an honorable discharge be buried at state veterans cemeteries that receive VA grant money, giving these members the same burial recognition as other veterans.
Supporters say spouses and minor children of eligible Guard and Reserve members can now be buried at these state cemeteries, and families can receive a plot allowance to help cover burial costs.
Supporters say the VA cannot reject a state's grant application just because the state plans to bury these members, which removes a barrier that has blocked states from making this choice.
critics: Critics say expanding burial eligibility to National Guard, Reserve, and ROTC members — plus their spouses and children — could fill limited cemetery space faster, leaving fewer plots for veterans who served on active duty.

Critics say allowing states to use VA grant funds to expand or improve cemeteries for these additional groups may shift federal cemetery dollars away from veterans who are already eligible for burial in national cemeteries.

117-s-2794.one_liner: Raise the life insurance cap for service members and veterans from $400,000 to $500,000
provisions: Raises the maximum life insurance payout for active and former service members from $400,000 to $500,000.
This applies to two government life insurance programs: one for people currently serving and one for veterans.
If a covered service member or veteran dies, their family can receive up to $100,000 more than before.

supporters: Supporters say raising the maximum payout from $400,000 to $500,000 gives military families $100,000 more to cover costs like housing, childcare, and debt after losing a loved one who served.
Supporters say the current $400,000 limit has not kept up with rising costs of living, and the increase brings the benefit closer to what a family would need to replace years of lost income.
Supporters say the change covers both active-duty members under Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance and veterans under Veterans' Group Life Insurance, so more families are protected.
critics: Critics say Congress has not released a full cost estimate for raising the cap by $100,000 across both insurance programs, making it hard to know the total impact on the federal budget.
Critics say the bill does not address the monthly premium rates service members pay, so some lower-income members may still not be able to afford the full $500,000 in coverage.

117-s-2551.one_liner: Require federal workers who buy goods and services to take AI training
provisions: The federal office that oversees government budgets must create a training program about artificial intelligence for government workers who handle purchasing and contracts.
The training covers what AI can do and what risks come with using it.
The program must be updated at least every two years.
The office must track how many workers complete the training and collect feedback from them.

supporters: Supporters say that requiring OMB to train government purchasing workers on AI capabilities and risks will help federal agencies make smarter decisions when buying AI tools or services.
Supporters say the rule that the program must be updated at least every two years means workers will stay current as AI technology keeps changing fast.
Supporters say tracking how many workers complete the training and collecting their feedback will help OMB improve the program over time.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a funding amount, so it is unclear how OMB will pay for building, running, and updating the training program across all executive agencies.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for when workers must complete the training, which could let agencies delay or skip participation without consequences.
Critics say requiring updates only every two years may not be often enough, since AI technology can change significantly in a shorter period of time.

117-s-2490.one_liner: Create a national historic site in Texas honoring a school that taught Mexican-American children
provisions: Makes the Blackwell School in Marfa, Texas part of the National Park System.
The school educated children of Mexican descent from 1885 to 1965, during a time when Texas schools were segregated by race.
The site cannot open until the federal government signs an agreement with the Marfa school district to share or receive the property.
The government can only get the land through donations, donated money, or trades — not by forcing anyone to give it up.
No private or local government land can be added to the site without the written permission of the owner.
The National Park Service must write a plan for how to manage the site.

supporters: Supporters say making the Blackwell School part of the National Park System would preserve the history of Mexican-descent children who were forced to attend a separate school in Marfa, Texas from 1885 to 1965 because of state-enforced segregation.

Supporters say the bill protects private property owners by requiring their written permission before any private or local government land can be added to the site, and by limiting how the federal government can get land to donations or trades only.

Supporters say the requirement that the federal government sign an agreement with the Marfa school district before the site can open gives the local community a direct role in decisions about the property.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a specific dollar amount for what it will cost each year to staff and run the site, making it hard to know the full expense to taxpayers.

Critics say placing the Blackwell School under shared management between the National Park Service and the Marfa school district could create disagreements over how the site is used, since the bill requires the site to be managed in line with National Park System rules.

Critics say the National Park Service is responsible for hundreds of sites across the country, and adding a unit focused on one school in a small Texas town could pull staff and money away from other park units.

117-s-3157.one_liner: Study why some workers cannot find jobs that match their credentials from other countries
provisions: The Department of Labor must research why some people cannot find jobs that match their foreign credentials.
The bill covers people who are legally in the country but not yet citizens, and people who have become naturalized citizens.
The study must include suggestions for how the government could help these workers find jobs that match their skills.
The Department of Labor must send the results of the study to Congress.

supporters: Supporters say the Department of Labor study will identify specific barriers stopping naturalized citizens and legal immigrants from finding jobs that match the professional credentials they earned abroad.
Supporters say requiring the study to include policy recommendations gives Congress a starting point for actual legislation to fix the credential gap problem.
Supporters say workers with foreign credentials who are already legally in the country represent an untapped source of skilled labor that the U.S. economy is not fully using.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires a study and sends it to Congress, meaning no rules actually change and no workers get direct help from this legislation.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for when the Department of Labor must finish the study or define what counts as a qualifying foreign credential, leaving key details open.
Critics say Congress already has reports on immigrant workforce barriers and that another study delays action that could benefit affected workers sooner.

117-s-3115.one_liner: Make permanent a rule requiring federal judges to hold yearly events for abuse survivors
provisions: Each federal district's chief judge must hold at least one public event per year.
The event must connect survivors of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, or stalking with free legal help.
Without this bill, the rule would have ended automatically after four years.
Judges would no longer be required to hold these events once the rule expired.
This bill removes the expiration date so the rule stays in place going forward.

supporters: Supporters say making the rule permanent means chief judges in every federal district must keep holding yearly events to connect domestic violence and stalking survivors with free legal help, so that access does not disappear when the original four-year window closes.
Supporters say without this bill, the requirement for judges to run these events would expire automatically, cutting off a structured path for survivors to find lawyers who work for free.
critics: Critics say the bill adds a standing duty to federal judges without providing extra staff or funding to organize and run these annual public events.

Critics say Congress could review the program every few years instead of making it permanent, which would allow lawmakers to check whether the events are actually connecting survivors with legal help before locking in the requirement.

117-s-3369.one_liner: Rename the VA medical center in Atlanta, Georgia after veteran Max Cleland
provisions: Renames the VA medical center in Atlanta, Georgia after Joseph Maxwell 'Max' Cleland.
Max Cleland is a Vietnam War veteran who lost three limbs in combat.
He later served as a U.S. Senator from Georgia and as head of the VA.
This is a name change only — no funding, programs, or services change.

supporters: Supporters say renaming the Atlanta VA medical center after Max Cleland honors a Georgia veteran who lost both legs and one arm in Vietnam and later led the VA itself.
Supporters say the name change recognizes Cleland's service both in combat and as a U.S. Senator from Georgia, giving veterans in Atlanta a facility named after someone who shared their experience.
Supporters say this bill changes only the name — no funding, staffing, or services are affected — so there is no cost to veterans currently using the center.
arguments.note: This bill is a naming designation with no policy, funding, or programmatic changes. No organized opposition arguments have been recorded in the public record.

117-s-3662.one_liner: Fund airports to temporarily test fire suppression systems without releasing PFAS chemicals
provisions: The federal government will pay 100% of the cost for airports to buy equipment that tests fire suppression systems without releasing PFAS chemicals into the ground or water.
PFAS are man-made chemicals found in some fire-suppression foam used at airports.
Right now, airports often have to release PFAS into the ground or water just to test their fire systems.
This new equipment lets them run the same test without releasing any PFAS.
Scientists have linked PFAS exposure to possible health problems in humans.

supporters: Supporters say the bill lets the federal government pay 100% of the cost for airports to buy equipment that tests fire suppression systems without releasing PFAS chemicals into the ground or water, removing any financial barrier for airports to make the switch.
Supporters say that right now airports must discharge PFAS into soil and water just to test their fire systems, and this bill gives them a way to run the same test with zero discharge.
Supporters say scientists have linked PFAS exposure to possible health problems, so stopping PFAS releases during routine airport fire tests could reduce risk for communities near airports.
critics: Critics say the bill is temporary and does not create a permanent funding commitment, meaning airports could lose access to federal money for this equipment once the temporary period ends.
Critics say the bill only pays for testing equipment and does not require airports to remove PFAS already discharged into the ground or water from past fire system tests.
Critics say the bill sets no deadline for airports to start using the new no-discharge equipment, so some airports may delay making the switch.

117-s-3846.one_liner: Keep funding grants that connect police and courts with mental health services
provisions: Keeps the Justice and Mental Health Collaboration Program running through the year starting October 2025
Gives grants to states, cities, and tribes to help police and courts work with people who have mental health problems
Lets grant money pay for training prosecutors on how to redirect people away from jail and into treatment
Lets grant money pay for programs where police officers and mental health workers respond to crisis calls together
Opens up grants to cover suicide prevention programs, case management, and the 988 mental health phone line
Keeps the Department of Justice's job of tracking and reporting how many people with mental illness are in prisons and jails

supporters: Supporters say the bill lets grant money pay for programs where police officers and mental health workers respond to crisis calls together, which can get people treatment instead of putting them in jail.
Supporters say expanding grants to cover the 988 mental health phone line and suicide prevention programs gives states and cities more ways to help people before a crisis turns into a criminal case.
Supporters say training prosecutors on how to redirect people away from jail and into treatment can lower the number of people with mental illness who end up in the criminal justice system.
critics: Critics say the bill keeps the Department of Justice tracking how many people with mental illness are in prisons and jails but does not require the government to take steps to reduce that number.

Critics say grants for co-responder programs still put police officers at the center of mental health crisis calls, and some mental health advocates argue that law enforcement involvement can make crises worse for some people.

Critics say the bill reauthorizes funding through FY2026 without requiring programs to show data proving that past grants reduced arrests or improved mental health outcomes for people in the criminal justice system.

117-s-3470.one_liner: Require agencies to report contractors linked to human trafficking to oversight offices
provisions: When a government agency gets a report confirming that a contractor, grant recipient, or their partners took part in human trafficking, the agency must report them to its suspension and debarment office — the office that can bar companies from getting future government contracts.
Under current law, agencies only have to consider reporting these contractors. This bill makes reporting required.
The Office of Management and Budget must send Congress a report on how well the government is following its own rules against human trafficking in contracts.

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a gap in current law by making it required — not just optional — for agencies to report contractors confirmed to have taken part in human trafficking to the suspension and debarment office, which can bar those companies from future government work.

Supporters say requiring the Office of Management and Budget to report to Congress on how well agencies are following anti-trafficking rules in contracts creates accountability and makes it harder for agencies to ignore the issue.
Supporters say that under current law, agencies can receive a confirmed report of human trafficking by a contractor and still choose not to act — this bill removes that choice.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for when agencies must make the referral to the suspension and debarment office, which could allow agencies to delay action even after a confirmed report.

Critics say the bill focuses only on the referral step and does not require the suspension and debarment office to take any specific action once a case is referred, leaving the outcome still uncertain.

Critics say the required Office of Management and Budget report to Congress does not come with enforcement tools, so if agencies are found to be out of compliance, there is no clear consequence written into the bill.

117-s-3451.one_liner: Speed up federal permits for tech projects including semiconductors and artificial intelligence
provisions: Six types of tech projects can now use a faster federal permitting process.
Those types include the semiconductor industry, artificial intelligence systems, and high-performance computing and advanced hardware.
Quantum computing and science, data storage and management, and cybersecurity are also included.
This faster process requires government agencies to review a project at the same time instead of one after another.

supporters: Supporters say the bill lets semiconductor plants, AI systems, quantum computing facilities, and three other tech project types use the FAST-41 process, which requires federal agencies to review permits at the same time instead of one after another, cutting total wait time.

Supporters say faster permits for data storage, high-performance computing, and cybersecurity projects could help the U.S. build more of this infrastructure without long delays caused by sequential agency reviews.
Supporters say adding these six tech categories to FAST-41 gives companies in semiconductors and AI a clear federal process to follow, which reduces uncertainty about how long permitting will take.
critics: Critics say running all agency reviews at the same time — instead of one after another — may give each agency less time to find environmental or safety problems in large projects like semiconductor fabrication plants or AI data centers.

Critics say the bill does not specify a minimum project size to qualify for the faster FAST-41 process, which could allow a wide range of data storage or AI facilities to skip the normal, longer review timeline.

Critics say tech projects like high-performance computing centers and semiconductor plants use large amounts of water and energy, and a faster review process may not leave enough time to study those impacts fully.

117-s-4359.one_liner: Rename the VA office in Atlanta, Georgia after Senator Johnny Isakson
provisions: The Department of Veterans Affairs office in Atlanta, Georgia will be officially renamed the Senator Johnny Isakson Department of Veterans Affairs Atlanta Regional Office.
The office can also be called the Isakson VA Atlanta Regional Office for short.
Johnny Isakson was a U.S. Senator from Georgia who served from 2005 until he resigned in December 2019 due to health problems.

supporters: Supporters say renaming the Atlanta Regional Office honors Senator Johnny Isakson, who chaired the Senate Veterans Affairs Committee and wrote laws that improved care for Georgia veterans.
Supporters say the bill recognizes Isakson's 14 years in the Senate, where he focused on veterans issues before resigning in December 2019 due to Parkinson's disease.

Supporters say giving the office a formal name — the Senator Johnny Isakson Department of Veterans Affairs Atlanta Regional Office — creates a lasting public record of his service to veterans in Georgia.
critics: Critics say Congress could spend its time on bills that change rules or funding for veterans, rather than renaming an existing office.
Critics say naming federal buildings and offices after individual politicians sets a precedent that may not reflect the views of all veterans who use the Atlanta Regional Office.

117-s-4003.one_liner: Create federal training programs to help police de-escalate crises
provisions: The Department of Justice will create training programs for police officers and mental health professionals.
The programs cover how to de-escalate tense situations and avoid using force.
They also teach officers how to respond when someone is having a mental health or suicidal crisis.
The federal government will give money to states to pay for this training.

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires the Department of Justice to build training that teaches officers how to respond to mental health and suicidal crises without using force, which could lower the number of people harmed during those encounters.
Supporters say the federal government will give grant money to states to pay for this training, so local police departments do not have to find the money on their own.
Supporters say teaching officers specific de-escalation tactics gives them more tools to handle tense situations before they turn dangerous.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a minimum number of training hours or require all police departments to use the new curriculum, which means many officers could go without the training.

Critics say putting police officers in charge of mental health crisis responses — even with new training — is not the same as sending trained mental health professionals, and this bill does not change who shows up to those calls.
Critics say the bill does not specify how much grant money each state will receive, so smaller or rural departments may not get enough funding to actually run the training programs.

117-s-442.one_liner: Require federal buildings to use the most energy-efficient lighting available
provisions: Federal buildings run by the General Services Administration must use the most efficient lighting systems available, not just any energy-efficient bulb.
The new rule covers the full lighting system — including sensors and how light is spread across a room — not just the bulbs.
When the government buys new lighting, it must choose the option that costs the least over the full life of the product, including energy costs.
The General Services Administration must share information with state, local, and tribal governments about how to buy and use these lighting systems.

supporters: Supporters say requiring federal buildings to use the most life-cycle cost effective lighting — including sensors and fixture distribution — will lower long-term energy costs for taxpayers, since cheaper upfront options often cost more in energy bills over time.
Supporters say the bill goes beyond just swapping bulbs by covering full lighting systems, which they argue will cut energy use more than current law allows.

Supporters say requiring the General Services Administration to share information with state, local, and tribal governments will help smaller agencies access the same cost-saving lighting options as the federal government.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a budget or cost limit for upgrading lighting systems across all GSA-managed federal buildings, which could lead to large unplanned spending.

Critics say requiring the "most" energy-efficient systems available — rather than systems that meet a set standard — could force agencies to constantly upgrade equipment as technology changes, adding ongoing costs.
Critics say the bill gives the GSA new duties to advise state, local, and tribal governments but does not provide funding or staff to carry out that work.

117-s-3895.one_liner: Keep the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom operating through 2024
provisions: Keeps the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom running through the end of 2024.
The commission tracks how countries around the world treat people because of their religion.
Without this bill, the commission would have lost its power to operate after 2022.
The commission sends yearly reports to Congress and the President listing countries with serious religious freedom problems.

supporters: Supporters say reauthorizing the commission through 2024 ensures Congress and the President keep receiving yearly reports that name specific countries with serious religious freedom problems, giving lawmakers documented facts to use in foreign policy decisions.

Supporters say that without this bill, the commission would have lost the power to operate after 2022, ending the U.S. government's ability to systematically track how governments that restrict religious practice treat people based on their religion.
critics: Critics say the commission sends yearly reports to Congress but has no power to require countries to change their policies, so religious minorities in those countries may see no direct result from its findings.

Critics say the State Department's Office of International Religious Freedom already monitors religious freedom conditions worldwide, raising questions about whether a separate commission creates overlap without adding unique value.

117-s-4524.one_liner: Stop courts from enforcing silence agreements in sexual harassment or assault cases
provisions: If someone signs a nondisclosure or nondisparagement agreement before a sexual harassment or assault dispute starts, that agreement cannot be enforced in court.
This applies to cases under federal, tribal, or state law.
Courts cannot use these pre-signed agreements to stop a person from speaking about sexual harassment or assault they experienced.

supporters: Supporters say the bill stops courts from enforcing nondisclosure agreements that were signed before a dispute began, which means people who experienced sexual harassment or assault can speak about what happened to them.
Supporters say the rule applies across federal, tribal, and state law cases, so it protects people no matter which court system handles their case.
Supporters say pre-signed nondisparagement agreements have been used to silence people who experienced workplace sexual harassment, and this bill removes that legal barrier.
critics: Critics say some nondisclosure agreements are signed as part of a fair settlement that both sides agreed to, and the bill would make those agreements unenforceable even when the person signed willingly.
Critics say the bill does not define how serious a sexual harassment claim must be before the rule applies, which could make it hard for courts to decide which cases are covered.
Critics say the bill does not set a time limit on how old a pre-dispute agreement can be, so agreements signed many years ago could also be voided under this new rule.

117-s-958.one_liner: Let health centers use federal grants to build clinics or mobile medical units
provisions: Health centers can now use federal grant money to construct or renovate buildings where they provide care.
Health centers can also use that same grant money to set up mobile medical clinics — vehicles or portable units that bring care to patients.
Before this bill, mobile clinics could only get grant funding if they were connected to a permanent, full-time location. Now they can qualify on their own.
These grants go to health centers that serve communities where people have trouble getting medical care.

supporters: Supporters say allowing mobile clinics to qualify for New Access Point grants on their own — without being tied to a permanent location — means more vehicles and portable units can reach patients in communities where access to primary care is limited.

Supporters say expanding grant uses to include building construction and renovation gives health centers more options to set up new delivery sites in medically underserved areas, not just pay for services.
Supporters say mobile clinics can serve rural or low-income communities where building a permanent facility is not practical, so removing the permanent-site requirement lets grants go further.
critics: Critics say that mobile clinics without a permanent, full-time site attached may make it harder for patients to get consistent follow-up care, since there is no fixed location tied to the clinic.
Critics say allowing grant funds to be spent on construction and renovation — uses not previously allowed — could reduce the share of money going directly to patient care in underserved communities.
Critics say mobile-only sites that are not connected to a permanent facility may be more difficult for federal agencies to monitor and verify are delivering care to the right populations.

117-s-4785.one_liner: Extend a $5,000 fee on convicted sex traffickers by 19 days
provisions: People or companies convicted of sex abuse or human trafficking crimes must pay a $5,000 fee on top of other penalties.
This fee was set to end on September 11, 2022, but the bill moves that end date to September 30, 2022.
Money from this fee goes into a fund for victims of human trafficking inside the U.S.

supporters: Supporters say the 19-day extension keeps the $5,000 fee active through September 30, 2022, so money convicted offenders owe does not stop flowing into the Domestic Trafficking Victims' Fund before the end of the fiscal year.

Supporters say without this extension, anyone convicted of sex abuse or human trafficking between September 11 and September 30, 2022 would not owe the $5,000 assessment, cutting off funding that goes directly to U.S. trafficking victims.
Supporters say the extension costs nothing to the government and keeps an existing penalty in place for people and companies found guilty of serious crimes.
critics: Critics say the bill only adds 19 days to a fee set to expire, and does not make the $5,000 assessment permanent, meaning Congress will need to act again or the fund loses this revenue source entirely.

Critics say the $5,000 fee only applies to a narrow set of offenses involving sexual abuse and human trafficking, so the Domestic Trafficking Victims' Fund depends on how many convictions happen to occur in a short 19-day window.
Critics say the bill does not increase the $5,000 amount or expand which crimes trigger the fee, so the total money reaching victims stays limited by the same rules already in place.

117-s-4900.one_liner: Extend and add security rules to federal small business research grant programs
provisions: Keeps two federal programs running through the year starting October 2024 — these programs give money to small businesses to do research that could turn into products.
Stops small businesses from getting grants if they have financial ties to certain foreign countries.
Requires government agencies that run these programs to check whether applicants have connections to foreign governments before approving their grants.
Small businesses that have already received many grants must meet stricter performance standards to keep getting money.
Government inspectors must audit small businesses that are subject to those stricter standards.
The Defense Department, Energy Department, Health and Human Services, and National Science Foundation must each report on whether these programs create national security risks.

supporters: Supporters say keeping the SBIR and STTR programs funded through FY2025 gives small businesses a reliable source of grants to turn research into products, without a gap in funding.
Supporters say blocking grants to small businesses with financial ties to certain foreign countries protects U.S. research from being shared with or controlled by foreign governments.
Supporters say requiring small businesses with many prior awards to meet stricter performance standards ensures that grant money goes to businesses that actually deliver results.
critics: Critics say the new requirement to check every applicant for foreign financial ties adds steps to the application process, which could slow down awards and push small businesses away from applying.
Critics say small businesses that have already received many grants may lose access to funding if they cannot meet the expanded performance standards, even if their past work was successful.

Critics say requiring four separate agencies — Defense, Energy, HHS, and NSF — to each write national security reports adds cost and staff time without a clear plan for how those reports will change the programs.

119-hconres-40.one_liner: Order the President to pull U.S. troops out of fighting with Iran
provisions: Tells the President to stop using U.S. military forces in any fighting against Iran.
The President must stop unless Congress officially declares war or votes to allow military action against Iran.
U.S. forces can stay if they are defending the United States, an ally, or a partner from an attack that is happening right now.
Under existing law, the President has up to 60 days to use military force before needing Congress to approve it.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would force the President to stop using U.S. military forces against Iran unless Congress votes to declare war or passes a specific authorization for military action against Iran.
Supporters say the existing 60-day clock under the War Powers Resolution has already run, and Congress has not voted to approve fighting Iran, so the President must pull back U.S. forces now.
Supporters say U.S. forces can still stay in the region to defend against an active attack, so the resolution does not leave allies unprotected.
critics: Critics say pulling U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran while threats are still active could make it harder to respond quickly if Iran or its partners launch a new attack on U.S. troops or allies.

Critics say the resolution ties the President's hands by requiring a full congressional vote before the military can act, even in fast-moving situations where waiting days or weeks for Congress could cost lives.

Critics say the line between 'defending from an imminent attack' and ongoing hostilities is unclear, and the resolution does not define it, which could create confusion about when U.S. forces are legally allowed to act.

119-hr-1011.one_liner: Give farmers and forest owners more money upfront to recover from natural disasters
provisions: Farmers can now get up to 75% of the cost of rebuilding or fixing farmland paid upfront, before the work is done — up from 25%
Farmers can get 50% of repair costs paid upfront, also up from 25%
Wildfire damage now counts for disaster payments even if the fire was started by humans or the government, as long as it spread naturally
Forest owners on private land can now get up to 75% of emergency costs paid upfront — currently they get nothing upfront
Forest owners must spend the money within 180 days of receiving it

supporters: Supporters say raising the advance payment from 25% to 75% for farmland rebuilding will help farmers who cannot afford to pay for repairs out of pocket before getting reimbursed.

Supporters say expanding eligibility to include human-caused wildfires that spread naturally will help farmers and forest owners who were left out of disaster programs even when their land was destroyed.

Supporters say allowing forest owners to get 75% of emergency costs paid upfront — when they currently receive nothing in advance — will help them act faster to restore private forest land after a disaster.
critics: Critics say the 180-day spending requirement for forest owners may be too tight, forcing landowners to rush decisions on expensive emergency measures.
Critics say expanding wildfire eligibility to fires started by the government or humans could increase program costs by covering disasters that were not natural events.
Critics say raising advance payments to 75% before work is completed increases the risk that funds are disbursed but the emergency measures are not finished or done correctly.

119-hr-1689.one_liner: Give Haitians in the US temporary permission to stay and work for 18 months
provisions: Gives Haitians in the US a temporary legal status called TPS starting August 3, 2025, lasting 18 months.
While they have this status, they can get a work permit.
While they have this status, they cannot be held by immigration officials just because of their immigration status.
While they have this status, they cannot be deported.

supporters: Supporters say the 18-month TPS designation starting August 3, 2025 would protect Haitians already in the US from deportation while Haiti deals with ongoing gang violence and political instability.
Supporters say giving Haitians work permits under TPS would let them earn income legally and support themselves without relying on government aid.

Supporters say the rule that stops immigration officials from detaining Haitians based only on their immigration status would reduce fear in Haitian communities and let people report crimes without risk.
critics: Critics say the bill forces the Secretary of Homeland Security to grant TPS to an entire country with no review process, removing the executive branch's ability to assess conditions on the ground before making the designation.

Critics say that blocking deportations for 18 months could make it harder for the government to remove Haitians who do not qualify for TPS or who have criminal records, since enforcement actions would be complicated by the blanket protections.

Critics say automatic TPS designations set by Congress rather than DHS could encourage more migrants to travel to the US expecting legal status, adding pressure to immigration courts already handling large backlogs.

119-hr-7613.one_liner: Require military and civilian aircraft to share location signals and strengthen air safety rules
provisions: Military helicopters must broadcast their location when flying in shared airspace, unless doing so would give away a secret mission.
Military helicopters on special missions in the Washington, DC area are not required to broadcast their location.
Those helicopters must go through a safety review and take steps to reduce the risk of a crash.
By December 31, 2031, military aircraft must be able to receive location signals from other planes and helicopters.
By December 31, 2031, civilian aircraft already required to broadcast their location must also be able to receive location signals.
The FAA must set limits on how long supervisory air traffic controllers can stay at their post without a break.
The FAA must notify people involved in close-call incidents in the air and review helicopter flight paths near Reagan National Airport.

supporters: Supporters say requiring military helicopters to broadcast their location using ADS-B Out as the default in shared airspace means civilian pilots and air traffic controllers can see where those aircraft are, reducing the risk of midair collisions.

Supporters say the December 31, 2031 deadline for both military and civilian aircraft to receive location signals from nearby planes means pilots will be able to see other aircraft on a display and take action to avoid a crash.
