Supporters say requiring the FAA to set limits on how long supervisory air traffic controllers can stay at their post addresses concerns that fatigue can lead to mistakes during high-traffic periods.
critics: Critics say military helicopters on special missions in the Washington, DC area are exempt from broadcasting their location, which means civilian pilots flying near Reagan National Airport will still not know where those aircraft are.

Critics say the December 31, 2031 deadline gives aircraft operators more than five years to install ADS-B In equipment, which they argue is too slow a response given recent close-call and collision incidents in busy airspace.

Critics say the bill does not set specific time limits for how long supervisory air traffic controllers can work at their post — it only tells the FAA to create those limits — leaving the key safety details undefined.

119-hres-1156.one_liner: Express support for tax policies that help working families
provisions: This is a resolution, not a law — it does not create new rules or change anything on its own.
It states that Congress supports tax policies for working families and recognizes the tax relief passed in the 2025 reconciliation act.
It only states a position and has no legal effect.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution shows Congress stands behind the tax cuts passed in the 2025 reconciliation act, which they say lowered taxes for working families.
Supporters say putting Congress on record in favor of working-family tax policies signals that these cuts should be kept in future budget talks.
critics: Critics say this resolution has no legal effect and does not create or protect any actual tax relief, since it only states a position.
Critics say the resolution backs the 2025 reconciliation act without specifying which families benefit or by how much, making it impossible to hold Congress accountable for results.

119-hr-6398.one_liner: Remove EPA review of federal projects already reviewed under another law
provisions: Right now, the EPA must review and give comments on big federal construction projects and other major federal actions. This bill removes that requirement.
Federal projects already go through a review process under a law called NEPA. This bill stops the EPA from doing a second review on top of that.
The change applies to new federal construction projects and proposed federal rules that already require NEPA review.

supporters: Supporters say removing the EPA review requirement will cut duplicate work, since federal construction projects already go through a full review under NEPA.
Supporters say requiring two separate reviews — one under NEPA and one from the EPA — slows down federal projects without adding new protections.
Supporters say the bill targets only projects that already require NEPA review, so environmental analysis still happens before any project moves forward.
critics: Critics say the EPA review under the Clean Air Act looks at air quality impacts specifically, which NEPA reviews do not always cover in the same depth.
Critics say removing the EPA's ability to comment on proposed federal regulations means air quality concerns could be left out of the rule-making process.
Critics say the change affects all new federal construction projects and proposed rules that go through NEPA, which could be a large number of actions where the EPA currently weighs in.

119-hr-6409.one_liner: Exempt states from air quality penalties when outside sources like wildfires cause the pollution
provisions: States can avoid federal sanctions if outside pollution — like wildfire smoke — causes their air quality problems.
This applies to areas rated severe or extreme for ozone, or serious for particle pollution.
States can also avoid federal fees for missing air quality targets if outside pollution is the cause.
To keep the exemption, states must prove every five years that outside pollution is still the cause.
An area cannot be labeled as failing air quality standards if the pollution comes from outside the United States.
Pollution from other countries counts as an outside source even when caused by human activity, not just natural events.

supporters: Supporters say states in severe or extreme ozone zones should not face federal sanctions or fees when wildfire smoke or other pollution from outside their borders is what caused them to miss air quality targets, since those states cannot control that pollution.

Supporters say areas should not be labeled as failing air quality standards when the pollution causing the problem comes from outside the United States, including pollution caused by human activity in other countries, because states have no power to regulate foreign emissions.
Supporters say the five-year renewal requirement keeps states accountable by making them re-prove that outside pollution is still the cause before they can keep the exemption.
critics: Critics say the bill lets states in serious, severe, or extreme pollution zones avoid penalties without having to show they reduced their own local emissions, which could slow progress in areas already failing federal air quality standards.

Critics say allowing foreign human-caused pollution — not just natural events like wildfires — to count as an exempt outside source gives states a broader reason to avoid meeting Clean Air Act requirements, since industrial emissions from other countries could qualify.

Critics say residents in nonattainment areas rated severe or extreme for ozone or serious for particle pollution could continue breathing unhealthy air without federal pressure on states to act, since sanctions and fees are the main tools the EPA uses to push states to fix their plans.

119-hres-965.one_liner: Set the rules for debating a bill about Haiti temporary protected status
provisions: This resolution sets the rules for how the House of Representatives will debate and vote on a separate bill called H.R. 1689.
The bill being debated would require the U.S. government to give Haitians temporary protected status.
Temporary protected status lets people from a certain country stay and work legally in the U.S. for a set time.
The U.S. grants this status to people whose home country has gone through a disaster, war, or other serious crisis.
This resolution is not the Haiti bill itself — it only controls how that bill gets debated on the House floor.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution brings H.R. 1689 to a House floor vote, which would require the DHS Secretary to grant Haitians the right to live and work legally in the U.S. under temporary protected status.

Supporters say H.R. 1689 — which this resolution allows to the floor — covers Haitians who cannot return home because of disaster or crisis, giving them a legal way to stay in the U.S. for a set period.
Supporters say the floor debate rules in this resolution give all House members the chance to vote on whether to extend TPS to Haitians.
critics: Critics say this resolution moves forward H.R. 1689, which would remove the DHS Secretary's power to choose whether Haiti meets the standard for temporary protected status — making the designation mandatory.
Critics say H.R. 1689, which this resolution puts on the House floor, would allow Haitians to live and work legally in the U.S. with no stated limit on how many people could receive TPS.
Critics say this resolution uses special floor rules to advance H.R. 1689 instead of letting it go through the normal committee process that other bills must follow.

119-hres-1174.one_liner: Set the rules for debating four bills about clean air and taxes
provisions: Lets Congress debate a bill that changes how the EPA handles air quality data when wildfires or other events affect the readings
Lets Congress debate a bill that changes how the EPA reviews laws proposed by Congress before they pass
Lets Congress debate a bill that sets rules for pollution that comes into the U.S. from other countries
Lets Congress debate a resolution that says tax rules should support working families

supporters: Supporters say bringing H.R. 6387 to the floor lets Congress fix how the EPA counts air quality data during wildfires, which currently can make counties look like they are breaking clean air rules even when the pollution came from a natural disaster.
Supporters say H.R. 6409 would give the EPA clear rules for handling pollution that blows in from other countries, so American communities are not penalized for emissions they did not create.
Supporters say scheduling debate on H. Res. 1156 opens the door for Congress to go on record supporting tax policies that benefit working families.
critics: Critics say this procedural resolution fast-tracks bills that would weaken EPA oversight, including H.R. 6398, which changes how the EPA reviews proposed laws before they are passed — reducing an independent check on new legislation.
Critics say H.R. 6387 could let states use wildfire or mitigation events as reasons to avoid meeting air quality standards under the Clean Air Act, even in areas with ongoing pollution problems.

Critics say bundling four separate measures — three Clean Air Act changes and a tax resolution — into one debate rule limits how much time members of Congress can spend examining each bill on its own.

119-hres-1175.one_liner: Set the debate rules for a vote on extending a U.S. surveillance law
provisions: This resolution sets the rules for how the House of Representatives will debate and vote on a separate bill about U.S. surveillance powers.
The bill being debated would extend the government's power to collect foreign intelligence under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) through October 20, 2027.
FISA lets the U.S. government collect information on people outside the country who may be threats to national security.
This bill would keep those powers active through October 20, 2027.
This resolution itself does not change any law — it only controls how the debate in the House is run.

supporters: Supporters say keeping FISA title VII active through October 20, 2027 gives Congress time to review the law and make changes before it expires again.
Supporters say a lapse in FISA title VII would force intelligence agencies to stop certain ongoing collection efforts, which cannot be restarted without new court approvals.
Supporters say FISA title VII is one tool the government uses to collect information on people outside the U.S. who may be national security threats.
critics: Critics say FISA title VII allows the government to collect data on U.S. persons when they communicate with foreign targets, and this extension through 2027 does not add new protections for those Americans.
Critics say this resolution limits debate time on H.R. 8035, which they argue does not give members enough time to offer amendments that would add privacy safeguards.
Critics say the bill extends government surveillance powers for more than three years without adding new limits on how long data collected under FISA title VII can be stored.

119-hr-4690.one_liner: Remove the rule requiring federal buildings to stop using fossil fuels by 2030
provisions: Cancels the rule that required new and renovated federal buildings to phase out fossil fuels by 2030
Tells the Department of Energy to act as if the phase-out rule never existed until new rules are written
Stops green building certification programs from blocking federal buildings from getting certified just because they use fossil fuels

supporters: Supporters say repealing the 2030 fossil fuel phase-out rule gives federal agencies more flexibility in how they power and heat buildings, instead of being locked into one type of energy source by a set deadline.

Supporters say the bill stops green building certification programs from rejecting federal buildings just because they use fossil fuels, which lets the government still earn energy efficiency credits without switching fuel sources.
Supporters say directing the Department of Energy to write new rules from scratch gives experts a chance to set performance standards based on updated cost and energy data.
critics: Critics say removing the requirement to phase out fossil fuels in federal buildings by FY2030 slows down a plan that was already in place to cut long-term energy costs and carbon output from government-owned buildings.

Critics say telling the Department of Energy to treat the phase-out rule as if it never existed creates a gap with no clear standard in place, leaving federal building projects without guidance until new rules are finished.

Critics say changing the green building certification rules to allow fossil fuel use could weaken the meaning of those labels, since federal buildings could earn high-performance ratings while still relying on gas or oil.

119-hr-2493.one_liner: Renew federal grants for health care in rural areas through 2030
provisions: Federal money for rural health care is renewed through 2030.
One set of grants helps rural doctors, clinics, and hospitals offer more services to more people.
A second set of grants helps local health care groups work together and share resources.
A third set of grants helps small rural health care providers give better care.
Grant money must be used to reach people in rural areas who have trouble getting health care.
Those same communities must be involved in planning how the money is spent.

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps federal grant money going to rural doctors, clinics, and hospitals through 2030, which helps communities where people already struggle to find health care close to home.
Supporters say one set of grants helps local health care groups share resources and work together, which can lower costs for small rural providers that cannot afford services on their own.
Supporters say the bill requires grant money to reach rural people who have the hardest time getting care, so funds go to those who need them most instead of areas that are easier to serve.
critics: Critics say the bill extends existing programs without requiring any proof that the three grant types have improved health outcomes in rural areas since they were first created.
Critics say the new rule requiring underserved communities to be involved in planning how grant money is spent could slow down how quickly funds reach rural clinics and hospitals that need help now.

Critics say the bill does not set specific dollar amounts for any of the three grant programs, leaving it unclear how much money will actually reach small rural health care providers each year through 2030.

119-hr-5200.one_liner: Require the FCC to study 911 outages and hold yearly public hearings on disasters
provisions: The FCC must publish a report on 911 outages that are not currently required to be reported to the government.
The report must also look at whether phone companies should include images or video when reporting outages.
The FCC must recommend rule changes to fix gaps in how outages are reported.
The FCC must hold public hearings once a year after any major event that knocked out phone or internet service for at least a week.
After each hearing, the FCC must release a public report on how many outages happened, how long they lasted, and steps to make networks more reliable.
All reports must be posted on the FCC's public website.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would force the FCC to study 911 outages that phone companies are not currently required to report, which could reveal gaps in emergency coverage that put lives at risk.
Supporters say requiring the FCC to hold public hearings after any event that knocked out service for at least a week gives the public a chance to see what went wrong and hold providers accountable.

Supporters say posting all reports on the FCC's public website means anyone — including local governments and first responders — can access data on outage counts, durations, and network reliability recommendations.
critics: Critics say the bill adds new reporting and hearing requirements to the FCC without providing funding, which could strain agency resources already used for other oversight work.
Critics say requiring phone companies to include images or video in outage reports may be hard to carry out in practice, especially during disasters when network capacity is already limited.

119-hr-1681.one_liner: Create a team to speed up federal reviews of broadband permits on public land
provisions: Creates a team made up of heads of federal land agencies to help those agencies process broadband permit requests.
The team holds regular calls to make sure each agency is keeping up with its backlog of permit requests.
The team sets goals for how fast permit requests should be reviewed and tracks whether agencies hit those goals.
The team must send Congress a report on how well it is working.

supporters: Supporters say the strike force will hold regular calls with agency heads at the Department of Agriculture and Department of the Interior to make sure broadband permit requests on federal lands do not sit untouched in backlogs.

Supporters say setting review goals and tracking whether agencies hit them gives broadband companies a more predictable timeline for building on public lands, which could speed up internet expansion in rural areas that cross federal territory.
Supporters say the required report to Congress means lawmakers can see whether agencies are meeting their goals and take action if they are not.
critics: Critics say the strike force can only set goals and hold calls — it has no power to approve permits itself, so agencies can miss their goals without facing any penalty.
Critics say the bill does not require specific deadlines for how fast permit requests must be reviewed, which means agencies could set low goals that require little change from what they already do.

Critics say the bill only covers permit requests on federal lands managed by agencies like the Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management, leaving out delays at the state and local level that also slow broadband construction.

119-hr-5201.one_liner: Require the FCC to report on whether companies follow the direct-dial 911 law
provisions: Requires the FCC to publish a report on whether companies that make multi-line phone systems are following the direct-dial 911 law.
Multi-line phone systems are used in places like offices, hotels, and schools.
The report must describe how well companies are following the rule and what is making it hard for others to comply.
The report must also include suggestions for changes to FCC rules or new laws if needed.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the FCC to publish a report will show whether companies that make multi-line phone systems — used in offices, hotels, and schools — are following the direct-dial 911 rule.
Supporters say the report must include suggestions for new FCC rules or laws if companies are not complying, which could lead to better 911 access for people in those buildings.
critics: Critics say the bill only requires a report, not any new rules or penalties, so companies that are not following the direct-dial 911 law may face no real consequences.
Critics say producing the report uses FCC staff time and resources without guaranteeing any action to fix compliance problems among multi-line phone system makers and vendors.

119-hres-1189.one_liner: Set the rules for House floor debate on four energy and environment bills
provisions: This resolution sets the rules for how the House will debate and vote on four other bills.
One bill removes federal rules that set energy efficiency standards for buildings.
One is a House statement expressing support for rural communities — it does not change any laws.

One bill changes the Endangered Species Act to speed up permits for landowners and reward private landowners who protect wildlife on their property. It also requires the government to publicly report on progress recovering at-risk species.
One bill removes the requirement to get a federal drilling permit for some geothermal energy projects. It also removes the environmental review requirement for those same projects.

supporters: Supporters say removing federal energy efficiency standards for buildings gives states and local governments more control over their own building codes, rather than requiring them to follow rules set in Washington.

Supporters say changing the Endangered Species Act to reward private landowners who protect wildlife on their property will bring more land into conservation, since most at-risk species live on private land.

Supporters say removing the federal drilling permit and environmental review requirements for some geothermal energy projects will speed up clean energy development on land where the risks are already well understood.
critics: Critics say removing the federal energy efficiency standards for buildings will lead to higher energy costs for people who live or work in those buildings over time, since less efficient buildings cost more to heat and cool.

Critics say removing the environmental review requirement for geothermal drilling projects under the National Environmental Policy Act means nearby communities and ecosystems get less say before drilling begins.

Critics say changing the Endangered Species Act to speed up permits for landowners could weaken protections for species that are already at risk of dying out, since fewer reviews means less oversight.

119-hres-1182.one_liner: State that the House supports rural communities in the 119th Congress
provisions: The House says it has supported rural areas through rules on energy, health care, manufacturing, and internet access.
This resolution does not create new laws, change any rules, or spend any money.
It is a statement of support only.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution formally recognizes rural communities as major suppliers of U.S. energy resources and critical providers of food production, giving those communities public acknowledgment in the congressional record.

Supporters say the resolution highlights four specific policy areas — energy, health care, manufacturing, and broadband connectivity — where the House of Representatives took action during the 119th Congress to benefit rural Americans.
Supporters say that even without spending money or changing rules, the resolution signals to rural communities that Congress sees their role in national economic stability.
critics: Critics say the resolution claims the House supported rural areas in energy, health care, manufacturing, and broadband policy but does not name a single bill passed or dollar spent to back up that claim.

Critics say using floor time on a non-binding statement of support does nothing to address real gaps in rural broadband access or rural health care availability, since the resolution creates no new programs or funding.

Critics say the resolution's broad language about congressional support for rural communities cannot be verified or measured, making it impossible to hold the House accountable for the claims it is making.

119-hr-5587.one_liner: Remove federal permit and review requirements for geothermal drilling on state and private land
provisions: Geothermal energy comes from heat stored underground and can be used to generate electricity or heat buildings.
Companies on private or state land no longer need a federal drilling permit for geothermal work.
This applies when they hold a state permit and the federal government owns less than half of the underground heat resources.
These projects do not need to go through a federal environmental review.
These projects do not need to check whether they might harm endangered plants or animals.
Historic preservation review is skipped unless the state has no law protecting historic sites.
These exemptions do not apply on land where Native American tribes hold ownership.

supporters: Supporters say removing the federal drilling permit requirement for geothermal projects on private and state land will speed up clean energy development, since companies will only need a state permit when the federal government owns less than half of the underground resources.

Supporters say skipping federal environmental review under NEPA will cut months or years off the time it takes to build geothermal projects, helping more homes and businesses access heat and electricity from the ground.
Supporters say the bill still requires state permits and keeps protections in place for Native American tribal lands, so local oversight remains.
critics: Critics say removing the requirement to check whether geothermal drilling might harm endangered plants or animals, even on private land, could put species at risk without any federal safety net.
Critics say skipping the National Historic Preservation Act review whenever a state already has its own historic protection law may leave gaps, since state laws vary widely in what they protect.
Critics say cutting out federal environmental review under NEPA means the public loses a formal chance to comment on drilling projects that could affect local water, land, and air.

119-hr-6387.one_liner: Expand what counts as an exceptional event for federal air quality rules
provisions: The EPA must leave certain pollution data out when checking if a state broke federal air quality rules.
A state can request this by proving a specific event — not everyday pollution from cars or factories — caused the spike.
Controlled burns and other human actions designed to copy natural events now count as valid exceptional events.
States can now point to hot, dry weather or still air as causes of their pollution readings; those conditions were not recognized as valid causes before.
The EPA must update its rules for handling air quality data affected by actions taken to reduce wildfire risk.
When several states file about the same event, the EPA must do a regional study covering all of them.

supporters: Supporters say that letting states point to hot, dry weather and still air as causes of pollution spikes will stop states from being penalized for air quality problems caused by weather, not by local factories or cars.

Supporters say that counting controlled burns as valid exceptional events means states can manage wildfire risk without worrying that the smoke data will count against them when the EPA checks for air quality violations.

Supporters say that requiring the EPA to run a regional study when several states file about the same event will give a fuller picture of how wildfires and other shared events affect air quality across state lines.
critics: Critics say that letting states exclude pollution data caused by hot, dry weather or still air could make it easier to hide ongoing air quality problems, since those conditions happen regularly in many parts of the country.

Critics say that expanding what counts as an exceptional event — including controlled burns — means more pollution readings can be left out when the EPA checks whether a state is meeting federal air quality standards, which could weaken public health protections.

Critics say the bill requires the EPA to update its rules and run new regional studies without setting a clear deadline or providing extra funding, which could slow down enforcement of clean air standards.

119-s-1020.one_liner: Give hydropower projects more time to start construction
provisions: Hydropower projects that got a license before March 13, 2020 can ask for more time before they have to start building.
Right now, these projects can get up to 8 extra years to start construction. This bill adds up to 6 more years on top of that.
The extra time comes in three 2-year blocks, so projects can ask for more time as they need it.
If a project's license already expired, FERC can bring it back to life as if it never ran out.

supporters: Supporters say that adding up to 6 more years — on top of the current 8-year extension — gives hydropower developers enough time to work through permitting delays, supply chain problems, and funding gaps that slowed projects licensed before March 13, 2020.
Supporters say the three 2-year block structure lets FERC check in on each project before granting more time, so only projects still making progress get the extra years.
Supporters say allowing FERC to bring back expired licenses means projects that already went through years of review do not have to restart the approval process from scratch.
critics: Critics say extending deadlines by up to 14 total years keeps rivers and waterways tied to project plans for a very long time, which can block other uses of those water resources and delay environmental reviews of whether conditions have changed.

Critics say reviving expired licenses — treating them as if they never ran out — removes the normal check where regulators decide if an old project still makes sense under current environmental and safety rules.

Critics say the bill does not require developers to show why they need the extra time, so projects that have stalled without a clear path forward could hold onto licenses for years without real progress.

119-hr-227.one_liner: Give clergy a two-year window to undo their Social Security and Medicare tax exemption
provisions: Some clergy and Christian Science practitioners can apply to skip paying Social Security and Medicare taxes on their church pay.
That exemption has been permanent — once granted, they could not undo it.
This bill opens a two-year window for those clergy to cancel their exemption and start paying into Social Security and Medicare.
Clergy who do not opt back in will have no Social Security or Medicare benefits from their church work.
That changes only if they have enough credits from other jobs.
The IRS must create a plan to let clergy know they can now undo their exemption.

supporters: Supporters say the two-year window lets clergy who regret their exemption start paying into Social Security and Medicare again, giving them access to retirement and health benefits they currently cannot get from their church work.
Supporters say clergy who never meant to give up Social Security and Medicare for life now have a clear path to reverse that decision before the window closes.
Supporters say the bill requires the IRS to create a plan to notify eligible clergy, making sure people actually learn they can undo their exemption rather than missing the option entirely.
critics: Critics say the bill gives clergy only two years to act, and those who miss the deadline remain permanently locked out of Social Security and Medicare benefits from their ministerial earnings with no future recourse.

Critics say clergy who opt back in must begin paying both the employee and employer share of Social Security and Medicare taxes on their church income, which can be a large added cost for ministers with modest salaries.

Critics say the bill does not specify what the IRS notification plan must include or when it must be completed, leaving no guarantee that all eligible clergy will actually be reached before the two-year window expires.

119-sconres-33.one_liner: Set the federal government's spending and revenue targets for 2026 through 2035
provisions: Sets targets for how much the government plans to spend and take in each year from 2026 through 2035.
Tells four committees — covering homeland security, immigration law, courts, and government operations — to send budget proposals by May 15, 2026.
Those proposals can add no more than $70 billion total to the deficit across 2026–2035.
In the Senate, these budget bills can pass with 51 votes instead of the usual 60, skipping a step that normally lets senators delay a vote.
Sets aside budget room for border security and immigration changes that do not add to the deficit.

supporters: Supporters say the 10-year spending plan gives Congress a clear map for cutting the deficit by setting firm limits on new spending from 2026 through 2035.
Supporters say letting budget bills pass with 51 Senate votes instead of 60 means border security and immigration enforcement changes can move faster without being blocked.
Supporters say the $70 billion cap on new deficit spending from the four committees keeps the budget process from adding too much to the national debt.
critics: Critics say using the 51-vote rule to bypass the normal 60-vote threshold removes a key check that lets the minority party slow down major spending decisions.
Critics say the instructions to the Homeland Security and Judiciary committees prioritize border and immigration spending while leaving out other areas like health care or education.
Critics say setting a $70 billion deficit limit across 10 years still allows Congress to add to the national debt, which already stands above $36 trillion.

119-hr-7567.one_liner: Renew federal farm and food programs through 2031
provisions: Keeps USDA farm and food programs running through 2031, when Congress will need to renew them again
Continues food assistance — known as SNAP or food stamps — for the roughly 42 million Americans who use it to buy groceries
Renews crop insurance that pays farmers when weather or other problems wipe out their crops
Keeps programs that pay farmers to protect soil, water, and wildlife on their land
Continues government loans that help farmers buy land, equipment, and supplies
Updates rules on who can buy U.S. farmland from outside the country
Funds farm research and programs for people living in rural towns and communities

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps SNAP benefits running through 2031 for the roughly 42 million Americans who use them to buy groceries each month.
Supporters say renewing crop insurance gives farmers a financial safety net when weather or other problems wipe out their crops, protecting the food supply.
Supporters say the bill continues programs that pay farmers to protect soil, water, and wildlife on their land, which helps prevent long-term damage to U.S. farmland.
critics: Critics say the bill extends USDA farm and food programs through 2031 without adding work requirements for able-bodied adults who receive SNAP benefits.
Critics say the bill does not do enough to limit which foreign individuals or companies can buy U.S. farmland, leaving national security risks in place.
Critics say farm commodity support payments go mostly to large farming operations, leaving small and mid-size family farms with a smaller share of the benefits.

119-s-1318.one_liner: Find Jewish veterans buried abroad under wrong grave markers and notify their families
provisions: Find Jewish veterans buried abroad in U.S. military cemeteries under grave markers that did not show they were Jewish.
Reach out to the families and descendants of those veterans.
The government must try to hire a nonprofit group to run this program for the first 10 years after the bill passes.

supporters: Supporters say the program would find Jewish veterans buried abroad in U.S. military cemeteries under markers that did not show their Jewish faith, correcting a wrong done to those soldiers.
Supporters say the bill requires the government to contact families and descendants of those veterans, giving relatives a chance to know the true record of their loved one's service.
Supporters say hiring a nonprofit to run the program for the first 10 years would keep costs lower than using a new government agency.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a specific budget or funding amount, making it unclear how the American Battle Monuments Commission will pay for the search and outreach work.
Critics say the bill does not define how many veterans are affected or set a timeline for completing the identification process, which could leave the program open-ended.
Critics say relying on a nonprofit contract for the first 10 years may create gaps in oversight, since the bill does not name standards the nonprofit must meet.

119-hr-7959.one_liner: Strengthen protections and payment rules for people who report tax cheats to the IRS
provisions: People who report tax fraud to the IRS can now keep their name private in court.
A judge can reveal their name only if the public benefit of knowing outweighs the risk to them.
When a whistleblower disputes their award, the judge must take a fresh look at the full case, not just check for obvious errors.
If the IRS is late notifying a whistleblower about their award, the IRS must pay interest on top of the award amount.
Whistleblowers can deduct lawyer's fees from their taxes, whether the award came through the required or optional payment program.
The IRS must include a list of up to 10 top tax avoidance schemes reported by whistleblowers in its yearly report to Congress.

supporters: Supporters say allowing whistleblowers to keep their names private in Tax Court proceedings will encourage more people to report tax fraud, since many fear retaliation from those they report on.
Supporters say switching to a fresh review of the full case — instead of only checking for obvious errors — means judges look at all the evidence when a whistleblower disputes their award amount.
Supporters say letting whistleblowers deduct lawyer fees from both the required and optional award programs, not just the required one, removes an unequal tax treatment between the two groups.
critics: Critics say requiring the IRS to pay interest on awards when it misses notification deadlines adds a new financial penalty that could cost the agency money on top of the awards themselves.

Critics say giving judges the power to reveal a whistleblower's identity when 'societal interest' outweighs harm leaves room for broad interpretation that could expose whistleblowers in more cases than intended.

Critics say requiring the IRS to publish a list of up to 10 top tax avoidance schemes in its yearly report to Congress could tip off tax planners about which strategies the IRS is watching most closely.

119-s-4465.one_liner: Extend the government's legal authority to monitor foreign communications for national security
provisions: Lets U.S. intelligence agencies collect electronic messages and calls of people outside the United States without getting a separate warrant for each person
Requires the government to get a court order before searching collected messages for information about an individual U.S. citizen or resident
Keeps the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court in charge of reviewing and approving the rules that govern how these collections work
Extends these collection powers for 5 more years, through 2031

supporters: Supporters say the 5-year extension through 2031 lets intelligence agencies keep collecting electronic messages and calls from people outside the United States without slowing down operations to get a separate warrant for each person.

Supporters say the law requires a court order before the government can search collected data for information about a U.S. citizen or resident, which protects Americans from being targeted without oversight.
Supporters say the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court will continue to review and approve the rules for how these collections work, keeping a check on how the power is used.
critics: Critics say the law allows intelligence agencies to collect a large amount of communications without individual review, which means messages from U.S. citizens or residents can be gathered before any court has approved targeting them.
Critics say the court order requirement only applies after data has already been collected, so Americans' communications can be stored and searched later without a warrant at the time of collection.

Critics say extending these powers for 5 more years through 2031 gives the government a long window to collect foreign communications with limited ability for the public to know how many Americans are affected.

119-hres-1224.one_liner: Set the rules for debating five separate bills in Congress
provisions: Sets the time limits and debate rules for five bills before the full House
One of the five bills covers farm programs through 2031
One bill requires parents to approve any changes to a child's name, pronouns, or bathroom access at public schools
One bill sets the federal government's spending plan for 2026 through 2035
One bill creates a program to find and correct grave markers for Jewish American soldiers buried overseas under wrong symbols
One bill changes clean air rules related to ethanol content in gas

supporters: Supporters say this rule brings five bills to the House floor for a vote, including a farm program that runs through 2031 and a federal spending plan that covers 2026 through 2035.
Supporters say the rule sets clear time limits for each bill, which keeps the House on schedule and lets members vote on all five measures in an organized way.
Supporters say one of the five bills would fix grave markers for Jewish American soldiers buried overseas under wrong religious symbols, a correction that affects veterans' families.
critics: Critics say the rule limits debate time on a 10-year budget plan covering fiscal years 2026 through 2035, which means members get little time to review decisions that affect trillions in spending.

Critics say bundling a parental consent rule for public schools, a farm bill, an ethanol clean air change, and a budget resolution into one rule forces a single vote on debate terms for five unrelated issues.

Critics say the rule does not allow members to change the debate schedule for individual bills, including the school policy bill that applies to any public school receiving federal funds under the Elementary and Secondary Education Act.

119-sres-690.one_liner: Let the Senate vote on multiple nominations at the same time
provisions: Lets the Senate group certain nominations together and vote on all of them in one vote, instead of voting on each person one at a time.
The nominations being grouped are already listed on the Senate's Executive Calendar — the waiting list of people nominated for government jobs.
This only changes how the Senate holds the vote, not who is nominated or what the positions are.

supporters: Supporters say grouping nominations already listed on the Executive Calendar into one en bloc vote allows the Senate to confirm more people faster, reducing the backlog of nominees waiting for a floor vote.
Supporters say because this resolution only changes how the vote is held — not who is nominated or what jobs they would fill — it saves Senate floor time that can be used for other work.
Supporters say en bloc voting is used for nominations that have already cleared committee review, so bundling them together does not skip any earlier steps in the process.
critics: Critics say when nominations from the Executive Calendar are grouped into a single vote, senators cannot vote against one specific nominee without voting against every nominee in the package.
Critics say combining multiple nominees into one vote makes it harder for the public to know how their senator stands on each individual person being confirmed to a government job.
Critics say even nominees who have already been listed on the Executive Calendar may raise concerns that deserve a separate vote, and en bloc consideration removes that option.

119-hconres-75.one_liner: Order the President to pull U.S. troops out of fighting against Iran
provisions: Tells the President to stop U.S. military forces from taking part in attacks on Iran by March 30, 2026.
The order does not apply if Congress votes to declare war on Iran or approves military action before that date.
U.S. forces can still defend themselves, American diplomats, military bases, or allied countries if attacked.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution would force U.S. military forces out of hostilities against Iran by March 30, 2026, unless Congress votes to authorize war — putting the decision in Congress's hands, where the Constitution places it.
Supporters say the self-defense clause still lets U.S. forces protect American troops, diplomats, and allies from attack, so the resolution does not leave the country defenseless.
Supporters say Congress has not declared war on Iran or passed an authorization for military force, making any ongoing hostilities a violation of the War Powers Resolution.
critics: Critics say the March 30, 2026 deadline could force a withdrawal before military objectives are met, limiting the President's ability to respond quickly to threats from Iran.
Critics say the resolution ties the President's hands during a fast-moving conflict, where waiting for a congressional vote could create dangerous delays in responding to Iranian action.
Critics say the self-defense exception is narrow and may not cover all the situations where U.S. forces could need to act against Iran's military or government.

119-hconres-96.one_liner: Express support for law enforcement officers and their contributions
provisions: Congress states that it supports law enforcement officers.
Congress recognizes the work that law enforcement officers do.
Congress recognizes the risks they take on the job.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution formally puts Congress on record backing law enforcement officers, which they argue gives officers public recognition for the on-the-job risks the text names.
Supporters say that Congress naming the contributions and sacrifices of officers sends a clear message of appreciation to the people who do this work every day.
critics: Critics say the resolution contains no funding, no policy changes, and no specific rules — meaning it does not change what happens to law enforcement officers or the communities they police.

Critics say that without addressing specific issues like officer training standards, oversight, or resources, a statement of support alone does not respond to the concrete concerns raised by both officers and the public.

119-hr-5625.one_liner: List states that free people charged with violent, sexual, or public disorder crimes before trial
provisions: The Department of Justice must publish a list every year of states and cities that release people before trial without requiring bail.
The list covers people charged with violent, sexual, or public disorder crimes — like murder, rape, break-ins, looting, or vandalism.
People on those charges can be released by signing a promise to appear in court, with no money paid upfront.
This bill does not change any state's bail laws — it only collects and publishes information about which states use this practice.

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires the DOJ to publish a yearly list of states and cities that release people charged with murder, rape, burglary, looting, or vandalism without paying bail, so voters can see which local governments use this practice.

Supporters say making this information public through the DOJ annual list helps the federal government track how many jurisdictions allow people charged with violent or sexual crimes to be released by signing a promise to appear in court with no money upfront.

Supporters say the list focuses on specific offense types — including violent acts, sexual crimes, and public disorder offenses like looting and vandalism — so the reporting is tied to charges the bill identifies as threats to public safety.
critics: Critics say the DOJ publication requirement singles out states and cities that choose cashless bail for violent or sexual charges, which puts pressure on local governments to change laws that were set by their own voters or legislatures.

Critics say the bill does not include data showing whether cashless bail leads to more crime. It only collects and publishes names of jurisdictions, without measuring what happens to people released on a signed promise to appear.

Critics say the bill covers a broad range of offenses — from murder to vandalism — under the same reporting rule, and does not distinguish between the seriousness of different charges when deciding which jurisdictions appear on the list.

119-hr-2853.one_liner: Crack down on organized theft rings that steal and resell goods across state lines
provisions: Lets prosecutors add up stolen goods over 12 months to reach the dollar amount needed for federal charges, instead of counting each theft separately.
Lets the government seize money and property tied to organized retail theft.
Makes organized retail theft a crime that can also be charged under federal money laundering laws.
Expands money laundering laws to cover people who use prepaid cards or gift cards to move stolen money.
Creates a center inside the Department of Homeland Security to coordinate federal agencies fighting organized retail theft rings.

supporters: Supporters say allowing prosecutors to add up stolen goods over 12 months to reach federal charging thresholds will help catch retail theft rings that spread small thefts across many stores to stay below the limit.
Supporters say connecting organized retail theft to federal money laundering laws gives prosecutors more tools to go after the full criminal network, not just the person caught at the store.
Supporters say the new DHS coordination center will help federal agencies share information and work together against retail crime rings that operate across state lines.
critics: Critics say adding organized retail theft as a money laundering predicate offense could expose low-level workers or small resellers to federal charges that were meant for serious financial crimes.
Critics say allowing 12-month aggregation of theft values to trigger federal charges could pull cases into federal court that local prosecutors and courts were already handling.
Critics say expanding money laundering laws to cover gift cards and prepaid cards could lead to federal charges against people with no connection to organized crime rings.

119-hr-2071.one_liner: Block U.S. money from going to foreign shrimp farms through international banks
provisions: Stops U.S. government money from going to international banks — like the International Monetary Fund — if those banks use the money to fund shrimp farms, shrimp processing, or shrimp exports in other countries.
Requires the Treasury Department to attach this condition every time it sends money to these international banks.

Requires a government watchdog agency to check every year whether U.S. representatives at these banks are following existing rules against funding foreign goods that compete with American farmers, and report the findings to Congress.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would stop U.S. money sent to international banks, like the International Monetary Fund, from being used to fund shrimp farms or shrimp exports in other countries, which they say competes directly with American shrimp fishers.
Supporters say the bill adds a condition — one not previously attached — requiring the Treasury Department to enforce this restriction every time it sends money to these international banks.

Supporters say the bill requires a government watchdog to check each year whether U.S. representatives at international banks are following existing rules against funding foreign goods that hurt American producers, filling a gap where no such annual check currently exists.
critics: Critics say the bill singles out one industry — shrimp — for special protection, while other American seafood producers who face the same kind of foreign competition would not be covered.
Critics say blocking international banks from funding foreign shrimp farming could reduce U.S. influence over how those banks operate, since other member countries may fill the funding gap instead.

Critics say the bill does not address the main reason foreign shrimp is cheaper — lower labor and production costs abroad — so restricting bank financing may not meaningfully help U.S. shrimp fishers.

119-hr-1346.one_liner: Let gas stations sell higher-ethanol fuel year-round in all states
provisions: Gas with 15% ethanol, called E15, can be sold during summer months — right now, most states cannot sell it in summer because it evaporates faster in heat and can worsen air quality
States that had already put rules in place to block E15 summer sales lose those rules when this bill passes, but they can apply to get new ones after that
Small oil refineries that are required to blend renewable fuel into their gas or diesel can get unused blending credits back from the EPA in some cases
The bill changes a Clean Air Act rule that set limits on how much summer gas is allowed to evaporate — those limits now apply the same way to E15 as they already do to regular E10 gas

supporters: Supporters say allowing E15 to be sold year-round gives drivers a cheaper fuel option, since E15 often costs less per gallon than regular E10 gas.
Supporters say the bill treats E15 the same as E10 under the Clean Air Act's summer evaporation rules, so there is no new special treatment — just equal standards for both fuel blends.
Supporters say small refineries will get unused blending credits returned by the EPA, which reduces costs for smaller fuel producers who struggle to meet renewable fuel volume requirements.
critics: Critics say E15 evaporates faster in summer heat than E10, and overriding state rules that were already in place could increase smog-forming pollution in areas that specifically chose to limit E15 sales.

Critics say states that had existing exclusions lose them automatically when the bill passes and must go through a new application process to get protections back, leaving a gap period with no state-level limits on E15.
Critics say expanding E15 sales year-round increases demand for corn-based ethanol, which some environmental groups argue drives up food prices and increases land and water use in farming states.

119-hres-1251.one_liner: Call on leaders to speak out against antisemitism and honor Jewish-American servicemembers
provisions: Calls on elected officials to publicly condemn antisemitism and take action against it
Calls on faith leaders and community leaders to do the same
Honors Jewish Americans who have served in the U.S. military
Commits to protecting all Americans, including Jewish Americans, from violence or persecution while worshipping

supporters: Supporters say asking elected officials to publicly condemn antisemitism gives Jewish Americans who face harassment or violence a clear signal that their government stands behind them.
Supporters say honoring Jewish Americans who served in the U.S. military recognizes a group that has contributed to national defense and deserves public recognition.
Supporters say committing to protect all Americans from violence while worshipping reinforces existing constitutional rights and puts Congress on record supporting religious safety.
critics: Critics say the resolution does not include any enforcement mechanism, funding, or legal change, so the call for officials to act has no binding effect.
Critics say a resolution that names one religious group may set a precedent for similar resolutions for other groups, raising questions about equal treatment under congressional procedure.
Critics say the language committing to protect Americans from persecution while worshipping overlaps with rights already guaranteed by the First Amendment, making the resolution largely symbolic.

119-hres-1252.one_liner: Honor law enforcement officers and express condolences to families of those killed on the job
provisions: States that Congress supports police and other law enforcement officers across the country.
States that Congress recognizes the need to give officers the equipment, training, and resources to stay safe while protecting the public.
States that Congress honors law enforcement officers for their acts of heroism and sacrifice.
States that Congress offers condolences and thanks to the families of officers who died in the line of duty.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution puts Congress on record recognizing the need to give officers the equipment, training, and resources to stay safe — which they argue sets a foundation for future funding decisions.
Supporters say the provision offering formal condolences and thanks from Congress to the families of officers who died in the line of duty gives those families official recognition they deserve.

Supporters say stating that Congress supports law enforcement officers across the country sends a clear signal to local agencies and officers that the federal government stands behind their work to keep communities safe.
critics: Critics say the resolution mentions giving officers equipment, training, and resources but includes no dollar amounts, no deadlines, and no binding requirements — meaning agencies are not required to act on anything it states.
Critics say the resolution honors officers for heroism and sacrifice but does not include any language about oversight, accountability standards, or data on how many officers die each year and why.

Critics say a resolution that only expresses support and condolences cannot require any changes to how law enforcement agencies operate, so it may have no effect on the safety conditions officers actually face.

119-hr-8365.one_liner: Add rules for court-appointed monitors who oversee local police departments
provisions: When a court orders a city or police department to make changes, it can appoint a monitor — an outside person who checks that those changes happen.
Before a monitor is picked, the public must be told and given a chance to comment.
One person can only be a monitor for one case at a time.
Monitors can only serve for up to five years.
Monitors must publicly report what they charge and what work they do.
There is a cap on how much monitors can be paid.
Monitors are allowed to do some of the work for free.

supporters: Supporters say the five-year term limit and one-case-at-a-time rule will stop monitors from holding long-term power over cities and police departments without fresh oversight.
Supporters say requiring monitors to publicly report their fees and capping how much they can be paid will stop cases where monitors have charged millions of dollars with little public review.
Supporters say allowing pro bono monitor work could lower costs to local governments that are already under court-ordered reforms.
critics: Critics say the five-year term limit could cut off oversight too soon in cases where police departments have not yet made the required changes, leaving reforms unfinished.

Critics say adding a public comment period before a monitor is picked could slow down civil settlement agreements and delay corrective action in departments with confirmed patterns of unconstitutional policing.
Critics say fee caps may make it harder to find qualified monitors willing to take on complex, multi-year oversight of large government agencies.

119-hr-8469.one_liner: Fund building projects on military bases and veterans services through September 2027
provisions: Gives money to the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force, and National Guard to build and repair military bases
Funds VA hospitals, veterans benefit payments, and military cemeteries for the year ending September 2027
Sets aside money to build and fix housing for military families who live on or near bases
Funds housing for service members who live on base without their families
Pays for the court that hears cases when veterans are denied benefits
Funds the upkeep of American war memorials and cemeteries in other countries
Sets rules for how all of these funds can and cannot be spent

supporters: Supporters say this bill funds the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force, and National Guard to build and repair military bases, keeping U.S. forces ready and housed through September 2027.

Supporters say the bill pays for VA hospitals, veterans benefit payments, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims, giving veterans access to health care and a place to appeal denied benefits.
Supporters say setting aside money for on-base family housing and unaccompanied service member housing helps military families who rely on base-provided homes and have few other options.
critics: Critics say the bill funds the NATO Security Investment Program, which sends U.S. dollars to build and upgrade military infrastructure in other countries, at a time when some lawmakers want to limit overseas spending.

Critics say the Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund, created under the 2022 PACT Act, is included in the bill. The VA has reported a fast-rising number of toxic exposure claims, raising questions about whether the fund is sized to meet demand.

Critics say the Base Closure Account receives funding under this bill, and some members argue that closing or consolidating domestic bases removes jobs and economic activity from local communities near those installations.

119-hr-6260.one_liner: Treat organizations that pay bail for defendants as insurance businesses under federal law
provisions: Groups that pay bail money for defendants must follow the same federal and state rules that apply to insurance companies.
This includes nonprofits and charities that pay bail for people who cannot afford it.
These groups must get a license from their state, just like insurance companies do.
State insurance boards can now oversee and regulate any group that pays bail.
The rule covers three types of bail: cash bail, criminal bail bonds, and immigration bail bonds.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would require nonprofits and charities that pay cash bail or criminal bail bonds to get a state insurance license, which gives state insurance boards the power to oversee how these groups operate and who they release.

Supporters say that subjecting bail funds to federal insurance fraud laws could reduce cases where defendants who may pose a public safety risk are released without oversight of the paying organization.

Supporters say the bill covers all three types of bail — cash bail, criminal bail bonds, and immigration bail bonds — closing what they call a gap in federal law that let bail funds operate outside insurance regulations.
critics: Critics say requiring nonprofits and charities that pay bail for low-income defendants to meet state insurance licensing requirements could force many of these groups to shut down, leaving poor defendants unable to afford release before trial.

Critics say applying federal insurance fraud law to organizations that pay immigration bail bonds could limit the ability of groups that help immigrants to post bond, affecting a specific category of defendants not covered by criminal bail rules.

Critics say that cash bail payments made by charitable groups do not involve the risk-pooling or premium collection that define insurance under state law, meaning the licensing requirements in this bill may not fit how these organizations actually work.

119-hres-1259.one_liner: Ask the President to push China to release five named people held in detention
provisions: Calls on the President to raise the cases of Pastor Jin Mingri, Pastor Gao Quanfu, his wife Pang Yu, Dr. Gulshan Abbas, and Jimmy Lai whenever he meets with China's leader Xi Jinping.
Asks the President to get proof that these people are alive and in good health.
Calls for these detainees to have access to lawyers of their choosing and to contact their families.
States that the U.S. stands for the right of people to practice their religion and speak freely without being jailed for it.

supporters: Supporters say raising the cases of Pastor Jin Mingri, Pastor Gao Quanfu, Pang Yu, Dr. Gulshan Abbas, and Jimmy Lai directly with Xi Jinping puts pressure on China to release people jailed for their faith or speech.
Supporters say asking for proof of life and access to independent lawyers gives families concrete information and basic legal protections for their loved ones.
Supporters say the resolution reinforces the U.S. position that jailing people for religious practice or free expression violates their basic rights.
critics: Critics say a non-binding resolution does not require the President to act, so it may not change how the U.S. handles talks with China.
Critics say singling out five individuals while thousands of others are detained in China could give the appearance that the U.S. is only willing to advocate for a small, select group.
Critics say pressing China on specific detainees during diplomatic meetings could make it harder to reach agreements on other issues like trade or security.

119-hres-1274.one_liner: Remove a rule requiring two bills to be combined in the farm bill
provisions: A rule passed on April 29, 2026 said that a bill about fuel choices at gas stations had to be added into the farm bill before it could pass.
This resolution cancels that rule, so the farm bill can move forward without the fuel bill attached to it.
The fuel choice bill — which deals with what kinds of fuel gas stations can sell — would continue on its own separate path.

supporters: Supporters say removing the April 29, 2026 rule lets the Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026 move forward on its own, without being held up by a separate bill about what fuels gas stations can sell.

Supporters say H.R. 1346, the Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act, covers fuel retail rules that are unrelated to farm programs and food policy, so combining them in one bill creates problems for both.
Supporters say the farm bill affects millions of people who rely on food programs and farm support, and it should not be delayed because of a dispute over a fuel choice bill.
critics: Critics say the House already voted on April 29, 2026 to require H.R. 1346 to be included in the farm bill, and this resolution cancels that vote without going through the same process.

Critics say removing H.R. 1346 from the farm bill makes it much harder for the Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act to pass, because it loses its place in a larger, must-pass piece of legislation.

Critics say fuel retailers and consumers who were counting on H.R. 1346 to change what fuels can be sold at gas stations now face an uncertain timeline with no guarantee the bill will come to a vote on its own.

119-hres-1275.one_liner: Set House debate rules for four bills and one resolution on bail, courts, and veterans
provisions: Lets the House vote on a bill that would make public a list of states and cities that allow cashless bail
Lets the House vote on a bill that would make it illegal to lie or cheat when paying bail to get out of jail
Lets the House vote on a bill that sets rules for when a court can appoint an outside person to watch over a government agency
Lets the House vote on a resolution that expresses support for law enforcement officers
Lets the House vote on a spending bill for military bases and the Department of Veterans Affairs for the year ending September 30, 2027

supporters: Supporters say that allowing a vote on H.R. 5625 would give the public a clear list of which states and cities allow cashless bail, making it easier to see how local bail policies differ across the country.

Supporters say that moving H.R. 6260 forward would close a gap in federal law by making it a crime to lie or cheat when paying bail, which they argue protects the justice system from being manipulated.
Supporters say that bringing H.R. 8469 to a vote ensures the House can act on military construction funding and Department of Veterans Affairs spending before the September 30, 2027 deadline.
critics: Critics say that bundling five separate and unrelated measures — including bail policy bills, a law enforcement support resolution, and a VA spending bill — into one rule prevents each from getting its own full debate.

Critics say that H.R. 8365, which sets new conditions on when courts can appoint outside monitors to watch government agencies, limits a tool judges currently use to enforce compliance with court orders.

Critics say that the cashless bail list in H.R. 5625 could be used to pressure states and cities into changing their own bail laws, even though bail policy has traditionally been decided at the state level.

119-hr-1041.one_liner: Stop the VA from reporting veterans to the gun background check system based only on having a financial manager
provisions: Right now, the VA sends names to a federal gun background check system when a veteran needs someone else to manage their benefits money.
This bill stops the VA from sending that information unless a judge has ruled that the veteran is a danger to themselves or others.
Veterans who have a money manager handling their VA benefits would no longer lose access to guns just because of that.
The change applies to both veterans and other people who get VA benefits.

supporters: Supporters say that having a money manager handle VA benefits should not automatically block a veteran from buying a gun, because needing financial help does not mean someone is dangerous.
Supporters say the bill requires a judge to find that a veteran is a danger to themselves or others before the VA can send their name to the federal gun background check system.
Supporters say the current rule removes gun rights from veterans and other VA beneficiaries without any court review, and this bill adds that legal step.
critics: Critics say that some veterans who need a fiduciary to manage their benefits may have mental health conditions that make access to firearms risky, and removing the automatic reporting could increase that risk.

Critics say the bill stops the VA from sending information to the federal gun background check system even when a veteran's need for a money manager is directly tied to a service-related mental health condition.
Critics say that waiting for a judge's order before reporting means some people in the VA fiduciary program could pass a background check and buy a gun before any court has reviewed their situation.

119-hr-1329.one_liner: Set a location and rules for a new Smithsonian museum about women's history
provisions: The museum will be built on the National Mall in Washington, DC, on a piece of land across from the National Museum of African American History and Culture.
The President has 180 days after the bill passes to pick a different location if needed.
The Smithsonian Board must get approval from federal agencies before the museum can be planned, designed, or built.
The museum will focus on the history and experiences of biological women in the United States.
The museum cannot describe or show any biological male as a female.
The advisory council must get input from people with different political viewpoints when creating exhibits and programs.

supporters: Supporters say placing the museum on the National Mall, across from the National Museum of African American History and Culture, gives women's history a permanent, high-visibility home equal to other national museums.

Supporters say requiring the advisory council to seek input from people with different political viewpoints will help the museum represent a wide range of women's lived experiences across the country.
Supporters say the rule limiting exhibits to biological women gives the museum a clear and focused mission centered on a group that has historically been underrepresented in national institutions.
critics: Critics say the provision banning the museum from describing any biological male as a female will exclude the history of transgender women and erase part of American women's history.
Critics say requiring approval from multiple federal agencies before the museum can be planned, designed, or built may slow construction and add costs without a clear benefit to the final museum.

Critics say the bill's definition of women as biological females reflects a political choice that will shape every exhibit and program the museum creates, making it harder to represent all people who identify as women.

119-sres-526.one_liner: Stop Senator pay on every day the government shuts down
provisions: Senators would not receive pay on any day the government is shut down.
Senators currently earn $174,000 a year, and this bill would pause those payments during any shutdown.
Federal workers already lose pay during shutdowns — this bill would make Senators lose pay too.

supporters: Supporters say that Senators earning $174,000 a year should not keep getting paid when the government shuts down, since federal workers already lose pay during shutdowns.
Supporters say this resolution gives Senators a personal reason to avoid shutdowns, because their own paychecks would stop on any day the government is closed.
critics: Critics say withholding Senator pay may not be legal under the 27th Amendment, which bars laws that change congressional pay from taking effect right away.
Critics say the pay pause would not affect Senators equally, since many are wealthy enough that losing $174,000 in annual salary would not pressure them to act faster.

119-hr-2616.one_liner: Require schools to get parent permission before changing a student's gender records
provisions: Public elementary and middle schools must ask parents before changing a student's name, pronouns, or gender on any school form.
Schools must ask parents before moving a student to a different locker room or bathroom based on gender.
Schools that do not get parent permission can lose certain federal education funding.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives parents the right to know before a school changes their child's name, pronouns, or gender markers on any school form.
Supporters say schools must get parent permission before moving a student to a different locker room or bathroom, keeping parents informed about their child's day-to-day school environment.
Supporters say schools that skip the parental consent step risk losing federal education funding, which supporters argue gives the rule real enforcement power.
critics: Critics say the bill requires schools to notify parents before changing a student's gender-related records or accommodations, which critics argue could put some students at risk of harm at home.

Critics say the law applies to all public elementary and middle school students, affecting children as young as kindergarten age, and removes the ability of school staff to use a student's preferred name or pronouns without first going through a formal consent process.

Critics say schools that serve low-income communities depend heavily on federal education funds, and the threat of losing that funding could pressure those schools to act against the needs of individual students.

119-hr-1993.one_liner: Create a coin marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks
provisions: The U.S. Treasury will make and sell special coins to mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks.
Each coin sold will include an extra fee on top of the purchase price.
That extra fee goes to the National September 11 Memorial and Museum in New York City to help pay for its upkeep.
If too many of these coins are made in a given year and they go over a legal limit, the extra fee is dropped from those coins.

supporters: Supporters say the bill requires a surcharge on every coin sale to be paid to the National September 11 Memorial and Museum, giving the museum a direct source of money for its operations and maintenance.
Supporters say the surcharge is built into each coin purchase, so the museum receives funding from people who choose to buy the coins without requiring new tax dollars.
Supporters say the bill creates a clear way for the public to mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks while sending money to the memorial through the surcharge on each sale.
critics: Critics say the bill removes the surcharge from coins sold above annual legal limits, meaning the museum loses the extra funding on the highest-volume sales.
Critics say because the surcharge is dropped once annual coin sales hit a legal cap, the museum cannot count on a steady or predictable amount of funding from this program.
Critics say the bill does not specify how large the surcharge on each coin will be, so the total amount the National September 11 Memorial and Museum may receive from sales is unclear.

119-hr-4544.one_liner: Make it easier to apply to start a new bank or credit union
provisions: Federal banking regulators must review how people apply to start a new bank or credit union and reduce duplicate requests for information.
If an applicant asks, regulators must assign one employee to guide them through the application process.
If an applicant asks, regulators must provide a list of similar banks or credit unions that are willing to act as mentors.
Regulators must look at the rules around how new banks raise startup money, while keeping protections for investors in place.
Each regulator must create a plan to help states and other groups understand how to apply to start a new bank or credit union.

supporters: Supporters say requiring regulators to assign a caseworker to guide applicants through the process will make it easier for community groups and local investors to start new banks or credit unions in areas that lack banking options.
Supporters say reducing duplicate information requests from different agencies will cut down the time and cost it takes to apply to open a new depository institution.
Supporters say the mentor list provision gives new applicants direct access to experienced banks and credit unions, which could help more de novo institutions successfully open.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set any deadlines for regulators to complete their review of the application process, which means agencies could delay changes indefinitely.
Critics say the caseworker and mentor provisions are optional — only triggered if an applicant asks — so applicants who do not know to request these resources may still face the same barriers.
Critics say the bill does not change the underlying capital-raising rules, only requiring a review, so new banks in low-income areas may still struggle to meet startup funding requirements.

119-hr-5317.one_liner: Change rules so some small bank deposits no longer count as brokered deposits
provisions: Right now, some deposits are labeled 'brokered,' which means banks face more government oversight for holding them.
This bill removes that label from certain deposits held at banks with less than $10 billion in total assets.
To qualify, those deposits must make up less than 20% of the bank's total money owed to others.
The bank must also be in good financial standing, or have a special exception from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC).
Banks that take in these deposits must still follow the same interest rate rules that apply to banks in weaker financial shape.

supporters: Supporters say removing the 'brokered deposit' label from custodial deposits at banks with less than $10 billion in assets would reduce government oversight requirements, lowering costs for small community banks.

Supporters say the bill's 20% liability cap and the requirement that banks be well-capitalized — or hold an FDIC waiver — limits who can benefit, keeping the change targeted to financially stable institutions.
Supporters say keeping the same interest rate rules that apply to weaker banks means community banks cannot use these deposits to offer risky rates that could threaten their stability.
critics: Critics say brokered deposits — including custodial ones — tend to leave banks quickly when the economy turns bad, and removing the oversight label could leave community banks exposed to sudden deposit outflows.

Critics say allowing custodial deposits up to 20% of a bank's total liabilities without the brokered deposit rules adds risk at small banks, which have fewer assets to absorb large, fast-moving withdrawals.
