Critics say the FDIC waiver option allows banks that do not meet the well-capitalized standard to still hold these less-regulated deposits, which could weaken the bill's financial safety guardrails.

119-hr-3234.one_liner: Let local banks hold more customer deposits through shared deposit networks
provisions: Raises the cap on how much money banks can hold through deposit-sharing networks, where banks split up large deposits to give customers more insurance coverage
Sets different caps based on the size of the bank — bigger banks can hold more, smaller banks hold less
Opens up deposit-sharing to more banks by letting banks with a health rating of 1, 2, or 3 (on a 1–5 scale, where 1 is best) qualify, instead of only the top two ratings

supporters: Supporters say raising the cap on deposit-sharing lets customers split large deposits across banks so more of their money is covered by FDIC insurance, beyond the standard $250,000 limit.
Supporters say the tiered cap system gives smaller community banks a way to keep local deposits in their communities rather than losing those accounts to bigger banks.
Supporters say expanding eligibility to banks with a CAMELS rating of 3 means more banks can offer this service, even if they are in good but not perfect financial health.
critics: Critics say allowing banks with a CAMELS rating of 3 — meaning regulators have found real problems with their cash reserves or money management — to join these networks could spread risk if those banks run into trouble.

Critics say the tiered cap system could allow larger banks to hold much more money through these networks than smaller banks, which may pull deposits away from the community banks the bill is meant to help.
Critics say loosening the rules on who can join deposit-sharing networks removes a key safeguard that was meant to keep these programs limited to the healthiest banks.

119-s-1003.one_liner: Let the government send shark attack warnings to cell phones
provisions: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is the government agency that runs emergency text alerts sent to cell phones.
Right now, the government can send emergency alerts for things like bad weather, missing children, and other dangers to people's lives.
This bill adds shark attacks to the approved list of emergencies that can trigger those alerts.

supporters: Supporters say that shark attacks put lives at risk just like the other emergencies the FCC already covers, such as severe weather and missing children, so the FCC should clearly allow these alerts.

Supporters say that right now it is unclear whether local governments can send a shark attack alert under the current rules, and this bill removes that confusion by giving the FCC a direct order to permit it.
Supporters say that beachgoers near an attack would get a cell phone warning in real time, which could stop more people from entering the water while a threat is still active.
critics: Critics say the FCC's current rules already allow alerts for any 'threat to life or property,' which means shark attacks may already be covered without a new law.
Critics say that shark attacks are rare events and that adding a specific category for them in federal law sets a precedent for writing many other narrow emergency types into FCC rules.
Critics say the bill does not include funding or a timeline for the FCC to act, so there is no guarantee the order would be issued quickly or at all.

119-s-2393.one_liner: Let the VA build a new medical facility in St. Louis, Missouri
provisions: Lets the Department of Veterans Affairs build a new medical complex at its St. Louis, Missouri location during the year starting October 2025.
The project includes a new building with patient beds, expanded clinic space, a combined office and warehouse building, a utility plant, and parking garages.
Sets a maximum dollar amount the government can spend on the project, though the exact cap is detailed in the full bill text.

supporters: Supporters say the St. Louis project will expand care by adding a new bed tower, larger clinic space, and a utility plant, giving veterans in Missouri more room to get medical treatment.

Supporters say combining the administrative offices and warehouse into one building at the St. Louis site reduces the cost of running separate facilities that currently handle those functions in different locations.

Supporters say setting a legal spending cap on the project holds the VA accountable to a fixed budget, which protects taxpayers from the kind of cost overruns that affected past VA construction projects.
critics: Critics say the bill does not publicly disclose the exact dollar cap for the St. Louis construction, making it impossible for the public to judge whether the spending limit is realistic before work begins.
Critics say funding parking garages as part of the project directs money toward infrastructure that does not directly provide medical services to veterans who need care.

Critics say authorizing construction of a new bed tower, clinical building, and utility plant without a confirmed completion date could mean veterans wait years before seeing any improvement in access to care.

119-hres-1299.one_liner: Create new federal housing programs and update housing rules
provisions: Creates new programs to help people get access to housing
Updates federal rules around how housing programs work
Changes requirements for who can qualify for housing help
Sets new rules for how housing money is spent at the federal level

supporters: Supporters say the bill creates new programs to connect more people to housing, which could help low-income households that currently have no path into federal housing assistance.
Supporters say the updated federal rules on how housing money is spent would reduce waste and make sure funds reach families more quickly.
Supporters say the changes to who can qualify for housing help would open the door to groups left out under the old requirements.
critics: Critics say the changes to who can qualify for housing help could shift limited federal dollars away from the people who need it most under the current rules.
Critics say setting new federal rules for how housing money is spent takes decision-making power away from state and local governments.
Critics say adding new programs without clear spending caps or cost estimates makes it hard to know how much this will cost taxpayers.

119-hres-1300.one_liner: Set the rules for House floor votes on three separate bills
provisions: Lets the House vote on a bill to stop the VA from sharing veteran records with the gun background check system.
Lets the House vote on a bill to raise disability pay for veterans and benefits for their surviving families.
Lets the House vote on a bill to place a Smithsonian museum about American women's history on the National Mall.
Skips a House rule that would normally delay a vote on certain resolutions from the Rules Committee.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution allows a House vote on a bill to stop the VA from sending veteran records to the Justice Department for use in gun background checks, which they say unfairly penalizes veterans who receive help managing their benefits.

Supporters say this moves forward a vote on raising disability pay and survivor benefits paid to the families of veterans who died from service injuries, giving those groups faster access to a floor vote.

Supporters say this lets the House vote on placing the Smithsonian American Women's History Museum on the National Mall, where it would sit alongside other national museums already open to the public.
critics: Critics say the bill to stop VA record sharing would remove from the background check system veterans who have been legally found unable to manage their own financial affairs, a group that could include people with serious mental health conditions.

Critics say the bill to raise veteran disability pay and survivor benefits paid to families of veterans who died from service injuries does not name a specific funding source or offset to cover the added payments, leaving the total cost unresolved before a vote.
Critics say waiving the clause 6(a) rule cuts short the review period that normally gives House members time to read Rules Committee reports before a vote is called.

119-hr-6047.one_liner: Add monthly payments and expand home loans for disabled veterans and survivors
provisions: Gives disabled veterans who already get a monthly payment for needing help with daily care an extra $833.33 per month
Raises monthly payments to surviving family members of veterans who died from a service-connected cause by an extra 1% at the next inflation increase, then 0.5% more at the one after that
Lets National Guard and reserve members qualify for VA home loans after 14 days of active duty, including annual training time
Extends current VA home loan fee rates through September 30, 2036
Raises fees for some VA loan refinancing and loan takeovers
Keeps a cap on pension payments for veterans living in hospitals or care facilities through September 30, 2036

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives disabled veterans who already receive an aid and attendance allowance an extra $833.33 per month to help cover the cost of daily care.
Supporters say National Guard and reserve members were not previously eligible for VA home loans based on annual training duty, but the bill changes that after just 14 days of active-duty service.

Supporters say surviving family members of veterans who died from service-connected causes will see their monthly DIC payments rise by an extra 1% at the next cost-of-living adjustment, and another 0.5% at the one after that.
critics: Critics say the bill keeps a cap on pension payments for veterans living in hospitals or care facilities through September 30, 2036, even as their care costs may rise.
Critics say the bill raises fees for some VA loan refinancing and loan assumptions, which could make it more expensive for veterans to refinance or transfer existing home loans.

Critics say the DIC increase adds only 1% at the first cost-of-living adjustment. The extra 0.5% at the second adjustment keeps the total raise below what critics say is needed to keep up with rising costs.

119-hr-7618.one_liner: Extend federal grants to protect U.S. battle sites through 2036
provisions: Keeps three National Park Service grant programs running through 2036, instead of ending in 2028.
These grants pay for buying, fixing, and adding information displays at U.S. battle sites.
Tells the National Park Service to study battle sites from the French and Indian War (1754–1763) for possible protection.
Tells the National Park Service to study battle sites from the Mexican-American War (1846–1848) for possible protection.

supporters: Supporters say extending the three grant programs from 2028 to 2036 gives communities eight more years of funding to buy, restore, and add information displays at battle sites before the programs would have expired.

Supporters say the bill directs the National Park Service to study French and Indian War (1754–1763) and Mexican-American War (1846–1848) sites, which are not currently covered by these grant programs.

Supporters say continuing the existing grant programs through 2036, rather than starting new ones, avoids the cost and time of building a separate funding structure for the three grant types already in place.
critics: Critics say the bill pushes the grant programs to 2036 without setting a spending limit, so there is no cap on how much federal money can go to battlefield acquisition and restoration over those eight years.

Critics say the bill does not include criteria for which French and Indian War or Mexican-American War sites the National Park Service must prioritize, which could lead to studies of sites with little public benefit.

Critics say funding battlefield preservation through 2036 means federal dollars are committed to these three grant programs for eight more years while other National Park Service needs compete for limited budgets.

119-hr-2860.one_liner: Renew a marine protection program covering Washington's Strait of Juan de Fuca and Puget Sound
provisions: Renews a program for seven years that protects marine waters, habitats, and wildlife in Washington's Strait of Juan de Fuca and Puget Sound.
Keeps a commission in place that gives resources and technical support to local groups working to protect those waters.
The commission must use science to create plans for restoring and protecting the marine environment.
The commission holds open meetings where the public can talk about policy for the marine ecosystem.

supporters: Supporters say renewing the program for seven years gives local marine resource committees steady access to technical support and resources to protect waters in Puget Sound and the Strait of Juan de Fuca.
Supporters say the commission is required to use science to build restoration and protection plans, rather than opinion or politics, which leads to more reliable decisions about the marine ecosystem.
Supporters say the open public meetings let residents, fishers, and tribal members talk directly about policy affecting the marine waters from the Canadian border to Snohomish County.
critics: Critics say the bill extends the commission for seven years without adding new tools to hold it accountable for results in restoring marine habitats or species.
Critics say the bill does not change how the commission is organized or add new ways to measure its progress, leaving the same structure in place for another full term.

Critics say local groups that depend on healthy waters, like fishing communities, may see little change since the bill does not require the commission to set specific targets for habitat or species recovery.

119-hconres-86.one_liner: Order the President to pull U.S. troops out of fighting with Iran
provisions: The President must remove U.S. military forces from any fighting against Iran unless Congress officially declares war or passes a law allowing it.
U.S. troops that are defending the U.S., an ally, or a partner from an immediate attack do not have to be pulled out right away.
If troops stay to defend against an immediate threat, the President must follow the War Powers Resolution, which gives a 60-day limit on military action without Congress approving it.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would require the President to pull U.S. troops out of fighting with Iran unless Congress votes to declare war or passes a specific law allowing military action — giving Congress its constitutional role in deciding when the country goes to war.
Supporters say the 60-day clock in the War Powers Resolution still applies, so troops used to stop an immediate attack cannot stay in combat indefinitely without Congress approving it.
Supporters say U.S. forces defending America, an ally, or a partner from an active attack are still allowed to act, so the resolution does not leave the country unable to respond to a real threat.
critics: Critics say requiring Congress to vote before the President can act against Iran could slow down the military's ability to respond quickly, since getting a declaration of war or a new law passed takes time.
Critics say the 60-day limit from the War Powers Resolution may not be enough time to finish a military operation against Iran if Congress does not move fast enough to authorize it.
Critics say the line between 'defending against an immediate attack' and other military action is unclear, which could create legal confusion about when troops must be removed.

119-hconres-84.one_liner: Order the President to pull U.S. troops out of Lebanon within seven days
provisions: Tells the President to remove all U.S. Armed Forces from Lebanon within seven days of this resolution passing.
Uses the War Powers Resolution, a 1973 law that lets Congress direct the President to end military operations.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution uses the 1973 War Powers Resolution to force the President to pull all U.S. troops out of Lebanon within seven days, giving Congress direct control over the decision.
Supporters say removing U.S. Armed Forces from Lebanon within one week stops American soldiers from being in an active conflict zone without a formal declaration of war from Congress.
critics: Critics say a seven-day deadline does not give military commanders enough time to safely move U.S. Armed Forces out of Lebanon without putting those troops at risk.

Critics say using the War Powers Resolution to force a full withdrawal blocks the President from responding to fast-changing security conditions in Lebanon that could affect U.S. interests in the region.

119-hres-518.one_liner: Set the rules for how the House debates and votes on Ukraine aid
provisions: This resolution sets the time limits and debate rules the House must follow when voting on H.R. 2913, the Ukraine Support Act.
It controls which changes to the bill members of Congress can propose during the debate.
After the House passes H.R. 2913, the Clerk of the House must send the bill to the Senate within one week.
This resolution only controls the debate process — it does not change U.S. policy toward Ukraine on its own.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution sets clear debate time limits and controls which amendments members can propose, giving the House a structured process for voting on H.R. 2913, the Ukraine Support Act.
Supporters say the one-week deadline for the Clerk of the House to send H.R. 2913 to the Senate keeps the bill moving without delays.
critics: Critics say limiting which amendments members can propose during debate blocks lawmakers from changing parts of H.R. 2913 they disagree with.
Critics say requiring the Clerk to transmit H.R. 2913 to the Senate within one week moves the bill forward before members have fully debated U.S. support for Ukraine.

119-hr-7726.one_liner: Require the federal government to cut funding to states that misuse child care money
provisions: Right now, the federal government can cut funding to states that misuse child care money — but it does not have to.
This bill changes that: if a state is found to have broken the rules of the Child Care and Development Block Grant program, the federal government must take action.
The strongest punishment is cutting off the state from receiving any more money from the program.
The program gives money to states to help low-income working families pay for child care.

supporters: Supporters say the bill changes the law so that the federal government is required by law to cut off Child Care and Development Block Grant funding to states that break program rules, instead of leaving that decision optional.
Supporters say the current optional enforcement has allowed states that misuse money meant for low-income working families to keep receiving grant funds without facing consequences required by law.
Supporters say requiring the Office of the Administration for Children and Families to act removes the possibility of choosing not to act when a state is found to be out of compliance.
critics: Critics say the bill could cut off child care funding to an entire state based on a finding of noncompliance, which would reduce access to subsidized child care for low-income working families who did not cause the violation.
Critics say the law does not define what counts as 'failing to comply substantially,' which means states may not know exactly what behavior triggers the mandatory funding cutoff.
Critics say removing the federal government's ability to choose a smaller penalty forces a one-size-fits-all response that does not account for the size or cause of a state's violation.

119-hres-1336.one_liner: Let the House vote on a budget bill the same day it is proposed
provisions: Normally, the House must wait one day before voting on a rules proposal, unless two-thirds of members agree to skip the wait.
This resolution removes that two-thirds vote requirement for one specific budget bill.
The House can now vote on the budget rules the same day they are introduced, through June 5, 2026.

supporters: Supporters say removing the two-thirds vote requirement lets the House vote on budget rules the same day they are introduced, which speeds up work on the budget bill tied to S.Con.Res.33.
Supporters say the normal one-day waiting period would slow down the process, and this resolution lets the Committee on Rules move the budget bill forward without delay through June 5, 2026.
Supporters say the two-thirds vote threshold is a high bar that can block action even when a majority agrees, and this resolution lets a simple majority move forward on the budget rules.
critics: Critics say waiving the one-day waiting period removes time for members to read and understand the rules before voting on a major budget bill.
Critics say the two-thirds vote requirement exists to make sure broad agreement exists before fast-tracking a rules change, and skipping it on a budget bill bypasses that protection.
Critics say allowing same-day votes on budget rules through June 5, 2026 means members could be forced to vote on rules for a major budget bill with little notice or debate.

119-s-2.one_liner: Fund border patrol and immigration enforcement agencies through 2029
provisions: Gives money to Customs and Border Protection for more staff, border technology, and enforcement activities.
Gives money to Immigration and Customs Enforcement for more staff, investigations, transportation, computers, and buildings.
Pays for ICE to make arrests related to immigration enforcement.
Lets state and local police departments work with ICE on immigration enforcement.
Gives extra money to the Department of Homeland Security to work with state and local agencies on enforcement.
All of this funding stays available through the end of 2029.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives Customs and Border Protection money for new staff and screening technology, which they say will help stop illegal crossings at the border.
Supporters say funding 287(g) agreements lets state and local police help ICE enforce immigration law, adding more officers to enforcement efforts without hiring all federal agents.
Supporters say locking in funding through FY2029 gives ICE and CBP a stable budget to plan operations, hire staff, and maintain facilities without waiting for yearly budget fights.
critics: Critics say the bill is passed through reconciliation, a process that bypasses the normal Senate debate rules, and that it adds to the federal deficit rather than being paid for with cuts elsewhere.

Critics say expanding 287(g) agreements means local police departments—who are funded by cities and counties—will take on immigration enforcement tasks, which critics argue pulls them away from local crime and public safety work.

Critics say paying for ICE arrests and detention transportation through FY2029 will lead to a large rise in the number of people detained, including immigrants with no criminal record, raising concerns about due process.

119-hres-1333.one_liner: Allow House votes on agriculture funding, child care grants, FAFSA fraud checks, and welfare rules
provisions: Allows the House to debate and vote on four separate bills at once
One bill funds the U.S. Department of Agriculture, rural programs, and the FDA through September 2027
One bill would cut child care grant money to states that don't follow federal rules
One bill would require a fraud check on every student financial aid (FAFSA) application to spot identity theft
One bill changes how welfare cash assistance (TANF) works — directing money to low-income families and adding steps to track and reduce incorrect payments

supporters: Supporters say the rule allows the House to debate and vote on four bills at once, including one that funds the U.S. Department of Agriculture, rural programs, and the FDA through September 2027, keeping those agencies operating.

Supporters say the FAFSA fraud check provision would require the Secretary of Education to screen every student aid application for identity theft, protecting students from having their financial aid stolen.
Supporters say the TANF changes would direct cash assistance funds specifically to low-income families and require states to track and report incorrect payments, reducing waste in the program.
critics: Critics say bundling four separate bills into one debate limits how much time members have to examine each bill, including the TANF changes that affect cash assistance rules for low-income families.

Critics say the child care grant bill would cut federal funding to states that don't meet federal rules, which could reduce the number of child care slots available to low-income families in those states.
Critics say the new TANF program integrity steps and fraud-reduction goals could create barriers that delay or deny benefits to eligible low-income families who already qualify under current rules.

119-s-254.one_liner: Let Alaska Natives sell, trade, and own ivory and bone products in any state
provisions: States cannot ban Alaska Natives from importing, selling, trading, giving, or owning ivory, bone, or baleen from marine animals.
Baleen is the stiff material inside a whale's mouth, often used in traditional crafts.
These products must be legally made by Alaska Natives as part of their traditional crafts or clothing.
This applies in all 50 states — no state can pass its own law to stop these sales.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects Alaska Natives' legal right to sell ivory, bone, and baleen items they make as part of their traditional crafts and clothing, which are already allowed under federal law.
Supporters say that without this bill, state-level bans could block Alaska Natives from selling their traditional items in other states, cutting off income tied to their cultural practices.
Supporters say the bill sets a clear rule across all 50 states so Alaska Native artisans do not face different restrictions depending on where they try to sell their work.
critics: Critics say allowing ivory, bone, and baleen products to move freely across all 50 states could make it harder for states to enforce their own wildlife protection laws, even for products that may be hard to tell apart from illegal ivory.
Critics say removing each state's ability to set its own rules on marine mammal products limits state authority to protect local wildlife markets from fraud or misuse of the Alaska Native exemption.

Critics say the bill does not include a clear way to verify that every product sold is a genuine Alaska Native handicraft, which could open the door to non-Native sellers using the exemption as cover.

117-hr-7946.one_liner: Give non-citizen veterans a path to stay in the US legally
provisions: Lets the Department of Homeland Security give non-citizen veterans who served in the US military the right to stay in the country as permanent residents
Stops the government from deporting a non-citizen veteran while their application to stay is still being decided
Requires the government to check whether someone is a veteran before starting the process to remove them from the country
Extends the time non-citizen veterans have to apply for US citizenship after serving in the military
Creates a new committee to advise the government on cases where a service member, veteran, or their close family member faces deportation
Requires the military and immigration agencies to work together to help active-duty recruits and veterans apply for US citizenship

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives non-citizen veterans who served in the U.S. military an opportunity to apply for permanent resident status before any removal decision is made.
Supporters say the bill stops the government from deporting a veteran while their application is still being decided, so no one who served is removed before their case is reviewed.

Supporters say requiring the military and immigration agencies to work together — and training Judge Advocate General Corps members as liaisons — helps active-duty recruits and veterans actually complete citizenship applications.
critics: Critics say the bill lets DHS waive many of the reasons a person can be denied entry or residency, which could allow veterans with serious criminal records to remain in the country.

Critics say creating a new Military Family Immigration Advisory Committee and requiring DHS to check veteran status before every removal case adds steps to the process and costs that have not yet been estimated or approved by Congress.

117-hr-5796.one_liner: Run a contest every two years to reward patents that solve humanitarian problems
provisions: The U.S. Patent and Trademark Office must hold a competition at least once every two years.
People and organizations can enter by submitting a patent application that addresses a humanitarian issue.
Winners get a certificate they can use to speed up other patent applications or reviews at the Patent Office.
This program replaces an older version of the same competition that was not written into law.

supporters: Supporters say making the Patents for Humanity program permanent law means the Patent Office must hold the competition at least once every two years, so it cannot be quietly dropped like the older version that had no legal backing.

Supporters say inventors working on humanitarian problems — like medicines for poor countries or tools for disaster relief — can use the winner's certificate to speed up their other patent applications, which gives them a real financial reason to focus on humanitarian work.
Supporters say writing the program into law gives companies and nonprofits more confidence to invest time in humanitarian patent work, since the competition is now guaranteed to continue.
critics: Critics say the certificate prize only speeds up Patent Office reviews, so it mostly helps large organizations that already file many patents and can benefit from faster processing — smaller inventors or nonprofits with only one patent get little value.
Critics say the bill does not set standards for what counts as a 'humanitarian issue,' which means the Patent Office has wide power to decide winners without clear rules that applicants can count on.
Critics say holding the competition only once every two years means long gaps between chances to win, which limits how many inventors the program can actually reach.

117-hr-7939.one_liner: Keep GI Bill and education benefits flowing to veterans during emergencies
provisions: Veterans can keep getting their monthly housing money even if their school switches to online classes during an emergency.
If a veteran has to drop a class because of an emergency, that class does not count against the total education time they are allowed to use.
Veterans get more time to use their GI Bill benefits if their school closes because of an emergency.
Veterans in job training programs can still get paid during emergency periods.
These rules, which were first used during COVID-19, now apply to any future emergency the President declares.

supporters: Supporters say veterans should keep receiving their monthly housing stipends when a school switches to online classes during an emergency, because the school made the decision to switch, not the veteran.
Supporters say if a school closes during an emergency and a veteran cannot finish a course, that course should not count against the total GI Bill time the veteran is allowed to use.

Supporters say making these COVID-19 protections permanent means veterans in any future presidential emergency will automatically keep their housing payments, work-study allowances, and GI Bill time extensions without waiting for Congress to pass new rules.
critics: Critics say paying full monthly housing stipends for distance learning during emergencies adds unplanned costs to the VA budget, since those stipends were originally set based on the cost of living near a physical campus.

Critics say linking these benefit expansions to any emergency the President declares, rather than a specific situation like COVID-19, gives the executive branch broad authority to trigger increased VA spending without additional congressional approval.

Critics say allowing veterans to extend GI Bill time limits every time a school closes during a declared emergency could push program costs beyond what Congress originally budgeted for those benefits.

117-hr-7535.one_liner: Prepare government computer systems to resist attacks from future quantum computers
provisions: Tells federal agencies to start moving their computer systems to stronger encryption after a government standards group publishes new security rules
The new encryption is designed to hold up against quantum computers, which can break the codes that protect most government data today
Within one year of this bill passing, a government budget office must send Congress a plan for protecting agency computers from quantum computer attacks
That same plan must include how much money it would take to make federal computer systems secure
The plan must also describe how the U.S. is working with international groups to set shared security standards

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects federal computer systems by requiring agencies to switch to stronger encryption after NIST publishes new post-quantum security standards, making it harder for future quantum computers to break into government data.

Supporters say the required report, due within one year of the bill passing, will give Congress a clear funding plan and show what it will cost to secure federal systems before quantum computers become a real threat.

Supporters say requiring the report to cover U.S. coordination with international standards groups helps make sure American security rules line up with global standards, reducing gaps that foreign actors could exploit.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for agencies to finish switching to post-quantum encryption — it only requires them to start prioritizing the move after NIST publishes standards, which could lead to slow or uneven progress.
Critics say the bill does not include any funding, meaning agencies must wait for a separate budget process to pay for the upgrades, which could delay protection of federal systems for years.

Critics say the one-year reporting requirement depends on NIST finishing its standards first, so if those standards are delayed, the whole timeline for protecting agency systems gets pushed back with no backup plan in the bill.

117-hr-1948.one_liner: Give VA healthcare workers the right to negotiate pay and performance rules
provisions: Right now, VA healthcare workers cannot use union bargaining to challenge decisions about their pay, their professional conduct reviews, or peer review processes.
This bill removes those limits, letting VA healthcare workers negotiate on those topics the same way other federal workers can.
This affects workers at the Veterans Health Administration, which employs around 400,000 people.

supporters: Supporters say removing the bargaining limits lets the roughly 400,000 VHA workers negotiate pay and conduct reviews the same way other federal employees already can.
Supporters say peer review and pay decisions affect worker rights, and blocking unions from those topics treats VHA employees as second-class federal workers.
Supporters say giving workers a voice in conduct and compensation decisions could help the VA keep experienced healthcare staff.
critics: Critics say allowing union bargaining over peer review processes could make it harder for the VA to remove healthcare workers who provide poor care to veterans.
Critics say letting unions negotiate professional conduct standards may slow down disciplinary action, since those cases would now go through a bargaining process.
Critics say expanding collective bargaining rights for 400,000 VHA employees could increase administrative costs and delay decisions that affect veteran care.

117-hres-1512.one_liner: Pass the 2023 defense bill with changes added by the House
provisions: The House voted to accept the Senate's version of the 2023 defense bill, then added its own changes to it
The bill is named after James M. Inhofe, a former U.S. Senator from Oklahoma
The final version must be agreed on by both the House and Senate before it goes to the President

supporters: Supporters say this resolution keeps moving the FY2023 defense bill forward, which authorizes about $858 billion for the military, including a 4.6% pay raise for service members.
Supporters say the process of the House adding its own changes before both chambers agree ensures that lawmakers from both sides have a voice in final defense policy.
Supporters say completing this step is needed to lock in funding for military programs and Pentagon operations before the fiscal year deadline passes.
critics: Critics say allowing the House to add its own changes to the Senate-passed bill reopens debates that had already been settled, which could delay final passage of the $858 billion defense budget.
Critics say the back-and-forth between chambers created by this process leaves defense contractors and military families waiting longer for certainty on funding decisions.
Critics say the House amendment process gives leadership too much control over which changes get added, limiting rank-and-file members' ability to shape the final bill.

117-hres-1508.one_liner: Set the rules for debating two immigration bills in the House
provisions: This bill sets the time and rules for how the House of Representatives debates two other bills
One of those bills would remove the limit on how many work-visa green cards can go to people from any one country
The other bill would give benefits to non-citizens who serve in the U.S. military

supporters: Supporters say H.R. 3648 would remove the per-country cap on employment-based green cards, which would help skilled workers from high-population countries like India who currently wait decades in the backlog.
Supporters say H.R. 7946 would give military benefits to noncitizen service members who risk their lives for the U.S. but are currently denied access to those benefits.
Supporters say bringing both bills to the House floor for a vote gives all members a chance to debate and decide on two immigration changes that affect hundreds of thousands of people.
critics: Critics say removing the per-country limit on employment-based green cards in H.R. 3648 would allow workers from a small number of large countries to take up most of the available spots, leaving workers from smaller countries with fewer chances.
Critics say H.R. 7946 raises questions about whether noncitizens should receive the same military benefits as U.S. citizens, including access to federal programs tied to citizenship status.
Critics say combining these two separate immigration bills into one rule forces members to vote on unrelated changes at the same time, limiting their ability to address each bill on its own merits.

117-hres-1510.one_liner: Set House rules for a vote on a bill about federal marriage law
provisions: Lets the House vote on a Senate amendment to a House bill about marriage law.
That bill would repeal the Defense of Marriage Act, a 1996 law that defined marriage as only between a man and a woman for federal purposes.
This rule governs only House action and does not require a separate Senate vote or Presidential approval.

supporters: Supporters say this rule allows the full House to vote on a bill that would repeal the 1996 Defense of Marriage Act, which currently blocks the federal government from recognizing same-sex marriages for benefits like Social Security and tax filing.

Supporters say the House passing this rule moves the bill one step closer to removing a federal law that treats same-sex married couples differently from opposite-sex married couples across more than 1,000 federal programs.
Supporters say the rule keeps the process moving by allowing a direct vote on the Senate amendment without requiring a separate Senate vote or new presidential action.
critics: Critics say the 1996 Defense of Marriage Act was written to protect each state's right to set its own marriage rules, and allowing a vote to repeal it would reduce that state authority.

Critics say the underlying bill the House would vote on goes further than the 1996 law by requiring all states to recognize same-sex marriages performed in other states, which critics say removes state control over marriage definitions.

Critics say moving this rule forward forces a House floor vote on a bill that changes how the federal government defines marriage without giving members enough time to review the full text of the Senate amendment.

117-hr-9640.one_liner: Require the IRS to audit and publish the tax returns of sitting presidents
provisions: The IRS must audit the tax return of every president while they are in office.
The IRS must post reports about each audit online so the public can read them.
The final report must include when the audit ended, what was reviewed, and any changes proposed to the return.
The rule covers the president's personal tax returns, their spouse's returns, and returns for any businesses they control.
Normally, tax returns are private — this bill makes an exception for presidents and their spouses.

supporters: Supporters say requiring the IRS to audit every president's tax return while in office closes a gap in the law — before this bill, no rule forced the IRS to review a sitting president's finances.
Supporters say posting audit reports online, including any proposed changes to the return, lets the public see whether a president is paying the right amount in taxes.
Supporters say covering the president's spouse and any businesses they control stops a president from hiding income by moving it into a company or a family member's return.
critics: Critics say making a president's tax return public breaks the same privacy rule that protects every other taxpayer, setting a different legal standard for one person based on the office they hold.

Critics say publishing detailed audit reports — including a list of audit materials and every proposed adjustment — could expose personal financial details that go beyond what voters need to judge a president's fitness for office.

Critics say the bill does not set a limit on how long the IRS must keep auditing or how many periodic reports it must release, which could keep a president's finances under review without a clear end date.

117-hr-8393.one_liner: Let Puerto Rico vote on statehood, independence, or becoming a self-governing nation with U.S. ties
provisions: Puerto Rico — home to about 3.2 million people — would hold a vote on November 5, 2023, to decide its political future.
Voters would choose one of three options: becoming a U.S. state, becoming a fully independent country, or becoming a self-governing nation that keeps formal ties to the U.S.
The Puerto Rico State Elections Commission would run a nonpartisan information campaign before the vote, with printed materials available at every polling location.
All ballots and voter information would be printed in both English and Spanish.
Each of the three options has its own set of steps the U.S. and Puerto Rico would follow after the vote to carry out the result.

supporters: Supporters say the vote would give all 3.2 million Puerto Ricans a direct say in their political future for the first time, choosing between statehood, independence, or free association.

Supporters say having the Elections Commission run a nonpartisan education campaign — with bilingual materials in English and Spanish at every polling location — ensures voters understand what each of the three options actually means before they decide.

Supporters say each option comes with a clear set of transition steps, so the result of the vote would not be left open-ended but would trigger a defined process to carry out whatever Puerto Ricans choose.
critics: Critics say the three options on the ballot — statehood, independence, and free association — do not include the current territorial status, which means some voters may feel their preference is not represented.

Critics say the bill does not guarantee that Congress will act on the result, meaning Puerto Ricans could vote for statehood or independence and still see no change if lawmakers in Washington choose not to follow through.

Critics say the transition steps outlined for each option are not fully detailed in the bill, leaving key questions about taxes, citizenship rights, and federal benefits unanswered before voters are asked to make a permanent choice.

117-s-1402.one_liner: Review how federal agencies support Native American languages
provisions: The President must check whether federal agencies are following rules that say they should support Native American languages.
The President must suggest ways for agencies to work together better on this.
A federal office called the Administration for Native Americans must survey how Native American languages are being used across the country.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would help Native American tribes by requiring the President to check if federal agencies are following existing laws that say they must support Native American languages.

Supporters say requiring the Administration for Native Americans to survey language use across the country would give tribes real data on how many people still speak their languages, which could help them get more resources.
Supporters say making agencies work together better on language support could reduce gaps where tribes fall through the cracks between different federal offices.
critics: Critics say the bill only asks for a review and a survey but does not require agencies to actually change how they operate or spend money, so it may not lead to real action.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for the President to make recommendations, which could allow the review to be delayed or never completed.
Critics say a survey of language use by the Administration for Native Americans has limits because it cannot force tribes to participate, which could leave out important communities.

117-hres-1519.one_liner: Set the rules for how the House will debate the Puerto Rico status vote bill
provisions: Lets the House debate H.R. 8393, a bill about Puerto Rico's political status, under a specific set of floor rules
Sets a time limit on how long members of Congress can speak about the bill before a vote
Controls which changes to the bill can be proposed during the debate

supporters: Supporters say this rule brings H.R. 8393 to the House floor for a vote, giving Puerto Rico's 3.2 million residents a formal path to choose a permanent political status for the first time.

Supporters say the set debate time limit keeps the process moving so Congress can finally vote on whether Puerto Rico becomes a state, gains independence, or enters free association with the United States.
Supporters say controlling which amendments can be offered prevents changes that could delay or block the vote on Puerto Rico's status options.
critics: Critics say the rule limits how long members can speak, which does not give Congress enough time to examine how each status option in H.R. 8393 would change federal benefits and tax rules for Puerto Ricans.
Critics say blocking most amendments shuts out members who want to change parts of the transition process laid out in H.R. 8393 before the bill goes to a final vote.
Critics say a closed or restricted rule on a bill affecting 3.2 million people means major concerns about the status options cannot be addressed on the House floor.

117-hres-1518.one_liner: Set the rules for Congress to debate and vote on five separate bills
provisions: This bill sets the rules for how and when Congress can debate and vote on five other bills.
One bill changes the rules for union bargaining for workers at Veterans Health Administration hospitals.
One bill blocks companies with conflicts of interest from getting federal government contracts.
One bill requires law enforcement to train officers on avoiding force, de-escalating situations, and handling mental health, behavioral health, and suicide crises.
One bill requires a federal weather agency to give the public updated rain and snow data.
One bill changes how the government describes its progress toward meeting its own goals.

supporters: Supporters say this rule brings five stalled bills to the House floor for a vote, including one that requires law enforcement agencies to train officers on de-escalation and handling mental health and suicide crises.

Supporters say packaging these bills together — covering VHA union bargaining, federal contract conflicts of interest, police training, weather data, and government goal-setting — speeds up action that would take longer if each bill moved separately.
Supporters say the rule gives Congress a clear path to vote on blocking companies with conflicts of interest from winning federal government contracts.
critics: Critics say bundling five unrelated bills — ranging from rain and snow data updates to Veterans Health Administration union rules — into one rule limits the time members can debate each issue on its own.
Critics say the rule may block members from offering amendments to the bill that changes collective bargaining rights for workers at Veterans Health Administration hospitals.
Critics say combining bills on police training requirements, federal acquisition rules, and weather agency duties makes it harder for members to vote against one bill without affecting the others.

117-hres-1529.one_liner: Set House floor rules for voting on two separate bills
provisions: Sets the rules for how the House will debate and vote on a bill that would let Congress see and release the President's tax returns
Sets the rules for how the House will debate and vote on a bill that would create one standard process for naming National Heritage Areas across the country
Controls how much time each side gets to speak and what changes can be proposed during each debate

supporters: Supporters say this rule brings H.R. 9640 to a full House vote, a bill that would give Congress the power to examine and publicly release the President's income tax returns under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986.

Supporters say the rule also advances S. 1942, which would create one uniform process for naming National Heritage Areas across the country, replacing the current mix of different rules used for each designation.
Supporters say the rule sets structured debate time for both sides on each bill, ensuring members get equal time to speak before any vote is held.
critics: Critics say this rule restricts which changes members can propose to H.R. 9640, limiting the ability to narrow or add conditions to the presidential tax return disclosure requirements before a final vote.

Critics say combining a bill about presidential tax returns with a bill about National Heritage Areas into one rule forces members to advance both at once, even if they support only one of the two underlying bills.

Critics say the rule's limits on debate time for S. 1942 reduce the time local communities and affected groups have had their concerns heard before the House votes on a new national standard for Heritage Area designations.

117-hres-1531.one_liner: Set the rules for voting on three separate bills in one combined session
provisions: Updates how the government measures whether its programs are meeting their goals.
Covers State Department spending and foreign aid for the year ending September 2022.
Bans the sale of fake ride-hailing vehicle signs and orders a study on driver and passenger assaults.
Sets a single debate and voting process for all three bills to be handled together.

supporters: Supporters say handling H.R. 2617, H.R. 4373, and H.R. 1082 under one debate and voting process moves all three bills forward faster instead of scheduling separate floor time for each.
Supporters say the ban on fake ride-hailing signs in H.R. 1082 gives police a clear rule to enforce against sellers of unauthorized vehicle signage, which has been used to trick passengers.
Supporters say the required study on fatal and non-fatal assaults in ride-hailing and for-hire vehicles will give Congress data on a safety gap that currently has no national tracking.
critics: Critics say bundling State Department foreign aid spending for fiscal year 2022 with unrelated ride-hailing safety rules limits members to a single up-or-down vote, preventing them from rejecting one bill without blocking the others.

Critics say H.R. 4373 covers State Department and foreign operations spending for a fiscal year that has already ended, raising questions about why funds are being approved after the spending period closed.
Critics say H.R. 1082 does not set a deadline or specify a funding amount for the assault study, meaning no report is guaranteed to be completed.

117-s-2796.one_liner: Expand how rural areas can use federal drug abuse grants
provisions: Lets rural communities use Department of Justice grant money for programs that offer alternatives to jail for people with opioid addiction
Lets those grant programs include efforts to reduce opioid overdose deaths in rural areas
Requires that at least 10% of grant money from this program goes to rural areas

supporters: Supporters say the 10% minimum requirement ensures rural areas — which have higher opioid overdose death rates than cities — get a guaranteed share of Department of Justice grant money instead of competing against larger programs.
Supporters say allowing grants to fund alternatives to jail for people with opioid addiction could reduce overdose deaths in rural communities, where treatment options are limited.
Supporters say community response programs funded by these grants give rural areas tools to treat addiction as a health problem rather than a crime.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a dollar amount for how much grant money rural areas must receive, only a 10% floor, which may not be enough to fund programs across many rural communities.
Critics say pilot programs for alternatives to incarceration could reduce consequences for drug offenses in rural areas where residents may prefer law enforcement responses.
Critics say the bill expands the uses of existing Department of Justice grants without adding new funding, meaning other communities could receive less money to make room for the 10% rural set-aside.

117-s-1466.one_liner: Create a federal program to study and protect salt lakes in the Great Basin
provisions: The U.S. Geological Survey, a federal science agency, must create a program to study salt lakes in Nevada, Utah, Oregon, California, Idaho, and nearby Great Basin states.
The program must track the health of those salt lakes over time.
The program must track the birds, fish, and other wildlife that live in and around those lakes.
The program must also work to protect those lake ecosystems and the wildlife that depend on them.

supporters: Supporters say the USGS program would track the health of salt lakes in Nevada, Utah, Oregon, California, and Idaho over time, giving scientists long-term data that does not currently exist for these lakes.
Supporters say monitoring the birds, fish, and other wildlife that depend on Great Basin salt lakes would help agencies detect population drops early, before species face larger threats.
Supporters say making the USGS responsible for both studying and protecting these lake ecosystems puts science and conservation in the same program, so data can lead directly to action.
critics: Critics say the bill gives the USGS broad authority to 'conserve' salt lake ecosystems across six or more states but does not set a budget, a spending cap, or a clear end date for the program.
Critics say adding a new federal monitoring and conservation program in states like Nevada and Utah could duplicate work that those state water and wildlife agencies already do.
Critics say the bill does not define what 'conservation' actions USGS is allowed to take, leaving open how much federal control the program could have over land and water use around these lakes.

117-s-2333.one_liner: Require equal pay and benefits for all Team USA athletes regardless of gender
provisions: Requires that male and female athletes representing the U.S. in international amateur competitions get the same pay and benefits.
Each sport's national governing body must report to the government every year on whether they are following this rule.
Full compliance with the equal pay rule was required by January 31, 2022.

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes a pay gap where female U.S. Olympic athletes have historically earned less than male athletes for the same international competitions.
Supporters say the yearly reporting rule holds each sport's national governing body accountable, making it harder to ignore unequal pay without consequence.
Supporters say the January 31, 2022 deadline means governing bodies cannot delay — they must act quickly to equalize pay and benefits across all amateur sports.
critics: Critics say the bill does not define what counts as equal 'benefits,' which could make it hard for governing bodies to know if they are actually in compliance.
Critics say smaller national governing bodies with limited budgets may struggle to raise pay for female athletes to match male athletes by the January 31, 2022 deadline.
Critics say the bill covers amateur athletes in international competition but does not address pay gaps in domestic or professional sports, leaving most athletes unaffected.

117-s-1942.one_liner: Create rules for how Congress sets up National Heritage Areas
provisions: Congress, not a federal agency, must be the one to officially create any new National Heritage Area.
The Department of the Interior can give money and advice to local groups that manage Heritage Areas.
All existing Heritage Areas, Heritage Corridors, and Heritage Partnerships become part of one official system.
The Department of the Interior must review and approve the management plan for each Heritage Area.
Before a new Heritage Area is created, a study must check whether the land has natural, historic, or cultural features that represent something important about American history.
The Department of the Interior must send reports to Congress on what is happening in each Heritage Area.

supporters: Supporters say requiring Congress, not a federal agency, to officially create any new National Heritage Area gives elected representatives more control over which places get federal recognition and money.

Supporters say bringing all existing Heritage Areas, Corridors, and Partnerships into one official system will help the Department of the Interior send resources and advice to local groups more consistently.

Supporters say requiring a study to check that land has real natural, historic, or cultural features before a Heritage Area is created will stop places from getting the designation without meeting a clear standard.
critics: Critics say requiring the Department of the Interior to review and approve management plans for every Heritage Area adds a new layer of federal oversight that could slow down decisions made by local communities.

Critics say the bill does not set a specific funding limit for the financial assistance the Department of the Interior can give to local coordinating entities, making it hard to predict the total cost to taxpayers.

Critics say requiring the Department of the Interior to send reports to Congress on each Heritage Area's activities creates more paperwork for both federal staff and the local groups that manage these areas.

117-s-1617.one_liner: Let the SBA declare disasters in rural areas to provide disaster loans
provisions: Lets the SBA declare a disaster in a rural area and offer disaster loans to people and businesses there.
Rural areas are places with fewer than 200,000 people, outside a large city or its surrounding suburbs.
The rural area must already be under a Presidential disaster declaration before the SBA can step in.
The state where the rural area is located must ask the SBA to make the declaration.
To qualify, a home, small business, nonprofit, or small farm must have major uninsured damage.
The damage must equal at least 40% of what the property was worth before the disaster.
A government watchdog must report on challenges rural communities face when getting disaster help, and suggest improvements.

supporters: Supporters say the bill fills a gap by letting the SBA declare its own disaster in rural areas — places with fewer than 200,000 people — so homes, small businesses, nonprofits, and small farms with at least 40% uninsured damage can access low-interest disaster loans.
Supporters say requiring a state request before the SBA acts keeps local governments in control, so federal help only comes where state leaders say it is needed.
Supporters say the required government watchdog report will find specific barriers rural communities face in getting disaster aid and push Congress to fix them with real policy changes.
critics: Critics say the bill requires a Presidential disaster declaration before the SBA can step in, which means rural areas hit by smaller disasters that do not reach that threshold still get no help.

Critics say the 40% damage threshold — based on pre-disaster property value — may be too high for low-income rural property owners whose homes were worth little to begin with, leaving them unable to qualify.
Critics say the bill creates a study but does not guarantee any new funding or faster loan processing, so rural communities may wait years before seeing real improvements to disaster access.

117-s-2834.one_liner: Create a public list of top brain and spinal cord injury rehab centers
provisions: Requires Medicare's parent agency to publish a list of rehab centers that specialize in brain and spinal cord injuries
The list must be updated every two years
To be included, a center must hold a federal research or training designation for brain or spinal cord injury work and treat a set minimum number of Medicare patients

supporters: Supporters say publishing a list of federally designated brain and spinal cord injury rehab centers will help Medicare patients find specialized care that is harder to locate without a central resource.
Supporters say requiring the list to be updated every two years means patients and doctors will have current information about which centers hold active federal research or training designations.
Supporters say tying inclusion to a minimum number of Medicare patients treated ensures the list only features centers with real experience serving the Medicare population.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a specific minimum number of Medicare patients a center must treat, leaving that threshold undefined and potentially excluding or including centers inconsistently.
Critics say updating the list only every two years may leave patients with outdated information if a center loses its federal designation between update cycles.

Critics say the bill focuses only on centers with federal research or training designations, which could leave off other qualified rehab facilities that treat brain and spinal cord injuries but do not hold those specific federal labels.

117-s-3168.one_liner: Extend the deadline for the government to confirm a tribal water rights deal
provisions: Moves the deadline for the Department of the Interior to publish a required confirmation from 2023 to April 30, 2025.
If Interior does not publish that confirmation by April 30, 2025, the water rights settlement agreement ends on May 1, 2025.
The confirmation must show that certain conditions have been met, including that the government has signed contracts for water rights with the White Mountain Apache Tribe.

supporters: Supporters say moving the deadline to April 30, 2025 keeps the White Mountain Apache Tribe's water rights settlement alive, since the Department of Interior did not publish its required confirmation by the original 2023 deadline.

Supporters say the extension gives Interior time to finish signing water rights contracts with the White Mountain Apache Tribe, which is one of the specific conditions that must be met before the settlement can take effect.
Supporters say without this change, the 2010 settlement agreement would have already ended, leaving the Tribe without the water rights that were negotiated over many years.
critics: Critics say the Department of Interior already missed the 2023 deadline, and pushing the date to April 30, 2025 delays confirmed water access for the White Mountain Apache Tribe by at least two more years.

Critics say the bill creates a hard cut-off: if Interior does not publish its findings by April 30, 2025, the entire settlement ends on May 1, 2025, with no replacement plan for the Tribe's water rights.

Critics say the government has had since 2010 to enter into water rights contracts with the White Mountain Apache Tribe, and a second deadline extension does not fix the conditions that caused the first deadline to be missed.

117-s-3308.one_liner: Let a Native American tribe in Arizona lease or store its water rights off tribal land
provisions: Lets the Colorado River Indian Tribes lease or trade part of their water rights to users in southern Arizona
Lets the tribe store its water underground at approved facilities in southern Arizona
Lets the tribe work with the Arizona Water Banking Authority to store water for future use
Requires federal approval of any lease, trade, or storage deal to make sure it follows environmental laws

supporters: Supporters say this bill lets the Colorado River Indian Tribes lease or trade part of their water rights to users in southern Arizona's Lower Basin, giving the tribe a way to earn money from water it is not currently using on its reservation.

Supporters say the option to work with the Arizona Water Banking Authority to store tribal water in underground facilities means the tribe can save water during wet years and use or sell it later when water is scarce.
critics: Critics say that moving tribal water off the reservation to southern Arizona through a lease or trade could make it harder for the tribe to get that water back if its own water needs grow in the future.

Critics say that requiring federal review under the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act for each lease, trade, or storage deal adds steps that could slow down or block the tribe from acting quickly with its own water.

117-s-3773.one_liner: Let the Confederated Tribes of the Chehalis Reservation sign land leases for up to 99 years
provisions: The Confederated Tribes of the Chehalis Reservation can now sign leases on their land for up to 99 years.
This applies to land the federal government holds for the tribe in western Washington State.
A 99-year term is the longest lease the tribe can sign under this bill — the tribe can still choose shorter leases.

supporters: Supporters say that allowing leases of up to 99 years gives the Confederated Tribes of the Chehalis Reservation enough time to attract businesses, housing developers, and energy projects that need long-term certainty before building on trust land in western Washington.

Supporters say other tribes across the country have already received the right to sign 99-year leases through similar bills, and this bill gives the Chehalis tribe the same leasing options those tribes already have.
Supporters say the tribe can still choose leases shorter than 99 years, so the bill adds flexibility without taking away any current options.
critics: Critics say a 99-year lease on trust land can outlast three or four generations of tribal leadership, meaning future Chehalis tribal members would inherit long-term land commitments they had no role in making.

Critics say under current federal law, shorter lease terms require the Bureau of Indian Affairs to review and approve renewals more often, and allowing a single 99-year term reduces how frequently that federal oversight of trust land use can happen.

117-s-3499.one_liner: Remove a requirement for the government to limit subcontractors in disaster contracts
provisions: This bill changes a law passed in 2006 about how the government responds to disasters.
That 2006 law told the Department of Homeland Security to write rules limiting how many layers of subcontractors companies could use on disaster response contracts.
The government no longer has to write those rules about subcontractor limits for disaster contracts.

supporters: Supporters say the 2006 provision requiring DHS to write subcontractor rules was never acted on, making it an obsolete requirement, and removing it cleans up the law without changing any rules that are actually in use.

Supporters say that removing the requirement to limit subcontractor tiers gives disaster response companies more freedom to quickly bring in local businesses and workers when responding to natural or man-made disasters.
critics: Critics say the 2006 law was passed because after Hurricane Katrina, contractors used many layers of subcontractors where each layer took fees, leaving less money for actual recovery work, and repealing this provision removes Congress's push to fix that problem.

Critics say that without a rule limiting subcontractor tiers on disaster contracts, the Department of Homeland Security will have no legal requirement to prevent the same contractor practices that hurt disaster recovery efforts before 2006.

117-s-4104.one_liner: Confirm the Hualapai Tribe's water rights in Arizona and fund a new water project
provisions: The U.S. confirms the Hualapai Tribe's legal rights to use water from the Colorado, Verde, and Bill Williams Rivers in Arizona.
The tribe gets 4,000 acre-feet — a unit of water volume — per year from the Central Arizona Project, a water delivery system serving Arizona.
Money from a trust fund can be used to build the Hualapai Water Project on the reservation.
That project would bring up to 3,414 acre-feet of Colorado River water per year to the reservation for homes, businesses, and industry.
Land outside the reservation can only be added to the tribe's holdings through an act of Congress.
The tribe and the U.S. government agree to drop certain legal claims against each other as part of this settlement.

supporters: Supporters say the bill gives the Hualapai Tribe legal rights to 4,000 acre-feet of water per year from the Central Arizona Project, ending years of uncertainty over water the tribe has long claimed.

Supporters say the Hualapai Water Project would bring up to 3,414 acre-feet of Colorado River water each year to the reservation, giving tribal members reliable water for homes, businesses, and industry.
Supporters say settling these water claims through a formal agreement avoids costly and lengthy court battles between the tribe, Arizona, and the federal government.
critics: Critics say the rule that future land outside the reservation can only be added through an act of Congress limits the tribe's ability to expand its land base without going through a slow political process.

Critics say agreeing to drop certain legal claims against the federal government as part of the settlement means the Hualapai Tribe gives up the right to pursue other water-related grievances in court.

117-s-4052.one_liner: Keep funding hearing screening programs for babies and young children through 2027
provisions: Three federal health agencies keep running programs that screen newborns for hearing loss and support young children who are deaf or hard of hearing.
These programs get money to keep going through 2027.
Families with babies or young children who have hearing problems can keep getting early help and services.
A government watchdog group will study how well state hearing screening programs are working.
That study will also look at whether some families have a harder time getting these programs than others.

supporters: Supporters say the bill keeps programs at three federal agencies — HRSA, CDC, and NIDCD — running through 2027, so newborn hearing screening can continue without interruption.
Supporters say families with babies and young children who are deaf or hard of hearing can keep receiving early intervention services that the reauthorized programs fund through 2027.
Supporters say the GAO study will check whether some families have a harder time accessing state hearing screening programs than others, which could point to where changes are needed.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set specific dollar amounts for the programs it extends through 2027, leaving actual funding levels unclear.
Critics say ordering a study on whether some families face barriers to hearing programs delays action — families who struggle to access services today must wait for a report before anything changes.
Critics say the bill extends programs run by three agencies through 2027 without requiring those agencies to show whether their current screening and intervention efforts are producing results.

117-s-3905.one_liner: Require companies doing federal work to report conflicts of interest
provisions: Updates the rulebook that controls how the government buys goods and services, to cover more types of conflicts of interest
Requires companies that work for the government to tell federal agencies when they have a conflict of interest
Limits what future government contracts a company can get if they have a conflict of interest
Requires each federal agency to set up its own process for catching and handling conflicts of interest

supporters: Supporters say the bill closes gaps in the current Federal Acquisition Regulation by requiring companies to report conflicts of interest that existing rules do not cover, which could protect taxpayer money from going to biased contractors.

Supporters say requiring each federal agency to set up its own conflict of interest process will make oversight more consistent across the government, since agencies currently handle these situations differently.

Supporters say limiting what future contracts a company can get if they have a conflict of interest will reduce cases where one company both advises the government on a contract and then wins that same contract.
critics: Critics say the new disclosure requirements placed on contractors could create extra paperwork and legal costs for small businesses that want to compete for government contracts.

Critics say giving each federal agency the power to set its own conflict of interest procedures could lead to uneven rules across agencies, making it harder for companies that work with multiple agencies to comply.
Critics say the bill does not set a deadline for the Federal Acquisition Regulatory Council to finish updating the rules, which means the changes could take years to take effect.

117-s-4834.one_liner: Keep funding programs that find and stop people who abuse children online
provisions: Keeps the National Strategy for Child Exploitation Prevention and Interdiction running through 2024
Keeps the National Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force Program running through 2024

supporters: Supporters say keeping the National Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force Program running through 2024 lets law enforcement keep working with local agencies to find and stop online predators.

Supporters say the National Strategy for Child Exploitation Prevention and Interdiction gives the government a clear plan to track and reduce crimes against children, and cutting it off early would leave that work unfinished.
critics: Critics say the bill only extends these programs through 2024 without adding new funding or tools, which may not be enough to keep up with growing online threats to children.
Critics say reauthorizing the Task Force Program without reviewing how well it has worked means Congress is continuing a program without checking if it is actually reducing child exploitation.

117-s-3875.one_liner: Map the highest natural disaster risk areas and give local governments help to prepare
provisions: The federal government must keep a public map showing how much natural disaster risk every part of the country faces.
That map must include data on how much money could be lost, how vulnerable the people living there are, and how ready the community is for a disaster.
The government must check and update those risk ratings at least once every five years.
The government will label the 50 areas in the country with the highest disaster risk as special high-priority zones.
In every state, at least 1 out of every 100 high-risk areas must also be labeled as a high-priority zone.
State, local, and tribal governments in those zones can apply for money and help from the federal government to get their communities ready for disasters.

supporters: Supporters say the bill helps state, local, and tribal governments in the 50 highest-risk areas get federal money and technical help to prepare for disasters before they happen.

Supporters say requiring the government to update risk ratings every five years means communities will have current data on money loss risk, social vulnerability, and disaster readiness — not outdated numbers.
Supporters say making the risk maps public gives every community free access to information about their disaster risk, so local leaders can plan better.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a minimum funding amount for the resilience zones, so state, local, and tribal governments may apply for help but receive little or no money.
Critics say labeling only 50 census tracts nationwide as top-priority zones leaves out thousands of other high-risk communities that could also need federal support.
Critics say updating the risk maps only once every five years may not be fast enough to reflect new threats, since climate patterns and community conditions can change quickly.

117-s-5087.one_liner: Extend a federal commission working to reduce violent crime against Native Americans
provisions: Gives the joint commission 18 more months to keep working.
Moves the deadline for the commission to publish its findings from 18 months to 36 months.
Requires the Department of the Interior and the Department of Justice to pay for the commission's work.
Lets the commission accept donated services or property from Native American tribes, colleges, or nonprofits.

supporters: Supporters say the 18-month extension gives the commission more time to finish its work on violent crime affecting Native Americans, who face murder rates more than 10 times higher than the national average in some areas.
Supporters say moving the deadline from 18 to 36 months allows the commission to gather better data before sending recommendations to Congress and the Departments of Interior and Justice.
Supporters say requiring Interior and Justice to fund the commission directly ensures the work does not stall due to budget gaps.
critics: Critics say extending the commission's timeline from 18 to 36 months delays concrete action on violent crime in Indian Country, where communities have already waited years for federal results.
Critics say the bill does not set a specific dollar amount for Interior and Justice to contribute, leaving funding levels unclear and potentially insufficient.
Critics say allowing the commission to accept donations from tribes and nonprofits could create conflicts of interest when those same groups are subjects of the commission's recommendations.

117-s-989.one_liner: Fund a center to help teach and preserve Native American languages
