provisions: The Department of Education can give money to a school or group to set up a center focused on Native American languages.
The center would help teachers and students learn and teach Native American languages.
The center would work to keep Native American languages alive by building tools and training for people who want to learn them.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would direct the Department of Education to fund a center that gives teachers and students tools to learn and teach Native American languages.
Supporters say the center would build training programs so that people in Native American communities have an opportunity to learn their languages from trained instructors.
Supporters say creating a dedicated resource center would help keep Native American languages in active use by developing materials that schools and communities can use.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a funding limit, leaving Congress without a clear cap on how much the Department of Education could spend on the center.
Critics say the bill does not require the center to report results, so there is no built-in way to measure whether the training and tools it produces are being used.
Critics say the bill targets a broad range of Native American language communities without specifying how the center would divide its resources among groups with different languages and needs.

117-s-4926.one_liner: Require the FBI to use child-focused teams when investigating crimes against children
provisions: Requires the FBI to use a team of specialists — not just agents — when investigating sexual abuse of children, child pornography, or child trafficking
Requires the FBI to include a trained child interviewer on these teams when possible
Requires the FBI to work with Children's Advocacy Centers, which are local organizations that already specialize in helping child victims

supporters: Supporters say requiring the FBI to use a multidisciplinary team — including a trained child forensic interviewer — means child victims are questioned by specialists who know how to talk to kids, not just federal agents, which can produce more reliable evidence.

Supporters say having the FBI work with Children's Advocacy Centers brings in local organizations that already specialize in helping child victims of sexual abuse and trafficking, instead of excluding them from federal investigations.
Supporters say a team-based approach means a child may not have to repeat their story to multiple separate investigators, which can reduce additional harm during the investigation.
critics: Critics say the bill's phrase 'if practicable' gives the FBI wide room to skip using a trained child forensic interviewer, which could make that part of the requirement easy to ignore.
Critics say the bill does not include any new funding to help FBI field offices build working relationships with Children's Advocacy Centers or bring trained interviewers onto their teams.

Critics say requiring the FBI to coordinate with local Children's Advocacy Centers could slow time-sensitive investigations if the local organizations and federal agents have different timelines or priorities.

117-s-5168.one_liner: Extend work permits for foreign ship crew doing cargo transfers to 180 days
provisions: Non-citizen ship workers who transfer liquid cargo between ships can get a permit to stay in the U.S. for up to 180 days instead of the current 29 days.
This only applies to crew members working on ships involved in international trade.
The extra time covers the length of ship-to-ship cargo transfer jobs, which often take longer than 29 days.

supporters: Supporters say the current 29-day permit limit forces companies to replace crews in the middle of ship-to-ship liquid cargo transfers, and the 180-day extension lets workers finish these jobs without interruption.
Supporters say the bill limits the longer permit only to alien crewmen on vessels in foreign trade doing liquid cargo transfers, so the change applies to a specific, narrow group of workers.
Supporters say matching the permit length to the actual duration of these transfer operations — which run longer than 29 days — keeps cargo moving without costly crew changes mid-job.
critics: Critics say the bill allows non-citizen ship workers to stay in U.S. waters for up to 180 days — more than six months — to perform liquid cargo transfer jobs, including oil and fuel shipments, that American maritime workers could fill.

Critics say raising the permit from 29 to 180 days is more than a sixfold increase in allowed stay time, and the bill sets no upper limit on how many alien crewmen can receive this extended permit at once.

Critics say the 180-day permit applies to ship-to-ship liquid cargo transfers, which are tied to U.S. energy supply chains, and giving foreign workers long-term access to these roles in American ports reduces jobs for U.S.-based crews.

117-s-5230.one_liner: Require police to report missing children to a second national database
provisions: Police must now send missing child reports to two national databases — NCIC and NamUs — instead of just one.
NamUs is a database run by the Department of Justice that tracks missing people and unidentified human remains across the country.
The two databases will be required to share data with each other to reduce gaps in records.
The Department of Justice must make a plan so that records move automatically from NCIC to NamUs.
Police departments and forensic teams will get guidance from DOJ on how to collect and report data on missing people and unidentified remains.
DOJ must report to Congress every two years on how both databases are working and how they share information with each other.

supporters: Supporters say requiring police to submit missing child reports to both NCIC and NamUs — instead of just NCIC — means the same case gets tracked in two national systems, making it less likely a child's case goes unnoticed.
Supporters say linking NCIC and NamUs through automatic data sharing will help investigators match missing person reports to unidentified human remains that are already in the system.
Supporters say the DOJ guidance to police and forensic teams on how to collect and report data will help standardize records across agencies that currently use different methods.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include dedicated funding to cover the cost of local police departments building the systems needed to submit reports to a second database.

Critics say sharing records between NCIC and NamUs raises questions about who can access sensitive missing person data and what rules will govern that access, since the bill leaves those details to DOJ to figure out later.
Critics say the two-year reporting requirement to Congress may not be frequent enough to catch problems with data sharing between the two systems early on.

118-hr-2379.one_liner: Rename a post office in St. Charles, Illinois, after Vietnam War veterans
provisions: Changes the official name of the post office at 616 East Main Street in St. Charles, Illinois
The new name is the 'Veterans of the Vietnam War Memorial Post Office'
No other changes are made to the post office or its services

118-hr-4394.one_liner: Fund water projects, energy programs, and nuclear security for the year starting October 2023
provisions: Gives the Army Corps of Engineers money to build and maintain water projects like flood walls, dams, and river channels across the country.
Funds the Bureau of Reclamation, which manages water supplies for farms and cities in 17 western states.
Sets aside money for Department of Energy programs covering solar and wind power, nuclear energy, oil and gas, and energy research.
Funds the National Nuclear Security Administration, which oversees the country's nuclear weapons and national defense programs.
Gives money to federal agencies that regulate electricity markets and nuclear power plants, including FERC and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
Makes the Bureau of Reclamation the main agency in charge of getting permits to build new water storage projects in certain areas of California.

supporters: Supporters say the bill funds the Bureau of Reclamation, which manages water supplies for farms and cities in 17 western states, keeping irrigation and drinking water systems running.
Supporters say the bill covers Department of Energy programs for solar, wind, nuclear, and fossil fuels at the same time, spreading research and energy production across multiple sources.

Supporters say making the Bureau of Reclamation the lead permitting agency for new water storage projects in California will speed up approvals that have taken years under the current multi-agency process.
critics: Critics say the bill funds both clean energy programs and fossil energy programs through the Department of Energy, directing federal dollars toward oil and gas at the same time as solar and wind.

Critics say giving the Bureau of Reclamation sole authority over permits for new California water storage projects removes other federal and state agencies from decisions that affect fish, rivers, and existing water rights.

Critics say combining Army Corps of Engineers construction, Department of Energy research, nuclear weapons funding, and water management into one bill ties together unrelated spending areas, making it harder to vote on each program separately.

118-hr-340.one_liner: Place financial penalties on foreign individuals and governments that fund Hamas
provisions: Blocks foreign people or companies that give money or help to Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, or their supporters from using U.S. banks for loans over $10 million
Stops those same foreign people or companies from buying U.S. weapons or military equipment
The President must give Congress a list of foreign governments that have repeatedly helped fund these groups
Any government on that list loses U.S. foreign aid and the ability to buy U.S. weapons for one year
U.S. officials at international banks must vote against giving money to those governments for one year
The President must report to Congress on where these groups get their money and equipment

supporters: Supporters say the bill would cut off Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad from U.S. financial systems by barring foreign individuals and companies that support these groups from getting loans over $10 million from U.S. banks.

Supporters say that by requiring the President to report foreign governments that fund these groups to Congress, the bill creates public accountability and lets lawmakers track which countries are enabling terrorist financing.
Supporters say removing U.S. foreign aid and blocking weapons sales to governments on the list for one year gives the U.S. direct leverage to pressure countries that repeatedly back these groups.
critics: Critics say the bill gives the President broad power to define who counts as a 'significant supporter' of these groups, which could lead to sanctions on foreign governments or companies based on limited evidence with little oversight.

Critics say cutting off U.S. foreign aid and blocking weapons purchases for any government on the list for a full year could damage diplomatic relationships with countries the U.S. relies on for regional stability, even if their support was indirect.

Critics say the waiver process, which lets the President skip sanctions when they conflict with 'U.S. national interests,' is loosely defined and could allow the executive branch to avoid enforcing the law's core requirements.

118-hr-4502.one_liner: Remove education requirements for federal cybersecurity jobs
provisions: Federal agencies can no longer set education requirements for cybersecurity jobs unless a state or local law already requires it.
If education is considered, it must directly match the skills needed for the job.
This applies to IT management jobs and jobs listed in a national framework for cybersecurity roles called NICE.
The federal office that oversees government hiring must post yearly updates on education rules for these jobs.
It must also share data on the education levels of people currently in those roles.

supporters: Supporters say removing degree requirements for NICE-designated cybersecurity positions will open up federal jobs to skilled workers who learned through training programs, military service, or self-study instead of a four-year college.
Supporters say requiring that education only count when it directly reflects job competencies will stop agencies from rejecting qualified candidates based on unrelated degrees.
Supporters say the rule requiring OPM to publish yearly updates on education changes and workforce education data will make federal hiring more transparent and easier to track over time.
critics: Critics say dropping minimum education requirements for IT Management Series and NICE-designated positions could make it harder for agencies to screen large pools of applicants without a consistent baseline standard.

Critics say the rule that education must directly match job competencies gives agencies broad room to interpret what counts as a match, which could lead to uneven hiring decisions across different federal departments.
Critics say the OPM annual reporting requirement does not include enforcement rules or penalties, meaning agencies could ignore the new standards without consequence.

118-hr-4364.one_liner: Fund Congress and its offices for the year starting October 2023
provisions: Gives the House of Representatives money to pay for its day-to-day operations for the year starting October 2023.

Funds four offices shared by both chambers: the Joint Economic Committee, the Joint Committee on Taxation, the Office of the Attending Physician, and the Office of Congressional Accessibility Services.
Gives the Capitol Police money to keep the Capitol building and the people who work there safe.
Funds the Congressional Budget Office, which figures out how much bills will cost, and the Office of Congressional Workplace Rights.
Funds the Library of Congress, including the Congressional Research Service and the Copyright Office.
Funds the Government Accountability Office, the Government Publishing Office, and the Architect of the Capitol, who manages and repairs Capitol buildings.
Funds the Congressional Office for International Leadership and the John C. Stennis Center, which trains people for public service, and sets rules for how all the money in this bill can be spent.

supporters: Supporters say funding the Capitol Police through this bill keeps the Capitol building and the lawmakers and staff who work there safe throughout the year.
Supporters say money for the Congressional Budget Office lets Congress see how much proposed laws will cost before voting on them, which helps members make more informed decisions.
Supporters say the Library of Congress and Congressional Research Service funding gives members of Congress and their staff the research and legal analysis they need to write and review laws.
critics: Critics say the bill funds the Congressional Office for International Leadership and the John C. Stennis Center for Public Service Training — whose work focuses on international exchange programs and career training, not on reviewing legislation or federal spending — while other federal agencies are being asked to reduce their budgets.
Critics say the bill covers only House operations and joint offices, leaving out the Senate entirely, which means it does not reflect the full cost of running Congress for the year.

Critics say the bill sets rules for how money can be spent but does not require lower funding levels for offices like the Architect of the Capitol, where construction and repair costs can grow from year to year without a set limit.

118-hres-559.one_liner: Declare that the United States will not allow Iran to get a nuclear weapon
provisions: States that the U.S. will use all means necessary to stop Iran from building a nuclear weapon.
States that the U.S. supports other countries taking steps to stop Iran from getting a nuclear weapon.
This is a resolution stating a policy position — it does not order specific military action or spending.

supporters: Supporters say the phrase 'all means necessary' sends a clear message to Iran that the U.S. will not allow it to build a nuclear weapon, which they argue makes an attack less likely.
Supporters say the resolution backs U.S. allies — like Israel — who may need to take their own steps to stop Iran's nuclear program, giving those partners a stronger legal and political footing.
Supporters say that because this is a policy statement and not a spending bill, it costs nothing and carries no risk of committing troops or dollars without further congressional action.
critics: Critics say the phrase 'all means necessary' is too open-ended and could be used to justify military action against Iran without a formal vote in Congress, which the Constitution requires.
Critics say the resolution does not define what counts as an 'acceptable' Iranian nuclear program, leaving key decisions to the executive branch with little oversight.

Critics say supporting allied 'freedom of action' without specific limits could draw the U.S. into a conflict started by another country, with no clear rules on when or how the U.S. would get involved.

118-hr-5692.one_liner: Send weapons to Ukraine and create an office to track how the money is spent
provisions: Sends weapons and military equipment to Ukraine's armed forces to resist Russia's attacks.
Pays to replace U.S. military weapons that were already pulled from American stockpiles and sent to Ukraine.
Creates a new government office called the Special Inspector General for Ukraine Assistance.
The new office runs audits and investigations to check whether money and weapons are being used correctly.
The new office reports waste, fraud, and problems to Congress, the State Department, and the Defense Department.

supporters: Supporters say sending weapons and military equipment to Ukraine's armed forces helps Ukraine resist Russian attacks without putting U.S. troops in the fight.
Supporters say paying to restock U.S. military weapons already sent to Ukraine keeps American defense stockpiles ready in case they are needed.
Supporters say the new Special Inspector General office will run audits and investigations to catch waste, fraud, and misuse of weapons or money before problems grow.
critics: Critics say the bill sends more weapons and military aid to Ukraine, which pulls resources from U.S. defense needs and could draw America deeper into the conflict.
Critics say creating a new government office adds spending and bureaucracy, and that oversight should be handled by offices that already exist.
Critics say replacing weapons taken from U.S. stockpiles costs money without a clear limit set in the bill, making the total price hard to pin down.

118-hres-756.one_liner: Set the debate and amendment rules for two government spending bills in the House
provisions: Sets time limits and debate rules for a bill that funds energy and water programs through September 2024.
Sets time limits and debate rules for a bill that funds Congress through September 2024.
Controls which changes House members can propose to each bill during floor debate.
Both bills cover spending for the year ending September 30, 2024.

supporters: Supporters say limiting debate time on H.R. 4394 and H.R. 4364 keeps the House on schedule so energy, water, and Congressional funding can be approved before the September 30, 2024 deadline.
Supporters say controlling which changes members can propose prevents unrelated additions from being attached to the energy, water, and Legislative Branch spending bills.
Supporters say setting clear debate rules for both fiscal year 2024 spending bills gives members enough time to speak while keeping the floor process moving.
critics: Critics say the rule restricts which amendments House members can offer on the energy and water funding bill, limiting their ability to change spending levels for specific programs.
Critics say capping debate time on the Legislative Branch funding bill reduces the chance for members to argue for or against how Congress spends money on its own operations.
Critics say a closed or restricted rule on both fiscal year 2024 bills takes power away from individual members and concentrates control over the final spending decisions in House leadership.

118-hres-741.one_liner: Set the House debate rules for a government funding bill covering 2024
provisions: This bill sets the rules for how the House of Representatives will debate a government funding bill for the year starting October 2023.
It controls how much time members of Congress get to speak about the funding bill before a vote takes place.
It determines whether members can offer changes to the funding bill during debate, before the final vote.
The rules it sets decide the order in which the House handles the funding bill on the floor.

supporters: Supporters say the rule sets a clear debate schedule so the House can vote on H.R. 5525 before the October 2023 government funding deadline, preventing a shutdown.
Supporters say limiting total floor time and setting a fixed speaking order keeps debate focused on the continuing appropriations bill and prevents delays.
Supporters say controlling which amendments can be offered stops members from adding unrelated items that could block the funding bill from passing.
critics: Critics say the rule limits how long members can speak about H.R. 5525, cutting short debate on a bill that funds the entire federal government.
Critics say restricting amendments blocks members from proposing changes to spending levels or policy riders before the final vote on the continuing appropriations bill.
Critics say setting the floor schedule through a closed rule removes the ability of the full House to decide how to handle H.R. 5525, concentrating that power in the Rules Committee.

118-hr-5525.one_liner: Keep the government funded and tighten rules on who can apply for asylum
provisions: Keeps the government funded through October 31, 2023. Defense, VA, and disaster relief stay at 2023 funding levels. Most other programs get an 8.1% funding cut.
Requires building a border wall along at least 900 miles of the U.S.-Mexico border. Current law requires only 700 miles of fencing.
Changes the bar for approving asylum claims. People must now show it is more likely than not they would face persecution. Before, they only needed to show a real chance.
People can only apply for asylum if they entered the U.S. at an official border crossing. Those who crossed between official crossings cannot apply.
People who traveled through another country before reaching the U.S. generally cannot apply for asylum. An exception applies if they sought and were denied asylum in that country first.
Fines for crossing the border without permission go from $50–$250 up to $500–$1,000. Overstaying a visa by 10 or more days becomes a crime with up to 6 months in jail on a first offense.
Limits when the government can let non-citizens stay temporarily in the U.S. while their immigration cases are reviewed.

supporters: Supporters say the bill prevents a government shutdown by keeping federal agencies funded through October 31, 2023, and protects defense, VA, and disaster relief programs from cuts by holding them at 2023 funding levels.

Supporters say requiring a border wall along 900 miles of the U.S.-Mexico border — up from the current 700-mile requirement — gives Border Patrol more physical infrastructure to stop illegal crossings.

Supporters say raising the asylum approval standard to 'more likely than not' and limiting applications to people who enter at official border crossings will reduce the number of people who use asylum claims to avoid removal after crossing illegally.
critics: Critics say the bill cuts funding for most federal programs by 8.1%, which would reduce services for Americans who rely on programs outside of defense, the VA, and disaster relief.

Critics say barring people from applying for asylum if they traveled through another country first would block many people fleeing violence from ever getting a hearing, even if they had no safe way to apply for protection along the route.

Critics say raising fines for illegal border crossings to up to $1,000 and making visa overstays of 10 or more days a crime punishable by up to 6 months in jail creates criminal penalties for people who may have missed deadlines due to backlogs in the immigration system.

118-hres-771.one_liner: State that the House supports Israel and condemns Hamas attacks
provisions: States that the House of Representatives stands with Israel during the current conflict with Hamas.
Says Israel has the right to defend itself.
Condemns Hamas for starting the war against Israel.
States that the U.S. will keep supporting Israel's security.
Supports sending emergency weapons and other help to Israel.
Calls for full enforcement of penalties against Iran to stop it from sending money to groups that carry out attacks.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution reflects Israel's right to self-defense, since Hamas launched the attack and Israel is responding to protect its people.
Supporters say calling for full enforcement of sanctions against Iran targets the financial networks that fund groups like Hamas, cutting off a key source of attack funding.
Supporters say the resolution's support for emergency weapons resupply gives Israel the specific military tools it needs to continue defending itself during an active conflict.
critics: Critics say the resolution's call for emergency weapons resupply could send more arms into an active conflict zone where reports show large numbers of Palestinian civilians have been killed.
Critics say the resolution condemns Hamas but does not mention any role for diplomacy or negotiation, leaving out tools that could reduce harm to civilians on both sides.

Critics say the resolution's blanket support for Israel's security actions does not address whether emergency military assistance complies with U.S. laws that restrict weapons transfers when civilians are at risk.

118-s-4199.one_liner: Add 66 new federal judges across 14 states over 10 years
provisions: Creates 63 new permanent federal judge positions spread across 13 states, added every two years from 2025 to 2035.
California gets 21 new judges, Texas gets 13, Florida gets 9, New York gets 5, and the other 9 states get between 1 and 3 each.
Creates 3 temporary judge positions in Oklahoma starting in 2025.
Adds new courthouse locations in El Centro, California; College Station, Texas; and Moab and Monticello, Utah.
A government watchdog agency must report to Congress on how many cases judges are handling and how much federal detention space is available.
Federal court officials must publish a public report every two years on how many more judges are needed.

supporters: Supporters say the bill adds 63 permanent federal judgeships over 10 years, including 21 in California and 13 in Texas, which are two of the states with the highest federal court caseloads in the country.
Supporters say new courthouse locations in El Centro, California and Moab and Monticello, Utah will let people in those areas attend federal court without traveling long distances.
Supporters say requiring a public report every two years on how many judges are needed will hold Congress accountable for keeping up with court demand.
critics: Critics say adding 63 permanent judgeships gives whichever president is in office from 2025 to 2035 the power to shape the federal courts for decades, since each judge serves a lifetime appointment.

Critics say the bill concentrates most new judgeships in just three states — California (21), Texas (13), and Florida (9) — while 9 other states each get only 1 to 3 judges, which may not match where delays are worst.

Critics say the three temporary judgeships in Oklahoma created in 2025 do not come with a clear plan for what happens when those positions expire, leaving uncertainty for courts and staff in that state.

118-hres-757.one_liner: Remove the current Speaker of the House from their position
provisions: Declares the Speaker of the House position empty, which would trigger a vote in the House to elect a new Speaker

supporters: Supporters say the resolution would trigger a new Speaker election, giving all 435 House members a direct vote to decide who leads the chamber.
Supporters say declaring the office vacant is the only way for members to force a leadership change when a majority believes the current Speaker should no longer hold the position.
critics: Critics say removing the Speaker without naming a replacement would leave the House without a presiding officer until a new Speaker wins a majority of votes from all 435 members, which could delay any House floor business during that time.
Critics say passing this resolution with a simple majority vote sets a pattern where any future Speaker could be removed over policy disagreements, making the position less stable.

118-hres-829.one_liner: Formally censure a sitting member of Congress
provisions: The House of Representatives votes to officially censure Representative Rashida Tlaib, which is a formal statement of disapproval by her colleagues
A censure does not remove a member from Congress or change their voting rights
The resolution states specific reasons for the censure, including her conduct related to events at the Capitol and statements about foreign conflicts

supporters: Supporters say the resolution uses the House's formal censure process to put members on record against Rep. Tlaib's conduct, including her role in a protest at the Capitol Complex and statements they say expressed support for groups the U.S. government has labeled terrorist organizations.
Supporters say a censure is the right tool here because it lets the House issue an official statement of disapproval without removing Rep. Tlaib from Congress or taking away her voting rights.
critics: Critics say the resolution labels Rep. Tlaib's statements about a foreign conflict as antisemitic and pro-terrorist, but those statements were political speech made by an elected member of Congress doing her job.

Critics say calling Rep. Tlaib's participation in a Capitol protest an 'insurrection' uses a term that describes a much more serious act, and the resolution does not remove her from office or change her voting rights in any way.

119-s-2806.one_liner: Keep the government running at last year's spending levels if Congress misses its budget deadline
provisions: If Congress does not pass a budget before the new government year starts, spending continues at the same levels as the year before.
Government programs, offices, and services that were funded last year keep running without interruption.
This stops the government from shutting down when Congress and the President cannot agree on a new budget in time.

supporters: Supporters say this bill would stop government shutdowns by keeping spending at the same levels as the year before if Congress misses its budget deadline.
Supporters say programs like Social Security payments, veterans services, and food safety inspections would keep running without interruption under the prior-year funding rate.
Supporters say this removes the threat of a shutdown being used as a bargaining tool when Congress and the President cannot agree on a new budget in time.
critics: Critics say automatically continuing prior-year spending levels removes pressure on Congress to pass a budget on time, since there is no longer a consequence for missing the deadline.
Critics say locking in prior-year spending levels could freeze funding for programs that Congress intended to grow or shrink in the new budget.
Critics say this bill shifts budget power away from Congress by allowing unchanged spending levels to continue without a vote on new appropriations.

119-s-3012.one_liner: Pay federal workers their regular wages during government shutdowns
provisions: Right now, federal workers who are required to keep working during a government shutdown do not get paid until the shutdown ends — this bill changes that.
Under this bill, those workers get their regular pay, benefits, and other payments while the shutdown is happening, not after.
The bill also covers some government contractors and active-duty military members who keep working during a shutdown.
The bill counts as if it became law on September 30, 2025.

supporters: Supporters say the bill ends a rule where federal workers — including active-duty military — must work during a shutdown without pay until it ends.
Supporters say workers would get their regular pay, benefits, and other payments while the shutdown is happening, not weeks later.
Supporters say the bill also protects some government contractors who keep working during shutdowns, a group left out of current law.
critics: Critics say the bill creates a standing pool of money set aside in advance to cover shutdown pay, which could make Congress less motivated to avoid shutdowns in the first place.
Critics say paying workers during a shutdown — rather than after — adds costs during a period when no full budget has been passed, making it harder to control spending.
Critics say the bill's rules about when agencies can use the funds, tied to whether a short-term funding bill is in effect, may be hard to track and enforce.

119-sconres-22.one_liner: Set the federal government's spending and income plan for 2026 through 2035
provisions: Sets the overall spending and income plan for the federal government for the year starting October 2025.
Plans out government spending and income levels for the nine years from 2027 through 2035.
Sets limits on how much Congress can spend in different areas like defense, health, and education.
Sets rules for Social Security and Postal Service spending to help the Senate keep the budget on track.
Creates room in the budget for Congress to save money through cuts, combinations, or changes to health savings accounts.
Sets rules for when senators can object to a bill for breaking the budget.
Covers how emergency spending is handled and how Congressional Budget Office cost estimates are used.

supporters: Supporters say the budget plan sets clear spending limits for defense, health, and education from 2026 through 2035, giving Congress a long-term roadmap instead of making last-minute decisions each year.
Supporters say the rules for when senators can object to overspending will help keep the deficit from growing, since any bill that breaks the budget can be blocked before it passes.
Supporters say the reserve funds let Congress find savings through cuts or changes to health savings accounts, which could reduce government costs without cutting core programs.
critics: Critics say a budget plan that locks in spending levels through 2035 limits future Congresses from responding to new needs, like an economic crisis or a public health emergency.
Critics say the rules around Social Security and Postal Service spending in the Senate could make it harder to increase funding for those programs, which affect tens of millions of Americans.
Critics say the emergency spending rules give too much flexibility to add costs outside the normal budget process, which could make it harder to track the true size of the deficit.

119-s-3385.one_liner: Keep health insurance tax credits in place for three more years through 2028
provisions: Before 2021, people who earned more than 4 times the federal poverty level could not get health insurance tax credits. That cutoff is about $62,000 for a single person or $127,000 for a family of four.
In 2021, that income cap was removed so people above those amounts could get credits too. This bill keeps the cap removed through 2028.
The tax credit lowers your monthly health insurance bill when you buy coverage through the government marketplace.
Without this bill, those payment percentages would go back up after 2025 and adjust upward each year for inflation. This bill pauses both changes through 2028.

supporters: Supporters say extending the removal of the 400% income cap through 2028 lets people earning above $62,000 (single) or $127,000 (family of four) keep getting tax credits to lower their monthly insurance bills.
Supporters say without this bill, the percentages used to calculate credits would rise after 2025 and keep rising with inflation each year, making coverage more expensive for marketplace shoppers.
Supporters say the three-year extension gives families more time to count on lower premiums while Congress works on a longer-term fix.
critics: Critics say extending these expanded credits through 2028 adds to the federal deficit, since the government pays out more in tax credits to people at higher income levels who may be able to afford coverage without help.
Critics say allowing households earning above $127,000 to receive subsidies means federal dollars go to families that were not eligible for this assistance before 2021.
Critics say a three-year extension delays a real decision about whether these higher subsidies should be permanent, leaving insurers and consumers uncertain about what comes after 2028.

119-s-2882.one_liner: Keeps the federal government funded through October 2025 and makes health insurance tax credits permanent
provisions: Keeps the federal government funded at 2025 spending levels through October 31, 2025.
Stops a government shutdown that would start October 1, 2025, unless Congress passes the full 2026 budget sooner.
Makes the health insurance tax credit permanent so people pay less for coverage bought through the government marketplace.
Cancels health coverage changes made in an earlier law called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including cuts to Medicaid.
Lets Washington D.C. spend its own local tax money at the rates in its 2026 local budget.
Makes funds that the federal budget office was holding available to spend.
Stops the federal budget office from blocking government spending on its own in the future.

supporters: Supporters say making the health insurance tax credit permanent will keep premiums lower for the millions of people who buy coverage through the government marketplace, preventing a price spike that would hit when the credit was set to expire.
Supporters say this bill stops a government shutdown on October 1, 2025, keeping federal workers paid and federal services running while Congress finishes the full 2026 budget.
Supporters say canceling the Medicaid cuts from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act protects low-income adults and children who rely on Medicaid from losing health coverage.
critics: Critics say keeping spending at 2025 levels through October 31, 2025, delays real budget decisions and locks in federal spending without making needed cuts or changes.
Critics say permanently extending the health insurance tax credit adds long-term costs to the federal budget without a plan to pay for it.
Critics say limiting the Office of Management and Budget's ability to hold back funds takes away a tool the executive branch uses to control how money is spent.

119-s-3386.one_liner: Fund health savings accounts and cut coverage for certain groups and procedures
provisions: From 2026 to 2027, the government puts $1,000 or $1,500 per year into the health savings accounts of people age 18 to 64 who have basic or catastrophic insurance plans and earn up to 700% of the poverty line — about $106,000 a year for a single person.
Starting in 2027, people with mid-level silver insurance plans who earn up to 250% of the poverty line — about $38,000 a year for a single person — get help paying their share of medical bills.
Starting in 2027, any adult can sign up for a catastrophic health plan; right now only people under 30 or those with certain exemptions can.
States that use their own money to give health coverage to non-citizens who do not qualify under federal rules get a smaller share of federal Medicaid money.
Medicaid and CHIP no longer have to cover people while their immigration status is being checked, and the federal government will only pay for that coverage after the check is complete.
Health plans sold through government insurance exchanges cannot cover gender-transition procedures, and Medicaid and CHIP cannot pay for them either.

supporters: Supporters say the bill puts $1,000 to $1,500 per year directly into health savings accounts for people earning up to about $106,000 a year who have basic or catastrophic plans, giving them more control over how they spend on health care.
Supporters say opening catastrophic plans to all adults starting in 2027 gives people a lower-cost coverage option that is currently blocked by age limits.
Supporters say cutting federal Medicaid payments to states that cover non-citizens who do not qualify under federal law stops the federal government from paying for benefits Congress did not approve.
critics: Critics say removing federal payment for Medicaid and CHIP coverage while immigration status is being verified could leave lawfully present immigrants without coverage for weeks or months during a paperwork delay.

Critics say banning exchange plans and Medicaid from covering gender-transition procedures takes away coverage that some medical groups say is necessary care for transgender people, including minors on CHIP.

Critics say reducing the federal Medicaid matching rate for states that cover non-citizens with their own state funds could force states to cut back coverage for millions of people in the broader Medicaid program to make up for lost federal dollars.

119-sres-412.one_liner: Allow the Senate to vote on a group of nominations all at once
provisions: The Senate can vote on several presidential nominations at the same time instead of holding a separate vote for each one.
This applies to nominations the Senate has already received but not yet voted on.
This vote only needs a simple majority to pass and does not require any action from the House or the President.

supporters: Supporters say voting on multiple nominations at the same time clears a backlog of nominees already sitting on the Executive Calendar who have not yet received a vote.
Supporters say the simple majority threshold means a small group of senators cannot delay or block the en bloc vote from moving forward.
Supporters say en bloc consideration saves Senate floor time by replacing dozens of separate votes with one combined vote.
critics: Critics say bundling nominations into one en bloc vote prevents senators from debating or casting a separate vote against individual nominees they have concerns about.
Critics say the simple majority rule gives the majority party full control over which nominees get individual review and which get swept through without separate scrutiny.
Critics say applying en bloc procedures to the full Executive Calendar could push through a large number of nominees at once without any individual examination of each person's record.

119-sres-377.one_liner: Approve multiple presidential nominees for government and ambassador jobs at once
provisions: Groups several presidential nominations together so the Senate can vote on all of them at one time instead of one by one
The nominees include people picked to lead roles at the Departments of Defense, Energy, Interior, and Labor
Also includes nominees to serve as U.S. ambassadors to Argentina, Greece, Liechtenstein, and Sweden

supporters: Supporters say grouping the Defense, Energy, Interior, and Labor nominees into one vote fills leadership gaps faster, since key agency posts stay empty longer when the Senate votes on each person one at a time.

Supporters say bundling the four ambassador nominees for Argentina, Greece, Liechtenstein, and Sweden into a single vote lets the Senate move through a backlog of uncontested nominees without taking up extra floor time.
Supporters say en bloc votes are a standard Senate tool when nominees have already cleared committee review and no senator has placed a hold on them.
critics: Critics say voting on all nominees — including those headed to the Departments of Defense and Energy — in one bundle gives individual senators less chance to raise concerns about a specific nominee before the vote is final.

Critics say combining ambassador picks for four different countries, such as Liechtenstein and Sweden, with domestic agency leaders in a single vote makes it harder for the public to track who was confirmed and when.
Critics say the en bloc process limits debate time, which means nominees for roles at the Department of Labor or Interior may receive less scrutiny than they would in a standalone vote.

119-sres-520.one_liner: Vote on multiple Senate nominations at once instead of one at a time
provisions: The Senate can vote on a group of nominations together in one vote instead of holding a separate vote for each person.
Only nominations already listed on the Senate's official pending list at the time of the vote are included.
This applies only to the current session of Congress and has no effect on future nominations.
This does not change any policy or law — it only changes how the Senate organizes its votes on nominations.

supporters: Supporters say grouping all pending nominations from the Executive Calendar into one vote saves Senate floor time, letting the chamber move faster on other business.
Supporters say the process only covers nominations already on the official pending list, so no new or unreviewed nominees can be added at the last moment.
Supporters say this change is limited to the current session of Congress and does not create a permanent new rule or affect future nominations.
critics: Critics say bundling multiple nominees into a single vote makes it harder for senators to vote no on one specific person without rejecting the entire group.
Critics say combining nominations reduces the chance for public debate and individual scrutiny of each nominee before a vote is cast.
Critics say even though this does not change any law, it shifts how senators are held accountable for each nomination by hiding individual votes inside a group decision.

119-sres-532.one_liner: Allow the Senate to vote on several nominations at once
provisions: The Senate voted to consider several nominees together in one vote, instead of voting on each person one at a time.
The nominees in this group were already on the Executive Calendar — the Senate's list of people nominated by the President who are waiting for a vote.
This is a one-time action that only applies to this specific group of nominees and does not change how future nominations are handled.

supporters: Supporters say combining the nominees already on the Executive Calendar into one en bloc vote saves Senate floor time, letting the chamber move through its backlog of pending nominations faster.

Supporters say each of these nominees had already been placed on the Executive Calendar, meaning they had gone through committee review and were waiting for a floor vote — the en bloc process does not skip any prior steps.
Supporters say this is a one-time action limited to this specific group and does not change the rules for how future nominations are handled.
critics: Critics say grouping multiple nominees into a single en bloc vote means senators cannot vote against one individual nominee without rejecting the entire group at once.

Critics say nominees on the Executive Calendar are being considered for different positions with different qualifications, and bundling them removes the chance to debate or question each person on their own record.
Critics say even a one-time en bloc vote can pressure senators to approve nominees they have concerns about in order to avoid blocking others in the same group.

119-hjres-25.one_liner: Cancel an IRS rule requiring crypto brokers to report decentralized finance sales
provisions: This resolution cancels an IRS rule published on December 30, 2024.
The rule required people who process DeFi transactions to report crypto sales to the IRS.
DeFi transactions are trades that happen without a bank or company in the middle.
Once canceled, the IRS cannot issue a new rule in the same form without a new act of Congress.

supporters: Supporters say the December 30, 2024 IRS rule wrongly treated DeFi software developers as brokers, even though they never hold customer funds or collect personal information the way a bank or company would.

Supporters say canceling the rule protects DeFi users and developers from reporting requirements that do not fit how peer-to-peer crypto trades work, since no middleman collects the data the IRS would require.
Supporters say blocking the IRS from reissuing this rule without a new act of Congress gives lawmakers — not a federal agency — control over how DeFi transactions are taxed and reported.
critics: Critics say nullifying the rule removes the only mechanism requiring DeFi transaction processors to report crypto sales to the IRS, making it harder to track taxable income from digital assets.
Critics say the December 30, 2024 rule was meant to close a reporting gap where crypto traders using DeFi platforms can avoid tax obligations that stock and bond traders must follow.

Critics say using the Congressional Review Act to cancel the rule permanently blocks the IRS from writing any similar DeFi reporting rule in the future without a separate vote of Congress, limiting the agency's ability to enforce tax law on digital assets.

119-hjres-24.one_liner: Cancel a 2024 Department of Energy energy efficiency rule for walk-in coolers and freezers
provisions: This bill cancels a rule the Department of Energy issued on December 23, 2024.
Walk-in coolers and freezers are large refrigerated rooms used in places like grocery stores and restaurants to keep food cold.
That rule required these units to meet higher energy efficiency standards than what was required before.
With the rule gone, manufacturers can keep building these units under the older standards that existed before December 2024.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the December 2024 rule lets manufacturers keep building walk-in coolers and freezers under the older standards, which they argue lowers production costs for grocery stores and restaurants.
Supporters say the Department of Energy's new efficiency standards would force businesses to buy more expensive equipment, putting a financial burden on small restaurant and grocery store owners.
Supporters say Congress has the right to reject federal agency rules it did not vote on, and this disapproval resolution uses that legal authority under chapter 8 of title 5 of the U.S. Code.
critics: Critics say the December 2024 rule was designed to reach the maximum energy efficiency that the DOE found was both technically possible and cost-justified, and canceling it means that energy savings will be lost for grocery stores and restaurants nationwide.

Critics say walk-in coolers and freezers run continuously and use large amounts of electricity, so lower efficiency standards will lead to higher energy bills over time for businesses that use this equipment.
Critics say the DOE already determined the new standards were economically justified, meaning the long-term savings would outweigh the upfront costs, and removing the rule takes away those benefits.

119-hjres-42.one_liner: Cancel a 2024 rule changing how appliance makers must report and label energy use
provisions: Cancels a Department of Energy rule from October 2024 that changed how companies prove and label the energy use of products like washing machines and dishwashers.
The cancellation also applies to rules for industrial equipment, like computer room air conditioners.
Companies go back to the energy reporting and labeling rules that were in place before October 2024.
Removes updated rules about how the government checks whether companies follow energy reporting requirements for these products.

supporters: Supporters say that canceling the October 2024 DOE rule removes new reporting and labeling requirements on companies that make washing machines, dishwashers, and industrial equipment like computer room air conditioners, reducing their paperwork burden.
Supporters say the pre-October 2024 rules were already working, and the new certification and enforcement changes were not needed to keep energy standards in place.
Supporters say Congress, not the DOE, should decide when to update how companies report and label energy use for consumer products.
critics: Critics say the October 2024 DOE rule helped align company reporting requirements with current energy standards, and canceling it leaves a gap in how the government checks whether washing machines and dishwashers meet those standards.
Critics say removing the updated enforcement provisions means the DOE loses tools it uses to verify that companies are correctly classifying their products under the right energy rules.

Critics say going back to the pre-October 2024 labeling rules means the DOE will have less information to determine whether products like computer room air conditioners are placed in the right category for energy standards.

119-hjres-20.one_liner: Cancel a rule setting energy efficiency standards for gas-fired tankless water heaters
provisions: Cancels a Department of Energy rule from December 26, 2024 that set energy efficiency standards for gas-fired tankless water heaters.
The rule required these water heaters to reach the highest efficiency level that was both technically possible and worth the cost to make.
Gas-fired tankless water heaters — also called instantaneous water heaters — heat water on demand instead of storing hot water in a tank.
With the rule canceled, manufacturers of these water heaters do not have to meet those efficiency standards.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution cancels the December 26, 2024 DOE rule, which means manufacturers of gas-fired tankless water heaters will not be forced to redesign their products to meet new efficiency standards.

Supporters say the DOE rule required these water heaters to reach the highest efficiency level technically possible, and removing that requirement gives manufacturers more freedom in what products they can build and sell.
Supporters say canceling the rule prevents the federal government from setting product design requirements that could limit the types of gas-fired tankless water heaters available to consumers.
critics: Critics say canceling this rule removes the requirement that gas-fired tankless water heaters meet the highest efficiency level the DOE found was both technically possible and worth the cost to produce.
Critics say without the December 26, 2024 rule, consumers who buy gas-fired tankless water heaters may end up with less efficient models that use more gas and cost more to operate each year.
Critics say the DOE rule was designed to lock in energy savings for households that use on-demand water heaters, and canceling it means those savings will not happen.

119-hjres-35.one_liner: Cancel an EPA rule setting up how oil and gas companies handle methane fee requirements
provisions: Oil and gas companies no longer have a set process for showing they follow the methane fee rules — the EPA published the canceled rule in November 2024.
Under the Methane Emissions Reduction Program, companies that release more methane than a set limit owe a yearly fee to the EPA.
'Netting' — combining methane releases from different company locations to stay under the fee limit — is no longer an option.
The process companies could use to apply for exemptions from the methane fee is also canceled.

supporters: Supporters say nullifying the November 2024 EPA rule removes a compliance process with multiple steps that oil and gas companies had to follow under the Methane Emissions Reduction Program.

Supporters say canceling the yearly fee means oil and gas companies no longer owe payments to the EPA when their methane releases go above the set threshold under the Methane Emissions Reduction Program.
Supporters say without the rule, oil and gas companies are no longer required to go through the EPA's formal exemption process to avoid the methane fee.
critics: Critics say the rule's yearly fee on methane releases above set thresholds gave oil and gas companies a financial reason to cut their emissions under the Methane Emissions Reduction Program.
Critics say nullifying the November 2024 rule removes the formal process companies used to combine methane releases from different locations — called netting — to show they stay under the fee limit.
Critics say without the rule, there is no set process for the EPA to collect charges from oil and gas companies that release more methane than allowed under the Methane Emissions Reduction Program.

119-hjres-88.one_liner: Cancel an EPA decision letting California set its own car pollution rules
provisions: Cancels an EPA notice published January 6, 2025 that gave California permission to enforce its own car emission rules.
Removes California's ability to apply its Advanced Clean Cars II (ACC II) standards, which the state had set for car makers.
Under federal law, states cannot set their own car emission rules without special permission from the EPA. This bill takes away the permission California received.

supporters: Supporters say this bill cancels the EPA's January 6, 2025 notice, which means California's Advanced Clean Cars II rules can no longer be enforced, so one national standard applies to all car makers instead of a separate California standard.

Supporters say California's ACC II rules require car makers to sell only zero-emission vehicles in California by 2035, and removing the EPA waiver prevents one state from setting rules that affect car production for the whole country.
Supporters say under federal law, states are not allowed to set their own car emission rules, and this bill restores that rule by taking away the special permission California received from the EPA.
critics: Critics say the EPA waiver granted to California under the Clean Air Act has allowed the state to set stricter emission rules since 1968, and this bill removes a legal permission that Congress built into federal law.

Critics say California's ACC II standards cover a market of over 35 million people, and at least 17 other states have adopted the same rules, so canceling the waiver would affect clean air protections across a large part of the country.
Critics say the ACC II rules were designed to cut tailpipe pollution from cars sold in California, and taking away the EPA waiver stops California from enforcing those limits on car makers.

119-hjres-61.one_liner: Cancel an EPA rule limiting toxic air pollution from rubber tire factories
provisions: The EPA published a rule on November 29, 2024 that set new limits on toxic chemicals that rubber tire factories can release into the air.
This bill cancels that rule.
The rule covered the rubber processing part of tire manufacturing specifically.
Canceling it means rubber tire factories no longer have to follow those new air pollution limits.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the EPA rule removes new air pollution limits on rubber tire factories that were not required before November 2024, which they argue reduces costs for manufacturers in the rubber processing industry.
Supporters say the original rule was added to respond to a 2020 court case, and Congress should decide whether those new limits are needed rather than leaving it to the EPA alone.
Supporters say rubber tire factories were already following older pollution rules, and the new requirements from the November 2024 rule added extra limits on top of what was already in place.
critics: Critics say canceling the rule means rubber tire factories no longer have to meet the new limits on toxic chemicals released into the air, leaving nearby communities exposed to hazardous air pollutants that the EPA found needed to be regulated.

Critics say the EPA published the rule on November 29, 2024 specifically to fix a gap in pollution rules for the rubber processing part of tire manufacturing — a gap a federal court identified in 2020 — and canceling it reopens that gap.
Critics say the rule targeted hazardous air pollutants from the rubber processing subcategory of tire factories, and without it, there are no updated federal limits covering those specific emissions.

119-hjres-75.one_liner: Cancel a 2025 rule setting energy standards for commercial refrigerators and freezers
provisions: A Department of Energy rule published on January 21, 2025 set new energy efficiency levels for commercial refrigerators, freezers, and refrigerator-freezers.
This bill cancels that rule, so the new efficiency levels do not take effect.
Commercial refrigeration equipment goes back to the older energy standards that were in place before January 2025.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the January 21, 2025 rule removes new energy standards that would have forced businesses like restaurants and grocery stores to buy more expensive commercial refrigerators and freezers.

Supporters say returning to the older efficiency standards gives equipment makers more time to adjust and keeps costs lower for small businesses that cannot afford to replace refrigeration equipment right away.
Supporters say the Department of Energy rule was set without enough proof that the new efficiency levels were both achievable and worth the cost to commercial buyers.
critics: Critics say blocking the January 21, 2025 rule means commercial refrigerators and freezers will keep using more electricity than they need to, raising energy bills for businesses that run this equipment every day.

Critics say the Department of Energy found the new standards were the most efficiency improvement that was both technically possible and economically justified, so canceling the rule throws out that analysis.

Critics say reverting to the older commercial refrigeration standards will slow down energy savings that would have added up across thousands of grocery stores, convenience stores, and food service businesses nationwide.

119-hjres-60.one_liner: Cancel a rule limiting off-road vehicle access in Glen Canyon National Recreation Area
provisions: A National Park Service rule from January 13, 2025 limited where off-road vehicles could go in Glen Canyon National Recreation Area.
Glen Canyon spans parts of northern Arizona and southeastern Utah.
The rule applied to all-terrain vehicles (ATVs) and off-highway vehicles.
This resolution cancels that rule, removing those limits on off-road vehicle use.

supporters: Supporters say the January 13, 2025 NPS rule blocked ATVs and off-highway vehicles from areas of Glen Canyon that riders had used for years, and this resolution restores that access.
Supporters say off-road vehicle recreation brings tourism dollars to communities in northern Arizona and southeastern Utah, and the NPS restrictions hurt local businesses that depend on that traffic.
Supporters say Congress, not a federal agency, should decide how public land in Glen Canyon is used, and this resolution asserts that authority.
critics: Critics say the January 13, 2025 NPS rule was created to protect soil, habitat, and wildlife in Glen Canyon from ATV and off-highway vehicle damage, and canceling it removes those protections.
Critics say Glen Canyon spans a large protected area across two states, and without the January 2025 rule, there are no limits on where ATVs and off-highway vehicles can go in that area.
Critics say the NPS went through a formal public review process before issuing the January 2025 rule, and this resolution wipes out that work without a similar review.

119-hjres-87.one_liner: Cancel the EPA's permission for California to use its own heavy-duty truck emission rules
provisions: Takes away the EPA's April 2023 decision to give California special permission to enforce its own emission rules for heavy-duty trucks.
Federal law normally blocks states from writing their own vehicle pollution standards, but California can ask the EPA for a waiver — this bill cancels one such waiver the EPA approved.

The canceled permission covered California rules on heavy truck emissions, truck engine warranty and maintenance standards, airport shuttle pollution standards, and zero-emission powertrain standards.
Without this permission, California cannot enforce those specific truck emission rules under federal law.

supporters: Supporters say the EPA's April 2023 waiver lets California set its own heavy-duty truck emission rules, which forces trucking companies to meet two different sets of standards — one federal and one state — raising costs for the industry.

Supporters say canceling the waiver means one national standard applies to heavy-duty trucks, airport shuttles, and zero-emission powertrains, which they argue makes it easier for truck makers to build one product for the whole country.

Supporters say California's zero-emission truck and powertrain rules could reduce the number of diesel trucks available nationwide, affecting supply chains and small trucking businesses that cannot afford to switch fleets quickly.
critics: Critics say the April 2023 waiver allowed California to enforce its Heavy-Duty Vehicle Emission Warranty and Maintenance rules, which require truck makers to stand behind their engines longer — and canceling it removes that protection for California truck owners and operators.

Critics say California has held a special waiver right under the Clean Air Act for decades, and this resolution takes away permission the EPA already reviewed and approved, blocking the state from enforcing its Advanced Clean Trucks and Zero Emission Airport Shuttle standards.

Critics say without the waiver, California cannot enforce its zero-emission powertrain standards, which were designed to cut pollution in communities near ports and airports where heavy truck traffic is highest.

119-hjres-89.one_liner: Cancel an EPA waiver letting California set its own pollution limits on heavy-duty trucks
provisions: Under the Clean Air Act, California is the only state allowed to set its own vehicle pollution limits instead of following the national standard.
In January 2025, the EPA gave California permission to enforce its own pollution rules for heavy-duty trucks and engines.
Those rules focus on cutting nitrogen oxide (NOX), a gas that contributes to smog, from large trucks.
This bill cancels that EPA permission, so California's heavy-duty truck pollution rules can no longer take effect.
Only this one waiver is affected — not any other California vehicle emission waivers.

supporters: Supporters say that canceling the EPA waiver stops California from setting separate pollution rules for heavy-duty trucks, which forces truck makers to build one version of their engines for California and a different version for the rest of the country.

Supporters say that the Clean Air Act gives only one state — California — the power to set its own truck emission limits, and that this unequal treatment puts an unfair burden on the trucking industry that moves goods across all 50 states.
Supporters say that Congress, not the EPA, should decide whether a single state's rules can override the national standard for large commercial trucks.
critics: Critics say that blocking this waiver takes away a legal right California has held under the Clean Air Act for decades — the right to set stricter limits on nitrogen oxide from heavy-duty trucks and engines.

Critics say that NOX from large trucks is a major source of smog, and that California's Omnibus Low NOX rules were designed to reduce that pollution for the millions of people who live near major freight routes in the state.

Critics say that this resolution only cancels one specific waiver — the Heavy-Duty Vehicle Omnibus Low NOX waiver published January 6, 2025 — and leaves California with no approved path to enforce those cleaner truck standards.

119-sjres-11.one_liner: Cancel a rule requiring offshore oil and gas companies to report underwater archaeological sites
provisions: A September 2024 BOEM rule required oil and gas companies to file a report on underwater historical sites before getting permission to drill on the Outer Continental Shelf.
Companies had to identify any objects or sites at least 50 years old on the sea floor in the area they planned to work.
Before that 2024 rule, companies only had to file these reports if a BOEM official had a specific reason to think something was buried in the area.
This bill cancels the 2024 rule, so companies go back to only filing these reports when BOEM specifically asks.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the 2024 rule removes a requirement that forced all oil and gas companies to file archaeological reports before drilling on the Outer Continental Shelf, even when there was no sign that any historical site was present.

Supporters say the old system — where BOEM only asked for a report when a regional director had a specific reason to believe something was buried — was enough to protect sites without adding paperwork to every project.
Supporters say requiring companies to search for and report on any object 50 years or older across an entire planned work area adds cost and delays to energy development without a proven need.
critics: Critics say the 2024 rule protected underwater historical sites by making companies check the sea floor before drilling, and canceling it means companies go back to only filing reports when BOEM specifically asks — which critics say is often too late.

Critics say without the 2024 rule, oil and gas operators can begin work on the Outer Continental Shelf without identifying material remains of human life or activities on the sea floor, which could lead to the permanent destruction of those sites.

Critics say the old trigger — a BOEM official having a specific reason to believe something is present — leaves gaps, because officials may not have information about a site until after a company has already started work in the area.

119-sjres-13.one_liner: Bring back automatic approvals and simplified forms for some bank mergers
provisions: Some bank merger applications can get automatic approval again — a September 2024 rule had removed that option.
Banks applying to merge can use a simplified form again; that same 2024 rule had gotten rid of it.
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency reviews bank merger applications under the rules it had before September 2024.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution restores automatic approval for certain bank merger applications, which the September 2024 OCC rule had eliminated, allowing mergers that meet existing standards to move forward without added wait times.
Supporters say banks can again use the simplified application forms that the 2024 rule discontinued, which reduces the cost and time burden on community banks seeking to merge.
Supporters say returning to the pre-September 2024 OCC review process gives banks a stable, predictable set of rules that existed before the 2024 changes.
critics: Critics say the resolution brings back automatic approvals for bank mergers, meaning the OCC would no longer be required to conduct a full review of every application before it is granted.
Critics say restoring the streamlined application forms means regulators receive less detailed information about proposed mergers, making it harder to assess effects on competition or consumers.
Critics say the 2024 OCC rule was put in place to increase scrutiny of bank consolidation, and nullifying it returns oversight to a process critics said was not thorough enough.

119-sjres-12.one_liner: Cancel an EPA rule on how oil and gas companies pay methane emission fees
provisions: Cancels the EPA's November 2024 rules on how oil and gas companies must comply with the federal methane fee program.
Oil and gas companies no longer have formal guidelines for figuring out when their methane or greenhouse gas emissions are high enough to trigger annual fees.
Takes away the method that let companies subtract lower emissions from one location against higher emissions from another to reduce what they owe.
Also removes the situations where the EPA said certain companies or operations could skip paying the methane fee.

supporters: Supporters say the November 2024 EPA rule added steps — like the netting method and company exemptions — that go beyond what the methane fee law requires, and canceling it removes procedures that Congress never directly approved.

Supporters say the rule gave EPA officials the power to decide which oil and gas operations could skip paying the methane fee through exemptions, a decision supporters say should be made by Congress, not the agency.
Supporters say the compliance rules placed new reporting and calculation burdens on oil and gas companies before those companies had a chance to challenge them.
critics: Critics say canceling the rule removes the only official process oil and gas companies had for calculating when their methane emissions are high enough to trigger the annual fee under the Inflation Reduction Act's methane program.

Critics say the netting method — which let a company subtract lower emissions at one site from higher emissions at another — was the main tool for making sure operators were not charged more than they owed, and removing it leaves no replacement.
Critics say without these compliance rules, the EPA has no working system to collect the methane fee, which Congress set up to cut greenhouse gas emissions from the oil and gas sector.

119-sjres-10.one_liner: End the national energy emergency the President declared on January 20, 2025
provisions: Ends the national energy emergency that the President declared on January 20, 2025
Stops government agencies from using emergency powers to speed up approval of oil, gas, coal, uranium, biofuels, and other energy projects
Cuts the fast-track permitting that let agencies skip some environmental review steps for energy projects
Removes the military's emergency authority to build infrastructure to fix energy supply and transport problems
Cancels the order directing agencies to speed up energy infrastructure in the Northeast, West Coast, and Alaska

supporters: Supporters say ending this emergency stops agencies from using fast-track powers to skip environmental review steps for oil, gas, coal, and uranium projects, which they argue bypasses important public safety checks.
Supporters say removing the military's emergency construction authority means energy infrastructure decisions go back through normal approval processes, keeping civilian oversight in place.
Supporters say canceling the order to speed up energy projects in the Northeast, West Coast, and Alaska lets those regions follow standard rules instead of emergency shortcuts.
critics: Critics say ending the emergency will slow down approval of oil, gas, and other energy projects, making it harder to fix supply and infrastructure problems the President identified on January 20, 2025.
Critics say without fast-track permitting, energy infrastructure projects in the Northeast, West Coast, and Alaska will face longer delays, which could affect energy supply in those areas.

Critics say removing the military's authority to assess and fix energy transport problems leaves known vulnerabilities in the country's ability to move energy resources without a clear plan to address them.

119-sjres-31.one_liner: Cancel an EPA rule keeping tighter pollution limits on some factories that switched categories
provisions: Cancels an EPA rule published in September 2024.
That rule required factories releasing certain toxic chemicals to keep following stricter pollution limits even after they officially switched to a lower pollution category.
Once this bill passes, those factories can switch categories and follow the less strict rules that normally apply to smaller pollution sources.
The chemicals this covers are ones that stay in the environment for a long time and collect in the bodies of animals and people.

supporters: Supporters say the September 2024 EPA rule went beyond what Section 112 of the Clean Air Act allows, because it kept major source rules in place for factories that had already cut their emissions enough to qualify as area sources under the law.

Supporters say canceling this rule gives factories that reduced their toxic chemical releases a fair path to follow the less strict area source standards they legally earned, instead of being held to major source limits indefinitely.

Supporters say the rule created ongoing costs for facilities that had already made real pollution cuts, and that Congress — not the EPA — should decide if those stricter standards stay in place permanently.
critics: Critics say this bill lets factories that release persistent and bioaccumulative chemicals — ones that build up in human and animal bodies over time — switch to weaker pollution limits just by changing their official category on paper, without actually reducing harm.

Critics say the EPA published the September 2024 rule specifically to close a loophole where major industrial sources could reclassify as area sources to avoid the stricter emission standards under Clean Air Act Section 112, and this bill reopens that loophole.

Critics say communities living near these factories will face higher exposure to hazardous air pollutants that do not break down in the environment, because the less strict area source rules allow higher emission levels than the major source standards the EPA rule required.

119-sjres-26.one_liner: Block one proposed sale of military equipment and services to Israel
provisions: Stops one specific proposed military sale to Israel from going through.
The bill covers only this one sale — it does not change rules for any other sale or agreement with Israel.
The bill does not name what equipment or services are included — the source describes them only as 'certain defense articles and services.'
If this resolution passes both chambers and is signed, that one sale cannot be completed.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would use Congress's legal authority under the Arms Export Control Act to stop one proposed arms sale to Israel from being completed, giving lawmakers a direct role in approving major weapons transfers.
Supporters say the bill is narrow — it blocks only this one sale and does not change any other U.S.-Israel defense agreements — so it is a targeted check on this specific executive branch decision.

Supporters say Congress and the public have not been told what 'certain defense articles and services' are included in this sale, and the sale should not go forward without that information being made clear.
critics: Critics say blocking this one sale sends a signal to Israel and other U.S. allies that arms agreements approved by the executive branch can be reversed by Congress, which creates uncertainty in defense partnerships.

Critics say the resolution covers only this one sale and leaves all other U.S.-Israel agreements in place, so it does not reflect a real shift in policy but does damage a specific security commitment.

Critics say the executive branch determined this sale served U.S. national security interests, and a congressional disapproval vote overrides that judgment without replacing it with an alternative plan.

119-sjres-28.one_liner: Remove CFPB oversight from large digital payment apps
provisions: Large payment apps that handle at least 50 million transactions a year will no longer be reviewed by the CFPB.
