The CFPB published this oversight rule in December 2024 — this bill wipes it out.
Only nonbank companies running payment apps were covered by the rule — banks have their own separate regulators.
The 50 million transaction threshold was set to cover the biggest payment app companies, not small businesses.

supporters: Supporters say the bill uses Congress's formal process to cancel a rule published in December 2024, which they argue is the correct way to reject agency actions that Congress did not specifically authorize.

Supporters say nonbank payment app companies that process at least 50 million transactions a year would have faced new rounds of CFPB compliance reviews under the rule, and removing it reduces that burden.

Supporters say nonbank payment apps already operate under state and existing federal laws, so the December 2024 rule added a new layer of federal supervision without granting those companies any new rights or protections.
critics: Critics say the bill removes the only federal consumer watchdog review for the largest nonbank payment apps — those handling at least 50 million transactions a year — with no replacement oversight in place.

Critics say banks that offer payment services are reviewed by their own federal regulators, but without this rule, large nonbank payment apps at the 50-million-transaction threshold have no equivalent federal consumer supervisor.

Critics say the CFPB set the 50-million-transaction threshold specifically to exclude small businesses and focus only on the biggest nonbank payment platforms, so this bill removes oversight of the largest companies in the market.

119-sjres-18.one_liner: Cancel a rule that would have capped overdraft fees at $5 at large banks
provisions: Very large banks can charge overdraft fees above $5 — a Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rule published December 30, 2024 that set this cap is cancelled
The cancelled rule gave large banks three options: charge no more than $5 per overdraft, set a higher fee with a stated reason, or treat overdrafts as loans with required disclosures to customers
With the rule gone, very large banks return to whatever overdraft fee policies they had before December 2024
Overdraft fees are charged when a customer spends more money than is in their account and the bank covers the difference

supporters: Supporters say the December 2024 CFPB rule overstepped federal authority by capping overdraft fees at $5, a price the government had no legal right to set for private banks.
Supporters say cancelling the rule lets banks set fees that reflect the actual cost of covering a customer's overdraft, rather than being locked into a $5 limit that may not cover that cost.

Supporters say the rule's requirement to treat overdrafts as loans with Truth in Lending Act disclosures added compliance burdens on very large financial institutions that could raise costs elsewhere for customers.
critics: Critics say cancelling this rule allows very large banks to charge overdraft fees well above $5, which most often hit low-income customers who have little money in their accounts.

Critics say the CFPB rule gave banks a fair choice — charge $5, set a higher fee with a stated reason, or disclose overdrafts as credit — and killing it removes all three consumer protections at once.
Critics say without the December 2024 rule, very large banks return to pre-2024 overdraft policies that in some cases charged customers $30 or more per overdraft transaction.

119-sjres-3.one_liner: Cancel an IRS rule requiring crypto platform operators to report digital asset sales
provisions: Cancels an IRS rule from December 30, 2024 that required certain crypto brokers to report information about digital asset trades to the IRS.
The canceled rule covered people and platforms that help others trade crypto on decentralized networks — meaning networks with no single company in charge.
Those crypto platforms and operators are no longer required to send trade details to the IRS.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the December 30, 2024 IRS rule protects decentralized crypto platforms, which have no single company in charge, from being forced to collect and report user trade data they may have no way to gather.
Supporters say the IRS rule placed the same reporting duties on decentralized networks as on traditional brokers, even though those networks do not hold customer accounts or control transactions.

Supporters say removing this rule lets DeFi developers and users operate without building costly compliance systems that the open-source, automated nature of their platforms makes nearly impossible to run.
critics: Critics say canceling this rule means the IRS loses access to trade details from decentralized crypto platforms, making it harder to catch people who do not report digital asset gains on their taxes.
Critics say the December 30, 2024 rule was meant to close a gap where crypto trades on decentralized networks went unreported, and nullifying it leaves that gap open.

Critics say without broker reporting requirements on DeFi platforms, the tax system treats crypto traders differently than stock or bond traders, who must have their trades reported to the IRS by their brokers.

119-sjres-49.one_liner: End the national emergency Trump used to add tariffs on most imports
provisions: Ends the national emergency that President Trump declared on April 2, 2025
Removes the 10% tariff that was added to most goods imported into the United States
Removes the extra tariffs that were added on top of the 10% for certain countries

supporters: Supporters say ending the 10% tariff on most imported goods would lower costs for American businesses that rely on foreign parts and for consumers who buy imported products.
Supporters say removing the extra tariffs placed on specific countries would reduce prices across industries like retail and manufacturing that depend on those trading partners.
Supporters say Congress, not the president, should decide whether tariffs stay in place, and this resolution restores that oversight.
critics: Critics say the 10% tariff gives the U.S. leverage to push trading partners to lower their own barriers on American exports, and ending it removes that pressure.
Critics say removing the tariffs on imports would expose American manufacturers to lower-priced foreign competition they were previously shielded from.
Critics say President Trump declared the April 2, 2025 emergency using legal authority granted to the executive branch, and Congress should not use a joint resolution to override that power.

119-sjres-37.one_liner: End the national emergency that added extra tariffs on imports from Canada
provisions: Cancels the national emergency that President Trump declared on February 1, 2025.
That emergency added a 25% extra tax on most goods coming into the U.S. from Canada.
Canadian energy products had a lower extra tax of 10% instead of 25%.
Ending the emergency would remove those extra tariffs.

supporters: Supporters say removing the 25% tariff on Canadian goods would lower costs for U.S. businesses and consumers who buy products from Canada, since that extra tax raises the price of imports.
Supporters say the 10% tariff on Canadian energy would also end, which they argue would reduce energy costs for American households and industries that depend on Canadian oil and gas.
Supporters say Congress has the power to end a national emergency under the National Emergencies Act, and this resolution uses that process to check the President's use of emergency trade powers.
critics: Critics say the 25% tariff on Canadian imports was put in place to pressure Canada on border security and fentanyl trafficking, and ending it would remove that leverage before those issues are resolved.
Critics say lifting the tariffs could hurt U.S. industries that compete with Canadian goods, since those industries have been protected by the extra 25% tax since February 1, 2025.
Critics say the President, not Congress, should decide when a national emergency ends, and that this resolution oversteps the role of the legislative branch in foreign trade policy.

119-sjres-34.one_liner: Block a proposed U.S. sale of military equipment and services to Israel
provisions: Blocks a proposed U.S. government sale of military equipment and services to Israel.
Under U.S. law, Congress can vote to stop any proposed government-to-government arms sale before it is completed.
For this resolution to take effect, both the House and Senate must pass it and the President must sign it.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution uses Congress's legal power to block a government-to-government arms sale to Israel before it is completed, which they argue gives elected lawmakers a direct say in U.S. weapons transfers.
Supporters say stopping this sale would limit the U.S. supply of defense articles and services to Israel during an active conflict, which they argue could reduce civilian harm in affected areas.
Supporters say the joint resolution process — requiring both the House and Senate to pass it — is the proper constitutional check on executive branch arms sale decisions.
critics: Critics say blocking this sale would weaken a long-standing U.S. defense partnership with Israel, which relies on U.S.-government arms transfers under existing foreign military sale agreements.

Critics say the resolution would need to pass both chambers and be signed by the President to take effect, making it unlikely to succeed and primarily a symbolic vote rather than a binding policy change.

Critics say stopping the sale removes defense articles and services that Israel says it needs for its own security, and that cutting off a government-to-government sale mid-process breaks commitments already in motion.

119-sjres-55.one_liner: Cancel a federal safety rule for hydrogen fuel systems in vehicles
provisions: Blocks a rule from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) about how hydrogen fuel systems must be built and tested in cars and trucks
The rule set safety standards for compressed hydrogen storage tanks in vehicles that run on hydrogen fuel
Canceling the rule means those NHTSA standards no longer apply

supporters: Supporters say blocking the NHTSA rule removes a federal mandate on compressed hydrogen storage tank testing that duplicates SAE International's SAE J2579 standard, which the auto industry already follows for hydrogen fuel system safety.

Supporters say canceling the rule reduces compliance costs for hydrogen vehicle manufacturers, who would otherwise need to meet two overlapping sets of technical requirements for the same high-pressure storage tanks.

Supporters say the NHTSA rule was finalized without enough time for automakers to test and validate their compressed hydrogen storage systems to the new federal specifications before production deadlines.
critics: Critics say removing the NHTSA standard leaves no federal safety floor for compressed hydrogen storage tanks, which hold fuel at pressures up to 10,000 pounds per square inch in passenger vehicles.

Critics say manufacturers who have already begun redesigning vehicles to meet NHTSA's compressed hydrogen storage rules now face uncertainty about which requirements will apply when those models reach consumers.
Critics say blocking the rule means hydrogen vehicles sold in the U.S. will not have to pass the federal crash and leak tests that NHTSA designed specifically for high-pressure hydrogen fuel systems.

119-sjres-59.one_liner: Order the President to stop military attacks on Iran unless Congress votes to allow them
provisions: Tells the President to end any U.S. military attacks on Iran that Congress has not approved.
The President can only keep U.S. forces fighting Iran if Congress declares war on Iran or passes a law specifically saying it is allowed.
This applies to attacks on Iran that are already happening and any future attacks that start without a vote from Congress.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would require the President to stop any ongoing U.S. military attacks on Iran unless Congress votes to approve them, putting the power to start a war back in Congress's hands as the Constitution requires.

Supporters say that under this resolution, no future military strikes on Iran could happen without a formal declaration of war or a specific law from Congress, which prevents one person from making the decision to go to war alone.
Supporters say this directly addresses current hostilities by applying the rule to attacks that are already happening, not just future ones.
critics: Critics say requiring a congressional vote before continuing military action against Iran could slow the U.S. military's ability to respond quickly to threats from Iran or its allies in the region.

Critics say the President already has authority under the 2001 and 2002 Authorizations for Use of Military Force to respond to threats, and this resolution could block action that is already legally permitted.
Critics say that if Iran is actively threatening U.S. forces or allies, this resolution could force a pause in operations while Congress debates, creating a gap in national defense.

119-sjres-53.one_liner: Block one proposed arms sale to Qatar
provisions: Stops a specific U.S. government sale of weapons and military equipment to Qatar.
The sale was already proposed and going through the normal approval process before Congress stepped in to block it.

supporters: Supporters say Congress should block this sale because Qatar has ties to groups that the U.S. has designated as security threats, and sending weapons and military equipment there could put those arms in dangerous hands.
Supporters say the normal approval process for this sale did not give Congress enough say, and this resolution is the proper way for lawmakers to stop a weapons transfer they disagree with.
critics: Critics say blocking this sale would damage the U.S. relationship with Qatar, which hosts a major American military base used for operations across the Middle East.

Critics say the sale was already going through the standard government review process, and rejecting it without naming specific problems with the equipment or the deal sets a bad precedent for future arms agreements.

119-hjres-104.one_liner: Cancel a rule that blocked coal leasing on 1.7 million acres in Montana
provisions: About 1.7 million acres of public land near Miles City, Montana are now open to be considered for coal leasing.
A November 2024 rule had set zero of those acres open to coal companies; this bill cancels that rule.
Coal leasing is when a company pays the government for the right to mine coal on public land.
The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) is the federal agency that wrote the rule being canceled here.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the November 2024 rule reopens about 1.7 million acres near Miles City, Montana to coal leasing review, which could bring mining jobs and lease payments to the federal government.
Supporters say the BLM's rule blocked all coal leasing on those acres without giving Congress a say, and this bill restores that decision to elected lawmakers.
Supporters say coal companies in Montana can now apply to lease public land again, which they argue supports local economies that depend on coal mining.
critics: Critics say the 2024 BLM rule protected 1,745,040 acres from coal development based on land management studies, and canceling it removes those protections permanently under the Congressional Review Act.
Critics say reopening those acres to coal leasing consideration could affect grazing, water, and wildlife on public lands that ranchers and others in eastern Montana currently use.
Critics say the BLM went through a formal review process before issuing the November 2024 rule, and this bill wipes out that work without requiring a new environmental review.

119-hjres-106.one_liner: Remove protected status from 21 areas covering 3.6 million acres in Alaska's Central Yukon
provisions: Removes protected status from 21 areas in Alaska's Central Yukon that together cover about 3.6 million acres.
The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) had set aside those areas as protected zones in November 2024.
Those 21 areas go back to being managed under the land plan that was in place before November 2024.

supporters: Supporters say removing the November 2024 protections will let the BLM manage the 3.6 million acres in Alaska's Central Yukon under the older land plan, which allowed more uses like mining and energy development.
Supporters say the 21 protected zones were set by the BLM without enough input from Alaska communities and local industries that depend on access to those lands.
Supporters say Congress has the right under the Congressional Review Act to block agency rules like this BLM plan before they take full effect.
critics: Critics say this resolution would strip protected status from all 21 areas of critical environmental concern and research natural areas, covering about 3.6 million acres of Alaska wilderness.
Critics say returning to the pre-November 2024 land plan removes conservation rules the BLM put in place to protect specific ecosystems and wildlife habitats across the Central Yukon region.
Critics say nullifying the BLM's Resource Management Plan means the agency cannot put the same protections back in place without new approval from Congress.

119-hjres-78.one_liner: Remove endangered species protection for a Bay-Delta smelt fish population
provisions: Cancels a rule published July 30, 2024 that gave the San Francisco Bay-Delta longfin smelt endangered species status
Takes away the legal protections that come with being listed under the Endangered Species Act of 1973
The longfin smelt is a small fish found in the San Francisco Bay and Delta area of California's Pacific Coast

supporters: Supporters say removing the July 30, 2024 endangered listing will free up water for California farmers and cities, since Endangered Species Act protections for the longfin smelt have been used to limit water pumping from the San Francisco Bay-Delta.

Supporters say the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service rule was based on flawed science, and that the San Francisco Bay-Delta longfin smelt population does not meet the legal standard for endangered status under the Endangered Species Act of 1973.
Supporters say canceling this rule gives Congress a check on federal agency rulemaking, using the process allowed under chapter 8 of title 5 of the U.S. Code.
critics: Critics say removing the endangered listing strips away all Endangered Species Act protections for the San Francisco Bay-Delta longfin smelt, a fish found only in a specific part of California's Pacific Coast, which they say puts the population at risk of extinction.
Critics say the July 30, 2024 rule was based on a scientific review by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, and that overturning it through a congressional resolution bypasses that process.

Critics say once this joint resolution passes, the Fish and Wildlife Service is barred from issuing a substantially similar rule in the future without new congressional action, which could permanently block protections for the species.

117-hjres-100.one_liner: Force railroads and their workers to accept unratified labor agreements
provisions: Makes railroads and their unions accept the most recent agreements they negotiated but had not yet voted to approve.
Workers and rail companies cannot reject or renegotiate these deals — they become binding when this bill is signed.
This applies to any side agreements and local deals made between individual railroads and their workers that were not yet ratified.

supporters: Supporters say that making the tentative agreements binding stops a rail strike that could shut down freight and passenger service across the country, affecting millions of people who depend on trains to move food, fuel, and goods.

Supporters say that workers and rail companies already negotiated these deals at the table, so forcing both sides to accept them is fair — it locks in what they already agreed to without starting over.

Supporters say that local carrier agreements and side letters are included, which means workers at individual railroads get the specific terms their own company negotiated, not a one-size-fits-all deal.
critics: Critics say that workers never got to vote on these agreements, and making unratified deals binding takes away union members' right to accept or reject a contract that affects their pay, schedules, and working conditions.
Critics say that blocking any renegotiation — even for side letters and local deals — means railroads and unions cannot fix problems in the agreements before they become permanent.
Critics say that Congress stepping in to force a contract on workers sets a precedent that companies can walk away from bargaining, knowing the government will impose a deal if talks break down.

119-hjres-105.one_liner: Cancel a 2025 BLM land plan limiting oil, gas, and coal activity in North Dakota
provisions: The Bureau of Land Management issued a land management plan in January 2025 for federal land in North Dakota — this bill cancels it.
Oil and gas development can again take place on low-potential federal land in North Dakota, where it was restricted under the 2025 plan.
Coal companies can again apply to lease federal land more than four miles from existing mines in North Dakota.
North Dakota's federal land goes back to being managed under the rules that were in place before January 2025.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the January 2025 plan restores access for oil and gas companies to low-potential federal land in North Dakota that the 2025 rules had restricted.
Supporters say coal companies can again apply to lease federal land more than four miles from existing mines in North Dakota, which the 2025 plan had prohibited.
Supporters say returning to the 1988 land management rules restores the same terms that allowed oil, gas, and coal development on North Dakota federal land before the January 2025 plan took effect.
critics: Critics say the 2025 plan restricted oil and gas development on low-potential federal land because drilling there was not expected to produce much output, so opening it again carries environmental risk for little economic gain.
Critics say the 2025 plan's four-mile limit on new coal leasing was designed to keep leasing near existing mines and limit how far coal operations spread across North Dakota's federal land.

Critics say reverting to the 1988 land management rules means North Dakota federal land will be managed under decisions made nearly 40 years ago, before newer surveys and environmental data were collected.

117-sjres-29.one_liner: Cancel a Department of Labor rule requiring companies to enforce COVID-19 vaccine-or-test policies
provisions: Cancel a Department of Labor rule issued on November 5, 2021, that set COVID-19 policies for large workplaces.
Under that rule, companies with 100 or more employees had to create a vaccine-or-test policy for workers.
Each worker had to either be fully vaccinated against COVID-19 or get tested for the virus every week.
If this bill passes, those workplace requirements no longer apply.

supporters: Supporters say the Department of Labor rule from November 5, 2021 forced companies with 100 or more employees to track and enforce vaccine or weekly testing requirements, creating paperwork and costs that fell on employers.
Supporters say workers at large companies should be able to choose their own health decisions without a federal rule requiring them to get vaccinated or submit to weekly COVID-19 tests.
Supporters say canceling this rule removes a mandate that applied to millions of workers across the country and returns that decision to employers and employees.
critics: Critics say the November 5, 2021 rule was designed to protect workers at large companies from COVID-19 spread, and removing it takes away a safety standard that required unvaccinated employees to get tested every week.
Critics say without the rule, companies with 100 or more employees no longer have to put any COVID-19 vaccination or testing policy in place, leaving workers with no guaranteed workplace protection.

Critics say the Department of Labor created this emergency standard because COVID-19 was still spreading widely in workplaces, and canceling it removes that protection before the public health situation was resolved.

117-sjres-13.one_liner: Cancel an EEOC rule requiring the agency to share its reasoning with employers before settling
provisions: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, or EEOC, is the federal agency that handles workplace discrimination complaints.
When the EEOC finds evidence that a company discriminated against workers, it issues a formal finding.
The canceled rule said the EEOC had to share the facts and legal reasons behind its finding with the employer.
That had to happen before the two sides could try to reach a settlement.
This resolution cancels that rule, so the EEOC no longer has to share those details first.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution restores the EEOC's ability to run settlement talks without having to hand over its full case file to employers before those talks begin.

Supporters say the old rule gave employers a chance to pick apart the EEOC's factual and legal reasoning before agreeing to settle, which supporters say slowed down or blocked relief for workers who faced discrimination.
Supporters say canceling the rule puts the EEOC back in control of when and how it shares information during the settlement process.
critics: Critics say the canceled rule was a fairness protection for employers, because it required the EEOC to explain the facts and legal reasons behind a discrimination finding before asking a company to settle.
Critics say without that rule, employers are asked to agree to a settlement without knowing the specific evidence or legal basis the EEOC used to reach its finding.
Critics say removing the rule makes it harder for employers, especially small businesses, to decide whether the EEOC's finding is accurate before entering the settlement process.

117-sjres-14.one_liner: Bring back EPA methane emission limits on oil and gas operations
provisions: Cancels an EPA rule published in September 2020 that had removed limits on how much methane oil and gas operations could release.
Brings back the methane emission limits that were in place before the 2020 rule changed them.
These limits apply to oil and gas equipment that is new, rebuilt, or changed — not to older, existing equipment.
Congress used a law called the Congressional Review Act, which lets it cancel recent federal rules within a set window of time.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would bring back methane emission limits that the EPA removed in its September 2020 rule, restoring limits on how much methane new and rebuilt oil and gas equipment can release into the air.
Supporters say methane is a potent heat-trapping gas, and removing the 2020 rule means the limits would apply again to new, reconstructed, and modified oil and gas sources under the Clean Air Act.
Supporters say Congress has the right to use the Congressional Review Act to cancel federal rules, and this resolution is a direct check on an EPA decision they say weakened air quality protections.
critics: Critics say restoring these methane limits puts new rules on oil and gas companies that build or upgrade equipment, raising the cost of expanding domestic energy production.

Critics say the 2020 EPA rule it cancels had removed what the agency called duplicative regulations, and this resolution forces companies to follow overlapping federal requirements for new and rebuilt sources.

Critics say the resolution only affects new, reconstructed, or modified equipment — not existing operations — which they argue makes the regulatory burden fall unevenly on companies trying to invest in updated infrastructure.

117-sjres-31.one_liner: Block one proposed sale of military equipment to Saudi Arabia
provisions: Blocks one sale of military equipment to Saudi Arabia that the U.S. government had already approved.
If this passes, the equipment cannot be sold or transferred to Saudi Arabia.
For this to become law, it must pass both the House and the Senate, then be signed by the President — or passed again with enough votes to override a veto.

supporters: Supporters say the sale should be blocked because Saudi Arabia has used U.S.-made weapons in Yemen, where air strikes have killed thousands of civilians, and allowing more military equipment to flow there could make the U.S. responsible for further harm.
Supporters say Congress has the legal right under the Arms Export Control Act to review and stop arms sales approved by the executive branch, and this resolution is a direct use of that power.
Supporters say halting the transfer gives the U.S. a tool to pressure Saudi Arabia over the treatment of political dissidents and journalists, which an approved sale removes.
critics: Critics say blocking the sale damages the U.S.-Saudi security partnership, which supports American military access to bases in the Middle East and helps counter Iranian influence in the region.
Critics say the sale already passed a formal government review and was found to meet U.S. national security standards, so a congressional override substitutes political judgment for that process.
Critics say canceling an approved defense contract could cost American manufacturing jobs and weaken U.S. arms exporters competing against Russian and Chinese suppliers for future deals.

117-sjres-15.one_liner: Cancel a 2020 rule defining when a bank counts as a lender
provisions: Cancels a rule the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency published in October 2020.
That rule said a bank counts as a lender only if it was named in the loan agreement when the loan was made.
The rule also counted a bank as a lender if it provided the money for the loan at the time it was made.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the October 2020 Office of the Comptroller of the Currency rule would close a loophole that lets payday lenders partner with banks to charge high interest rates that state laws would otherwise ban.
Supporters say the rule allowed non-bank lenders to avoid state consumer protection laws by simply having a bank's name on the loan agreement at the time the loan was made.
Supporters say nullifying this rule would give states back the power to enforce their own interest rate caps on loans made to their residents.
critics: Critics say the October 2020 Office of the Comptroller of the Currency rule gave banks a clear legal test — a bank is the lender if it is named in the loan agreement when the loan is made.
Critics say removing the rule about who funded the loan when it was made creates legal uncertainty for banks that work with outside companies to offer loans to customers.
Critics say canceling this rule could reduce access to credit for borrowers who rely on partnerships between banks and financial technology companies.

117-sjres-37.one_liner: Cancel the CDC rule requiring masks on planes, trains, and buses
provisions: Removes the CDC rule from February 3, 2021 that required people to wear masks on airplanes, trains, buses, and at airports and transit stations.
That rule applied to all public transportation to slow the spread of COVID-19.
Once canceled, there is no longer a federal mask rule for travelers on public transportation.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the CDC's February 3, 2021 rule would end the federal requirement for travelers to wear masks on airplanes, trains, and buses, giving people the freedom to choose for themselves.
Supporters say the CDC mask rule for public transportation was put in place for COVID-19, and Congress has the right under chapter 8 of title 5 to cancel agency rules it did not vote on.

Supporters say removing the federal mask mandate for airports and transit stations lets airlines, train companies, and bus operators set their own health policies instead of following a one-size-fits-all federal rule.
critics: Critics say the CDC's February 3, 2021 rule was designed to slow the spread of COVID-19 on planes, trains, and buses, where people sit close together for long periods, and canceling it removes the only federal protection for travelers in those spaces.

Critics say once this resolution passes, there will be no federal mask rule covering public transportation at all, which could put older travelers and people with health conditions at greater risk in airports and transit stations.

Critics say Congress is using the Congressional Review Act to block a public health rule made by medical experts at the CDC, taking away a tool that was meant to protect all passengers on public conveyances.

117-sjres-32.one_liner: Cancel a federal rule requiring COVID-19 vaccines for health care workers
provisions: Cancels a rule from November 5, 2021 that required health care workers to be fully vaccinated against COVID-19.
Health care facilities that take Medicare or Medicaid money had to follow this vaccine rule as a condition of getting that money.
If this resolution passes, those facilities no longer have to require COVID-19 vaccines for their staff.

supporters: Supporters say removing the rule would let health care facilities that take Medicare or Medicaid money decide their own vaccine policies instead of being forced by the federal government to require COVID-19 shots for all staff.

Supporters say the November 5, 2021 rule threatened facilities with losing Medicare and Medicaid funding if they did not require vaccines, and canceling it protects those facilities from that financial pressure.
Supporters say staff who work at Medicare and Medicaid facilities should not have to choose between getting a COVID-19 vaccine and keeping their job.
critics: Critics say the November 5, 2021 rule required staff vaccination as a condition of Medicare and Medicaid participation, and canceling it removes a protection for patients — including elderly and low-income people — who are most at risk from COVID-19.

Critics say health care workers who are not vaccinated against COVID-19 could spread the virus to vulnerable patients in Medicare and Medicaid facilities, and this resolution takes away the federal rule that was meant to stop that.

Critics say CMS set the vaccine requirement because health care facilities serve sick people, and ending that rule for all facilities that receive Medicare or Medicaid funding raises the risk of COVID-19 outbreaks in those settings.

117-sjres-35.one_liner: Block one proposed arms sale to Egypt
provisions: Blocks a sale of certain military weapons and services from the U.S. to Egypt.
Congress would use its power to reject this specific sale before it goes through.

supporters: Supporters say Congress should use its power to block this sale because Egypt has been cited by the U.S. State Department for human rights abuses, and sending weapons could allow those abuses to continue.

Supporters say the Arms Export Control Act gives Congress the right to reject specific foreign military sales, and this resolution uses that law to stop these defense articles and services from being transferred to Egypt.
Supporters say blocking the sale sends a message that the U.S. will not approve arms transfers to governments under human rights scrutiny, without ending the broader U.S.-Egypt relationship.
critics: Critics say rejecting this sale weakens the U.S.-Egypt security partnership, which helps the U.S. maintain stability in the Middle East and access to the Suez Canal.

Critics say blocking the transfer of these defense articles and services pushes Egypt to buy weapons from other countries, like Russia or China, reducing U.S. influence over how those weapons are used.
Critics say the executive branch negotiated this sale under existing law, and using a joint resolution to override it limits the President's ability to manage foreign policy and military alliances.

117-sjres-38.one_liner: End the COVID-19 emergency the President declared on March 13, 2020
provisions: Ends the COVID-19 national emergency that the President declared on March 13, 2020.
Special powers that federal agencies were given because of that emergency would end.
Programs and rules that were only active because of the emergency declaration would stop being in effect.

supporters: Supporters say ending the March 13, 2020 emergency declaration would stop special powers that federal agencies were given during COVID-19, returning government programs to the normal rules that were in place before the emergency.

Supporters say the National Emergencies Act gives Congress the right to end a presidential emergency declaration, and they argue the COVID-19 crisis no longer rises to the level needed to keep those powers active.

Supporters say programs and funding streams that only exist because of the emergency declaration — including certain FEMA disaster funds tied to it — would stop, which they say is the correct step now that COVID-19 is no longer a public crisis.
critics: Critics say ending the emergency would also stop a federal rule that let the health department skip its normal approval process, which allowed millions of people to get medical care faster during COVID-19 without waiting for standard reviews.

Critics say the emergency let the federal Medicare and Medicaid agency pause reviews to check who still qualifies for Medicaid, and ending the emergency could cause low-income families to lose health coverage before those reviews are finished.

Critics say the emergency allowed doctors to see Medicare patients by video call from their homes without the usual location rules, and ending it could cut off that option for patients in rural areas who have no other way to reach a doctor.

117-sjres-33.one_liner: Raise the U.S. debt limit by $2.5 trillion
provisions: Raises the cap on how much money the federal government can borrow, from about $36.1 trillion to about $38.6 trillion
The debt limit is a legal ceiling on how much the government can borrow to pay bills Congress has already approved spending
Without this increase, the government would not be allowed to borrow more money to cover those approved costs
The new borrowing cap stays in place until Congress votes to change it again

supporters: Supporters say that without raising the borrowing cap from $36.1 trillion to $38.6 trillion, the government could not pay bills that Congress already approved — including Social Security checks, military salaries, and Medicare payments.
Supporters say the debt limit does not allow new spending; it only lets the government borrow money to cover costs that have already been voted on and approved by law.

Supporters say failing to raise the $2.5 trillion cap could cause the U.S. to miss payments on its debt for the first time, which could raise borrowing costs for the government and for everyday Americans.
critics: Critics say raising the cap by $2.5 trillion, bringing total allowed debt to $38.6 trillion, adds to a debt load that already costs hundreds of billions of dollars per year in interest payments alone.
Critics say the new $38.6 trillion cap has no expiration date, meaning Congress faces no deadline to address borrowing levels until it chooses to vote again.
Critics say repeated debt limit increases allow Congress to approve more spending without making equal cuts elsewhere, adding to the total amount owed by the federal government.

117-sjres-60.one_liner: Cancel a 2022 rule setting requirements for federal charter school grants
provisions: Cancels a Department of Education rule published on July 6, 2022.
That rule set the requirements and selection process for who could get federal Charter Schools Program grants.
The grants covered went to state governments, charter management organizations, and individual charter school developers.

supporters: Supporters say the 2022 Department of Education rule added new selection criteria that made it harder for state governments, charter management organizations, and charter school developers to qualify for federal Charter Schools Program grants.

Supporters say canceling the rule returns the grant process to earlier standards that let more types of charter schools compete for federal funding without meeting the added requirements set in July 2022.
Supporters say the rule's priorities favored certain applicants over others, limiting which charter management organizations and developers could access grants under the Charter Schools Program.
critics: Critics say the 2022 rule required Charter Schools Program grant applicants to show their schools would not harm nearby public schools, and canceling it removes that protection for communities.

Critics say the rule set open enrollment requirements as part of the selection criteria for state entity grants and developer grants, and nullifying it means federal funds could go to charter schools without those conditions.

Critics say removing the rule's requirements lets charter management organizations and developers receive federal grants without having to meet standards designed to protect students with disabilities and English learners.

117-sjres-39.one_liner: Cancel a federal rule requiring vaccines and masks in Head Start programs
provisions: Head Start programs give early learning and services to low-income children.
A November 2021 rule required Head Start staff and volunteers to get COVID-19 vaccines and wear masks.
Staff and volunteers at Head Start programs would no longer need to get COVID-19 vaccines or wear masks.

supporters: Supporters say removing the vaccine requirement gives Head Start programs the freedom to hire more staff, since some workers left or refused to join because of the mandate.
Supporters say the 2021 rule forced Head Start programs to follow federal health rules that Congress never voted on, and this resolution restores congressional control over those decisions.
Supporters say mask requirements for staff and volunteers in Head Start classrooms were never approved by lawmakers, and nullifying the rule corrects that process.
critics: Critics say the 2021 rule protected low-income children in Head Start — a group less likely to have access to private healthcare — by requiring staff to be vaccinated against COVID-19.
Critics say removing the mask requirement means young children in Head Start programs, who are too young to be vaccinated, lose a key layer of protection from adults around them.

Critics say the Department of Health and Human Services followed the law when it issued the November 2021 rule, and nullifying it removes a safety standard that was already in place for thousands of Head Start sites.

117-sjres-55.one_liner: Bring back the 2020 rules for how the government reviews environmental effects before major projects
provisions: Cancels a rule the Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) put in place in April 2022.
The 2022 rule had switched back to environmental review guidelines that were used before 2020; this bill cancels it and brings the 2020 rules back.
Under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), federal agencies must review how their actions affect the environment — this bill determines which version of those review rules applies.

supporters: Supporters say that canceling the 2022 CEQ rule brings back the 2020 environmental review rules, which they argue allowed federal agencies to complete NEPA reviews faster by setting clearer time limits and narrowing the scope of required analysis.
Supporters say the 2020 rules reduced delays for infrastructure, energy, and transportation projects by limiting how many indirect effects federal agencies had to study during environmental reviews.
Supporters say restoring the 2020 rules gives project developers more certainty about how long the federal review process will take.
critics: Critics say this resolution cancels the 2022 CEQ rule that had restored longstanding NEPA review standards used for decades before the 2020 changes, which critics argue weakened protections for communities living near federal projects.

Critics say the 2022 rule required agencies to look at a broader range of environmental effects, including climate impacts, and that canceling it means fewer of those effects will be studied before projects are approved.
Critics say bringing back the 2020 rules makes it harder for the public — especially low-income communities near federal projects — to participate in the NEPA review process.

117-sjres-46.one_liner: Cancel a 2022 rule that changed how asylum officers screen people during fast-track deportation
provisions: Asylum screening in fast-track deportation cases goes back to the process used before March 2022
The three-part test is restored: officers check separately for a credible fear of persecution, a reasonable chance of persecution, and a reasonable chance of torture
Under the 2022 rule, those three checks had been replaced by one combined test — a single 'credible fear of persecution or torture' — which no longer applies

supporters: Supporters say the 2022 rule replaced three separate checks — credible fear of persecution, reasonable chance of persecution, and reasonable chance of torture — with a single combined test, and restoring all three checks means each type of danger is reviewed on its own terms.

Supporters say the single combined test in the 2022 rule made it harder for officers to distinguish between different legal grounds for protection, and the three-part test gives a clearer structure for deciding who qualifies under expedited removal screening.
critics: Critics say the 2022 rule was built to make fast-track deportation screening faster by combining three checks into one, and reversing it will slow down screening for asylum seekers already in expedited removal.

Critics say going back to the three-part test raises the number of separate hurdles an asylum seeker must clear before getting a full hearing, and this could lead to more people being deported before their claims are fully reviewed.

117-sjres-41.one_liner: Reinstate 2019-era limits on abortion counseling and referrals at federally funded family planning clinics
provisions: Cancels a rule from October 2021 that changed how federally funded family planning clinics operate.
Clinics must follow the rules set in May 2019 instead.
Under those rules, doctors at these clinics cannot counsel patients about abortion or refer them to abortion providers.
When a clinic provides both family planning and abortion services, those activities must be kept physically and financially separate.
Removes a health equity focus that the 2021 rule had added to these programs.

supporters: Supporters say that putting the 2019 rules back in place keeps federal Title X family planning dollars from going to clinics that give abortion referrals, which Congress intended when it separated family planning funding from abortion services.

Supporters say the rule should require physical and financial separation between abortion-related activities and family planning activities, so taxpayer-funded programs stay focused on services like birth control, STI testing, and cancer screenings.
Supporters say removing the 2021 rule stops the federal government from requiring family planning providers to counsel patients about abortion as part of their standard care.
critics: Critics say nullifying this rule would force doctors at federally funded clinics to withhold information about abortion from patients who ask, limiting what medical providers can legally tell patients about all of their pregnancy options.

Critics say returning to the 2019 physical and financial separation requirement makes it harder for clinics that serve low-income patients to operate, because maintaining two separate facilities or accounting systems raises costs for providers who may already have limited budgets.

Critics say removing the health equity focus added in the 2021 rule takes away a standard that directed family planning programs to reduce gaps in care for patients based on race, income, and geography.

117-sjres-63.one_liner: End the national COVID-19 emergency declared on March 13, 2020
provisions: Ends the national emergency that President Trump declared on March 13, 2020 for COVID-19.
Once ended, any special government powers or rules tied to that emergency declaration stop applying.

supporters: Supporters say the March 13, 2020 emergency gave the president power to waive federal contracting rules and redirect FEMA disaster funds without a congressional vote, and this resolution ends that authority.
Supporters say the emergency let the Executive Branch suspend specific Medicare billing rules since 2020 without Congress passing a new law, and ending it returns that decision to Congress.

Supporters say the resolution ends the president's Stafford Act authority, which has allowed the federal government to fund COVID-related costs outside the normal budget approval process since March 2020.
critics: Critics say ending the emergency would cut off FEMA reimbursements to state and local governments for COVID-related costs that have been paid out since March 2020.
Critics say Medicare telehealth waivers that let millions of seniors see doctors by video and get reimbursed through Medicare are tied to the emergency and could stop if the resolution passes.
Critics say the Medicaid continuous enrollment rule — which has prevented low-income people from losing Medicaid coverage since 2020 — depends on the emergency declaration staying active.

118-hjres-26.one_liner: Cancel a DC law that changed criminal definitions, sentencing rules, and jury trial rights
provisions: Throws out a Washington DC law passed in 2022 that changed how crimes are defined in DC courts.
The cancelled law had changed the rules for how judges decide sentences for people convicted of crimes.
The cancelled law had given people accused of some lower-level crimes the right to ask for a jury trial instead of a judge-only trial.
Congress has the power to cancel DC laws, and this bill uses that power to stop the 2022 law from taking effect.

supporters: Supporters say Congress was right to cancel the 2022 DC law because the changes to sentencing guidelines would have made punishments lighter for people convicted of crimes in DC.
Supporters say the 2022 law expanded jury trial rights for lower-level crimes, which they argue would slow down DC courts and make it harder to process cases.
Supporters say Congress has a duty under the Constitution to review DC laws, and this bill is a proper use of that power to block changes they believe would weaken public safety.
critics: Critics say Congress is overriding a law that DC's own elected council passed, taking away the city's ability to set its own criminal justice rules.
Critics say the 2022 law made DC criminal codes clearer by adding written definitions for parts of crimes, and canceling it leaves outdated and vague rules in place.
Critics say giving people accused of certain misdemeanors the right to a jury trial is a basic legal protection, and this bill removes that option for DC residents.

118-hjres-109.one_liner: Cancel an SEC accounting rule for companies that hold cryptocurrency for customers
provisions: Since March 2022, an SEC rule required companies that hold cryptocurrency for their customers to list those holdings as debts on their financial records.
This bill removes that requirement — companies no longer have to record customer crypto as a debt on their books.
In October 2023, a government watchdog agency found this SEC bulletin counted as a formal federal rule, giving Congress the power to vote to cancel it.
Congress used a law that lets it cancel recent federal rules by a majority vote in both chambers.

supporters: Supporters say the SEC's March 2022 rule forced banks and companies holding crypto for customers to list those assets as debts on their balance sheets, which made it harder for regulated banks to offer crypto services to customers.

Supporters say removing this rule lets banks and financial companies hold cryptocurrency on behalf of customers without it counting against their financial health, which opens the door for more mainstream companies to offer crypto storage.

Supporters say Congress had the legal right to cancel this rule after a government watchdog found in October 2023 that the SEC bulletin counted as a formal federal rule under the Congressional Review Act.
critics: Critics say the SEC's March 2022 rule was designed to protect customers by making sure companies that hold crypto clearly show those obligations on their books, and removing it reduces transparency about who is responsible if customer funds are lost.

Critics say that without the requirement to record customer crypto holdings as debts, companies may take on more risk with those assets without it showing up in their financial records, leaving customers less protected.

Critics say the SEC created this rule specifically to address the risks of holding crypto for users, and canceling it through a Congressional vote bypasses the normal process for changing financial safety rules.

118-hjres-24.one_liner: Cancel a DC law that let non-citizens vote in local elections
provisions: Non-citizens living in DC can no longer vote in DC local elections.
DC passed a law in 2022 letting non-citizens vote in DC local elections if they lived there and met other requirements.
Congress canceled that DC law.

supporters: Supporters say voting is a right tied to U.S. citizenship, and allowing noncitizens to vote in DC local elections — as the 2022 DC law did — blurs that line for the roughly 50,000 noncitizen residents who would have been eligible.

Supporters say Congress has the power to review and cancel DC laws under the U.S. Constitution, and used that power here to block a rule that let people who are not citizens decide who runs DC's local government.
Supporters say local elections, like those for DC Mayor and DC Council, shape laws that apply to all residents, and only citizens should have a say in choosing those officials.
critics: Critics say DC's 2022 law only applied to local DC elections — not federal ones — and canceling it takes away a voice from noncitizen residents who live, work, and pay taxes in DC.
Critics say Congress stepping in to nullify a law passed by DC's own elected council limits DC's ability to govern itself, since DC residents have no voting representation in Congress to push back.

Critics say noncitizen residents who met DC's residency and other requirements under the 2022 law are directly affected by local DC decisions on schools, housing, and public safety, but now have no vote in choosing the leaders who make those decisions.

118-hjres-27.one_liner: Cancel a 2023 rule that expanded federal oversight of rivers, streams, and wetlands
provisions: The Clean Water Act is the main federal law protecting rivers, streams, and wetlands from pollution.
In January 2023, the EPA and Army Corps of Engineers published a new rule about which water bodies fall under that law.
It widened the list — covering more rivers, streams, and wetlands as "Waters of the United States."
This resolution cancels the 2023 rule.
After that, the 2020 rule takes effect again — it covered a smaller set of rivers, streams, and wetlands.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the 2023 rule and returning to the 2020 rule would remove federal oversight from streams and wetlands that are not directly connected to larger navigable waters, giving farmers and land developers more control over how they use their own property.

Supporters say the 2023 rule's wider definition of 'Waters of the United States' gave the EPA and Army Corps of Engineers the power to require permits for ditches, ponds, and seasonal streams on private land, creating costs and delays for agriculture and construction.

Supporters say Congress, not federal agencies, should decide which water bodies fall under the Clean Water Act, and using the Congressional Review Act to cancel the 2023 rule is a way to reassert that authority.
critics: Critics say returning to the narrower 2020 definition removes Clean Water Act protections from millions of miles of streams and tens of millions of acres of wetlands that filter pollution before it reaches drinking water sources.

Critics say the 2023 rule restored protections that had been in place for decades under the Clean Water Act, and canceling it leaves rivers and wetlands downstream from unprotected water bodies more exposed to contamination.

Critics say wetlands covered by the 2023 rule but not the 2020 rule absorb floodwaters and reduce storm damage, and removing federal oversight of those wetlands increases flood risk for nearby communities.

118-hjres-42.one_liner: Cancel DC rules on police neck restraints, body cameras, and discipline records
provisions: Removes DC rules that stopped police from using certain neck holds
Removes DC requirements for extra steps officers had to follow when using body cameras
Removes DC rules that made police discipline records available to the public

supporters: Supporters say the DC Council overstepped by passing rules that limit how police can respond to dangerous situations, and that removing the ban on certain neck restraints gives officers more tools to safely control resisting suspects.
Supporters say the extra body camera steps required by the DC act slowed officers down and that removing those requirements lets police focus on doing their jobs instead of added paperwork.
Supporters say Congress has the authority under the Home Rule Act to reject DC laws, and this resolution uses that power to protect public safety.
critics: Critics say the resolution removes a ban on neck restraints that DC passed after research showed those holds have caused deaths and serious injuries during arrests.
Critics say striking down the DC law takes away public access to police discipline records, making it harder for DC residents to know if officers have a history of misconduct.
Critics say the body camera rules that are being removed were meant to make sure footage was recorded and preserved correctly, and removing them reduces accountability for how police use force.

118-hjres-45.one_liner: Cancel a federal rule that paused student loan payments and erased some debt
provisions: Brings back federal student loan payments that were paused by a 2022 Department of Education rule
Student loan debt that was set to be wiped out under that rule would no longer be canceled
The 2022 rule from the Department of Education — put in place on October 12, 2022 — no longer applies

supporters: Supporters say the October 12, 2022 rule let the Department of Education cancel federal student loan debt without a vote in Congress, and that Congress — not a federal agency — should decide how to spend or forgive that money.
Supporters say bringing back loan payments means borrowers who agreed to repay their loans are held to the same terms as borrowers who already paid theirs off, treating all borrowers the same way.
Supporters say wiping out student loan debt through the 2022 rule would cost the federal government hundreds of billions of dollars that was never approved through the normal budget process.
critics: Critics say the 2022 rule paused payments for millions of federal student loan borrowers, and ending that pause forces those borrowers to restart payments even if their financial situations have not improved.
Critics say debt that was set to be discharged under the October 12, 2022 rule will now remain on borrowers' records, meaning people who expected that relief will owe the full amount again.
Critics say lower-income borrowers and those who attended schools that closed or misled students are among the groups most affected by losing the debt discharge the 2022 rule was meant to provide.

118-hjres-30.one_liner: Cancel a rule letting retirement fund managers consider climate factors when investing
provisions: Cancels a Department of Labor rule from December 2022.
That rule let managers of workplace retirement and pension plans factor in climate change and other social issues when choosing investments.
Under the same rule, those managers could also use climate and social concerns when voting on shareholder decisions on behalf of plan members.
Removing this rule takes away the explicit permission to use those factors in investment and voting choices.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the December 2022 Department of Labor rule will refocus retirement plan managers on financial returns only, removing pressure to weigh climate or social factors that may not improve investment performance.

Supporters say the rule gave retirement plan managers permission to vote on shareholder resolutions and board nominations using climate and social criteria, and canceling it ensures those votes reflect members' financial interests instead.
Supporters say workers in pension and retirement plans did not choose to have their savings used to advance environmental or social goals, and this resolution removes that option from plan managers.
critics: Critics say the December 2022 rule allowed retirement plan managers to account for climate-related financial risks — like stranded fossil fuel assets — and canceling it may leave workers exposed to those risks in their retirement accounts.

Critics say removing the rule creates legal uncertainty for retirement plan managers, who may now face liability for using climate or environmental data even when that data is financially relevant to their investment decisions.

Critics say the rule also covered shareholder voting rights, and canceling it takes away a tool plan managers used to push companies for disclosures that could affect the long-term value of workers' retirement savings.

118-hjres-39.one_liner: Cancel a rule that put tariffs on hold for solar panels from four countries
provisions: A September 2022 Department of Commerce rule put tariffs on hold for solar panels finished in Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, or Vietnam using parts made in China.
To get that tariff hold, a panel could not already be facing a separate trade penalty.
This resolution cancels that 2022 rule.
Solar panels from those four countries that had been avoiding tariffs under the old rule would face tariffs again.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the 2022 rule means solar panels from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam that used Chinese-made parts will face tariffs again, closing a gap that allowed those imports to avoid trade penalties.

Supporters say the 2022 Commerce Department rule let Chinese-made solar panel parts enter the U.S. without the extra fees — designed to protect U.S. factories from cheaper foreign competition — that were already in place for Chinese goods.

Supporters say U.S. solar cell and module manufacturers, who compete directly with imports from those four countries, lost sales because the tariff hold kept foreign panel prices lower than they would otherwise be.
critics: Critics say bringing tariffs back on panels from those four countries will raise costs for U.S. solar energy projects that planned their budgets around the lower prices the 2022 rule made possible.

Critics say the 2022 rule was already narrow — a solar panel could only avoid tariffs if it was not already facing a separate trade penalty — so the resolution removes a limited protection, not a broad loophole.

Critics say ending the tariff hold will disrupt supply chains for U.S. solar installers and developers who have been sourcing panels from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam under the terms the 2022 rule set out.

118-hjres-44.one_liner: Stop treating guns with stabilizing braces as rifles under the National Firearms Act
provisions: Guns with stabilizing braces no longer need to meet the registration rules that apply to rifles under federal law.
An ATF rule published on January 31, 2023 had set up a test for deciding when a gun with an attached brace counts as a rifle.
Under that rule, some guns with stabilizing braces were classified as rifles and had to be registered with the federal government.
This bill cancels that ATF rule.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the January 31, 2023 ATF rule means guns with stabilizing braces will no longer be forced to go through the registration process that applies to rifles under the National Firearms Act.
Supporters say the ATF rule created an unclear test that left millions of legal gun owners uncertain about whether their firearms had to be registered, and this bill removes that uncertainty.
Supporters say people with disabilities who use stabilizing braces to steady firearms will not have their equipment reclassified and regulated as rifles.
critics: Critics say canceling the ATF rule means guns with stabilizing braces that are designed to be fired from the shoulder will no longer have to be registered under the National Firearms Act, removing a tracking tool used by law enforcement.
Critics say the January 31, 2023 rule gave the ATF a clear legal process for deciding when a braced firearm counts as a rifle, and this bill eliminates that process entirely.

Critics say short-barreled rifles regulated under the National Firearms Act require a $200 tax and background check to transfer, and this bill removes those requirements for braced firearms that function the same way.

118-hjres-74.one_liner: End a national emergency that froze assets of people threatening Yemen's stability
provisions: Ends a national emergency that President Obama declared on May 16, 2012.
That emergency let the U.S. government freeze the money and property of people seen as threats to peace in Yemen.
Once this resolution passes, that emergency and its rules no longer apply.

supporters: Supporters say ending the May 16, 2012 emergency returns power to Congress, since the emergency has let the executive branch freeze people's money and property for over 12 years without a new vote.

Supporters say that once this resolution passes, the U.S. government can no longer use the 2012 emergency rules to block the funds or property of people connected to Yemen without going through normal legal steps.
critics: Critics say the 2012 emergency gave the U.S. a tool to freeze the assets of people seen as threats to Yemen's peace, and ending it removes that tool before the situation in Yemen is resolved.

Critics say that without the rules from the May 16, 2012 declaration, people who were blocked from accessing frozen money or property could regain that access, even if they are still seen as dangers to Yemen's stability.

118-hjres-7.one_liner: End the national COVID-19 emergency declared on March 13, 2020
provisions: Ends the national emergency that President Trump declared on March 13, 2020 for COVID-19
Closing this emergency removes certain government powers that only apply during a declared emergency
Any rules or actions that were only allowed because of this emergency declaration would no longer have that legal basis

supporters: Supporters say the March 13, 2020 declaration gave the President powers that belong to Congress — like redirecting FEMA funds and waiving federal agency rules without a vote — and this joint resolution takes those powers back.

Supporters say COVID-19 no longer causes the kind of widespread shutdown it did in 2020, so there is no reason to keep an emergency declaration that expands executive authority beyond its normal limits.

Supporters say the National Emergencies Act gives Congress the right to end any presidential emergency, and this resolution uses that process to close a declaration that has been running for over two years.
critics: Critics say ending the March 13, 2020 declaration removes the authority that let FEMA and the SBA quickly approve disaster funds and emergency loans for businesses and families still affected by the pandemic.

Critics say some federal health programs — including HHS waivers that allowed faster Medicare approvals — depended on this emergency declaration, and those programs lose their footing if the declaration ends.
Critics say Congress has not passed replacement laws to keep these programs running, so agencies would have no ground to continue work they have been doing since March 2020.

118-hjres-71.one_liner: End the national emergency declared for Iraq in 2003
provisions: Ends a national emergency that President Bush declared on May 22, 2003.
That emergency was about stabilizing Iraq.
Once this passes, the emergency declaration is no longer active.

supporters: Supporters say the May 22, 2003 emergency declaration has been active for over 20 years, well past the Iraq stabilization mission it was created for, and ending it removes an executive power that was meant to be temporary.

Supporters say terminating the 2003 declaration returns to Congress the authority to decide when a national emergency exists, rather than leaving an open-ended presidential declaration in place with no expiration.

Supporters say the specific goal named in the May 22, 2003 declaration — stabilizing Iraq — is no longer an active U.S. military mission, so the legal basis for keeping the emergency in force no longer applies.
critics: Critics say ending the May 22, 2003 declaration could affect Executive Order 13303, signed the same day, which protected the Development Fund for Iraq and Iraqi oil proceeds from U.S. court judgments and legal claims.

Critics say the bill terminates the emergency without a review of which federal authorities were issued under it, risking unintended gaps in U.S. legal and financial arrangements tied to the 2003 Iraq stabilization framework.

Critics say Congress should identify and replace any still-active orders tied to the May 22, 2003 declaration before ending it, rather than terminating the emergency and addressing those gaps afterward.

118-hjres-70.one_liner: End the national emergency the U.S. declared about Libya in 2011
provisions: Ends the national emergency that President Obama declared about Libya on February 25, 2011
A national emergency gives the government extra powers — like freezing money or blocking trade tied to another country — that go away once the emergency is ended
Congress can end a national emergency by passing a joint resolution, which is what this bill does

supporters: Supporters say the Libya emergency declared on February 25, 2011 has lasted over 15 years, and the extra government powers — like freezing money and blocking trade tied to Libya — should not stay in place without a current reason.
Supporters say ending this emergency through a joint resolution is how Congress is supposed to work, taking back powers that were given to the President for a specific moment that has passed.
Supporters say removing these emergency powers stops the executive branch from using tools tied to a 2011 crisis to take actions that were never voted on by Congress.
critics: Critics say the special powers tied to the 2011 emergency — including the ability to freeze Libyan assets and block certain trade — may still be needed because Libya remains unstable and those tools help protect U.S. interests.
Critics say ending the emergency removes legal cover for actions already taken under it, and could make it harder for the government to respond quickly if conditions in Libya get worse.
Critics say Congress ending a national emergency by joint resolution sets a pattern that could limit the President's ability to act fast in future foreign crises.

118-hjres-68.one_liner: End a 2006 emergency order freezing assets tied to the Congo conflict
provisions: Ends a national emergency that President George W. Bush declared on October 27, 2006.
The emergency had blocked U.S.-held money and property belonging to certain people connected to the conflict in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Once ended, those asset freezes put in place under that emergency order would no longer be in effect.

supporters: Supporters say the national emergency from October 27, 2006 has been in place for nearly 20 years, and ending it removes asset freezes that may no longer match current conditions in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Supporters say the 2006 emergency order blocked U.S.-held money and property from specific people tied to the DRC conflict, and Congress should decide whether those freezes still serve their original goal.
Supporters say this resolution ends asset freezes that have continued since 2006 without new approval from lawmakers, restoring congressional oversight over an emergency that has lasted two decades.
critics: Critics say ending the 2006 emergency would lift the freeze on U.S.-held funds and property belonging to people connected to the DRC conflict, allowing those blocked assets to move freely again.
Critics say the DRC still has ongoing armed conflict, and terminating the October 27, 2006 declaration removes a direct financial pressure tool used against groups tied to that violence.

Critics say if this emergency is ended, the Treasury Department would need to restart sanctions from scratch under a separate law, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), losing the existing freeze protections in the meantime.

118-sjres-11.one_liner: Cancel an EPA rule setting pollution limits for heavy-duty trucks and large vehicles
provisions: Cancels an EPA rule published on January 24, 2023, that set new pollution limits for heavy-duty trucks, buses, and other large vehicles.
The canceled rule covered two types of air pollution from those vehicles: ozone and fine particles in the air.
Brings back the pollution rules that were in place before January 2023.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would cancel the January 2023 EPA rule that put new pollution limits on heavy-duty trucks and buses, removing requirements that vehicle makers say raise the cost of building those vehicles.

Supporters say returning to the pollution standards that were in place before January 2023 gives trucking companies and manufacturers time to adjust without being forced to meet stricter ozone and fine particle limits right away.
Supporters say Congress, not the EPA alone, should decide when and how to change emission rules for heavy-duty vehicles that move goods across the country.
critics: Critics say this resolution would wipe out the January 2023 EPA rule that cut ozone and fine particle pollution from heavy-duty trucks and buses — two types of air pollution linked to lung disease and smog.

Critics say going back to the pre-January 2023 standards means heavy-duty vehicles will be allowed to release more ozone and fine particles, putting people who live near highways and freight routes at greater risk.
Critics say the 2023 EPA rule was already set to apply to new vehicle models, so canceling it now would delay cleaner air for communities most exposed to truck and bus exhaust.

118-hjres-79.one_liner: End a 2004 national emergency that blocked money and exports to Syria
provisions: Lifts a freeze on money and property of certain people tied to Syria that has been in place since May 11, 2004
Brings back the ability to export certain goods to Syria that were blocked under that emergency
The original emergency was put in place by President George W. Bush because of Syria's support for terrorist activity in Iraq

supporters: Supporters say the emergency has been in place since May 11, 2004 — over 20 years — and that ending it would lift the freeze on property and allow goods to flow to Syria again, which could help ordinary Syrian people access trade and resources.
Supporters say the conditions that led President Bush to block Syrian property and exports in 2004 have changed enough that keeping this emergency active is no longer needed.
Supporters say Congress has the power to end national emergencies, and terminating this one would restore normal trade and property rules that apply to other countries.
critics: Critics say the original 2004 emergency was put in place because Syria supported terrorist activity in Iraq, and lifting the property freeze could allow money and assets tied to those same networks to move freely again.

Critics say ending the block on exports to Syria removes a tool the U.S. has used for over 20 years to pressure the Syrian government, and doing so without a full review of current conditions could weaken U.S. security interests.

Critics say unfreezing the property of certain people connected to Syria could benefit individuals who were originally targeted for supporting terrorism, since the resolution ends all restrictions tied to the May 11, 2004 emergency.

118-sjres-10.one_liner: Remove the VA's ability to offer abortion-related care to veterans and their covered family members
provisions: The VA can no longer provide abortion-related care to veterans.
Family members of veterans covered under CHAMPVA, the VA's civilian health program, also lose access to that care.
This cancels a rule the VA put in place in September 2022.

supporters: Supporters say the VA's 2022 rule went beyond what Congress authorized, and this resolution restores the rule that the VA should not provide abortion-related care.
Supporters say veterans seeking abortion care should use civilian providers, and the VA's limited resources should stay focused on service-connected injuries and conditions.
Supporters say CHAMPVA family members are civilian dependents, and removing their access to VA-covered abortion care keeps the program within its original purpose.
critics: Critics say nullifying the 2022 rule means veterans in states with abortion bans will have no VA facility to turn to, leaving them without a federal healthcare option they had access to starting September 2022.
Critics say the rule change also cuts off CHAMPVA beneficiaries — family members of disabled or deceased veterans — who had gained access to this care under the 2022 rule.
Critics say veterans who need abortion care due to rape, incest, or health risks will face added barriers because the VA, their primary healthcare system, can no longer provide that service.

118-hjres-98.one_liner: Cancel a federal labor board rule that changed when two companies count as joint employers
provisions: Cancels a rule the National Labor Relations Board published on October 27, 2023.
That rule said two companies could both be considered employers of the same workers if they shared control over pay, hours, or working conditions.
Under the canceled rule, simply having the ability to influence those conditions was enough — a company did not need to directly set them.
The previous standard required a company to exercise direct and immediate control over workers to be considered their employer.
Canceling this rule returns the joint employer standard to what it was before October 2023.

supporters: Supporters say the October 2023 NLRB rule went too far by making a company a joint employer just for having the ability to influence workers' pay or hours — even if it never actually did so, and canceling it means companies are only responsible for workers they directly and immediately control.

Supporters say the rule threatened how franchise businesses work, since it could have forced corporate brands and local franchise owners to bargain together with workers, affecting hundreds of thousands of franchise locations across the country.
Supporters say returning to the standard that existed before October 2023 gives businesses clear rules about when they are legally responsible for another company's employees.
