critics: Critics say the pre-2023 standard let large companies use franchisees and contractors to avoid responsibility for workers' pay and conditions, even when those large companies set the rules that workers had to follow every day.

Critics say canceling this rule removes workers' ability to bargain directly with the company that actually controls their hours, wages, and working conditions, leaving them only able to negotiate with smaller businesses that may have little power to make changes.
Critics say the NLRB's October 2023 rule simply reflected how work actually happens today, where one company can shape a worker's job without being named on their paycheck.

118-sjres-111.one_liner: Block one proposed sale of military equipment to the government of Israel
provisions: Blocks one specific proposed sale of military items and services to Israel.
The sale was proposed by the executive branch under a law that lets Congress vote to stop it.
If this resolution passes both the House and Senate, the sale cannot go forward.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution uses Congress's legal authority under the Arms Export Control Act to block one specific sale of military items and services to Israel, giving elected lawmakers a direct vote on where U.S. weapons go.
Supporters say the executive branch proposed this sale without enough congressional input, and this resolution is the only tool Congress has under current law to stop it before it goes through.
Supporters say blocking this specific sale would pause the transfer of defense articles to Israel while questions about how those items are used remain unanswered.
critics: Critics say rejecting this one sale would damage the U.S.-Israel defense relationship by cutting off specific military items and services that Israel's government formally requested through an established legal process.
Critics say the resolution overrides a decision made by the executive branch, which has primary responsibility for managing foreign military sales and coordinating with allies.

Critics say if this resolution passes both the House and Senate, it sets a precedent for using disapproval votes to block individual arms sales to close U.S. partners, which could slow future military cooperation.

118-sjres-23.one_liner: Restore limits on which areas can be labeled critical habitat by a federal fisheries agency
provisions: The National Marine Fisheries Service manages fish, marine mammals, and other water species listed as endangered or threatened.
Areas labeled 'critical habitat' face legal restrictions on development and other activities nearby.
In 2022, the agency issued a rule that removed earlier limits on which areas could get that label.
This bill cancels the 2022 rule, bringing back those earlier limits on critical habitat labeling.

supporters: Supporters say this bill cancels the June 24, 2022 rule from the National Marine Fisheries Service, which removed earlier limits on which areas could be labeled critical habitat — restoring those limits protects landowners and businesses from legal restrictions on development near water areas.

Supporters say the 2022 rule allowed the agency to label areas as critical habitat too broadly, and canceling it returns clearer rules about when those development restrictions can apply to land near fish and marine mammal habitats.
critics: Critics say canceling the 2022 rule brings back earlier limits that made it harder for the National Marine Fisheries Service to protect the land and water areas that endangered fish and marine mammals need to survive.

Critics say the 2022 rule was designed to give the agency more tools to designate critical habitat, and removing it weakens legal protections for threatened species by restricting which areas can qualify for that status.

118-sjres-115.one_liner: Block one proposed U.S. export license for military equipment and training to Israel
provisions: This resolution blocks one proposed change to a U.S. export license that would let military equipment, training services, and technical information be sent to Israel.
As a joint resolution, it must pass both the House and the Senate, then go to the President — who can sign it or veto it.
If it becomes law, the U.S. government cannot move forward with the specific license change named in the resolution.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would block a specific U.S. export license change that allows military equipment, training services, and technical data to be sent to Israel, giving Congress a direct way to stop that transfer.

Supporters say the joint resolution process — requiring both the House and Senate to vote — ensures that elected lawmakers, not just the executive branch, have a say in approving major arms-related license changes.
Supporters say that if this resolution passes and becomes law, the named license amendment cannot move forward, which they argue is the right use of congressional oversight over weapons exports.
critics: Critics say blocking this specific license amendment would limit Israel's access to U.S. military equipment and training services that they argue are needed for Israel's defense.
Critics say the joint resolution process adds a political obstacle to a license change that has already gone through the standard export review process, slowing down support to a U.S. ally.
Critics say that if the President vetoes this resolution, as is allowed under the process, it shows the resolution is unlikely to stop the license amendment and may only serve as a symbolic vote.

118-sjres-117.one_liner: Reject a Presidential report about money Ukraine owes the United States
provisions: Rejects a report the President sent to Congress about Ukraine's debt to the United States.
Blocks the effect of that Presidential report on Ukraine's debt obligations to the US government.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution stops the President's report from changing what Ukraine owes the US government without Congress voting to approve it first.
Supporters say blocking the report keeps Ukraine's debt obligations to the United States in place, since only Congress has the power to change how foreign debts are handled.
critics: Critics say rejecting the Presidential report removes official guidance on Ukraine's debt to the US, leaving those obligations without a clear legal framework.
Critics say blocking the report limits the President's ability to manage the US government's financial relationship with Ukraine during an active conflict.

118-sjres-113.one_liner: Block one proposed sale of weapons and military equipment to Israel
provisions: Blocks a proposed U.S. sale of weapons and military equipment to Israel.
To take effect, this resolution must pass both the House and Senate.
This type of resolution uses a process that lets Congress formally reject a foreign arms sale the U.S. government has already proposed.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution would stop a proposed sale that includes 155mm artillery shells, which have been fired into densely populated areas of Gaza where more than 1 million civilians were sheltering.
Supporters say U.S. law — specifically the Leahy Law — bars arms transfers to foreign military units credibly accused of human rights abuses, and they argue this proposed sale breaks that rule.
Supporters say requiring both the House and Senate to approve the resolution is the exact check the Arms Export Control Act created so Congress can reject executive arms deals it disagrees with.
critics: Critics say blocking this sale leaves Israel short of key munitions it needs to continue military operations against Hamas, which carried out the October 7, 2023 attacks that killed approximately 1,200 Israeli civilians.

Critics say the president holds constitutional authority over foreign policy and arms sales, and a joint resolution of disapproval lets Congress override that authority in ways courts have historically left to the executive branch.
Critics say cutting off weapons to Israel mid-conflict could signal to Iran and other regional actors that U.S. security commitments to allies can be reversed by a single legislative vote.

118-sjres-18.one_liner: Restore a 2019 rule making it harder for non-citizens to get a green card
provisions: Cancels a 2022 rule from the Department of Homeland Security about green card approvals.
Brings back a 2019 rule that raised the bar for who can get a green card.
Non-citizens were more likely to be denied if the government thought they might use benefits like Medicaid or food stamps.
This applies to people trying to enter the country and those applying for permanent resident status.

supporters: Supporters say bringing back the 2019 rule means the government can more carefully check if someone applying for a green card might need Medicaid, food stamps, or other public benefits before approving them.
Supporters say the 2022 rule made it too easy for people who may rely on government benefits to get permanent resident status, and this resolution fixes that.
Supporters say the change applies to both people trying to enter the country and those already here applying for permanent residency, closing a gap they say the 2022 rule created.
critics: Critics say the 2019 rule being restored caused many immigrants — including those with U.S. citizen children — to drop Medicaid and food programs they were legally allowed to use, out of fear it would hurt their green card chances.
Critics say the rule discourages non-citizens from using benefits like Medicaid even when sick, which public health groups say leads to untreated illness spreading in communities.
Critics say the 2022 rule was put in place because courts and health agencies found the 2019 rule caused harm, and this resolution ignores those findings.

118-sjres-24.one_liner: Cancel a 2022 rule that changed the northern long-eared bat to endangered status
provisions: In November 2022, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service changed the northern long-eared bat from 'threatened' to 'endangered' under the Endangered Species Act.
Under federal law, 'endangered' means a species is in danger of dying out. 'Threatened' means it could become endangered.
This bill cancels that 2022 rule. The bat goes back to 'threatened' status.
The 2022 rule also ended a set of rules that applied only when the bat was listed as 'threatened.' This bill brings those rules back.

supporters: Supporters say moving the northern long-eared bat back to 'threatened' status restores a species-specific set of rules that gave landowners, loggers, and energy developers clearer guidance on what activities were allowed in bat habitat.

Supporters say the Fish and Wildlife Service's 2022 rule to list the bat as 'endangered' placed stricter limits on land use across the bat's range in the eastern U.S., and this resolution removes those stricter limits.
Supporters say Congress has the right under the Congressional Review Act to cancel agency rules it disagrees with, and this resolution uses that legal process to reverse the November 30, 2022 rule.
critics: Critics say the northern long-eared bat was moved to 'endangered' because its population collapsed — white-nose syndrome, a fungal disease, has killed millions of bats — and canceling the 2022 rule removes the stronger legal protections the species needs to survive.

Critics say 'endangered' status under the Endangered Species Act triggers stricter rules against harming the bat or its habitat, and returning it to 'threatened' status weakens those protections for a species already in sharp decline.
Critics say the species-specific rule that this resolution brings back was written for a bat population that was larger and less at risk, and it no longer fits the bat's current condition.

119-sjres-33.one_liner: Block one proposed sale of weapons and military equipment to Israel
provisions: Blocks one specific proposed sale of military goods and services to Israel — it does not affect any other arms deals with Israel.
A joint resolution of disapproval is the tool Congress uses to reject a sale the President has already announced. If it passes both chambers and becomes law, the named sale cannot go forward.
Under U.S. law, when the President plans to sell military equipment to a foreign government, Congress gets a window of time to vote to stop it.
This resolution applies only to this one sale — it does not change U.S. policy on selling military goods to Israel in general.

supporters: Supporters say Congress has the legal right to block this sale, and this resolution uses the exact tool U.S. law gives Congress to reject a Presidential arms sale before it goes through.

Supporters say blocking this one sale sends a message to Israel without ending the broader U.S.-Israel arms relationship, since the resolution only applies to this specific deal and leaves all other sales in place.
Supporters say the sale should not move forward because Congress has not had a full vote on whether these particular defense articles and services should be transferred to Israel.
critics: Critics say rejecting this sale weakens a U.S. ally's ability to defend itself, since Israel would not receive the specific defense articles and services the President already agreed to provide.
Critics say the resolution goes against the President's authority to manage foreign military sales, which U.S. law gives the executive branch the power to negotiate and announce.
Critics say blocking this one sale could signal to other allies that U.S. arms commitments can be reversed by Congress after the President has already made an official offer.

119-sjres-54.one_liner: Block one proposed U.S. defense sale to the United Arab Emirates
provisions: This resolution blocks one specific proposed sale of U.S. defense items and services to the United Arab Emirates.
If this resolution passes, the sale cannot go forward.
U.S. law gives Congress a set window of time after the president reports a planned arms sale to pass a resolution like this one and stop it.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would use the legal window that U.S. law gives Congress to stop a specific proposed sale of American defense items and services to the UAE before it goes through.

Supporters say blocking this sale would prevent U.S. weapons and military services from reaching the UAE at a time when some lawmakers have raised concerns about how the UAE has used American arms in regional conflicts.
Supporters say Congress has a responsibility to review arms sales reported by the president, and this resolution exercises that check directly on this specific proposed deal.
critics: Critics say stopping this specific sale would damage the U.S. relationship with the UAE, a key partner that helps the U.S. maintain influence in the Middle East.

Critics say the president already reviewed and approved this proposed arms deal, and using the congressional review window to block it could signal to other allies that U.S. weapons sales are unreliable.
Critics say if this sale is blocked, the UAE could turn to other countries — such as Russia or China — to buy the defense articles and services it was seeking from the U.S.

119-sjres-41.one_liner: Block one proposed U.S. sale of defense equipment to Israel
provisions: Blocks one specific sale of U.S. weapons or military equipment that was set to go to Israel.
The sale had already been approved by the President's administration before Congress introduced this resolution.
Congress has the legal power to vote to stop any arms sale the President approves — this resolution uses that power for this one sale.
If this passes both the House and Senate and becomes law, only this one sale is stopped — other U.S. military sales are not affected.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution uses Congress's legal authority under U.S. law to block one specific weapons sale to Israel that the President's administration already approved, giving elected lawmakers a direct vote on the deal.
Supporters say stopping this one approved sale lets Congress put limits on U.S. arms transfers to Israel during an active conflict without ending all military cooperation between the two countries.
critics: Critics say this resolution only stops one specific sale — all other U.S. military sales to Israel remain in place — which they argue makes the action largely symbolic and does not change overall U.S. military support.

Critics say overriding a sale the President's administration already approved sets a precedent that could slow future arms deals and reduce U.S. influence with allies who depend on reliable access to American military equipment.

118-sjres-43.one_liner: Cancel the Department of Education rule that created the SAVE student loan repayment plan
provisions: Cancels a Department of Education rule published on July 10, 2023
Removes the SAVE plan, which was a new repayment option for federal student loan borrowers based on income
The SAVE plan covered loans in the Direct Loan program and the Federal Family Education Loan program

supporters: Supporters say the SAVE plan, published July 10, 2023, went beyond what Congress authorized, and Congress should decide loan repayment rules — not the Department of Education.
Supporters say canceling the SAVE plan stops what they call an unlawful income-driven repayment option that could cost taxpayers hundreds of billions of dollars over time.
Supporters say removing the SAVE plan restores the repayment rules that were in place before the July 2023 rule changed how borrowers in the Direct Loan and FFEL programs repay their loans.
critics: Critics say canceling the SAVE plan takes away a repayment option that let Direct Loan and FFEL borrowers pay less each month based on how much they earn.
Critics say the resolution eliminates a rule that helped lower-income borrowers avoid defaulting on their federal student loans by capping payments at a share of their income.
Critics say removing the SAVE plan means borrowers who enrolled in it after July 2023 would lose the specific payment terms they were counting on.

118-sjres-32.one_liner: Cancel a CFPB rule requiring lenders to track and report small business loan data
provisions: This bill cancels a Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) rule published on May 31, 2023.
The canceled rule required banks and lenders to collect information about small business loan applications.
That information included who applied, what type of business they ran, and whether they were approved.
Lenders would have had to send all of this data to the CFPB.
As of July 31, 2023, a federal court had paused enforcement of this rule while a related lawsuit moved through the courts.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the May 31, 2023 CFPB rule removes a burden on banks and lenders who would have had to collect and report detailed data on every small business loan application.
Supporters say the rule was already paused by a federal court on July 31, 2023, so making that cancellation permanent gives lenders clear rules to follow instead of waiting on a lawsuit.
Supporters say requiring lenders to send applicant data — including business type and approval status — to the CFPB creates privacy risks for small business owners.
critics: Critics say the canceled rule would have required lenders to report who applied for small business loans, which could have helped identify if certain groups, like minority-owned businesses, were being denied credit unfairly.
Critics say without the data collection requirement, the CFPB loses a key tool to spot lending discrimination under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act.
Critics say Congress is using this resolution to permanently block a rule before the courts have finished deciding whether it is legal.

118-sjres-42.one_liner: Cancel a federal rule about how food assistance programs handle discrimination complaints
provisions: The Food and Nutrition Service (FNS), which runs programs like SNAP (food stamps), issued a rule in May 2022 about how to handle discrimination complaints.
This resolution cancels that rule using a law called the Congressional Review Act, which lets Congress undo federal rules.
The FNS based this rule on a 2020 Supreme Court case called Bostock v. Clayton County.
That case said firing or punishing someone for being gay or transgender counts as sex discrimination.
The FNS rule said food programs must treat complaints about discrimination against gay or transgender people as sex discrimination complaints.

supporters: Supporters say the FNS did not have the authority to extend the Bostock ruling — a 2020 Supreme Court case about employment law — to food programs like SNAP without Congress passing a new law first.
Supporters say the FNS issued this rule in May 2022 without submitting it to Congress and the GAO as required by the Congressional Review Act, which means Congress has the right to cancel it.
Supporters say decisions about how anti-discrimination rules apply to federal food programs serving tens of millions of SNAP participants should be made by Congress, not a federal agency.
critics: Critics say canceling this rule removes the requirement that state agencies and program operators treat complaints from gay or transgender SNAP participants as sex discrimination complaints.
Critics say the FNS rule was built directly on the 2020 Bostock Supreme Court decision, and nullifying it means federal food programs would no longer follow that court ruling.
Critics say without this rule, LGBTQ+ people using FNS programs would lose the formal process for filing discrimination complaints that the May 2022 policy put in place.

118-sjres-4.one_liner: Declare the Equal Rights Amendment valid and remove its ratification deadline
provisions: The Equal Rights Amendment says the government cannot treat people differently based on sex.
Congress first proposed the ERA in 1972 and set a deadline of March 22, 1979 for states to approve it, then extended that deadline to June 30, 1982.
38 states have voted to approve the ERA, but 3 of those states did so after the deadline passed.
Five states that had already approved the ERA later voted to take back their approval.
This bill says those deadlines do not matter and that the ERA counts as part of the Constitution.
The ERA's legal status has been the subject of court cases, which this bill would resolve by declaring it valid.

supporters: Supporters say the ERA should count as part of the Constitution because all 38 required states have voted to approve it, and the original 1972 proposal did not include any rule saying Congress could set a deadline for ratification.
Supporters say this bill would end years of court cases about the ERA's legal status by declaring it valid, giving women and girls a clear constitutional right against sex discrimination.

Supporters say that states like Nevada, Illinois, and Virginia ratified after the 1982 deadline because the deadline was added by Congress, not written into the amendment itself, so it should not block the ERA from taking effect.
critics: Critics say that Congress set a clear deadline of June 30, 1982, and three states missed it, which means the ratification process was not completed under the rules that were in place.
Critics say that five states voted to take back their approval of the ERA, and this bill ignores those rescissions, raising questions about whether a state can ever change its vote.

Critics say that declaring the ERA valid through a simple joint resolution, rather than a new ratification process, goes around the rules in Article V of the Constitution for how amendments are added.

118-sjres-38.one_liner: Cancel a rule that waived Buy America requirements for electric vehicle chargers
provisions: This resolution cancels a Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) rule issued in February 2023.
Before this resolution passed, charger makers could use parts from anywhere as long as final assembly happened in the US.
Installation had to begin before October 1, 2024.
Starting July 1, 2024, chargers had to use US-made parts for more than 55% of their total parts cost.
Steel and iron housing parts for EV chargers were never covered by the waiver and always had to meet Buy America rules.

supporters: Supporters say the FHWA waiver let charger makers use foreign parts for up to 55% of total component costs, which breaks the Buy America rules required by the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.
Supporters say canceling the waiver protects US manufacturing jobs, since the rule allowed overseas parts in federally funded EV chargers until June 30, 2024.
Supporters say the waiver created an uneven playing field, where steel and iron housing parts had to meet Buy America rules but internal components did not.
critics: Critics say the waiver was needed because US factories could not yet supply enough EV charger parts to meet demand, and canceling it could slow the buildout of the national charging network.
Critics say removing the waiver makes it harder for charger makers to meet the October 1, 2024 installation deadline, since sourcing all components domestically takes more time and raises costs.
Critics say the 55% US-parts threshold set for July 1, 2024 was already a step toward full compliance, and ending the waiver early removes flexibility that the FHWA said was necessary.

118-sjres-58.one_liner: Cancel the DOE's 2023 efficiency standards for gas furnaces sold in the U.S.
provisions: Gas furnaces no longer have to meet the efficiency levels the Department of Energy set in December 2023.
The canceled rule covered two types of furnaces: standard home gas furnaces and gas furnaces built for mobile homes.
Without this rule, the efficiency requirements that existed before December 2023 stay in place for furnace makers.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the December 2023 DOE rule means furnace makers will not have to redesign standard home gas furnaces and mobile home gas furnaces to meet new efficiency levels, which they say would have raised the purchase price of those products.

Supporters say the older efficiency requirements that existed before December 2023 will stay in place, so furnace makers can keep building the same products without being forced into costly changes on a short timeline.
Supporters say mobile home residents, who often have lower incomes and fewer options for replacing equipment, would have been especially hurt by higher furnace prices caused by the new standards.
critics: Critics say the December 2023 DOE standards for standard home gas furnaces and mobile home gas furnaces were designed to cut how much natural gas those furnaces burn, which would lower monthly energy bills for households over time.

Critics say without the rule, furnace makers can keep selling less efficient gas furnaces, meaning buyers will pay more in gas costs each year compared to what they would have paid under the new standards.

Critics say mobile home residents stand to lose the most because the canceled rule specifically set new efficiency levels for mobile home gas furnaces, a product type that has not seen updated federal standards in years.

118-sjres-44.one_liner: Order the removal of U.S. troops from hostilities in Niger within 30 days unless Congress approves
provisions: Tells the President to pull U.S. troops out of fighting in Niger within 30 days of this resolution passing.
The 30-day clock applies to any fighting in or connected to Niger, even if it takes place nearby.
U.S. troops can stay only if Congress passes a formal declaration of war or votes to specifically approve the military action in Niger.
If no congressional vote happens within those 30 days, the withdrawal must happen.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution enforces the War Powers Resolution by requiring the President to remove U.S. troops from Niger within 30 days unless Congress votes to authorize the fighting.
Supporters say no formal declaration of war or specific authorization for military action in Niger has been passed by Congress, so U.S. forces should not be engaged in hostilities there.
Supporters say the 30-day deadline gives Congress time to debate and vote, putting the decision to go to war in Niger back in the hands of elected lawmakers instead of the executive branch.
critics: Critics say a forced 30-day withdrawal could leave U.S. partners in Niger without support, since American forces are working with local troops on counterterrorism missions in the region.

Critics say the resolution's broad scope — covering any hostilities 'affecting' Niger, even those nearby — could restrict U.S. military operations beyond Niger's borders that are not directly tied to Niger.

Critics say requiring a full declaration of war or specific congressional authorization within 30 days sets a hard deadline that does not give diplomats or military planners enough time to manage a safe exit.

118-sjres-60.one_liner: Block one proposed sale of U.S. weapons and military equipment to Turkey
provisions: Blocks one specific proposed sale of U.S. weapons and military equipment to Turkey from going forward.
The sale included defense articles and services — the legal terms for military hardware and related support.
Congress used a joint resolution — a formal vote passed by both the House and Senate — to stop this sale.

supporters: Supporters say Turkey bought Russian S-400 missile systems, which got it removed from the U.S. F-35 program. They say transferring more U.S. defense articles and services to Turkey while it keeps Russian equipment could let Russia study how American weapons operate.

Supporters say Turkey has used military force against Kurdish groups in Syria who fought alongside U.S. troops against ISIS. They say approving a defense sale to Turkey rewards military action taken against a U.S. partner on the ground.

Supporters say Congress has the legal authority under the Arms Export Control Act to disapprove proposed foreign military sales. They say using a joint resolution here puts lawmakers on record about whether this specific transfer serves U.S. interests.
critics: Critics say Turkey is a NATO ally that hosts the Incirlik Air Base, which U.S. forces use for operations in the region. They say blocking the transfer of defense articles and services weakens that alliance and reduces U.S. influence over how Turkey arms itself.

Critics say the State Department and Pentagon both reviewed and approved this proposed sale before Congress voted to block it. They say overriding that executive branch decision with a joint resolution makes it harder for the U.S. to manage defense relationships with partner countries.

Critics say if Turkey cannot buy U.S. military equipment, it is more likely to purchase weapons from Russia or China. They say the joint resolution removes U.S. leverage and could push a NATO member closer to adversary suppliers.

118-sjres-57.one_liner: Cancel a Treasury rule letting states count compliance costs as committed COVID relief spending
provisions: In 2021, the federal government sent COVID-19 relief money to states and cities to help them recover.
States had to officially commit that money by December 31, 2024, and fully spend it by December 31, 2026.
A 2023 Treasury rule let states count paperwork, audit, reporting, and environmental compliance costs as committed by the 2024 deadline.
Under that rule, states reported estimated amounts of those costs to the Treasury by April 30, 2024.
This resolution cancels that 2023 Treasury rule, so those administrative costs no longer count toward the 2024 commitment deadline.

supporters: Supporters say the 2023 Treasury rule went beyond what Congress allowed when it set the December 31, 2024 obligation deadline in the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021, because Congress meant actual program spending commitments, not administrative paperwork costs.

Supporters say letting states count audit, reporting, and environmental compliance costs as obligated funds by the 2024 deadline lets states keep COVID relief money in reserve longer than Congress intended.
Supporters say canceling this rule makes sure all COVID relief money sent to states in 2021 is committed to real recovery spending, not administrative overhead.
critics: Critics say the 2023 Treasury rule covered costs that federal law requires states to pay, like audits and environmental reviews, and states already reported estimated amounts of these costs to Treasury by April 30, 2024.
Critics say canceling this rule could cause states to lose access to COVID relief funds they were counting on for administrative compliance work that must be finished before December 31, 2026.
Critics say states built their spending plans around the 2023 rule, and removing it now changes the rules after states already met the April 2024 reporting deadline.

118-sjres-51.one_liner: Order U.S. troops removed from combat operations in Syria not approved by Congress
provisions: Orders the President to pull U.S. troops out of military combat in Syria.
Covers only military operations in Syria that Congress has not voted to approve.
For this to become law, both the House and Senate must pass it, and the President must sign it or Congress must override a veto.

supporters: Supporters say the War Powers Resolution of 1973 requires congressional approval for U.S. troops to stay in combat, and this resolution enforces that law by ordering withdrawal from Syria operations that Congress has never voted to authorize.

Supporters say the resolution specifically covers only military operations in Syria that Congress has not approved, which means U.S. troops are currently in active combat there without a single congressional vote on record.

Supporters say the Constitution gives Congress, not the President alone, the power to commit U.S. forces to military hostilities, and this resolution reclaims that authority for the specific, unapproved Syria operations.
critics: Critics say the Authorization for Use of Military Force that Congress passed in 2001 after the September 11 attacks already gives the President legal authority to conduct military operations against terrorist groups in Syria, making this resolution's withdrawal order based on a false premise.
Critics say ordering the removal of U.S. troops under this resolution could allow groups like ISIS to rebuild in Syria, reversing gains made by U.S.-backed forces already operating there.

Critics say the bill's own passage process — requiring both chambers to pass it and then either a presidential signature or a veto override — gives the President a simple veto pen to block any congressionally ordered Syria withdrawal indefinitely.

118-sjres-9.one_liner: Remove federal protections for the lesser prairie-chicken
provisions: Takes the lesser prairie-chicken off the federal threatened and endangered species list, where it was placed in November 2022.
The northern population of the bird had been listed as threatened; this removes that status.
The southern population had been listed as endangered; this removes that status.
Without these protections, land use rules that applied to areas where the bird lives no longer apply under federal law.

supporters: Supporters say removing the lesser prairie-chicken from the federal threatened and endangered species list will lift land use rules that currently restrict farming, ranching, and energy development in areas where the bird lives across states like Texas, Oklahoma, and Kansas.
Supporters say the 2022 Fish and Wildlife Service rule placed burdens on private landowners by limiting how they can use their own land, and this resolution ends those federal restrictions.

Supporters say the northern population's threatened status and the southern population's endangered status were added without enough proof that federal protections are needed beyond what states already provide.
critics: Critics say removing the endangered status from the southern population of the lesser prairie-chicken takes away the strongest federal protections for a group of birds that scientists identified in November 2022 as facing the highest risk of extinction.

Critics say without the 2022 rule, there are no federal land use requirements to protect the bird's habitat, meaning oil and gas drilling, farming, and other activities can expand into areas where the bird nests and breeds.

Critics say the Fish and Wildlife Service followed the legal process under the Endangered Species Act to list both populations, and overturning the rule through Congress bypasses that science-based review.

119-hjres-117.one_liner: Take Congressional action on the national emergency the President declared July 30, 2025
provisions: This bill responds to a national emergency declared by the President on July 30, 2025.
The bill falls under Emergency Management as its policy area.
No bill text or official summary was provided, so no further details about what this bill does can be stated without speculation.

supporters: Supporters say the bill responds to a real emergency that the President formally declared on July 30, 2025, and that Congress acting on it keeps the legislative branch involved in emergency management decisions.
Supporters say emergency management bills tied to a specific declared emergency help make sure federal resources and authority are used in a focused, time-limited way rather than left open-ended.
critics: Critics say no official bill text or summary has been provided for this legislation, which makes it impossible to know what powers, funding levels, or affected groups are actually involved in the July 30, 2025 emergency response.

Critics say Congress should not move forward on a bill under the emergency management policy area without disclosing what specific rules would change or how long emergency powers triggered by the July 30, 2025 declaration would last.

118-sjres-61.one_liner: Cancel a federal rule requiring states to track and cut highway CO2 emissions
provisions: A 2023 federal rule told every state to measure how much carbon dioxide their roads and highways produce — this bill cancels that rule.
States no longer have to set targets for reducing CO2 from transportation.
State transportation departments and regional planning groups no longer have to send reports to the federal government showing whether CO2 from roads is going down.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the 2023 FHWA rule removes a federal mandate that forced state transportation departments and regional planning groups to set declining CO2 targets, giving states back control over their own road planning.
Supporters say states no longer having to file federal progress reports on highway CO2 levels reduces paperwork and costs for state agencies.
Supporters say the rule put unfunded requirements on states by demanding CO2 targets tied to transportation without providing money to help meet them.
critics: Critics say canceling the December 7, 2023 rule removes the only federal system that required states to measure and report whether CO2 from roads and highways is going up or down.
Critics say without the rule, state transportation departments and metropolitan planning organizations have no shared standard for tracking highway greenhouse gas emissions across the country.

Critics say the rule only required states to set targets and file reports — it did not ban any projects — so canceling it eliminates accountability without reducing any actual burden on road builders.

118-sjres-89.one_liner: Stop US troops from building and running a floating pier off the Gaza coast
provisions: Orders the US military to stop all work building, maintaining, and running the floating pier off the coast of Gaza.
States that Congress never voted to approve this use of US troops for the pier.
The pier was put in place without Congress first passing a law or resolution allowing it.

supporters: Supporters say Congress never voted to approve US troops building or running the pier, and this resolution would enforce that rule by ordering the military to stop all pier work.
Supporters say the War Powers Act gives Congress the power to approve or stop military operations, and using troops for the pier without a vote bypasses that power.
Supporters say ending the pier mission would pull US service members out of a role that Congress did not authorize and has not overseen.
critics: Critics say stopping the pier mid-operation could cut off a supply route that the US government said was meant to bring food and aid into Gaza.
Critics say the resolution would force the military to abandon equipment and logistics already in place, wasting resources already spent on the pier mission.
Critics say the President has authority as Commander in Chief to direct short-term military operations, and this mission does not require a separate act of Congress.

118-sjres-62.one_liner: Block a rule that let Paraguay ship fresh beef into the United States
provisions: Restores the block on fresh beef from Paraguay entering the United States
Cancels a rule from November 2023 that set conditions for Paraguay to ship beef to the U.S.
The canceled rule required that no foot-and-mouth disease cases had been found in Paraguay's beef-producing regions for the 12 months before any shipment
Beef under that rule also had to come from farms where no animals had ever had foot-and-mouth disease
That rule would have let U.S. inspectors visit Paraguay's slaughter plants to check records and operations

supporters: Supporters say the November 2023 rule only requires APHIS to conduct periodic inspections of Paraguay's slaughter plants, leaving no continuous U.S. oversight to confirm that the 12-month FMD-free condition is being met before each shipment.

Supporters say the rule puts American cattle ranchers at a disadvantage by giving Paraguayan producers U.S. market access through periodic plant visits while domestic ranchers face continuous federal inspection requirements.

Supporters say the farm-level requirement — that no cattle on a supplying farm ever had foot-and-mouth disease — depends on records kept by Paraguayan producers, with no independent U.S. confirmation of that history.
critics: Critics say the November 2023 APHIS rule already required that no FMD cases be diagnosed in Paraguay's beef-producing regions for 12 months before any shipment, a condition this resolution cancels before it could take effect.
Critics say APHIS completed a formal risk analysis and concluded that fresh beef could be safely imported from Paraguay under these conditions, and this resolution sets aside that scientific finding.
Critics say the rule gave U.S. inspectors the authority to conduct on-site evaluations of Paraguay's slaughter facilities and review their records — an oversight tool this resolution removes.

119-hjres-131.one_liner: Cancel a 2024 rule limiting oil and gas leasing in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge
provisions: In 2020, a federal decision made about 1.6 million acres of Alaska's Arctic National Wildlife Refuge available for oil and gas leasing.
A 2024 federal rule had cut the land open for leasing from about 1.6 million acres down to 400,000 — the legal minimum.
This bill cancels that 2024 rule.
With the 2024 rule gone, the additional restrictions on those 1.2 million acres are removed.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the 2024 rule restores access to the full 1.6 million acres of the Coastal Plain program area, reversing a cut that had locked away about 1.2 million acres from oil and gas leasing.

Supporters say returning to the 2020 record of decision opens more land in areas identified by law as having the highest potential for finding oil and gas, which could increase domestic energy production.

Supporters say the 2024 rule went beyond what Congress required, since the law only mandates a minimum of 400,000 acres be made available, and the original 2020 decision offered four times that amount.
critics: Critics say the 2024 rule protected about 1.2 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge that the Bureau of Land Management identified as important for conservation, and canceling it removes those protections.
Critics say restoring leasing access across 1.6 million acres puts at risk wildlife habitats and Indigenous land uses in areas the 2024 environmental review found should be off-limits.

Critics say the 2024 rule was based on a supplemental environmental impact statement completed that year, and canceling it through this resolution skips the standard review process for undoing that environmental analysis.

119-hjres-140.one_liner: Reopen 225,504 acres of Minnesota forest land to mining and energy leasing
provisions: Cancels a 2023 federal order that blocked mining and energy leasing on about 225,504 acres of national forest land in Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties, Minnesota.
That land had been off-limits to mineral and geothermal leasing for 20 years under the canceled order.
The land sits near the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and the Rainy River Watershed in northeastern Minnesota.
Mining and geothermal energy companies can now apply to lease and explore this land again.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution reopens 225,504 acres of Minnesota national forest land that a 2023 federal order had locked out of mineral and geothermal leasing for 20 years, giving mining and energy companies the ability to apply for leases again.

Supporters say the Bureau of Land Management blocked this land without an act of Congress, and this resolution restores congressional authority over how federal land in Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties is used.
Supporters say allowing mineral exploration on these acres could bring mining jobs and tax revenue to northeastern Minnesota communities near the Rainy River Watershed.
critics: Critics say this resolution removes protections the Bureau of Land Management put in place in 2023 specifically to shield the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and the Rainy River Watershed from the potential harm of mineral and geothermal drilling.

Critics say the 1854 Ceded Territory of the Lake Superior Chippewa — tribal land with treaty-protected hunting and fishing rights — sits within the affected area, and reopening it to leasing could threaten those rights and the water quality the tribe depends on.
Critics say the original 20-year withdrawal was meant to give time to study risks before any leasing decision, and canceling it now cuts that review short for all 225,504 acres.

119-hjres-72.one_liner: End the national immigration emergency the President declared on February 1, 2025
provisions: Cancels the national emergency the President declared on February 1, 2025.
Ends any special powers the President gained from declaring that emergency.
Returns immigration decisions made under that emergency to the normal process, which requires Congress to vote on them.
Uses Congress's power under federal law to cut short a presidential emergency before it would end on its own.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would end the special powers the President gained from the February 1, 2025 emergency, returning control over immigration decisions to Congress, where federal law says those decisions belong.

Supporters say the emergency declaration let the President act on immigration without a Congressional vote, and this bill uses Congress's existing legal authority to restore that check on executive power.
Supporters say any immigration rules put in place under the February 1, 2025 emergency would have to go back through the normal lawmaking process, which requires approval from elected lawmakers.
critics: Critics say ending the emergency would remove tools the President was using to respond quickly to border conditions, forcing immigration decisions through a Congressional process that can take months.
Critics say the February 1, 2025 emergency gave the executive branch the speed needed to act on immigration without waiting for Congress, and canceling it slows that response.

Critics say using Congress's power to cut the emergency short overrides a decision the President made under authority granted by federal law, setting a precedent for Congress to block future emergency declarations.

119-hjres-130.one_liner: Bring back coal mining permits on federal land in Wyoming's Buffalo Field Office
provisions: The BLM's Buffalo Field Office controls federal land in Wyoming that sits above coal deposits.
A November 2024 BLM rule stopped coal companies from getting new government permits to mine that coal.
This resolution brings back the 2015 rules, which let coal companies apply for new mining permits on that land.

supporters: Supporters say that reversing the November 2024 BLM rule would reopen federal land in Wyoming's Buffalo Field Office to new coal mining permit applications, which they argue protects coal industry jobs in the region.

Supporters say the 2024 BLM rule went too far by making all BLM-managed coal in the Buffalo Field Office unavailable, and that the 2015 resource management plan already set rules for responsible leasing that should still apply.

Supporters say Congress has the authority under the Congressional Review Act to cancel agency rules, and using that power here puts elected officials — not BLM staff — in charge of decisions about Wyoming coal lands.
critics: Critics say the 2024 BLM rule came after a federal court found that BLM had not properly studied the climate effects of coal leasing in the Buffalo Field Office under the National Environmental Policy Act, and reversing the rule ignores that court ruling.

Critics say canceling the rule forces BLM to offer coal leasing permits on Wyoming federal land without completing the climate impact review the court required, putting the government back in legal conflict with the Western Organization of Resource Councils court decision.

Critics say the BLM rule was based on a full environmental review of the Buffalo Field Office planning area, and overturning it removes those protections for federal lands in Wyoming without replacing them with any new environmental review process.

119-hjres-142.one_liner: Cancel a DC tax law and bring back federal tax rules for DC residents
provisions: Cancels a DC law passed on December 20, 2025 that changed how DC's tax rules matched federal tax rules.
Brings back a higher standard tax deduction for DC residents — the amount DC had before the December 2025 law changed it.
Makes tips tax-free again for DC workers — the December 2025 DC law had kept tips taxable after a federal law stopped taxing them.
Restores a tax write-off that lets owners of certain commercial buildings in DC deduct the full cost in one year instead of spreading it out.
Removes a DC child tax credit that the December 2025 DC law had added back.

supporters: Supporters say this would restore the tip income exemption for DC workers, bringing DC back in line with the federal rule that stopped taxing tips after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed.
Supporters say this would bring back the higher standard tax deduction for DC residents that the December 20, 2025 DC law had reduced.
Supporters say this would restore the full first-year write-off for owners of certain commercial buildings in DC, a tax benefit the December 2025 DC law had removed.
critics: Critics say this removes the DC child tax credit that the December 20, 2025 DC law had added back for DC families.
Critics say this overrides a decision made by the DC Council on December 20, 2025, taking away DC's ability to set its own tax rules separate from federal law.

Critics say this forces DC to automatically adopt tax changes from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including the standard deduction increase and the commercial building write-off, without allowing DC to choose which of those rules apply to its residents.

119-sjres-86.one_liner: Cancel an EPA rule approving South Dakota's plan to reduce haze in national parks
provisions: Cancels an EPA rule published on August 28, 2025 that approved South Dakota's plan for reducing haze in national parks and wilderness areas.
Federal law requires states to submit plans for improving air visibility in national parks — this bill removes South Dakota's currently approved plan.
The cancelled rule covered South Dakota's second round of work under the national program to reduce haze in protected natural areas.

supporters: Supporters say the EPA overstepped by approving South Dakota's plan, and that the state should have more control over how it meets federal air quality goals without federal sign-off on the specific details.
Supporters say removing the August 28, 2025 EPA rule lets South Dakota revise or replace its second-period haze plan without being locked into the version the EPA already approved.
Supporters say Congress has the power under Chapter 8 of Title 5 to cancel agency rules it disagrees with, and this bill is a proper use of that authority.
critics: Critics say blocking the EPA's August 28, 2025 approval leaves South Dakota without a valid haze plan, which federal law requires all states to have for protecting visibility in national parks and wilderness areas.

Critics say the cancelled rule covered South Dakota's second round of required work under the national haze program, and rejecting it could delay air quality improvements in protected natural areas for years.
Critics say without an approved state plan in place, the EPA may be required to step in and write a federal plan for South Dakota, giving the state less control, not more.

119-sjres-80.one_liner: Reopen about half of Alaska's National Petroleum Reserve to oil and gas drilling
provisions: The National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska covers about 23 million acres on Alaska's North Slope.
A 2022 rule closed about 48% of that land to oil and gas drilling to protect wildlife and support local communities that rely on the land for food.
This resolution cancels the 2022 rule and brings back the 2020 rule, which kept more of that land open to drilling.
The land that was closed under the 2022 rule would be open again to oil and gas companies seeking leases.

supporters: Supporters say the 2022 rule wrongly closed about 48% of the 23-million-acre National Petroleum Reserve to oil and gas leasing, and reversing it would let energy companies access more of that land.
Supporters say returning to the 2020 plan would increase the area available for drilling leases on Alaska's North Slope, which they say supports U.S. energy production and Alaska jobs.
Supporters say Congress, not a federal agency, should decide how much of the 23-million-acre reserve stays off-limits to oil and gas companies.
critics: Critics say the 2022 rule protected wildlife habitat and the ability of local Alaska Native communities to hunt and fish on land in the National Petroleum Reserve, and canceling it removes those protections.
Critics say reopening the roughly 11 million acres that the 2022 rule closed to leasing puts at risk the subsistence food sources that nearby communities depend on.
Critics say the 2020 plan that this resolution restores gave oil and gas companies access to more of the 23 million acres without the same safeguards for surface resources and wildlife.

119-sjres-104.one_liner: Pull U.S. troops from any fighting with Iran that Congress has not approved
provisions: Tells the President to pull U.S. troops out of any fighting with or inside Iran.
This rule kicks in unless Congress has officially declared war on Iran or voted to allow military action there.
Does not stop the U.S. from defending against an attack on American troops, bases, or staff in other countries.

supporters: Supporters say the bill enforces the Constitution's rule that only Congress can authorize war, by requiring either a formal declaration of war or a congressional vote before U.S. troops can fight against Iran.
Supporters say the bill does not leave American troops defenseless — it still allows the U.S. military to respond if American soldiers, bases, or staff in other countries are attacked.
Supporters say that without this resolution, the President can order U.S. forces into hostilities against Iran without any vote from the 535 elected members of Congress.
critics: Critics say the bill limits the President's ability to act quickly as Commander in Chief, since getting a congressional vote could take days or weeks while a military threat is already unfolding.

Critics say the line between 'defending against an attack' and 'hostilities against Iran' is unclear, which could cause confusion about what U.S. forces are legally allowed to do in a fast-moving conflict.
Critics say directing the removal of U.S. forces from ongoing operations before Congress acts could create a gap in military readiness in the region.

119-sjres-95.one_liner: Cancel an IRS rule about how partnerships pay the corporate minimum tax
provisions: Cancels an IRS rule that told partnerships how to calculate and pay the Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax
The Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax is a federal tax that makes sure large companies pay at least a set minimum amount in taxes each year
Partnerships — businesses owned by two or more people or companies — would no longer have this IRS guidance to follow
Once canceled, the IRS cannot put out a new rule on the same topic unless Congress approves it first

supporters: Supporters say the IRS issued this rule without enough input from Congress, and canceling it restores lawmakers' control over how the Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax applies to partnerships.
Supporters say partnerships — businesses owned by two or more people or companies — should not have to follow complex IRS interim guidance that was put out without a full rulemaking process.

Supporters say the Congressional Review Act gives Congress the right to block agency rules like this one, and using it here ensures the IRS must get approval before writing a new rule on the same topic.
critics: Critics say that without this IRS guidance, partnerships have no clear instructions for how to calculate and pay the Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax, leaving businesses unsure of what they owe.

Critics say the Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax was created to make sure large companies pay at least a minimum amount in taxes each year, and removing the guidance makes that tax harder to apply to partnerships.
Critics say canceling the rule blocks the IRS from issuing any new guidance on this topic unless Congress votes to allow it, which could leave partnerships without answers for a long time.

119-sjres-84.one_liner: Cancel a rule that changed health insurance marketplace sign-up windows and requirements
provisions: Health insurance marketplaces are not required to run open enrollment only between November 1 and December 31 each year.
Marketplaces no longer have to check whether 75% of people signing up through special enrollment periods qualify before letting them enroll.
People protected under DACA — a program for people brought to the U.S. as children — can still sign up for health coverage through the marketplace and state low-income health programs.
Health insurers can still count sex-trait modification procedures as required coverage under their plans.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution blocks a rule that would have banned DACA recipients — people brought to the U.S. as children — from signing up for marketplace health plans and state Basic Health Programs, keeping coverage available for that group.

Supporters say without the rule, marketplaces are not forced to verify eligibility for 75% of special enrollment applicants before letting them enroll, which they say removes barriers for people who lose coverage mid-year.
Supporters say nullifying the rule lets health insurers keep covering sex-trait modification procedures as essential health benefits under their plans.
critics: Critics say blocking the rule removes a requirement that marketplaces check whether at least 75% of special enrollment applicants qualify before enrolling them, which they say allows ineligible people to receive subsidies they do not qualify for.

Critics say rejecting the rule keeps DACA recipients eligible for federally subsidized marketplace plans and state Basic Health Programs, which they say extends federal health benefits to people without lawful permanent resident status.
Critics say nullifying the rule forces insurers to count sex-trait modification procedures as required coverage, which they say raises plan costs across the individual and small group markets.

119-sjres-103.one_liner: Cancel a Department of Veterans Affairs rule on reproductive health services
provisions: Cancels a rule the Department of Veterans Affairs made about reproductive health services.
Congress used a law called the Congressional Review Act, which lets Congress vote to cancel rules made by federal agencies.
If this passes and is signed into law, that VA rule would no longer be in effect.
The VA could not put a similar rule back in place without new approval from Congress.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would cancel a VA rule that allowed VA facilities to provide abortion services, which they argue Congress never clearly authorized the VA to offer.
Supporters say using the Congressional Review Act means Congress — not a federal agency — would decide whether the VA can offer these services, keeping that power with elected officials.
Supporters say if the rule is canceled, the VA could not put a similar reproductive health rule back in place without a new vote in Congress, giving lawmakers lasting control over the policy.
critics: Critics say canceling this rule would end abortion access for women veterans and servicemembers at VA facilities, a group that has grown to over 2 million people.

Critics say the VA rule was put in place to make sure veterans could get reproductive health care even in states where abortion is banned under state law, and removing it would leave those veterans without options.

Critics say the Congressional Review Act provision that blocks the VA from issuing a similar rule without new Congressional approval could permanently limit care for veterans, even in medical emergencies.

117-hjres-17.one_liner: Remove the deadline for states to ratify the Equal Rights Amendment
provisions: The Equal Rights Amendment, first sent to states in 1972, would ban the government from treating people differently based on their sex.
Right now, a deadline blocks any new state from counting toward the 38 states needed to add the amendment to the Constitution.
This resolution removes that deadline, so any state that ratifies the amendment in the future would count toward the total.
The amendment becomes part of the Constitution if three-fourths of states — 38 out of 50 — ratify it.

supporters: Supporters say removing the deadline would allow the three states that ratified the ERA after the original cutoff — Nevada in 2017, Illinois in 2018, and Virginia in 2020 — to count toward the 38 states needed to add it to the Constitution.

Supporters say the ERA, first sent to states in 1972, would add a clear constitutional ban on sex discrimination by the government, and no rule in the Constitution requires Congress to set a deadline when proposing an amendment.
Supporters say 37 states have already ratified the amendment, meaning the country is one state away from the 38 needed, and removing the deadline is the only step left to let that count.
critics: Critics say five states that had ratified the ERA later voted to take back their ratification, and this resolution does not say whether those rescissions are valid, leaving the real count of supporting states unclear.

Critics say the Supreme Court has not ruled on whether states can rescind a ratification or whether a 50-year gap between a proposal and final ratification is legally allowed, so adding the ERA to the Constitution this way could face court challenges.

Critics say the 1972 proposal included a ratification deadline as part of its terms, and Congress changing those terms decades later, after most states already voted, sets a new precedent for how amendments can be added.

119-sjres-98.one_liner: Order the president to stop U.S. military action against Venezuela without a congressional vote
provisions: Tells the president to pull U.S. military forces out of any fighting in or against Venezuela.
The president can only keep forces there if Congress passes a formal declaration of war or a separate vote allowing military force.
Does not stop the U.S. from defending itself if attacked or if an attack is about to happen.

supporters: Supporters say the bill enforces the Constitution, which gives Congress — not the president — the sole power to declare war, and no declaration of war or authorization to use military force against Venezuela has been passed by Congress.

Supporters say the bill requires the president to withdraw U.S. troops from any fighting in or against Venezuela unless Congress holds a formal vote first, which puts the decision to go to war in the hands of elected lawmakers.

Supporters say the bill still lets the U.S. military defend itself if attacked or if an attack is about to happen, so pulling forces out of unauthorized hostilities does not leave the country open to harm.
critics: Critics say the bill would force the president to get a Congressional vote before acting, which could delay a military response during a fast-moving crisis involving Venezuela.

Critics say the self-defense carve-out only covers direct attacks or threats of imminent attack, which is a narrow exception that may not cover all situations where U.S. forces or interests in the region face danger.

Critics say removing forces from hostilities on Congress's timeline, rather than the military's, could put U.S. personnel already in the region at greater risk before a withdrawal can be safely carried out.

119-sjres-118.one_liner: Order U.S. troops removed from any military action involving Iran not approved by Congress
provisions: Tells the President to pull U.S. troops out of any military fighting in or against Iran.
Only applies to military actions that Congress has not voted to allow.
Does not affect any military actions involving Iran that Congress already approved.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would force the President to remove U.S. troops from any military fighting in or against Iran that Congress never voted to allow, putting war decisions back in Congress's hands as the Constitution requires.

Supporters say that without a congressional vote, U.S. military action against Iran lacks legal authority, and this resolution closes that gap by requiring withdrawal from any such unauthorized hostilities.
Supporters say the resolution is narrow — it only targets military actions Congress has not approved, so it does not touch any Iran-related operations that Congress already authorized.
critics: Critics say the resolution could limit the President's ability to respond quickly to attacks from Iran or Iran-backed groups, since pulling troops out would require waiting for Congress to act.
Critics say the line between 'authorized' and 'unauthorized' military action is not always clear, and this resolution could cause confusion about which operations must stop and which can continue.
Critics say removing U.S. forces from ongoing hostilities mid-conflict, without a congressional vote to re-authorize them, could put troops and regional allies at risk.

119-hjres-139.one_liner: Add a balanced budget requirement to the U.S. Constitution
provisions: Caps federal spending each year at the average amount the government collected in taxes over the previous three years, adjusted for population growth and inflation.
Debt payments do not count toward the spending cap.
Congress can spend above the cap only if two-thirds of members in both the House and Senate vote yes on a recorded vote.
Spending above the cap is also allowed during any year a war is officially declared by Congress.
Any new tax or tax rate increase must be approved by two-thirds of all members in both the House and Senate before it can become law.
These rules take effect five years after enough states ratify the amendment.

supporters: Supporters say capping federal spending at the average of the last three years of tax receipts, adjusted for population and inflation, would force Congress to stop spending more than the government takes in each year.
Supporters say requiring a two-thirds vote in both the House and Senate to raise taxes protects taxpayers by making it harder for Congress to increase tax rates without broad agreement.
Supporters say the five-year delay before the rules take effect gives Congress time to adjust spending without sudden cuts to programs people depend on.
critics: Critics say the two-thirds supermajority required to spend above the cap would make it nearly impossible to respond quickly to a recession or natural disaster, since 67% of both chambers would need to agree before any extra spending could happen.

Critics say the rule tying the spending cap to past tax receipts means that during an economic downturn, when tax revenue drops, the government would be forced to cut spending at the exact moment people need help most.

Critics say the two-thirds vote requirement to raise any tax rate would give a minority of members in Congress the power to block tax changes, even if a majority of elected representatives support them.

118-hjres-136.one_liner: Cancel the EPA's 2027 pollution and battery standards for cars, trucks, and SUVs
provisions: Cancels an EPA rule from April 2024 that set pollution limits for cars, trucks, and SUVs starting with 2027 models.
Greenhouse gas limits that rule placed on those vehicles no longer apply.
Battery durability rules for electric and hybrid vehicles set by that rule are removed.
Changes the EPA made to how fuel economy is measured are undone.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the EPA rule removes greenhouse gas emission limits on 2027 and later model cars, trucks, and SUVs, which they argue would have forced automakers to sell more electric vehicles than buyers currently want.
Supporters say removing the battery durability requirements set by the April 2024 rule lowers production costs for electric and hybrid vehicles, which they say were being passed on to car buyers.
Supporters say undoing the EPA's changes to how fuel economy is measured stops a system they claim gave electric vehicles an unfair advantage over gas-powered cars in efficiency ratings.
critics: Critics say the April 2024 EPA rule set greenhouse gas emission standards for model year 2027 and later light-duty and medium-duty vehicles, and canceling it means those vehicles will emit more carbon dioxide per mile with no federal limit.

Critics say removing the battery durability rules leaves buyers of electric and hybrid vehicles with no federal standard guaranteeing how long or how far a battery must last before it can be replaced.
Critics say reversing the EPA's fuel economy measurement updates makes it harder for consumers to accurately compare the real energy costs of gas-powered cars versus electric and hybrid models.

118-hjres-165.one_liner: Cancel a 2024 Education Department rule on sex discrimination in federally funded schools
provisions: Congress uses a law called the Congressional Review Act to cancel a rule the Education Department published on April 29, 2024.
The rule being canceled was based on Title IX, the federal law that bans sex discrimination in schools that get federal money.
The 2024 rule's new definitions of sex-based harassment no longer apply.
Schools no longer have to follow the complaint steps the 2024 rule added for sex-based harassment cases.

supporters: Supporters say the 2024 rule changed how Title IX defines sex-based harassment in ways Congress never approved, and this resolution restores the original meaning of the law.
Supporters say schools should not have to follow the complaint steps added by the April 29, 2024 rule, which they argue created extra burdens for schools handling harassment cases.
Supporters say using the Congressional Review Act is the proper way for Congress to cancel agency rules that go beyond what federal law allows.
critics: Critics say canceling the 2024 rule removes protections for students who face sex-based harassment in schools that receive federal funding under Title IX.

Critics say the new definitions of sex-based harassment in the April 29, 2024 rule gave clearer guidance to schools on what counts as harassment, and removing them leaves students without those protections.
Critics say the complaint steps the 2024 rule added helped make sure schools handled harassment cases in a fair and consistent way, and canceling the rule takes that away.

119-sjres-116.one_liner: Pull US troops out of military actions against Iran not approved by Congress
provisions: Tells the US military to stop taking part in any fighting in or against Iran.
Only covers military actions that Congress has not voted to allow.
This is a joint resolution, so both the House and Senate must vote to pass it.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would force Congress to vote before U.S. troops take part in any fighting in or against Iran, which is what the Constitution requires.
Supporters say the resolution targets only military actions that Congress has not voted to allow, so it does not touch operations that already have congressional approval.
Supporters say requiring both the House and Senate to pass this resolution gives the American people a voice in whether the country goes to war with Iran.
critics: Critics say the resolution could tie the President's hands during a fast-moving crisis with Iran, where waiting for Congress to act could put U.S. troops at risk.
Critics say existing military force authorizations passed by Congress in 2001 and 2002 may already give the President legal cover for some actions against Iran, making this resolution unnecessary.
Critics say removing U.S. forces from hostilities before a diplomatic or military situation is resolved could weaken American leverage in the region.

119-sjres-123.one_liner: Order the removal of U.S. troops from any unauthorized conflict with Iran
provisions: Orders the President to pull U.S. troops out of any military fighting with or against Iran that Congress has not voted to approve
Covers all forms of military combat involving U.S. forces and Iran, not just a declared war
Uses a type of resolution that lets Congress end military action that started without a Congressional vote

supporters: Supporters say the resolution would require Congress to vote before U.S. troops can take part in any military fighting with or against Iran, returning a power the Constitution gives to Congress — not the President.

Supporters say the resolution covers all types of military combat, not just a declared war, so the President cannot send forces into battle against Iran through smaller actions that avoid a full war vote.
Supporters say the resolution uses a legal tool that lets Congress stop military action that began without its approval, giving lawmakers a direct way to end unauthorized fighting.
critics: Critics say ordering U.S. forces out of hostilities could put troops and allies at risk if Congress takes days or weeks to vote while a military situation is moving fast.
Critics say the President, as Commander in Chief, needs to act quickly against threats from Iran, and a required Congressional vote could delay or block a necessary military response.
Critics say the resolution does not set a clear dollar limit, troop number, or timeline — leaving it unclear exactly which ongoing military activities it would require to stop.

119-sjres-107.one_liner: Cancel an IRS rule defining when wind and solar projects qualify for clean electricity tax credits
provisions: Cancels an IRS rule that set standards for when wind and solar projects count as having 'started construction.'
That rule applied to two tax credits — the Clean Electricity Production Credit and the Clean Electricity Investment Credit — which are set to end once certain building milestones are reached.
Wind and solar developers used this rule to know if their project qualified for those credits before they end.

supporters: Supporters say canceling the IRS rule removes standards that allowed wind and solar developers to lock in tax credits — the Clean Electricity Production Credit and Clean Electricity Investment Credit — before those credits were set to end, which they argue stretched out subsidies Congress intended to phase out.

Supporters say the IRS rule gave wind and solar project developers a way to claim credits even if their projects were not fully built, and removing it tightens the rules around who actually qualifies.
Supporters say Congress, not the IRS, should decide the construction standards that determine when these credits apply to wind and solar facilities.
critics: Critics say canceling this rule takes away clear guidelines that wind and solar developers relied on to know whether their projects qualified for the Clean Electricity Production Credit or Clean Electricity Investment Credit before those credits expired.
Critics say without the IRS rule, wind and solar companies that already started planning or building projects based on those standards could lose access to tax credits they expected to receive.
Critics say the rule gave certainty to developers of applicable wind and solar facilities, and removing it creates confusion about which projects count as having begun construction under federal law.

119-sjres-32.one_liner: Block one proposed U.S. weapons sale to Israel
provisions: Stops one specific proposed sale of weapons and military equipment from the United States to Israel.
The sale was already in progress under a foreign military sales process before Congress voted to block it.
If passed and signed, the sale cannot go through as proposed.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution uses the Arms Export Control Act's congressional review process, which gives Congress the formal power to block a proposed foreign military sale before it is completed.
Supporters say the resolution targets one specific proposed sale of defense articles and services to Israel, not a broader cut to all U.S. military assistance.

Supporters say members of Congress have raised concerns about how the weapons in this sale could be used, and the resolution gives elected officials a direct way to act on those concerns through the existing review window.
critics: Critics say Israel is a security partner, and they consider stopping this in-progress sale to be a break in what they see as a U.S. commitment to fulfill approved arms agreements.
Critics say the sale was already moving through the foreign military sales process before Congress voted to block it, which they say creates uncertainty about how future arms deals will be handled.
Critics say other U.S. allies may become less confident that approved arms sales will be completed if Congress can block them after the process has already started.

119-sjres-139.one_liner: Cancel an EPA rule that rejected Colorado's state plan for reducing haze
provisions: Cancels an EPA rule that rejected Colorado's own plan to cut regional haze — the smoky air that reduces visibility in national parks and wilderness areas.
Because the EPA rejected Colorado's plan, the state was set to follow a federal haze plan instead of its own.
Congress used the Congressional Review Act — a law that lets Congress vote to block a recently issued government rule — to cancel this EPA action.
If this resolution passes, Colorado's state haze plan goes back into effect.
