supporters: Supporters say this resolution restores Colorado's own haze reduction plan, which the state designed to cut smoky air in its national parks and wilderness areas, instead of forcing a federal plan on the state.

Supporters say the EPA's rejection of Colorado's plan took away the state's right to manage its own air quality, and using the Congressional Review Act to cancel that EPA rule gives that control back to Colorado.
critics: Critics say the EPA rejected Colorado's state haze plan because it did not cut enough smoky air pollution to protect visibility in national parks and wilderness areas, and restoring that plan means weaker protections than the federal plan would have required.

Critics say blocking the EPA rule through the Congressional Review Act removes a layer of federal review that was meant to make sure state haze plans actually meet Clean Air Act standards for reducing regional haze.

119-sjres-124.one_liner: Order the removal of U.S. troops from unauthorized military actions against Cuba
provisions: Tells the President to pull U.S. military forces out of any conflict in or against Cuba.
Applies only to military actions that Congress has not voted to approve.
Covers both fighting inside Cuba and military attacks directed at Cuba from outside.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would stop the President from using U.S. military forces in or against Cuba without a vote from Congress, which they argue is required by law.
Supporters say the resolution covers all uses of force — both troops sent inside Cuba and military attacks aimed at Cuba from outside — closing gaps that could let presidents act without approval.
Supporters say Congress has not passed any law allowing military action against Cuba, so any current or future hostilities would have to stop until lawmakers vote on the matter.
critics: Critics say pulling military forces back could limit the President's ability to respond quickly if U.S. interests or personnel near Cuba face a sudden threat.
Critics say the resolution does not define what counts as 'hostilities,' which could cause confusion about which military activities near Cuba must stop.

Critics say directing the removal of forces through a joint resolution may conflict with the President's role as commander-in-chief, raising questions about which branch controls troop movements in fast-moving situations.

119-sjres-138.one_liner: Block one proposed sale of defense articles and services to Israel
provisions: Stops one specific proposed sale of military equipment and services to the government of Israel.
If this resolution passes, that sale cannot go forward.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would block the specific proposed sale of military equipment and services to Israel, giving Congress a direct vote on arms transfers it believes should not go forward.
Supporters say stopping this sale would let Congress exercise its oversight role over foreign military sales, which are usually approved without a full congressional vote.
critics: Critics say blocking this specific sale would weaken the U.S.-Israel defense partnership by cutting off military equipment and services Israel has already been promised.
Critics say rejecting this proposed sale sends a signal to U.S. allies that weapons agreements with America are not reliable, which could affect future partnerships.

119-sjres-114.one_liner: Pull US troops from any military action against Iran not approved by Congress
provisions: Tells the President to withdraw US military forces from any fighting in or against Iran that Congress has not voted to approve.
Covers military action taking place inside Iran and military action aimed at Iran from outside its borders.
Takes the form of a joint resolution, meaning both the House and Senate must pass it for it to take effect.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would require the President to stop any military action inside Iran or aimed at Iran from outside its borders unless Congress has voted to approve it, restoring Congress's constitutional role in deciding when the U.S. goes to war.

Supporters say that because the resolution covers both attacks inside Iran and attacks launched toward Iran from other locations, it closes loopholes that could allow military operations without a formal vote.
Supporters say Congress has not passed a law authorizing fighting with Iran, and this resolution forces that missing approval to be addressed before U.S. troops are put at risk.
critics: Critics say the resolution would block the President from responding quickly to attacks from Iran or Iranian-backed forces, since waiting for both the House and Senate to pass a joint resolution could take days or weeks.

Critics say the resolution's requirement that both chambers pass it before any military action is authorized could leave U.S. forces without legal cover during fast-moving threats that require an immediate response.
Critics say directing a full withdrawal from hostilities could signal to Iran that the U.S. will not act militarily, which they argue could encourage further Iranian aggression in the region.

119-sjres-132.one_liner: Restore federal consumer bureau financial risk checks for active-duty troops and their families
provisions: A Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) rule required financial companies to be checked for risks they posed to active-duty troops.
Those checks covered risks to the troops and their families.
The CFPB withdrew that rule, which ended the checks.
This resolution blocks the withdrawal and brings those checks back.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would bring back CFPB checks on financial companies that posed risks to active-duty troops and their families, protections that were removed when the CFPB withdrew the rule.
Supporters say without these checks, lenders and financial companies face no federal review for how their products affect servicemembers, leaving military families without that layer of oversight.
Supporters say the original rule was designed to catch specific risks to troops — like high-cost loans or unfair terms — and blocking the withdrawal restores that protection.
critics: Critics say the CFPB had the legal authority to withdraw the rule, and this resolution uses a congressional tool to override a regulatory decision that was within the agency's power.

Critics say bringing back the checks adds compliance costs for financial companies that serve military communities, which could make it harder or more expensive for those companies to offer products to servicemembers.
Critics say the resolution does not include new requirements or updated standards, so restoring the old rule may not address whatever gaps or problems led the CFPB to withdraw it in the first place.

119-sjres-184.one_liner: Pull US troops out of any military fighting against Iran not approved by Congress
provisions: Tells the President to remove US military forces from any fighting involving Iran that Congress has not voted to approve.
Covers military actions happening inside Iran and attacks directed at Iran.
Congress has not passed a separate law approving military hostilities against Iran, so this resolution would require those forces to be withdrawn.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution would require the President to withdraw forces because Congress has never passed a law approving military action against Iran, meaning any current fighting automatically falls under the mandatory removal order.

Supporters say the resolution closes a gap by covering both operations inside Iran and attacks launched at Iran from outside its borders, so the military could not stay engaged by moving to nearby waters or airspace.

Supporters say returning the authorization decision to Congress means elected lawmakers — not the President alone — would have to vote before any military campaign against Iran could legally continue.
critics: Critics say the resolution's mandatory withdrawal language contains no exception for active combat, which would require pulling US forces out mid-operation with no time set aside to safely exit the fight.

Critics say that because Congress has not yet passed a replacement authorization, enforcing the resolution could leave US ships and aircraft in the region with no legal authority to defend themselves if attacked.

Critics say the resolution's broad scope — covering all attacks 'directed at Iran' — means the US could not respond to an Iranian strike on American forces without first returning to Congress for a new vote.

119-sjres-141.one_liner: Restore a rule against deceptive and unfair medical debt collection
provisions: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau removed a rule about how debt collectors can collect medical debt.
This bill cancels that removal and puts the rule back in effect.
Debt collectors would again have to follow restrictions on deceptive and unfair practices when collecting medical debt.
Congress is using its power under federal law to block a federal agency from removing one of its own rules.

supporters: Supporters say this bill would restore rules that stop debt collectors from using deceptive or unfair methods to collect medical bills, protections that were removed when the CFPB withdrew Regulation F.

Supporters say medical debt affects tens of millions of Americans, and without the reinstated rule, debt collectors face no federal restrictions on misleading tactics when pursuing patients for unpaid medical bills.

Supporters say Congress has the legal right under federal law to block a federal agency from withdrawing its own rules, and this bill is a proper use of that power to keep patient protections in place.
critics: Critics say the CFPB removed the medical debt collection rule through its own review process, and Congress using the Congressional Review Act to override that decision limits how agencies can update or repeal their own regulations.

Critics say restoring Regulation F adds compliance costs and legal restrictions on debt collectors trying to recover legitimate unpaid medical debts, which could affect how providers and collectors recoup those funds.

Critics say the CFPB is the agency responsible for consumer financial rules, and blocking its decision to withdraw this rule through a congressional disapproval resolution sets a precedent for Congress to override agency judgment on technical regulatory matters.

119-sjres-99.one_liner: Cancel a federal rule that ended automatic work permit extensions for non-citizens
provisions: Cancels a USCIS rule that ended automatic extensions of work permits for non-citizens waiting on immigration decisions
Brings back the automatic extension of Employment Authorization Documents — the official work permits issued by the federal government
Non-citizens who have pending immigration applications will again receive automatic extensions on their work permits while they wait
USCIS, the agency that handles immigration paperwork, would be required to resume granting these automatic extensions

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would bring back automatic extensions on Employment Authorization Documents, so non-citizens with pending immigration applications can keep working while they wait for a decision.
Supporters say without automatic extensions, workers could lose their jobs even if they did nothing wrong — just because USCIS is slow processing their paperwork.
Supporters say requiring USCIS to resume automatic extensions protects employers too, since businesses would not have to fire workers over a processing delay.
critics: Critics say the USCIS rule that this resolution cancels was meant to give the government more control over who holds active work permits during the immigration review process.

Critics say bringing back automatic extensions means non-citizens can keep working even when their underlying immigration status is still unresolved, which critics argue skips a key step in the approval process.
Critics say Congress should let USCIS manage its own rules about Employment Authorization Documents rather than using a disapproval resolution to override the agency.

119-sjres-130.one_liner: Keep in place a federal rule on how banks sign customers up for overdraft coverage
provisions: In 2024, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau issued a policy saying banks cannot sign customers up for overdraft coverage without getting clear consent first.
The bureau later issued a rule to cancel that 2024 policy.
This resolution uses a federal law to block that cancellation rule.
Because the cancellation is blocked, the original policy stays in effect and banks must still follow it.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution keeps the 2024 Consumer Financial Protection Bureau policy in place, which requires banks to get clear consent from customers before signing them up for overdraft coverage.
Supporters say that without this resolution, the bureau's cancellation rule would take effect and bank customers could be enrolled in overdraft programs without giving clear permission first.
Supporters say Congress has the authority under federal disapproval law to block the bureau's cancellation rule and restore the original consumer consent requirement.
critics: Critics say the bureau chose to cancel the 2024 policy through its own regulatory process, and this resolution uses a federal disapproval law to override that agency decision.
Critics say financial institutions made changes based on the bureau's decision to cancel the 2024 rule, and blocking that cancellation creates uncertainty for banks trying to follow the rules.
Critics say the bureau, not Congress, is the agency responsible for setting overdraft rules for bank customers, and this resolution removes that authority from the bureau.

119-sjres-188.one_liner: Block the EPA's removal of air pollution limits on coal and oil power plants
provisions: The EPA issued a rule that removed air pollution limits on coal and oil power plants.
This bill cancels that EPA rule.
If this bill passes, the pollution limits the EPA removed go back into effect for coal and oil power plants.

supporters: Supporters say this bill would restore air pollution limits on coal and oil power plants that the EPA removed, protecting people who live near those plants from hazardous air pollution.
Supporters say that without this bill, coal and oil power plants would no longer have to meet the emission standards for toxic air pollutants that were in place before the EPA repealed them.
Supporters say Congress has the right to cancel EPA rules it disagrees with under the Congressional Review Act, and this bill uses that authority to bring back the removed limits.
critics: Critics say this bill would force coal and oil power plants to follow pollution rules that the EPA already decided were unnecessary, which could raise operating costs for those plants.
Critics say the EPA went through a formal process to repeal these emission standards and found reasons to remove them, and Congress should let that decision stand.
Critics say restoring these limits could affect the electricity supply from coal and oil plants, which some regions still depend on for power.

119-sjres-60.one_liner: Cancel an EPA rule that raised how much air pollution Indiana power plants can release
provisions: Cancels an EPA rule published in May 2025.
That rule had raised how much nitrogen oxide — a type of air pollutant — Indiana power plants were allowed to release.
With this rule canceled, Indiana power plants return to the lower emission limits that were in place before May 2025.
The canceled rule had applied to the months of May through September each year, starting in 2024.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution cancels the EPA's May 2025 rule that raised nitrogen oxide limits for Indiana power plants, returning those plants to the lower emission limits that were in place before that rule took effect.

Supporters say the May–September ozone season is when nitrogen oxide pollution most harms air quality in downwind states like Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Michigan, and they argue Indiana power plants should not release more pollution during those months.

Supporters say Congress has the authority under the Congressional Review Act to block federal agency rules, and this resolution is the proper way to use that authority to reject the EPA's May 2025 change.
critics: Critics say that blocking this EPA rule forces Indiana power plants back to emission limits the EPA determined were too strict, based on the agency's finding that those original limits did not reflect what the plants could realistically achieve.

Critics say the May 2025 EPA rule made a needed adjustment to Indiana's nitrogen oxide budget after court decisions changed how the Cross-State Air Pollution Rule applies, and canceling it removes that correction.

Critics say restoring the lower nitrogen oxide limits could raise compliance costs for Indiana power plants during the May–September period, which utility groups say may affect electricity prices for customers in the state.

119-sjres-69.one_liner: Block a US Fish and Wildlife Service plan to manage barred owls in three states
provisions: Congress voted to cancel a US Fish and Wildlife Service rule about managing barred owls in Washington, Oregon, and California.
That rule gave the government a plan to shoot barred owls in those three states.
Shooting barred owls was part of a plan to protect spotted owls, which share the same forests.
When Congress cancels a rule this way, the agency cannot issue a new rule that does the same thing.

supporters: Supporters say the rule gave the Fish and Wildlife Service a plan to shoot barred owls in national forests across Washington, Oregon, and California — a program covering pilot sites in all three states that had not been directly authorized by Congress before.

Supporters say canceling this rule under chapter 8 of title 5 of the U.S. Code also blocks the agency from writing any new rule with the same shooting program, which ends this approach entirely without requiring a future congressional vote to stop it.

Supporters say the rule called for a shooting program planned to run across multiple pilot sites in three states over a 10-year period, affecting barred owls that are not listed as threatened or endangered under federal law.
critics: Critics say the spotted owl is listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act, and the barred owl removal plan was the Fish and Wildlife Service's primary active strategy to slow the spotted owl's decline across Washington, Oregon, and California.

Critics say that because Congress used chapter 8 of title 5 to cancel this rule, the agency is permanently blocked from issuing a similar barred owl removal rule — taking away the government's main spotted owl recovery tool in all three states.

Critics say the Fish and Wildlife Service ran controlled pilot studies before writing this rule, and those studies showed that spotted owl populations grew in forest areas where barred owls were removed, meaning the rule was built on documented field results.

119-sjres-163.one_liner: Direct the President to pull U.S. troops out of unauthorized fighting with Iran
provisions: Tells the President to pull U.S. military forces out of any fighting with Iran.
This rule only kicks in if Congress has not voted to declare war or approve the fighting.
Does not stop the U.S. from defending itself if attacked — including protecting American troops or buildings in other countries.
Uses the War Powers Act, a law that gives Congress — not the President — the power to decide when the U.S. goes to war.
Covers any current or future military action against Iran that Congress has not voted to approve.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution enforces the War Powers Act, which gives Congress — not the President — the power to decide when the U.S. goes to war with Iran.
Supporters say that without a Congressional vote to declare war or approve military action, any U.S. fighting with Iran is unauthorized, and this resolution would require troops to be withdrawn.
Supporters say the resolution still allows the U.S. military to defend itself if attacked, so American troops and facilities in other countries would still be protected.
critics: Critics say the resolution could limit the President's ability to respond quickly to threats from Iran before Congress has time to vote on authorizing military force.
Critics say that requiring Congressional approval before acting against Iran could weaken U.S. deterrence, making it harder to stop Iran from taking hostile actions against American forces or allies.
Critics say the resolution applies to any current or future military action against Iran, which could force a withdrawal even in situations where stopping would put American troops at greater risk.

119-sjres-185.one_liner: Order US troops out of combat against Iran that Congress did not approve
provisions: Tells the President to pull US troops out of any military fights involving Iran that Congress has not voted to approve
Covers military action happening inside Iran and attacks directed at Iran
Does not apply to military actions that Congress has already voted to allow

supporters: Supporters say this resolution would require the President to end military fights involving Iran that Congress has not voted to approve, which supporters say the Constitution requires before troops can be sent into combat.
Supporters say the resolution covers both attacks inside Iran and attacks directed at Iran, closing what they see as a loophole that has allowed military action without a formal vote.
Supporters say the carve-out for already-authorized operations means ongoing missions approved by Congress would not be affected.
critics: Critics say the word 'hostilities' is not defined in the resolution, which they say could create confusion about which military activities must stop and which can continue.
Critics say pulling troops from unapproved operations could leave US forces or allies exposed if a fast-moving conflict with Iran requires an immediate military response before Congress can vote.
Critics say the resolution limits the President's ability to act quickly in a crisis, since getting a Congressional vote can take days or weeks while a military threat may require action in hours.

119-sjres-77.one_liner: End the national emergency that added a 25% import tax on most goods from Canada
provisions: Cancels the national emergency Trump declared on February 1, 2025 about Canadian imports.
That emergency added a 25% extra tax on most goods shipped from Canada into the U.S.
Canadian energy products like oil and natural gas had a lower 10% extra tax instead of 25%.
Canceling the emergency removes those extra import taxes on Canadian goods.

supporters: Supporters say ending the emergency would remove the 25% extra tax on Canadian goods, lowering costs for U.S. businesses and consumers who buy products imported from Canada.
Supporters say the 10% tariff on Canadian oil and gas has raised energy prices, and canceling the emergency declared on February 1, 2025 would bring those costs down.
Supporters say Congress, not the president, should control trade policy, and this resolution takes back that authority by ending the emergency Trump declared.
critics: Critics say the 25% tariff on Canadian imports gives the U.S. leverage to push Canada on trade and border issues, and removing it weakens that pressure.
Critics say ending the emergency would eliminate the 10% tariff on Canadian energy, making it harder for U.S. energy producers to compete with cheaper Canadian oil and gas.
Critics say canceling the February 1, 2025 emergency sends a signal to trading partners that the U.S. will back down from tariffs, reducing future negotiating power.

119-sjres-71.one_liner: End the national energy emergency the President declared on January 20, 2025
provisions: Ends the national emergency about energy that the President declared on January 20, 2025.
Takes away the emergency powers federal agencies were using to speed up approvals for energy projects.
Stops agencies from using special permit rules under environmental laws to fast-track energy construction.
Ends the order for the Department of Defense to study how it gets and moves energy resources.
Removes the authority to spend emergency military construction money on energy projects.

supporters: Supporters say ending the January 20, 2025 emergency declaration will stop federal agencies from bypassing normal environmental review rules that were put in place to protect communities near energy projects.

Supporters say removing emergency permitting powers means energy construction projects in the Northeast, West Coast, and Alaska will have to go through standard approval steps, giving local groups and states more say.
Supporters say canceling the order for the Department of Defense to study energy transport removes a task that Congress did not specifically approve or fund.
critics: Critics say taking away emergency powers will slow down approvals for domestic energy projects at a time when the original order stated that U.S. energy supply and infrastructure are not meeting the country's needs.
Critics say stopping the use of emergency military construction authority means the Pentagon can no longer spend those funds to fix energy supply problems it finds in the Northeast and West Coast.
Critics say ending the fast-track permitting rules under environmental laws will delay energy infrastructure projects that agencies were already moving forward under the emergency order.

119-sjres-81.one_liner: End the national emergency used to add a 40% tariff on most imports from Brazil
provisions: Ends a national emergency that President Trump declared on July 30, 2025.
That emergency was used to add a 40% extra tax on most goods imported from Brazil.
Some products were not taxed under that rule — including aircraft parts, wood pulp, precious metals, energy products, and fertilizers.
Ending the emergency would remove the legal basis for that 40% tariff.

supporters: Supporters say ending the emergency would remove the 40% tariff on Brazilian imports, lowering costs for U.S. businesses and consumers who buy goods like food, clothing, and manufactured products from Brazil.
Supporters say the 40% tariff was added through an emergency declaration, and Congress has the power to end emergencies it believes are not justified by a real national security threat.

Supporters say removing the tariff could help U.S. industries that depend on Brazilian inputs, since the exemptions for aircraft parts, wood pulp, and fertilizers left many other sectors still paying the 40% extra cost.
critics: Critics say the 40% tariff gives the U.S. leverage in trade talks with Brazil, and ending it too soon could remove pressure on Brazil to change trade practices that the executive order was meant to address.

Critics say the President has broad legal authority to declare national emergencies for trade purposes, and Congress overriding that authority through this resolution limits the executive branch's ability to act quickly on trade issues.

Critics say the tariff exemptions for energy products, precious metals, and fertilizers show the policy was designed carefully to protect key U.S. industries, and the remaining 40% tariff on other goods should stay in place to protect American manufacturers.

119-sjres-76.one_liner: Restore original emissions deadlines for oil and natural gas facilities
provisions: Cancels an EPA rule from July 31, 2025 that gave oil and natural gas companies more time to meet pollution control standards.
Oil and gas facilities must meet the original deadlines for controlling leaks from equipment, storage tanks, and vents.
The Methane Super Emitter Program — which tracks large releases of methane gas — goes back to its original start date.
States must submit their pollution control plans by the original deadline, not the extended one.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution restores the original deadlines for oil and gas facilities to control leaks from equipment, storage tanks, and vents — deadlines the EPA had extended in its July 31, 2025 rule.

Supporters say bringing back the original start date for the Methane Super Emitter Program means large methane releases will be tracked sooner, reducing greenhouse gas pollution from oil and natural gas sites.
Supporters say states should not get extra time to submit their pollution control plans, and restoring the original state plan deadline keeps environmental protections on schedule.
critics: Critics say the July 31, 2025 EPA rule gave oil and gas companies needed extra time to install control devices for equipment leaks, storage vessels, and vent systems, and canceling that extension forces companies to meet deadlines they may not be ready for.

Critics say delaying the Methane Super Emitter Program had a reason behind it, and reverting to the original implementation date could cause problems for facilities that planned around the extended timeline.

Critics say states were given more time to submit pollution control plans because the work is complex, and removing that extension puts pressure on state agencies that may not have enough staff or resources to meet the earlier deadline.

119-sjres-82.one_liner: Cancel an HHS rule requiring the department to follow rulemaking law as written
provisions: Cancels a rule from the Department of Health and Human Services that required the department to follow the exact text of the Administrative Procedure Act when making regulations.
The Administrative Procedure Act is the law that sets the steps all federal agencies must follow when creating or changing rules.
With this HHS rule gone, the department no longer has its own written policy requiring it to stick to what that law says word for word.

supporters: Supporters say canceling this rule removes a requirement that was already covered by federal law, since the Administrative Procedure Act already applies to all agencies without HHS needing its own separate written policy repeating it.
Supporters say the HHS rule added an extra layer of internal policy that could slow down the department's ability to update health regulations when urgent changes are needed.
Supporters say Congress, not a single department, should decide how agencies interpret the Administrative Procedure Act, so HHS should not have its own binding text-based policy on that law.
critics: Critics say removing this rule means HHS no longer has a written commitment to follow the exact text of the Administrative Procedure Act, which could make it easier for the department to issue regulations that bend or skip required steps.

Critics say the Administrative Procedure Act sets the process that protects the public's right to comment on new rules, and without HHS's written policy reinforcing that, those comment rights could be weakened for the millions of people affected by HHS programs.

Critics say this disapproval resolution targets a rule that kept one of the largest federal departments — which oversees Medicare, Medicaid, and public health — accountable to the law's exact wording, and canceling it reduces that accountability.

119-sjres-88.one_liner: End the national emergency President Trump declared to put tariffs on most imports
provisions: President Trump declared a national emergency on April 2, 2025, to put tariffs on imported goods.
That emergency placed a 10% tariff on most goods coming into the U.S. from other countries.
Some trading partners faced extra tariffs on top of that 10%.
This resolution ends that emergency.
Ending the emergency would remove those tariffs from most imported goods.

supporters: Supporters say the 10% tariff on most imported goods has raised the cost of everyday products for American consumers, from electronics to clothing.
Supporters say the extra duties placed on specific trading partners led those countries to put their own tariffs on American exports, hurting U.S. farmers and manufacturers who sell goods abroad.

Supporters say this resolution uses Congress's authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to end the April 2, 2025 emergency declaration, returning trade policy decisions to the legislative branch rather than the executive.
critics: Critics say the 10% base tariff has brought in billions of dollars in federal revenue and gives U.S. factories a price advantage over cheaper foreign goods entering the country.

Critics say the extra tariffs on specific trading partners are a tool the president is using to push for better trade deals, and ending the April 2, 2025 emergency would remove that leverage before negotiations are finished.

Critics say removing both the 10% tariff and the additional duties on specific trading partners means the U.S. would give up its bargaining position with nothing guaranteed in return from those countries.

119-sjres-89.one_liner: Bring back coal leasing on federal land in Wyoming's Buffalo Field Office
provisions: Coal on federal land in Wyoming's Buffalo Field Office area becomes available for companies to apply to lease again.
The Bureau of Land Management must follow its 2015 land-use plan for that Wyoming area rather than the 2024 update.
Under the 2015 plan, private companies can apply to mine coal on federal land in that area.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution would restore the 2015 BLM land-use plan, which allows private companies to apply to mine coal on federal land in the Buffalo Field Office area in Wyoming.

Supporters say that reopening coal leasing applications on federal land in the Buffalo Field Office could generate royalty payments to the federal government and support local coal industry jobs in Wyoming.
Supporters say the 2024 BLM rule was finalized in November 2024 and can be reversed under the Congressional Review Act, which lets Congress cancel recent federal agency rules.
critics: Critics say the resolution overturns a BLM rule that was written to satisfy a federal court order requiring the agency to study the climate effects of coal leasing in the Buffalo Field Office under the National Environmental Policy Act.
Critics say canceling the 2024 rule forces BLM to use the 2015 plan, which the court found did not properly evaluate alternatives to limit or stop coal leasing as required by law.
Critics say the resolution removes protections that BLM put in place after reviewing climate impacts of coal extraction on federally managed land in the Buffalo Field Office planning area.

119-sjres-83.one_liner: Pull US troops from any armed conflict Congress has not voted to allow
provisions: Requires the President to remove US troops from any armed conflict Congress has not voted to allow.
Covers any conflict — current or future — where Congress did not pass a vote before US troops got involved.
Congress must pass a formal vote approving military action for US troops to remain in a conflict.

supporters: Supporters say the bill enforces the Constitution's rule that only Congress — not the President — can authorize military force, by requiring a formal Congressional vote before US troops can remain in any armed conflict.

Supporters say the provision covering current conflicts would end ongoing military actions that were never approved by Congress, stopping troops from staying in hostilities without a public vote by elected representatives.
Supporters say requiring Congress to pass a vote for every conflict gives the American public more control over when and where US troops fight.
critics: Critics say the requirement to get a Congressional vote before troops can remain in a conflict could leave US forces in danger during fast-moving military situations where there is no time to wait for Congress to act.
Critics say the provision covering current conflicts could force a sudden withdrawal of US troops already deployed, which could put allied forces at risk and destabilize ongoing military operations.

Critics say the President's role as Commander-in-Chief has long included the authority to respond to threats quickly, and this bill would limit that authority in ways that could weaken US military response.

119-sjres-91.one_liner: Bring back oil and gas leasing to 1.6 million acres in Alaska's Arctic refuge
provisions: Opens about 1.6 million acres of Alaska's Arctic National Wildlife Refuge Coastal Plain to oil and gas leasing — up from 400,000 acres allowed under a December 2024 rule
About 1.2 million of those acres had been off-limits to leasing since December 2024; this bill removes that restriction
By law, the acres made available for leasing must include the parts of this land most likely to contain oil

supporters: Supporters say nullifying the 2024 rule would reopen about 1.6 million acres of the Coastal Plain to oil and gas leasing, compared to only 400,000 acres allowed under the rule being cancelled.
Supporters say the bill ensures that leasing must happen in the areas most likely to contain oil and gas, which they argue gives the U.S. better access to domestic energy resources in Alaska.
Supporters say the 2024 rule blocked 1.2 million acres from any leasing or exploration, and removing that restriction gives energy companies more options to find and produce oil.
critics: Critics say the 1.2 million acres that the 2024 rule protected were set aside to conserve wildlife habitat and other resources in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge Coastal Plain, and this bill removes those protections.

Critics say the 2024 BLM rule followed an environmental review process and chose a leasing option specifically designed to limit damage to the Coastal Plain area, and this bill wipes out that decision.

Critics say requiring leases to be placed in the areas with the highest potential for hydrocarbons means drilling activity would be concentrated in the most ecologically sensitive parts of the 1.6 million acre program area.

119-sjres-90.one_liner: Order the president to stop U.S. military action against Venezuela without a vote from Congress
provisions: Tells the president to pull U.S. military forces out of any fighting in or against Venezuela.
The president can only keep those forces there if Congress formally declares war or passes a specific vote allowing it.
Does not stop the U.S. from defending itself if the U.S. is attacked or about to be attacked.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution restores Congress's role in deciding when the U.S. goes to war, since the Constitution gives Congress — not the president — the power to declare war against a country like Venezuela.
Supporters say that without a formal vote from Congress, U.S. troops should not be involved in hostilities in or against Venezuela, and this resolution enforces that rule.
Supporters say the self-defense exception in the resolution means the U.S. can still protect itself if attacked, so pulling forces out does not leave the country exposed.
critics: Critics say the resolution ties the president's hands in fast-moving situations, since waiting for Congress to pass a war declaration or authorization vote could delay a military response to threats from Venezuela.
Critics say the phrase 'imminent armed attack' in the self-defense exception is vague and could cause confusion about when the president is legally allowed to act without a congressional vote.

Critics say removing U.S. forces from any ongoing operations in or against Venezuela could weaken U.S. leverage in the region and signal to other governments that Congress will block the use of military force.

119-sjres-7.one_liner: Cancel an FCC rule letting schools loan Wi-Fi hotspots to students for home use
provisions: Cancels a rule the FCC published in August 2024.
That rule let schools and libraries in the E-Rate program buy discounted Wi-Fi hotspots and lend them to students, staff, and library visitors for use at home.
Schools that used the rule had to make sure the hotspots were used mainly for school or learning activities.
After this bill, E-Rate funds cannot be used to buy Wi-Fi hotspots for students or staff to take home.

supporters: Supporters say the FCC's August 2024 rule went beyond what E-Rate was designed to fund, because the program was set up to connect schools and libraries as buildings, not to pay for home internet service for individual students or staff.
Supporters say Congress, not the FCC, should decide if E-Rate money can be spent on hotspots that students take home, and that canceling this rule returns that decision to lawmakers.
Supporters say removing the rule stops E-Rate funds from being used for hotspots lent to library patrons and school staff at home, keeping the program focused on in-building connectivity.
critics: Critics say the canceled rule was the only way schools in the E-Rate program could use discounted funds to get Wi-Fi hotspots into the hands of students who have no internet at home, a group sometimes called the 'homework gap.'

Critics say the FCC's rule required schools to set acceptable use policies so hotspots were used mainly for educational purposes, and blocking the rule removes that option even with those safeguards in place.
Critics say students, school staff, and library patrons who rely on borrowed hotspots for schoolwork will lose access to that equipment because E-Rate funds can no longer pay for it.

119-sres-616.one_liner: Request a State Department report on human rights conditions in Honduras
provisions: Asks the State Department to put together a report on human rights conditions in Honduras
Uses a process in the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 that lets Congress formally request this kind of report from the executive branch
Does not change any laws, policies, or spending — it only requests information

supporters: Supporters say section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 gives Congress the legal right to formally request this report, and this resolution uses that tool to get information directly from the State Department about human rights conditions in Honduras.
Supporters say the report could help Congress make future decisions about U.S. foreign assistance to Honduras, since U.S. law ties aid decisions to a country's human rights record.
critics: Critics say the State Department already releases annual human rights reports on Honduras through its regular process, which makes this resolution a request for information that is already publicly available.

Critics say the resolution does not change any laws, policies, or spending, so even if the report finds serious human rights problems in Honduras, the resolution itself cannot require any action to address them.

119-sjres-190.one_liner: Cancel a rule about how the immigration appeals court handles cases
provisions: Cancels a rule that changed how the Board of Immigration Appeals — the court that reviews immigration judge decisions — runs its process.
The Board of Immigration Appeals is part of the Executive Office for Immigration Review, which runs federal immigration courts across the country.
Once this resolution passes, the Board of Immigration Appeals goes back to following the older appeals procedures that were in place before the rule took effect.

supporters: Supporters say canceling this rule returns the Board of Immigration Appeals to its older procedures, which they argue gave both sides more time and process to make their case.

Supporters say the new rule changed how appeals were handled at the Board of Immigration Appeals in ways that Congress did not approve, and this resolution restores congressional oversight over immigration court procedures.
Supporters say the Board of Immigration Appeals handles thousands of cases each year, and going back to the prior rules gives immigrants more consistent protections during the appeals process.
critics: Critics say this resolution cancels a rule designed to make the Board of Immigration Appeals run more efficiently, which could slow down decisions for the large backlog of immigration cases already waiting in federal immigration courts.

Critics say removing the updated appellate procedures means the Executive Office for Immigration Review loses tools it put in place to reduce delays, leaving immigrants and enforcement agencies waiting longer for final decisions.

Critics say the rule that Congress is canceling was meant to streamline how the Board of Immigration Appeals reviews immigration judge decisions, and undoing it adds steps back into a process that was already taking too long.

119-sjres-196.one_liner: Cancel a Department of Education rule on federal student loan programs
provisions: Cancels a set of rules the Department of Education issued about federal student loans, called the 'Reimagining and Improving Student Education' regulations.
Under a law called the Congressional Review Act, Congress can vote to cancel a federal agency's rule — this resolution does that for this specific rule.
If passed and signed, the Department of Education cannot bring back this same rule without Congress passing a new law first.

supporters: Supporters say the 'Reimagining and Improving Student Education' regulations went beyond what Congress authorized the Department of Education to do, and this resolution uses the Congressional Review Act to bring that power back to elected lawmakers.
Supporters say canceling these rules protects taxpayers by stopping loan forgiveness or repayment changes that were not approved by Congress, which controls federal spending.
Supporters say the Congressional Review Act block means the Department of Education cannot quietly bring back the same rules later without a vote in Congress first.
critics: Critics say the 'Reimagining and Improving Student Education' rules were designed to help federal student loan borrowers — including those in repayment hardship — and canceling them removes those protections.

Critics say using the Congressional Review Act here means the Department of Education cannot issue any rule that is 'substantially the same' without a new law, which limits future fixes for student loan borrowers.

Critics say this resolution wipes out regulations that were already finalized after a public comment process, and borrowers who were counting on those rules will lose access to relief programs tied to them.

119-sjres-172.one_liner: Require the President to pull U.S. troops out of any unauthorized fighting against Iran
provisions: The President must remove U.S. troops from any fighting against Iran that Congress has not approved.
Two things could allow military action to continue: Congress declaring war on Iran, or Congress passing a vote giving the President permission to use military force.
The bill still lets the U.S. fight back if Iran attacks U.S. troops, people, or U.S.-run buildings in other countries.

supporters: Supporters say the bill follows the Constitution, which gives Congress — not the President — the power to declare war, meaning military action against Iran requires a vote in Congress before U.S. troops are sent into hostilities.
Supporters say the bill still allows U.S. forces to fight back if Iran attacks American troops, personnel, or U.S.-run facilities in other countries, so it does not leave the military defenseless.
Supporters say removing troops from unauthorized hostilities against Iran protects service members from being placed in a war zone without Congress first approving it.
critics: Critics say the bill could slow the President's ability to respond quickly to threats from Iran, since getting a formal declaration of war or a military force authorization from Congress takes time.

Critics say the self-defense exception — which allows fighting back against attacks on U.S. troops or facilities — may be too narrow, leaving the President unable to act against Iranian-backed groups operating in other countries.
Critics say the resolution could signal to Iran that the U.S. is limited in how it can respond, which they argue weakens the country's position in the region.

118-hr-4821.one_liner: Fund the Interior Department, EPA, and related agencies for the year starting October 2023
provisions: Gives money to the Department of the Interior, which manages national parks, public lands, and wildlife programs.
Funds the EPA to keep its environmental programs running.
Pays for health care for Native American and Alaska Native communities through the Indian Health Service.
Sets aside money for the Bureau of Indian Affairs and Bureau of Indian Education to serve tribal communities.
Sends money to arts and culture organizations, including the Smithsonian Institution, the National Gallery of Art, and the Kennedy Center.
Sets rules for how agencies can and cannot use the money this bill provides.

supporters: Supporters say the bill funds the Bureau of Land Management and National Park Service to manage more than 245 million acres of public land, paying for park rangers, trail upkeep, and wildlife programs that serve millions of visitors each year.

Supporters say the Indian Health Service, which provides health care to about 2.6 million Native Americans and Alaska Natives, would keep receiving money for clinics and medical services that many tribal communities have no other way to access.

Supporters say the Bureau of Indian Education would get funding to run more than 180 schools on reservations, giving Native students access to basic education that depends almost entirely on federal support.
critics: Critics say the bill allocates roughly $207 million to the National Endowment for the Arts and $207 million to the National Endowment for the Humanities — a combined $414 million — for cultural programs that critics argue are not a core responsibility of the federal government.

Critics say the bill's rules bar the Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management from moving funds between accounts mid-year without returning to Congress for approval, which critics argue prevents agencies from quickly shifting resources when wildfires or other land emergencies break out.

Critics say the EPA receives roughly $9 billion through this bill, locking in funding for air and water enforcement programs that critics argue were written by agency staff rather than authorized in law by Congress.

118-hres-798.one_liner: Condemn support for designated terrorist groups at colleges and call for a federal investigation
provisions: Condemns support of Hamas, Hezbollah, or other groups the U.S. has designated as terrorist organizations at colleges.
Congress states that this support may make colleges hostile for Jewish students, faculty, and staff.
Calls on the Department of Education to have its Office for Civil Rights look into incidents at colleges.
Where problems are found, calls for the Office for Civil Rights to take action.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution is needed because groups like Hamas and Hezbollah are U.S.-designated terrorist organizations, and showing support for them at colleges creates a hostile environment for Jewish students, faculty, and staff.
Supporters say directing the Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights to investigate campus incidents gives Jewish students a formal way to report harassment and get federal action taken.
Supporters say that without this resolution, colleges may not feel pressure to address pro-terrorist activity that Title VI of the Civil Rights Act is meant to protect against.
critics: Critics say the resolution does not define what 'support' means, which could lead the Office for Civil Rights to investigate protected speech like political protests or classroom discussions about Hamas or Hezbollah.
Critics say the call for the Office for Civil Rights to 'take action' is vague and could result in colleges restricting student and faculty speech beyond what the First Amendment allows.
Critics say the resolution only names a hostile environment for Jewish students but does not address similar concerns for Muslim, Arab, or Palestinian students who also report harassment on campuses.

118-s-3998.one_liner: Make temporary federal judge positions permanent in 10 states
provisions: Turns temporary judge positions into permanent ones in federal courts in Alabama, Arizona, California, Florida, Hawaii, Kansas, Missouri, New Mexico, North Carolina, and Texas.
Permanent judges have lifetime appointments, while temporary judges serve for a set number of years until the position expires.
This change lets those courts keep those judges on the bench long-term instead of losing them when the temporary term ends.

supporters: Supporters say converting temporary judgeships to permanent ones in 10 states — including Texas, California, and Florida — lets courts keep experienced judges instead of losing them when their terms expire.
Supporters say permanent judges, who serve lifetime appointments, can take on long-term cases and reduce backlogs in busy federal districts without having to be replaced mid-case.
Supporters say the change gives these 10 federal districts more stable staffing, since temporary positions can go unfilled when terms end and no replacement is named.
critics: Critics say turning temporary judgeships into permanent lifetime appointments removes the built-in check that comes with a set term, making it harder to adjust court size if caseloads drop.
Critics say adding permanent judgeships in states like Alabama, Kansas, and Hawaii locks in a larger federal judiciary long-term, which increases ongoing salary and benefit costs for those courts.
Critics say the bill was introduced in 2024 under one Congress, and converting these seats permanently gives whoever appoints the judges — the sitting President — a lasting influence on those courts.

118-hres-773.one_liner: Remove Representative George Santos from his seat in the House of Representatives
provisions: The House votes on whether to remove George Santos from his seat in Congress.
Passing this resolution requires a two-thirds vote of all House members.
The Senate and the President have no role — only the House acts on this.
If it passes, Santos stops serving as a Member of Congress right away.

supporters: Supporters say the House Ethics Committee voted 6-0 to recommend expulsion after finding that Santos used campaign funds for personal items, giving House members a documented record to base their vote on.
Supporters say Santos faces 23 federal criminal charges, including wire fraud and identity theft, and that keeping him in office lets him vote on laws while those charges are pending.
Supporters say the two-thirds vote rule — requiring at least 290 of 435 House members to agree — already sets a high bar that protects against removing members for minor or political reasons.
critics: Critics say only three members of Congress have ever been expelled in U.S. history, all during or just after the Civil War, and none were removed before a criminal conviction, making this resolution a break from that historical standard.
Critics say Santos has not been convicted of any crime, and removing him before a court verdict would set a new standard that allows the House to expel members based on charges alone.

Critics say Santos was elected by voters in New York's 3rd congressional district, and expelling him before trial removes a representative those voters chose before any court has ruled on the charges.

119-hconres-108.one_liner: Order U.S. troops out of hostilities in Lebanon within seven days
provisions: Tells the President to pull U.S. military forces out of any active fighting in Lebanon within 7 days of this resolution passing.
Does not stop the U.S. from working with Lebanon's own military forces.
Does not stop the U.S. from protecting its embassies or other official buildings in Lebanon.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution uses Section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution to require the President to end U.S. military involvement in active fighting in Lebanon within 7 days, which they argue restores Congress's role in deciding when American forces are sent into combat.
Supporters say the 7-day deadline gives the executive branch time to withdraw forces in an orderly way while still acting quickly to stop unauthorized military action.

Supporters say the resolution keeps two key exceptions in place — the U.S. can still work with the Lebanese Armed Forces and still protect its embassies and official buildings — so core U.S. interests in Lebanon are not abandoned.
critics: Critics say the 7-day withdrawal deadline does not give military commanders enough time to safely remove forces or hand off responsibilities without putting troops at risk.

Critics say the resolution's exceptions for working with the Lebanese Armed Forces and protecting diplomatic facilities do not cover other U.S. operations, such as counterterrorism support or intelligence sharing, which would be forced to stop.

Critics say the word 'hostilities' in the resolution is not clearly defined, which means it is unclear whether ongoing advisory missions or intelligence operations would trigger the 7-day clock and require a full withdrawal.

118-hres-838.one_liner: Set the House debate rules for three government spending bills
provisions: Sets the rules for how the House votes on and debates three separate spending bills
One of those bills covers money for the Department of the Interior and environment programs for the year ending September 30, 2024
A second bill covers money for transportation and housing programs for the same year
A third bill covers emergency money related to the attacks in Israel for the year ending September 30, 2024
This bill does not spend any money itself — it only controls how Congress handles those three spending bills

supporters: Supporters say this rule creates an organized process for the House to debate and vote on three separate spending bills — H.R. 4821, H.R. 4820, and H.R. 6126 — without needing to pass a separate procedural vote for each one.

Supporters say setting a clear debate structure for H.R. 6126 lets Congress move quickly on emergency funding tied to the attacks in Israel, rather than leaving that bill waiting for floor time under uncertain terms.

Supporters say combining the Interior funding bill, the transportation and housing bill, and the Israel emergency supplemental into one rule reduces the total number of procedural steps the House must complete before reaching a final vote on any of them.
critics: Critics say packaging H.R. 4821, H.R. 4820, and H.R. 6126 into a single rule means members cannot separately reject the debate terms for just one of those three bills — they must accept or reject all three debate structures together.

Critics say the rule gives House leadership the power to control how H.R. 6126 — the emergency spending bill tied to the Israel attacks — is handled on the floor, rather than letting the full chamber decide those terms.

Critics say linking the debate structure for unrelated spending areas — Interior and environment programs, transportation and housing programs, and emergency Israel aid — inside one procedural package makes it harder for members to draw a clear line between domestic spending decisions and emergency foreign policy funding.

119-hr-5408.one_liner: Set deadlines for first union contracts and require arbitration if talks fail
provisions: Once a union wins the right to negotiate at a company, the employer must start contract talks within 10 days.
Both sides must make every reasonable effort to reach and sign a deal.
If no deal is reached after 90 days, either side can ask a federal agency called the FMCS to help mediate.
If mediation fails after 30 days, a panel of arbitrators steps in and makes a final, binding decision that lasts two years.
The arbitration panel must weigh the employer's expected financial future and workers' cost of living when making its decision.
During negotiations, the employer must keep current wages, hours, and working conditions in place.
Even if the union loses its official status, the employer must still bargain.

supporters: Supporters say the 10-day deadline to start talks and the 90-day limit before mediation kicks in will stop employers from stalling after workers vote to unionize, which currently can drag on for years without a first contract.
Supporters say the requirement to keep current wages, hours, and conditions in place during negotiations protects workers from having their pay or schedules cut while a deal is being worked out.
Supporters say the arbitration panel's two-year binding decision gives both sides a firm contract, ending the limbo that leaves newly unionized workers without guaranteed terms.
critics: Critics say forcing binding arbitration after just 120 days — 90 days of talks plus 30 days of mediation — takes away an employer's right to negotiate freely and hands a panel of arbitrators the power to set wages and conditions the business must live with for two years.

Critics say the rule that an employer must keep bargaining even after a union loses its official certification status forces companies to negotiate with a representative that workers may no longer want.

Critics say the arbitration panel's authority to set a two-year binding contract based on the employer's expected financial future could force small businesses to agree to terms they cannot afford, with no exit option during the two-year period.

119-hr-7128.one_liner: Extend the terrorism risk insurance program through 2034 and tighten its rules
provisions: The program pays back part of what insurance companies lose when a terrorist attack causes property damage or injures people.
The program is extended through 2034 — without this bill, it would have ended sooner.
Starting in 2029, an attack must cause a larger total amount of losses before the program steps in to cover insurers.
The Treasury Department gets clear legal authority to publicly explain how it decides whether something counts as a terrorist attack.

supporters: Supporters say extending the program through 2034 gives insurance companies the stability they need to keep offering terrorism coverage to businesses and property owners.
Supporters say the program helps make sure that if a major attack happens, private insurers will not have to pay all the losses alone, which keeps insurance available in the market.
Supporters say giving the Treasury Department clear legal authority to explain how it certifies an attack as terrorism makes the process more open to the public.
critics: Critics say raising the loss threshold starting in 2029 means smaller attacks may no longer trigger federal help for insurers, leaving some companies to cover those losses on their own.
Critics say the bill does not set a specific dollar amount for the new 2029 loss threshold, so insurers and businesses cannot plan ahead for how much coverage they may actually need.
Critics say extending the program through 2034 continues a government backstop that private insurance markets have had over 20 years to replace on their own.

119-hr-7401.one_liner: Require SBA employees to sign a conflict-of-interest statement before working on any loan
provisions: Before an SBA employee can work on a loan — reviewing it, approving it, or helping start it — they must sign a written statement saying they have no conflict of interest with that loan.
If a conflict of interest comes up after signing, the employee must report it.
The written statement must also confirm the employee understands the conflict-of-interest rules that apply to their job.
The SBA must write new rules to carry out these requirements.

supporters: Supporters say requiring SBA employees to sign a written conflict-of-interest statement before working on any loan will make it harder for employees to approve loans that benefit people they have financial ties to.

Supporters say the rule that employees must report new conflicts of interest after signing gives small business owners a better chance at a fair review, since the problem must be flagged even if it comes up mid-process.

Supporters say having the SBA write new regulations to carry out these requirements creates a clear, enforceable process that existing federal ethics rules do not already provide for SBA loan work specifically.
critics: Critics say the bill adds a paperwork step — a signed written statement — for every SBA employee involved in loan origination, review, or approval, which could slow down the lending process for small businesses waiting on funds.

Critics say federal employees are already required by law to disclose financial conflicts of interest and recuse themselves, so this bill may duplicate rules that are already in place without fixing a proven gap.
Critics say the bill does not set a penalty for employees who sign the statement falsely, which could make the new certification requirement hard to enforce in practice.

119-hr-2478.one_liner: Let investment companies pause mutual fund withdrawals when they suspect elder financial fraud
provisions: Investment companies and transfer agents can pause a mutual fund withdrawal for up to 15 days if they think someone age 65 or older is being financially scammed.
The same applies to people 18 or older who cannot protect themselves because of a mental or physical condition.
If the company confirms exploitation is happening, it can pause the withdrawal for 10 more days.
A state regulator or court can extend the pause beyond those time limits.
During any pause, the money must be held in a bank account.
Companies and transfer agents must tell the SEC if they choose to follow these rules.
The SEC must issue recommendations on how to better protect adults from financial exploitation.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects adults age 65 or older, and adults with mental or physical impairments, by letting investment companies pause a mutual fund withdrawal for up to 15 days when they suspect financial exploitation is happening.
Supporters say that if a company confirms exploitation is taking place, it can add 10 more days to the pause, giving law enforcement or family members more time to step in before the money is gone.
Supporters say requiring the SEC to issue recommendations on protecting these adults means the government must take concrete follow-up steps, not just pass a law and move on.
critics: Critics say the bill gives investment companies the power to block a person's own withdrawal for up to 25 days—and longer if a court gets involved—without the account holder's agreement, which could trap people out of their money when they need it.

Critics say adults with disabilities who have urgent financial needs, like paying for medical care, could be locked out of their funds for weeks if a company misjudges a normal transaction as exploitation.
Critics say the bill does not set clear penalties if a company wrongly delays a redemption, which means account holders may have no quick way to get their money back if the company makes a mistake.

119-hr-2913.one_liner: Send aid to Ukraine and impose penalties on Russia if it keeps attacking
provisions: Creates a fund to pay for rebuilding Ukraine after the war.
Gives the U.S. the power to lend military equipment to Ukraine and nearby European countries through 2028.
Extends the U.S. military's power to send weapons, training, and intelligence to Ukraine's forces through 2027.
Tells the State Department to help strengthen the armies and border forces of Baltic countries.
The President must check regularly whether Russia is still attacking Ukraine or blocking peace talks.

If the President finds Russia is still attacking or blocking peace, the U.S. must charge at least 500% in extra taxes on all goods imported from Russia — a $10 Russian product would face $50 in added taxes.
That same finding would freeze U.S. bank accounts and block visas for Russian officials, and freeze the assets of Russian oil, mining, and nuclear companies.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects U.S. security by extending military aid and intelligence support to Ukraine through 2027 and keeping the lend-lease program for military equipment open through 2028, which they argue limits Russia's ability to expand the war into NATO countries.

Supporters say the 500% tariff on Russian imports — meaning a $10 Russian product would cost $60 total — along with freezing assets of Russian oil, mining, and nuclear companies, would put direct economic pressure on Russia to stop the war or enter real peace talks.

Supporters say the reconstruction trust fund and stronger Baltic military forces would help stabilize the region and reduce long-term costs for the U.S. by building up European allies to handle more of their own defense.
critics: Critics say extending military aid and intelligence support to Ukraine through 2027, and keeping the lend-lease authority open through 2028, risks pulling the U.S. deeper into a conflict with no clear end date or exit plan.

Critics say the 500% tariff on Russian goods could raise prices for U.S. businesses and consumers who rely on Russian materials like oil and minerals, since the cost of those taxes often gets passed on to buyers.

Critics say the bill gives the President broad power to trigger major sanctions and tariffs based on a personal determination about Russia's actions, with little role for Congress to check or vote on those decisions.

119-hr-7892.one_liner: Require identity checks before releasing federal student aid to flagged applicants
provisions: Starting October 1, 2026, the Department of Education must run every federal student aid application through a system that looks for signs of identity fraud.
If an application looks suspicious, the Department of Education must alert the applicant and every college listed on their application.
Colleges cannot release federal financial aid money to a flagged applicant until they confirm who that person is — either face-to-face or by live video call.
Once a college confirms the applicant's identity, it must report that back to the Department of Education.
The Department of Education must write the rules colleges have to follow when checking applicants' identities.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would protect federal student aid money by requiring every FAFSA application to go through a fraud detection system starting October 1, 2026, stopping identity thieves from collecting aid meant for real students.

Supporters say flagging suspicious applications and requiring colleges to verify applicants in person or by live video gives schools a clear process to confirm someone is who they say they are before any aid money is released.
Supporters say having the Department of Education write the rules for identity checks gives all colleges the same standard to follow, making the process consistent across schools.
critics: Critics say requiring in-person or live video verification for flagged applicants could create barriers for students in rural areas or without reliable internet access, delaying or blocking their aid.
Critics say the bill puts the burden of identity verification on colleges without providing funding to cover the cost of setting up verification systems or staffing the process.

Critics say students flagged by the fraud detection system could have their aid held up even if they are real applicants, since the bill does not set a deadline for how quickly schools must complete the verification process.

119-hr-8464.one_liner: Require federal agencies to pause and check payments that show signs of fraud
provisions: Federal agencies must stop and review a payment request if they have documented reasons to think it might be fraudulent or wrong.
Any pause on a payment must target only the specific part that looks risky — not the whole payment.
Pauses must last only as long as it takes to confirm whether the payment is correct.
The Treasury Department must send back payment requests that its fraud-detection system flags as high-risk, so the agency can review them.
Federal workers who follow this law in good faith cannot be held personally responsible if something goes wrong in the process.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would cut down on fraudulent federal payments by requiring agencies to pause and review payment requests when they have documented, specific reasons to think fraud is present — not just a general suspicion.
Supporters say the rule that pauses must target only the risky part of a payment, not the whole amount, means most payments go through on time while only the suspicious portion gets held back.
Supporters say requiring Treasury to return high-risk payments flagged by its Do Not Pay system adds a second layer of review that could catch errors agencies miss on their own.
critics: Critics say the bill gives agencies broad power to pause payments without clear deadlines, and even though it says pauses must be short, there is no set time limit written into the law to enforce that.

Critics say people or businesses waiting on federal payments — such as contractors, benefit recipients, or grant holders — could face delays even when their payments turn out to be fully legitimate, because the review process takes time.
Critics say the good-faith protection for federal workers who pause payments removes accountability if agencies apply the fraud-risk rules too broadly or inconsistently.

119-hr-8312.one_liner: Create a new Treasury office to find and stop fraud in federal spending
provisions: Creates a new office inside the Treasury Department to look into fraud in government spending
The new office checks on any government payment or award of $50,000 or more
It also reviews how COVID relief money, disaster funds, and economic recovery payments were used
A government tool called 'Do Not Pay' — which checks a person's identity before they get government money — moves under Treasury's control
Federal agencies must share data with each other to catch fraud and stop wrong payments before they go out
When the new office finds signs of a crime, it must quickly send that information to the Justice Department

supporters: Supporters say moving the 'Do Not Pay' system to Treasury will stop wrong payments before they go out, since agencies will share data with each other to catch fraud earlier.

Supporters say the new Office of the Inspector General for Fraud, Accountability, and Recovery (OIGFAR) will check any federal award of $50,000 or more, creating a clear process to catch waste across the government.
Supporters say requiring OIGFAR to quickly send signs of crime to the Justice Department means more fraud cases will lead to actual prosecution, not just reports.
critics: Critics say creating a new inspector general office inside Treasury adds another layer of bureaucracy that may overlap with the 74 inspector general offices that already exist across federal agencies.

Critics say requiring data sharing agreements between federal agencies and private entities raises privacy concerns for people who receive government payments, since their personal information moves across more systems.
Critics say focusing OIGFAR's review on COVID relief funds and disaster payments — money already spent — may not recover those dollars and pulls attention away from preventing future fraud.

119-hr-8428.one_liner: Require federal employees who manage public funds to take anti-fraud training every two years
provisions: Federal workers in roles that involve managing or overseeing government money must complete an anti-fraud training program every two years.
Roles covered include program administrators, financial managers, disbursement officials, auditors, and grants managers.
The training covers how to spot fraud risks, how to use government fraud-detection tools, and how to report suspected fraud or waste.
The Office of Personnel Management keeps records of who has finished the training.
States, local governments, and tribal governments can also access the training for their own employees who run federally funded programs.
Federal agencies can require proof of completed training before giving out grants or awards.
Within two years of the law taking effect, Treasury and OMB must send Congress a report on how the program is running.

supporters: Supporters say requiring federal workers in roles like grants manager, auditor, and disbursement official to complete anti-fraud training every two years will help catch and prevent improper payments before they happen.

Supporters say making the training available to state, local, and tribal governments means more people managing federally funded programs will know how to spot fraud risks and use government fraud-detection tools.
Supporters say allowing agencies to require proof of completed training before giving out grants adds a clear accountability step that connects training to real federal dollars.
critics: Critics say the bill does not include a cost estimate, so Congress has no way to know how much it will cost to build, run, and maintain the training program across all covered federal agencies.

Critics say adding a mandatory two-year training requirement for program administrators, financial managers, and other covered roles may pull staff away from their regular duties without clear proof that the training reduces fraud.
Critics say the requirement for Treasury and OMB to report to Congress only two years after the law takes effect may not give enough time to measure whether the program is actually working.

119-hr-7757.one_liner: Require online platforms to set up safety rules for users under 18
provisions: Websites where more than one-third of content is sexual must use technology to identify minors and block their access to that content.
Social media platforms must set default options for minors that limit addictive features and stop strangers from sending them messages.
Parents get tools to control their child's privacy settings and account on social media platforms.
Disappearing messages are not allowed for minors on social media platforms.
Video game platforms must give parents tools to limit who their child talks to and stop the child from making purchases.
AI chatbots must tell users who are minors that they are talking to a computer, not a person, and must share suicide and crisis hotline numbers.
The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general can take action against platforms that break these rules.

supporters: Supporters say the bill protects minors by requiring websites where more than one-third of content is sexual to use technology to identify and block children from accessing that material.

Supporters say the bill gives parents real control by requiring social media and video game platforms to provide tools that let parents manage their child's privacy settings, limit who they talk to, and block in-game purchases.
Supporters say requiring AI chatbots to tell minors they are talking to a computer — and to share suicide and crisis hotline numbers — reduces the risk of young users being misled or harmed.
critics: Critics say the requirement for platforms to identify whether users are minors could force websites to collect more personal data from all users, raising privacy concerns for adults and children alike.

Critics say banning disappearing messages for minors on social media platforms limits a feature that many teenagers use to communicate privately, and may be difficult for platforms to enforce without age verification systems that do not yet exist at scale.

Critics say the bill puts enforcement in the hands of the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general, but does not set clear technical standards for what counts as valid age-identification technology, leaving platforms uncertain about how to comply.
