119-hr-915.one_liner: Let small businesses use Small Business Administration loans to buy software and cloud services
provisions: The Small Business Administration (SBA) runs a loan program for small businesses that cannot get affordable credit on their own.
This bill adds software and cloud computing services to what those SBA loans can pay for.
Covered software includes tools for payroll, human resources, sales, billing, and accounting.
Loans can also cover software that tracks inventory or helps run day-to-day business operations.
Business tools that use artificial intelligence count as covered software under this bill.

supporters: Supporters say that small businesses that cannot get affordable credit on their own will now be able to use SBA 7(a) loans to pay for payroll software, billing tools, and accounting programs they could not afford before.

Supporters say that including AI-powered business tools as covered software gives small businesses access to the same technology that larger companies already use for HR, inventory tracking, and daily operations.

Supporters say that covering cloud computing services under the 7(a) program means small businesses can borrow to run core operations — like payroll processing and sales functions — without relying on high-interest credit.
critics: Critics say the bill does not set a dollar cap on how much of a 7(a) loan can go toward software, which could lead small businesses to take on long-term debt to pay for monthly subscription fees.
Critics say that allowing loans to cover AI tools is risky because that technology changes fast, and a business could end up repaying a loan for software that no longer works for them.

Critics say the 7(a) program was built to help businesses get capital for things like equipment and real estate, and adding recurring cloud service costs could increase the risk of defaults that the SBA's loan guaranty fund has to cover.

119-hres-1335.one_liner: Condemn fraud against the U.S. government and call for checking who qualifies before payments
provisions: The House condemns anyone who tries to cheat or steal from U.S. government programs.
The House says new rules to stop fraud and wrong payments from government programs would help the country's finances.
Government programs should check whether someone qualifies before sending them money.

supporters: Supporters say the resolution backs eligibility checks before payments go out, which would stop money from going to people or groups who don't qualify for a federal program.
Supporters say new rules to catch fraud and wrong payments — as the resolution calls for — would protect tax dollars and help the country's finances over time.
Supporters say formally condemning anyone who cheats government programs puts the House on record that stealing from federal programs is wrong.
critics: Critics say the resolution uses the phrase 'improper payment' without defining it, which could group actual fraud together with simple paperwork errors made by government agencies — two very different problems.
Critics say requiring eligibility checks before every payment could delay or block benefits for people who do qualify, such as seniors or people with disabilities waiting on federal programs.
Critics say the resolution names no specific programs, dollar amounts, or enforcement tools, so it is hard to see how it would lead to real changes in how fraud is caught or stopped.

119-hres-1140.one_liner: Set House debate rules for a bill about speeding up union contract timelines
provisions: This resolution allows the House to bring H.R. 5408 to the floor for debate and a vote.

H.R. 5408, the bill this resolution covers, would change how long it takes for workers and employers to reach a first contract after workers vote to form a union under the National Labor Relations Act.
The resolution itself does not change any labor rules — it only sets the terms for how the House debates H.R. 5408.

supporters: Supporters say this resolution gives the House a chance to vote on H.R. 5408, which would set faster deadlines for workers and employers to reach a first contract after a union vote under the National Labor Relations Act.
Supporters say H.R. 5408 addresses a gap in the NLRA where employers can delay first-contract talks for months or years after workers vote to form a union, leaving those workers without a contract.

Supporters say bringing H.R. 5408 to the floor through this resolution lets lawmakers debate specific changes to NLRA timelines that currently leave newly formed unions without enforceable contract deadlines.
critics: Critics say the resolution limits how long the House can debate H.R. 5408, which they argue prevents a full review of how new contract deadlines under the NLRA would affect employers of different sizes.

Critics say H.R. 5408 would force employers to reach a first contract on a government-set schedule, which they say removes flexibility from both sides to negotiate terms that fit their specific workplace under the NLRA.

Critics say the resolution fast-tracks a vote on H.R. 5408 before lawmakers can fully study how shorter time-to-contract rules would affect industries where negotiations are complex, such as construction or healthcare.

119-hr-8466.one_liner: Require federal agencies to create anti-fraud plans for emergency spending
provisions: Each federal agency must write a plan within one year to stop fraud and bad payments in emergency spending, like disaster relief or pandemic funds.
The Office of Management and Budget must write rules that tell agencies what their fraud-prevention plans need to cover.
Agency plans must include steps to spot the risk of losing money to fraud — and put safeguards in place before the money goes out when possible.
Plans must include tools to watch payments and flag unusual transactions as they come in.
Agencies must review and resubmit their plans at least every three years.
The Office of Management and Budget must send all agency plans to Congress each year, along with suggestions for new laws on emergency spending.

supporters: Supporters say requiring each federal agency to write a fraud-prevention plan within one year would create clear steps to catch bad payments before emergency money — like disaster relief or pandemic funds — goes out the door.

Supporters say having the Office of Management and Budget send all agency plans to Congress each year gives lawmakers a way to track whether agencies are actually following through on reducing fraud in emergency spending.
Supporters say building in payment monitoring tools to flag unusual transactions as they come in could catch fraud faster than waiting until after the money is spent.
critics: Critics say the bill adds new reporting work for federal agencies — including writing plans, reviewing them every three years, and resubmitting to OMB — without providing dedicated funding to carry out those tasks.
Critics say the one-year deadline for all agencies to submit fraud-prevention plans may not be enough time for large agencies managing complex emergency programs to build reliable internal controls.

Critics say the bill relies on the Office of Management and Budget to write guidance and review plans, which puts a heavy coordination burden on one office during the same emergencies the bill is meant to address.

119-hr-8646.one_liner: Fund the USDA, FDA, and food assistance programs for the year starting October 2026
provisions: Pays for SNAP, the program that helps low-income Americans buy groceries each month.
Gives money to WIC, which provides food and nutrition help to pregnant women, new mothers, and children under age five.
Covers school lunch and breakfast programs that feed children at low or no cost.
Keeps food safety workers on the job to inspect meat, poultry, and egg products sold across the country.
Sets aside money for rural housing loans and business support in small towns and farming communities.
Funds the FDA, which checks that food, drugs, and medical devices are safe.
Backs farm insurance programs that pay out when farmers lose crops or income.

supporters: Supporters say the bill funds SNAP, which helps roughly 42 million low-income Americans buy groceries each month, and WIC, which provides food and nutrition support to pregnant women and children under age five.
Supporters say the bill keeps food safety inspectors working to check meat, poultry, and egg products before they reach store shelves, protecting consumers from unsafe food.
Supporters say rural housing loans and business funding in the bill give small farming towns access to money that private banks often will not lend.
critics: Critics say the bill funds SNAP without adding work requirements for able-bodied adults without dependents, letting people who can work receive monthly grocery benefits with no conditions.
Critics say farm crop insurance payments in the bill flow mostly to large farming operations, not the small family farms that need financial protection the most.
Critics say the bill increases spending across USDA, FDA, and rural development programs without cutting any existing ones, adding to federal costs with no offset.

119-hres-1399.one_liner: Require the House Ethics Committee to keep and release records on harassment settlements
provisions: The House Ethics Committee must keep all written records and documents tied to money paid to settle sexual harassment claims by members of Congress.
The committee must release those records to the public.
This covers any communications, agreements, or payments connected to sexual harassment settlements involving House members.

supporters: Supporters say the bill would force the House Ethics Committee to release all written records, agreements, and payment amounts tied to sexual harassment settlements involving House members, giving the public the right to know how their money was spent.
Supporters say that making these records public holds members of Congress accountable, since taxpayer funds or public resources may have been used to pay settlement costs.
Supporters say requiring the committee to preserve all communications and documents prevents records from being destroyed or hidden before the public can see them.
critics: Critics say releasing settlement records could expose the names and personal details of victims who chose to settle privately, which may discourage future victims from coming forward.
Critics say that making all agreements and communications public could violate the privacy rights of accusers, since many settlements include confidentiality terms that both sides agreed to.
Critics say the bill does not set limits on what details must be released, which could mean sensitive personal information about victims gets shared alongside records about the accused members.

119-hres-1398.one_liner: Allow the House to debate and vote on the defense budget and other bills
provisions: Lets the House vote on the defense spending plan for the year starting October 2026.
Opens debate on the national security and State Department spending plan for the year ending September 2027.
Schedules a vote on extending a Social Security disability insurance test program.
Sets up a vote on a statement marking one year since the Working Families Tax Cuts passed.

supporters: Supporters say this rule moves the fiscal year 2027 defense spending bill (H.R. 8800) to the House floor, letting Congress set military funding and troop strength levels before the October 2026 deadline.

Supporters say the rule also brings the State Department and national security spending bill (H.R. 8595) to a vote, keeping funding for U.S. diplomacy and security programs on track through September 2027.
Supporters say scheduling a vote on H.R. 8884 prevents the Social Security disability insurance test program from expiring without a chance for Congress to reauthorize it.
critics: Critics say bundling four unrelated items — defense spending, State Department funding, a Social Security program extension, and a tax cut anniversary resolution — into one rule forces members to vote on all of them together rather than judging each on its own.

Critics say including H. Res. 1383, a statement marking one year since the Working Families Tax Cuts, adds a political messaging item to a rule that also controls defense and Social Security votes, limiting separate debate on each.
Critics say the rule may limit or block amendments to H.R. 8800 and H.R. 8595, reducing the ability of members to propose changes to how defense and national security money is spent.

119-hres-1345.one_liner: Set House floor rules for votes on fraud prevention and budget bills
provisions: Opens the House floor for a vote on a bill to set up a new fraud-prevention office inside the Treasury Department.
Brings to the House floor a bill that lets the government pause or split up payments when fraud is suspected.
Schedules a vote on a House statement condemning government fraud and saying benefits should be checked before payments go out.
Also schedules a vote on S. 2, a budget bill written through a special fast-track process.
That fast-track process limits how long the Senate can debate the bill.

supporters: Supporters say the new Treasury fraud office created by H.R. 8312 would add a permanent Inspector General focused only on catching improper payments before they go out, filling a gap that existing agencies have not covered.
Supporters say H.R. 8464 gives the government a tool to pause or split up payments when fraud is suspected, so taxpayer money is not sent out while a problem is still being investigated.
Supporters say using the fast-track reconciliation process for S. 2 allows the budget bill to pass the Senate with a simple majority instead of needing 60 votes to end debate.
critics: Critics say the fast-track process used to schedule S. 2 limits how long the Senate can debate a major budget bill, reducing the time lawmakers have to review its full effects.

Critics say the payment-pausing authority in H.R. 8464 could delay or cut off benefits for real people while the government investigates a fraud claim, with no clear timeline for when payments would resume.
Critics say H.R. 8312 creates a brand-new government office without stating how much it will cost to run or how it will coordinate with fraud offices that already exist inside federal agencies.

119-s-629.one_liner: Expand emergency aid for farmers and forest landowners hit by natural disasters
provisions: Raises the upfront payment farmers can get to replace damaged farm structures from 25% to 75% of the cost, and for repairs or restoration from 25% to 50% of the cost
Lets forest landowners get up to 75% of their emergency costs paid upfront — they could not get any advance payment before this bill
Gives farmers 180 days to spend their emergency funds instead of 60 days
Adds human-caused wildfires that spread because of natural conditions as events that qualify for emergency aid
Covers damages from wildfires the federal government caused

supporters: Supporters say raising the advance payment for replacing damaged farm structures from 25% to 75% of the cost lets farmers buy materials right after a disaster, instead of paying most of the cost themselves while waiting for reimbursement.

Supporters say forest landowners can now get up to 75% of their emergency costs paid upfront — they received zero advance payment before this bill — so they can hire workers and start repairs without taking on debt.
Supporters say extending the spending window from 60 days to 180 days gives farmers enough time to find contractors and get materials, since 60 days is often too short after a major natural disaster.
critics: Critics say covering human-caused wildfires that spread due to natural conditions expands the number of events that qualify for federal emergency aid, which could increase total program spending beyond current budget levels.

Critics say paying out 75% of costs before the repair work is finished and verified raises the risk that some funds will not be used for the intended emergency measures, and may be hard to recover if the work is never completed.

Critics say adding coverage for wildfires caused by the federal government creates a new spending path for damages that might otherwise be handled through separate federal liability or claims processes.
